title: Expected learning outcomes
text:
5MO104 Basic and molecular genetics, 15 ECTS, Umeå University. This site covers the theory and ethics content. The course book is Hartwell et al., Genetics: From Genes to Genomes, and the site follows its order.


After the course, a student should be able to:

show knowledge of basic genetics, and understanding of how inheritance is governed by molecular mechanisms;
explain how inheritance is studied at the level of cells and organisms, and how allele frequencies in populations vary with different factors;
test, interpret and statistically evaluate results;
study, present and discuss original literature in English;
reflect on ethical problems in the application of genetic knowledge.




Running through every part, a student should be able to:

B1. find a gene, variant, disease or organism in the core public databases (NCBI, Ensembl, OMIM, ClinVar, gnomAD, model-organism databases) and extract a specific fact;
B2. run a sequence similarity search (BLAST) and read the result;
B3. search PubMed for original papers on a genetic question;
B4. use R to test genetic ratios and Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium (χ²);
B5. use R to simulate simple genetic processes, such as crosses, drift and bottlenecks;
B6. load a downloaded table or sequence (TSV, CSV, FASTA) into R and summarise or plot it;
B7. write small R functions of their own.

title: Three-point crosses
text:
About this lecture
In Linkage & recombination we measured the distance between two genes from a testcross. Following three linked genes in one cross gives more than three distances: it gives the order of the genes, and it shows the double crossovers that a two-point cross cannot see.

The three-point testcross: a triple heterozygote × a triple recessive tester; 8 offspring classes.
A five-step recipe: parentals (most common), double crossovers (rarest), the gene in the middle, the two distances.
Why the outer distance must count the double crossovers twice.
Expected double crossovers from the product rule; the coefficient of coincidence and interference.
A worked Drosophila example on the X chromosome: cv, ct and v.

Book: Hartwell, Genetics: From Genes to Genomes, linkage and recombination chapter (the three-point cross sections).

This unit is mostly a method, and the method is short. The skill students should leave with is reading eight class counts and, in a few minutes, writing down the gene order, two distances and the interference. Everything rests on the previous unit: recombination frequency, the testcross as a direct readout of gametes, and map units. The new ideas are the double crossover class, which tells the order, and interference, which tells us that crossovers are not independent events. The product rule from Probability & the chi-square test comes back to compute the expected number of double crossovers.

title: Three-point crosses
text:
What two-point crosses leave open
Suppose two-point testcrosses give cv–ct 7 cM, ct–v 13 cM and cv–v 19 cM.

Order. 7 + 13 = 20 ≈ 19, so ct is probably in the middle. But with sampling noise in three separate crosses, and distances that do not add up exactly, the order can be ambiguous, especially for close genes.
Hidden double crossovers. Two crossovers between cv and v put cv and v back together in the parental combination. A two-point cross counts that chromatid as parental, so the long distance comes out too short.
Effort. Three separate crosses, three sets of flies.

A three-point cross answers all three in one cross: it measures both intervals in the same offspring and shows the double crossovers directly.

Start from what the students can already do. With three two-point distances they can guess the order by additivity: the two short distances should add up to the long one. But 7 + 13 is 20, not 19, and with real data and small samples the mismatch can be bigger. The second point is the important one conceptually: a double crossover between the outer genes leaves them in the parental combination, so in a two-point cross it is invisible. That is the same reason RF never exceeds 0.5, from the previous unit, now at short range. A third marker in between catches these events, because the middle gene changes partner.

title: Three-point crosses
text:
The three-point testcross


Female: heterozygous for three X-linked genes, v (vermilion eyes), cv (crossveinless wings) and ct (cut wings), with v on one X and cv ct on the other.
Male: recessive for all three (v cv ct / Y). He adds only recessive alleles, so each offspring’s phenotype shows which egg it came from.
Each egg carries one of 2^3 = 8 combinations of alleles: 8 phenotype classes.


This is the testcross logic from Mendel, scaled up to three genes. The tester contributes nothing visible, so offspring classes equal female gametes. For X-linked genes in Drosophila there is a bonus: sons get the father’s Y and daughters get his recessive X, so in both sexes the phenotype is the maternal X. We use females as the heterozygous parent for a second reason: Drosophila males do not cross over in meiosis, so a heterozygous male would give no recombinants at all. Note that we do not yet know the order of the three genes on the chromosome; the figure lists them in an arbitrary order. Finding the order is the first goal.

The 8 classes come in reciprocal pairs: each crossover makes two complementary chromatids, so the two members of a pair have similar counts.

The + sign is the usual fly shorthand for the wild-type allele. First thing to do with any three-point data: pair the classes. Two classes form a pair when they are exact opposites at all three loci: v + + and + cv ct, + + + and v cv ct, and so on. Their counts are similar because one crossover produces both products in equal numbers. If a pair has very unequal counts, something else is going on, such as reduced viability of one phenotype. The counts are invented for teaching, but they were made to fit the real map of the X chromosome, which we check at the end.

title: Three-point crosses
section: What each kind of crossover produces
text:
What each kind of crossover produces

A single crossover moves an end gene to the other chromosome. A double crossover, one in each interval, moves only the middle gene.

This is the key picture of the lecture. Use generic letters A, B, C, in the true order, with B in the middle. No crossover gives the two parental chromosomes. A crossover in region I, between A and B, gives A b c and a B C: A has changed partner. A crossover in region II changes C’s partner. Two crossovers, one in each region, swap the middle segment only: A b C and a B c. The outer genes are still in their parental combination, which is why a two-point cross between A and C would call these chromatids parental. Since two crossovers are rarer than one, the double crossover classes are the rarest pair. So: find the rarest pair, compare it with the parentals, and the gene that has switched is the middle one.

title: Three-point crosses
section: Steps 1–2: pair up and find the parentals
text:
Steps 1–2: pair up and find the parentals
Step 1. Pair the reciprocal classes: (1, 2), (3, 4), (5, 6), (7, 8).
Step 2. The largest pair is parental: no crossover in either interval. Here v + + (812) and + cv ct (799).
So the female was v cv+ ct+ / v+ cv ct: v was on one X, cv and ct on the other. The parentals tell you the phase of the heterozygote, even if you were not told it.

The parentals are the most common classes as long as all the genes are linked, which they are when every recombinant class is well below a quarter. A frequent student mistake is to assume that the parentals are + + + and v cv ct, that is, all mutant alleles on one chromosome. That is only true when the heterozygote is in coupling for all three genes. Here the female carried v on one X and cv ct on the other, a mixed phase, and the data say so. Always read the parentals from the counts, not from an assumption.

Only ct has changed partner. A double crossover moves only the middle gene, so ct is in the middle:
cv \;-\; ct \;-\; v \qquad (\text{or } v - ct - cv\text{: the same map read backwards})
The parental chromosomes in the true order: cv+ ct+ v / cv ct v+.

This is the whole trick. Pick a DCO class, find the parental class that agrees with it at two of the three loci; the locus where they disagree is the middle one. Check with the other DCO class: it must give the same answer. The direction of the map does not matter; cv-ct-v and v-ct-cv are the same order. A useful check: if you try the other two orders, the class you would call “double crossover” is much more common than the singles, which makes no sense. The R exercise does exactly this for all three orders, and so does the demo.

title: Three-point crosses
section: Rewrite the classes in the right order
text:
Rewrite the classes in the right order

In the order cv–ct–v, each class shows its crossovers: one switch of colour = one crossover.

Rewriting the data in the correct order is the step students skip and then get lost. Blue alleles came from the cv+ ct+ v chromosome, red from cv ct v+. The two parental classes are all blue or all red. In 63 and 66, cv has switched: a crossover between cv and ct, region I. In 128 and 121, v has switched: a crossover between ct and v, region II. In 6 and 5, only ct has switched: one crossover in each region. The map at the bottom is the result of the next step.

title: Three-point crosses
Three-point crosses
section: Why two-point crosses underestimate long distances
text:
Why two-point crosses underestimate long distances
Ignore ct and score only cv and v, as a two-point cross would:




Recombinant for cv–v?




SCO in I (129)
yes


SCO in II (249)
yes


DCO (11)
no: cv and v are back in the parental combination



RF_{\text{two-point}}(cv\text{–}v) = \frac{129 + 249}{2000} = 0.189 \quad\text{vs}\quad 7.0 + 13.0 = 20.0\ \text{cM}
Each DCO is two crossovers that look like zero: 0.189 + 2 \times \frac{11}{2000} = 0.200.
Adding up short intervals is more accurate than measuring a long one directly. That is why maps are built from closely spaced markers.

This connects back to the map functions of the previous unit. Over long distances, even-numbered crossovers are invisible, so RF grows more slowly than the true distance and never passes 0.5. The three-point cross shows the effect at short range, with real counts: 11 double crossovers, 22 crossovers in total, went missing from the two-point estimate. Map functions such as Haldane’s are a way to correct for this when there is no marker in between. With a marker in between, you can count the crossovers directly.

title: Three-point crosses
section: How many double crossovers do we expect?
text:
How many double crossovers do we expect?
If crossovers in the two intervals were independent, the product rule (Probability & the χ² test) gives:
P(\text{DCO}) = RF_{\text{I}} \times RF_{\text{II}} = 0.070 \times 0.130 = 0.0091
\text{expected DCO} = 0.0091 \times 2000 = \mathbf{18.2}
We observed 11. Fewer double crossovers than independence predicts: a crossover in one interval seems to make a crossover in the neighbouring interval less likely.

This is the product rule again: P(A and B) = P(A) times P(B) if A and B are independent. Here A is “crossover in region I” and B is “crossover in region II”. The calculation uses the RFs that include the DCOs, which is the right estimate of each interval’s crossover probability. The observed number is well below the expected one. We could have got 11 instead of 18 by chance, and we look at that on a later slide, but the deficit is typical: in Drosophila and in many other organisms, crossovers that are close together are rarer than independence predicts.

title: Three-point crosses
Three-point crosses
text:
Interference in real chromosomes

Crossovers are spaced out. In Drosophila, mice and humans, a crossover makes another one nearby less likely. Over short intervals (a few cM) double crossovers are almost never seen: interference is close to complete.
Interference fades with distance. Over long distances, two crossovers on one chromosome arm are again roughly independent.
At least one crossover per bivalent. Most organisms make at least one crossover per pair of homologues; it holds the pair together until anaphase I and helps them separate correctly (Chromosome theory & sex linkage).
Not universal. The fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe shows essentially no interference.

Map functions encode this: Haldane assumes no interference; Kosambi builds some in (Linkage & recombination).

Keep this slide qualitative. The mechanism of interference is still studied; the useful picture is that once a crossover is designated, it inhibits other crossovers nearby along the chromosome axis. The consequence for mapping: over short distances, we can treat RF as additive and DCOs as nearly absent, and over long distances, map functions are needed. The link to nondisjunction in the first unit of this part: bivalents without a crossover are prone to missegregation, which is one reason why chromosomes evolved to ensure one obligate crossover.

title: Three-point crosses
section: Is the interference real, or noise?
text:
Is the interference real, or noise?
Only 11 double crossovers were observed. Small counts are noisy:

If there were no interference (CoC = 1), we would expect 18.2 DCOs, but a cross of 2000 flies could easily give 13 or 24.
In the Exercise in R you simulate 1000 such crosses with no interference: the CoC lands between about 0.63 and 1.43 in 95% of them, and is as low as 0.60 in only about 2% of them.
So 0.60 is fairly strong evidence for interference, but with fewer flies it would not be.

A CoC computed from 2 or 3 double crossovers says very little. Rare classes need large crosses.

This brings back the theme of sampling noise from Part 1. CoC is a ratio of two counts, one of them small, so it is noisy. The simulation in R gives a feel for the spread; a proper test would compare the observed DCO count with the expected count, for example with a Poisson or binomial model, which is beyond what we need. Practical message: if a three-point cross has zero double crossovers in 200 offspring, you cannot conclude complete interference: with 2 expected, zero happens about one time in seven.

title: Three-point crosses
section: Try it: find the middle gene
text:
Try it: find the middle gene




Interactive demo. It starts on the fly data with no order chosen; each class is drawn as a chromosome, blue for alleles from the most common class’s chromosome, red for the other. Click each of the three orders in turn. With v in the middle or cv in the middle, the demo says “not this order”: the pair it would call double crossovers has 249 or 129 offspring, more than a single crossover pair, and the CoC comes out far above 1. With ct in the middle, the rarest pair, 6 and 5, is the DCO, the distances are 7.0 and 13.0 cM, CoC 0.60 and I 0.40. Then click maize: here the female is in coupling, so the parentals are all mutant and all wild type, and the middle gene is gl. Finally click random a few times and let the room call the order before you click.

title: Three-point crosses
section: The recipe, and the usual mistakes
text:
The recipe, and the usual mistakes


Do not assume the parentals are + + + and all-mutant: read them off the counts.
Do not forget to add the DCOs to both intervals.
Rewrite the classes in the correct gene order before you classify the single crossovers.
Expected DCO uses the RFs (fractions), not cM: 0.070 × 0.130, not 7 × 13.


The recipe on one slide, for revision. Students who follow the five steps in order rarely go wrong. The list of mistakes comes from years of exam answers. The last one gives absurd numbers quickly (7 x 13 x 2000 is 182000 double crossovers), so a sanity check catches it: expected DCOs can never exceed the smaller SCO-plus-DCO count.

section: Our map and the real map
text:
Our map and the real map
Genetic map positions on the Drosophila X chromosome, from NCBI Gene (field “MapLocation”, taken from FlyBase):

“1-20” means chromosome 1 (the X), 20 cM from the tip. The real order is cv–ct–v, with about 8 and 13 cM between them. Our (invented) counts give the same order and similar distances.
Maps like this were built in the 1910s–1930s from thousands of crosses like this one, starting with Sturtevant’s map of the X in 1913 (Linkage & recombination).

Close the loop with the real chromosome. The counts in the worked example are invented, so that we can use round numbers, but they were made to match the real map: NCBI Gene records the classical genetic map positions from FlyBase, 1-12 for crossveinless, 1-20 for cut, 1-33 for vermilion. The first number is the chromosome, the second the position in centimorgans. Our map puts cv at 0 because a three-point cross only gives relative positions; adding 12 to each puts it on the standard map. In the Linkage exercise students look up these positions in FlyBase themselves.

title: Three-point crosses
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Three-point testcross
triple heterozygote × triple recessive; 8 classes = 8 gamete types; 4 reciprocal pairs


Parental classes
the largest pair; tells the phase of the heterozygote


Double crossover (DCO) classes
the smallest pair; only the middle gene has changed partner


Interval distance
(SCO in that interval + DCO) / N


Outer distance
sum of the two intervals; a two-point cross underestimates it by 2 × DCO / N


Expected DCO
RFI × RFII × N (product rule, if independent)


Coefficient of coincidence
CoC = observed DCO / expected DCO


Interference
I = 1 − CoC; usually positive (fewer DCOs than expected)


Worked example
cv – 7.0 cM – ct – 13.0 cM – v; CoC 0.60, I 0.40




The summary is the revision sheet. The two ideas to keep: the rarest pair reveals the middle gene, and the double crossovers count in both intervals. Interference is the one new biological fact: crossovers are not independent, they repel each other.

title: Three-point crosses
text:
Where this leads

Human linkage & LOD scores (next). In humans we cannot set up a testcross with thousands of offspring. Instead we combine small families and weigh the evidence for linkage with a likelihood, the LOD score.
Genome analysis (Part 4). Genetic maps in cM are now anchored to DNA sequence in base pairs; markers such as SNPs replace visible phenotypes.
Rearrangements & aneuploidy (Part 5). In an inversion heterozygote, recombinant chromatids from crossovers inside the inversion are lost, so map distances across it shrink.


Point forward. The logic of counting recombinants carries over to humans, but the data are scarce, so the statistics change: next time we write down the probability of a family’s data as a function of the recombination frequency, and compare it with no linkage. The exercise today has the paper problems, the demo, and an R page where students write one function for a given gene order, run it over all three orders with map, and pick the order with the rarest double crossovers.

title: Exercise in R: three-point crosses
Exercise in R: three-point crosses
Exercise in R: three-point crosses
text:
Before you start
This page builds on the by-hand part of the Exercise, so do that first. You need the packages readr, dplyr, purrr and ggplot2. Download drosophila_v_cv_ct.csv and maize_lg_gl_bm.csv and save them in a data/ folder of your R project. Both are invented teaching data (see data/README.md); the fly file holds the lecture’s example.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(ggplot2)

title: Exercise in R: three-point crosses
text:
Tasks
You already know map_dbl() (Extensions to Mendel), which calls a function for each element of a list and returns a number for each. This unit’s new idiom is a function that returns a one-row tibble, called for each element with map(). map() returns a list of tibbles, one per element, and list_rbind() stacks them into one tibble, with one row per input. This is how you compare one analysis under several hypotheses side by side.
R1. (the data) Read the fly data. Each row is one class: the alleles the offspring got from the heterozygous female (+ = wild type) and the count n. Compute N, and use slice_max() and slice_min() to pull out the two most common and the two rarest classes. (The first n in slice_max(n, n = 2) is the column; the second says how many rows to keep.) Which gene differs between the rarest classes and the parentals?
fly <- read_csv("data/drosophila_v_cv_ct.csv") |> select(-note)
fly
N <- sum(fly$n)
N
fly |> slice_max(n, n = 2)
fly |> slice_min(n, n = 2)
R2. (classify the classes for one order) Take the most common class as the reference parental chromosome. For each gene, TRUE means the offspring got the allele from the same chromosome as the reference. A crossover between two neighbouring genes shows up as a change from TRUE to FALSE (or back). Classify each class for the order cv–ct–v with case_when(), and add up the counts per class type.
parental <- fly |> slice_max(n, n = 1)
fly2 <- fly |>
  mutate(cv_same = cv == parental$cv,
         ct_same = ct == parental$ct,
         v_same  = v  == parental$v,
         region1 = cv_same != ct_same,      # crossover between cv and ct
         region2 = ct_same != v_same,       # crossover between ct and v
         class = case_when(region1 & region2 ~ "DCO",
                           region1 ~ "SCO cv-ct",
                           region2 ~ "SCO ct-v",
                           TRUE ~ "parental"))
fly2 |> select(v, cv, ct, n, class)
fly2 |> group_by(class) |> summarise(n = sum(n))
Check the four totals against the lecture.
R3. (one function, one order) Write a function three_point(df, order) that does R2 for any data frame and any order (a character vector of the three column names, left to right) and returns the two distances in cM, the observed and expected DCOs, the CoC and the interference as a one-row tibble. df[[g]] picks the column whose name is stored in g. Note that sum(df$n[sw1]) already includes the DCOs, which have a crossover in region I too.
three_point <- function(df, order) {
  top  <- df |> slice_max(n, n = 1)            # one parental class
  same <- function(g) df[[g]] == top[[g]]      # allele from the same chromosome as top?
  sw1  <- same(order[1]) != same(order[2])     # crossover in region I
  sw2  <- same(order[2]) != same(order[3])     # crossover in region II
  N    <- sum(df$n)
  r1   <- sum(df$n[sw1]) / N                   # SCO I + DCO
  r2   <- sum(df$n[sw2]) / N                   # SCO II + DCO
  n_dco   <- sum(df$n[sw1 & sw2])
  exp_dco <- r1 * r2 * N
  tibble(order = paste(order, collapse = "-"),
         dist1 = 100 * r1, dist2 = 100 * r2,
         n_dco = n_dco, exp_dco = exp_dco,
         coc = n_dco / exp_dco, interference = 1 - coc)
}
three_point(fly, c("cv", "ct", "v"))
R4. (all three orders with map()) There are only three different orders, one for each gene in the middle (reading a map backwards gives the same order). Put them in a list, run three_point() on each with map(), stack the results with list_rbind(), and pick the order with the fewest DCOs with slice_min(). What happens to the CoC for the wrong orders?
orders <- list(c("ct", "v", "cv"), c("v", "cv", "ct"), c("cv", "ct", "v"))
all_orders <- map(orders, \(o) three_point(fly, o)) |> list_rbind()
all_orders
all_orders |> slice_min(n_dco)
R5. (reuse: maize, and the two-point distance) Your function works for any three-point data set. Run it on the maize data of B1 over all three orders and sort by n_dco with arrange(). Then go back to the flies and compute the two-point cv–v distance, ignoring ct. Compare it with the three-point outer distance, 7.0 + 13.0 cM.
maize <- read_csv("data/maize_lg_gl_bm.csv") |> select(-note)
maize_orders <- list(c("gl", "lg", "bm"), c("lg", "gl", "bm"), c("lg", "bm", "gl"))
map(maize_orders, \(o) three_point(maize, o)) |> list_rbind() |> arrange(n_dco)

top <- fly |> slice_max(n, n = 1)
outer_rec <- (fly$cv == top$cv) != (fly$v == top$v)   # cv and v in a new combination
100 * sum(fly$n[outer_rec]) / sum(fly$n)
R6. (how noisy is the CoC?) The flies gave CoC = 0.60 from only 11 DCOs. Could that happen with no interference? Write simulate_tp(), which draws N offspring with sample() from the four class types (parental, SCO in I, SCO in II, DCO), with probabilities from the Background of the exercise, and returns the CoC. Its arguments r1, r2 and I have default values (as in Linkage & recombination), so simulate_tp(2000) simulates the fly intervals with no interference. Run it 1000 times with I = 0 and 1000 times with I = 0.4, using map_dbl(), and plot the two distributions.
simulate_tp <- function(N, r1 = 0.07, r2 = 0.13, I = 0) {
  p_dco <- (1 - I) * r1 * r2
  probs <- c(parental = 1 - r1 - r2 + p_dco, sco1 = r1 - p_dco,
             sco2 = r2 - p_dco, dco = p_dco)
  kids <- sample(names(probs), N, replace = TRUE, prob = probs)
  n1 <- sum(kids %in% c("sco1", "dco"))
  n2 <- sum(kids %in% c("sco2", "dco"))
  n_dco <- sum(kids == "dco")
  n_dco / (n1 / N * n2 / N * N)                # the CoC
}
set.seed(33)
simulate_tp(2000)
coc_sims <- tibble(I = rep(c(0, 0.4), each = 1000)) |>
  mutate(coc = map_dbl(I, \(i) simulate_tp(2000, I = i)))
coc_sims |> group_by(I) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(coc), low = quantile(coc, 0.025), high = quantile(coc, 0.975))

ggplot(coc_sims, aes(x = coc, fill = factor(I))) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.1, boundary = 0, position = "identity", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.60, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "coefficient of coincidence", y = "simulated crosses",
       fill = "true interference",
       title = "CoC in 1000 simulated crosses of 2000 flies") +
  theme_minimal()

coc_sims |> filter(I == 0) |> summarise(p_as_low = mean(coc <= 0.604))
What fraction of the crosses without interference give a CoC as low as the flies’ 0.60? How would the spread change with 500 flies instead of 2000?

title: Exercise in R: three-point crosses
text:
Where this leads
The pattern one function, many hypotheses, one tibble comes back in Human linkage & LOD scores, where you compute the likelihood of family data for many values of the recombination frequency θ and find the one that fits best. The simulation in R6 is the same idea as the χ² simulations in Probability & the χ² test: when a formula is awkward, simulate the null hypothesis.

title: RNA-mediated regulation
text:
About this lecture
Transcription is not the last word. Small RNAs, about 22 nucleotides long, pair with mRNAs and turn them down. They were found twice: once by geneticists studying worm larvae that developed at the wrong pace, and once by researchers trying to switch genes off with antisense RNA.

lin-4 and let-7: how a genetic screen found the first microRNAs.
RNA interference (RNAi): double-stranded RNA silences genes.
miRNA biogenesis: Drosha, Dicer, RISC.
Seed matching: why nucleotides 2–8 matter, and how to find target sites.
siRNA vs miRNA; long non-coding RNAs such as XIST.
RNAi as a lab tool for reverse genetics.

Book: Hartwell, Genetics: From Genes to Genomes, the chapter on RNA-based regulation (non-coding RNAs).

The unit has a genetics story at its centre: the lin-4 and lin-14 mutants of C. elegans, analysed with the same tools as the lac mutants (dominance, gain and loss of function, epistasis). The mechanism then comes from biochemistry, and the practical payoff is RNAi as a tool, which leads into reverse genetics in the next unit. The R exercise finds let-7 seed matches in the HMGA2 3’UTR, a real oncology example.

title: RNA-mediated regulation
text:
A post-transcriptional layer










RNA
Size
Made from
Acts on
Effect




miRNA
~22 nt
its own gene (hairpin)
many mRNAs, partial pairing via the seed
less translation, mRNA decay


siRNA
~21 nt
long double-stranded RNA (virus, transposon, or the experimenter)
mRNAs with perfect complementarity
cleavage of the target


piRNA
24–31 nt
piRNA clusters, germ line
transposon RNAs
silences transposons in the germ line


lncRNA
> 200 nt
its own gene
chromatin, other RNAs, proteins
many; e.g. XIST silences an X



Humans have about two thousand miRNA genes in miRBase; a typical miRNA has hundreds of predicted targets, and most human mRNAs carry at least one conserved miRNA site.

Give students the map before the details. The rule of thumb: siRNAs come from long double-stranded RNA and pair perfectly, so they cut their target. miRNAs come from the genome’s own hairpins and pair imperfectly, mainly through the seed, so they turn many targets down a little each. piRNAs protect the germ line against transposons; we mention them only for completeness. lncRNAs are a heterogeneous group defined by length and lack of protein-coding potential; XIST from the last unit is the best understood one. The numbers are deliberately rough: miRBase’s count changes between releases and many annotated miRNAs are doubtful.

title: RNA-mediated regulation
text:
A genetic screen finds lin-4
In C. elegans, each cell division in the larva happens at a fixed stage (L1–L4). Heterochronic mutants do the right things at the wrong time.

lin-4(lf): cells repeat L1-type divisions in later stages (retarded). Recessive.
lin-14(lf): cells skip L1 fates and jump ahead (precocious): the opposite phenotype.
lin-14(gf): dominant alleles that look like lin-4(lf). They delete part of the lin-14 3′UTR; the protein is normal.
Double mutant lin-4(lf); lin-14(lf) is precocious: lin-14 is epistatic, so lin-4 acts upstream as a negative regulator of lin-14.

In 1993 the Ambros and Ruvkun labs found that lin-4 makes no protein: only a ~22-nt RNA, complementary to repeated sites in the lin-14 3′UTR. (Nobel Prize 2024.)

This is the same reasoning as in the Extensions to Mendel and lac units. Opposite phenotypes suggest opposite roles. The double mutant shows the phenotype of lin-14 loss, so lin-14 is downstream, and lin-4 must negatively regulate it. The gain-of-function lin-14 alleles are the clincher: they are dominant (cis-acting, like Oc!), and map to the 3’UTR, not the coding sequence. So the 3’UTR contains a site through which lin-4 acts. When Victor Ambros’ lab cloned lin-4, they found no open reading frame, only a 22-nt and a 61-nt RNA. Gary Ruvkun’s lab showed that the lin-14 3’UTR has seven sites complementary to lin-4. For seven years this looked like a worm curiosity.

title: RNA-mediated regulation
text:
lin-4 turns down lin-14

The lin-14 3′UTR is a cis-acting element, like lacO: deleting it makes the gene escape regulation, dominantly. The lin-4 RNA is the trans-acting factor.

Walk through the curves. In the wild type, LIN-14 protein is high in L1 and falls when lin-4 RNA appears late in L1, although lin-14 mRNA levels stay much the same. That is post-transcriptional regulation: same mRNA, less protein. Without lin-4, or without the sites in the lin-14 3’UTR, LIN-14 stays high, and the cells think they are still in L1. Without lin-14, cells act as if L1 were already over. Ask: why is lin-14(gf) dominant while lin-4(lf) is recessive? Because the gf allele’s own mRNA escapes regulation in cis, regardless of the other allele; while one copy of lin-4 makes enough RNA to regulate both lin-14 alleles in trans.

title: RNA-mediated regulation
text:
let-7: the first conserved microRNA
In 2000, let-7 was found by the same kind of screen: another heterochronic gene, again a ~22-nt RNA, acting on the 3′UTRs of later-stage regulators (lin-41, hbl-1).

let-7 turned out to be conserved: the mature let-7 of worms, flies and humans is identical over its first 22 nucleotides, and it is expressed at the same transition, from larval/embryonic to adult fates.
Suddenly small regulatory RNAs were not a worm oddity. Cloning projects found hundreds in animals and plants: they were named microRNAs.
Human let-7 targets include HMGA2, LIN28B and RAS genes; let-7 is often low in tumours, and HMGA2 is a growth-promoting oncogene.


The conservation result is what changed the field. Pasquinelli and colleagues showed that the let-7 RNA sequence is identical in many bilaterian animals, including humans, and that its expression is timed with the larval-to-adult switch in worms and flies. In the Find it task students compare worm and human let-7 in miRBase and see this for themselves. The human connection: LIN28 binds let-7 precursors and blocks their processing, while let-7 represses LIN28: a double-negative loop that keeps stem cells young or lets them mature. HMGA2 has seven let-7 sites in its 3’UTR, which students count in R.

title: RNA-mediated regulation
text:
RNA interference
Fire, Mello and colleagues (1998) injected RNA into worms to silence the unc-22 gene:







Injected RNA
Silencing




sense strand
weak


antisense strand
weak


double-stranded RNA
strong, with only a few molecules per cell, spreading through the body and into the progeny



Double-stranded RNA is cut by Dicer into ~21-nt siRNAs; one strand guides Argonaute (in RISC) to cut any mRNA that matches perfectly. Natural roles: defence against viruses and transposons. (Nobel Prize 2006.)

The surprise in the 1998 paper was that the earlier antisense experiments worked because the antisense preparations were contaminated with some double-stranded RNA. Only a few molecules of dsRNA per cell were enough: catalytic, not stoichiometric. In worms the silencing signal is amplified by RNA-dependent RNA polymerases and spreads between cells and even to the next generation. Plants had shown the effect earlier as “co-suppression”: adding extra copies of a petunia pigment gene made some flowers white instead of darker purple. The shared machinery between RNAi and miRNAs is Dicer and Argonaute.

title: RNA-mediated regulation
text:
How a microRNA is made

Drosha cuts the hairpin out in the nucleus; Dicer cuts off the loop in the cytoplasm; the guide strand goes into Argonaute (RISC). siRNAs use the same Dicer and Argonaute, but start from long double-stranded RNA.

Keep it to the names and the order. Drosha with its partner DGCR8 is the nuclear processor; Exportin-5 carries the pre-miRNA out; Dicer makes the duplex; one strand, the guide, is kept, usually the one whose 5’ end is less tightly paired. The guide is the mature miRNA you see in miRBase, named 5p or 3p after the arm of the hairpin it comes from, for example hsa-let-7a-5p. Genetic note: Dicer mutant mice die early in development, and Dicer mutant worms are sterile with heterochronic defects: the miRNA pathway is essential.

title: RNA-mediated regulation
text:
Seed matching

Animal miRNAs find targets mainly through the seed, nucleotides 2–8 from the 5′ end. A target site in the mRNA (usually the 3′UTR) is the reverse complement of the seed, sometimes with an A opposite nucleotide 1.

Read the figure: let-7a is drawn 3’ to 5’ so it lines up antiparallel with the mRNA. The seed GAGGUAG (nt 2 to 8) pairs with CUACCUC in the mRNA, followed by an A opposite nt 1: an 8mer, the strongest site type. This is the real site at UTR positions 21 to 28 of HMGA2, the first of the seven let-7 sites. The rest of the miRNA pairs only partly, which is why one miRNA can regulate hundreds of mRNAs. TargetScan, which students use in the Find it task, ranks targets by site type, number of sites, and whether the sites are conserved across species. A 7-nt site occurs by chance about once every 16 kb (4 to the 7th), so a single site means little; conserved and multiple sites mean more.

The last row is the practical warning: an siRNA designed against one gene also has a seed, and it can turn down hundreds of other mRNAs that happen to carry a seed match. That is the main source of off-target effects in RNAi screens. The standard control is to use two or more siRNAs with different sequences against the same gene: a real phenotype should be reproduced by all of them; an off-target phenotype will not.

title: RNA-mediated regulation
section: Regulatory RNA in genetics and disease
text:
Regulatory RNA in genetics and disease

Target-site mutations act in cis. Chromosomal rearrangements in benign tumours (e.g. lipomas) cut HMGA2 off from its 3′UTR. The truncated mRNA loses its seven let-7 sites, escapes repression, and makes too much protein: a dominant gain of function, like lin-14(gf).
miRNA mutations act in trans. A point mutation in the seed of MIR96 causes dominant progressive hearing loss in humans (and in the diminuendo mouse). The mutant miRNA loses its normal targets and gains new ones.
The miRNA pathway is a drug target. Patisiran, an siRNA drug approved in 2018, silences the TTR gene in hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis.


Three examples, one for each of: cis-acting sites, trans-acting regulators, and therapy. HMGA2: in many lipomas and other tumours a translocation breaks HMGA2 between its coding exons and the 3’UTR; the fused or truncated mRNA lacks the let-7 sites, and experiments showed that the loss of let-7 regulation alone is enough to make HMGA2 oncogenic (Mayr, Hemann and Bartel, 2007). MIR96: the mutations are in the seed and act dominantly, because the mutant miRNA from one allele is a new, wrong regulator in the hair cells. Patisiran is delivered in lipid nanoparticles to the liver, which makes most TTR; it is a direct application of the 1998 RNAi discovery.

title: RNA-mediated regulation
text:
Long non-coding RNAs
lncRNAs are transcripts longer than 200 nt that do not encode a protein. Some work in cis, on the chromosome they are made from; others in trans.

XIST (from the last unit): made from the X that will be silenced; coats that X in cis and recruits silencing complexes. Deleting XIST on one X means that X cannot be inactivated.
Many lncRNAs act as scaffolds for chromatin complexes, or as decoys that soak up miRNAs or proteins.
Many more are transcribed but of unknown function. Genetics is the test: does deleting it, or its promoter, change a phenotype?


Keep the lncRNA part short and honest: there are tens of thousands of annotated lncRNA genes, and for most we do not know if the RNA itself does anything. Some act through the act of transcription, not through the RNA. XIST is the clearest case and links back. The cis/trans question applies again: XIST acts only on the chromosome it comes from, which can be shown genetically by putting an XIST transgene on an autosome: that autosome becomes silenced.

title: RNA-mediated regulation
section: RNAi as a tool for reverse genetics
text:
RNAi as a tool for reverse genetics
Forward genetics goes from a phenotype to the gene. Reverse genetics starts from a gene and asks: what happens if I remove it? RNAi made this easy.

Worms: feed them E. coli that make dsRNA against a gene. A library covering about 86 % of predicted C. elegans genes allowed genome-wide RNAi screens (2003).
Flies: transgenic hairpin RNAs (often combined with tissue-specific GAL4 drivers, next unit).
Mammalian cells: transfect siRNAs or express shRNAs.

Limits: RNAi gives a knockdown (a hypomorph), not a null; efficiency varies; off-target effects via the seed. Today CRISPR–Cas9 knockouts are often preferred, but RNAi remains useful for genes whose knockout is lethal, and for tuning dosage.

This bridges to Development and model organisms. The worm feeding library (Kamath and colleagues, Ahringer lab, 2003) was one of the first genome-wide reverse-genetic screens in an animal. Genetically, an RNAi phenotype is like a hypomorphic allele: partial loss of function. That has advantages (you can see phenotypes for genes whose null alleles die early) and disadvantages (a weak knockdown can miss a phenotype; you cannot do clean complementation tests). Controls: several independent siRNAs, and rescue with a version of the gene that the siRNA cannot target (silent changes in the target site).

Before you start
This page builds on the by-hand part of the Exercise, so do that first. You need the packages dplyr, stringr and ggplot2. Download HMGA2_3UTR.fa and save it in a data/ folder of your R project. It is the 3′UTR of the human HMGA2 canonical transcript (ENST00000403681.7) from Ensembl release 116, 2999 nt, downloaded on 2026-11-20; see the data README for how it was cut out. The miRNA sequences are from miRBase release 23.1 and are typed into the code below.
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)

title: Exercise in R: RNA-mediated regulation
text:
Tasks
The R in this unit reuses idioms from Part 3 and Part 4: reading FASTA by hand, chartr() for complementing, and str_locate_all() for finding every match of a pattern. One new helper: case_when() from dplyr, a vectorised “if … else if … else” that gives each row the value of the first condition that is true.
R1. (read the UTR) Read the FASTA file with readLines(), keep the header, and paste the remaining lines into one string utr. How long is it? Print the first 60 nt.
R2. (seed and site) Store let-7a-5p (miRBase MIMAT0000062) as let7a <- "UGAGGUAGUAGGUUGUAUAGUUU". Convert U to T so it matches the DNA in the file, take nt 2–8 with str_sub(), and write a function revcomp() that returns the reverse complement of a DNA string. What is the 7mer-m8 site?
revcomp <- function(s) {
  # complement with chartr(), then reverse the letters
}
R3. (find and classify the sites) Use str_locate_all() to list every 7mer-m8 match. Then do a better job: find every match to the 6-nt core (the site without its first letter: it pairs with nt 2–7), and for each one look at the base just before it (a C there pairs with nt 8) and just after it (an A there sits opposite nt 1). Use case_when() to label each site 8mer, 7mer-m8, 7mer-A1 or 6mer, and count the types. Compare with TargetScan’s numbers from the Find it task.
core6 <- str_sub(site7, 2)
hits <- tibble(start = str_locate_all(utr, core6)[[1]][, "start"]) |>
  mutate(before = str_sub(utr, start - 1, start - 1),
         after  = str_sub(utr, start + 6, start + 6),
         type   = case_when(...))
R4. (plot) Plot the sites along the UTR: position on the x axis, site type on the y axis, one point per site, and a grey bar for the UTR itself (annotate("segment", ...)). Are the sites clustered or spread out?
R5. (chance and controls) a) How many 7mer-m8 matches to one seed would you expect by chance in 2999 nt? And 6-nt matches? b) Write seed_sites(mirna, utr), which returns the number of 7mer-m8 matches for a miRNA, and apply it with sapply() to let-7a, miR-1 (UGGAAUGUAAAGAAGUAUGUAU) and miR-21 (UAGCUUAUCAGACUGAUGUUGACU). What do the controls tell you?

title: Exercise in R: RNA-mediated regulation
text:
Where this leads
In Development & model organisms you go from one gene to many species: you join an ortholog table to a gene list with left_join() and draw a presence/absence heat map of developmental genes across yeast, worm, fly, fish and mouse.

title: Rearrangements & aneuploidy
text:
About this lecture
The previous lecture built a normal chromosome: one centromere, two telomeres, a fixed band pattern. This one is about what happens when structure or number goes wrong, and why the consequences show up in the next generation.

Deletions and duplications: dosage changes; recurrent ones caused by repeats.
Inversions: no DNA lost, yet crossovers inside them give unbalanced gametes.
Translocations: reciprocal and Robertsonian; how the carrier’s chromosomes segregate; the Philadelphia chromosome.
Aneuploidy: nondisjunction in meiosis I and II; trisomy 21 and the maternal age effect; sex-chromosome aneuploidies.
Polyploidy: crops with whole extra genomes, and why triploids are sterile.

Book: Hartwell, Genetics: From Genes to Genomes, the chapter on chromosomal rearrangements and changes in chromosome number.

The genetic thread through the whole lecture is meiosis. A rearrangement or a missing chromosome in one cell is a cytology fact; what makes it genetics is what the carrier passes on. Many carriers of a balanced rearrangement are perfectly healthy, and the problem appears only in their children or as reduced fertility. Students know mitosis, meiosis and nondisjunction from Part 2 (chromosome theory); today’s demo is the same meiosis demo, in its nondisjunction mode. Keep the key word “balanced” in view: does a cell or gamete have the right amount of every part of the genome, or not?

title: Rearrangements & aneuploidy
text:
Four kinds of rearrangement

A rearrangement starts with double-strand breaks that are rejoined the wrong way, or with recombination between repeats at the wrong place. Balanced rearrangements (inversions, reciprocal translocations) keep every gene, just in a new order; unbalanced ones (deletions, duplications) change the amount.

Read the figure row by row. The letters are blocks of genes; the red dot is the centromere. Deletion: a segment is missing. Duplication: a segment is present twice, here in tandem. Inversion: a segment is cut out and put back the other way round; paracentric if the centromere is outside the inverted segment, pericentric if it is inside (which can move the centromere and change the arm ratio). Reciprocal translocation: two non-homologous chromosomes swap ends. The notation from the last lecture applies: del, dup, inv, t, with the breakpoints in parentheses. Ask the room which of these can be seen in a G-banded karyotype: those that change the band pattern by more than a few megabases.

title: Rearrangements & aneuploidy
text:
Recurrent rearrangements come from repeats

Non-allelic homologous recombination (NAHR): crossing over between two similar low-copy repeats that are not at the same position. It gives a deletion and a reciprocal duplication of exactly the segment between the repeats.

Low-copy repeats, also called segmental duplications, are stretches of more than about 10 kb that are more than 95 percent identical and occur at several places in the genome. When homologous chromosomes pair at the wrong copy, a crossover between them is unequal. Because the breakpoints are set by the repeats, unrelated patients carry nearly identical deletions; that is why these are called recurrent genomic disorders and why they have fixed names. 22q11.2 deletion syndrome is the most common, around 1 in 3000 to 1 in 6000 births. The 17p12 pair is the cleanest example of reciprocity: the duplication of a 1.4 Mb segment containing PMP22 causes Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease type 1A, and the deletion of the same segment causes HNPP, a different nerve disease. One gene, three copies versus one copy, two diseases. Sturtevant’s Bar eye in Drosophila (1925) was the first unequal crossing over to be studied.

title: Rearrangements & aneuploidy
text:
Deletions
A heterozygote for a deletion has only one copy of the genes in the deleted segment.

Haploinsufficiency: for some genes, one copy is not enough. Large deletions are usually harmful; homozygous deletions are usually lethal.
Pseudodominance: a recessive allele on the normal homologue is expressed, because the deletion uncovers it. Drosophila geneticists used overlapping deletions to map genes: a recessive mutation is uncovered only by deletions that remove its locus.
In meiosis, the normal homologue forms a deletion loop where it has no partner.










Human deletion syndrome
Region
Typical size
Key gene(s)




Cri-du-chat

varies

22q11.21
≈ 2.5–3 Mb
TBX1 (heart, face)

Pseudodominance is the genetic signature of a deletion: a recessive phenotype appears in a heterozygote. It made deletion mapping possible: cross a recessive mutant to a series of flies carrying overlapping deletions, and the mutation lies in the region removed by every deletion that uncovers it. The same logic, with molecular deletions in yeast or bacteria, is still used. In humans, the most common deletion syndromes arise by NAHR, as on the previous slide, mostly as new mutations. A deletion syndrome is a contiguous gene syndrome: many genes are lost, and some features can be traced to single genes, such as the narrowing of the aorta in Williams syndrome to the loss of one copy of the elastin gene ELN. Students find these in ClinVar and MedGen in the exercise. Deletions below about 5 Mb are invisible in a routine karyotype; they are found with microarrays or sequencing.

title: Rearrangements & aneuploidy
text:
Duplications

Dosage: three copies of a gene instead of two can change the phenotype. Drosophila Bar eye is a tandem duplication; flies with the segment three times on one chromosome (double-Bar) have even smaller eyes. Human CMT1A is a duplication of PMP22.
In meiosis, the duplicated segment forms a duplication loop, and the repeat makes further unequal crossing over possible: duplications beget duplications.
Evolution: a duplicated gene is free to change. One copy keeps the old job, the other can gain a new one. Gene families arose like this, for example the α- and β-globin genes, and the red and green opsin genes on the X.

Duplications are usually less harmful than deletions of the same size: having a little too much is better tolerated than too little.

Bar is the classic: Sturtevant showed that Bar reverted and also gave double-Bar at a low rate, and explained both by unequal crossing over between the tandem copies; Bridges later saw the duplicated bands in salivary gland chromosomes. The dosage point links to aneuploidy later today: a trisomy is a duplication of a whole chromosome. The evolutionary point links back to the T2T genome: many of the new protein-coding genes in T2T-CHM13 are in recent segmental duplications that the old reference could not resolve. Red–green colour blindness often results from unequal crossing over between the tandem opsin genes on the X, which is why it is so common in men.

title: Rearrangements & aneuploidy
text:
Inversions
An inversion loses nothing: an inversion homozygote, or a heterozygote, usually has a normal phenotype. Exceptions: a breakpoint inside a gene, or a gene moved next to heterochromatin (position-effect variegation, previous lecture).









Paracentric
Pericentric




Centromere
outside the inverted segment
inside it


Band pattern
changes within one arm
can change the arm ratio


Crossover in the loop gives
a dicentric + an acentric
two chromosomes with a duplication and a deficiency



In a heterozygote, the two homologues can only pair gene by gene if one of them forms an inversion loop.
A common harmless human variant is the pericentric inversion of chromosome 9, inv(9)(p12q13), found in about 1–3% of people.

The genetic problem with inversions arises in heterozygotes during meiosis, which is the next slide. Inversion homozygotes pair normally and have no problem. Over evolution, inversions are common differences between species: humans and chimpanzees differ by several pericentric inversions, and many Drosophila populations carry inversion polymorphisms that keep favourable combinations of alleles together. Inversions are usually detected by a change in band order, or today by sequencing with long reads.

title: Rearrangements & aneuploidy
section: Why crossovers in inversions make bad gametes
text:
Why crossovers in inversions make bad gametes


Paracentric: the crossover chromatids become a dicentric (torn at anaphase I) and an acentric fragment (lost). Gametes with them are unbalanced.
Pericentric: the crossover chromatids each have a duplication of one end and a deficiency of the other.
Either way, only the non-crossover chromatids give viable offspring. Inversion heterozygotes have reduced fertility, and recombinants for genes inside the inversion seem to be suppressed.


Derive the products on the board using the figure. Normal: centromere A B C D E; inverted: centromere A D C B E. In the loop, one crossover between B and C joins the normal chromatid’s centromere part, A B, to the inverted chromatid’s centromere part read backwards, C D A: a chromosome with a centromere at each end. The leftover pieces, E D C on one side and B E on the other, join into a fragment with no centromere. The dicentric is stretched between the poles at anaphase I and breaks; the acentric is lost. In animals, the cell often directs the dicentric into the polar body, so the egg can be fine, but in plants and in males fertility drops. Crossing over itself is not suppressed: it happens, but its products die. Geneticists use this: Drosophila balancer chromosomes carry several overlapping inversions, a dominant visible marker and a recessive lethal, and keep a mutation on the homologue intact for generations without selection.

title: Rearrangements & aneuploidy
text:
Reciprocal translocations

A balanced carrier is usually healthy. At meiosis I the four chromosomes pair as a cross (quadrivalent). Each gamete gets two of the four, and only alternate segregation gives balanced gametes.

The cross forms because each part of each chromosome pairs with its homologous part. Then two of the four go to each pole. Alternate segregation, normal plus normal and translocation plus translocation, gives two kinds of balanced gamete: completely normal, and a balanced carrier like the parent. Adjacent-1 keeps homologous centromeres apart but puts one normal and one translocated chromosome together: each gamete has a duplication of one tip and a deficiency of the other. Adjacent-2, where homologous centromeres go to the same pole, is rarer and also unbalanced. In plants this shows up as semisterility: about half of the pollen and ovules abort. In human carriers it shows up as recurrent miscarriage or a child with an unbalanced karyotype. How often each mode happens is measured, not predicted from first principles; if all six ways of sending two chromosomes to each pole were equally likely, a third of gametes would be balanced, and the R exercise simulates exactly that. Translocations also cause pseudolinkage: genes near the breakpoints on the two different chromosomes are inherited together, because only alternate gametes survive.

title: Rearrangements & aneuploidy
text:
Robertsonian translocations
Two acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, 22) fuse at or near their centromeres. The long arms survive as one chromosome; the tiny short arms (repeats and rDNA) are lost without harm.

A carrier has 45 chromosomes, e.g. 45,XX,rob(14;21), and is healthy. About 1 in 1000 people carry a Robertsonian translocation.
Their gametes, from a trivalent (14, 21, rob):









Gamete
Zygote with a normal gamete
Outcome




14 + 21
46, normal
healthy


rob(14;21)
45, balanced carrier
healthy


rob(14;21) + 21
46, but three copies of 21q
translocation Down syndrome


14 alone
monosomy 21
lethal


rob(14;21) + 14
trisomy 14
lethal


21 alone
monosomy 14
lethal



About 4% of Down syndrome is translocation Down syndrome, and it can recur in a family.

Students met acrocentric chromosomes last lecture; the five pairs carry the rDNA on their short arms, so losing two short arms is harmless. The trivalent in the carrier can send the three chromosomes to the poles in several ways; the table lists the six two-plus-one outcomes. Several end in early miscarriage. The important clinical difference from ordinary trisomy 21: a translocation trisomy has 46 chromosomes, and one of the parents may be a carrier, so the recurrence risk is much higher than for free trisomy 21. Empirically, the risk of a child with Down syndrome is about 10 to 15 percent when the mother carries rob(14;21), and about 1 percent when the father does. A carrier of rob(21;21) can only make gametes with two copies of 21q or none, so every pregnancy that survives has Down syndrome. That is why a karyotype is done for every child with Down syndrome: it tells the family whether the risk can recur.

title: Rearrangements & aneuploidy
text:
The Philadelphia chromosome
Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML): in most patients, the leukaemic cells carry t(9;22)(q34;q11).

The small derivative chromosome 22, der(22), is the Philadelphia chromosome (Nowell and Hungerford, 1960; shown to be a translocation by Janet Rowley in 1973).
The breakpoints fall inside two genes: BCR on 22q11 and ABL1 on 9q34. The joint makes a fusion gene, BCR::ABL1.
The fusion protein is a tyrosine kinase that is always on, and drives the cells to divide.
Imatinib (2001) blocks the kinase: one of the first drugs designed against the product of a specific mutation.

This is a somatic rearrangement in blood stem cells: it is not inherited.

This is the clearest case of a rearrangement whose effect comes from the breakpoint itself rather than from dosage. Neither BCR nor ABL1 alone is the problem; the fusion is a new gene, with the start of BCR (which makes it dimerise) and the kinase domain of ABL1 (which normally is tightly regulated). The modern notation BCR::ABL1 with a double colon means a fusion. Students look up both genes in NCBI Gene in the exercise; note that BCR lies only about 2 Mb from the 22q11.2 deletion region, so 22q11 shows up twice today for two very different reasons. Cancer genetics in Part 7 comes back to fusion genes and oncogenes. Detection: karyotype, FISH with probes for both genes, or RT-PCR for the fusion transcript, which also measures how well treatment works.

title: Rearrangements & aneuploidy
text:
Aneuploidy: nondisjunction
Euploid: whole sets of chromosomes (n, 2n, 3n…). Aneuploid: one or a few chromosomes too many or too few: monosomy (2n − 1), trisomy (2n + 1), nullisomy (2n − 2), tetrasomy (2n + 2).
Most aneuploidy comes from nondisjunction: chromosomes that fail to separate in meiosis.








Error in
What fails to separate
Gametes from that meiosis




Meiosis I
the homologues
2 × n + 1 (one copy from each grandparent), 2 × n − 1


Meiosis II
the sister chromatids in one cell
1 × n + 1 (two identical copies), 1 × n − 1, 2 × n



A trisomic zygote from an MI error has two different homologues from that parent; one from an MII error has two copies of the same homologue (apart from crossovers). DNA markers near the centromere tell which division failed.

Students met nondisjunction with Bridges’ X chromosomes in Drosophila in Part 2; now we use it on autosomes and in humans. Count the gametes on the board, or use the demo on the next slide. The marker logic is how we know that most trisomy 21 is maternal and mostly from meiosis I: genotype the child, the mother and the father at polymorphic markers on chromosome 21. If the child has two maternal alleles that differ at markers near the centromere, the two chromosomes came from different homologues, so meiosis I. Crossing over makes this rule apply to centromere-near markers only, because a crossover can make the two sister chromatids differ further out. Mitotic nondisjunction after fertilisation gives mosaics, with normal and aneuploid cell lines side by side; about 1 to 2 percent of Down syndrome is mosaic.

title: Rearrangements & aneuploidy
section: Try it: nondisjunction in meiosis I and II
text:
Try it: nondisjunction in meiosis I and II




Interactive demo from Part 2 (chromosome theory), here in its nondisjunction mode with two chromosome pairs, labelled 21 and 2; only chromosome 21 nondisjoins. Blue is the homologue this person got from their father, red the one from their mother. Step through with Next. In meiosis I mode, both homologues go to the same pole at anaphase I, and the four gametes are two with both a blue and a red 21 (labelled n + 1 = 3) and two with none (n − 1 = 1). Switch to meiosis II mode and step again: meiosis I is normal, then in one cell the sister chromatids stay together, giving one gamete with two identical copies, one with none and two normal ones. Ask: if this person is a woman and the egg with two 21s is fertilised by a normal sperm, which grandparent’s chromosome 21 does the child carry in each case? Point out that chromosome 2 segregates normally, so each gamete is n + 1 or n − 1 for chromosome 21 only. The demo has no crossing over, which is a simplification.

Human aneuploidies

No autosomal monosomy survives to birth, and of the autosomal trisomies only 13, 18 and 21 (the chromosomes with the fewest genes) do.
About half of first-trimester miscarriages are chromosomally abnormal; trisomy 16 is the most common, and is never born alive.
Sex-chromosome aneuploidies are tolerated because extra X chromosomes are inactivated, and the Y carries few genes.


The frequencies are rounded and vary between studies and with maternal age and prenatal screening; the point is the order of magnitude and the pattern. Gene dosage explains the pattern: chromosome 21 is one of the smallest and most gene-poor, so three copies are survivable; the gene-rich chromosomes are not. Chromosome 16 trisomy, the most common trisomy in miscarriages, shows how often aneuploid embryos form, and how strongly selection removes them; aneuploidy in human eggs is far more frequent than in most other species studied. For the sex chromosomes, X inactivation (Part 6) silences all but one X, so 47,XXY and 47,XXX are mild. Turner syndrome is the only viable monosomy, but even it is mostly lethal before birth: survivors are thought to be often mosaic.

title: Rearrangements & aneuploidy
text:
The maternal age effect

The risk of trisomy 21 is ≈ 1 in 1000 pregnancies for mothers aged 20–29 and ≈ 1 in 47 at 40–44. Monosomy X shows no such rise.

The data are from a Danish nationwide registry of more than half a million pregnancies followed after first-trimester screening, including diagnoses made before birth, so the numbers are higher than live-birth figures (many affected pregnancies end in miscarriage or termination). On a log scale the trisomy 21 curve rises more than twenty-fold from the twenties to the early forties; trisomy 18 rises even more steeply. Monosomy X is flat: most 45,X cases have lost the paternal sex chromosome, so the mother’s age does not matter. Triploidy, mostly from two sperm fertilising one egg, is flat too. The students reproduce this plot in R. Why the mother? About 90 percent of trisomy 21 is maternal in origin, most of it from meiosis I. Human oocytes enter meiosis I before the mother is born and stay arrested in prophase I, with homologues held together by crossovers and cohesin, for up to 50 years. The cohesin is not renewed, so it wears out with age, and the homologues come apart early or go to the same pole. Sperm are made continuously from stem cells, and paternal age has little effect on trisomy.

title: Rearrangements & aneuploidy
text:
Polyploidy
Polyploids have three or more complete sets: triploid (3n), tetraploid (4n) and so on. Rare in animals, common in plants: much of our food is polyploid.








Crop
Ploidy
Origin




Bread wheat
6x = 42 (AABBDD)
allopolyploid: three ancestral species


Cotton, rapeseed
4x
allopolyploid of two species


Potato
4x = 48
autopolyploid: doubled sets of one species


Cultivated strawberry
8x = 56
allopolyploid


Banana (Cavendish), seedless watermelon
3x
sterile triploids, seedless




Autopolyploid: extra sets from the same species. Allopolyploid: sets from two or more species, after hybridisation and chromosome doubling.
Polyploids are often bigger (larger cells), and allopolyploids are fertile because each chromosome has a partner from its own species.


Most flowering plants have a polyploid ancestor somewhere in their history. Bread wheat combines the genomes of three wild grasses, through two rounds of hybridisation and doubling; each of its 21 chromosome types comes in an A, a B and a D version, and they pair only with their exact partner, so meiosis works like a diploid’s. Polyploidy can be induced with colchicine, which blocks the spindle so the chromosomes double without cell division. Seedless watermelons are made by crossing a tetraploid with a diploid: the triploid offspring are sterile, which is the point. In animals, polyploidy is rare, partly because it disturbs sex determination; triploid human conceptions occur in about 1 to 2 percent of pregnancies and miscarry. Farmed triploid oysters are sterile and put their energy into growth rather than spawning.

title: Rearrangements & aneuploidy
text:
Why triploids are sterile
In a triploid, each chromosome has three homologues. At meiosis I, a trivalent sends 2 copies to one pole and 1 to the other, at random.
For each chromosome type, the gamete gets 1 or 2 copies with probability ½ each. With x chromosome types, a gamete is balanced (euploid: all 1 or all 2) with probability
P(\text{balanced}) = 2 \times \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^x




x
P(balanced gamete)




a toy triploid
3
2/8 = 0.25


banana, 2n = 3x = 33
11
2/2048 ≈ 0.001


triploid watermelon, 2n = 3x = 33
11
≈ 0.001



Almost every gamete is aneuploid, so triploids are (nearly) sterile. Bananas are propagated by cuttings.

This is the product rule from Part 1 at work. Each trivalent is an independent event, so the probability that all x chromosome types happen to give one copy is one half to the power x, and the same for all giving two copies; add them. With 11 chromosome types it is about one in a thousand, so seeds almost never form; the black specks in a banana are aborted ovules. The same calculation explains why autotetraploids have reduced fertility, and why allopolyploids, which pair as bivalents, do not. The R exercise checks the formula by simulation with rbinom and replicate. The assumption that the extra copy goes to either pole at random is a simplification; trivalents can also fall apart into a bivalent and an unpaired univalent, which makes things worse rather than better.

title: Rearrangements & aneuploidy
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Deletion / duplication
unbalanced; dosage effects; recurrent ones by NAHR between low-copy repeats (22q11.2, 7q11.23, 17p12)


Pseudodominance
a deletion uncovers a recessive allele on the other homologue: used for deletion mapping


Inversion
balanced; crossover in the loop → dicentric + acentric (paracentric) or dup + def (pericentric); recombinants “suppressed”


Reciprocal translocation
balanced carrier; quadrivalent; only alternate segregation gives balanced gametes; semisterility


Robertsonian translocation
two acrocentrics fuse; carrier has 45 chromosomes; can give translocation Down syndrome


Philadelphia chromosome
t(9;22) in CML; BCR::ABL1 fusion kinase; somatic


Nondisjunction
MI: n + 1 gametes carry both homologues; MII: two copies of one


Trisomy 21
≈ 90% maternal, mostly MI; risk rises steeply with maternal age


Sex-chromosome aneuploidy
45,X; 47,XXY; 47,XYY; 47,XXX; tolerated thanks to X inactivation


Polyploidy
auto- and allopolyploids; triploids sterile: P(balanced) = 2 · (½)x




The revision sheet. The common thread: balanced versus unbalanced. A balanced rearrangement is usually harmless for its carrier, but meiosis turns it into unbalanced gametes, so the problems show up as reduced fertility, miscarriages and affected children. Aneuploidy and polyploidy are the same principle at the level of whole chromosomes and whole sets.

title: Rearrangements & aneuploidy
text:
Where this leads

Next: Bacterial genetics (recap). A very different kind of chromosome: one circle, no meiosis, but genes moved between cells by conjugation, transduction and transformation.
Organelle inheritance. Mitochondria have their own chromosome, inherited only through the egg, and their own kind of dosage: heteroplasmy.
Part 6: Eukaryotic regulation. X inactivation, the dosage compensation that makes sex-chromosome aneuploidy survivable.
Part 7: Cancer genetics. Fusion genes like BCR::ABL1 and the loss of chromosome segments in tumours.
Ethics. Prenatal screening for trisomies raises its own questions.


Point forward. The exercise has pen-and-paper problems on the products of inversion and translocation heterozygotes, nondisjunction, and the triploid formula; the meiosis demo in nondisjunction mode; database tasks on 22q11.2 deletion, Williams syndrome and BCR and ABL1. The R part plots the Danish maternal-age data on a log scale and simulates the gametes of a translocation carrier and a triploid.

title: Prokaryotic regulation (recap)
text:
About this lecture
Recap from 5MO103. You have met the lac operon in Microbiology and basic molecular biology: a repressor, an operator, three genes, and lactose as the switch. Today we look at it as geneticists. Jacob and Monod worked out the model in 1961 from mutants, before anyone had purified the repressor or sequenced the operator.

The mutant classes: constitutive (I−, Oc) and uninducible (Is).
Merodiploids (partial diploids made with an F′ plasmid) to test dominance.
Cis vs trans: a mutation that acts in trans changes a diffusible product (a protein); one that acts only in cis changes a site on the DNA.
Complementation between lacZ− and lacY−.
Briefly: attenuation of the trp operon.

Book: Hartwell, Genetics: From Genes to Genomes, the chapter on gene regulation in prokaryotes.

This is a recap unit, so keep it light on mechanism and heavy on reasoning. Students know the cartoon. What is new is the logic: how do you deduce from phenotypes alone that lacI makes a diffusible protein while lacO is a stretch of DNA? The tools are the same ones they used in Part 1 and Part 3: dominance (Extensions to Mendel), and the complementation test (Mutation unit). The F′ plasmid comes from the Bacterial genetics recap in Part 5. We simplify throughout: no CAP and cAMP, no leaky basal expression, and the inducer is IPTG, which works without permease or beta-galactosidase.

title: Prokaryotic regulation (recap)
section: The lac operon in one picture
text:
The lac operon in one picture


lacZ (β-galactosidase), lacY (permease) and lacA are transcribed together, as one mRNA, from one promoter (P).
The repressor (LacI) is made all the time from its own gene. It binds the operator (O) and blocks transcription.
The inducer (allolactose, made from lactose; or IPTG in the lab) binds the repressor, which then lets go of O.


Quick recap only, two minutes. The operon idea: several genes, one promoter, one mRNA, one switch. The repressor is an allosteric protein: one site binds DNA, another binds the inducer, and binding the inducer changes the shape so that the DNA-binding site no longer fits the operator. We ignore CAP-cAMP (catabolite repression, glucose) today; it adds a second, positive switch on top. In the lab, Jacob and Monod used gratuitous inducers like TMG and later IPTG: they induce but are not broken down, so the lacZ genotype does not affect how much inducer there is. We assume that throughout the exercise and demo.

title: Prokaryotic regulation (recap)
section: Jacob & Monod: hunting for regulatory mutants
text:
Jacob & Monod: hunting for regulatory mutants
Screen E. coli on indicator plates (e.g. X-gal, which turns blue when β-galactosidase cuts it), with and without inducer. Two odd kinds of mutants stood out:








Phenotype
What it means
Mutations found




Constitutive
enzymes made with or without inducer
lacI− (no working repressor); lacOc (operator that repressor cannot bind)


Uninducible
enzymes never made, although lacZ and lacY are intact
lacIs (“super-repressor”: cannot bind inducer)


Structural
one enzyme missing, regulation normal
lacZ−, lacY−



Both lacI− and lacOc give the same phenotype in a haploid cell. How can you tell them apart? You need a second copy of the operon in the same cell.

The genetic approach: find mutants with an interesting phenotype first, then ask what kind of thing is broken. Constitutive mutants were the clue that something actively keeps the genes off. Note that in a haploid, I minus and O c look identical: both are constitutive. Mapping showed them at slightly different positions, next to each other, which is not enough to say what they are. The decisive experiment is dominance in a partial diploid. The super-repressor I s was found a few years later (1964); it is an uninducible mutant that maps in lacI, not in lacZ or lacY.

title: Prokaryotic regulation (recap)
section: Merodiploids: a second copy on an F′
text:
Merodiploids: a second copy on an F′
An F′ plasmid is an F factor that has picked up a piece of the chromosome (here the lac region). Transfer it by conjugation into a recipient, and the cell has two copies of the lac genes: a partial diploid, or merodiploid.

Notation: F′ genotype / chromosome genotype, e.g. F′ I+ / I−.
Now you can ask the questions from Part 1 and Part 3:

Dominance: in I+/I−, which phenotype wins? (Extensions to Mendel)
Complementation: do two mutations on different copies restore the wild type? (Mutation unit)
Cis vs trans: does the mutation affect only the genes on its own DNA molecule, or both copies?



This is the same trick as in diploid organisms: put two alleles in one cell and see what happens. Bacteria are normally haploid, so Jacob and Monod used F-prime plasmids (from the Bacterial genetics recap in Part 5) to make them partially diploid for the lac region. “Cis” means on the same DNA molecule; “trans” means on the other molecule. The key insight is this: a product that diffuses through the cell, like a protein, can act on both copies, so it acts in trans. A site on the DNA can only affect what is physically next to it, so it acts only in cis.

title: Prokaryotic regulation (recap)
section: Cis vs trans: the two decisive merodiploids
text:
Cis vs trans: the two decisive merodiploids


A. F′ I+ / I− is inducible: I+ is dominant and works on both copies. The lacI product diffuses: it is a protein.
B. F′ O+ Z+ / Oc Z− is inducible for β-gal: the Oc mutation only affects the lacZ next to it. lacO is a DNA site.


Walk through panel A. The chromosome makes no repressor, but the F-prime does, and that repressor reaches the operator on the chromosome as well. So I+ is dominant over I-, just as a working enzyme allele is usually dominant over a null allele (Extensions to Mendel: haplosufficiency). Panel B is the cleverer one. The Oc copy is always on, but it carries Z minus, so it makes only inactive beta-galactosidase. The F-prime copy has a normal operator and Z plus, and is properly repressed. So active beta-gal is made only with inducer. Oc did not help the lacZ+ gene on the other molecule: it acts only in cis. Put the other way round, F-prime O+ Z minus over Oc Z plus is constitutive: the working lacZ sits next to the broken operator. That pair of experiments is the cis-trans test.

title: Prokaryotic regulation (recap)
section: The super-repressor Is and the full logic
text:
The super-repressor Is and the full logic
Is makes a repressor that binds the operator but not the inducer. In F′ I+ / Is, the Is repressor sits on both operators: Is is dominant, in trans. Only an Oc in cis can escape it.









Strain (F′ / chromosome)
β-gal
permease
Conclusion

inducible
inducible
wild type


I− (haploid)
constitutive
constitutive
repressor needed to turn genes off


F′ I+ / I−
inducible

I+ dominant, acts in trans


F′ I+ / Is
none
none
Is dominant, acts in trans


F′ I+ Oc / Is O+

F′ Z+ Y− / Z− Y+
inducible
