Rule: a mutation that is dominant in trans changes a diffusible product; one that acts only in cis changes a DNA site.

I s is a dominant gain-of-function allele in the sense of Extensions to Mendel: the mutant repressor has lost the ability to respond, and it wins over the normal one because it keeps the operators blocked. Read the table row by row and ask the class to predict before revealing. The permease column in the Oc Z minus row: the chromosome copy is Oc and Y+, so permease is made all the time. This is exactly the table the R exercise rebuilds from a single function. A side note for the curious: some lacI mutations (I minus d) are dominant negative: the repressor is a tetramer, and poisoned subunits ruin mixed tetramers. That is the same idea as dominant-negative collagen mutations in Extensions to Mendel.

title: Prokaryotic regulation (recap)
text:
Try it: lac merodiploids




Interactive demo. It opens on F-prime O+ Z+ over Oc Z minus, without lactose: the F-prime copy is repressed, the chromosome copy is transcribed but has Z minus, so no active beta-gal; permease is made from the chromosome. Click “+ lactose”: now beta-gal comes from the F-prime. Phenotype: beta-gal inducible, permease constitutive. Then try the presets in order: I minus (constitutive), F-prime I+ over I minus (inducible again: trans), I s (nothing), F-prime I+ over I s (still nothing: I s is trans-dominant), and finally put Oc on the F-prime in the I s cell to show that a cis-acting operator escapes even the super-repressor. Ask the class to predict before each click.

title: Prokaryotic regulation (recap)
text:
Complementation in the operon
F′ Z+ Y− / Z− Y+: each copy makes the protein the other cannot. The cell has both enzymes, inducibly. So lacZ and lacY are different genes, even though they share one promoter and one mRNA.

This is the complementation test from the Mutation unit (Part 3), done in a bacterium.
Benzer called the unit defined by the cis–trans test a cistron. In modern words: a gene that encodes one polypeptide.
Caveat: polarity. A nonsense mutation early in lacZ also lowers lacY expression from that copy (transcription and translation are coupled in bacteria). Such polar mutations can fail to complement lacY− although the lacY gene itself is fine.


Link back to the complementation grid in the Mutation unit. Two recessive loss-of-function mutations complement when they are in different genes, because each copy supplies the missing product. Here the twist is that two genes share one transcription unit, and the test still separates them. Polarity is the classic complication: in bacteria, if ribosomes fall off the mRNA at an early stop codon, the downstream part of the mRNA is left bare and is degraded or terminated (Rho), so the downstream genes are also expressed poorly. Students only need to know that polarity exists and why it can fool a complementation test. That is why Jacob and Monod were careful to use missense alleles.

title: Prokaryotic regulation (recap)
section: A second way to switch: trp attenuation
text:
A second way to switch: trp attenuation

The trp operon (tryptophan synthesis) has a repressor too (TrpR, active with tryptophan). On top of that, the leader mRNA senses tryptophan through translation of a short leader peptide with two Trp codons. Deletions of the attenuator region raise trp expression even with the repressor working: another cis-acting site.

Keep this to one slide. The trp operon makes the enzymes for tryptophan synthesis, so it is on when tryptophan is scarce: a repressible rather than an inducible system. The repressor TrpR needs tryptophan as a corepressor. Attenuation is the second, finer control. Transcription and translation are coupled, so the position of the ribosome on the leader decides which hairpin forms in the RNA that RNA polymerase has just made. With lots of tryptophan, the ribosome zips through region 1, covers region 2, and the 3:4 terminator forms. With little tryptophan the ribosome stalls on the Trp codons in region 1, region 2 pairs with 3, and the terminator cannot form. Genetically, attenuator deletions act in cis, like Oc. Only bacteria can do this, because eukaryotes separate transcription (nucleus) from translation (cytoplasm).

title: Prokaryotic regulation (recap)
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Operon
several genes, one promoter, one mRNA; lacZ, lacY, lacA


Negative control
LacI repressor binds lacO; inducer releases it


Constitutive mutants
I− (no repressor), Oc (operator cannot bind repressor)


Uninducible mutant
Is (repressor cannot bind inducer)


Merodiploid
F′ / chromosome; a partial diploid to test dominance


Trans-acting
I+ over I−, and Is over I+: the gene makes a diffusible protein


Cis-acting
Oc affects only genes on its own DNA molecule: a DNA site


Complementation
Z− and Y− on different copies give both enzymes (watch out for polarity)


Attenuation
trp leader hairpins; ribosome stalling on Trp codons decides termination




The one sentence to take away: dominance tells you which allele wins, and cis versus trans tells you whether the gene acts through a product that moves or through a place on the DNA. That logic carries straight over to eukaryotes, where enhancers are cis-acting sites and transcription factors are trans-acting proteins.

title: Prokaryotic regulation (recap)
text:
Where this leads

Next: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics. Enhancers and promoters are cis-acting elements, and transcription factors are trans-acting proteins, the same logic as lacO and lacI. Chromatin adds a layer that bacteria do not have.
RNA-mediated regulation. Small RNAs that turn genes down after transcription, discovered, like the lac mutants, through a genetic screen.
Development & model organisms. Mutant screens like Jacob and Monod’s, scaled up to find the genes that build an embryo.


Point forward. In the exercise students predict merodiploid phenotypes by hand, then check their answers in the demo, and look up lacZ and lacI in NCBI Gene to see that lacI lies right next to the operon it controls but has its own promoter. In R they write the whole Jacob-Monod logic as one function and run it over every possible merodiploid with expand_grid.

Before you start
This page builds on the by-hand part of the Exercise, so do that first. You need the packages readr, dplyr, tidyr, stringr and purrr. Download jacob_monod_table.csv and save it in a data/ folder of your R project. It lists the expected phenotypes of eleven classic strains; the course team typed them in from the textbook summaries of Jacob and Monod’s work, so they are qualitative results, not measurements.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(purrr)

title: Exercise in R: Prokaryotic regulation (recap)
text:
Tasks
New idiom today: expand_grid() from tidyr. It makes a tibble with one row for every combination of the vectors you give it, like writing out every cell of a Punnett square. expand_grid(x = 1:2, y = c("a", "b")) gives four rows: 1 a, 1 b, 2 a, 2 b.
We write a genotype as a string such as "I+ O+ Z+ Y+", with - for loss of function, s for the super-repressor and c for the constitutive operator. An F′ genotype uses the same format, or "none" for a haploid. str_match() pulls out the character after a gene letter: str_match("I+ Oc Z- Y+", "O(.)")[, 2] is "c".
R1. (the rules as a function) Complete lac_expression(chrom, fprime, lactose). It returns a named logical vector: is active β-galactosidase made, and is permease made? Follow the three steps from the Background of the exercise: which repressor is in the cell, which operators are free, and what each transcribed copy makes.
lac_expression <- function(chrom, fprime, lactose) {
  copies <- if (fprime == "none") chrom else c(chrom, fprime)
  I <- str_match(copies, "I(.)")[, 2]   # one value per copy: "+", "-" or "s"
  O <- str_match(copies, "O(.)")[, 2]
  Z <- str_match(copies, "Z(.)")[, 2]
  Y <- str_match(copies, "Y(.)")[, 2]
  # step 1: are normal operators blocked? (TRUE/FALSE)
  repressed <- ...
  # step 2: which copies are transcribed?
  on <- ...
  # step 3: what do the transcribed copies make?
  c(bgal = any(on & Z == "+"), permease = any(on & Y == "+"))
}

lac_expression("I+ O+ Z+ Y+", "none", lactose = FALSE)
lac_expression("I+ O+ Z+ Y+", "none", lactose = TRUE)
lac_expression("I- O+ Z+ Y+", "I+ O+ Z+ Y+", lactose = FALSE)
R2. (phenotype) Write phenotype(chrom, fprime, enzyme), which calls lac_expression() without and with lactose and returns "inducible", "constitutive" or "none" for one enzyme ("bgal" or "permease"). Test it on Oc and on F′ I+ / Is.
R3. (every strain) Use expand_grid() to build all single copies: three lacI alleles × two lacO × two lacZ × two lacY. Paste each row into a genotype string. Then use expand_grid() again to pair every chromosome with every F′ (including "none"). Add the two phenotypes with map2_chr(), which works like map_chr() but walks along two vectors at once. How many strains are there? How many are inducible for β-gal?
copies <- expand_grid(I = c("+", "-", "s"), O = c("+", "c"), Z = c("+", "-"), Y = c("+", "-")) |>
  mutate(genotype = paste0("I", I, " O", O, " Z", Z, " Y", Y))

all_cells <- expand_grid(chrom = copies$genotype, fprime = c("none", copies$genotype)) |>
  mutate(bgal     = map2_chr(chrom, fprime, \(c, f) phenotype(c, f, "bgal")),
         permease = map2_chr(chrom, fprime, \(c, f) phenotype(c, f, "permease")))
R4. (check against Jacob and Monod) Read data/jacob_monod_table.csv. Join your model’s predictions onto it with left_join() by chrom and fprime, and add a column agree that is TRUE when both enzymes match. Does your function reproduce every classic result?
R5. (looking for cis action) Use filter() on all_cells to list merodiploids whose chromosome carries Oc but whose β-galactosidase is nevertheless inducible. What do these strains have in common, and what do they show about lacO? Then count the haploid phenotype combinations: how many of the 24 haploids are both β-gal-none and permease-none, and why?

title: Exercise in R: Prokaryotic regulation (recap)
text:
Solutions






Solutions: In R





R1. Any Is repressor blocks every normal operator, whatever the inducer. Otherwise normal repressor blocks normal operators only without inducer. With no working repressor at all, nothing is blocked. An Oc copy is transcribed whatever happens.
lac_expression <- function(chrom, fprime, lactose) {
  copies <- if (fprime == "none") chrom else c(chrom, fprime)
  I <- str_match(copies, "I(.)")[, 2]
  O <- str_match(copies, "O(.)")[, 2]
  Z <- str_match(copies, "Z(.)")[, 2]
  Y <- str_match(copies, "Y(.)")[, 2]
  repressed <- if (any(I == "s")) TRUE else if (any(I == "+")) !lactose else FALSE
  on <- O == "c" | !repressed
  c(bgal = any(on & Z == "+"), permease = any(on & Y == "+"))
}
lac_expression("I+ O+ Z+ Y+", "none", lactose = FALSE)
    bgal permease
   FALSE    FALSE
lac_expression("I+ O+ Z+ Y+", "none", lactose = TRUE)
    bgal permease
    TRUE     TRUE
lac_expression("I- O+ Z+ Y+", "I+ O+ Z+ Y+", lactose = FALSE)
    bgal permease
   FALSE    FALSE
The last one is F′ I+ / I− without lactose: repressed, because the F′ repressor works in trans.
R2.
phenotype <- function(chrom, fprime, enzyme) {
  off <- lac_expression(chrom, fprime, lactose = FALSE)[[enzyme]]
  on  <- lac_expression(chrom, fprime, lactose = TRUE)[[enzyme]]
  if (off) "constitutive" else if (on) "inducible" else "none"
}
phenotype("I+ Oc Z+ Y+", "none", "bgal")
[1] "constitutive"
phenotype("Is O+ Z+ Y+", "I+ O+ Z+ Y+", "bgal")
[1] "none"

title: Exercise in R: Prokaryotic regulation (recap)
text:
Where this leads
expand_grid() comes back whenever you need every combination of a few factors. In Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics you reshape a GTEx expression table with pivot_longer() and summarise it by tissue and sex with group_by() and summarise().

title: Probability & the χ² test
text:
About this lecture
Mendel’s laws predict ratios, such as 3:1 or 9:3:3:1. Real crosses give counts, such as 5474 round and 1850 wrinkled seeds. Today we connect the two.

Probability rules: the product rule (AND), the sum rule (OR) and conditional probability (“given that …”).
Families: the chance that 2 of 4 children are affected (the binomial), and “at least one”.
Testing a ratio: why observed counts never match the expected ones exactly, and the χ² goodness-of-fit test, which tells us whether the gap is bigger than chance would give.
p-values: what they mean, what “fail to reject” means, and Fisher’s claim that Mendel’s data fit too well.

Book: Hartwell, Mendel’s principles chapter (the sections on probability and on the chi-square test).

Set the scene: last lecture gave the laws of segregation and independent assortment and the ratios they predict. Today is about the bridge between a predicted ratio and a real pile of seeds or children. Two halves. First, probability rules, which they met at upper-secondary school: we recap them with genetics examples and add two new tools, conditional probability and the binomial. Second, the chi-square test, which most of them have only heard of by name. We build it from scratch, with Mendel’s own numbers. Reassure them that the maths stays at fractions and squaring. The one formula to take away is the sum of (O minus E) squared over E.

title: Probability & the χ² test
section: A cross is a random experiment
text:
A cross is a random experiment
Each child (or seed) of Aa × Aa is a fresh, independent draw:

each parent passes on A or a with probability ½ each (segregation);
the egg and the sperm are chosen independently of each other;
one child’s genotype says nothing about the next child’s genotype.

So a Punnett square is a probability table: each cell is one equally likely outcome. “3:1” means P(dominant phenotype) = ¾ for each offspring. It is not a promise that exactly 3 out of every 4 will be dominant.
Two rules let us combine these probabilities, and we use them all through the course: in pedigrees, in mapping and in population genetics.

Recap from upper-secondary school and from the Mendel lecture. The key reframe is that a ratio is a probability per offspring, not a quota for a family. Students often believe that if the first three children are unaffected the fourth “must” be affected. Kill this now: each child is an independent draw, and the coin has no memory. Mention that this simple model assumes complete dominance, no lethality and fair segregation. The Extensions to Mendel unit relaxes these assumptions.

title: Probability & the χ² test
text:
Product rule and sum rule


Product rule: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B), if A and B are independent.
Sum rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B), if A and B are mutually exclusive (cannot both happen).


Walk through the square. Each cell is “this egg AND this sperm”: the two gametes are independent, so we multiply, half times half is a quarter. The dominant phenotype is “AA OR Aa OR aA”: these cells are mutually exclusive (a child has one genotype), so we add, giving three quarters. Point out the two conditions: multiply only for independent events, add only for events that cannot happen together. A common error is to add probabilities of events that overlap. Note also that all cells sum to 1, which is a free check on any calculation.

title: Probability & the χ² test
section: Using both rules: a dihybrid cross
text:
Using both rules: a dihybrid cross
AaBb × AaBb, with the two genes on different chromosomes (independent assortment):

P(aabb) = P(aa) × P(bb) = ¼ × ¼ = 1/16
P(A_B_) = P(A_) × P(B_) = ¾ × ¾ = 9/16
P(A_bb or aaB_) = 3/16 + 3/16 = 6/16

This works for any number of genes. For AaBbCc × AaBbCc:
P(aabbcc) = \tfrac14 \times \tfrac14 \times \tfrac14 = \tfrac{1}{64}
No 64-cell Punnett square is needed. Split the cross into one gene at a time, then multiply.

This is the payoff of the product rule: the forked-line or “one gene at a time” method. Independent assortment is exactly the statement that the genes are independent events, so their probabilities multiply. Do the trihybrid on the board to show how much faster it is than a Punnett square. Warn: this only holds for unlinked genes. Linked genes break independence, and that is the Linkage unit. The 9/16 and 1/16 are the 9 and 1 of 9:3:3:1, which we test with chi-square later today.

title: Probability & the χ² test
text:
Conditional probability: “given that …”
Two Aa carriers have a child who is unaffected. What is the chance that this child is a carrier?

Knowing something shrinks the table. We only count the outcomes that are still possible:
P(\text{carrier} \mid \text{unaffected}) = \frac{P(\text{carrier and unaffected})}{P(\text{unaffected})} = \frac{1/2}{3/4} = \frac23

This is the single most-used calculation in pedigree risk, and the classic exam trap: students answer one half, which is the carrier probability before we knew the phenotype. Once we know the child is unaffected, the aa cell is impossible, so we renormalise over the three remaining equally likely cells, two of which are carriers. Read the vertical bar as “given”. The formula is just the picture written down: the share of the remaining area that is carrier. Preview: in the Pedigrees unit we chain this, for example the probability that two unaffected siblings of affected children have an affected child is 2/3 times 2/3 times 1/4.

title: Probability & the χ² test
section: Families: how many children are affected?
text:
Families: how many children are affected?
Aa × Aa, four children. Each child is affected (aa) with p = ¼. What is P(exactly 2 affected)?

P(k \text{ of } n) = \binom{n}{k}\, p^k\, (1-p)^{n-k}, \qquad \binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!} \text{ ("$n$ choose $k$")}

Build the binomial from the two rules. One particular birth order, such as affected, affected, unaffected, unaffected, has probability a quarter times a quarter times three quarters times three quarters by the product rule. There are 6 such orders, which are mutually exclusive, so by the sum rule we multiply by 6. The 6 is “4 choose 2”: the number of ways to pick which 2 of the 4 children are the affected ones. Count them on the slide. Only then show the general formula, and say that n choose k is just that count. For small n they can list the orders by hand. Point out the bar chart: the most likely family has 1 affected child, not “exactly one quarter of 4”. Bars sum to 1.

title: Probability & the χ² test
text:
“At least one”: use the complement
P(at least one of 4 children affected) has many cases (1, 2, 3 or 4). The opposite event has only one case:
P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - P(\text{none}) = 1 - \left(\tfrac34\right)^4 = 1 - \tfrac{81}{256} \approx 0.68

“None affected” means every child is unaffected, so by the product rule it is (¾)⁴.
Not 4 × ¼ = 1, which would make an affected child certain. Adding is wrong here, because “child 1 affected” and “child 2 affected” can both happen.


The complement trick is a standard move. The wrong answer, 4 times a quarter equals 1, is worth showing because many students produce it: it adds events that are not mutually exclusive, which breaks the sum rule’s condition. With 5 children the naive sum would exceed 1, which is an obvious absurdity. Check against the bar chart on the previous slide: 1 minus 0.316 is 0.684.

title: Probability & the χ² test
section: Real counts deviate from the ratio
text:
Real counts deviate from the ratio

Every dot is a family simulated with the 3:1 rule exactly true. With 20 seeds the fraction ranges from 0.50 to 0.90. With 2000 seeds it stays close to 0.75.

Deviation from the expected ratio is normal. It is sampling variation, or chance.
Small samples deviate a lot (in proportion); large samples deviate little.
The question is never “does it match exactly?” but “is the deviation larger than chance would usually produce?”


This is the motivation for a statistical test. Everything here obeys 3:1 perfectly, and yet a family of 20 can come out 10 to 10, which looks like 1:1. So we cannot judge by eye. We need a yardstick for how big a deviation chance produces, and that yardstick depends on sample size. The chi-square test is that yardstick. Note the data were simulated in R with rbinom and a fixed seed; students simulate the same thing in the exercise.

title: Probability & the χ² test
text:
The χ² statistic
Turn “how far is observed (O) from expected (E)?” into one number:
\chi^2 = \sum_{\text{classes}} \frac{(O - E)^2}{E}
Mendel’s F2 seeds: 5474 round, 1850 wrinkled, total N = 7324. H0: 3:1.

χ² = 0.263




Square, so that positive and negative deviations do not cancel.
Divide by E, so that a deviation of 19 counts for more when only 1831 were expected than when 5493 were.


Do this slowly on the board. Expected counts come from the total times the hypothesised proportion, never from the ratio numbers themselves. The deviations always sum to zero, which is a useful check. Why square: otherwise plus and minus cancel. Why divide by E: a deviation of 19 is small relative to 5493 and relatively larger relative to 1831. Under the null hypothesis the counts vary by roughly the square root of E, so dividing the squared deviation by E puts every class on the same scale. A chi-square of 0 is a perfect fit; bigger means a worse fit. Now we need to know what values chance alone produces.

title: Probability & the χ² test
text:
Degrees of freedom
The degrees of freedom (df) count how many classes are free to vary once the total is fixed.

2 classes (round, wrinkled): once N and the round count are known, the wrinkled count is fixed. df = 1.
k classes, with the ratio given in advance: df = k − 1.

More classes give more terms in the sum, so χ² tends to be bigger by chance alone. The df tells us which reference curve to use.

Keep df concrete: it is the number of independent counts. With k classes and a fixed total, k minus 1 of them determine the last. That is the rule for a goodness-of-fit test against a ratio given in advance, which is every test today. Mention briefly that if you estimate a parameter from the data, as in the Hardy-Weinberg test, you lose another degree of freedom; that comes in the Hardy-Weinberg unit. The average value of chi-square under the null hypothesis is equal to df, which is a nice anchor: chi-square of 0.26 on 1 df is below average.

title: Probability & the χ² test
text:
The χ² distribution

If H0 is true, repeating the experiment many times gives χ² values that follow this curve. Most are small; large values are rare.

The curve is what chance alone produces when the hypothesis is true and the counts are large enough. The df = 1 curve is piled up near zero; with more df the bulk moves right, and its average equals df. The dashed lines cut off the top 5% of each curve. A chi-square beyond that line would happen less than 1 time in 20 if H0 were true. In the exercise they simulate 10 000 F2 samples under 3:1 and see their histogram trace exactly the df = 1 curve. That is the honest meaning of this curve.

title: Probability & the χ² test
text:
The p-value
p-value = P(χ² at least as large as the observed one, if H0 is true) = the area of the tail to the right of the observed χ².

Rule: if χ² > the 5% critical value (p < 0.05), reject H0: the deviation is too big to blame on chance.
Mendel’s seeds: χ² = 0.263 < 3.84, so p > 0.05 (exactly, p = 0.61). The data are consistent with 3:1.


Define the p-value in words before showing any number: assuming the hypothesis is true, how often would chance give a fit this bad or worse? A small p-value means “rarely”, so we doubt the hypothesis. The table is how this was done before computers, and it is still how they will do it in an exam: compare the statistic with the critical value for the right df. Read the table: going right gives stricter thresholds; going down, more df need a bigger chi-square. For Mendel’s seeds, a p of 0.61 means that 61% of honest 3:1 experiments with 7324 seeds would deviate at least this much. Stress that 0.05 is a convention, not a law of nature.

title: Probability & the χ² test
text:
“Fail to reject” is not “proven”

p < 0.05: the data are unlikely under H0. We reject H0. (We may still be wrong in 1 in 20 tests of a true H0.)
p ≥ 0.05: we fail to reject H0. The data are consistent with H0, but this does not prove it.

Other ratios may fit too: 5474:1850 is also consistent with 2.95:1.
Small samples can rarely reject anything. 6:4 seeds gives χ² = 1.2 against 3:1 (p = 0.27).

A p-value is not the probability that H0 is true.


This is the conceptual heart of the second half. Hypothesis tests are asymmetric: they can give evidence against a hypothesis, but a non-significant result is an absence of evidence, not proof. Use the 6:4 example: with 10 seeds even a ratio that looks like 1.5:1 cannot be told apart from 3:1. Mention the two errors in plain words: rejecting a true hypothesis (which happens 5% of the time by design) and failing to reject a false one (common in small samples). The last bullet is the most common misreading of p-values in published papers too.

title: Probability & the χ² test
text:
Two rules for using χ²
1. Use counts, never percentages or proportions.
60% vs 40% against 3:1:

The same proportions are much stronger evidence when N is large. A percentage throws N away.
2. Every expected count should be at least 5. Otherwise the χ² curve is a poor approximation. Pool classes, collect more data, or use an exact test.

Two practical rules, both frequent exam and lab-report errors. Percentages: chi-square scales with N, because the same proportional deviation is far more convincing with more data. Feeding percentages in silently pretends N is 100. Expected counts of at least 5: the smooth chi-square curve is an approximation to a discrete reality. With tiny expected counts the approximation fails, and R warns “Chi-squared approximation may be incorrect”. In the demo, try N = 20 with 9:3:3:1: the aabb class expects 1.25, and the demo shows a warning.

text:
Try it: χ² goodness of fit




Live demo. Start at 3:1 with N = 100, where the counts sit exactly on the expected 75:25, so chi-square is 0 and p is 1. Drag the aa bar up slowly: watch the contributions, chi-square and the tail area. Ask the room to predict the count at which p drops below 0.05. With 75 A_ it happens at 37 aa (75:37 gives p = 0.0495), which surprises most people: 75:37 is about 2:1. Press “simulate under H0” a few times: these are honest 3:1 samples, and they still wobble. Then “simulate 1000×”: the grey histogram follows the df = 1 curve, and the fraction of simulations beyond the observed value is the p-value, estimated by brute force. Switch to 9:3:3:1 and N = 20 to show the expected-count warning, and to N = 7324 to show how tightly large samples sit on the ratio.

title: Probability & the χ² test
section: Fisher: Mendel’s data fit too well
text:
Fisher: Mendel’s data fit too well


In 1936 R. A. Fisher added up χ² over many of Mendel’s experiments. The total was smaller than chance would usually allow.
With honest sampling, p-values are spread evenly between 0 and 1. A whole series of p-values close to 1 is itself suspicious.
Here: the 7 monohybrid experiments give a total of 2.14 on 7 df. A fit this close happens only about 1 time in 20.

Possible explanations include unconscious bias in classifying ambiguous seeds, selective reporting, or an assistant “helping”. The debate continues; you will look up a modern analysis in the exercise.

A lovely twist that shows the test cutting both ways. Under a true hypothesis, chi-square should average about df. Mendel’s seven experiments sum to 2.14 when we expect about 7. Fisher’s full analysis over all of Mendel’s experiments gave an even more extreme left-tail probability. Present this fairly: nobody doubts Mendel’s laws, which have been confirmed countless times; the question is how the published numbers came about. Explanations range from honest misclassification of borderline phenotypes, to stopping counting when the ratio looked right, to deliberate tidying. In the exercise students find a modern reanalysis in PubMed and estimate the left-tail probability by simulation in R.

title: Probability & the χ² test
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Product rule
independent events, AND: multiply


Sum rule
mutually exclusive events, OR: add


Conditional
P(B given C): count only the outcomes still possible. P(carrier | unaffected, Aa × Aa) = 2/3


Binomial
P(k of n) = (n choose k) pᵏ (1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ


At least one
1 − P(none)


χ²
Σ (O − E)²/E, with E = N × expected proportion


df
k − 1 for k classes and a ratio given in advance


p-value
P(χ² this large or larger, if H0 is true). p < 0.05: reject H0


Fail to reject
consistent with H0, not proof of it


Rules
counts not percentages; all E ≥ 5


Too good
χ² far below df, repeatedly, is suspicious too




Revision sheet. Recite the chi-square recipe once more: state H0 as a ratio, compute expected counts from the total, sum (O minus E) squared over E, find df as classes minus one, compare with the critical value or compute the p-value, and conclude in words about the biology. The words matter: “consistent with 3:1”, never “proves 3:1”.

title: Probability & the χ² test
text:
Where this leads

Extensions to Mendel: modified ratios such as 9:7 and 12:3:1. You use χ² to decide which ratio fits.
Pedigrees: conditional probability and the product rule give carrier and disease risks in families.
Linkage: a χ² test against 1:1:1:1 is the first test for whether two genes are linked.
Hardy–Weinberg: χ² again, with one df lost because the allele frequency is estimated from the data.
In R (this unit’s exercise): chisq.test, pchisq, dbinom, and simulation with replicate().


Chi-square is the workhorse statistic of transmission genetics, and it returns in nearly every unit of Part 1 and Part 2. Point out the new R idiom, simulation under the null hypothesis with replicate, because it is a general way to get a p-value for any statistic, even when no textbook curve exists. That idea comes back in drift simulations and in the Hardy-Weinberg unit.

title: Exercise in R: probability & the χ² test
text:
Before you start
This page builds on the by-hand part of the Exercise, so do that first. You need the packages ggplot2, readr and dplyr. Download mendel_monohybrid.csv and save it in a data/ folder of your R project.

title: Exercise in R: probability & the χ² test
text:
Tasks
R1–R3 check your hand calculations. R4–R6 introduce this unit’s new idiom: simulation under the null hypothesis with replicate(). replicate(n, expr) evaluates the expression expr n times and collects the results in a vector. If the expression contains random draws, every evaluation is a new random experiment. This lets you see the distribution of any statistic under H0, without a formula.

R1. chisq.test on Mendel’s data
chisq.test(x, p = ...) tests the counts in x against the proportions in p, which must sum to 1.
obs <- c(round = 5474, wrinkled = 1850)
chisq.test(obs, p = c(3, 1) / 4)

dihybrid <- c(round_yellow = 315, round_green = 108,
              wrinkled_yellow = 101, wrinkled_green = 32)
chisq.test(dihybrid, p = c(9, 3, 3, 1) / 16)
Check the χ² values and df against the lecture. Then use chisq.test to check your answers to B6–B9 in the exercise.


R2. χ² by hand, then the p-value with pchisq
pchisq(q, df) gives the area to the left of q under the χ² curve. The p-value is the area to the right, so use lower.tail = FALSE. qchisq goes the other way and gives critical values.
N    <- sum(obs)
expd <- N * c(3, 1) / 4
expd
chi2 <- sum((obs - expd)^2 / expd)
chi2
pchisq(chi2, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
qchisq(0.95, df = 1:4)
Confirm that chi2 and the p-value match chisq.test, and that qchisq reproduces the 5% row of the table in the Background of the exercise.


R3. Family composition with dbinom and pbinom
dbinom(k, size, prob) is P(exactly k), and pbinom(k, size, prob) is P(at most k).
dbinom(2, size = 4, prob = 1/4)        # exactly 2 of 4 affected
dbinom(0:4, size = 4, prob = 1/4)      # the whole distribution
1 - dbinom(0, size = 4, prob = 1/4)    # at least one of 4
pbinom(1, size = 4, prob = 1/4)        # at most one of 4
Then answer: two carriers have 5 children. What is the probability that at least 2 are affected? Check B4 in the exercise with dbinom as well.


R4. Simulate 10 000 F2 samples under 3:1
First write a small function that computes χ² from counts and proportions. Then write a function that simulates one F2 of 7324 seeds under H0 with sample() and returns its χ². Finally, replicate() it 10 000 times.
library(ggplot2)

chisq_stat <- function(obs, p) {
  expd <- sum(obs) * p
  sum((obs - expd)^2 / expd)
}
chisq_stat(c(5474, 1850), c(3, 1) / 4)

one_f2 <- function(N = 7324) {
  seeds <- sample(c("round", "wrinkled"), N, replace = TRUE, prob = c(3, 1) / 4)
  obs   <- table(factor(seeds, levels = c("round", "wrinkled")))
  chisq_stat(obs, c(3, 1) / 4)
}

set.seed(1866)
sims <- replicate(10000, one_f2())
length(sims)
summary(sims)
mean(sims >= 3.84)
The factor(..., levels = ...) makes sure that table() always reports both classes, even in the (unlikely) case that one is missing.
Now plot the simulated values as a histogram, on the density scale, with the χ² curve for df = 1 (dchisq) on top:
sim_df   <- data.frame(chi2 = sims)
curve_df <- data.frame(x = seq(0.02, 8, by = 0.02))
curve_df$density <- dchisq(curve_df$x, df = 1)

ggplot(sim_df, aes(x = chi2)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 0.25, boundary = 0,
                 fill = "grey75", colour = "white") +
  geom_line(data = curve_df, aes(x = x, y = density), colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.263, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 8), ylim = c(0, 1.5)) +
  labs(x = "chi-squared statistic", y = "density",
       title = "10 000 simulated F2 samples of 7324 seeds under 3:1")
Does the curve describe the simulations? What fraction of the simulated χ² values are ≥ 3.84, and why is that the number you would expect?


R5. How often is χ² at least as small as Mendel’s?
A p-value looks at the right tail: how often is the fit this bad or worse? Fisher’s question looks at the left tail: how often is the fit this good or better?
mean(sims <= 0.263)
pchisq(0.263, df = 1)
For seed shape alone, is Mendel’s fit suspiciously good?


R6. All seven of Mendel’s experiments together
The file data/mendel_monohybrid.csv has Mendel’s F2 counts for all seven traits (from Mendel’s 1866 paper, as tabulated in Hartwell, Mendel’s principles chapter). Compute χ² for each trait with your chisq_stat function, then add them up. The sum of independent χ² values is again χ², with df equal to the sum of the dfs (here 7 × 1 = 7).
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
mendel <- read_csv("data/mendel_monohybrid.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
mendel <- mendel |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(n    = dominant + recessive,
         chi2 = chisq_stat(c(dominant, recessive), c(3, 1) / 4)) |>
  ungroup()
mendel |> select(trait, dominant, recessive, n, chi2)

total <- sum(mendel$chi2)
total
pchisq(total, df = 7)
Now check the left-tail probability by simulation. This time rmultinom() draws the counts for each experiment directly, which is faster than sample() for large N:
one_mendel <- function(sizes) {
  chis <- sapply(sizes, function(N) {
    obs <- rmultinom(1, size = N, prob = c(3, 1) / 4)
    chisq_stat(obs, c(3, 1) / 4)
  })
  sum(chis)
}
set.seed(1936)
sims7 <- replicate(10000, one_mendel(mendel$n))
mean(sims7 <= total)
Which trait fits worst, and which fits best? How often would seven honest experiments of these sizes fit as well as Mendel’s did? Relate your answer to Fisher’s argument and to what you read in F1 in the exercise.

About 4.9% of the simulated values are ≥ 3.84, close to 5%, because 3.84 is by definition the value that χ²(1) exceeds 5% of the time. Stem length fits worst (χ² = 0.61), and cotyledon colour fits best (χ² = 0.015). Every one of the seven χ² values is below 1, the average under H0. Their sum is 2.14, while about 7 is expected. Both the χ² formula (pchisq(2.14, 7) = 0.048) and the simulation (0.048) say that seven honest experiments fit this well only about 1 time in 20. No single experiment is suspicious, but together they fit better than chance usually allows. Fisher made the same argument over many more of Mendel’s experiments and got a much smaller probability. As Weeden (F1) concludes, the bias is real, but its cause (misclassifying borderline seeds, leaving out experiments, or “tidying” the numbers) cannot be settled from the counts alone.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
About this lecture
We cannot set up crosses in humans. To learn how a human trait is inherited, we read the family tree that already exists: the pedigree.

The standard symbols of a pedigree, and how to name each person (II-3).
The hallmarks of five modes of inheritance: autosomal recessive, autosomal dominant, X-linked recessive, X-linked dominant and Y-linked. Mitochondrial inheritance gets a brief mention.
A strategy: do not try to prove a mode; rule modes out, one family at a time.
Risk calculations: the 2/3 carrier probability, partners from the population, and children of relatives.
Complications: incomplete penetrance, new mutations and ascertainment bias.

You already know Mendel’s laws, the χ² test and the probability rules (product rule, sum rule, conditional probability). Today we use all three. Book: Hartwell, Mendel’s principles chapter (pedigrees) and the chromosome theory chapter (sex-linked traits).

The whole lecture is one skill: look at a family tree and say which modes of inheritance it allows. Students already have the tools: segregation of one gene from the Mendel unit, and conditional probability from the probability unit. Today we only add two things: the drawing conventions, and the transmission rules for the X and Y chromosomes. Stress the strategy early: we rule modes out. A pedigree rarely proves a mode; it often excludes several. The risk part at the end reuses the 2/3 they met in the probability unit, now with a family attached.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
Why humans need pedigrees
In peas or flies we choose the cross: true-breeding parents, a test cross, hundreds of offspring. In humans we can do none of this.




Experimental organism
Humans




Crosses
chosen by the geneticist
chosen by the people


Offspring per family
hundreds
usually 1–4


Generation time
days to weeks
25–30 years


Genotypes of parents
known (true-breeding lines)
unknown



So we collect what already happened: who is affected, and how they are related, over as many generations as we can trace. One family is small, so a 3:1 ratio is rarely visible. Instead we look for patterns that are impossible under a given mode.

The point is the contrast with the Mendel unit. There we chose the parents and counted hundreds of offspring, so a chi-square test against 3:1 was natural. Here a family has two or three children, so ratios are useless within one family; with three children, 0, 1, 2 or 3 affected are all quite likely. What a pedigree does give us is structure: who passed what to whom. A single impossible transmission, such as an affected child of two unaffected parents under dominant inheritance, excludes a mode no matter how small the family is. That is why the analysis is about exclusion. Mention that clinical genetics still draws pedigrees routinely, now often next to DNA tests.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
The symbols


Generations are roman numerals from the top; people are numbered left to right within a generation, so “II-2” names one person.
The proband is the affected person through whom the family came to attention. Remember this: it matters for bias later.
Half-filled means a known (or obligate) heterozygous carrier. Most pedigrees do not show carriers, because nobody has tested them.


Go through the symbols quickly; they are a convention, not a concept. Squares are males, circles females, diamonds sex unknown. Filled means affected. A diagonal slash means deceased. A horizontal line between two people is a mating; a double line means the partners are related (consanguineous). The vertical line of descent drops to a horizontal sibship line, and the children hang from it in birth order, left to right. The arrow marks the proband. Some books mark X-linked carrier women with a dot in the centre instead of half-filling; we use half-filled for all carriers. Point out that carriers are only drawn when we know: either by a test, or because the logic of the pedigree forces it (an obligate carrier).

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
Autosomal recessive


The affected person is aa; both parents are usually unaffected carriers (Aa × Aa), so ¼ of their children are expected to be affected.
The trait skips generations: it appears among siblings, often with no affected ancestor.
Consanguinity (a double line) is common: relatives are more likely to carry the same rare allele.
Examples: phenylketonuria (PKU), cystic fibrosis.


Read the figure from the bottom. IV-1 and IV-3 are affected but their parents are not: so the allele was hidden in both parents, which is the hallmark of a recessive trait. Both parents must be carriers, so III-2 and III-3 are obligate carriers even though nobody tested them. They are first cousins, which is the classic clue: a rare recessive allele from a shared grandparent can come down both sides. Both sexes are affected, as expected for an autosome. Note what is missing: no affected people in generations I to III. That is common for rare recessive diseases. Ask: what would rule out AR? Only two affected parents with an unaffected child, because aa × aa can only give aa.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
Autosomal dominant


Every affected person has an affected parent (with full penetrance and no new mutation): the trait appears in every generation.
Affected (Aa) × unaffected (aa) gives ½ affected children, of either sex.
Male-to-male transmission (father → son) is possible. A son gets his father’s Y, not his X, so this rules out X-linkage.
Examples: Huntington disease, Marfan syndrome.


The pattern is vertical: affected people in each generation, each with an affected parent. Most affected people are heterozygous, because the disease allele is rare, so the cross is Aa × aa and half the children are affected. Here 5 of 8: in small families, expect noise around one half. The key line is I-1 to II-2 to III-1: father to son to grandson. A father gives his son a Y chromosome, so a trait that goes from father to son cannot be on the X. This is the single most useful observation for separating autosomal dominant from X-linked dominant. What rules out AD? An affected child of two unaffected parents; we will see later that new mutations and incomplete penetrance can produce exactly this, which is why the assumptions matter.

title: Pedigree analysis
section: Sex linkage, just enough for pedigrees
text:
Sex linkage, just enough for pedigrees
Recap only; Part 2 (Chromosome theory) covers sex chromosomes properly.

Females are XX; males are XY. A male has one X, so he is hemizygous for X-linked genes: a single recessive allele shows.
A father gives his X to every daughter and his Y to every son.
A mother gives one of her two X chromosomes to each child, ½ each.
Notation: XA and Xa for the two alleles on the X; XaY is an affected male for an X-linked recessive trait.









Parents
Sons
Daughters




XAXa (carrier) × XAY
½ XaY affected
½ XAXa carriers, none affected


XAXA × XaY (affected)
all XAY unaffected
all XAXa carriers




This slide gives just what pedigree reading needs; meiosis, sex determination and dosage compensation come in Part 2. The two transmission rules carry everything: fathers pass X to daughters and Y to sons; mothers pass either X with probability one half. From the rules, the two crosses in the table follow directly; have the students derive them with a Punnett square, using X^A and X^a as the gametes. The second row is the reason an affected man’s grandsons, through his daughters, can be affected: his daughters are obligate carriers. Mention hemizygous: males have no second copy to mask a recessive allele, which is why X-linked recessive diseases are much more common in males.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
X-linked recessive


Mostly males are affected; an affected female needs an affected father and a carrier mother.
Affected males are related through unaffected carrier females: the trait passes from grandfather to grandson via a daughter.
No male-to-male transmission: an affected father gives his Xa to every daughter and to no son.
Examples: Duchenne muscular dystrophy, haemophilia A, red–green colour blindness.


Point to I-2, a carrier woman: half her sons are affected (II-4), half her daughters are carriers (II-2). II-2 in turn has two affected sons among four children. This is the “knight’s move” pattern: grandfather or great-uncle to grandson, through women who are not affected. On the right, II-4 is an affected man: all his daughters are carriers (III-5), none of his sons is affected. What rules out XR? An affected woman with an unaffected son (she is XaXa, so every son gets Xa), or an affected daughter whose father is unaffected. Male-to-male transmission does not strictly rule out XR, if the mother happens to be a carrier, but it makes XR much less likely. The demo shows this case.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
X-linked dominant


An affected father has all daughters affected and no affected sons.
An affected (heterozygous) mother passes it to ½ of her sons and ½ of her daughters: here it looks just like autosomal dominant.
More affected females than males, often with milder symptoms in females.
Example: X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets (PHEX).


X-linked dominant is rare, and easy to confuse with autosomal dominant, because an affected mother gives the same one-half to both sexes under either mode. The families that decide it are those with an affected father. Under XD all his daughters are affected and none of his sons; under AD each child, of either sex, has a one-half chance. One unaffected daughter or one affected son of an affected father rules XD out. Females are more often affected because they have two X chromosomes, and therefore two chances to carry the allele. Females are often milder because of X inactivation, which comes in Part 6.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
Y-linked and mitochondrial


Y-linked: only males, from father to every son. There are few Y genes; examples involve male fertility.
Mitochondrial: from the mother to all her children; fathers never transmit. Severity varies because cells carry a mixture of normal and mutant mitochondria (heteroplasmy). Example: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy. Full story in Part 5 (Organelle inheritance).


Both are quick. Y-linked inheritance is strict father-to-son, with no females ever affected, because the Y passes only from father to son. The Y carries few genes, mostly for male development and fertility, so Y-linked pedigrees are rare in the clinic. Mitochondria come from the egg, so the mother passes them to all her children and a father passes them to none. In real families the pattern is blurred by heteroplasmy, so not every child of an affected mother is equally affected; that is the topic of the organelle inheritance unit in Part 5. The demo and the exercises use only the four nuclear modes.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
A strategy: rule modes out
Do not ask “which mode is it?”. Ask “which modes are impossible?”, family by family. With full penetrance and no new mutations:







You see in one family
Rules out




Affected child, both parents unaffected
AD and XD


Both parents affected, an unaffected child
AR


Father → son transmission, mother unaffected
XD (and makes XR unlikely)


Affected father, unaffected daughter
XD


Affected mother, unaffected son
XR


Affected daughter, unaffected father
XR




Check each mode against every parent–child trio.
Among the modes left, prefer the one that needs fewest extra assumptions, such as carriers marrying in from the population.


This is the slide to copy into notes. Each row is a single trio: father, mother, child. Each impossible trio is a proof that the mode is wrong, under our assumptions. Go through the rows and ask students to justify each from the transmission rules. For the first row under XD: an affected daughter needs an affected parent, and an affected son needs an affected mother, so both are ruled out. Step 2 is about likelihood, not logic: AR is almost never strictly ruled out, because any unaffected person could be a carrier. But if AR needs three unrelated people who married in to all be carriers of a rare allele, it is a poor explanation.

title: Pedigree analysis
section: Consistent is not the same as proven
text:
Consistent is not the same as proven
A pedigree often fits several modes. Look at fig04 again (X-linked recessive):

AR also fits, if I-1 and I-2 are both carriers and II-1, who married in, is a carrier too. For a rare allele that is unlikely, but it is not impossible.
AD is ruled out: III-1 is affected but his parents II-1 and II-2 are not.
XD is ruled out: affected sons of an unaffected mother.

So we say “consistent with X-linked recessive”, and we prefer it because it needs no extra carriers. More families, or a DNA test, can settle it.


Students tend to want one right answer. Make the point that the honest result of pedigree analysis is a list of modes that remain, ranked by how plausible they are. In fig04, AR survives the logic test but needs the in-law II-1 to carry the same rare allele. XR needs nothing extra beyond a carrier grandmother. That is why we favour XR. In the demo, you can test each mode: it will report consistent or ruled out, show a set of genotypes that works, and name the people who married in and must be carriers.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
Demo: which mode?




This pedigree was generated under a hidden mode. Test X-linked recessive first: it is ruled out, and the demo rings the trio, an affected mother with an unaffected son. Then test AD, XD and AR: all three are consistent. Ask the class which is most likely. Under XD the affected father I-1 must have all daughters affected and no sons; he has exactly that, and so does III-3. Under AD that pattern has probability one half per child, about 1/32 for these five children. Under AR, two people who married in must be carriers. Then press reveal. Press “new pedigree” for another family if time allows. The demo assumes full penetrance and no new mutations, so it can rule out a mode that a real family would still allow.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
Risk 1: the 2/3 carrier probability
Two unaffected parents have a child with PKU (autosomal recessive). So both parents are Aa. What is the chance that their unaffected daughter is a carrier?

Aa \times Aa \;\rightarrow\; \tfrac14\,AA,\; \tfrac12\,Aa,\; \tfrac14\,aa

She is not aa, so we condition on “unaffected” (recap: Probability and the χ² test):

P(Aa \mid \text{unaffected}) = \frac{1/2}{1/4 + 1/2} = \frac{2}{3}.


The answer is 2/3, not 1/2: knowing she is unaffected removes the aa quarter.
Her parents are obligate carriers: probability 1.


This is the conditional probability from the probability unit, in a family setting. Students often say one half, because Aa is half of the Punnett square. But the Punnett square includes aa, and we already know she is not aa. Among the three unaffected quarters, two are Aa and one is AA. Draw the Punnett square, cross out aa, count what is left. Point out that the parents’ carrier status is not a probability at all: an affected child proves it.

title: Pedigree analysis
section: Risk 2: a partner from the population
text:
Risk 2: a partner from the population
The unaffected sister (carrier probability 2/3) has a child with a man from the population. He has no family history. Assume a carrier frequency of 1/50.

P(\text{child } aa) = \underbrace{\tfrac23}_{\text{she is }Aa} \times \underbrace{\tfrac1{50}}_{\text{he is }Aa} \times \underbrace{\tfrac14}_{\text{both pass }a} = \tfrac{1}{300}.


Product rule: three independent events must all happen.
Where does 1/50 come from? If a disease affects 1 in 10 000 births, then q = 1/100 and the carrier frequency 2pq ≈ 1/50. That is Hardy–Weinberg, in Part 7 (Hardy–Weinberg).
If both partners have an affected sibling: 2/3 × 2/3 × 1/4 = 1/9.


Build the risk as a chain: she must be a carrier, he must be a carrier, and both must pass on a. Each is a probability and they multiply. The population carrier frequency is the weak link; it depends on the population, and for most diseases the clinic looks it up. Here we treat 1/50 as an assumption. Make clear that the 1/50 is derived, not looked up: incidence 1/10 000 means q squared = 1/10 000, so q = 1/100 and 2pq is about 2/100 = 1/50. The last line is a classic exam problem: two unaffected people who each have an affected sibling. Compare 1/300 with 1/9: family history moves the risk by a factor of about 30.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
Consanguinity raises recessive risk
Relatives share alleles by descent from common ancestors. If one great-grandparent carried a rare allele, it can come down both sides of a cousin marriage and meet again in a child.

For a rare allele, an unrelated partner is almost never a carrier of the same allele. A cousin is much more likely to be, because the allele may be in the family.
The child of first cousins is homozygous by descent at about 1/16 of its genes.
This is why consanguinity in a pedigree is a hint for autosomal recessive inheritance, and why rare recessive diseases are more common in families and populations where cousin marriage is frequent.


Keep this qualitative. The one number is 1/16, the inbreeding coefficient of a child of first cousins: the probability that the two copies of a gene in that child are copies of the same ancestral allele. It does not mean the child has a 1/16 risk of disease: the risk depends on whether the shared ancestors carried a disease allele at all. The key idea is that relatedness makes the second carrier much more likely when the allele is rare. Do not moralise: in many parts of the world cousin marriage is common and most children are healthy; the increase in absolute risk is modest. Inbreeding returns in Part 7 with Hardy–Weinberg.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
Complications
Our rules assumed full penetrance and no new mutations. Real families break both.

Incomplete penetrance (from Extensions to Mendel): a person carries a dominant allele but is unaffected. An AD trait then skips a generation and can look recessive.
New mutations: an affected child of two unaffected parents under AD. Most cases of achondroplasia arise this way.
Ascertainment bias: families reach the clinic because they have an affected child. Families with Aa × Aa parents but no affected child are never seen.

Each one can make a correct mode look “ruled out”, so read impossible trios with these in mind.

These three are why a real geneticist does not apply the rule-out table blindly. Incomplete penetrance: an obligate carrier, such as an unaffected parent between an affected grandparent and an affected grandchild, is the tell-tale sign. New mutations: for dominant diseases that reduce reproduction, many cases are new; an isolated affected child of unaffected parents is then expected, not paradoxical. Ascertainment is subtler and gets its own slide: it does not break transmission rules, it distorts ratios.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
Ascertainment bias: the numbers
Take many Aa × Aa families with 3 children. Each child is affected with probability q = 1/4.

All families: 1/4 of the children are affected.
Families seen in the clinic (at least one affected child): the fraction is higher, because the families with 0 affected are missing. Expected affected per ascertained family:


\frac{n q}{1-(1-q)^n} = \frac{3 \times 0.25}{1 - 0.75^3} = \frac{0.75}{0.578} = 1.30,

so the fraction affected is 1.30/3 ≈ 0.43, not 0.25.
A naive count in clinic families would wrongly reject the 1/4 of a recessive trait. We simulate this in R in the exercise.

The denominator is the probability that a family has at least one affected child, one minus the probability that all three are unaffected. Dividing by it rescales the expected count to the families we actually see. With 3 children, 42% of Aa × Aa families have no affected child and are invisible, so the observed fraction is inflated to 0.43. With larger families the bias shrinks. Historically this was a real problem for testing Mendelian ratios in humans; corrections such as counting only the non-proband siblings exist. In the exercise students reproduce this with rbinom and replicate, then filter, and compare with this formula.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
Summary

A pedigree is the human substitute for a controlled cross; families are small, so we look for impossible transmissions, not ratios.
AR: skips generations, both sexes, often consanguinity. AD: every generation, ½ of children, male-to-male possible.
XR: mostly males, through carrier mothers, no father-to-son. XD: affected father → all daughters, no sons.
Y-linked: father → every son. Mitochondrial: mother → all children (Part 5).
Rule modes out trio by trio; among those left, prefer the one with the fewest extra carriers. Consistent ≠ proven.
Risks: unaffected sibling of a patient 2/3 carrier; multiply independent steps; consanguinity raises recessive risk.
Watch for incomplete penetrance, new mutations and ascertainment bias.


Recap the two-step strategy once more, since it is what students will use in the exam: exclude by impossible trios, then rank what remains by plausibility. Remind them of the three numbers: one quarter for a carrier couple, two thirds for an unaffected sibling, one half for a dominant parent. Everything else is the product rule.

title: Pedigree analysis
text:
Where this leads

Part 2: Chromosome theory explains sex chromosomes and X-linkage in full, and LOD scores use pedigrees to map disease genes.
Part 5: Organelle inheritance treats mitochondrial inheritance and heteroplasmy.
Part 7: Hardy–Weinberg gives the population carrier frequencies we assumed today, and the inbreeding coefficient.
In the exercise: analyse pedigrees by hand, look up real diseases in OMIM, MedGen and ClinVar, and simulate ascertainment bias in R.


Pedigrees are not a dead end. In Part 2 the same family trees are used to find where a disease gene lies on a chromosome, by asking whether it is inherited together with a marker. The population numbers we assumed today come from Hardy–Weinberg. The exercise links today to the databases: OMIM and MedGen record the mode of inheritance of each disease, and ClinVar records which variants in a gene cause it.

title: Exercise in R: pedigree analysis
text:
Before you start
This page builds on the by-hand part of the Exercise, so do that first. You need the packages dplyr and ggplot2.

title: Exercise in R: pedigree analysis
text:
Tasks
This unit’s new R idiom is simulation with rbinom and replicate, then filtering. rbinom(n, size, prob) draws n binomial random numbers: with size = 1 each draw is 1 (affected) with probability prob, otherwise 0. replicate(N, expr) runs expr N times and collects the results; here each run is one family. We then keep only some families with filter, as a clinic does without meaning to. Use set.seed so that your numbers match the solutions.
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

Risk as a function
R1. Write a function p_child_affected(p_carrier_mother, p_carrier_father) that returns the probability that a child is affected by an autosomal recessive disease. Check it on two known carriers (answer ¼). Then use it for B6 in the exercise: an unaffected sister of a PKU patient and a man from a population with carrier frequency 1/50. Also compute B7 (both partners have an affected sibling).
p_child_affected <- function(p_carrier_mother, p_carrier_father) {
  p_carrier_mother * p_carrier_father * 1/4
}

p_child_affected(1, 1)          # two known carriers
p_child_affected(2/3, 1/50)     # unaffected sib of a patient x person from the population
1 / p_child_affected(2/3, 1/50) # as "1 in ..."
p_child_affected(2/3, 2/3)      # both partners have an affected sib
R2. The carrier frequency depends on the population. Compute the risk from R1 for carrier frequencies 1/25, 1/50 and 1/100 in one tibble. Your function works on whole vectors, so no loop is needed.
tibble(carrier_freq = c(1/25, 1/50, 1/100)) |>
  mutate(risk = p_child_affected(2/3, carrier_freq),
         one_in = round(1 / risk))


Simulating families
R3. Simulate 10 000 families with Aa × Aa parents and three children each. rbinom(3, size = 1, prob = 1/4) is one family; replicate makes 10 000 of them, one per column. What fraction of all children are affected? How many families have 0, 1, 2 and 3 affected children?
set.seed(1)
n_fam <- 10000
n_kids <- 3
q <- 1/4
kids <- replicate(n_fam, rbinom(n_kids, size = 1, prob = q))
dim(kids)        # 3 rows (children) x 10000 columns (families)
kids[, 1:5]      # the first five families: 1 = affected
mean(kids)       # fraction of all children who are affected

families <- tibble(family = 1:n_fam, n_affected = colSums(kids))
families |> count(n_affected)
R4. A clinic only sees families that have at least one affected child. Keep only those families. What fraction of their children are affected? Compare with the analytic value \(\frac{nq}{1-(1-q)^n}\) affected per family, divided by \(n\).
clinic <- families |> filter(n_affected >= 1)
nrow(clinic)
sum(clinic$n_affected) / (n_kids * nrow(clinic))   # fraction affected among their children

expected_per_family <- n_kids * q / (1 - (1 - q)^n_kids)
expected_per_family
expected_per_family / n_kids
R5. Make a bar chart that compares the fraction of affected children in all families and in the clinic’s families, with a dashed line at the Mendelian ¼.
summary_tbl <- bind_rows(
  families |> mutate(group = "all families"),
  clinic   |> mutate(group = "families with >= 1 affected")
) |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(n_families = n(),
            frac_affected = sum(n_affected) / (n_kids * n()))
summary_tbl

ggplot(summary_tbl, aes(x = group, y = frac_affected)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2a6f97", width = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1/4, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(frac_affected, 3)), vjust = -0.4) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "fraction of children affected",
       title = "Aa x Aa sibships of 3: ascertainment raises the affected fraction") +
  ylim(0, 0.5)
R6. Does the bias grow or shrink with family size? Compute the analytic fraction \(\frac{q}{1-(1-q)^n}\) for \(n = 1, \dots, 6\). Explain the value for \(n = 1\).
sizes <- 1:6
round(q / (1 - (1 - q)^sizes), 3)

title: Organelle inheritance
text:
About this lecture
Everything so far in the course has been about genes in the nucleus, which follow Mendel’s laws because meiosis deals out chromosomes fairly. Mitochondria and chloroplasts carry their own small genomes, outside the nucleus, and these follow quite different rules.

The mitochondrial and chloroplast genomes: small, circular, many copies per cell.
Where they came from: endosymbiosis, and the gene transfer to the nucleus that followed.
Maternal (uniparental) inheritance: reciprocal crosses give different results.
Heteroplasmy, the bottleneck and the threshold effect: why the children of one mother can be so different.
Two human diseases: MELAS (m.3243A>G) and LHON (m.11778G>A).
Mitochondrial donation, and why it raises ethical questions.

Book: Hartwell, Genetics: From Genes to Genomes, organelle inheritance chapter.

This is the last unit of Part 5. The pedigree unit in Part 1 gave mitochondrial inheritance one slide: from the mother to all her children, never from the father. Today we explain why, and why real families do not look as clean as that rule. The key new idea is that a cell has hundreds or thousands of copies of the organelle genome, not two, so a “genotype” becomes a proportion. Once students see that, the variable severity of mitochondrial disease, the bottleneck and the threshold all follow. The previous unit, bacterial genetics, is the right warm-up: mitochondria and chloroplasts are former bacteria.

text:
Two genomes outside the nucleus

Lengths from NCBI RefSeq: human mtDNA NC_012920.1, Arabidopsis thaliana chloroplast NC_000932.1.
Organelle genes are not dealt out by meiosis. They are passed on with the cytoplasm, and the egg supplies almost all of it.

Give the scale first: the mitochondrial genome is about 200 000 times smaller than the nuclear genome. But a cell has many copies of it, so mtDNA can be up to a few percent of a cell’s DNA. Other organisms vary a lot: yeast mtDNA is about 86 kb, plant mitochondrial genomes are often several hundred kb, and the chloroplast genomes of land plants are mostly 120 to 160 kb. The last row is the headline of today: no meiosis, so no segregation in Mendel’s sense, and no 1:1 contribution from the two parents. The figure for cpDNA genes counts the gene features in the RefSeq record, some of which are duplicated in the inverted repeats.

title: Organelle inheritance
text:
The human mitochondrial genome


13 proteins, all subunits of the respiratory chain and ATP synthase (ND1–6, ND4L, CYTB, COX1–3, ATP6, ATP8); 22 tRNAs and 2 rRNAs to translate them.
Extremely compact: no introns, genes overlap (ATP8/ATP6 by 46 bp), only one larger non-coding region (the control region, or D-loop).
Its own genetic code: UGA is tryptophan, not stop.


Walk around the circle. The rRNAs and most genes are on one strand (outer ring); ND6 and eight tRNAs are on the other (inner ring). The tRNAs, in orange, sit between the larger genes; the whole strand is transcribed as long polycistronic RNAs that are cut at the tRNAs. Some protein genes do not even end in a complete stop codon: the stop codon is finished when the mRNA gets its poly-A tail. You check that in the R exercise. The two red points are today’s disease variants. The m. prefix in m.3243A>G means a position in the mitochondrial reference sequence, just as c. means coding sequence. The different genetic code is one sign that mtDNA has been evolving on its own for a very long time.

title: Organelle inheritance
section: Most mitochondrial proteins come from the nucleus
text:
Most mitochondrial proteins come from the nucleus

A human mitochondrion contains more than 1000 different proteins. Only 13 are encoded by mtDNA.
All the rest, including the mtDNA polymerase (POLG), the ribosomal proteins and most respiratory chain subunits, are nuclear genes, translated in the cytosol and imported.
Even the chloroplast’s key enzyme is split: Rubisco’s large subunit (rbcL) is in the cpDNA, the small subunit (RBCS) in the nucleus.









Mitochondrial disease caused by…
Inheritance
Example




a variant in mtDNA
maternal, variable (heteroplasmy)
MELAS, LHON


a variant in a nuclear gene for a mitochondrial protein
Mendelian (AR, AD, X-linked)
POLG disorders, many cases of Leigh syndrome




This slide prevents a common error: “mitochondrial disease” does not mean “maternally inherited”. Many mitochondrial diseases, especially in children, are autosomal recessive, because the gene is in the nucleus. So when a pedigree of a mitochondrial disease shows an affected child of two unaffected parents, with a 1 in 4 recurrence, that is a nuclear gene and Part 1 applies. The organelle and the nucleus depend on each other: neither genome alone can make a working mitochondrion. That interdependence is the long-term result of endosymbiosis, on the next slide.

title: Organelle inheritance
text:
Where organelles came from: endosymbiosis
Mitochondria descend from an alphaproteobacterium, and chloroplasts from a cyanobacterium, each taken up by a host cell more than a billion years ago.








Evidence
Bacteria
Mitochondria and chloroplasts




Genome
one circular chromosome
small circular DNA


Ribosomes
70S, sensitive to e.g. chloramphenicol
bacteria-like, also sensitive


Division
binary fission
divide by fission, not made from scratch


Membranes
inner + outer (Gram-negative)
double membrane


DNA sequence
—
rRNA and protein genes group with alphaproteobacteria / cyanobacteria in phylogenetic trees



Over time, most of the symbiont’s genes moved to the nucleus or were lost. Pieces of mtDNA still land in our chromosomes (NUMTs, nuclear mitochondrial DNA segments).

This connects to the previous unit: bacteria swap DNA, and organelles are former bacteria that have handed most of their genome over to the host. The strongest evidence is the sequence evidence: a tree of 16S-type rRNA puts mitochondria among the alphaproteobacteria and chloroplasts among the cyanobacteria. Gene transfer to the nucleus is still going on in plants, and in humans NUMTs are a practical nuisance: when you sequence mtDNA, reads from nuclear copies can look like low-level heteroplasmy. Why keep any genes in the organelle at all? One idea is that genes for very hydrophobic membrane proteins are hard to import, so they stay where the protein is needed.

title: Organelle inheritance
text:
Maternal inheritance


In humans and most animals:

the egg carries a very large number of mitochondria (and mtDNA copies, of the order of 100 000);
the sperm brings very few, in its midpiece, and they are tagged and destroyed in the early embryo.

So mtDNA comes from the mother, and only women pass it on.

Reciprocal crosses differ. That is the classic test for organelle inheritance:



Cross
Offspring




mutant ♀ × normal ♂
all carry the mutation


normal ♀ × mutant ♂
none do



For nuclear genes, reciprocal crosses give the same result (Mendel, Part 1), except for X-linked genes.


Two separate reasons make inheritance maternal: the huge numerical difference (the egg has orders of magnitude more mtDNA than a sperm), and active destruction of the paternal mitochondria after fertilisation. Recall from the Mendel unit that Mendel did reciprocal crosses and got identical results: that told him that egg and pollen contribute equally. A difference between reciprocal crosses points to either sex linkage or organelle inheritance. Sex linkage gives a difference that depends on the sex of the offspring; organelle inheritance gives a difference that depends only on the sex of the parent. Ask the class: how would you tell the two apart in a pedigree? Answer on the next slide.

title: Organelle inheritance
text:
Maternal inheritance in a pedigree


Affected or carrier mother → every child gets the variant, at different levels.
Father → no child, whether the children are sons or daughters.
Both sexes are affected. It looks like neither autosomal nor X-linked inheritance.


Compare with the one-line version from the pedigree unit (fig06 there). The new element is the percentage under each person: the fraction of their mtDNA that carries the variant. In the left family the mother has 40 percent and is healthy; her four children have 85, 55, 10 and 30 percent. Only the 85 percent son is affected. The 55 percent daughter is healthy, but one of her children reaches 70 percent and is affected. On the right, an affected father passes nothing, and that holds in every generation. So the rule “mother to all children” is true for the variant but not for the disease: severity is a matter of degree. The rest of the lecture explains where the spread of percentages comes from.

title: Organelle inheritance
text:
Uniparental inheritance in other organisms
