title: Exercise in R: Mendel, segregation & assortment
text:
Where this leads
Every simulated cross above was a little off from its expected ratio, and so were all of Mendel’s. In Probability & the χ² test you measure such deviations in R with chisq.test(), and use replicate() to run a simulation many times. sapply() comes back in Part 2.

title: Extensions to Mendel
text:
About this lecture
Mendel picked traits that behave simply: one gene, two alleles, one fully dominant, no interactions, no environment. Most traits are not that tidy. Today we keep Mendel’s two laws (segregation and independent assortment) and change the assumptions about how genotype becomes phenotype.

One gene: incomplete dominance and codominance, why some alleles are dominant at the molecular level, multiple alleles, lethal alleles, pleiotropy, penetrance and expressivity, and the environment.
Two genes: genes acting in the same pathway change the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 into 9 : 3 : 4, 9 : 7, 12 : 3 : 1, 13 : 3 or 15 : 1. These are still 16ths, merged.
Strategy: given an F₂, turn the counts into 16ths, guess which classes merged, then test the guess with χ² (from Probability and the χ² test).

Book: Hartwell, the chapter on extensions to Mendel’s laws.

The key message: the laws of transmission do not change. Alleles still segregate 1:1 and unlinked genes still assort independently. What changes is the mapping from genotype to phenotype. Every odd ratio in this lecture can be derived from an ordinary Punnett square, then relabelled. Students who remember that will never need to memorise the ratios. The χ² test from the previous unit comes back at the end, as the tool for choosing between candidate ratios. Linkage, which breaks independent assortment, is a different story and comes in Part 2.

title: Extensions to Mendel
section: Dominance is a relation between two alleles
text:
Dominance is a relation between two alleles


Complete dominance: the heterozygote looks like one homozygote (Pp is purple). F₂ phenotypes 3 : 1.
Incomplete dominance: the heterozygote is in between. Red × white snapdragons give pink F₁, and the F₂ is 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white: phenotype ratio = genotype ratio.
Codominance: the heterozygote shows both phenotypes in full. IAIB red cells carry both A and B antigens: blood type AB.

“Dominant” describes a pair of alleles, not one allele, and not how common it is.

Start from the snapdragon: it is the cleanest way to show that segregation still works perfectly. The F1 is pink, which looks like blending, but the F2 brings back red and white unchanged, in 1:2:1. Blending inheritance would never give back the parental types. In the incomplete-dominance case you can read the genotype straight off the phenotype, so the phenotype ratio is the genotype ratio. Codominance differs from incomplete dominance: the heterozygote is not an average, it shows both products side by side, as A and B antigens on the same red cell. Stress that dominance is a relation: the I-A allele is codominant with I-B but dominant over i. Also the misconception: a dominant allele is not necessarily common; polydactyly alleles are dominant and rare.

title: Extensions to Mendel
section: Why is an allele dominant? The molecular view
text:
Why is an allele dominant? The molecular view


Most loss-of-function alleles are recessive: half the normal protein is usually enough (haplosufficient).
Haploinsufficiency: half is not enough, so a loss-of-function allele is dominant (e.g. PAX6 and aniridia).
Dominant negative: the mutant protein spoils the normal one in a complex (e.g. mutant collagen chains in osteogenesis imperfecta).
Gain of function: the mutant protein does something new or too much (e.g. an over-active FGFR3 receptor in achondroplasia).


This links the Mendelian words to the molecular biology students know from 5MO103. Ask first: if a mutation destroys an enzyme, why is the heterozygote usually normal? Because one working copy gives about half the enzyme, and pathways usually have spare capacity. So recessive is the default for loss-of-function alleles. Then the three ways around this. Haploinsufficiency: a dosage-sensitive gene, where 50% is below the threshold. Dominant negative: in a dimer, random pairing in a heterozygote leaves only 1/4 of dimers fully normal, which is worse than the 1/2 from a plain null allele; for tetramers it is only 1/16. Gain of function: the mutant protein is active when it should not be. Achondroplasia comes back in Find it: FGFR3 variants make the receptor overly active.

title: Extensions to Mendel
text:
Multiple alleles
A population can carry many alleles of one gene, even though each diploid person carries at most two.
ABO blood groups (gene ABO, which encodes a glycosyltransferase):










Genotype
IAIA, IAi
IBIB, IBi
IAIB
ii




Blood type
A
B
AB
O



IA and IB are codominant with each other; both are dominant over i (no working enzyme). Three alleles give 6 genotypes but 4 phenotypes.
An allelic series: rabbit coat colour, C (full colour) > cch (chinchilla) > ch (Himalayan) > c (albino). Each allele is dominant over those to its right.
With n alleles there are n(n + 1)/2 genotypes: 3 alleles → 6, 4 alleles → 10.

ABO combines two ideas: multiple alleles, and different dominance relations between different pairs. The A allele adds N-acetylgalactosamine and the B allele adds galactose to the same precursor (the H antigen); the O allele makes no active enzyme. So A and B are codominant, both products are present, and O is recessive because it makes nothing. The rabbit series is the textbook allelic series and sets up the Himalayan allele, which comes back on the environment slide. The formula n(n+1)/2 is n homozygotes plus n(n-1)/2 heterozygotes; a quick check of their combinatorics from the probability unit.

title: Extensions to Mendel
section: Lethal alleles and pleiotropy: the yellow mouse
text:
Lethal alleles and pleiotropy: the yellow mouse


Cuénot (1905): yellow × yellow mice always gave yellow and agouti offspring, in a ratio near 2 : 1, never 3 : 1. Yellow mice never bred true.
The AYAY embryos die. AY is dominant for coat colour but recessive for lethality.
One allele affecting several traits is pleiotropy. Another example: the sickle-cell allele of HBB affects red cell shape, anaemia, organ damage and resistance to malaria.
A 2 : 1 ratio among the survivors of a monohybrid cross is the signature of a recessive lethal.


This is the classic case where a ratio looked wrong and the explanation was a missing class. Ask students to predict yellow x yellow first: they will say 3:1. Then show 2:1 and ask what has happened. The test for the hypothesis: yellow mice are always heterozygous, so yellow x agouti should give 1:1, and pregnant yellow x yellow females should show about a quarter of embryos dying early. Pleiotropy: the same allele has one effect we see (coat colour, dominant) and one we infer (lethality, recessive). That shows again that “dominant” belongs to a trait, not to an allele. In the exercise, students test 2:1 against 3:1 with χ².

title: Extensions to Mendel
text:
Penetrance and expressivity


Penetrance: the fraction of individuals with a genotype who show the trait at all. Incomplete penetrance can make a dominant trait skip a generation in a pedigree.
Expressivity: how strongly the trait shows in those who have it. Polydactyly can be one small extra digit, or extra digits on all four limbs.
BRCA1: carriers of a pathogenic variant have a much higher lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancer, but not all of them get cancer. They inherit a raised risk, not the disease.
Causes: other genes (modifiers), the environment, and chance.


Keep the two words apart: penetrance is yes/no at the level of individuals, expressivity is the degree among affected individuals. Penetrance is a fraction of genotypes, so it can only be measured when we know the genotype, which is why molecular testing changed our estimates of penetrance for BRCA1. Do not quote penetrance numbers for BRCA1 here: they differ between studies and populations, and they change. The important qualitative fact is: autosomal dominant, incomplete penetrance. In the pedigrees unit, incomplete penetrance is the classic trap: an unaffected parent between two affected generations does not rule out dominant inheritance. In Find it students look up the mode of inheritance in MedGen/OMIM.

title: Extensions to Mendel
text:
The environment changes the phenotype
The same genotype can give different phenotypes in different environments.

Himalayan rabbits (chch) and Siamese cats carry a temperature-sensitive allele of the gene for tyrosinase, the first enzyme in melanin synthesis.
The enzyme works at lower temperature and fails at body-core temperature, so only the cool extremities (ears, nose, paws, tail) are dark.
Shave a patch on a Himalayan rabbit’s back and keep it cold while the fur regrows: the new fur grows in dark.
In humans, phenylketonuria (PKU): the same genotype gives severe intellectual disability on a normal diet and near-normal development on a low-phenylalanine diet.

Genotype sets a range of possible phenotypes. The environment picks a point in that range.

The rabbit experiment is the cleanest demonstration that the genotype of every skin cell is the same; only the temperature differs. The allele makes a protein that folds correctly at lower temperature. PKU is the human example where knowing the environment lets us change the phenotype: newborn screening plus diet. This leads to the idea of the norm of reaction, which returns with quantitative traits in Complex traits. It also explains part of incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity from the previous slide.

title: Extensions to Mendel
text:
Two genes, one pathway: epistasis
Epistasis: the genotype at one gene hides the effect of another gene. Mendel’s 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 is still there underneath; some classes look the same.

Recessive epistasis, 9 : 3 : 4. Labrador retrievers, BbEe × BbEe: ee dogs make no dark pigment in the hair, so they are yellow whatever their B genotype. ee is epistatic to B; B is hypostatic.

Epistasis is about genes, not alleles: one gene masks another. Contrast with dominance, which is about two alleles of the same gene. The pathway picture: a later step only matters if the earlier step happens. Here E is needed for dark pigment in the hair at all, and B decides whether that dark pigment is black or brown. The pathway is simplified: in reality E (MC1R) acts as a switch between dark and yellow pigment, but the logic is the same. Yellow Labradors with bb still show it: their nose and lips are brown rather than black. That is a hint that the B genotype is still there, just hidden in the coat. Point out how 9:3:4 comes from 9:3:3:1 with the last two classes merged: B_ee (3) and bbee (1).

title: Extensions to Mendel
text:
Complementary genes: 9 : 7
Both steps of the pathway are needed; losing either one gives the same mutant phenotype.
\text{colourless} \xrightarrow{\ \text{enzyme A}\ } \text{colourless} \xrightarrow{\ \text{enzyme B}\ } \text{purple}

Bateson and Punnett (sweet pea): two white varieties crossed gave an all-purple F₁. The F₁ selfed gave 9 purple : 7 white.
The parents were AAbb and aaBB. Each could make what the other could not, so the F₁ AaBb has both enzymes.
Only A_B_ is purple (9). A_bb, aaB_ and aabb are all white (3 + 3 + 1 = 7).
Also called duplicate recessive epistasis: aa hides B, and bb hides A.

Two white parents with a coloured F₁ is the same logic as a complementation test: the mutations are in different genes.

This is the slide that sets up the complementation test in the Mutation unit. When two recessive mutants with the same phenotype are crossed and the offspring are wild type, the mutations are in different genes; they complement. If they were in the same gene, the F1 would still be mutant. Point out the merged classes: 3 + 3 + 1 = 7. The pathway explains why: you get purple only if both steps work. Ask students what an F1 test cross AaBb x aabb would give: 1 purple : 3 white.

title: Extensions to Mendel
text:
Dominant epistasis: 12 : 3 : 1
A dominant allele at one gene blocks the pathway, so it hides the other gene.
\text{white} \xrightarrow{\ \text{step 1}\ } \text{green} \xrightarrow{\ \text{enzyme B}\ } \text{yellow} \qquad \text{(}A\text{\_ blocks step 1)}
Summer squash fruit colour, WwYy × WwYy:

White = 9 + 3 = 12, yellow 3, green 1: 12 : 3 : 1.
The W allele (dominant) is epistatic to Y/y. Only ww plants show what the Y gene does.

Now the first two classes merge instead of the last two. The dominant W allele stops pigment production early, so W_ fruit is white whatever Y is. In ww plants the pathway runs: green pigment is made, and Y_ converts it to yellow; yy plants stay green. Compare with recessive epistasis: there the epistatic genotype was the homozygous recessive (ee), here it is any genotype with one dominant allele (W_). That is why the merged class is 12 instead of 4. Test cross: WwYy x wwyy gives 2 white : 1 yellow : 1 green.

title: Extensions to Mendel
text:
Dominant suppression 13 : 3 and duplicate genes 15 : 1


Dominant suppression, 13 : 3
\text{colourless} \xrightarrow{\ \text{enzyme B}\ } \text{pigment} A_ makes an inhibitor of enzyme B.

Coloured only if aaB_: 3.
A_B_, A_bb, aabb are colourless: 9 + 3 + 1 = 13.
Chickens: White Leghorn (CCII) × White Wyandotte (ccii) → F₂ 13 white : 3 coloured. I suppresses C.


Duplicate genes, 15 : 1
\text{precursor} \xrightarrow{\ \text{enzyme A}\ \text{or}\ \text{enzyme B}\ } \text{product}

Two redundant genes do the same job; one working copy of either is enough.
Only aabb lacks the product: 1. All others: 15.
Shepherd’s purse: triangular seed capsules unless aabb (ovoid).



Two more ways to merge classes. In dominant suppression, a dominant allele of one gene makes a suppressor that stops the other gene’s product from acting. Unlike 12:3:1, the double recessive aabb is colourless too, because it lacks enzyme B, so it joins the big class: 13. Make students explain why aabb is white: no inhibitor, but also no enzyme. Duplicate genes are common in plants with genome duplications, such as shepherd’s purse, which is tetraploid. Redundancy is also why many single knockouts in model organisms have no visible phenotype; you need to knock out both copies. Test crosses: 13:3 gives 3 colourless : 1 coloured; 15:1 gives 3 : 1.

Nothing about meiosis has changed. The test-cross column is worth a minute: a test cross has the four classes in 1:1:1:1, so merging the same classes gives the test-cross ratio. 9:3:4 merges aaBb and aabb, giving 1:1:2. A test cross is a good second check when two ratios fit an F2 about equally well. Note that 13:3 and 15:1 give the same 3:1 test cross; only the F2 tells them apart.

title: Extensions to Mendel
section: Explore: pathways and the Punnett square
text:
Explore: pathways and the Punnett square




Interactive demo. It opens on recessive epistasis 9:3:4. Click the aaBB square: enzyme A is missing, so the pathway stops at yellow, even though enzyme B is there. Then click Aabb: enzyme A works, B does not, and the dog is brown. Then switch presets: complementary (9:7) and click aaBB and AAbb, the two white parents of the sweet pea cross; then AaBb, the purple F1. Dominant epistasis: click aabb (green) and AaBb (white, inhibitor on). Dominant suppression: only aaB_ squares are coloured. Duplicate: only aabb lacks the product. End on “no interaction” to show that the same 16 squares give 9:3:3:1 when the two pathways are separate. The static fallback for print is the figure on the previous slide.

title: Extensions to Mendel
text:
Strategy: collapse the F₂ into 16ths

How many phenotype classes? Two classes from a dihybrid cross points to 9 : 7, 13 : 3 or 15 : 1; three classes to 9 : 3 : 4, 12 : 3 : 1 (or 9 : 6 : 1); four to 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
Convert to 16ths: count ÷ total × 16.
Match to sums of 9, 3, 3, 1. For example 4 = 3 + 1, 7 = 3 + 3 + 1, 12 = 9 + 3, 13 = 9 + 3 + 1, 15 = 9 + 3 + 3.
Test the candidates with χ², with df = number of classes − 1.
Explain it with a pathway, and check with a test cross if you can.

Worked example. Sweet pea F₂: 382 purple, 290 white (672 plants).

382/672 × 16 = 9.1 and 290/672 × 16 = 6.9 → try 9 : 7.
Expected 378 and 294: χ² = 4²/378 + 4²/294 = 0.097, df = 1, p = 0.76. Fits.
Under 3 : 1 instead: χ² = 118, p ≈ 10⁻²⁷. Rejected.


The point of step 2 is that it turns counts into something you can compare with ratio tables at a glance. Students should be able to do steps 1 to 3 in their head. The χ² step is from the previous unit; the only new thing is that we now have several candidate ratios to compare. Note a warning: any ratio that merges classes of a ratio that fits will also fit, because merging throws away information. For example, if 9:3:4 fits, then 9:7 (merge brown with yellow) will usually fit too. Choose the ratio that has the same number of classes as the phenotypes you can actually tell apart. The exercise works through exactly that with R. Worked numbers: (382-378)^2/378 + (290-294)^2/294 = 0.042 + 0.054 = 0.097.

title: Extensions to Mendel
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Incomplete dominance
heterozygote in between; F₂ 1 : 2 : 1 (snapdragon)


Codominance
heterozygote shows both; IAIB = type AB


Molecular dominance
haploinsufficiency, dominant negative, gain of function


Multiple alleles
many alleles in a population; ABO; allelic series


Recessive lethal
2 : 1 among survivors; yellow mouse AY


Pleiotropy
one gene, several traits


Penetrance / expressivity
whether a genotype shows / how strongly


Environment
temperature-sensitive tyrosinase in Himalayan rabbits


Epistasis
one gene hides another; F₂ ratios are merged 16ths


Ratios
9 : 3 : 4, 9 : 7, 12 : 3 : 1, 13 : 3, 15 : 1


Strategy
counts → 16ths → candidate ratios → χ² → pathway




Run through the table as a quick check. The two ideas to take away: dominance is about alleles of one gene, epistasis is about two genes; and all the odd dihybrid ratios are the same 16 squares with some phenotypes merged. If students can draw the pathway and colour a 4 by 4 Punnett square, they can derive any ratio in the table.

title: Extensions to Mendel
text:
Where this leads

Pedigree analysis (next unit): incomplete penetrance, variable expressivity and new mutations make human pedigrees harder to read.
Mutation and complementation: the 9 : 7 cross is a complementation test. Two recessive mutants that give a wild-type F₁ have mutations in different genes.
Linkage: when two genes are close on a chromosome, the dihybrid classes are no longer 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, for a quite different reason.
Complex traits: many genes and the environment together give continuous variation.


Point forward. The most immediate use is pedigrees, where incomplete penetrance and de novo mutations (achondroplasia: about 80% of cases are new mutations) change how we read a family tree. Complementation is the experimental version of the 9:7 logic. Linkage is the other big reason a dihybrid ratio may not be 9:3:3:1, and students must not confuse it with epistasis: linkage changes the frequency of genotype classes, epistasis changes how genotype classes map to phenotypes. Finally, complex traits extend the environment and modifier ideas to many genes at once.

title: Exercise in R: extensions to Mendel
text:

in R, apply one function to a whole list of hypotheses with purrr::map_dbl() or sapply(), and collect the results in a tibble.

title: Exercise in R: extensions to Mendel
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

in R, apply one function to a whole list of hypotheses with purrr::map_dbl() or sapply(), and collect the results in a tibble.

title: Exercise in R: extensions to Mendel
text:
Before you start
This page builds on the by-hand part of the Exercise, so do that first. You need the packages readr, dplyr, purrr, tidyr and ggplot2. Download labrador_f2.csv and save it in a data/ folder of your R project.

title: Exercise in R: extensions to Mendel
text:
Tasks
New idiom today: apply one function to every element of a list. You write a function once, put the hypotheses in a named list, and let purrr::map_dbl() (or base R sapply()) call the function for each hypothesis. map_dbl(xs, f) returns a numeric vector, one value per element of xs, named like xs. Inside map_dbl() you can write a short function as \(h) ..., where h is one element of the list.
The data. data/labrador_f2.csv has coat colours of 384 Labrador pups from matings between black BbEe parents. This is an invented teaching dataset, shaped like pooled kennel records. The recorder split the yellow pups into “fox red” and “cream”, because she wondered if the shade was a third Mendelian class. (In real yellow Labradors the shade varies a lot and is not explained by B or E: this is variable expressivity.)
R1. Load the data and look at it. Add a column with each count expressed in 16ths. Which ratio do the 16ths suggest?
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

f2 <- read_csv("data/labrador_f2.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
f2
f2 |> mutate(sixteenths = round(16 * count / sum(count), 2))
R2. Write two functions: chisq_stat(obs, ratio), which returns the χ² statistic for observed counts obs and a ratio such as c(9, 3, 4), and chisq_p(obs, ratio), which returns the p-value with df = number of classes − 1 (use pchisq() with lower.tail = FALSE). Check chisq_p(obs, c(9, 3, 3, 1)) against chisq.test().
obs <- setNames(f2$count, f2$coat)   # a named vector: black, chocolate, fox red, cream

chisq_stat <- function(obs, ratio) {
  expected <- sum(obs) * ratio / sum(ratio)
  # ... return the chi-square statistic
}
chisq_p <- function(obs, ratio) {
  # ... use chisq_stat() and pchisq()
}
R3. Each hypothesis says which recorded classes belong together and what the ratio is. group gives, for each of the four recorded classes (black, chocolate, fox red, cream), the number of the class it belongs to under that hypothesis. tapply() adds up the counts within each group. Use map_dbl() to compute χ² and p for every hypothesis, and collect them in a tibble sorted by p. Then get the same p-values with sapply().
collapse <- function(obs, group) tapply(obs, group, sum)

hypotheses <- list(
  "9:3:3:1" = list(group = c(1, 2, 3, 4), ratio = c(9, 3, 3, 1)),
  "9:3:4"   = list(group = c(1, 2, 3, 3), ratio = c(9, 3, 4)),
  "9:7"     = list(group = c(1, 2, 2, 2), ratio = c(9, 7)),
  "12:3:1"  = list(group = c(1, 1, 2, 3), ratio = c(12, 3, 1)),
  "15:1"    = list(group = c(1, 1, 1, 2), ratio = c(15, 1))
)
collapse(obs, hypotheses[["9:3:4"]]$group)   # black, chocolate, all yellow

results <- tibble(
  hypothesis = names(hypotheses),
  df    = map_int(hypotheses, \(h) length(h$ratio) - 1L),
  chisq = map_dbl(hypotheses, \(h) chisq_stat(collapse(obs, h$group), h$ratio)),
  p     = map_dbl(hypotheses, \(h) chisq_p(collapse(obs, h$group), h$ratio))
) |>
  arrange(desc(p))
results
Which hypotheses are rejected at α = 0.05? Two hypotheses fit. Which one would you choose, and why?
R4. Make a tibble of observed and expected counts for the best-fitting ratio, 9 : 3 : 4 (black, chocolate, yellow), and plot them side by side with pivot_longer() and geom_col(position = "dodge").
R5. (yellow mice) Yellow × yellow mice gave 118 yellow and 62 agouti pups (invented counts). Put the two hypotheses 2:1 and 3:1 in a named list and use your chisq_stat() and chisq_p() with map_dbl() to test both. Which fits? What does that tell you about AYAY?

text:
Solutions






Solutions: In R





R1. The 16ths are about 8.8 : 3.2 : 2.2 : 1.9. Black and chocolate look like 9 and 3, but fox red and cream are close to 2 and 2, not 3 and 1. Together they make 4.0, which suggests 9 : 3 : 4.

chisq_stat <- function(obs, ratio) {
  expected <- sum(obs) * ratio / sum(ratio)
  sum((obs - expected)^2 / expected)
}
chisq_p <- function(obs, ratio) {
  pchisq(chisq_stat(obs, ratio), df = length(obs) - 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
}
obs <- setNames(f2$count, f2$coat)
chisq_p(obs, c(9, 3, 3, 1))

The same p-value. 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 is rejected: the split of yellow into fox red and cream is not 3 : 1.

The 9 : 7 model is just 9 : 3 : 4 with chocolate and yellow merged, so it fits whenever 9 : 3 : 4 fits; but chocolate and yellow pups clearly look different, and 9 : 7 cannot explain that. A model has to explain every class you can tell apart. Do not pick a model just because its p-value is highest; here the two p-values are for tests with different df and different data groupings. The fox red / cream split is not a Mendelian class: it is variation in the shade of yellow (expressivity).

title: Exercise in R: extensions to Mendel
text:
Where this leads
In Pedigree analysis you write a risk function that works on a whole vector of carrier frequencies at once, and simulate families with replicate().

title: Human linkage & LOD scores
text:
About this lecture
In flies we map genes with designed testcrosses and thousands of offspring. In humans we have neither: we get the families that exist, with a handful of children each. So we need statistics to say whether a disease gene is linked to a marker, and how far apart they are.

Why human linkage needs a different approach, and what a DNA marker is.
Counting recombinants in a pedigree: informative meioses and phase.
The likelihood L(θ) of the data, and the LOD score: \text{LOD}(\theta) = \log_{10} \dfrac{L(\theta)}{L(0.5)}.
The LOD curve, its maximum θ̂, the threshold of 3 for linkage and −2 for exclusion.
Adding LODs across families.
The story of Huntington disease: from a linked marker in 1983 to the gene in 1993.

Book: Hartwell, Genetics: From Genes to Genomes, linkage and mapping chapter (the section on mapping in humans).

This unit closes Part 2. Everything so far in Part 2 assumed we could choose the crosses: testcrosses in Drosophila, thousands of flies, recombination frequency read off directly. In humans the logic of linkage is exactly the same (recombination fraction theta is the RF from Linkage & recombination), but the data are small and messy. The new idea is to compare two hypotheses, linked at theta versus unlinked, by how probable each makes the observed family. Students have met the binomial in Probability & the chi-square test, and pedigrees in Pedigree analysis; today combines them.

title: Human linkage & LOD scores
text:
Why humans need statistics







In Drosophila (Linkage & recombination)
In humans




We choose the cross: a testcross with a known double heterozygote
We take the families that exist


Hundreds or thousands of offspring
2–5 children per family


Phase known: we built the parent’s chromosomes
Phase often unknown: which marker allele is with the disease allele?


Mutant markers chosen to be visible
Markers must be DNA variants that differ between the parent’s two homologues


RF = recombinants / total; test with χ²
Combine many small families, each too small for χ²



So for humans we ask a different question: how much more probable are these families if the disease gene and the marker are linked at distance θ than if they are unlinked?

Go row by row. The first row is the fundamental problem: no experimental crosses in humans, for obvious ethical reasons. The second is the size problem: a single family gives at most a few meioses, so a chi-square test (which needs expected counts of at least 5) cannot be used family by family. The third is phase, which gets its own slide. The fourth is markers: in flies we use visible mutants; in humans we use DNA differences that have no effect on the phenotype at all. The solution, due to Newton Morton in 1955, is a likelihood-based score that can be computed for each family and simply added across families.

title: Human linkage & LOD scores
text:
Markers: something we can follow

A marker is a DNA site where people differ. It need not do anything; we only need to tell the two homologues of a parent apart, so that we can see which one each child got.

The first human disease linkages with DNA markers used RFLPs, restriction fragment length polymorphisms: a single base change creates or destroys a restriction site, which changes the length of a fragment on a Southern blot. RFLPs usually have two alleles, so many parents are homozygous and their meioses tell us nothing. Microsatellites, short tandem repeats such as CA repeated 6 to 30 times, have many alleles, so most people are heterozygous: they made the human genetic maps of the 1990s. Today SNP arrays or sequencing type hundreds of thousands of single-base variants at once; each is less informative, but there are so many that several are always close to any gene. Part 4 (Genomic variation) returns to SNPs. Stress the take-home line: a meiosis is informative only if the parent is heterozygous at the marker, and (for the disease) we can tell which disease allele was passed on.

title: Human linkage & LOD scores
text:
Counting recombinants in a family

Autosomal dominant disease (D), marker with alleles 1, 2, 3. II-1’s mother is 3/3, so each child’s paternal marker allele can be read: 1 or 2. Children who got D with 1, or d with 2, are non-recombinant; III-4 got D with 2: recombinant.

Walk through it. Generation I: the affected grandfather is homozygous 1/1 at the marker, so the D he passed to II-1 must sit on a chromosome with marker allele 1. II-1 therefore has D 1 on one homologue and d 2 on the other: his phase is known. His wife is 3/3, so she always passes 3, and the other allele of each child came from II-1. Affected children (D) who carry 1 got the parental D 1 chromosome; unaffected children with 2 got d 2; both are non-recombinant. III-4 is affected but carries 2: a crossover between the disease gene and the marker happened in his father’s meiosis. Six meioses, one recombinant. The naive estimate of theta is 1/6, about 0.17. But is this evidence of linkage at all? With only 6 meioses, one recombinant could easily come from an unlinked marker. The rest of the lecture answers that.

title: Human linkage & LOD scores
text:
Phase: known or unknown

Without the grandparents we do not know which marker allele travels with D. Each phase has prior probability ½; under the other phase, the same children count as 5 recombinants instead of 1. The likelihood averages over both phases, and the evidence is weaker.

Phase is the linkage phase from Linkage & recombination: coupling versus repulsion, here D 1 / d 2 versus D 2 / d 1. In a testcross we built the parent, so we knew. In a human family we infer it from the previous generation, when it is available. If the grandparents are dead or untyped, we must consider both phases. Under phase 1 the family has 1 recombinant out of 6; under phase 2 it has 5. Each phase is equally likely before we look at the children, so the likelihood is the average. Today we mostly work with phase-known families, where the arithmetic is simplest; the demo and the R exercise also let you switch to phase unknown. Note the maximum LOD drops from 0.63 to 0.33: not knowing the phase costs information.

title: Human linkage & LOD scores
text:
The likelihood of the data
Each informative meiosis is recombinant with probability θ and non-recombinant with probability 1 − θ, independently. A family with n informative meioses and k recombinants (phase known) has probability

L(\theta) = \theta^{k}\,(1-\theta)^{n-k}.

This is the binomial from Probability & the χ² test, without the binomial coefficient (it is the same for every θ, so it cancels below).



θ
0.01
0.1
1/6
0.3
0.5




L(θ) for n = 6, k = 1
0.0095
0.059
0.067
0.050
0.0156



Read as a function of θ with the data fixed, L(θ) is the likelihood. The θ with the highest likelihood, θ̂ = k/n, is the best estimate.

Compute two columns on the board. At theta = 0.1: 0.1 times 0.9 to the 5th = 0.1 times 0.590 = 0.059. At theta = 0.5: 0.5 to the 6th = 1/64 = 0.0156. The shift in viewpoint is the important thing: a probability is about data given the parameter; a likelihood is the same number, read as a function of the parameter for the data we actually have. The maximum is at k/n, the obvious estimate, 1/6 here. Note that theta = 0.01 makes the data less likely than 0.1: a family with one recombinant out of six is not evidence for very tight linkage.

title: Human linkage & LOD scores
section: The LOD score: linked vs unlinked
text:
The LOD score: linked vs unlinked
Compare “linked at θ” with “unlinked” (θ = 0.5) by the ratio of likelihoods, on a log10 scale:

\text{LOD}(\theta) = \log_{10}\frac{L(\theta)}{L(0.5)} = \log_{10}\frac{\theta^{k}(1-\theta)^{n-k}}{0.5^{\,n}}

Worked example (fig. on the previous slides: n = 6, k = 1) at θ = 0.1:

L(0.1) = 0.1 × 0.95 = 0.0590; L(0.5) = 0.56 = 1/64 = 0.0156.
Ratio = 0.0590 / 0.0156 = 3.78: the family is 3.8 times more probable if the genes are linked at θ = 0.1.
LOD(0.1) = log10 3.78 = 0.58.

LOD = “logarithm of the odds”. LOD 1 = odds 10 : 1; LOD 2 = 100 : 1; LOD 3 = 1000 : 1.

The LOD score is a likelihood ratio, written as a base-10 logarithm. Why the logarithm? Because independent families multiply their likelihoods, and logarithms turn products into sums: that is what lets us add LOD scores later. Why base 10? Historical convenience: a LOD of 3 is easy to read as odds of a thousand to one. Positive LOD favours linkage, negative favours no linkage, zero is neutral. At theta = 0.5 the LOD is always exactly 0, because the numerator and denominator are the same.

title: Human linkage & LOD scores
text:
The LOD curve

One family, n = 10 meioses. Compute LOD(θ) for every θ from 0 to 0.5: the curve peaks at θ̂ = k/n, and its height is the strength of the evidence. With k = 0, LOD(0) = 10 × log10 2 = 3.01. With k > 0, LOD(0) = −∞: one recombinant rules out θ = 0.

Read the curves from the top. k = 0: every child is non-recombinant, the curve is highest at theta = 0, where LOD = n log10 2 = 0.301 per meiosis. So you need at least 10 fully informative, phase-known meioses without a recombinant to reach 3. k = 1: the peak drops to 1.60 at theta = 0.1, and the curve plunges to minus infinity at 0, because a recombinant is impossible under complete linkage. k = 2 and 3: lower and flatter peaks. A single family of ten children is enormous in human terms and still rarely reaches 3. That is why we need many families. The curve is what the demo and the R exercise draw.

title: Human linkage & LOD scores
text:
Why 3? And why −2?

LOD ≥ 3: accept linkage. The data are 1000 times more likely under linkage at θ̂ than under no linkage.
LOD ≤ −2: reject linkage at that θ (exclusion). The data are 100 times more likely under no linkage.
In between: inconclusive, collect more families.

Why so strict? Before you look, linkage is unlikely: a randomly chosen marker has only about a 1 in 50 chance of lying close enough to a given gene to show linkage. Odds of 1000 : 1 from the data, against a prior of about 1 : 49, give roughly 20 : 1 in favour, so about a 5 % chance that a “significant” linkage is false. That matches the familiar 5 % level.
Threshold from Morton (1955), Am J Hum Genet (PMID 13258560), who introduced the LOD score for human linkage.

This is the key conceptual slide. The threshold of 3 is not arbitrary: it reflects that most markers are not linked to any given gene, so the prior odds of linkage are low. Multiply the prior odds, roughly 1 to 49, by the likelihood ratio, 1000, and you get posterior odds of about 20 to 1, which is the same as a 5 percent error rate. That is Bayes’ rule in one line; students do not need to name it. The minus 2 threshold is used to exclude a region: if the LOD is below minus 2 for all theta below some value, the gene is not within that distance of the marker. For genome scans with many markers, stricter thresholds such as 3.3 are used; Complex traits in Part 7 meets the same multiple-testing problem in GWAS. The 1 in 50 prior is a rough classical figure; do not over-interpret it.

title: Human linkage & LOD scores
text:
Adding families

Families are independent, so their likelihoods multiply and their LODs add: \text{LOD}_\text{total}(\theta) = \sum_\text{families} \text{LOD}_i(\theta). Five families (invented data), none above 1.8 alone, sum to 6.35 at θ̂ = 3/36 = 0.083.

This is the practical power of the LOD score. Five small families, each inconclusive, together give strong evidence. Add the curves at each theta, then find the maximum of the sum. For phase-known families the total maximum is at total recombinants over total meioses, 3 out of 36. Note one subtlety: you must add the curves first and then take the maximum, not add the individual maxima, because each family peaks at a different theta. The sum of the individual maxima here would be 6.9, which is too high. The demo and R exercise make students do this.

title: Human linkage & LOD scores
text:
Try it: the LOD curve




Start with one family, 10 meioses, 1 recombinant: maximum 1.60 at theta 0.1. Move k to 0: the maximum jumps to 3.01 at theta 0. Move n down to 6 with k 0: 1.81, not enough. Then click “five families”: the thin curves are the families, the thick curve is the sum; max 6.35 at 0.083. Remove families one by one and watch the total drop below 3. Tick “phase ?” on one family to see how much an unknown phase costs. Finally “unlinked marker”: three families with about half recombinants; the curve is never positive and is below minus 2 for theta below about 0.18, so linkage closer than that is excluded.

title: Human linkage & LOD scores
text:
Exclusion: a real example
DRPLA (dentatorubral–pallidoluysian atrophy) is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disease that looks much like Huntington disease. Is it caused by the same gene?
Kondo et al. (1990, J Med Genet, PMID 1969487) typed four DRPLA families for the HD-linked marker D4S10 (probe G8):

The LOD score was negative at all θ, and −2.215 at θ = 0.15.
So the DRPLA gene is not within about 15 cM of D4S10: it is not the HD gene, and DRPLA is a distinct disease.

Negative evidence is useful: exclusion rules out regions, and so narrows the search.

This is a clean, published use of the minus 2 rule. The question was whether DRPLA and HD are allelic, that is, different mutations in the same gene. If they were, DRPLA families would show the same tight linkage to D4S10 that HD families do. Instead the LOD is negative everywhere, and below minus 2 at theta = 0.15, so linkage at that distance or closer is excluded. The DRPLA gene was later found on chromosome 12 (the ATN1 gene, again with an expanded CAG repeat); that is a pointer for curious students, not something to examine.

title: Human linkage & LOD scores
text:
Not yet significant
Youngman et al. (1989, Genomics, PMID 2574148) tested a new marker, D4S90, near the tip of chromosome 4p:

In HD families: maximum LOD 2.14 at θ = 0.00.
2.14 is above 0 (favours linkage) but below 3: “provisional”, not proof.
In reference families, D4S90 mapped 6 cM from D4S10, at the far end of 4p16.3; HD itself lay about 4 cM distal to D4S10.

A LOD of 2 means odds of 100 : 1 from the data, which is still not enough given the low prior. The answer is more meioses.

A real result that sits in the grey zone. Its maximum is at theta = 0, which means no recombinants were seen between HD and D4S90 in the families typed, but there were too few informative meioses to reach 3. Ask: how many more phase-known, non-recombinant meioses would push it over 3? Each adds 0.30, so 3 more. The CEPH reference families mentioned in the abstract are large three-generation families, typed for many markers by labs worldwide, which made the first human genetic maps; they are exactly the “many families” of the previous slides.

title: Human linkage & LOD scores
section: Huntington disease: from linkage to gene
text:
Huntington disease: from linkage to gene

Gusella et al. (1983) “A polymorphic DNA marker genetically linked to Huntington’s disease”, Nature 306:234–238 (PMID 6316146). The 1993 gene: Huntington’s Disease Collaborative Research Group, Cell 72:971–983 (PMID 8458085).

Huntington disease was the first human disease gene mapped with an anonymous DNA marker, with no idea in advance of where it was. The 1983 paper reports that the HD gene is linked to a polymorphic DNA marker on chromosome 4. It was also lucky: very few DNA markers existed at the time, and one of them happened to lie close to the HD gene. Linkage gave the region, but finding the gene took ten more years: more markers, physical maps of 4p16.3, and finally haplotype analysis and exon trapping. The 1993 paper found a new gene, IT15, now called HTT, with a CAG repeat that was expanded on HD chromosomes in all 75 families examined. HTT is the gene students looked up in the Mendel exercise. Today, with a genome sequence, the step from a linked region to the gene is much shorter.

title: Human linkage & LOD scores
text:
The Venezuelan families
Some of the key HD families live in Venezuela: very large extended kindreds with many affected people, studied by Nancy Wexler and a US–Venezuelan collaboration.

By 2004 the Venezuelan kindreds comprised 18 149 individuals over 10 generations (Wexler et al. 2004, PNAS, PMID 14993615).
A large pedigree with many affected people and known phase gives many informative meioses: exactly what a LOD score needs.
Such pedigrees made linkage possible, and later also the study of what modifies age of onset.

Mapping in humans depends on families who agree to take part. That raises ethical questions about consent, about learning one’s own risk, and about benefit to the families, which come back in the Ethics module.

A pedigree of this size is rare and extraordinarily valuable. Huntington disease is autosomal dominant with late onset; most people at risk in such a family do not know whether they carry the allele. The linkage marker immediately made predictive testing possible, years before the gene was known, which raised difficult questions: do you want to know? Many at-risk people chose not to. This is a good place to mention that the Ethics module discusses predictive genetic testing. The 18,149 individuals and 10 generations come from the 2004 PNAS abstract.

title: Human linkage & LOD scores
section: What linkage can and cannot do
text:
What linkage can and cannot do







Linkage analysis is good for
It struggles with




Monogenic diseases with clear inheritance (HD, cystic fibrosis, DMD)
Traits influenced by many genes, each with a small effect


Large families with many affected members
Small families, uncertain diagnosis


Finding the region, often a few cM (millions of bases)
Pinpointing the variant: needs fine mapping and sequencing


Few markers needed (one every ~10 cM)
Incomplete penetrance and phenocopies blur recombinant counts



Cystic fibrosis (CFTR, 1989) and many other disease genes were found this way: linkage first, then the gene. For common diseases, the field moved to association studies (GWAS), which use unrelated people instead of families.

Linkage needs recombinants within families; there are only a few crossovers per chromosome per meiosis, so families localise a gene to a region of a few centimorgans, which in humans is a few million base pairs and can hold dozens of genes. For complex traits, where each gene has a small effect, linkage in families has little power; genome-wide association studies, which exploit very old recombinations in the population (linkage disequilibrium), took over in the 2000s. GWAS is in Complex traits, Part 7. Incomplete penetrance from Extensions to Mendel causes trouble here: an unaffected carrier looks like a recombinant. Real software models penetrance explicitly; we keep full penetrance.

title: Human linkage & LOD scores
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Marker
a DNA variant (RFLP, microsatellite, SNP) used to tell a parent’s homologues apart


Informative meiosis
the parent is heterozygous at the marker and at the disease locus, so the child can be scored R or NR


Phase
which marker allele is on the same homologue as the disease allele; known from grandparents, else average over both (½ each)


Likelihood (phase known)
L(θ) = θk (1 − θ)n−k; maximal at θ̂ = k/n


LOD score
LOD(θ) = log10[L(θ) / L(0.5)]; LOD(0.5) = 0


Thresholds
≥ 3 linkage (odds 1000 : 1); ≤ −2 excluded at that θ


Many families
LODs add at each θ; then find the maximum of the sum


k = 0
LOD(0) = n × 0.301: at least 10 non-recombinant meioses for LOD 3


Huntington
linked to G8 on chromosome 4 in 1983; gene (HTT, CAG repeat) in 1993




If students remember three things: the LOD is a log likelihood ratio comparing linked with unlinked; 3 and minus 2 are the thresholds, and 3 is strict because linkage is unlikely a priori; and LODs add across families. Everything else follows from the binomial.

title: Human linkage & LOD scores
text:
Where this leads

Part 2 complete. From chromosomes (Chromosome theory & sex linkage) through recombination frequencies and maps (Linkage & recombination, Three-point crosses) to human families (today): the same θ throughout.
Genomic variation (Part 4). SNPs and haplotypes: the markers behind modern mapping, and how to find their frequencies in gnomAD.
Complex traits (Part 7). When many genes matter, families are replaced by GWAS in unrelated people, and the LOD threshold of 3 is replaced by a genome-wide p-value threshold.
Ethics. Predictive testing for Huntington disease began with the linked marker.


Close the loop of Part 2. The recombination fraction was measured directly in Drosophila; in humans it is estimated by maximum likelihood. The exercise today: count recombinants in pedigrees by hand, compute LODs, use the demo to add families, find the HTT region in the UCSC Genome Browser and Gusella’s paper in PubMed, and in R write a lod() function and draw the curve.

title: Exercise in R: human linkage & LOD scores
Exercise in R: human linkage & LOD scores
Exercise in R: human linkage & LOD scores
text:
Before you start
This page builds on the by-hand part of the Exercise, so do that first. You need the packages dplyr, ggplot2, purrr, readr and tidyr. Download hd_families.csv and save it in a data/ folder of your R project. The families in it are invented teaching data.
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)
library(readr)
library(tidyr)

title: Exercise in R: human linkage & LOD scores
text:
Tasks
You already know how to write functions with arguments (Mendel, Linkage & recombination) and how to apply a function to a list with map_dbl() (Extensions to Mendel). This unit’s new idiom is to evaluate a function over a grid of parameter values, here θ = 0, 0.01, …, 0.5, to get a curve, and then to find the maximum of that curve, first by looking it up on the grid with which.max(), then exactly with optimize(). optimize(f, interval, maximum = TRUE) searches an interval for the value of x where the one-argument function f(x) is largest, and returns it as $maximum together with the function value $objective.
R1. (the LOD function) Write lod(theta, n, k) for a phase-known family with n informative meioses and k recombinants. Check it against your answers: the family of fig. 1 in the lecture (n = 6, k = 1) at θ = 0.1 gave 0.58, and your B2 family (n = 8, k = 2) gave 0.45 at θ = 0.25. What do you get at θ = 0.5? At θ = 0, with and without recombinants?
lod <- function(theta, n, k) {
  L_theta <- theta^k * (1 - theta)^(n - k)   # likelihood if linked at theta
  L_half  <- 0.5^n                           # likelihood if unlinked
  log10(L_theta / L_half)
}
lod(0.1, n = 10, k = 1)
lod(0.5, n = 10, k = 1)
lod(0, n = 10, k = 1)
lod(0, n = 10, k = 0)
Add your own calls for n = 6, k = 1 and n = 8, k = 2.
R2. (a LOD curve with map_dbl) Make a grid of θ values from 0 to 0.5 in steps of 0.01. Use map_dbl() to compute the LOD for one family (n = 10, k = 1) at every θ, put the result in a tibble, and plot the curve with the thresholds +3 and −2. Where is the maximum?
thetas <- seq(0, 0.5, by = 0.01)
curve1 <- tibble(theta = thetas,
                 lod   = map_dbl(thetas, \(t) lod(t, n = 10, k = 1)))
curve1 |> filter(theta %in% c(0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5))
curve1 |> slice_max(lod)

ggplot(curve1, aes(theta, lod)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(3, -2), linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-3, 3.5)) +
  labs(x = "recombination fraction theta", y = "LOD score",
       title = "One family: 10 meioses, 1 recombinant") +
  theme_minimal()
At θ = 0 the LOD is -Inf; ggplot draws that point at the bottom edge of the panel, which is why the curve drops straight down there.
R3. (adding families) Read data/hd_families.csv (the comment = "#" argument skips the description lines at the top). Keep the phase-known families. Because the arithmetic in lod() works element by element, it accepts whole columns: expand_grid() makes one row per family and θ, and mutate() computes all LODs at once. Then add the families at each θ with group_by(theta) and summarise(). Plot each family and the total.
fams <- read_csv("data/hd_families.csv", comment = "#", show_col_types = FALSE)
fams
known <- fams |> filter(phase == "known")

curves <- expand_grid(known, theta = thetas) |>
  mutate(lod = lod(theta, n, k))
nrow(curves)

total <- curves |>
  group_by(theta) |>
  summarise(lod = sum(lod))
total |> filter(theta %in% c(0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5))

ggplot(curves, aes(theta, lod)) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = family)) +
  geom_line(data = total, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(3, -2), linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-3, 7)) +
  labs(x = "recombination fraction theta", y = "LOD score",
       title = "Five phase-known families and their sum (black)") +
  theme_minimal()
Why is nrow(curves) 255? Does any single family reach 3? Does the total?
R4. (finding θ̂) Find the maximum of the total on the grid with slice_max() and with which.max(). Then write a function total_lod(theta) of θ alone and maximise it exactly with optimize(). Compare θ̂ with total recombinants / total meioses.
total |> slice_max(lod)
total$theta[which.max(total$lod)]

total_lod <- function(theta) sum(lod(theta, known$n, known$k))
best <- optimize(total_lod, interval = c(0, 0.5), maximum = TRUE)
best
sum(known$k) / sum(known$n)
Why does the grid give 0.08 and not the exact value?
R5. (phase unknown) Family F in the file has an unknown phase. Write lod_unknown(theta, n, k), which averages the likelihood over both phases. Compare the known and unknown versions for n = 6, k = 1 at θ = 0.1 and at their maxima. Then add family F to the five others and find the new θ̂ and maximum LOD.
lod_unknown <- function(theta, n, k) {
  L_theta <- 0.5 * (theta^k * (1 - theta)^(n - k) + theta^(n - k) * (1 - theta)^k)
  log10(L_theta / 0.5^n)
}
c(known = lod(0.1, 6, 1), unknown = lod_unknown(0.1, 6, 1))
optimize(\(t) lod(t, 6, 1), c(0, 0.5), maximum = TRUE)$objective
optimize(\(t) lod_unknown(t, 6, 1), c(0, 0.5), maximum = TRUE)$objective

all_lod <- function(theta) total_lod(theta) + lod_unknown(theta, 6, 1)
optimize(all_lod, c(0, 0.5), maximum = TRUE)
R6. (how many meioses?) Use map_dbl() over the family size n this time. (a) For a phase-known family with no recombinants, compute LOD(0) for n = 1, …, 15. Which is the smallest n with LOD ≥ 3? (b) With exactly one recombinant, the maximum is at θ̂ = 1/n. What is the smallest n that reaches 3? (c) And with two recombinants?
ns <- 1:15
tibble(n = ns, lod_at_0 = map_dbl(ns, \(n) lod(0, n, 0))) |> filter(n >= 8)

tibble(n = 10:30, max_lod = map_dbl(10:30, \(n) lod(1 / n, n, 1))) |>
  filter(max_lod >= 3) |> head(1)
tibble(n = 10:40, max_lod = map_dbl(10:40, \(n) lod(2 / n, n, 2))) |>
  filter(max_lod >= 3) |> head(1)

title: Exercise in R: human linkage & LOD scores
text:
Where this leads
The pattern of this page, a function of one parameter evaluated over a grid and then maximised, is maximum likelihood estimation, the workhorse of statistical genetics. You meet curves over a parameter again in Drift and selection (Part 7). In Complex traits (Part 7), GWAS replaces family LOD scores with association tests at hundreds of thousands of SNPs.

title: Linkage & recombination
text:
About this lecture
Mendel’s second law says that alleles of different genes go into gametes independently. That is only true for genes on different chromosomes, or far apart on one. Genes close together on a chromosome are linked: they tend to travel together. Measuring how much they travel together turns out to be a ruler for the chromosome.

Linkage: excess parental types in a testcross. Coupling and repulsion.
Recombination frequency (RF), and where recombinants come from: crossing over at the four-strand stage.
Map distance in centimorgans (cM), and Sturtevant’s first genetic map (1913).
Why RF never exceeds 50%, and map functions (Haldane, Kosambi) that correct for multiple crossovers.
Testing for linkage with the χ² test.

Book: Hartwell, Genetics: From Genes to Genomes, linkage, recombination and mapping chapter.

This unit picks up two threads. From Mendel: the law of independent assortment, which we flagged as needing genes on different chromosomes. From Chromosome theory & sex linkage: genes sit on chromosomes, chromosomes are replicated into two sister chromatids, and homologues pair in prophase I. Put those together and you can predict linkage before seeing any data. The rest of Part 2 builds on today: Three-point crosses uses the same ideas to order three genes at once and to measure interference; Human linkage & LOD scores does the same thing in families, where we cannot set up testcrosses. The R part today is about writing functions with default arguments: two map functions.

title: Linkage & recombination
text:
Independent assortment has exceptions

1905: Bateson, Saunders and Punnett crossed sweet peas differing in flower colour and pollen shape. The F2 was far from 9 : 3 : 3 : 1: the two parental combinations were much too common. They called it coupling (and, for the reverse arrangement, repulsion), without an explanation.
1911: Thomas Hunt Morgan saw the same in Drosophila with X-linked genes, and proposed the explanation: the genes are on the same chromosome, and they are separated only when the homologues exchange segments.

For a dihybrid testcross AaBb × aabb, recall what Mendel predicts:



Unlinked genes (Mendel)
Linked genes




4 classes, 1 : 1 : 1 : 1
4 classes, 2 large + 2 small


50% new combinations
less than 50% new combinations




The sweet pea story is worth telling because it shows how a good observation can sit unexplained for years. Bateson was a champion of Mendel but sceptical of the chromosome theory, and he did not connect coupling to chromosomes. Morgan did, and with his students Sturtevant and Bridges turned it into gene mapping. Recall the testcross from the Mendel unit: the tester gives only recessive alleles, so the offspring classes are a direct readout of the gametes of the dihybrid. That is why all mapping in experimental organisms is done with testcrosses, or crosses that act like them.

A testcross with linked genes
Drosophila: pr (purple eyes) and vg (vestigial wings), both recessive, both on chromosome 2. F1 females from pr+ vg+ / pr+ vg+ × pr vg / pr vg are testcrossed to pr vg / pr vg males.

\text{RF} = \frac{\text{recombinants}}{\text{total}} = \frac{155 + 146}{2620} = 0.115 = 11.5\%
Invented teaching numbers, consistent with the real pr–vg distance in FlyBase.

Read the table as gametes of the F1 mother, because the father only contributes pr vg. The two big classes have the allele combinations the F1 got from its parents: pr+ vg+ from one, pr vg from the other. Those are parental. The two small classes are new combinations, recombinants. Notice that the two parental classes are about equal, and the two recombinant classes are about equal; that is a useful check on your classification. Why F1 females? Drosophila males do not cross over in meiosis, so a testcross of F1 males would give only parental types. That is a quirk of flies, not a general rule, and it is a question in the exercise. The numbers are invented for teaching, but chosen to fit the FlyBase map positions of pr and vg, about 13 cM apart.

title: Linkage & recombination
text:
Coupling and repulsion


Coupling (cis): the two dominant alleles on one homologue, A B / a b.
Repulsion (trans): one dominant allele on each homologue, A b / a B.
“Parental” means as in the chromosomes the F1 received, not “dominant” or “wild type”.


The slash notation separates the two homologues: what is to the left of the slash is on one chromosome, what is to the right on the other. This is the first time in the course that the genotype AaBb is not enough: Ab/aB and AB/ab have the same alleles but different arrangements, called the linkage phase. Same recombination frequency, opposite labels: in repulsion, the wild-type and double-mutant flies are the rare recombinant classes. A quick way to find the parental classes in any data set: they are the two largest classes, as long as the genes are linked. Phase becomes a central problem in human linkage, where we usually do not know it.

title: Linkage & recombination
text:
Recombination frequency
\text{RF} = \frac{\text{number of recombinant offspring}}{\text{total number of offspring}}







RF
Meaning




0
complete linkage: no recombinants at all (genes very close)


between 0 and 0.5
linked: parental types in excess


0.5
unlinked: 1 : 1 : 1 : 1, as for genes on different chromosomes




RF is a property of the pair of genes (and of the organism and sex), not of the cross: coupling and repulsion give the same RF.
RF is measured in gametes. A testcross lets you count them directly.
The larger the distance between two genes on the chromosome, the larger the RF, up to 0.5.


RF of 0.5 is what independent assortment gives: half of the gametes of AaBb are parental (AB, ab) and half are new (Ab, aB). So unlinked genes and genes far apart on the same chromosome look the same in a cross. That is an important point: “unlinked” is a statement about inheritance, not about which chromosome a gene is on. We come back to why RF cannot exceed 0.5 later today. The idea that RF grows with distance is Morgan’s: a longer stretch of chromosome gives more room for an exchange.

title: Linkage & recombination
section: Where recombinants come from: crossing over
text:
Where recombinants come from: crossing over
Recap from Chromosome theory & sex linkage: in prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair. Each is already replicated into two sister chromatids, so the pair (a bivalent) has four chromatids.

Non-sister chromatids can break and rejoin, swapping segments: a crossover.
Under the microscope a crossover is a chiasma (plural chiasmata), where non-sister chromatids cross.
Most chromosome pairs need at least one chiasma to segregate correctly in meiosis I.
Physical proof (1931): Creighton & McClintock in maize, and Stern in Drosophila, used chromosomes with visible marks. Genetic recombinants always carried the physically swapped chromosome.


Janssens described chiasmata in 1909 and suggested they were sites of exchange; Morgan used that to explain linkage. The 1931 experiments are elegant: in maize, one chromosome 9 carried a knob at one end and a piece of another chromosome at the other, so it could be recognised in the microscope. When the genetic markers recombined, the cytological markers recombined too. That tied genetic recombination to a physical exchange between chromosomes. The molecular mechanism, double-strand breaks repaired using the homologue, is beyond this course. One point to keep: crossing over happens between non-sister chromatids, after replication. Next slide.

title: Linkage & recombination
text:
The four-strand stage


A crossover involves 2 of the 4 chromatids. The other two stay parental.
So a meiosis with one crossover between A and B gives 2 parental and 2 recombinant products: 50%, not 100%.
If a fraction f of meioses have one crossover between A and B (and none have two): RF = f / 2.


This is the most common source of confusion in linkage problems, so spend time here. Students often think: a crossover happened, so the gamete is recombinant. No: a crossover makes two of the four meiotic products recombinant. Hence the factor one half. Example: if 20 percent of meioses have a chiasma between A and B, RF is 10 percent and the map distance is 10 cM. Evidence that crossing over happens at the four-strand stage, not before replication, comes from tetrad analysis in fungi, where all four products of one meiosis can be recovered together: tetrads with exactly two recombinant spores are the rule.

title: Linkage & recombination
text:
From RF to map distance
Map unit or centimorgan (cM): the distance in which, on average, 1 crossover per 100 chromatids occurs.

For short distances, a crossover rarely happens twice, so 1 cM ≈ 1% recombinants: pr–vg RF = 11.5% → about 11.5 cM.
Equivalently: d (in morgans) = expected number of crossovers per chromatid = ½ × mean number of chiasmata in the interval.
Map distances add up: if A–B = 5 cM and B–C = 8 cM, then A–C = 13 cM (if B is in the middle).
Additivity gives the gene order: the gene in the middle is the one whose two distances add up to the third.

Named after Morgan; 100 cM = 1 morgan (M).

Two definitions of map distance compete in students’ heads: the percentage of recombinants, which you can measure, and the expected number of crossovers, which is what is additive. They agree for short intervals, and the rest of the lecture is about why they diverge for long ones. The chiasma version: each chiasma involves two of four chromatids, so the expected number of crossovers per chromatid is half the expected number of chiasmata per bivalent. A chromosome arm with one chiasma on average in every meiosis is 50 cM long. Additivity is what makes a map a map: it is the reason the genes can be drawn on a line.

title: Linkage & recombination
text:
Sturtevant’s first genetic map (1913)

Alfred Sturtevant, an undergraduate in Morgan’s lab, put five X-linked genes in order using his own and others’ crosses: y – w – v – m – r. The order still holds. Data: J. Exp. Zool. 14: 43–59 (1913).

Sturtevant was still an undergraduate. He realised, in his own words, that the percentage of crossovers could be used as an index of distance, and he spent most of a night making the map. He used neighbouring intervals to build it and added them up, exactly as on the previous slide: yellow to white 1.0, white to vermilion 29.7, vermilion to miniature 3.0, and vermilion to rudimentary 26.9, which puts rudimentary at 57.6. Then he checked the long distances directly. Yellow to rudimentary came out at 37.6 percent, not 57.6, and he guessed the reason: double crossing over. He even saw that the long intervals are measured less precisely. We use his real numbers in the R exercise. The letters in his paper are different from modern symbols: B, C and O, P, R, M stand for y, w, v, m and r.

title: Linkage & recombination
text:
Why RF can never exceed 50%


Two crossovers between A and B can involve 2, 3 or 4 of the chromatids, and on average give 50% recombinants.
More generally: a chromatid is recombinant for A and B if it has an odd number of crossovers between them, and parental if even (0, 2, 4…).
As the distance grows, odd and even become equally likely, so RF → 0.5. A double crossover inside the interval is invisible with two markers.


The key fact is the last bullet: what matters for a chromatid is whether it has an odd or even number of crossovers between the two loci. Two crossovers on the same chromatid swap the middle segment and swap it back, so the outer markers look parental. The figure shows the four equally likely kinds of double crossover, assuming that each crossover picks its two chromatids at random (no chromatid interference). Average: two of four products recombinant. Long intervals have many crossovers, odd and even become equally likely, and RF levels off at one half. This is why unlinked genes and genes far apart on the same chromosome look the same. The demo shows it moving.

RF underestimates long distances




Map distance (sum of short intervals)

Sturtevant (1913). Short distances: RF ≈ map distance. Long distances: RF falls below the map distance, because double crossovers are missed.
Rule: build maps from short intervals, then add. Never read a long RF directly as map distance.

These are Sturtevant’s own numbers. The first two rows are short intervals and agree by construction. The middle row is fine too. The last two are long, and RF is well below the sum of the intervals. Note also that the w–r and y–r numbers do not agree well with each other, although y and w are only 1 cM apart. The samples behind them are small, 898 and 693 flies; a long distance is measured less precisely. Even Sturtevant’s intervals of about 30 cM were already long enough to hide some double crossovers, which is one reason modern positions are a bit larger: FlyBase puts vermilion at 33 and rudimentary at 54. The exercise has students look these up.

title: Linkage & recombination
text:
Map functions: Haldane
A map function converts between map distance d (in morgans) and RF. Haldane (1919) assumed crossovers occur independently, at random along the chromosome (a Poisson process).

Number of crossovers on a chromatid in the interval: Poisson with mean d.
Recombinant if that number is odd: P(odd) = ½(1 − e−2d).

\text{RF} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(1 - e^{-2d}\right) \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad d = -\tfrac{1}{2}\ln(1 - 2\,\text{RF})



d

0.10 M
0.50 M

RF (Haldane)
0.010

Back the other way: y–r, RF = 0.376 → d = −½ ln(1 − 0.752) = 0.70 M = 70 cM.

Haldane’s derivation in one line: if the number of crossovers k is Poisson with mean d, the probability that k is odd is one half times one minus e to the minus 2d. You do not need to derive it; you do need to use it in both directions, with a calculator. At small d, e to the minus 2d is about 1 minus 2d, so RF is about d: map distance and RF agree for short intervals, as they should. At large d, the exponential vanishes and RF goes to one half. Applied to Sturtevant’s y–r value, Haldane gives 70 cM, more than his 57.6 from adding intervals. That overshoots, and the reason is the next slide.

title: Linkage & recombination
text:
Map functions: Kosambi, and interference




Real crossovers are not independent: one crossover makes another one nearby less likely. This is interference, measured properly in Three-point crosses.
Kosambi (1944) allows for interference:
\text{RF} = \tfrac{1}{2}\tanh(2d) d = \tfrac{1}{4}\ln\frac{1 + 2\,\text{RF}}{1 - 2\,\text{RF}}
y–r: Kosambi gives 49 cM, Haldane 70 cM, the sum of intervals 57.6 cM.

All three agree for short intervals. They differ only when RF is large.

The graph shows the three relationships. The dashed line is RF equals d, valid only without multiple crossovers. Haldane is the lowest curve: with independent crossovers, doubles are most common. Kosambi lies between: with interference, double crossovers are rarer, so RF stays closer to d for longer. Sturtevant’s two long pairs, the orange points labelled w–r and y–r, sit near or between the curves, and the three short ones lie a little above the dashed line, which says his map slightly underestimated those distances. Kosambi is the usual choice for plant and animal maps; Haldane is common in human genetics software. Which is right depends on the organism. The practical message: use a map function only for moderate RF; above about 0.35 the answer is very sensitive to the function and to sampling noise. In R today you write both functions, with Haldane as the default.

title: Linkage & recombination
text:
Demo: crossovers and saturation




The demo draws one bivalent, with crossovers placed at random (Poisson, no interference) and each crossover joining a random blue and a random red chromatid. Press “1 meiosis” a few times: point out that a single crossover between A and C makes two of the four products recombinant, and two crossovers can give zero, two or four. Then press “+1000”: the table shows RF for each pair of loci next to Haldane’s prediction and d/100. A–B and B–C at 25 cM come out near 0.20 (Haldane 0.197), but A–C at 50 cM comes out near 0.32, not 0.40, the sum of the two RFs, and not 0.50. Turn on “simulate the curve”: the grey points follow Haldane and level off at one half. Finally set spacing to 80: A–C is 160 cM apart, and RF is indistinguishable from 0.5, as for genes on different chromosomes.

title: Linkage & recombination
text:
Testing for linkage with χ²
Is an excess of parental types real, or chance? Use the χ² test from Probability & the χ² test.

First check that each gene alone segregates 1 : 1 (otherwise poor viability of one class can mimic linkage).
Then test parental vs recombinant against 1 : 1 (H0: unlinked, RF = 0.5), with df = 1.

Example (invented): testcross, 50 offspring: 15 A B, 17 a b, 9 A b, 9 a B.

Gene A: 24 A : 26 a; gene B: 24 B : 26 b. Both fine.
Parental 32, recombinant 18, expected 25 : 25.

\chi^2 = \frac{(32-25)^2}{25} + \frac{(18-25)^2}{25} = 3.92, \quad \text{df} = 1, \quad p = 0.048
Just significant at 5%: weak evidence for linkage, RF ≈ 18/50 = 0.36. More offspring would settle it.

Why not just test all four classes against 1:1:1:1 with three degrees of freedom? Because a deviation from 1:1:1:1 can have three causes: linkage, or one gene segregating unequally (for example because the mutant flies survive less well), or both. The 1-df parental versus recombinant test isolates linkage. Testing each gene first is good practice. In the pr vg example the test is overwhelming: chi-square is over 1500. In real mapping the problem is the opposite: loosely linked genes, RF 0.35 to 0.45, need hundreds of offspring to separate from 0.5. In humans, where families are small, the χ² approach does not work at all, and we need LOD scores, in Human linkage & LOD scores.

title: Linkage & recombination
text:
Real maps: some facts

Sex differences. Drosophila males have no meiotic crossing over: their genes are completely linked. That is why mapping crosses use F1 females. In humans the female map is roughly one and a half times longer than the male map.
cM is not bp. In humans, about 1 cM ≈ 1 Mb on average, but crossovers cluster in hotspots, and are rare near centromeres.
Same chromosome ≠ linked. Genes more than about 50 cM apart on one chromosome assort (nearly) independently. y and r on the Drosophila X are about 54 cM apart in FlyBase.
Uses. Gene order and distance; finding markers close to a gene of interest, for plant and animal breeding and for human disease genes.


These are the facts that make linkage maps different from physical maps. A genetic map measures how often crossovers happen, not how many base pairs there are, so it stretches where crossovers are frequent and shrinks where they are rare. The fly male oddity is real and useful: a male fly’s chromosomes pass on intact. Mendel’s seven traits are a nice illustration of the third point: some of his genes are on the same pea chromosome, but far enough apart to assort independently. The last bullet points ahead: in human genetics, linkage to a nearby DNA marker was how disease genes such as HTT were first located, the topic of the last unit in this part.

title: Linkage & recombination
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Linkage
genes close on one chromosome: parental combinations in excess, RF < 0.5


Coupling / repulsion
A B / a b vs A b / a B: same RF, opposite parental classes


Recombination frequency
RF = recombinants / total offspring of a testcross


Crossing over
between non-sister chromatids at the four-strand stage; one crossover → 2 of 4 products recombinant


Map distance
1 cM = 1 crossover per 100 chromatids; ≈ 1% RF for short distances; distances add


RF ≤ 0.5
recombinant ⇔ odd number of crossovers; multiple crossovers make RF level off at ½


Haldane
RF = ½(1 − e−2d), d = −½ ln(1 − 2RF); independent crossovers


Kosambi
RF = ½ tanh(2d); allows for interference


χ² for linkage
check 1 : 1 per gene, then parental vs recombinant against 1 : 1, df = 1




The revision sheet. The three ideas that do most of the work: recombinants are the small classes; one crossover gives half recombinant products; and RF is a saturating function of distance, so map from short intervals and add. The formulas for the map functions are worth knowing in both directions.

title: Linkage & recombination
text:
Where this leads

Next: Three-point crosses. With three genes in one testcross, the double crossovers become visible: they give the gene order at once, and show whether crossovers interfere with each other.
Human linkage & LOD scores. In human families there are no testcrosses and few offspring. The LOD score asks how much more likely the data are under linkage than under RF = 0.5, and maps disease genes such as HTT.
Rearrangements & aneuploidy (Part 5): inversions suppress recombination in heterozygotes, and a chromosome without a crossover can missegregate.
Complex traits (Part 7): genome-wide association is linkage thinking on a population scale.


Point forward. Today’s exercise: testcross problems on paper, the crossover demo, FlyBase map positions for the classic X-linked markers, and in R two map functions with a default argument, applied to Sturtevant’s original data. Three-point crosses is the natural next step: Sturtevant himself already noticed that one crossover tends to prevent another nearby, which is interference.
