Before you start
This page builds on the by-hand part of the Exercise, so do that first. You need the packages dplyr, purrr, readr and ggplot2. Download sturtevant1913.csv and save it in a data/ folder of your R project.
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)

title: Exercise in R: linkage & recombination
text:
Tasks
The new idiom today is a function argument with a default value. In function(d, method = "haldane"), d must always be given, but method can be left out: then it is "haldane". You can still write method = "kosambi" to override it. match.arg() checks that the value is one of the allowed choices and stops with a clear error message otherwise (try cM_to_rf(10, "kosambo")). Many R functions you already use work like this: chisq.test(x, p = ...) has a default p (equal proportions), and mean(x, na.rm = FALSE) a default na.rm.
You met map_dbl() in Extensions to Mendel: map_dbl(xs, f) calls f once for each element of xs and returns the results as a numeric vector. Inside it, \(x) ... is a short function of one argument x.

R1. RF from a testcross
The testcross from the lecture (pr and vg in Drosophila; invented numbers):
testcross <- tibble(
  phenotype = c("wild type", "purple vestigial", "purple", "vestigial"),
  genotype  = c("pr+ vg+ / pr vg", "pr vg / pr vg", "pr vg+ / pr vg", "pr+ vg / pr vg"),
  type      = c("parental", "parental", "recombinant", "recombinant"),
  n         = c(1170, 1149, 155, 146)
)
testcross

testcross |>
  group_by(type) |>
  summarise(n = sum(n)) |>
  mutate(fraction = n / sum(n))
What is the RF? Then change testcross to the maize data of B1 in the exercise and check your answer.


R2. Two map functions, with a default
Write two functions that convert between map distance in centimorgans and RF. Both have the argument method, with Haldane as the default.
cM_to_rf <- function(d, method = "haldane") {
  method <- match.arg(method, c("haldane", "kosambi"))
  m <- d / 100                       # centimorgans -> morgans
  if (method == "haldane") {
    0.5 * (1 - exp(-2 * m))
  } else {
    0.5 * tanh(2 * m)
  }
}

rf_to_cM <- function(rf, method = "haldane") {
  method <- match.arg(method, c("haldane", "kosambi"))
  if (method == "haldane") {
    m <- -0.5 * log(1 - 2 * rf)
  } else {
    m <- 0.25 * log((1 + 2 * rf) / (1 - 2 * rf))
  }
  100 * m                            # morgans -> centimorgans
}

cM_to_rf(10)                         # method left out: Haldane
cM_to_rf(10, method = "kosambi")
cM_to_rf(c(1, 10, 50, 100, 200))     # works on a whole vector
rf_to_cM(0.115)                      # pr-vg
rf_to_cM(0.115, "kosambi")           # arguments can also be given by position
rf_to_cM(cM_to_rf(37))               # there and back again
rf_to_cM(0.5)
Check your answers to B6 in the exercise with these functions. Why does rf_to_cM(0.5) give Inf?


R3. Plot the map functions with map_dbl()
Compute RF for every distance from 0 to 200 cM with both functions. For Kosambi, the extra argument goes inside a short function \(x) cM_to_rf(x, method = "kosambi").
curves <- tibble(d = 0:200) |>
  mutate(haldane = map_dbl(d, cM_to_rf),
         kosambi = map_dbl(d, \(x) cM_to_rf(x, method = "kosambi")))
curves |> filter(d %in% c(5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200))

ggplot(curves, aes(x = d)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = d / 100, colour = "RF = d (no double crossovers)"), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(aes(y = haldane, colour = "Haldane")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = kosambi, colour = "Kosambi")) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dotted") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 0.6)) +
  labs(x = "map distance d (cM)", y = "recombination frequency",
       colour = NULL, title = "Two map functions") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
Up to which distance do the three lines agree to within 0.01?


R4. Sturtevant’s 1913 data
The file sturtevant1913.csv has Sturtevant’s real counts: for each pair of X-linked genes, the number of recombinant flies and the total. His map put y at 0.0, w 1.0, v 30.7, m 33.7 and r 57.6. Compute the RF for each pair, the map distance from his map, and the distance that each map function gives for the measured RF.
sturtevant <- read_csv("data/sturtevant1913.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
map_1913 <- c(y = 0, w = 1.0, v = 30.7, m = 33.7, r = 57.6)

sturtevant |>
  mutate(rf         = recombinant / total,
         map_dist   = abs(map_1913[gene2] - map_1913[gene1]),
         haldane_cM = rf_to_cM(rf),
         kosambi_cM = rf_to_cM(rf, method = "kosambi")) |>
  select(gene1, gene2, rf, map_dist, haldane_cM, kosambi_cM) |>
  arrange(map_dist) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
map_1913[gene2] looks up each gene’s map position by name in the named vector. For which pairs do RF and map distance agree? For y–r, which map function comes closer to Sturtevant’s 57.6?


R5. Simulate crossovers: where Haldane comes from
If crossovers happen independently, the number of crossovers on one chromatid in an interval of d cM is a Poisson random number with mean d/100. rpois(n, lambda) draws n such numbers. The chromatid is recombinant if the number is odd: k %% 2 == 1 (%% is the remainder after division).
set.seed(1)
table(rpois(10, lambda = 0.5))       # 10 chromatids, 50 cM

sim_rf <- function(d, n = 10000) {
  crossovers <- rpois(n, lambda = d / 100)   # crossovers on one chromatid, between the loci
  mean(crossovers %% 2 == 1)                 # recombinant if the number is odd
}

set.seed(1913)
sim <- tibble(d = seq(10, 200, by = 10)) |>
  mutate(simulated = map_dbl(d, sim_rf),
         haldane   = cM_to_rf(d))
sim |> filter(d %in% c(10, 50, 100, 150, 200))

ggplot(sim, aes(x = d)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = haldane), colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(aes(y = simulated)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(x = "map distance d (cM)", y = "recombination frequency",
       title = "Simulated (points) and Haldane (line)") +
  theme_minimal()
sim_rf also has a default argument, n = 10000. Call sim_rf(50, n = 100) a few times: how much does the answer vary? Why does the simulation match Haldane’s curve and not Kosambi’s?


R6. Testing for linkage with chisq.test()
A testcross gives 15 A B, 17 a b, 9 A b and 9 a B (the lecture example). First check that each gene segregates 1 : 1, then test parental against recombinant.
gene_A   <- c(A = 15 + 9,  a = 17 + 9)
gene_B   <- c(B = 15 + 9,  b = 17 + 9)
par_rec  <- c(parental = 15 + 17, recombinant = 9 + 9)

chisq.test(gene_A)$p.value           # default p: equal proportions
chisq.test(gene_B)$p.value
chisq.test(par_rec)

chisq.test(c(parental = 1170 + 1149, recombinant = 155 + 146))
chisq.test() uses its own default here: without p =, it tests against equal proportions, which is exactly 1 : 1. Then check B7 in the exercise.

title: Quiz: genetics as information
text:
Short questions on the vocabulary and ideas of the first lecture. Try each one on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. What is the difference between a gene, an allele and a locus? Use HBB and sickle-cell disease in your answer.






Hint





One is an address, one is what lives there, and one is a version of it.









Answer





The locus is the position on the chromosome (for HBB, band 11p15.4 on chromosome 11). The gene is the DNA sequence at that position that encodes a product (HBB, encoding β-globin). An allele is one version of the gene: HbA (normal) and HbS (sickle) are two alleles of HBB.




Q2. A person has the genotype HbA/HbS. Are they homozygous or heterozygous at HBB? How many different HBB alleles can one person carry at most, and why?






Hint





How many copies of chromosome 11 does a body cell have?









Answer





Heterozygous: the two alleles differ. One person carries at most two alleles at an autosomal locus, because a diploid cell has two copies of each autosome, one from each parent. A population can contain many more alleles than two.




Q3. “Huntington disease is caused by a dominant allele, so it must be common.” What is wrong with this statement?






Hint





Does dominance say anything about how many people carry the allele?









Answer





Dominance describes what the heterozygote looks like: if Aa shows the same phenotype as AA, then A is dominant. It says nothing about the frequency of the allele in the population. The Huntington allele is dominant and rare. Allele frequencies are a question for population genetics.




Q4. In sickle-cell disease, one base change in HBB changes codon 6 from GAG to GTG. Which amino acid change does this cause, and why does it make the haemoglobin behave differently?






Hint





Look up GAG and GTG in the genetic code. One of the two amino acids is charged, the other hydrophobic.









Answer





GAG codes for glutamate (Glu, negatively charged) and GTG for valine (Val, hydrophobic). The valine sits on the surface of the protein and makes a sticky patch, so deoxygenated HbS molecules stick together into long fibres that distort the red cell into a sickle shape.




Q5. Is the sickle allele HbS dominant, recessive or codominant to HbA? Explain why there is more than one correct answer.






Hint





Compare the heterozygote with the two homozygotes for (a) disease, and (b) the types of haemoglobin found in the blood.









Answer





For the disease, HbS is recessive: HbA/HbS carriers are usually healthy, and only HbS/HbS has the disease. For the haemoglobin protein, the alleles are codominant: a heterozygote makes both HbA and HbS, and both appear on a gel. Dominance is defined for one phenotype at a time, so the answer depends on which phenotype you look at.




Q6. A database search lists HBB with the organism “Homo sapiens”, and Hbb-bs with “Mus musculus”. Why is one written in capitals and the other not? Are they the same gene?






Hint





Gene naming conventions differ between species. “Same gene” in two species has a technical name.









Answer





Human gene symbols are written all in capitals; mouse symbols have only the first letter capitalised. Both are β-globin genes, but because the β-globin cluster has duplicated separately in different mammal lineages, the mouse genes do not pair one-to-one with human HBB. Genes in different species that descend from one ancestral gene are orthologs; for HBB the relationship is complicated by duplications (paralogs). For a clean one-to-one example, see human CFTR and mouse Cftr.




Q7. The human genome is about 3,100 Mb with about 20,000 protein-coding genes. The axolotl genome is about 29,000 Mb with about 24,000 protein-coding genes. Compute the genes per Mb for each. What explains the difference?






Hint





Divide genes by Mb. Then think about what fills the rest of a large genome.









Answer





Human: \(20{,}000 / 3{,}100 \approx 6.5\) genes per Mb. Axolotl: \(24{,}000 / 29{,}000 \approx 0.8\) genes per Mb, about eight times fewer. The axolotl does not have many more genes; its genome is larger because it has more non-coding DNA, mostly repeated sequences such as transposable elements, and very long introns. This is the C-value paradox: genome size does not follow gene number or complexity.




Q8. Why can we learn about a human disease gene by studying a mouse, a zebrafish or even a fly?






Hint





What is an ortholog, and what tends to happen to the function of a gene over evolution?









Answer





Many genes are conserved: the human gene has an ortholog in the model organism that descends from the same ancestral gene and often has a similar function. For example, human CFTR and mouse Cftr are one-to-one orthologs whose proteins are about 79% identical. Model organisms can be crossed, mutated and studied in ways that are impossible in humans, and the results often carry over.




Q9. Which of the four approaches (transmission, molecular, genomic, population) is each study using?

Counting how many children of two carriers have sickle-cell disease.
Sequencing HBB to find the GAG→GTG change.
Comparing the frequency of HbS in regions with and without malaria.
Comparing the whole genomes of human and mouse to find shared genes.







Hint





Ask what is being measured: offspring of crosses, one gene’s DNA or protein, whole genomes, or allele frequencies in groups.









Answer






Transmission (inheritance in families). b. Molecular (one gene’s DNA). c. Population (allele frequencies in groups). d. Genomic (whole genomes).





Q10. A fly with white eyes carries two copies of the mutant allele w. The normal red-eyed allele is written w+. What does the “+” mean, and what does the name of the white gene tell you about how it was discovered?






Hint





Is the white gene needed to make white eyes or red eyes?









Answer





The “+” marks the wild-type allele, the standard allele in laboratory stocks. The gene is named after its mutant phenotype: it was found because flies lacking a working copy had white eyes. The working gene is in fact needed to make red eyes.

title: Exercise: genetics as information
Exercise: genetics as information
Exercise: genetics as information
text:
Background
Recap from 5MO103. Information flows DNA → RNA → protein → phenotype. A gene is a DNA segment that encodes a functional product. Its position on a chromosome is its locus.
Vocabulary.

An allele is one version of a gene. A diploid individual carries two alleles at each autosomal locus.
Genotype: the alleles carried, e.g. AA, Aa, aa. Phenotype: what is observed or measured.
Homozygous: two identical alleles. Heterozygous: two different alleles.
Wild type (w+): the standard allele in a lab population. Mutant: a changed allele.
If Aa has the same phenotype as AA, then A is dominant and a is recessive for that phenotype. In this unit we assume complete dominance; Extensions to Mendel adds the other cases.

Sickle-cell disease. The human gene HBB (chromosome 11) encodes β-globin. In the sickle allele HbS, codon 6 changes from GAG to GTG, and glutamate (Glu) becomes valine (Val). Databases count the start methionine too, so they write this change as c.20A>T, p.Glu7Val.
Genomes. Genome size (in megabases, Mb = 106 bp) varies more than 10,000-fold across life, but the number of protein-coding genes varies far less. Most of a large genome is non-coding: introns, intergenic DNA, repeats such as transposable elements. Some genomes are also large because of polyploidy.
Orthologs are genes in different species that descend from one gene in their common ancestor. Paralogs arise by duplication within one genome.

text:
Find it
These are your first database tasks. Take them slowly and check the organism every time: searching a gene symbol gives hits in many species.
F1. NCBI Gene: HBB. Go to NCBI Gene. Type HBB human in the search box and press Search. In the results table, click the row where the Name/Gene ID is HBB and the Organism is Homo sapiens.

Under “Also known as”, which familiar name for the protein do you see?

F2. Ensembl: HBB. Go to Ensembl. Choose Human in the species box, type HBB and press Go. Click the gene result HBB (Human Gene). On the gene page:

F3. CFTR: chromosome and mouse ortholog. a. In NCBI Gene, search CFTR human and open the Homo sapiens entry. On which chromosome is CFTR, and what is its cytogenetic location? What is the official full name? b. In Ensembl, open human CFTR. In the left-hand menu, under Comparative Genomics, click Orthologues. Find Mouse in the table. What is the mouse gene called? What type of orthology is it (the “Type” column, e.g. 1-to-1)? What is the “Target %id”? c. Click the mouse gene. On which mouse chromosome is it?
F4. (optional) The Alliance of Genome Resources: is there a CFTR in fly or yeast? Go to the Alliance of Genome Resources, search CFTR and open the Homo sapiens gene. Scroll to Orthology.

With the default (stringent) filter, which species are listed?
Change the stringency filter to the least strict setting (“No filter”/“All”). Do any fly (D. melanogaster) or yeast (S. cerevisiae) genes appear? How many prediction methods support them?
What does this tell you about whether fly or yeast has a true CFTR ortholog?

title: Exercise: genetics as information
text:
Hints






Hint B3: counting codons and nucleotides





Write the sequence in triplets and number the codons 1, 2, 3, … from ATG. Codon n covers nucleotides \(3n-2\) to \(3n\). So nucleotide 20 is in codon 7 (nucleotides 19–21). Codon 7 counting the Met is amino acid 6 without the Met.









Hint B7: orthologs and paralogs





Find the node in the tree where two genes last shared an ancestor. If that node is a speciation (the human–mouse split), the genes are orthologs. If it is a duplication, they are paralogs.









Hint F1–F3: finding your way in NCBI Gene and Ensembl





In NCBI Gene, the search result is a table with columns Name/Gene ID, Description, Location and Organism. The Location column already shows the cytogenetic band. In Ensembl, the gene page has a left-hand menu; Orthologues is under Comparative Genomics. If you land on a “Search results” page, make sure you click a Gene result for Human.

title: Exercise: genetics as information
text:
Solutions






Solutions: By hand





B1. a. w+/w+: homozygous, red eyes. b. w+/w: heterozygous, red eyes (w+ is dominant). c. w/w: homozygous, white eyes. w+ is the wild type; w is the mutant.
B2. “HBB is a gene at a locus on chromosome 11. HbA and HbS are two alleles of it. A person with the genotype HbS/HbS has the phenotype sickle-cell disease.”
B3. a. ATG GTG CAT CTG ACT CCT GAG GAG AAG → Met Val His Leu Thr Pro Glu Glu Lys. b. Without Met: Val(1) His(2) Leu(3) Thr(4) Pro(5) Glu(6) Glu(7) Lys(8). Amino acid 6 is glutamate. c. Nucleotides 19–21 are codon 7 (GAG), so nucleotide 20 is the A in the middle of GAG. A→T gives GTG, which codes for Val. The protein becomes Met Val His Leu Thr Pro Val Glu Lys. Traditional name: Glu6Val; database name: c.20A>T, p.Glu7Val (the same change, counted with the Met).
B4. c.19 is the first base of codon 7 (GAG). G→A gives AAG, which codes for Lys. The change is p.Glu7Lys (traditionally Glu6Lys). This is the haemoglobin C allele; ClinVar lists NM_000518.4(HBB):c.19G>A (p.Glu7Lys).
B5. Disease row: the heterozygote looks like HbA/HbA, so HbS is recessive for disease. Gel row: the heterozygote shows both bands, so the alleles are codominant for the haemoglobin protein. It is not a contradiction because dominance is a statement about one phenotype. Each allele makes its own protein (codominance at the protein level), but half normal haemoglobin is enough to avoid disease under normal conditions (recessive at the level of disease).
B6. a. E. coli: \(4{,}290 / 4.6 \approx 933\) genes per Mb. Yeast: \(6{,}021 / 12.1 \approx 498\). Human: \(20{,}054 / 3{,}099.4 \approx 6.5\). b. \(20{,}054 / 933 \approx 21.5\) Mb, which is less than 1% of the real 3,099 Mb. c. Introns, large intergenic regions, and repeated sequences (especially transposable elements), plus centromeres, telomeres, regulatory DNA and genes for non-coding RNAs.
B7. a. The tree has a duplication node at the root (G → G1, G2). Below each of G1 and G2 is a speciation node (human, mouse). b. Orthologs: human G1–mouse G1, and human G2–mouse G2 (they last shared an ancestor at the speciation). Paralogs: human G1–human G2, mouse G1–mouse G2, and also human G1–mouse G2 and human G2–mouse G1 (their last common ancestor is the duplication). c. The mouse would have a single gene G. Both human G1 and human G2 would be orthologs of mouse G: a one-to-many (in Ensembl, “1-to-many”) orthology. Human G1 and G2 would be paralogs of each other. This is roughly what has happened in the β-globin cluster, which is why there is no simple 1-to-1 mouse ortholog of human HBB.
B8. a. Transmission, human families (a pedigree or family study). b. Molecular/transmission genetics in yeast: a fast, single-celled organism where thousands of mutants can be screened. (A genomic screen, testing every gene, also fits.) c. Molecular, in the mouse: knock out the Cftr ortholog and look at the phenotype. The mouse is a mammal with lungs and a gut similar to ours. d. Population, in humans: compare HbS allele frequencies between populations.









Solutions: Find it





All facts checked in November 2026 (NCBI Gene; Ensembl release 116 on GRCh38; Alliance of Genome Resources).
F1. NCBI Gene, HBB. Click path: NCBI Gene → search HBB human → row HBB, Homo sapiens → Gene ID 3043. a. Official full name: hemoglobin subunit beta. b. Gene ID: 3043. c. Chromosome 11. d. Location 11p15.4: “p” is the short arm of chromosome 11 (“q” is the long arm), and 15.4 is the band (region 1, band 5, sub-band 4) counted outwards from the centromere. HBB lies near the tip of the short arm. e. Also known as: beta-globin (other aliases listed are CD113t-C and ECYT6). The gene has 3 exons.
F2. Ensembl, HBB. Click path: Ensembl → Human → HBB → Go → HBB (Human Gene) → ENSG00000244734. a. ENSG00000244734. b. Chromosome 11: 5,225,464–5,229,395, reverse strand (GRCh38). The gene is read from right to left on the standard chromosome map. c. In release 116 the transcript table lists 19 transcripts (most protein-coding, some “nonsense mediated decay” or “retained intron”). Your number may differ in a later release, which is why we note the release. Many extra transcripts come from new long-read evidence; most of the protein is made from one main transcript. d. HBB-201 (ENST00000335295) is the MANE Select and Ensembl canonical transcript. It matches RefSeq NM_000518.5 and encodes 147 aa (146 aa in the mature chain, after the start Met is removed).
Optional observation: if you open Orthologues for HBB, Ensembl lists orthologs in many species, but no mouse gene. The β-globin genes duplicated separately in the primate and rodent lineages, so mouse Hbb-bs and Hbb-bt do not pair one-to-one with human HBB (compare B7c). That is why F3 uses CFTR for the mouse ortholog.
F3. CFTR. a. Click path: NCBI Gene → CFTR human → Gene ID 1080. Chromosome 7, location 7q31.2 (long arm). Official full name: CF transmembrane conductance regulator (the older name “cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator” is still widely used). b. Click path: Ensembl → Human → CFTR → ENSG00000001626 → Comparative Genomics → Orthologues → Mouse. The mouse gene is Cftr (ENSMUSG00000041301). Type: 1-to-1. Target %id: about 79% (78.7% in release 116), meaning about 79% of the mouse protein’s amino acids are identical to the aligned human ones. c. Mouse Cftr is on mouse chromosome 6 (GRCm39). Chromosome numbers are not shared between species.
F4. Alliance of Genome Resources. Click path: alliancegenome.org → search CFTR → CFTR (Homo sapiens, HGNC:1884) → Orthology. a. With the stringent default filter, only vertebrates are listed: zebrafish cftr, mouse Cftr, rat Cftr, and frog (Xenopus tropicalis cftr; X. laevis cftr.L and cftr.S). b. With no filter, many fly and yeast genes appear: in fly a gene actually named Cftr, plus Mrp4, Mrp5, Sur and several CG-numbered genes; in yeast YOR1, YCF1, STE6, YBT1 and others. Each is supported by only one or two prediction methods (e.g. Ensembl Compara, PANTHER), against about ten for the mouse ortholog. c. Fly and yeast have related ABC-transporter genes, the same protein family as CFTR, but no high-confidence one-to-one ortholog. Gene families are conserved across all eukaryotes; a specific member like CFTR may only be clearly traceable among vertebrates.

Where this leads
The next unit, Mendel, uses the vocabulary from today to predict what happens when two heterozygotes are crossed (Aa × Aa), first by hand and then by simulating the cross in R. You will look up the HBB gene again in Mutation (its variants in ClinVar) and in Hardy–Weinberg (allele frequencies).
Next: Exercise in R: read genome data into R, compute genes per Mb, and plot genome size against gene number on log scales.

title: Basic and molecular genetics
text: Course material for Basic and molecular genetics (5MO104, 15 ECTS, Umeå University). The material follows the course book, Hartwell et al., Genetics: From Genes to Genomes. On top of the genetics, every unit trains you to find information in public databases and to analyse it in R.

title: Basic and molecular genetics
text:
Where to start

Learning outcomes: what we are trying to teach.
Install R and the packages you need: do this before the first exercise.
Glossary: the terms used in the course.

title: Basic and molecular genetics
text:
How each unit works
Work through the sidebar from top to bottom. Each unit has:

a lecture (slides, in green);
a quiz (in blue) to check that you understood the concepts;
an exercise, in this order:

By hand: genetics problems on paper.
Explore: an interactive demo (in orange).
Find it: look up real genes, diseases and variants in public databases.

an exercise in R: a small analysis or simulation that builds on the exercise.

title: Basic and molecular genetics
text:
Topics

Part 1: Mendelian genetics. Genes and alleles, Mendel’s laws, probability and the χ² test, extensions to Mendel (dominance, lethality, epistasis, penetrance), and pedigree analysis.
Part 2: Chromosomes and mapping. Meiosis, sex linkage and nondisjunction; linkage and recombination; three-point crosses; human linkage and LOD scores.
Part 3: DNA, mutation and gene function. DNA and replication (recap), mutation and complementation, and gene expression (recap).
Part 4: Genome analysis. Restriction enzymes, PCR and sequencing; genome annotation and BLAST; genomic variation across populations.
Part 5: Chromosomes in detail. Chromatin, centromeres and telomeres; rearrangements and aneuploidy; bacterial genetics (recap); mitochondrial and chloroplast inheritance.
Part 6: Gene regulation and development. The lac operon as genetic analysis; eukaryotic regulation, epigenetics and X inactivation; RNA-mediated regulation; development and model organisms.
Part 7: Cancer, populations and complex traits. Cancer genetics; Hardy–Weinberg; drift and selection; heritability and GWAS.
Ethics. Genetic testing, privacy, germline editing, and ethical review of research.

See Canvas for the most up-to-date study instructions.

title: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
text:
About this lecture
So far we followed alleles through one family. Now we follow them through a whole population: what fraction of people carry each allele and each genotype?

Allele and genotype frequencies, and how to count them.
The Hardy–Weinberg principle: random mating turns allele frequencies p and q into genotype frequencies p², 2pq, q², and keeps them there.
Its assumptions, and the χ² test for HWE (df = 1).
The de Finetti triangle, a picture of all possible populations.
Uses: carrier frequencies from disease incidence (the 1/50 from the pedigrees unit), X-linked traits, and inbreeding (F).

Book: Hartwell, the population genetics chapter. You need the product rule and the χ² test from Part 1.

This unit starts population genetics, which runs for the next two units. The key shift is from the Punnett square of one cross to the “Punnett square of a population”, where the gametes come from a pool. Students have already used the result: in the pedigrees unit, the 1/50 carrier frequency was promised to come from Hardy–Weinberg. Today we deliver it. HWE is also a null model: like 3:1 in Mendel’s crosses, it is what we expect when nothing interesting is happening, and departures tell us something about the population. The next unit, Drift and selection, is about the forces that make populations depart from it.

title: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
text:
Allele and genotype frequencies
The MN blood group has two codominant alleles, M and N, so every genotype can be seen. A classic textbook sample of 6129 people:

Allele frequencies: count alleles, two per person.

p = f(M) = \frac{2 \times 1787 + 3039}{2 \times 6129} = \frac{6613}{12258} = 0.540, \qquad q = f(N) = 1 - p = 0.460.

Shortcut: p = f(MM) + ½ f(MN) = 0.292 + 0.248 = 0.540.

Two kinds of frequency, and students mix them up. A genotype frequency counts people; an allele frequency counts gene copies, two per person. Homozygotes contribute two copies of their allele, heterozygotes one of each. Codominance matters here only because it lets us see every genotype; with a dominant allele we could not count the heterozygotes directly, which is exactly why HWE is useful for recessive diseases. The numbers are from a classic textbook sample; we test them for HWE later in the lecture and in the demo.

title: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
section: Random mating: the population’s Punnett square
text:
Random mating: the population’s Punnett square


If gametes meet at random, an egg carrying A (probability p) meets a sperm carrying A (probability p) with probability p², by the product rule.
So the genotype frequencies are **p_² : 2_pq : _q_²**, and they add up to (p + q)² = 1.
The allele frequency in the next generation is p² + pq = p: unchanged.


This is the whole derivation. The product rule from the probability unit does all the work: two independent draws from a gene pool. The heterozygote appears twice, A from the egg and a from the sperm or the other way round, which is the source of the 2. The last line is the important one: random mating does not change the allele frequency. Hardy, a mathematician, wrote this in 1908 to answer the question why dominant alleles do not spread until they take over the population: they do not, because dominance changes how a genotype looks, not how often an allele is passed on. Weinberg found it independently the same year.

title: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
text:
The Hardy–Weinberg principle
In a large, randomly mating population with no selection, mutation or migration:

Genotype frequencies are **p_², 2_pq, _q_², after one** generation of random mating, whatever they were before.
Allele and genotype frequencies then stay constant from generation to generation.

Note what it does not say:

It does not say p = q = 0.5. Any p can be in equilibrium.
It does not say a dominant allele becomes common. Dominance affects phenotypes, not allele frequencies.
It is a null model: like 3:1 in a cross, it is what we test against.


Emphasise point 1: one generation is enough, which is very different from most equilibria in nature. Take a population made by mixing pure AA and aa: no heterozygotes at all. After one round of random mating, genotypes are p squared, 2pq, q squared. The demo shows this with the Mendel F2 preset: an F2 is one generation of random union of gametes and sits exactly on the HWE curve. The misconception that dominant alleles become common is very widespread; ask the class for a counterexample: Huntington disease is dominant and rare, and blood group O is recessive and common in many populations.

title: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
text:
Rare alleles hide in heterozygotes


For a rare allele, almost all copies are in heterozygotes: at q = 0.1 there are 18 carriers for every aa person; at q = 0.01, about 200.
So selection against a rare recessive phenotype removes very few copies. This is why recessive disease alleles persist (next unit).
Heterozygote frequency 2pq is highest, 0.5, at p = q = 0.5.


Read the plot at q equals 0.1. The orange curve is at 0.18, the red one at 0.01. The ratio 2pq over q squared is 2p over q, about 2 over q for rare alleles. At q equals 0.01 that is about 200 carriers per affected person. This matters for medicine: carrier screening finds far more people than disease screening. It matters for evolution: even if every aa person died, the allele frequency would fall only very slowly, because selection cannot see the carriers. Mention eugenics here briefly: early twentieth-century proposals to remove recessive diseases by sterilising affected people would have had almost no effect on allele frequencies, exactly for this reason.

In real human populations these are rarely all true, yet most loci are close to HWE: the forces are weak at most loci, and one generation of random mating restores the proportions.

Random mating is with respect to this locus. People choose partners by height or language, but not by their MN blood group, so MN is in HWE even though mating is not random overall. Of the six rows, only non-random mating and population structure act on genotype frequencies directly while leaving allele frequencies alone; the other four change allele frequencies and are the subject of the next unit. The final point surprises students: if all the assumptions are false, why does HWE fit? Because most forces are weak per generation, and one generation of random mating is enough to reset the genotype proportions to match the current allele frequencies.

title: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
text:
Testing HWE with χ²
TCF7L2 SNP rs7903146 in 99 people of north-west European ancestry (CEU, 1000 Genomes): 52 CC, 32 CT, 15 TT.

p = (2 × 52 + 32)/198 = 0.687, q = 0.313.
Expected: 99 × 0.687² = 46.7, 99 × 2 × 0.687 × 0.313 = 42.6, 99 × 0.313² = 9.7.
χ² = (52 − 46.7)²/46.7 + (32 − 42.6)²/42.6 + (15 − 9.7)²/9.7 = 6.1.
df = 3 − 1 − 1 = 1: three classes, minus 1 because the counts add up to N, minus 1 because p was estimated from the same data.
p = 0.013 < 0.05: reject HWE at the 5% level? Fewer heterozygotes than expected (F = 0.25).

But we tested 15 SNP–population pairs in the exercise; one at p ≈ 0.01 is roughly what chance gives. More on this in GWAS.

Go step by step; this is the χ² from Part 1 with one new idea, the lost degree of freedom. In Mendel’s crosses the expected ratio came from theory, so df was the number of classes minus one. Here p is estimated from the same counts, and each estimated parameter costs one degree of freedom, leaving 1. The critical value at 5% with df 1 is 3.84. The data are real: from the 1000 Genomes CEU sample, via Ensembl. Is this population really out of HWE? Probably not: in the R exercise students test 15 SNP–population pairs, and with 15 tests at 5% we expect about 0.75 false rejections. This is the multiple-testing problem that returns with the 5 times 10 to the minus 8 threshold in the complex traits unit. Another sample of the same population would likely not reject.

title: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
text:
The de Finetti triangle


Every population is a point: horizontal position = q, height = frequency of Aa. The corners are pure AA, pure Aa and pure aa.
Populations in HWE lie on the parabola f(Aa) = 2pq.
Below the parabola: too few heterozygotes (inbreeding, population structure). Above: too many (heterozygote advantage, mixing of two distinct populations in one generation, genotyping errors).


The triangle is a compact way to see all three genotype frequencies at once. Each point inside an equilateral triangle has three distances to the sides that add up to the height; those are the three genotype frequencies. In practice it is easiest to read it as in the slide: q along the base, heterozygote frequency as the height. The vertical distance to the parabola measures the departure, and the inbreeding coefficient F is that distance as a fraction of 2pq. The point at F equals 1 lies on the base: no heterozygotes, as in a set of fully inbred lines.

title: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
text:
Demo: the de Finetti triangle




The demo starts at inbreeding F equals 0.25 with p equals 0.5. Drag the point onto the parabola: χ² falls to 0. Drag it up: excess heterozygotes. Then change N without moving the point: χ² grows in proportion to N. The same departure from HWE is invisible in 20 people and overwhelming in 1000. For the HWE test, χ² is in fact exactly N times F squared. Try the Mendel F2 preset: it sits on the parabola at its top.

SS people (sickle-cell disease) are missing from samples of healthy adults: selection acts on genotypes, so HWE fails for this locus among adults.
The χ² test is weak here: the expected counts are small (< 5). The direction is still informative.
Why is HbS common at all? Heterozygote advantage against malaria: next unit.


This connects the HBB thread of the course to populations. In both 1000 Genomes samples, there are no SS individuals at all, while HWE predicts one or two in each. That alone is weak evidence, but gnomAD, with tens of thousands of people, shows the same deficit clearly: about 9 observed against about 39 expected. Two reasons: sickle-cell disease shortens life, especially without treatment, and sequencing projects of adult cohorts often exclude people with severe childhood disease. Either way, the population of adults is not a random sample of the zygotes formed at fertilisation. HWE applies at conception, before selection. Ask: what would you expect at birth? Close to HWE. Note the χ² caveat: with expected counts below 5, the χ² approximation is poor; an exact test would be used in practice.

Population structure: the Wahlund effect
SLC24A5 rs1426654 (a pigmentation SNP): the A allele is almost fixed in Europe and rare in Africa.

Each population on its own is close to HWE. Pooling populations with different p gives far too few heterozygotes.
No inbreeding is involved: people mate within populations, so the pooled “population” does not mate at random.
Lesson: test HWE within a population, and remember that hidden structure looks like inbreeding.


This is the Wahlund effect, named after the Swedish geneticist Sten Wahlund, who described it in 1928. Mixing two populations, one mostly AA and one mostly GG, gives many homozygotes of both types and few heterozygotes, compared with what the pooled allele frequency predicts. The pooled sample has F equals 0.67, which looks like heavy inbreeding, but it is pure structure. The same effect causes false associations in GWAS if cases and controls come from populations with different ancestry: a point we come back to in the complex traits unit.

title: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
text:
X-linked genes


Males are hemizygous: the frequency of affected males is the allele frequency q.
Females follow HWE: q² affected, 2pq carriers.
So an X-linked recessive trait is about 1/q times more common in males. For red–green colour blindness (q ≈ 0.08), about 8% of men but under 1% of women.


This links back to the pedigrees unit, where X-linked recessive traits were mostly seen in males. Hardy–Weinberg makes it quantitative. Males show the allele directly, so male incidence is the best estimate of q. Females need two copies. The colour-blindness numbers are typical textbook values for northern European men; frequencies vary between populations. For a rare X-linked disease such as haemophilia A, with q around 1 in 5000 males, affected females are vanishingly rare, about q squared.

title: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
text:
Carrier frequency from disease incidence
The pedigrees unit assumed a carrier frequency of 1/50 for PKU. Where does it come from?

\text{incidence} = q^2 = \frac{1}{10\,000} \;\Rightarrow\; q = \frac{1}{100}, \qquad 2pq = 2 \times 0.99 \times 0.01 \approx 0.0198 \approx \frac{1}{50}.


For a rare allele, carrier frequency ≈ 2q = 2√incidence.
Cystic fibrosis in north-west Europe, incidence about 1 in 2500 births: q ≈ 1/50, carriers ≈ 1/26.
Check in gnomAD: CFTR F508del (rs113993960) has allele frequency 0.014 in non-Finnish Europeans (carriers ≈ 1/35; F508del is not the only CF allele), but only 0.0015 in Finns.


This is the slide that pays off the promise from the pedigrees unit. The calculation assumes HWE for the disease locus, which is reasonable: selection against a rare recessive disease barely affects genotype proportions at conception. It also assumes all disease alleles act as one allele; for CF, F508del is the commonest of many alleles, which is why its own frequency gives a lower carrier rate than the incidence. The Finnish value is a teaser for the next unit: CF is rare in Finland, while some other recessive diseases are much more common there. That is the founder effect.

title: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
section: Inbreeding and the inbreeding coefficient F
text:
Inbreeding and the inbreeding coefficient F
F = the probability that the two alleles in a person are identical by descent: copies of one ancestral allele. With inbreeding, genotype frequencies become

f(AA) = p^2 + Fpq, \qquad f(Aa) = 2pq(1-F), \qquad f(aa) = q^2 + Fpq.


Heterozygotes fall by a factor (1 − F); the missing ones become homozygotes. Allele frequencies do not change.
Child of first cousins: F = 1/16 (pedigrees unit). Selfing plants approach F = 1.
The rarer the allele, the bigger the effect on aa:

F has two readings. As a probability: the chance that a person’s two alleles at a locus are copies of the same ancestral allele. As a summary of genotype data: one minus observed over expected heterozygosity. In a population with inbreeding, both readings give the same number. The table shows why consanguinity matters most for very rare recessive diseases: when q is 0.001, almost every affected child of first cousins got both copies from a shared ancestor. Keep the tone neutral: in many countries cousin marriage is common and most children are healthy; the absolute risk increase is small for any one disease. The pedigrees unit computed the same thing for a single family.

title: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
text:
What HWE is used for

Estimating carrier frequencies for genetic counselling and screening.
Checking data: in genome-wide genotyping, SNPs that depart strongly from HWE in healthy controls are often genotyping errors and are removed before a GWAS.
Detecting forces: departures point to selection, population structure or inbreeding.
A starting point for population genetics: the next unit asks what happens when the assumptions fail.


Quality control is a very practical use that students will meet if they ever analyse genotyping data: a SNP assay that cannot tell heterozygotes from homozygotes shows a huge heterozygote deficit, and HWE filtering removes it. The usual threshold is very strict, such as p below 10 to the minus 6, because with a million SNPs some will fail HWE by chance. In cases, a departure could be a real association, which is why the filter is applied in controls.

title: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
text:
Summary

Allele frequency: count gene copies, p = f(AA) + ½ f(Aa).
Random mating gives **p_², 2_pq, _q_²** in one generation, and keeps p constant. Dominance does not change allele frequencies.
Assumptions: random mating, large population, no selection, mutation or migration, one population.
χ² test for HWE: expected counts from the estimated p, df = 1.
Rare alleles are mostly in carriers: carrier frequency ≈ 2√incidence (PKU: 1/10 000 → 1/50).
X-linked: males affected at q, females at q².
Inbreeding (F) and population structure (Wahlund) both give a heterozygote deficit; heterozygote advantage can give an excess.


The three numbers to remember: p squared, 2pq, q squared; df equals 1; and carrier frequency about 2 times the square root of the incidence. Students should be able to do the χ² test for HWE by hand in an exam.

title: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
text:
Where this leads

Next: Drift, selection, mutation, migration: what happens to p when the assumptions fail, including why HbS is common where malaria is.
Complex traits: HWE filters in GWAS quality control; population structure as a source of false associations.
In the exercise: HWE by hand, the de Finetti demo, real genotype counts from 1000 Genomes and gnomAD, and an hwe_test() function in R applied to many SNPs with pmap.


Today we kept p constant. Next time we let it move. The sickle-cell example will return as heterozygote advantage, and the Finnish CF value as the founder effect.

Exercise in R: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
Exercise in R: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
text:
Before you start
This page builds on the by-hand part of the Exercise, so do that first. You need the packages dplyr, purrr, tidyr, readr and ggplot2. Download hwe_snps.csv and save it in a data/ folder of your R project.
The file holds genotype counts for 7 SNPs in 1000 Genomes phase 3 populations, downloaded from the Ensembl REST API (release 116, endpoint /variation/human/<rsid>?population_genotypes=1) on 20 November 2026. allele_A is the reference allele on the forward strand of GRCh38 and allele_a the other allele; the source column records the query. Population codes: GBR British, FIN Finnish, CEU Utah residents of north-west European ancestry, YRI Yoruba, GWD Gambian, CHB Han Chinese, ALL all 26 populations pooled.

title: Exercise in R: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
text:
Tasks
New idiom today: pmap. In Extensions to Mendel you used map_dbl(xs, f) to call a function once for each element of one list. pmap(list(a, b, c), f) walks along several vectors in parallel and calls f(a[1], b[1], c[1]), then f(a[2], b[2], c[2]), and so on. Inside mutate, the vectors are columns, so pmap calls f once per row. If f returns a one-row tibble, the result is a list-column of tibbles, which tidyr::unnest spreads into ordinary columns.
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)

A function for the HWE test
R1. Write hwe_test(nAA, nAa, naa). It should compute N, p, the three expected counts, χ², the p-value with pchisq(chisq, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE), and F = 1 − Hobs/Hexp, and return them as a one-row tibble. Test it on the MN blood group sample (1787, 3039, 1303) and on the “excess heterozygotes” preset of the demo at N = 200 (40, 140, 20), and compare with the exercise.
hwe_test <- function(nAA, nAa, naa) {
  n <- nAA + nAa + naa
  p <- (2 * nAA + nAa) / (2 * n)
  q <- 1 - p
  obs <- c(nAA, nAa, naa)
  expd <- n * c(p^2, 2 * p * q, q^2)
  chisq <- sum((obs - expd)^2 / expd)
  tibble(n = n, p = p,
         exp_AA = expd[1], exp_Aa = expd[2], exp_aa = expd[3],
         chisq = chisq,
         p_value = pchisq(chisq, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE),
         F = 1 - (nAa / n) / (2 * p * q))
}
hwe_test(1787, 3039, 1303)   # MN blood group
hwe_test(40, 140, 20)        # excess heterozygotes


Many SNPs at once
R2. Read data/hwe_snps.csv. Use pmap inside mutate to run hwe_test on every row, and unnest the result. Show gene, population, N, p, χ², the p-value and F, rounded. Which SNP–population pairs depart from HWE at the 5% level?
snps <- read_csv("data/hwe_snps.csv")
snps |> select(rsid, gene, population, n_AA, n_Aa, n_aa)

results <- snps |>
  mutate(test = pmap(list(n_AA, n_Aa, n_aa), hwe_test)) |>
  unnest(test)

results |>
  select(gene, population, n, p, chisq, p_value, F) |>
  mutate(across(c(p, chisq, F), \(x) round(x, 3)),
         p_value = format.pval(p_value, digits = 2, eps = 1e-300))
R3. Look more closely at the two kinds of departure. (a) For HBB (rs334, HbS), compare the observed and expected numbers of HbS homozygotes (n_aa and exp_aa). (b) List the rows with p < 0.05, with observed and expected heterozygotes. For each one, decide whether it is most likely chance, population structure, or selection. How many rejections at the 5% level would you expect among 15 tests if every population were in HWE?
results |> filter(gene == "HBB") |> select(population, n_aa, exp_aa)
results |> filter(p_value < 0.05) |> select(gene, population, n_Aa, exp_Aa, F, p_value)


A de Finetti triangle in ggplot2
R4. Draw the triangle, the HWE parabola and one point per SNP–population pair, at x = q and y = nAa/N. Colour the points by whether HWE is rejected. coord_fixed(ratio = sqrt(3) / 2) makes the triangle equilateral. check_overlap = TRUE drops labels that would overlap.
tri <- tibble(x = c(0, 1, 0.5, 0), y = c(0, 0, 1, 0))
parab <- tibble(q = seq(0, 1, by = 0.01), H = 2 * q * (1 - q))
pts <- results |>
  mutate(q = 1 - p, H = n_Aa / n, label = paste(gene, population))

ggplot() +
  geom_path(data = tri, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_line(data = parab, aes(q, H), colour = "darkgreen") +
  geom_point(data = pts, aes(q, H, colour = p_value < 0.05), size = 2.5) +
  geom_text(data = pts, aes(q, H, label = label), size = 2.8, vjust = -0.8,
            check_overlap = TRUE) +
  annotate("text", x = c(-0.03, 1.03, 0.5), y = c(-0.04, -0.04, 1.04),
           label = c("AA", "aa", "Aa")) +
  coord_fixed(ratio = sqrt(3) / 2) +
  labs(x = "frequency of allele a (q)", y = "frequency of heterozygotes Aa",
       colour = "reject HWE (p < 0.05)") +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")


Carriers and inbreeding
R5. Write carrier_freq(incidence) that returns 2pq for a recessive disease of a given incidence. Apply it to PKU (1/10 000), cystic fibrosis (1/2500) and a rare disease (1/100 000) in one call. Show the answers as “1 in …”.
carrier_freq <- function(incidence) {
  q <- sqrt(incidence)
  2 * q * (1 - q)
}
incidence <- c(PKU = 1/10000, CF = 1/2500, rare = 1/100000)
round(carrier_freq(incidence), 4)
round(1 / carrier_freq(incidence))
R6. Make a tibble with q = 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001, and compute f(aa) under random mating and for a child of first cousins (F = 1/16), and their ratio. Compare with E3 in the exercise.
inbreeding <- tibble(q = c(0.1, 0.01, 0.001)) |>
  mutate(random = q^2,
         cousins = q^2 + (1/16) * (1 - q) * q,
         ratio = cousins / random)
inbreeding

title: Exercise in R: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
text:
Where this leads
pmap + a function that returns a tibble is a general pattern: one analysis per row of a table. In Drift, selection we turn from testing a population at one moment to following p over many generations, with a for loop.

title: Genomic variation
text:
About this lecture
The reference genome from the last unit is one genome. No living person has exactly that sequence. This lecture is about the differences: what kinds there are, how we find them in thousands of people, and why some alleles are common in one part of the world and rare in another.

Kinds of variant: SNPs, indels, microsatellites (STRs) and copy-number variants (CNVs).
Naming a variant: rs numbers, HGVS names, and the strand problem.
Haplotypes and linkage disequilibrium (LD).
Genotyping by arrays vs sequencing; the big databases: dbSNP, 1000 Genomes, gnomAD.
Population differences, with two case stories: lactase persistence and the sickle-cell allele and malaria.
Personal genomics: what a consumer genome test can and cannot tell you.

Book: Hartwell, Genetics: From Genes to Genomes, chapter on variation between individual genomes.

This closes Part 4. The genetics leads: variants are alleles, and everything from Part 1 (dominance, segregation, pedigrees) applies to them. What is new is the scale: we can now see millions of alleles in thousands of people. The two case stories are chosen because they connect molecular genetics, population genetics and human history, and because students have met HBB and rs334 in every unit of this part. The exercise looks up both variants in gnomAD, Ensembl and dbSNP; the R part downloads allele frequencies from Ensembl and joins them with a population table.

title: Genomic variation
text:
How different are two genomes?







Comparison
Differences




Two unrelated people
about 1 SNP per 1,000 bp, so a few million SNPs


One person vs the reference genome (1000 Genomes)
4.1–5.0 million sites: mostly SNPs, plus indels and structural variants


Variants in a typical genome that change a protein
about 10,000 amino-acid changes; on the order of 100 that break a gene (loss of function)


Human vs chimpanzee
about 1.2% of aligned bases (SNPs only)



Most variants are neutral: in introns or between genes, or silent. A few change a protein (like HbS) or gene regulation (like lactase persistence).

The numbers give a sense of scale. The 4.1 to 5.0 million figure comes from the final 1000 Genomes Project paper (2015); the range reflects ancestry, because the reference genome is mostly from a few people, and people of African ancestry, with the most genetic diversity, differ from it at the most sites. The loss-of-function point is surprising to students: a healthy person typically carries some broken genes, mostly heterozygous and mostly in genes where one working copy is enough. That is the recessive carrier state from Part 1, at genome scale. The chimp number is often misquoted; it is about 1.2 percent of single bases in aligned regions, and more if indels are counted.

title: Genomic variation
text:
Kinds of variant










Type
Size
Mutation rate
Example




SNP (SNV)
1 bp
~10−8 per bp per generation
HbS, rs334


Indel
1–50 bp
lower than SNPs
CFTR F508del


STR (microsatellite)
1–6 bp unit, repeated
10−3–10−4 per locus
HTT CAG repeat; forensic markers


CNV
1 kb to Mb

AMY1 (salivary amylase) copy number




SNP strictly means a single-nucleotide variant common enough to be a polymorphism (often defined as at least 1 percent); SNV is the general term including rare ones. Indels inside a coding sequence cause frameshifts unless their length is a multiple of three, as in F508del, which removes one phenylalanine. Microsatellites mutate by polymerase slippage during replication, a thousand to ten thousand times faster than SNPs, so they have many alleles per locus. That made them the markers of choice for linkage mapping in the 1990s (the LOD-score unit in Part 2) and for forensic DNA profiles today. Expansions of some trinucleotide repeats cause disease: Huntington disease, met in the Mendel unit, appears with 40 or more CAG repeats in HTT. CNVs cover more base pairs in total than SNPs. A well-studied example is AMY1: populations with traditionally starch-rich diets have, on average, more copies of the salivary amylase gene.

title: Genomic variation
text:
Naming a variant
The sickle-cell variant has several names, and you need to recognise them all:







Name
Meaning




rs334
dbSNP reference SNP number: a stable ID for the position, whatever the alleles


NC_000011.10:g.5227002T>A
genomic: chromosome 11 (GRCh38), position 5,227,002, T → A on the plus strand


NM_000518.5:c.20A>T
coding: position 20 of the HBB coding sequence, A → T on the gene’s strand


p.Glu7Val (traditionally Glu6Val)
protein: glutamate 7 → valine (counting the start Met)



HBB lies on the minus strand, so the plus-strand T>A and the coding A>T are the same change. Databases such as gnomAD and Ensembl list alleles on the plus strand; check the strand before you compare.

This slide prevents a lot of confusion in the exercise. dbSNP gives each variant position an rs number; rs334 covers several possible alleles at that base (T to A is HbS; T to C and T to G are other, rare variants). HGVS names say exactly which sequence they are relative to. The c. numbering starts at the A of the ATG start codon; p. numbering counts the start methionine, which is why HbS is p.Glu7Val in HGVS but Glu6Val in the older haemoglobin literature, as noted in Genetics as information. The same strand issue applies to the lactase SNP: the literature calls it LCT minus 13910 C to T, on the gene’s strand, while Ensembl and gnomAD list rs4988235 as G to A on the plus strand.

title: Genomic variation
text:
Haplotypes and linkage disequilibrium


A haplotype is the set of alleles on one chromosome. Nearby alleles are inherited together unless a crossover separates them.
Linkage disequilibrium (LD): alleles at nearby sites are associated in a population. It decays with distance and with time.


LD is linkage (Part 2) seen at population level. In a family, linkage means that alleles close together on a chromosome go into the same gamete unless there is a crossover between them. In a population, over many generations, crossovers gradually break up the associations, but between very close sites they rarely happen, so the associations survive. Walk through the figure: the new mutation appears on one chromosome, so at first it is always found with that chromosome’s alleles. Each generation, crossovers swap in other chromosome stretches at the ends. After many generations only a short stretch around the mutation is still shared by all carriers. A young allele that rose fast because of selection, such as lactase persistence, sits on an unusually long shared haplotype, which is one of the ways selection is detected.

title: Genomic variation
text:
Why LD matters

Tag SNPs. Within an LD block, one SNP predicts its neighbours. A genotyping array with ~0.5–1 million SNPs captures much of the common variation of a genome.
Association studies (GWAS). A SNP associated with a trait may not be the cause itself; it may be in LD with the causal variant nearby. (Complex traits, Part 7.)
Mapping, old and new. Linkage (Part 2) uses crossovers in families, a few per chromosome per meiosis, so it locates genes to a few Mb. LD uses the crossovers of thousands of generations, so it narrows the region down to kb.
Ancestry. LD and haplotypes differ between populations; the longest LD blocks are in populations that went through bottlenecks.


The practical point is tagging: you do not need to genotype every SNP, because many are redundant. That is what makes cheap genotyping arrays work, and why GWAS hits are regions rather than single bases. The comparison with Part 2 is worth making explicitly: a LOD-score study in a few families sees only the crossovers in those meioses, so it can only say that the gene is somewhere in a region of several megabases. A population sample implicitly contains the crossovers of all the ancestors, so association can be much finer. Populations of African ancestry have the shortest LD blocks, because they have the longest history at large population size; populations that passed through bottlenecks, such as the Finns, have longer blocks.

title: Genomic variation
text:
Genotyping: arrays vs sequencing










SNP array
Exome sequencing
Whole-genome sequencing




What is read
~0.5–2 million known SNPs
the ~1–2% of the genome that codes for protein
(almost) all 3.1 Gb


Finds new or rare variants
no
yes, in exons
yes, everywhere


Indels, STRs, CNVs
poorly
some
yes (best with long reads)


Typical use
consumer tests, GWAS, ancestry
rare disease diagnosis
research, clinical genomics, gnomAD


Cost
lowest
middle
highest (falling)



An array can only find what it was designed to look for. A disease variant that is rare or private to one family needs sequencing.

Arrays work by hybridisation: each spot carries probes for the two alleles of one known SNP, and the sample DNA lights up one or both. They are cheap and accurate for common SNPs, which is why direct-to-consumer companies use them. Their weakness is the flip side: they cannot see variants they were not designed for, and they are unreliable for very rare variants even if a probe exists. Exome sequencing targets the coding part, where most known disease-causing variants lie, which is why it became the first-line test for rare monogenic diseases. Whole-genome sequencing is becoming cheap enough to replace both. The coverage concept from Digital analysis of DNA applies: a heterozygote is called when enough reads show each allele.

title: Genomic variation
text:
The variation databases



Database
What it holds
Use it for




dbSNP (NCBI)
catalogue of known variants with rs numbers
the ID, position and HGVS names of a variant


1000 Genomes
2,504 people from 26 populations in 5 continental groups
frequencies in well-defined populations (also in Ensembl)


gnomAD
about 730,000 exomes and 76,000 genomes (v4)
frequencies in genetic ancestry groups; how rare is this variant?


ClinVar (NCBI)
variants with a clinical interpretation
is this variant pathogenic?


Ensembl / UCSC
all of the above on the genome
context: gene, consequence, LD



A variant’s population frequency is key evidence in diagnostics: an allele that is common in healthy people cannot cause a rare, severe, dominant disease.

These are the databases of the Find it tasks. 1000 Genomes is small but carefully sampled by population, which is why we use it in R: each sample comes from a defined population such as the Yoruba in Ibadan (YRI) or the Finnish (FIN). gnomAD is much larger but groups people by genetic ancestry; it is the standard reference for how rare a variant is. The last sentence is the most important clinical use of population data: if a variant is found in one percent of healthy people in gnomAD, it cannot be the cause of a disease that affects one in a million, unless penetrance is very low. Ethics: these databases hold data from real people, which raises questions about consent and re-identification that the ethics module returns to.

title: Genomic variation
text:
Allele frequencies differ between populations


About 85–90% of human genetic variation is found within any population; only a small part separates populations.
But some alleles differ sharply. The causes: genetic drift (chance, strongest in small populations), migration, and natural selection.


The figure is drawn from the same Ensembl data that students use in R: each dot is one of the 26 populations of the 1000 Genomes Project. Make the first point before the second, because students easily over-interpret differences: Lewontin showed in 1972 that most variation is within populations, and genome data confirm it. Two people from the same population differ at nearly as many sites as two people from different continents. But for a few alleles, frequency differences are large, and those are interesting because drift alone rarely produces such large differences at a single locus while the rest of the genome stays similar. Selection is the usual explanation, as in the two stories that follow. Drift, selection and migration are treated quantitatively in Part 7.

title: Genomic variation
text:
Lactase persistence








Population (1000 Genomes)
rs4988235 A (= LCT −13910T)
Expected lactase persistent (1 − (1 − q)2)




Utah, N. and W. European ancestry (CEU)
0.74
0.93


British (GBR)
0.72
0.92


Finnish (FIN)
0.59
0.83


Toscani, Italy (TSI)
0.09
0.17


Yoruba, Nigeria (YRI); Han Chinese (CHB)
0
0




The variant lies in an intron of the neighbouring gene MCM6, about 14 kb upstream of LCT, in an enhancer that keeps LCT on in adults. A regulatory variant, not a protein change.
Persistence is dominant: one T allele is enough, so phenotype frequency is 1 − (1 − q)2 (assuming Hardy–Weinberg proportions, Part 7).
Herding populations in East Africa and the Middle East have other persistence alleles in the same enhancer.


The frequencies are from the R data (Ensembl REST, 1000 Genomes phase 3). The north–south gradient within Europe, 74 percent in CEU but 9 percent in Tuscany, is striking and matches the distribution of lactase persistence measured with lactose-tolerance tests. Do not overclaim the calculation: it assumes random mating, which is the Hardy–Weinberg unit in Part 7; here it is just the product rule from Part 1 applied to two alleles. The absence of the European allele in the Yoruba sample does not mean that no Africans are lactase persistent: several East African pastoralist populations carry different variants, for example −14010 G to C, which are not in the 1000 Genomes populations. This convergent evolution is strong evidence for selection: the same phenotype evolved several times where milk was drunk.

title: Genomic variation
text:
Sickle cell and malaria

The HbS allele (rs334 A) reaches 0.10–0.14 in the West and East African 1000 Genomes samples (YRI, ESN, MSL, GWD, LWK), is lower in the African-diaspora samples (ACB, ASW) and is absent from the European and East Asian samples.

This is the classic example of balancing selection. HbS/HbS is sickle-cell disease, which before modern medicine was usually fatal in childhood, so selection removes HbS alleles. But HbA/HbS carriers are protected against severe falciparum malaria, so where malaria is common they survive better than HbA/HbA people, and selection also keeps HbS alleles in the population. The equilibrium frequency depends on the balance between these two costs. The geographic distribution of HbS matches the historical range of malaria; similar stories exist for HbC, the thalassaemias and G6PD deficiency. In the diaspora populations in Barbados and the US, HbS is at lower frequency because of admixture and because malaria selection stopped. The quantitative treatment, with fitness values and the equilibrium formula, is in the drift and selection unit in Part 7. With q = 0.14 in YRI, about 24 percent of people are carriers and about 2 percent of births have sickle-cell disease, if genotypes follow Hardy–Weinberg proportions; students compute this in R.

title: Genomic variation
section: Variants and families: back to pedigrees
text:
Variants and families: back to pedigrees
Population frequencies feed directly into the risk calculations of Part 1:

Carrier probability of a partner. For a recessive disease with allele frequency q, a random partner is a carrier with probability about 2q: for HbS in YRI (q = 0.14), 2 × 0.14 × 0.86 ≈ 0.24.
Risk for a child of a known carrier and a random partner: ¼ × 0.24 = 0.06.
Interpreting a new variant in a family: is it in gnomAD? At what frequency? Does it co-segregate with the disease in the pedigree?

The same variant can be common and protective in one setting and a cause of disease in another: genotype and environment together make the phenotype.

This links the population view back to the pedigree unit, where the probability that an unrelated partner was a carrier was often just given. Now students can look it up. Use the 2pq approximation (Part 7 gives the justification); for rare alleles it is about 2q. The second bullet multiplies the probability that the partner is a carrier by the one-quarter risk of a carrier-by-carrier cross. The third bullet is how clinical geneticists classify variants of uncertain significance: rarity in population databases, segregation in the family, predicted effect on the protein. It sets up the ethics module’s discussion of what to tell patients about uncertain findings.

title: Genomic variation
text:
Personal genomics







A consumer genome test (array) can tell you
It cannot tell you




your genotype at known common SNPs (e.g. rs4988235, rs671, rs12913832)
rare or private variants in your genes (unless sequenced)


carrier status for some common recessive alleles
that you are not a carrier of every allele of a disease


ancestry estimates by comparison with reference populations
a single “true” ancestry: results depend on the reference panels


relatives who used the same service
your risk of complex diseases with certainty: effects are small, and environment matters



Your genome is also partly your relatives’ genome, and it is hard to make anonymous. These are questions for the ethics module.

Bring it to the students’ own lives. The SNPs from the R exercise are typical consumer-test SNPs: lactase persistence, alcohol flush (ALDH2 rs671, common in East Asia, where the A allele reduces the activity of the enzyme that breaks down acetaldehyde), eye colour (HERC2 rs12913832, which affects OCA2 expression). The limits are the array limits from two slides back, plus interpretation: most traits are complex (Part 7) and each SNP explains little. A negative carrier result on an array only covers the alleles on the array. Privacy: because relatives share half their genome, a person who uploads their data also reveals information about relatives who did not consent; consumer databases have been used to identify suspects via distant relatives. The ethics module takes this up.

title: Genomic variation
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Kinds of variant
SNP (1 bp), indel (1–50 bp), STR (repeat count, fast-mutating), CNV (kb–Mb copy number)


One genome vs the reference
4.1–5.0 million sites differ (1000 Genomes)


Naming
rs number (dbSNP); HGVS g./c./p.; watch the strand: rs334 is T>A on plus, c.20A>T on HBB


Haplotype, LD
alleles on one chromosome; nearby alleles stay associated; LD decays with distance and time


Arrays vs sequencing
arrays read known common SNPs cheaply; sequencing finds rare and new variants


Databases
dbSNP, 1000 Genomes (26 populations), gnomAD (frequencies), ClinVar (clinical meaning)


Population differences
most variation is within populations; large differences at single loci suggest selection


Lactase persistence
rs4988235 A: 0.74 in CEU, 0 in YRI and CHB; regulatory; dominant; positive selection


Sickle cell
rs334 A: 0.10–0.14 in West and East African samples; heterozygote advantage against malaria




The revision table. The habit to take away: when you meet a variant, find its rs number, its position and strand, its consequence and its frequency in populations, and ask why it is as common as it is.

title: Genomic variation
text:
Where this leads

Exercise: variant types and LD by hand; gnomAD, Ensembl and dbSNP for rs4988235 and rs334.
Exercise in R: download-style tables of allele frequencies and populations, left_join() them, and plot frequencies by population.
Part 5: Rearrangements and aneuploidy. The large structural variants: deletions, inversions, translocations.
Part 7: Hardy–Weinberg, drift and selection. The quantitative theory behind today’s stories: why HbS stays at about 10% in malaria regions, and how fast an allele like lactase persistence can spread.
Ethics. Consent, privacy and personal genomics.


Point forward. Part 7 returns to both case stories with numbers: the Hardy–Weinberg unit uses genotype counts like those in gnomAD, and the drift and selection unit simulates heterozygote advantage.

title: Exercise in R: genomic variation
text:
Tasks
You met left_join() in Genome annotation, where both tables had a column called chromosome. This time the key has different names in the two tables (population in one, code in the other); join_by(population == code) says which columns to match. Two more join verbs help you check your data: anti_join(x, y) returns the rows of x that have no match in y, and cross_join(x, y) makes every combination of rows.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
R1. (look at the data) Read both files. How many rows does each SNP have in the frequency table? With 26 populations and two alleles, you might expect 52. Look at rs4988235 in three populations to see why some are missing.
freqs <- read_csv("data/snp_frequencies.csv")
pops <- read_csv("data/populations.csv")
freqs
pops
freqs |> count(snp, gene)
freqs |> filter(snp == "rs4988235", population %in% c("YRI", "CEU", "CHB"))
R2. (join the population information) Add the superpopulation to each frequency row. Then use anti_join() to check that every population code in freqs was found in pops.
freqs_pop <- freqs |>
  left_join(pops, by = join_by(population == code))
freqs_pop |> select(snp, population, allele, frequency, superpopulation) |> head(4)
freqs |> anti_join(pops, by = join_by(population == code)) |> nrow()
R3. (one effect allele per SNP, zeros included) We want the frequency of the effect allele of each SNP in all 26 populations, including those where it was not seen. Make a small table of the effect alleles, combine every population with every SNP using cross_join(), then left_join() the frequencies. Combinations without a match get NA, which here means “not observed”, so replace it with 0 using coalesce().
effect <- tribble(
  ~snp,         ~allele, ~trait,
  "rs4988235",  "A",     "lactase persistence (LCT -13910T)",
  "rs334",      "A",     "sickle-cell allele HbS (HBB Glu7Val)",
  "rs1426654",  "A",     "lighter skin (SLC24A5 Ala111Thr)",
  "rs12913832", "G",     "blue eyes (HERC2/OCA2)",
  "rs671",      "A",     "alcohol flush (ALDH2 Glu504Lys)"
)
eff <- pops |>
  cross_join(effect) |>
  left_join(freqs |> select(snp, population, allele, frequency),
            by = join_by(code == population, snp, allele)) |>
  mutate(frequency = coalesce(frequency, 0))
nrow(eff)
eff |> filter(snp == "rs4988235") |> arrange(desc(frequency)) |> select(code, superpopulation, frequency) |> head(6)
Why must the join use three columns (code == population, snp and allele)? Compare your top six with Find it F3.
R4. (summarise by continent) Compute the mean effect-allele frequency over the populations of each superpopulation, for each SNP.
eff |>
  group_by(snp, superpopulation) |>
  summarise(mean_freq = round(mean(frequency), 3), .groups = "drop") |>
  print(n = 25)
Which SNP shows the largest difference between superpopulations? Which allele is found almost only in one continental group?
R5. (plot frequency by population) Order the populations by superpopulation, then draw one bar per population, coloured by superpopulation, with one panel per trait.
eff <- eff |> mutate(code = factor(code, levels = pops |> arrange(superpopulation) |> pull(code)))
ggplot(eff, aes(x = code, y = frequency, fill = superpopulation)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ trait, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "1000 Genomes population", y = "allele frequency", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5), legend.position = "top")
Describe the pattern for lactase persistence within Europe (GBR, FIN, IBS, TSI, CEU). Where is HbS found?
R6. (from allele to genotype frequencies) For lactase persistence and HbS, compute in a few populations the expected fraction of heterozygotes (2q(1 − q)), homozygotes (q2) and people with at least one copy (1 − (1 − q)2), assuming Hardy–Weinberg proportions. For which trait is “at least one copy” the relevant number, and for which is “homozygotes”?
eff |>
  filter(snp %in% c("rs4988235", "rs334"), code %in% c("YRI", "GWD", "LWK", "CEU", "GBR", "FIN", "TSI", "CHB")) |>
  mutate(q = frequency,
         het = round(2 * q * (1 - q), 3),
         hom = round(q^2, 4),
         at_least_one = round(1 - (1 - q)^2, 3)) |>
  select(snp, code, q, het, hom, at_least_one) |>
  arrange(snp, desc(q))

title: Exercise in R: genomic variation
text:
Where this leads
The same idea, joining a table of measurements with a table that describes the samples, is the core of most genomic data analysis. In Part 6 you join gene-expression data with tissue information, and in Part 7 you use genotype counts like these to test Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium with a χ² test.

title: Genome annotation
text:
About this lecture
The last unit read DNA in pieces: one PCR product, or millions of short reads. A genome project puts the pieces together into chromosomes, and annotation marks what is on them: where the genes are, what they encode, and which genes in other species they resemble.

Assembly: from reads to contigs to chromosomes, and why repeats make it hard.
Finding genes: open reading frames (ORFs) in bacteria; exons, splice signals and codon bias in eukaryotes.
Evidence: RNA-seq, homology (BLAST) and conservation.
Genome browsers: one gene seen as stacked tracks.
Comparative genomics and gene families: orthologs, paralogs, and the globins as an example.

The running example is again HBB, now seen in its genomic neighbourhood.
Book: Hartwell, Genetics: From Genes to Genomes, chapter on genome sequencing and annotation.

This lecture is the most bioinformatic of the course, but the questions are genetic: where is a gene, what does it do, and how is it related to other genes? Students used NCBI Gene and Ensembl in the first unit to find the chromosome of HBB and CFTR. Today they find out where those annotations come from. The exercise has a six-frame ORF finder demo, a BLASTp search with the beta-globin protein, a look at the beta-globin locus in a genome browser, and the R part reads a BioMart export of all human protein-coding genes.
