Today a bacterial genome costs less than a lab course, and projects aim at all eukaryotic species.

The table is not for memorising; it shows the pace. The first genomes were read with Sanger sequencing and clone-by-clone strategies; from the late 2000s, next-generation sequencing made genomes cheap, and long reads made them complete. The human reference used everywhere in this course, GRCh38, still has gaps in the most repetitive regions; the T2T assembly filled them in 2022. The organisms in the table are the same as in the genome-size table from Genetics as information, and the size column links back to the C-value paradox: genome size says little about gene number.

title: Genome annotation
text:
Assembly: putting the reads together


Reads that overlap come from neighbouring positions; merging them gives contigs (contiguous sequences).
A repeat longer than the reads cannot be placed: its reads fit at every copy. The assembly breaks there.
Long reads (10–100 kb) span repeats and join contigs into scaffolds and whole chromosomes.


Assembly is a puzzle with millions of pieces, many of them identical. The key concept is the repeat: about half of the human genome consists of repeated sequences, mostly transposable elements, plus segmental duplications and the huge satellite arrays at centromeres. With 150-base reads, any repeat longer than about 150 bases is ambiguous. That is why the early human genome had hundreds of gaps, and why long-read technologies changed genome assembly. Gene families come back at the end of the lecture: recently duplicated genes are themselves long repeats and are hard to assemble.

title: Genome annotation
text:
What does annotation mean?








Kind
Question
Example for HBB




Structural
Where are the genes, exons, start and stop codons?
chr11:5,225,464–5,229,395, minus strand, 3 exons


Functional
What does the product do?
β-globin, the β chain of adult haemoglobin, carries O2


Relational
Which genes is it related to?
paralogs HBD, HBG1, HBA1 …; ortholog mouse Hbb-b1




The human genome has about 20,000 protein-coding genes (20,107 in Ensembl release 116), plus many genes for non-coding RNAs.
Protein-coding sequence is only about 1–2% of the genome.
Annotation is a model built from evidence, and it changes between releases. Always note the release you used.


The HBB coordinates are those of Ensembl release 116 on GRCh38; they are the span of all annotated transcripts, so they can change slightly between releases even when the gene does not. The 20,107 comes from the BioMart export used in the R exercise. Make the point that annotation is not observed directly; it is predicted from evidence and curated, which is why NCBI RefSeq and Ensembl give slightly different gene counts, and why the count has drifted down over the years from early guesses of 100,000 genes. The last bullet is the reason every data file in this course records its release.

title: Genome annotation
section: Finding genes in bacteria: open reading frames
text:
Finding genes in bacteria: open reading frames
An open reading frame (ORF) is a stretch from a start codon (ATG) to the next in-frame stop codon (TAA, TAG, TGA) with no stop in between.

DNA has six reading frames: three on each strand.
In random DNA, 3 of 64 codons are stops, so a stop comes on average every 64/3 ≈ 21 codons.
The chance of 100 codons in a row without a stop is (61/64)100 ≈ 0.008. A long ORF is unlikely by chance, so it is probably a gene.
Bacterial genes have no introns and are densely packed (about 1 gene per kb), so long ORFs find most of them.


This is the probability reasoning from Part 1 applied to sequences. Each codon is a stop with probability 3/64, independently in random sequence, so the run length until a stop is geometric with mean 64/3. The product rule gives the chance of a run of 100 non-stop codons: 61/64 to the power 100, about 0.8 percent. In a genome of several megabases there are many thousands of ORF-sized windows, so some random long ORFs still appear, and real gene finders also use codon usage, ribosome binding sites and homology. Short genes are the hard case: the lambda cro gene is only 66 codons and is easy to miss with a 100-codon cut-off, which the demo shows.

title: Genome annotation
text:
Try it: six-frame ORF finder




Interactive demo. It starts on a 3.3 kb region of phage lambda around the repressor gene cI and the cro gene, with a 100 amino acid cut-off. Grey ticks are stop codons. Point out that ORFs appear where stops are missing over long stretches. Compare with the green annotation track: rexA and cI on the reverse strand, cII and O on the forward strand. cro (66 aa) is missing at 100 aa; lower the cut-off to 60 and it appears, together with a few random ORFs. The cII ORF is longer than the annotated gene because the finder takes the first ATG; the real start is a later ATG. Then switch to random DNA: at 100 aa almost nothing; the longest ORF is under 100 aa. Then the HBB mRNA: a single long ORF of 147 aa in frame +3, which is beta-globin.

title: Genome annotation
section: Eukaryotic genes are harder to find
text:
Eukaryotic genes are harder to find








Feature
Problem for a gene finder
Signal that helps




Introns
the ORF is split into exons, often short
splice sites: introns start with GT and end with AG


Large intergenic regions
genes are far apart (human: about 6 genes per Mb)
promoters, CpG islands near the 5’ end


Alternative splicing
one gene, several transcripts
RNA evidence


Pseudogenes
look like genes but are broken
stop codons or frameshifts in the “ORF”


Codon bias

each species prefers some synonymous codons in real genes



HBB is 1.6 kb from transcription start to end but codes for only 147 amino acids (444 nt): 3 exons, 2 introns.

The contrast with bacteria is the point. In a bacterium, a long ORF is nearly always a gene; in human DNA, the coding parts are short exons separated by introns that are often thousands of bases long, so there is rarely a long ORF to find. Gene finders therefore look for combinations of signals: splice sites, start and stop codons in the right frame across exons, codon usage typical of real genes, and promoter features. Codon bias is the observation that synonymous codons are not used equally; real coding sequence has the species’ typical bias, random sequence does not. Pseudogenes such as HBBP1 in the globin cluster look gene-like but carry disabling mutations. Recall the genetic code from the Mutation unit: the third codon position is where most synonymous variation sits.

title: Genome annotation
text:
Evidence: RNA, protein and conservation

Modern annotation pipelines (Ensembl, NCBI RefSeq) combine RNA-seq reads (where transcripts are), protein homology (a known protein from another species aligned back to the DNA), conservation across species, and ab initio signals (ORFs, splice sites). Curators check difficult genes by hand.

Walk through the tracks from top to bottom. RNA-seq: reads from messenger RNA pile up on exons; reads that are split across an intron show exactly where the exon junctions are. Protein homology: if a mouse or zebrafish protein aligns to the human DNA in three blocks, those blocks are probably exons. Conservation: sequence that has stayed the same over millions of years of evolution is likely to have a function, because mutations there were removed by selection; exons stand out. Each kind of evidence has blind spots, for example a gene expressed only in one embryonic tissue has little RNA-seq support, which is why pipelines combine them.

title: Genome annotation
text:
Homology search with BLAST

Homologous genes share an ancestor. When two sequences are much more similar than chance allows, we infer homology, and often a similar function.

BLAST, the Basic Local Alignment Search Tool, is the most used program in biology. The idea is a heuristic: instead of aligning the query to every database sequence fully, which would be too slow, it looks for short exact word matches (seeds) and extends only those. The alignment here is real: human versus mouse beta-globin, first 40 residues; over the whole 147 residues, 118 are identical. Stress the language: similarity is measured, homology is inferred. Two proteins are homologous or not; there is no such thing as 80 percent homologous. 80 percent identical is correct.

title: Genome annotation
section: Which BLAST, and how to read it
text:
Which BLAST, and how to read it









Program
Query
Database
Use




blastn
DNA
DNA
identify a read or PCR product (the mystery read in the last unit)


blastp
protein
protein
find homologous proteins


blastx
DNA, translated in 6 frames
protein
what might this DNA encode?


tblastn
protein
DNA, translated in 6 frames
find unannotated genes for a protein in a genome











Column
Meaning
Rule of thumb




Per. Ident
% identical positions in the aligned region
high identity over a short stretch can still be chance


Query Cover
% of the query in the alignment
low cover: only one domain matches


E value
hits this good expected by chance in this database
< 10−10: homologous; > 0.01: be careful



Proteins detect distant relatives better than DNA: the code is redundant, and similar amino acids score positively.

The E value depends on the database size, so the same alignment gets a larger E value in a bigger database; it is not a p-value, but it can be read in a similar way. The protein point is important for the exercise: human and fish beta-globin genes have diverged a lot at the DNA level, especially at third codon positions, but the proteins are still clearly similar. blastx and tblastn translate in all six frames, which is exactly what the ORF finder did by hand. In the exercise students run blastp with the human beta-globin protein and see paralogs and orthologs in the same hit list.

title: Genome annotation
section: Genome browsers: tracks on a coordinate
text:
Genome browsers: tracks on a coordinate

The UCSC Genome Browser and Ensembl show a region of a chromosome with tracks stacked underneath: genes and transcripts, RNA-seq, conservation, variants (dbSNP, ClinVar), regulatory elements. Always check the assembly (GRCh38 here); coordinates differ between assemblies.

The figure is drawn from the Ensembl 116 positions of the five globin genes and the pseudogene HBBP1; the conservation and variant tracks are schematic. The important things to read in a browser are the coordinate and assembly at the top, the strand of each gene (here all on the minus strand, so the genes are read from right to left), and the exon structure. The beta-globin cluster is a classic: the genes lie in the same order as they are switched on during development, embryonic epsilon first, then the fetal gamma genes, then adult delta and beta. A locus control region further upstream (to the right here) is needed for high expression of all of them; that comes back in the eukaryotic regulation unit. Note rs334, the HbS variant, in the variant track: it is the subject of the Genomic variation unit.

title: Genome annotation
text:
Comparative genomics: conservation means function

Compare genomes of related species: what stayed the same is probably important; what differs may explain differences between species.
Orthologs (same gene in different species) usually keep the same function, so model organisms tell us about human genes: mouse Hbb-b1 vs human HBB, 80% identical proteins.
Synteny: blocks of genes stay in the same order on chromosomes of related species. A gene’s neighbours help to identify its ortholog.
Only a few percent of the human genome is under strong evolutionary constraint, but that includes many non-coding elements, such as enhancers.


Comparative genomics is how most human genes were first given a function: a human gene is assigned the function of its yeast, fly or mouse ortholog, which was studied genetically, with mutants. This is the link to Part 6, development and model organisms. Conservation also finds regulatory DNA: the locus control region of the globin cluster is conserved between human and mouse although it codes for nothing. The figure of a few percent under constraint comes from comparisons of many mammal genomes; it is clearly larger than the 1 to 2 percent that is protein-coding, so a lot of functional DNA is non-coding.

title: Genome annotation
text:
Gene families: duplication and divergence

Gene duplication gives a spare copy, which can keep the old function, take a new one (fetal vs adult haemoglobin) or decay into a pseudogene (HBBP1). Related genes in one genome are paralogs; the same gene in two species are orthologs.

The globin family is the textbook example. An ancestral globin gene duplicated into the myoglobin and haemoglobin lineages, then the haemoglobin gene into alpha-like and beta-like genes, which ended up on different chromosomes (16 and 11), and then each cluster duplicated further. The identity column is from BLASTp of human beta-globin against each protein, run for this course: delta is 93 percent identical (a recent duplication), the gamma and epsilon genes about 73 to 76 percent, alpha only 43 percent. Myoglobin has exactly the same three-dimensional fold, but BLAST cannot detect the similarity from sequence: a lesson that no hit does not prove no homology. The fetal gamma chains bind oxygen more tightly than adult beta chains, which lets the fetus take oxygen from the mother’s blood: a new function after duplication. In sickle-cell disease, drugs that turn fetal haemoglobin back on (hydroxyurea) help because gamma chains do not carry the HbS mutation.

text:
The human genome in numbers
From the Ensembl BioMart export used in the R exercise (release 116, GRCh38):

RBFOX1 2.47 Mb, CNTNAP2 2.30 Mb, … DMD 2.24 Mb



Gene density differs ten-fold between chromosomes. The trisomies that are compatible with survival to birth (13, 18, 21) involve gene-poor chromosomes.

These are the numbers students get in R; they should not memorise them, but the patterns are worth noticing. Chromosome 19 is famously gene-dense; chromosomes 13, 18 and the Y are gene-poor. The link to the aneuploidy unit in Part 5: the only autosomal trisomies seen in live births are of chromosomes 13, 18 and 21, which carry relatively few genes, so having an extra copy upsets fewer gene doses. The longest genes are huge mostly because of enormous introns; DMD, the Duchenne muscular dystrophy gene from the pedigree unit, is 2.2 Mb, and its size is one reason why new mutations in it are common. HBB, at 4 kb, is short.

title: Genome annotation
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Assembly
overlapping reads → contigs → scaffolds; repeats longer than reads break assemblies; long reads help


Annotation
structural (where), functional (what), relational (related to what); a model that changes between releases


ORF
ATG to stop with no stop between; random DNA has a stop every ~21 codons; long ORFs are likely genes


Eukaryotic gene finding
exons and introns (GT…AG), codon bias, promoters; combined with RNA-seq, homology and conservation


BLAST
seed, extend, report; blastn/blastp/blastx/tblastn; read identity, coverage and E-value


Genome browser
tracks on a chromosome coordinate; note the assembly (GRCh38) and strand


Orthologs / paralogs
same gene in two species / related genes in one genome, from duplication


Human genome
~20,000 protein-coding genes, 1–2% coding, 6.5 genes per Mb on average




The revision table. If students remember three things: annotation is evidence-based and versioned; an ORF’s length is a statistical argument; and BLAST hits are read through identity, coverage and E-value, with orthologs and paralogs in the same hit list.

title: Genome annotation
text:
Where this leads

Exercise: find ORFs in the demo, BLASTp the β-globin protein, look at the globin locus in Ensembl or UCSC, and export a gene list from BioMart.
Exercise in R: read the BioMart export with read_tsv(), count genes per chromosome, join with chromosome lengths and plot gene density.
Next: Genomic variation. Annotation describes one reference genome; sequencing many people shows how genomes differ: SNPs such as rs334, indels and copy-number variants.
Part 5: Rearrangements and aneuploidy. Gene density helps to explain which aneuploidies are survivable.


Point forward to the variation unit, which uses the same browsers and the Ensembl REST API to pull allele frequencies across populations. BioMart comes back in R in the next unit as the idea of downloading a table from a database and joining it with another table.

Before you start
This page builds on the Exercise; do Find it F3 (the BioMart export) first, so you know where the file comes from. You need the packages readr, dplyr and ggplot2. Download the two files and save them in a data/ folder of your R project:

human_genes.tsv (830 kB): all 20,107 human protein-coding genes on chromosomes 1–22, X, Y and MT, from Ensembl BioMart, release 116 (GRCh38).
chromosome_lengths.tsv: the length of each chromosome, from the Ensembl REST API (GRCh38.p14).

See data/README.md for the exact queries.

title: Exercise in R: genome annotation
text:
Tasks
New idiom: read_tsv() on a database export. read_tsv() reads tab-separated files, the format most databases use for downloads (BioMart, UCSC Table Browser, GWAS Catalog …). Exports often have column names with spaces and brackets, such as Gene start (bp). In R you refer to such a name with backticks, `Gene start (bp)`, and the easiest thing is to rename() the columns once, right after reading.
Also new: left_join(). left_join(x, y, by = "key") keeps every row of x and adds the columns of y from the row with the same value in the key column. You will use it again in the next unit.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
R1. (read the export) Read the file, look at what read_tsv() reports about the column types, and rename the columns. Check that every gene has the biotype you asked for, and count the genes without a name.
genes <- read_tsv("data/human_genes.tsv")
genes
genes <- genes |>
  rename(gene = `Gene name`, chromosome = `Chromosome/scaffold name`,
         start = `Gene start (bp)`, end = `Gene end (bp)`, biotype = `Gene type`)
genes |> count(biotype)
genes |> filter(is.na(gene)) |> nrow()
Why does read_tsv() read chromosome as text (chr) and not as a number?
R2. (genes per chromosome) Count the genes on each chromosome with count(). Alphabetical order would put “10” before “2”, so turn the chromosome into a factor with the levels in their natural order.
chrom_order <- c(1:22, "X", "Y", "MT")
per_chrom <- genes |>
  count(chromosome, name = "n_genes") |>
  mutate(chromosome = factor(chromosome, levels = chrom_order)) |>
  arrange(chromosome)
print(per_chrom, n = 25)
Which chromosome has the most genes? Is that surprising, given its size?
R3. (join with chromosome lengths) The number of genes means more per Mb of DNA. Read the second table and join it to the counts by chromosome. The join key must have the same type in both tables, so we turn the factor back into text before joining. Then compute genes per Mb, and look at the densest and the sparsest chromosomes.
lengths <- read_tsv("data/chromosome_lengths.tsv", col_types = "cd")
lengths
density <- per_chrom |>
  mutate(chromosome = as.character(chromosome)) |>
  left_join(lengths, by = "chromosome") |>
  mutate(length_mb = length_bp / 1e6,
         genes_per_mb = n_genes / length_mb,
         chromosome = factor(chromosome, levels = chrom_order))
density |> arrange(desc(genes_per_mb)) |> print(n = 6)
density |> arrange(genes_per_mb) |> print(n = 4)
overall <- sum(density$n_genes) / (sum(density$length_bp) / 1e6)
overall
(col_types = "cd" tells read_tsv() that the first column is character and the second double, so chromosome “1” is read as text, matching the gene table.)
R4. (plot gene density) Plot genes per Mb for the nuclear chromosomes as a bar chart, with a dashed line at the genome average. Leave out the mitochondrial genome (why?).
density |>
  filter(chromosome != "MT") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = chromosome, y = genes_per_mb)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2a6f97") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = overall, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "chromosome", y = "protein-coding genes per Mb",
       title = "Gene density of human chromosomes (Ensembl 116, GRCh38)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
Compare with your answers to B6 in the exercise.
R5. (gene length) Add a column with the length of each gene (end - start + 1, because both ends are included). Summarise it, list the five longest genes, and look up four genes you know from earlier units. Then plot the distribution on a log scale.
genes <- genes |> mutate(length = end - start + 1)
summary(genes$length)
genes |> arrange(desc(length)) |> select(gene, chromosome, length) |> head(5)
genes |> filter(gene %in% c("HBB", "DMD", "CFTR", "HTT")) |> select(gene, chromosome, start, end, length)

ggplot(genes, aes(x = length)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "#2a6f97") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "gene length (bp, log scale)", y = "number of genes") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
Why are the mean and the median so different? There is a small extra peak just below 1,000 bp: what kind of gene could be that short? (Hint: which genes have no introns?)
R6. (the globin cluster in the table) Filter the table to the genes that start between 5.2 and 5.3 Mb on chromosome 11 and sort them by position. Compare with the browser view in the lecture and with B5.
genes |>
  filter(chromosome == "11", start >= 5200000, start < 5300000) |>
  arrange(start) |>
  select(gene, start, end, length)
Some of these “genes” are hundreds of kb long, much longer than in B5, and two have no name. What does that tell you about using the gene start and end from an annotation table?

title: Gene expression (recap)
text:
About this lecture
Recap of 5MO103 (Microbiology and basic molecular biology). You know how a cell reads a gene. Here we ask the geneticist’s version of the question: where in a gene can a mutation act, and what does it do?

The anatomy of a gene, and six real HBB mutations that hit six different steps.
Transcription and RNA processing: promoters, caps, poly(A) tails and splicing.
Splicing mutations, and alternative splicing: one gene, many transcripts (CFTR in Ensembl and UniProt).
Translation and the genetic code, and how frameshift mutants proved that the code is read in triplets (Crick and Brenner).

Book: Hartwell, Genetics: From Genes to Genomes, Gene expression: the flow of information from DNA to RNA to protein chapter.

This is a recap unit, so keep the biochemistry short; students have the full mechanism from 5MO103. The new angle is the mutation one: in the previous unit every mutation was a change in a codon. Here we see that a mutation in a promoter, a splice site or a poly(A) signal can be just as damaging, and that one gene can give several proteins. The beta-thalassaemias are the running example because HBB is so small and so well studied; nearly every step of expression has a known disease mutation. About eight content slides.

title: Gene expression (recap)
text:
Where can a mutation act?

Six real disease variants in one small gene, HBB (all classified as pathogenic in ClinVar). Only two of them change a codon.

Walk along the gene from left to right. The promoter variant at c.-78 sits in the TATA box, 28 bases before the transcription start, and reduces transcription, so less beta-globin is made: beta-plus thalassaemia (reduced output). HbS is the missense change students know. The two intron 1 variants damage splicing: c.92+1 destroys the GT of the donor site, c.93-21 creates a new AG acceptor inside the intron. c.118C>T is the codon 39 nonsense allele from the mutation unit. The last one is in the poly(A) signal AATAAA in the 3’ UTR. Beta-zero means no beta-globin at all from that allele, beta-plus means some. Numbering: c.-78 is 78 bases before the A of ATG; c.92+1 is the first intron base after coding base 92; c.93-21 is 21 bases before coding base 93; c.*111 is 111 bases after the stop codon. The numbers are from the HGVS names in ClinVar.

title: Gene expression (recap)
text:
Transcription, in brief

RNA polymerase II binds the promoter with general transcription factors (TFIID binds the TATA box, about 25–30 bp upstream of the start).
It reads the template strand 3′ → 5′ and makes RNA 5′ → 3′, so the RNA has the same sequence as the coding strand (with U for T). That is why genes are written as the coding strand.
Enhancers and transcription factors set how much RNA is made, and where and when: Part 6.

The genetic lens. Promoter mutations change how much product is made, not what it is. HBB c.-78A>C changes the TATA box CATAAAA to CATACAA: less transcription, β+-thalassaemia. Such cis-acting mutations affect only the copy of the gene on the same chromosome.

The template versus coding strand point links back to the DNA recap: the coding strand is the one that matches the mRNA, and it is also the strand used for c. numbering. A cis-acting element is a DNA sequence that controls only the gene on the same molecule; a trans-acting factor is a diffusible product (a protein or RNA) that can act on both copies. The cis/trans distinction is the core of the lac operon logic in Part 6, so plant it here. The TATA sequence on the slide is the genomic sequence around c.-78 from Ensembl.

title: Gene expression (recap)
text:
Processing: cap, tail and splicing
A eukaryotic pre-mRNA is processed while it is being made:








Step
What happens
A mutation that breaks it




5′ cap
a 7-methylguanosine is added to the 5′ end; needed for export and translation



3′ end
the RNA is cut about 10–30 nt after AAUAAA, and a poly(A) tail is added
HBB c.*111A>G: AATAAA → AATGAA, β+


Splicing
the spliceosome removes introns: GU at the 5′ end (donor), a branch-point A, AG at the 3′ end (acceptor)
HBB c.92+1G>A (donor), c.93-21G>A (new acceptor)



Introns can be long. CFTR spans about 189 kb of chromosome 7, and its mRNA is 6.1 kb: only about 3 % of the gene ends up in the mRNA.

The point to land is that the splice signals are short and simple: GU, AG, a branch point and some weaker flanking sequences. That means a single base change can destroy a site or create a new one. The spliceosome is made of snRNPs that recognise these sites by base pairing, which is why the consensus is so important. The CFTR numbers come from the Ensembl snapshot used in the R exercise: the MANE Select transcript has 27 exons, 6070 nt of exon, over a span of 188,641 bp of genome.

title: Gene expression (recap)
text:
Splicing mutations

About one in ten disease-causing point mutations affects splicing. A “silent” or intronic change is not always harmless.

Three patterns. Destroying a donor or acceptor site (c.92+1G>A in HBB, or CFTR c.1585-1G>A, the acceptor of exon 12) means the normal splice is lost: the spliceosome skips the exon, keeps the intron, or uses a weaker cryptic site nearby. Creating a new site: HBB c.93-21G>A (traditionally IVS-I-110) makes a new AG 19 bases upstream of the normal acceptor; most transcripts use it and keep 19 nt of intron, which shifts the reading frame, but some normal splicing remains, so it is a beta-plus allele. It is one of the most common beta-thalassaemia alleles around the Mediterranean. Exon skipping: if the skipped exon is a multiple of 3 long, the frame is kept and the protein just lacks a piece; CFTR exon 10 (183 nt) is the example on the next slide. The one-in-ten figure is a rough literature estimate; give it as an order of magnitude.

title: Gene expression (recap)
section: Alternative splicing: one gene, many products
text:
Alternative splicing: one gene, many products


Most human multi-exon genes are alternatively spliced: exons can be included or skipped, and different starts and ends can be used.
CFTR in Ensembl (release 116): 45 transcripts, of which one is the MANE Select transcript (ENST00000003084, = RefSeq NM_000492.4): 27 exons, a protein of 1480 amino acids.
UniProt P13569 lists 3 isoforms. Isoform 2 lacks residues 404–464: exactly the 61 codons of exon 10.




Ensembl’s transcripts include everything with evidence: full-length coding transcripts, fragments, transcripts that keep an intron, and transcripts predicted to be destroyed by nonsense-mediated decay. Many are rare. MANE Select is one transcript per gene, agreed between NCBI and Ensembl, that is used as the default for reporting variants; ClinVar’s CFTR names all use NM_000492.4. UniProt lists isoforms only when there is protein-level or strong evidence, which is why it has 3 rather than 45. Exon 10 (exon 9 in the old legacy numbering) is 183 nt. A poly-T tract just upstream of it in intron 9 varies in length between people: with only five Ts (the 5T allele), exon 10 is skipped in most transcripts, and the protein without exon 10 does not work. 5T is associated with male infertility from absent vas deferens and with mild CF when combined with a severe allele. Students compute these numbers themselves in the R exercise.

title: Gene expression (recap)
text:
Translation, and nonsense-mediated decay

The ribosome starts at the first AUG in a good context, and reads codons in one frame until a stop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA).
tRNAs match codons by base pairing with their anticodon; the third position pairs loosely (wobble), which is why many synonymous codons differ only in the third base.
Nonsense-mediated decay (NMD). In a normal mRNA the stop codon is in the last exon. If a premature stop codon lies well upstream of the last exon–exon junction, the mRNA is recognised and destroyed.

The genetic lens. NMD means that a nonsense allele such as CFTR G542X (in exon 12 of 27) usually makes almost no protein, not a short one: it behaves as a null allele. Ensembl labels transcripts with such early stops with the biotype nonsense_mediated_decay: CFTR has 11 of them.

Wobble explains the pattern students found in the mutation R exercise: almost all silent changes are at the third codon position. NMD is a quality-control system: during splicing, protein complexes are deposited at each exon-exon junction; the first ribosome removes them as it translates; a stop codon that leaves junction complexes behind it marks the mRNA as faulty. The genetic consequence is that most nonsense and frameshift alleles act as nulls, which is why they are usually recessive, and why truncated dominant-negative proteins are rare. A nonsense codon in the last exon escapes NMD and can make a truncated protein. Drugs that make the ribosome read through stop codons have been tried for nonsense alleles such as G542X.

title: Gene expression (recap)
text:
The genetic code








Property
Meaning
How we know




Triplet
3 bases per amino acid (43 = 64 codons ≥ 20 amino acids)
Crick–Brenner frameshifts (next slide)


Non-overlapping, no gaps
each base belongs to one codon; reading from a fixed start
single base changes alter one amino acid (HbS)


Degenerate
61 sense codons for 20 amino acids; 3 stops
silent mutations


(Nearly) universal
the same in bacteria, plants and animals, with small exceptions (e.g. UGA = Trp in vertebrate mitochondria)
human genes are expressed correctly in E. coli



The meaning of the codons was found biochemically: Nirenberg and Matthaei (1961) showed that poly-U RNA makes poly-phenylalanine, so UUU = Phe; by 1966 all 64 codons were assigned.

Each property has a genetic or biochemical proof. Non-overlapping: if codons overlapped, a single base change would alter two or three adjacent amino acids; HbS and every other point mutation change only one. Degenerate: silent substitutions exist, and the codon table in the R exercise shows six codons for Leu, Ser and Arg. Universal: that is what makes it possible to make human insulin in bacteria. The mitochondrial exceptions come back in the organelle inheritance unit in Part 5. The cell-free translation experiments with synthetic RNAs (Nirenberg, Khorana) cracked the meanings; Crick and Brenner’s genetic experiment established the triplet nature before any codon was assigned.

title: Gene expression (recap)
section: Crick & Brenner: the code is read in triplets
text:
Crick & Brenner: the code is read in triplets

Crick, Barnett, Brenner and Watts-Tobin (1961) used proflavin to make frameshift mutants in the rII gene of phage T4. Combining them:

one (+) or one (−): mutant. (+)(−) close together: wild type again (intragenic suppression).
(+)(+) or (−)(−): mutant. (+)(+)(+) or (−)(−)(−): wild type.

Only a code read in threes from a fixed start explains this, years before any codon was known.

This is the genetic proof that matters for this course, because it used only crosses and phenotypes. Proflavin causes single-base insertions or deletions. They started with one rII mutant, called it plus by definition, and selected revertants; most revertants carried a second mutation nearby of the opposite sign, minus. Recombining mutations of the same sign showed that two pluses are still mutant but three pluses restore function. The region between the changes is translated in the wrong frame, so the protein is only near normal if that region is short and tolerant, which is why the suppressed mutants were close together and near the start of the gene, in a non-essential region. The sentence analogy in the figure is the one Crick used. Exercise B2 in the mutation unit did exactly this with the HBB sequence.

title: Gene expression (recap)
text:
Where this leads

Exercise in R: an exon-coordinate table for all 45 CFTR transcripts (Ensembl 116): exon and transcript lengths with group_by() and summarise(), and an exon diagram with geom_segment().
Part 4: Genome analysis. Finding genes and open reading frames in raw sequence, and browsing exons, transcripts and variants in Ensembl and UCSC.
Part 6: Gene regulation. How transcription factors, enhancers, chromatin and RNAs control how much of each transcript is made.


Point forward. This closes Part 3: DNA, how it changes, and how it is read. Part 4 turns to the tools for reading whole genomes. The R exercise of this unit is the first one to summarise a real database table by groups, which is the main R skill for the rest of the course.

title: Exercise in R: Gene expression (recap)
Exercise in R: Gene expression (recap)
Exercise in R: Gene expression (recap)
text:
Before you start
This page builds on F1–F3 of the Exercise. You need the packages readr, dplyr and ggplot2. Download cftr_exons_ensembl116.csv and save it in a data/ folder of your R project.
The file has one row per exon for all 45 CFTR transcripts in Ensembl release 116 (GRCh38), downloaded from the Ensembl REST API on 2026-11-20; data/README.md gives the exact query. Coordinates are on chromosome 7 and include both ends, so an exon from start to end is end - start + 1 nt long. CFTR is on the + strand, so exon_rank 1 is the leftmost exon.

title: Exercise in R: Gene expression (recap)
text:
Tasks
New idiom: grouped summaries. group_by() splits a table into groups (here: one group per transcript), and summarise() then computes one row per group: n() counts rows, sum(), min() and max() work on a column within each group. .groups = "drop" removes the grouping afterwards. You have seen grouped summaries before; here they turn a long exon table into a transcript table.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
R1. (look at the table) Read the file. How many rows are there? Count the transcripts of each biotype: use distinct() first, so that each transcript counts once rather than once per exon.
exons <- read_csv("data/cftr_exons_ensembl116.csv")
exons
exons |> distinct(transcript_name, biotype) |> count(biotype, sort = TRUE)
R2. (exon lengths) Add an exon_length column. Keep only the MANE Select transcript, and find its number of exons, its shortest and longest exon, and the total length. Then list the internal exons (not the first or last) whose length is a multiple of 3, using the remainder operator %%. Skipping any of these keeps the reading frame (exercise B3).
exons <- exons |> mutate(exon_length = end - start + 1)
mane <- exons |> filter(mane_select)
mane |> select(exon_rank, start, end, exon_length) |> print(n = 27)
mane |> summarise(n_exons = n(), shortest = min(exon_length), longest = max(exon_length),
                  total = sum(exon_length))
mane |> filter(exon_rank > 1, exon_rank < 27, exon_length %% 3 == 0) |>
  select(exon_rank, exon_length)
R3. (transcript lengths) Summarise every transcript: number of exons, transcript length (sum of exon lengths) and genomic span (first start to last end). What fraction of the span of the MANE transcript ends up in the mRNA? Then list the protein-coding transcripts by protein length, and compare biotypes.
tx <- exons |>
  group_by(transcript_name, biotype, mane_select, protein_length) |>
  summarise(n_exons = n(),
            tx_length = sum(exon_length),
            span = max(end) - min(start) + 1,
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(exon_fraction = tx_length / span)
tx |> filter(mane_select) |> select(transcript_name, n_exons, tx_length, span, exon_fraction)
tx |> filter(biotype == "protein_coding") |>
  arrange(desc(protein_length)) |>
  select(transcript_name, protein_length, n_exons, tx_length) |>
  print(n = 21)
tx |> group_by(biotype) |> summarise(transcripts = n(), median_exons = median(n_exons))
R4. (which exon is skipped?) UniProt isoform 2 has 1419 amino acids. In R3, find the Ensembl transcript with that protein length, and compare its exons with the MANE exons using %in%. First compare on start, then on end. Why do the two comparisons give different answers? How many nucleotides do 1480 − 1419 amino acids correspond to?
cftr218 <- exons |> filter(transcript_name == "CFTR-218")
mane |> filter(!(start %in% cftr218$start)) |> select(exon_rank, start, end, exon_length)
mane |> filter(!(end %in% cftr218$end)) |> select(exon_rank, start, end, exon_length)
cftr218 |> filter(exon_rank == 1) |> select(exon_rank, start, end)
(1480 - 1419) * 3
R5. (an exon diagram) Draw the protein-coding transcripts with at least 20 exons, one per row, as geom_segment(): a thin line from the first to the last base of each transcript (the introns), and a thick segment for each exon. Shade exon 10 with annotate(). Positions are in kb from the start of the leftmost transcript. Then zoom in on 60–80 kb with coord_cartesian(). Which transcripts lack exon 10?
keep <- tx |> filter(biotype == "protein_coding", n_exons >= 20) |> pull(transcript_name)
keep
plot_ex <- exons |> filter(transcript_name %in% keep)
gene_start <- min(plot_ex$start)
plot_ex <- plot_ex |> mutate(start_kb = (start - gene_start) / 1000, end_kb = (end - gene_start) / 1000)
introns <- plot_ex |> group_by(transcript_name, mane_select) |>
  summarise(from = min(start_kb), to = max(end_kb), .groups = "drop")
exon10 <- mane |> filter(exon_rank == 10) |>
  mutate(start_kb = (start - gene_start) / 1000, end_kb = (end - gene_start) / 1000)

p <- ggplot(plot_ex, aes(y = transcript_name)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = exon10$start_kb - 0.5, xmax = exon10$end_kb + 0.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "orange", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_segment(data = introns, aes(x = from, xend = to, yend = transcript_name), linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = start_kb, xend = end_kb, yend = transcript_name, colour = mane_select),
               linewidth = 5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "firebrick", `FALSE` = "steelblue"),
                      labels = c(`TRUE` = "MANE Select", `FALSE` = "other")) +
  labs(x = "position from the start of CFTR (kb)", y = NULL, colour = NULL,
       title = "CFTR protein-coding transcripts with at least 20 exons (Ensembl 116)") +
  theme_minimal()
p
p + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(60, 80)) + labs(title = "Zoom: 60-80 kb, around exon 10 (shaded)")

text:
Where this leads
The exon table is the same information a genome browser draws as its gene track. In Part 4: Genome analysis you read a larger table exported from Ensembl BioMart, count genes per chromosome, and join tables with left_join(). In Part 6, group_by() and summarise() summarise gene expression across tissues from GTEx.

title: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
text:
About this lecture
Every cell in your body has the same genome, yet a liver cell makes albumin and a red-cell precursor makes haemoglobin. The difference is regulation. Eukaryotes use the same cis/trans logic as the lac operon, plus a layer that bacteria lack: chromatin, whose states can be copied from cell to cell without any change in the DNA sequence.

Promoters, enhancers and transcription factors; motifs; regulatory mutations.
Chromatin and epigenetics: histone modification, DNA methylation, position-effect variegation.
Genomic imprinting: Prader–Willi and Angelman syndromes.
X inactivation: XIST, the Lyon hypothesis, calico cats, mosaicism and skewing.
Dosage compensation in flies and worms.

Book: Hartwell, Genetics: From Genes to Genomes, the chapter on gene regulation in eukaryotes.

This is the longest unit of Part 6. The thread through it: the same cis versus trans reasoning from the lac operon, then three phenomena that look non-Mendelian at first sight (imprinting, X-inactivation mosaics, position effects) and that make sense once you know that chromatin states are inherited through cell division. X inactivation connects back to X-linkage in Part 2 and to X-linked pedigrees in Part 1: it explains why carrier females are sometimes affected.

title: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
text:
What is different in eukaryotes?









Bacteria (lac)
Eukaryotes




Unit of transcription
operons: several genes, one mRNA
usually one gene, one promoter


DNA packaging
nearly naked DNA
chromatin: DNA wrapped on nucleosomes


Typical control
repressor blocks polymerase
activators recruit polymerase; default is often “off”


Regulatory DNA
operator next to the promoter
enhancers up to ~1 Mb away, combined with promoter elements


Signals
a few regulators per operon
many transcription factors in combination


Coupling
transcription and translation coupled
separated by the nuclear envelope; splicing, export


Memory
lost when the signal goes
chromatin states can be inherited through mitosis




Run through the table quickly. The two big differences for genetics: first, chromatin makes the default state of many genes “off”, so activators matter more than repressors; second, chromatin states can be maintained through cell divisions, giving cellular memory. That memory is what we will call epigenetic. Attenuation, which we saw in the trp operon, cannot work in eukaryotes, because the ribosome never meets the nascent mRNA while it is being made.

title: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
text:
Promoters, enhancers and transcription factors


Core promoter (e.g. TATA box): where general transcription factors (GTFs) and RNA polymerase II assemble.
Proximal elements and enhancers: binding sites for activators (or repressors). Enhancers work at a distance, in either orientation; the DNA loops, and Mediator links them to the polymerase.
In lac terms: enhancers and promoters are cis-acting sites (like lacO); transcription factors are trans-acting proteins (like LacI).


The point to land is the parallel with the lac operon. A mutation in an enhancer affects only the copy of the gene on the same chromosome: cis. A mutation in a transcription factor gene affects every target gene on both chromosomes: trans. One gene usually has several enhancers, each driving expression in a different tissue or at a different stage, which is why a regulatory mutation can remove expression from one tissue only. Silencers and insulators also exist; we skip them here.

title: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
text:
Transcription factors and their motifs
A transcription factor has a DNA-binding domain that recognises a short motif (6–12 bp), and an activation (or repression) domain that recruits co-factors.

Motifs are degenerate: GATA1 binds (A/T)GATA(A/G); SOX2 binds ACAATG-like sites. A position weight matrix gives the probability of each base at each position; a sequence logo draws it.
A 6-bp motif turns up by chance about every 46 = 4096 bp, so a genome has hundreds of thousands of copies. Combinations of factors, chromatin and spacing decide which sites matter.
Combinatorial control: a few hundred to a couple of thousand factors, used in combinations, specify many cell types.

JASPAR is the open database of such motifs. You will look up GATA1 and SOX2 in the exercise.

GATA1 is the master regulator of red blood cell and megakaryocyte development; its motif is literally the letters GATA, flanked by A or T before and A or G after. SOX2 is one of the factors that keeps embryonic stem cells pluripotent, often binding together with OCT4 at composite sites; JASPAR even has a matrix for the Pou5f1::Sox2 pair. Make the counting point: a motif of length 6 is expected once every 4096 bp in random sequence, so on 3 billion bp there are close to a million matches per strand. That is why motif scanning alone predicts far more sites than are bound in a cell. The R part of the RNA-regulation unit does exactly this counting for microRNA seed sites.

title: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
section: Regulatory mutations: same protein, different place or time
text:
Regulatory mutations: same protein, different place or time
A mutation in a cis-regulatory element changes where or when a gene is expressed, not the protein it makes.








Example
Mutation
Effect




Lactase persistence
−13910 C>T, in an intron of MCM6, ~14 kb upstream of LCT
enhancer stays active in adult gut: lactase made after weaning (dominant)


Preaxial polydactyly
point mutations in the ZRS enhancer, ~1 Mb from SHH
SHH switched on in the wrong part of the limb bud: extra thumb or toe


Fly wing spots (yellow)
gains and losses of enhancer sites between Drosophila species
pigment pattern changes; coding sequence unchanged



Genetic signature: cis-acting (affects only the allele on the same chromosome), often tissue-specific, and often dominant.

These are three classic examples of how evolution and disease use regulatory DNA. Lactase persistence: most mammals turn off lactase after weaning; in many Europeans an enhancer variant keeps it on. One copy is enough, so lactase persistence is dominant. The ZRS is a limb enhancer sitting in an intron of a different gene, LMBR1, a million base pairs from its target SHH; a single base change gives an extra digit, while SHH coding mutations cause holoprosencephaly, a completely different and much more severe phenotype. Why dominant: an enhancer gain switches on one allele where it should be off, and one active allele is enough to change the phenotype. Link forward: most GWAS hits for complex traits in Part 7 lie in non-coding, presumably regulatory, DNA.

title: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
text:
Chromatin: open and closed


Histone acetylation loosens chromatin; acetyl groups are added by HATs and removed by HDACs. H3K4me3 marks active promoters.
H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 mark silent chromatin. Reader proteins (HP1, Polycomb) bind them and compact the fibre.
Transcription factors recruit the enzymes that write these marks, so chromatin states follow, and then stabilise, regulatory decisions.


Keep the chemistry light. The nomenclature H3K4me3 reads: histone H3, lysine 4, three methyl groups. Students need two lists: marks that go with active chromatin (acetylation, H3K4me3) and marks that go with silent chromatin (H3K9me3, H3K27me3). The reader-writer loop is what gives memory: a reader that binds a mark recruits a writer that puts the same mark on neighbouring nucleosomes, and after replication the marks on old histones guide marking of the new ones. Heterochromatin is the cytological name for the compact, silent state; euchromatin for the open state. The Eukaryotic chromosome unit in Part 5 covered heterochromatin at centromeres and telomeres.

title: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
text:
DNA methylation and epigenetic memory
In mammals, cytosines in CpG dinucleotides can be methylated (5-methylcytosine). Methylated CpG islands at promoters keep genes silent.

After replication, each CpG is hemi-methylated (old strand methylated, new strand not). The maintenance enzyme DNMT1 recognises this and methylates the new strand: the pattern is copied.
De novo methyltransferases (DNMT3A/B) set new patterns, for example in the germ line.

Epigenetics: heritable changes in gene expression, through cell division (and sometimes across generations), without a change in DNA sequence.
Genetic evidence: Drosophila position-effect variegation. An inversion that puts white+ next to heterochromatin gives eyes with red and white patches. The DNA of white+ is unchanged; heterochromatin spreads into it in some cells and not others, and each cell’s descendants keep the state.

The key idea is that a pattern of methylation on a palindromic CpG site can be copied, just like the base sequence: the hemi-methylated site is the template. That is the textbook example of an epigenetic mechanism. Position-effect variegation, discovered by Muller in the 1930s, is the genetic proof that chromatin states are clonally inherited: the patches in the eye are clones. Modifier screens for enhancers and suppressors of variegation found many of the chromatin proteins, including HP1 (Su(var)2-5). That is a mutant screen in the Jacob-Monod tradition, applied to chromatin. Note the careful definition: most “epigenetic” inheritance we discuss is through mitosis; inheritance across generations is rare in mammals because the germ line erases most marks, except at imprinted genes.

title: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
text:
Genomic imprinting
For a few hundred genes in mammals, only the copy from one parent is expressed. The other is silenced by methylation set in the parent’s germ line, and the imprint is reset each generation.

The same deletion in 15q11–q13 gives Prader–Willi syndrome if it is on the paternal chromosome and Angelman syndrome if it is on the maternal one.

Imprinting breaks a Mendelian assumption: that it does not matter which parent an allele comes from (Mendel’s reciprocal crosses in Part 1). For imprinted genes, it does. In the 15q11-q13 region, the SNRPN cluster (here one box for simplicity; it includes several snoRNA genes that matter most for Prader-Willi) is expressed only from the paternal chromosome, and UBE3A only from the maternal chromosome, at least in neurons. Delete the region on the paternal 15, and the child has no paternal-only genes: Prader-Willi (hypotonia, then overeating and obesity, learning disability). Delete it on the maternal 15: Angelman (severe learning disability, seizures, happy demeanour). Uniparental disomy gives the same results: two maternal 15s is Prader-Willi. In mice, Igf2 is paternally expressed and its neighbour H19 maternally expressed. The parental-conflict hypothesis: paternally expressed genes tend to promote growth of the fetus, maternally expressed genes restrain it.

title: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
text:
Imprinting in a pedigree
For a gene expressed only from the maternal allele (like UBE3A in neurons):

A child is affected only if the mutation comes from the mother.
A man carrying the mutation is unaffected (if he got it from his father) and passes it on silently: his children are unaffected carriers, but his daughters’ children have a ½ risk.
So the trait seems to skip generations, then appear in every child of carrier women at a ½ risk.

The allele is transmitted by normal Mendelian segregation; only its expression depends on the parent of origin.

Draw a quick pedigree on the board: a carrier grandfather, his unaffected carrier son and carrier daughter; the son’s children are all unaffected whether or not they inherit the mutation; the daughter’s children are affected with probability one half. Ask the room what they would conclude from such a pedigree if they did not know about imprinting: probably incomplete penetrance or sex-limited expression. This is a good reminder from the Pedigree analysis unit that the mode of inheritance has to be inferred carefully. The exercise has a problem of exactly this kind.

title: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
text:
X inactivation: the Lyon hypothesis

Mary Lyon (1961): in female mammals, one X in each cell is inactivated early in development, the choice is random, and it is kept in all descendant cells. The inactive X is the Barr body; it is coated by the long non-coding RNA XIST (from the X-inactivation centre, Xq13).

Lyon reasoned from coat-colour mosaics in female mice heterozygous for X-linked coat genes: the patches meant that only one X allele was being used in each patch. Barr and Bertram had seen a dense body in the nuclei of female cat neurons in 1949, which turned out to be the inactive X. XIST was found in 1991; it is expressed only from the inactive X and spreads along it in cis, recruiting silencing complexes (including Polycomb, H3K27me3) and later DNA methylation. XIST is itself a lncRNA, which is a bridge to the next unit. In humans the choice happens around implantation in the embryo proper; in mouse extra-embryonic tissues it is the paternal X that is always inactivated, an example of imprinting meeting X inactivation.

title: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
text:
Consequences of X inactivation

Every female is a mosaic for X-linked genes. Heterozygous women for X-linked recessive conditions have patches of normal and mutant cells; e.g. in anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia carriers have patches of skin without sweat glands.
Calico and tortoiseshell cats are almost always female: they need two X alleles (XO and Xo). A male calico is usually XXY.
Number of Barr bodies = number of X − 1: XX and XXY have one; X0 (Turner) has none; XXX has two. That is why X aneuploidy is far less severe than autosomal aneuploidy (Part 5).
Some genes escape inactivation (e.g. in the pseudoautosomal regions), which is why X0 and XXY are not normal.


Connect to Part 2 and to Pedigree analysis: in X-linked recessive inheritance, carrier females are usually unaffected, because about half of their cells use the normal X, which is enough for most genes. “Usually” is the key word, and skewing on the next slide explains the exceptions. The calico point is a nice test of understanding: an orange and black cat needs both X alleles, so it needs two X chromosomes; a male calico must be XXY (Klinefelter-like) or a chimera. The aneuploidy point links to Rearrangements and aneuploidy in Part 5: trisomy 21 is severe, but XXX women are often unaware of it. The genes that escape inactivation are expressed from two X in females and one in males, which explains the phenotypes of Turner (missing a second dose) and Klinefelter syndromes.

title: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
text:
Skewed X inactivation
On average, half the cells use the maternal X. But the choice is made in a small number of progenitor cells, so one female can be far from 50 : 50 by chance, like getting 7 heads in 8 coin tosses.

Skewed X inactivation: ≥ 80 : 20 (some studies use 90 : 10) in a tissue.
Causes: chance (few progenitors), selection against cells that use a harmful X, or mutations in the X-inactivation centre.
Consequence: a heterozygous carrier of an X-linked recessive disease can be affected if most of her cells use the mutant X: a manifesting carrier (e.g. of Duchenne muscular dystrophy or haemophilia A).
Monozygotic female twins can differ for an X-linked trait if their X inactivation differs.


This is binomial sampling again, the same idea as Mendel’s small samples in Part 1. If N progenitors each choose at random, the fraction that chose the maternal X has standard deviation the square root of one quarter over N. With N = 16 the standard deviation is 0.125, so about 2 percent of females are 80:20 or more by chance alone; with N = 4 it is much more common. The demo lets students see this. Selection is the other big cause: in female carriers of some severe X-linked mutations, cells that use the mutant X die or grow slowly, giving extreme skewing in blood. That is used clinically to identify carriers.

title: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
text:
Try it: an X-inactivation mosaic




Interactive demo. Left: a patch of tissue from one female. N progenitor cells each choose the maternal (orange) or paternal (black) X at random, then grow into clonal patches. Right: the percentage of cells in this embryo, and a histogram over 1000 embryos with the same N, with the share that are skewed at least 80:20. Suggested tour: start at N = 16 (seed 1: 9 of 16 progenitors chose the maternal X, cells 50:50; 2.3 percent of embryos skewed). Press “new embryo” a few times. Then N = 2: half of all embryos are completely skewed, and the patches are huge. Then N = 256: almost exactly 50:50 every time, fine-grained. Finally “cell mixing”: the same proportions, but salt and pepper, as in blood, where cells move. Ask: what decides patch size in a cat’s coat? Mostly how much the cells migrate and mix, not N.

title: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
text:
Dosage compensation in other species

The problem is the same everywhere: one sex has two X chromosomes and the other has one. The solutions differ: inactivate one X (mammals), double the single X (Drosophila males, the MSL complex), or halve both X (C. elegans hermaphrodites). Mutations that break dosage compensation are sex-specific lethals, e.g. msl mutations kill Drosophila males but not females.

The genetics point: the genes for dosage compensation were found as mutants that kill only one sex. In Drosophila the male-specific lethal (msl) genes encode a complex, with two non-coding roX RNAs, that binds the male X and raises its transcription about twofold through histone H4 lysine 16 acetylation. In C. elegans the dosage compensation complex, related to condensin, binds both X chromosomes of the hermaphrodite and halves their output. Birds (ZW females) compensate only partially. Note that sex determination is different again: in Drosophila it is set by the X-to-autosome ratio, not by the Y, which is why XO flies are sterile males (Part 2).

title: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
section: Seeing it in data: XIST in GTEx
text:
Seeing it in data: XIST in GTEx
The GTEx project measured RNA in 54 tissues from about 950 deceased donors. XIST is a clean test of what you just learned:

In women, XIST is expressed in every tissue (from the inactive X); in men it is essentially absent.
A Y-linked gene such as RPS4Y1 shows the opposite pattern.
Careful: GTEx’s default summary is the median over all samples. Most tissues have about twice as many male as female samples, so the pooled median of XIST is the male value, close to 0, everywhere except female-only tissues.

You will see this in the exercise and pull the per-sex data in R.

This slide previews the R exercise and makes a statistics point: a summary statistic over a mixture of two very different groups can hide one of them. In GTEx v10 the pooled median XIST in skeletal muscle is 0.04 TPM, while the female median is about 18 and the male median 0.02. In uterus, ovary and vagina, which only have female donors, the median XIST is 50 to 100 TPM. A handful of samples break the rule (for example a male sample with high XIST), which could be a sample mix-up or a donor with a 47,XXY karyotype; GTEx does not say, so we should not guess.

title: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Promoter, enhancer
cis-acting DNA; enhancers act at a distance via looping and Mediator


Transcription factor
trans-acting protein; binds a short, degenerate motif (GATA1: WGATAR)


Regulatory mutation
changes where/when, not what; cis-acting, often tissue-specific, often dominant


Chromatin marks
acetylation, H3K4me3 = active; H3K9me3, H3K27me3 = silent


DNA methylation
5mC at CpG; DNMT1 copies the pattern after replication


Epigenetics
heritable expression state without sequence change; e.g. position-effect variegation


Imprinting
parent-of-origin expression; 15q11–q13: PWS (paternal loss), AS (maternal loss)


X inactivation
one X per cell, random, clonal; XIST; Barr bodies = X − 1


Skewing
chance (few progenitors) or selection; manifesting carriers


Dosage compensation
mammals: inactivate; flies: double in males; worms: halve in hermaphrodites




Revision sheet. The common theme across imprinting, X inactivation and position effects: a choice is made in one cell (or in a parent’s germ line) and then copied to descendants through chromatin. Genetically, all three give phenotypes that look odd at first: patchy, parent-dependent, or variable between relatives.

title: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
text:
Where this leads

Next: RNA-mediated regulation. XIST is a long non-coding RNA. The next unit adds microRNAs and RNAi, a second layer of control after transcription.
Development & model organisms. Transcription-factor cascades (gap, pair-rule, Hox genes) and chromatin memory (Polycomb keeps Hox genes off) build the body plan.
Part 7: Complex traits. Most GWAS signals lie in non-coding, regulatory DNA.


Point forward. In the exercise students predict X-linked phenotypes with mosaicism and imprinting by hand, look up motifs in JASPAR and XIST in GTEx and NCBI Gene, and in R they reshape and summarise GTEx data to see how a pooled median hides the female XIST signal.

title: Exercise in R: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
Exercise in R: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
Exercise in R: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
text:
Before you start
This page builds on the by-hand part of the Exercise, so do that first. You need the packages readr, dplyr, tidyr and ggplot2. Download both files and save them in a data/ folder of your R project:

gtex_median_tpm.csv: median expression (TPM, transcripts per million) of seven genes in each of the 54 GTEx tissues, all samples pooled;
gtex_sex_tpm.csv: one row per sample, the TPM of XIST and of the Y-linked gene RPS4Y1 in four tissues, with the donor’s sex.

Both are real data from the GTEx Portal API, release GTEx v10 (GENCODE v39), downloaded on 2026-11-20; see the data README for the exact queries. The first lines of each file, starting with #, record the source; read_csv(..., comment = "#") skips them.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

title: Exercise in R: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
text:
Tasks
New idiom today: long vs wide, and grouped summaries. A wide table has one column per gene. A long table has one row per measurement, with a column saying which gene it is. pivot_longer() turns wide into long; pivot_wider() goes back. Long tables are what group_by() + summarise() and ggplot2 work with: “for each gene”, “colour by gene” and “facet by tissue” all need the gene as a column, not as column names.
The genes: GAPDH (a glycolysis enzyme, expressed everywhere), ALB (albumin, liver), INS (insulin, pancreatic β cells), HBB (β-globin, red blood cells), MYH7 (β-myosin heavy chain, heart and slow skeletal muscle), XIST (X-inactivation lncRNA) and RPS4Y1 (a ribosomal protein gene on the Y chromosome).
R1. (wide to long) Read data/gtex_median_tpm.csv. How many rows and columns does it have? Use pivot_longer() to make a long table med_long with columns tissue, gene and tpm. How many rows does it have now, and why?
med <- read_csv("data/gtex_median_tpm.csv", comment = "#", show_col_types = FALSE)
med_long <- med |>
  pivot_longer(-tissue, names_to = "gene", values_to = "tpm")
R2. (where is each gene on?) For each gene, find the tissue with the highest median (slice_max() after group_by(gene)). Then summarise each gene over tissues: the median of the medians, the maximum, and the number of tissues above 10 TPM. Which genes are tissue-specific and which are expressed nearly everywhere? Anything surprising?
R3. (a heat map) Plot med_long as a heat map with geom_tile(): genes on the x axis, tissues on the y axis, fill = log10(tpm + 1). Why do we take the log, and why add 1?
R4. (XIST and RPS4Y1) Filter med_long to XIST and RPS4Y1, use pivot_wider() to put the two genes side by side, and sort by XIST. Which tissues top the list? XIST is expressed from the inactive X in every female cell, so why is its median close to 0 in, say, skeletal muscle?
R5. (summarise by sex) Read data/gtex_sex_tpm.csv. With group_by(tissue, gene, sex) and summarise(), compute for each group the number of samples, the median TPM and the fraction of samples above 1 TPM. Then compute the pooled median per tissue and gene (ignoring sex), with the number of female and male samples. Explain the pooled XIST median.
R6. (plot by sex) Make box plots of TPM by sex, with facet_grid(gene ~ tissue) and a log y axis (scale_y_log10(); add 0.01 so that zeros can be plotted). Are there samples that break the pattern? Suggest possible explanations, and say what you cannot conclude from these data.

Where this leads
group_by() + summarise() and pivot_longer() are the workhorses for any table of measurements. In RNA-mediated regulation you go back to sequences: you find microRNA seed matches in a 3′UTR with str_locate_all() and plot where they are.

title: The eukaryotic chromosome
text:
About this lecture
In Part 2 a chromosome was a line with genes on it, and meiosis moved those lines around. This lecture looks at the physical object: a single, very long DNA molecule packed with proteins, with special sequences that let it be copied and segregated without falling apart.

Chromatin: how 2 m of DNA fits in a nucleus; nucleosomes and higher-order packing.
Euchromatin and heterochromatin, and what happens to a gene moved next to heterochromatin.
Banding and karyotypes: how chromosomes are recognised and named (1p36.33, 47,XY,+21).
Centromeres: the attachment point for the spindle.
Telomeres: why linear ends are a problem, and how telomerase solves it.
What a chromosome needs: yeast artificial chromosomes.
The telomere-to-telomere (T2T) human genome, which finally sequenced centromeres and telomeres.

Book: Hartwell, Genetics: From Genes to Genomes, the eukaryotic chromosomes chapter.

This opens Part 5, which follows the book’s chapters on chromosomes in detail: the chromosome itself today, then rearrangements and aneuploidy, then bacterial genomes (a recap) and organelle genomes. Students know DNA replication from 5MO103, so the end-replication problem is a new application of something they know, not new biochemistry. Keep the questions genetic: what does a chromosome need in order to be inherited faithfully, and what goes wrong when it lacks it? Chromatin and gene regulation come back in Part 6 (eukaryotic regulation, X inactivation); today we only need the structural picture.

title: The eukaryotic chromosome
text:
The packaging problem




Number




Haploid human genome (T2T-CHM13)
3.055 × 109 bp


Diploid nucleus
≈ 6.1 × 109 bp in 46 molecules


Length of B-DNA
0.34 nm per bp


Total DNA per diploid nucleus
≈ 6.1 × 109 × 0.34 nm ≈ 2 m


Diameter of a nucleus
≈ 5–10 µm


Chromosome 1 (248 Mb) as naked DNA
≈ 8.4 cm


Chromosome 1 at metaphase
≈ 10 µm



The DNA must be compacted about 10 000-fold at mitosis, yet stay readable for transcription and replication in interphase. Chromatin solves both problems.

Do the arithmetic with the room. 248 million base pairs times 0.34 nanometres is 84 millimetres, about 8 centimetres of DNA for one chromosome, which at metaphase is around 10 micrometres long: roughly ten-thousand-fold compaction. The whole diploid set is about two metres in a nucleus a few micrometres across. The point is not the exact numbers but the scale: packaging cannot be a random tangle, because the cell has to find genes, copy every base exactly once per cycle, and separate 46 molecules without breaking them. Chromatin is DNA plus protein; by mass it is roughly half protein.

title: The eukaryotic chromosome
section: Nucleosomes: the first level of packing
text:
Nucleosomes: the first level of packing


A nucleosome core is 147 bp of DNA wrapped about 1.7 turns around a histone octamer: two each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4.
Linker DNA (about 20–80 bp) joins the cores; histone H1 binds where DNA enters and leaves. One nucleosome per ≈ 200 bp.
Histones are small, very basic (Lys, Arg) proteins: their positive charge binds the negative phosphate backbone. They are among the most conserved proteins known.


Walk the figure from left to right. The 11-nanometre fibre, beads on a string, is what you see when chromatin is spread out in low salt; nuclease digestion of chromatin gives DNA fragments in multiples of about 200 base pairs, which is how the nucleosome repeat was discovered. The compact 30-nanometre fibre is seen in vitro; in living cells, imaging suggests a less regular, irregularly folded fibre, so present it as “further folding” rather than a fixed structure. Loops anchored at their bases (by cohesin and condensin, which students will meet again) and condensation give the metaphase chromosome. Conservation: histone H4 differs at only two of its 102 amino acids between peas and cows, a classic example. The histone tails stick out of the core and carry chemical modifications; that is the hook for gene regulation in Part 6.

text:
Euchromatin and heterochromatin









Euchromatin
Heterochromatin

open, decondensed
compact, stains darkly


Genes
gene-rich, mostly active
gene-poor, mostly silent


Replication
early in S phase
late in S phase
