H3K9 methylation + HP1 protein


Examples
most of the chromosome arms
centromeres, telomeres, 1q12, 9q12, Yq12




Constitutive heterochromatin is always condensed, in every cell: mostly repetitive satellite DNA around centromeres.
Facultative heterochromatin is condensed in some cells only. The best-known example is the inactive X in female mammals (Part 6).


The terms come from cytology in the 1920s: heterochromatin stayed dark through interphase while euchromatin faded. Today we define them by function and chemistry. Constitutive heterochromatin is built on repeats, mostly satellite DNA, that would be dangerous if they recombined freely: unequal crossing over between repeats makes deletions and duplications, which is the next unit. Facultative heterochromatin is the inactive X, the Barr body, which is a whole chromosome silenced in some cells and not others; X inactivation has its own demo in Part 6. The large heterochromatic blocks 1q12, 9q12 and 16q11.2 vary in size between healthy people; such variants are written for example 1qh+ on a karyotype and have no clinical effect.

title: The eukaryotic chromosome
text:
Position effect: heterochromatin can spread
In Drosophila, the inversion In(1)wm4 moves the eye-colour gene white+ from the euchromatin of the X to a spot next to the centromeric heterochromatin.

The white+ allele is unchanged, but the eye is mottled: red and white patches.
In some cells heterochromatin spreads into white+ and silences it; in others it does not. Each choice is made early and inherited by the cell’s descendants, so you see clones of red and white cells.
This is position-effect variegation (PEV): the phenotype depends on where a gene sits, not only on its sequence.

Genetic lessons: a rearrangement can change a phenotype without changing any gene, and chromatin state is passed from a cell to its daughters.

PEV is the classic genetic evidence that heterochromatin is a state that can spread along the chromosome. Screens for mutations that suppress or enhance the mottling found the genes for heterochromatin proteins, among them HP1 (encoded by Su(var)2-5) and the H3K9 methyltransferase Su(var)3-9: genetics found the biochemistry. Point forward: inversions are one of the rearrangements in the next unit, and this is one way an inversion with no lost DNA can still have a phenotype. Variegation is also a clue for epigenetic inheritance, which is Part 6.

title: The eukaryotic chromosome
text:
Chromosome anatomy and banding

G-banding: metaphase chromosomes are treated with trypsin and stained with Giemsa. Each chromosome shows a fixed, reproducible pattern of dark and light bands, about 400–550 bands per haploid set in a routine karyotype, and up to about 850 at high resolution.

The banding pattern is the chromosome’s barcode; it is how cytogeneticists recognise each chromosome and spot a missing or extra piece. Dark G bands are AT-rich, gene-poor and replicate late; light bands are GC-rich and gene-rich. Band names are read from the centromere outward: chromosome, arm, region, band, then sub-bands after the dot. So 1p36.33 is near the tip of the short arm of chromosome 1, and 1q44 near the tip of the long arm. Students have already seen band names in NCBI Gene’s Location field (for example CFTR at 7q31.2), and now they know what the name means. The right side of the figure classifies chromosomes by centromere position; the acrocentrics matter in the next unit, because two of them can fuse at their centromeres (a Robertsonian translocation) with almost no loss of genes.

title: The eukaryotic chromosome
text:
The karyotype and its notation
A karyotype is the full set of chromosomes of a cell, arranged in pairs by size, centromere position and banding. It is written in a standard notation (ISCN):







Karyotype
Meaning




46,XX
normal female


46,XY
normal male


47,XY,+21
male with trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)


45,X
one X only (Turner syndrome)


46,XX,del(5)(p15.2)
deletion in 5p, from band 5p15.2 to the end


46,XY,t(9;22)(q34;q11.2)
reciprocal translocation between 9q34 and 22q11.2



The format is: total chromosome number, sex chromosomes, then any abnormality with its breakpoints.

A karyotype is made from cells arrested in metaphase, usually blood lymphocytes stimulated to divide, or amniotic or chorionic villus cells before birth. Read each row aloud. The first number is always the chromosome count. Every row from the third down is the subject of the next unit: trisomy 21, monosomy X, a terminal deletion (5p15.2 deletion causes cri-du-chat syndrome), and the translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 that makes the Philadelphia chromosome in chronic myeloid leukaemia. The resolution of a G-banded karyotype is a few megabases; smaller changes need molecular methods such as microarrays or sequencing, which is how the copy-number syndromes in the next unit are found today.

title: The eukaryotic chromosome
text:
Centromeres
The centromere is where the kinetochore assembles and spindle microtubules attach. Without one, a chromosome is lost at cell division.









Budding yeast
Humans




Type
point centromere
regional centromere


DNA
≈ 125 bp, three elements (CDEI–III)
α-satellite: 171-bp repeats in arrays of several Mb


Defined by
the DNA sequence
mainly by chromatin: the histone variant CENP-A




CENP-A replaces H3 in centromeric nucleosomes and marks the centromere epigenetically. Rare neocentromeres form on non-satellite DNA, and α-satellite without CENP-A does not work.
A chromosome with two centromeres (dicentric) is torn apart at anaphase; one with none (acentric) is lost.


Yeast is the exception that made centromeres tractable: its centromere is short enough to clone, and cloning it was how artificial chromosomes became possible (later today). Human centromeres are huge arrays of a 171-base-pair monomer, arranged in higher-order repeats that are nearly identical over megabases, which is why they could not be assembled until recently. The key concept is epigenetic specification: what makes a centromere a centromere is the CENP-A chromatin on it, and CENP-A is copied to the daughter chromosomes. Dicentric and acentric chromosomes come back in the next unit: a crossover inside a paracentric inversion loop makes exactly one of each. Some organisms, such as C. elegans, have holocentric chromosomes with kinetochores along their whole length.

title: The eukaryotic chromosome
text:
Telomeres: protecting the ends
A telomere is the end of a linear chromosome: a long array of a short repeat, plus proteins.

Vertebrates: 5’-TTAGGG-3’ repeated, a few kb up to about 15 kb in human cells. Tetrahymena: TTGGGG. Arabidopsis: TTTAGGG.
The G-rich strand runs 5’ → 3’ towards the end and sticks out as a single-stranded 3’ overhang (≈ 50–300 nt).
The overhang tucks back into the double helix to form a t-loop, held by a protein complex called shelterin.

Why ends need protecting: a cell treats a bare DNA end as a double-strand break. Unprotected ends get degraded or fused to each other, making dicentric chromosomes that break again at the next division.

Telomeres solve two problems; this slide is the first, end protection. Hiding the end in a t-loop and coating it with shelterin stops the DNA damage response from “repairing” the end by joining it to another chromosome. Barbara McClintock saw this in maize in the 1930s and 40s: broken chromosome ends fused and went through breakage-fusion-bridge cycles, while natural ends did not. The repeat is remarkably conserved: humans and other vertebrates share TTAGGG, and many other organisms have similar G-rich repeats. In the reference genome, the chromosome’s top strand at the p end reads CCCTAA, because it is the C-rich strand that runs 5’ to 3’ away from the p-terminal end; the R exercise shows this directly.

title: The eukaryotic chromosome
text:
The end-replication problem

DNA polymerase only extends an existing 3’ end, and needs an RNA primer to start. On the lagging strand, the last primer at the very end cannot be replaced by DNA: there is no 3’ end upstream of it to extend.

This is replication from 5MO103, followed to the very end of the molecule. Panel (a): the parental strand whose 3’ end is at the chromosome end is copied discontinuously. Each Okazaki fragment starts with an RNA primer; inner primers are removed and the gap is filled by extending the fragment to the left. The last primer has nothing to its right to extend from, so after removal its gap stays open, and the new strand is shorter. In the next round, that shorter strand is a template, so one of the daughter molecules is shorter. In practice, nucleases also resect the ends to make the 3’ overhang, which adds to the loss. Panel (b) is the solution and the next slide. The problem was pointed out independently by Olovnikov and by Watson in the early 1970s.

title: The eukaryotic chromosome
text:
Telomerase
Telomerase is a reverse transcriptase that carries its own RNA template.

Two core parts: the protein TERT (telomerase reverse transcriptase, gene TERT on 5p15.33) and the RNA TERC (also called hTR, gene TERC on 3q26.2).
The template in human TERC reads 3’-CAAUCCCAAUC-5’. It pairs with the 3’ end of the overhang, and TERT adds TTAGGG units by copying it.
Afterwards the ordinary replication machinery fills in the C-rich strand.

Discovered in the ciliate Tetrahymena by Carol Greider and Elizabeth Blackburn (1985). Changing bases in the RNA template changed the repeats added, which proved the RNA is the template. Nobel Prize 2009, with Jack Szostak.

Telomerase is the reverse of the central dogma in a small way: RNA to DNA, like a retroviral reverse transcriptase, and TERT is in fact related to those enzymes. Ciliates were the right organism because their macronucleus has many thousands of small chromosomes (including thousands of copies of a tiny rDNA minichromosome) and so a huge number of telomeres. The template experiment is a lovely piece of genetics: Yu, Blackburn and colleagues mutated the template in Tetrahymena and the cells’ telomeres acquired the mutant repeat. The exercise has a by-hand version. Both genes are on chromosomes you can look up in the Find it part; note that TERT itself sits only about 1.3 Mb from the end of chromosome 5.

title: The eukaryotic chromosome
text:
Telomeres, ageing and cancer



Cell type
Telomerase
Telomeres




Germline, early embryo
active
maintained


Stem and progenitor cells
low to moderate
shorten slowly


Most somatic cells
off
shorten each division


≈ 85–90% of cancers
re-activated
maintained


Most other cancers
off; ALT (recombination)
maintained




Cultured human fibroblasts stop dividing after about 40–60 divisions (the Hayflick limit): short telomeres trigger senescence. Short telomeres act as a counter of cell divisions.
Turning telomerase back on (often via mutations in the TERT promoter) lets cancer cells divide indefinitely.
Loss-of-function mutations in telomerase genes cause telomere biology disorders, such as dyskeratosis congenita: bone-marrow failure and other tissues that need many divisions.


The table summarises where telomerase is on. Replicative senescence is a tumour-suppressor mechanism: a cell that has divided too many times stops. Cancer cells must escape it, and most do so by reactivating telomerase; TERT promoter mutations are among the most common non-coding mutations in cancers such as melanoma and glioblastoma. The minority that do not use telomerase maintain telomeres by recombination between telomeres, called ALT, alternative lengthening of telomeres. The genetic diseases go the other way: patients inherit a faulty telomerase component and their highly proliferative tissues fail. Dyskeratosis congenita can be X-linked (DKC1, a telomerase-associated protein), autosomal dominant (TERC, TERT) or autosomal recessive: a good example of one phenotype with several genes and modes of inheritance. Students look it up in the exercise. Be careful with “telomeres explain ageing”: short telomeres correlate with age, but ageing has many causes.

title: The eukaryotic chromosome
text:
What does a chromosome need?
In the early 1980s, yeast geneticists tested which DNA elements a molecule needs to behave like a chromosome. They put each construct into yeast cells and measured how stably it was inherited:







Construct
Behaviour in yeast




Circular plasmid, selectable marker only
not maintained: no replication


+ ARS (origin of replication)
replicates, but is lost from many cells at each division


+ ARS + CEN (centromere)
stable, about one copy per cell, segregates like a chromosome


Linear, ARS + CEN, no telomeres
degraded from its ends


Linear, ARS + CEN + TEL at both ends
a minichromosome; more stable the longer it is



Three elements make a chromosome: an origin, a centromere and two telomeres.

This is the genetic definition of a chromosome, found by building one. Each element was cloned by its function: ARS by its ability to make a plasmid replicate, CEN (Clarke and Carbon, 1980) by making a plasmid segregate stably, and TEL by Szostak and Blackburn, who showed that Tetrahymena telomere ends stabilise a linear plasmid in yeast, the first hint that telomere function is conserved. The last row has a surprise: short linear minichromosomes still segregate poorly, and stability improves with length. That observation made people try very large inserts, which gave the yeast artificial chromosome.

title: The eukaryotic chromosome
text:
Yeast artificial chromosomes


A YAC (Burke, Carle and Olson, 1987) carries 100 kb to over 1 Mb of foreign DNA, far more than a plasmid (≈ 10 kb) or a phage (≈ 20–45 kb).
YACs were used to build the first physical maps of human chromosomes in the 1990s. Their weakness: inserts were often chimeric (two unrelated pieces joined) or rearranged.
The Human Genome Project then switched mostly to BACs, bacterial artificial chromosomes of 100–300 kb based on the E. coli F plasmid (see the bacterial genetics recap, later in this part).


The YAC puts the previous slide into practice: the vector is grown as a circular plasmid in E. coli, cut to expose the telomere sequences and the cloning site, and the two arms are ligated to a large fragment of genomic DNA. Selecting for both yeast markers, TRP1 on one arm and URA3 on the other, keeps only cells that carry a complete construct with both arms. The capacity was the selling point: whole human genes such as DMD, over 2 Mb, could be studied in a few clones. The drawback was instability and chimerism. BACs, built on the F factor that students know from conjugation, are smaller but much more stable, and they became the workhorses of the clone-by-clone human genome sequence. Artificial chromosomes are still used to build synthetic yeast chromosomes and to carry large human genes into mice.

title: The eukaryotic chromosome
section: Complete at last: the T2T human genome
text:
Complete at last: the T2T human genome

The reference genome from 2001–2013 (GRCh38) left about 8% unsequenced: centromeres, big satellite blocks, the short arms of the acrocentrics, and the telomeres. In 2022 the Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) Consortium published T2T-CHM13: 3.055 Gb with no gaps, adding nearly 200 Mb of sequence (Nurk et al., Science 2022).

Why could the repeats not be assembled before? Short sequencing reads, a few hundred bases, cannot be placed inside a multi-megabase array of nearly identical 171-base-pair repeats. T2T used long reads: PacBio HiFi reads of about 20 kb that are very accurate, and Oxford Nanopore reads of more than 100 kb. CHM13 is a cell line from a complete hydatidiform mole, which arises when an egg without a nucleus is fertilised by one sperm whose genome then doubles. So the genome is almost entirely homozygous, with only one version of each chromosome to assemble. A later version, CHM13 v2.0, added a Y chromosome from another person. The figure is drawn to scale from the UCSC browser’s CenSat track for this assembly: the active centromere of chromosome 1 is a 4.5 Mb alpha-satellite array, and the 1q12 heterochromatin block is 13 Mb of HSat2 satellite, which GRCh38 left as an 18 Mb gap. The new sequence includes 99 predicted protein-coding genes, many in segmental duplications. Students explore this assembly in the Find it and R tasks.

title: The eukaryotic chromosome
text:
Try it: read a telomere
The first 60 bases of chromosome 1 in T2T-CHM13 (UCSC genome hs1), as stored in the reference:
CACCCTAAACCCTAACCCCTAACCCTAACCCTAACCCTAACCCTAACCCTAACCCCTAAA
and the last 60 bases of the same chromosome:
AGGGTTAGGGTTAGGGTTAGGGTTAGGGTTAGGGTTAGGGTTAGGGTTAGGGTTAGGGTT

Find the repeat in each. Why does one end read CCCTAA and the other TTAGGG?
Spot the slight irregularities at the start (CCCCTAA, CCCTAAA). Real telomeres are not perfect.
In the R exercise you count the repeats along the first and last 10 kb and see where the telomere ends.


Give them a minute. The reference stores one strand, the top strand, read 5’ to 3’ from the p end to the q end. At the q end, the top strand runs 5’ to 3’ towards the end, so it is the G-rich strand: TTAGGG. At the p end, the strand that runs towards the end is the bottom strand, which is G-rich, so the top strand there is its reverse complement: CCCTAA. Same telomere, read from the other side. The irregular repeats are real: telomeres contain occasional variant repeats, especially near the junction with the rest of the chromosome. These sequences were downloaded from the UCSC REST API for the hs1 assembly on 2026-11-20. In the older GRCh38 reference, the first 10 kb of chromosome 1 are all N.

title: The eukaryotic chromosome
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Nucleosome
147 bp around a histone octamer (H2A, H2B, H3, H4 ×2); one per ≈ 200 bp


Packing
≈ 2 m of DNA per diploid nucleus; ≈ 10 000-fold compaction at metaphase


Heterochromatin
compact, gene-poor, late-replicating; constitutive (satellites) or facultative (inactive X)


Position-effect variegation
a gene moved next to heterochromatin is silenced in some cells only


G-banding, karyotype
reproducible band pattern; names like 1p36.33; notation 47,XY,+21


Centromere
kinetochore site; yeast 125 bp; human Mb arrays of 171-bp α-satellite; marked by CENP-A


Telomere
TTAGGG repeats with a 3’ overhang and shelterin; hides the end from DNA repair


End-replication problem
the last lagging-strand primer cannot be replaced: ends shorten each division


Telomerase
TERT + TERC RNA template; active in germline and most cancers


Minimal chromosome
origin (ARS) + centromere (CEN) + two telomeres (TEL): the YAC


T2T-CHM13
first gapless human genome, 3.055 Gb, 2022




The summary is the revision sheet. If they keep one idea: a chromosome is inherited faithfully only if it can be replicated (origins), segregated (one centromere) and kept whole (two telomeres). Each of these comes back in the next unit as something that can go wrong: dicentric and acentric fragments from inversions, fusions at centromeres in Robertsonian translocations, and lost or extra chromosomes in aneuploidy.

title: The eukaryotic chromosome
text:
Where this leads

Next: Rearrangements & aneuploidy. Deletions, duplications, inversions and translocations change the structure of chromosomes; nondisjunction changes their number. You will meet dicentric and acentric chromosomes, Robertsonian fusions of acrocentrics, and the 9;22 translocation from the karyotype slide.
Bacterial genetics (recap). A circular chromosome has no end-replication problem; the F plasmid behind BACs is the agent of conjugation.
Organelle inheritance. Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own small, circular chromosomes.
Part 6: Eukaryotic regulation. Histone modifications, chromatin and X inactivation as gene regulation.


Point forward. The exercise has pen-and-paper problems on packing arithmetic, band names, the telomerase template and artificial chromosomes, then database tasks in NCBI Gene, the UCSC browser and MedGen. The R part reads the first and last 10 kb of chromosome 1 from the T2T genome and counts telomere repeats along them with str_count.

title: Exercise in R: the eukaryotic chromosome
Exercise in R: the eukaryotic chromosome
Exercise in R: the eukaryotic chromosome
text:
Before you start
This page builds on the Exercise, especially B9 (why one chromosome end reads CCCTAA and the other TTAGGG). You need the packages dplyr, ggplot2 and stringr.
Download the two data files into a folder data/ next to your script or R Markdown file:

data/chm13_chr1_pter_10kb.fa: the first 10 kb of chromosome 1;
data/chm13_chr1_qter_10kb.fa: the last 10 kb of chromosome 1;
data/README.md says where they come from.

Both are real sequence from the complete human genome T2T-CHM13 v2.0 (UCSC genome hs1), downloaded on 2026-11-20 through the UCSC REST API, for example https://api.genome.ucsc.edu/getData/sequence?genome=hs1;chrom=chr1;start=0;end=10000. Each file is the top strand of the reference, read 5’ → 3’ from the p end of the chromosome towards the q end.
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)

title: Exercise in R: the eukaryotic chromosome
text:
Tasks
You already know the stringr functions str_sub (cut out part of a string), str_count (count matches of a pattern) and reading FASTA files by hand, from Parts 3 and 4. This unit’s new idiom is counting in windows: make a table with one row per window start, cut out each window with str_sub, and count in each window with str_count. Because both functions work on whole vectors, one mutate does all the windows at once, without a loop.
R1. (read the sequences) Write a function read_fasta_seq(path) that reads a one-record FASTA file and returns the sequence as a single string. Read both files. Check the header line and the lengths, and print the first 60 bases of the p end and the last 60 bases of the q end.
read_fasta_seq <- function(path) {
  lines <- readLines(path)
  paste(lines[-1], collapse = "")   # drop the header line, glue the rest together
}
pter <- read_fasta_seq("data/chm13_chr1_pter_10kb.fa")
qter <- read_fasta_seq("data/chm13_chr1_qter_10kb.fa")
readLines("data/chm13_chr1_pter_10kb.fa", n = 1)
nchar(pter)
nchar(qter)
str_sub(pter, 1, 60)
str_sub(qter, -60, -1)
R2. (count the repeats) Count TTAGGG and CCCTAA in each 10-kb sequence with str_count. Which motif dominates at which end? Explain with B9.
tibble(end    = c("p end (start of chr1)", "q end (end of chr1)"),
       TTAGGG = str_count(c(pter, qter), "TTAGGG"),
       CCCTAA = str_count(c(pter, qter), "CCCTAA"))
R3. (repeat density in windows) Cut the p-end sequence into 100-bp windows, count CCCTAA in each, and plot the counts along the sequence. A window made only of telomere repeats holds 100/6 ≈ 16.7 repeats; draw that as a dashed line. Where does the telomere end? Use the rule “a window with at least 8 repeats is telomeric” and find the last such window.
win <- 100
windows <- tibble(start = seq(1, nchar(pter), by = win)) |>
  mutate(window  = str_sub(pter, start, start + win - 1),
         repeats = str_count(window, "CCCTAA"))
windows |> select(start, repeats) |> slice(24:30)
windows |> filter(repeats >= 8) |> summarise(last_start = max(start))

ggplot(windows, aes(x = start, y = repeats)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2a6f97", width = win * 0.9) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = win / 6, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "position from the start of chr1 (bp)",
       y = "CCCTAA repeats per 100 bp",
       title = "T2T-CHM13 chr1, first 10 kb") +
  theme_minimal()
R4. (a gap inside the telomere) Your plot has a dip to almost zero around position 900–1100, inside the telomere. Look at that stretch with str_sub(pter, 880, 1000). Which slightly different repeat is there? Count it per window and in total.
str_sub(pter, 880, 1000)
windows <- windows |> mutate(variant = str_count(window, "CCCTCA"))
windows |> select(start, repeats, variant) |> slice(8:12)
sum(windows$variant)
R5. (both ends) Put the window counting into a function count_windows(seq, motif, win = 100). Use it for CCCTAA at the p end and TTAGGG at the q end, measure positions as distance from the chromosome end, and plot the two ends side by side with facet_wrap. Estimate how far each telomere reaches into the chromosome.
count_windows <- function(seq, motif, win = 100) {
  tibble(start = seq(1, nchar(seq), by = win)) |>
    mutate(repeats = str_count(str_sub(seq, start, start + win - 1), motif))
}
both <- bind_rows(
  count_windows(pter, "CCCTAA") |> mutate(end = "p end: CCCTAA", from_end = start - 1),
  count_windows(qter, "TTAGGG") |> mutate(end = "q end: TTAGGG", from_end = nchar(qter) - (start + 99))
)
both |>
  group_by(end) |>
  summarise(telomere_windows = sum(repeats >= 8),
            reaches_bp       = max(from_end[repeats >= 8]) + 100)

ggplot(both, aes(x = from_end, y = repeats)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2a6f97", width = 90) +
  facet_wrap(~ end) +
  labs(x = "distance from the chromosome end (bp)", y = "repeats per 100 bp") +
  theme_minimal()
R6. (is it chance?) How many times would CCCTAA turn up in 10 kb of random sequence? Shuffle the bases of the p-end sequence with sample() (this keeps the base composition but destroys the order) and count again. Compare with the rough expectation 10 000 / 46, which assumes all four bases are equally common.
set.seed(1)
bases <- str_split(pter, "")[[1]]
table(bases)
shuffled <- paste(sample(bases), collapse = "")
str_count(shuffled, "CCCTAA")
nchar(pter) / 4^6

Telomere repeats per 100-bp window, measured from each end of chromosome 1.


Both telomeres of chromosome 1 in this assembly are about 3 kb (2.7 kb at the p end, 3.0 kb at the q end), with variant or degenerate repeats in their inner part. That is at the short end of the range for human cells (a few kb up to about 15 kb). The reference is one assembly from one cell line, CHM13, and telomere length differs between cells, chromosome ends, tissues and people, and shortens with age. A real cell’s telomere length is a distribution, not a single number.

[1] 2.441406
In the shuffled sequence, CCCTAA appears 5 times in 10 kb; the rough expectation for random sequence with equal base frequencies is 10 000 / 4096 ≈ 2.4 (it is a bit higher here because this stretch is rich in C and A). The real sequence has 361 copies, almost all packed into the first 2.7 kb. The telomere is clearly not chance.

title: Exercise in R: the eukaryotic chromosome
text:
Where this leads
Counting a motif in windows is a general tool: the same code finds CpG islands, satellite arrays or restriction sites along a sequence. In Rearrangements & aneuploidy (next), you work with probabilities of aneuploid gametes and simulate how a translocation carrier’s chromosomes segregate. In Organelle inheritance you return to rbinom and replicate to simulate the mitochondrial bottleneck.

title: Ethics of genetic knowledge
text:
About this lecture
All course long you have predicted genotypes, computed risks and looked up variants. This lecture asks: what happens when those answers concern real people?

A framework: four principles, plus consent, privacy and the right not to know.
Genetic testing: diagnostic, predictive, carrier and prenatal tests, and findings nobody asked for. Direct-to-consumer tests.
Privacy: why a genome cannot be made anonymous, and how genealogy databases now solve crimes.
Editing the germline: embryo editing, mitochondrial replacement and gene drives.
History: eugenics, and the Swedish Institute for Racial Biology and sterilisation laws.
Ethical review of research in Sweden, and the laws on biobanks and genetic data.

The aim is not to give you the right answers. It is to help you see the conflict, name the principles involved and argue for a position. The exercise gives you cases and a literature search.

This is the ethics module of the course (1 ECTS). It links back to almost every unit: Huntington disease and the half risk from the Mendel unit, Y-linked inheritance from pedigrees, mitochondrial inheritance from Part 5, CRISPR-based tools and databases from Part 4. Make it clear from the start that ethics is not opinion without structure. We use a small, standard vocabulary (four principles, consent, privacy, the right not to know), and a good argument uses the facts of genetics correctly. Many questions have no single right answer, but there are clearly bad answers: ones that get the genetics wrong, or ignore someone whose interests are at stake.

title: Ethics of genetic knowledge
text:
Why genetic information is special
A blood glucose value is about you, today. A genotype is different:

It is shared. Your relatives carry half, a quarter or an eighth of your alleles. A result about you is also partly a result about them, and they did not consent.
It predicts. A Huntington disease allele says something about your health decades from now, sometimes with no treatment available.
It is permanent and identifying. You can change a password, not a genome. A genome is a unique identifier, and it can be read from a few cells.
It is reproductive. Carrier and prenatal tests inform choices about future people.
Its meaning changes. A variant of uncertain significance today may be classified as pathogenic next year (think of the ClinVar classification from the pedigree exercise).


Each bullet links to genetics they have done. Shared: the coefficient of relationship, one half for first-degree relatives, is Mendelian segregation. Predictive: an autosomal dominant late-onset disease with full penetrance turns a genotype into a forecast. Identifying: we will see how few markers are needed. Reproductive: carrier testing is the Aa x Aa cross. Changing meaning: ClinVar classifications and review status change as evidence accumulates; a result from five years ago may need to be re-read. These five properties are why genetics gets its own laws in many countries, including Sweden’s Genetic Integrity Act, which we meet at the end.

title: Ethics of genetic knowledge
text:
A framework: four principles

The four principles of biomedical ethics (Beauchamp and Childress, Principles of Biomedical Ethics, 1st edition 1979). Each is a reason that counts; in real cases they conflict, and the work is to weigh them.

These four principles are the most widely used framework in medical ethics. Autonomy: respect people’s own informed choices. Beneficence: act for the person’s good. Non-maleficence: avoid causing harm. Justice: distribute benefits, risks and costs fairly. None of them is absolute, and the interesting cases are the ones where they pull in different directions. Example: a doctor finds a BRCA1 variant. Beneficence says tell the patient’s sisters, who could get screening. Autonomy and privacy say the patient decides whom to tell. Justice asks whether everyone has access to the screening that would follow. In the exercise, every case asks you to name which principles are in tension. Other frameworks exist (consequences, duties, virtues, rights), and the principles are a practical summary rather than a full theory.

title: Ethics of genetic knowledge
section: Consent, privacy and the right not to know
text:
Consent, privacy and the right not to know

Informed consent: a person agrees to a test or to research voluntarily, after understanding what it involves, its risks, and what will happen to the sample and the data. Consent can be withdrawn.
Broad consent: agreeing that a stored sample may be used in future research that nobody can describe yet. Common in biobanks; debated, because it is hard to be “informed” about the unknown.
Privacy and confidentiality: genetic results are sensitive data. Who may see them: relatives, employers, insurers, the police?
The right not to know: a person may choose not to learn a genetic result about themselves. This is part of autonomy, and it is why tests are offered, never imposed.
The family problem: one person’s result reveals risk for relatives. The right to know of one person can collide with the right not to know of another.


These are the concepts that make genetics different from most of medicine. Stress the right not to know: in most of medicine, more information is assumed to be better, but for an untreatable late-onset disease many at-risk people choose not to be tested, and that choice must be respected. The family problem is the core of several cases in the exercise: a test on one identical twin is a test on both; a test on a grandchild of a Huntington patient can reveal the status of the parent in between. In Sweden, the Ethical Review Act requires consent to be voluntary, explicit and specific to the research (section 17); broad consent is handled through ethical review and the Biobanks Act.

title: Ethics of genetic knowledge
text:
Kinds of genetic testing

The same lab method can serve very different purposes. The ethics depends on who is tested, why, and what can be done with the answer.

Walk along the life course. Carrier testing applies the Aa x Aa cross from the Mendel unit: two healthy carriers have a one in four risk per child. Prenatal testing is about a fetus, and the decision belongs to the pregnant woman. Newborn screening in Sweden (the PKU test) is offered to all newborns for treatable conditions; the dried blood spots are stored in the PKU biobank, which we return to under biobanks. Diagnostic testing explains a disease someone already has; it is the least controversial, but it can still reveal risks for relatives. Predictive testing of a healthy person is the most ethically loaded, especially when there is no treatment. The band at the bottom is the reason incidental findings come up in every kind of test once we sequence exomes or genomes. The colour code says who the result is mainly for.

title: Ethics of genetic knowledge
text:
Predictive testing: Huntington disease
Recall the Mendel unit: Huntington disease is autosomal dominant with late onset. A child of an affected parent (Aa × aa) has a ½ risk. Since the HTT CAG-repeat expansion was found (Huntington’s Disease Collaborative Research Group 1993, PMID 8458085), a healthy person at risk can learn their genotype.

No cure. A positive result is a forecast, not a treatment plan.
International guidelines: counselling before and after, a free choice without coercion, and a minimum age of 18 (MacLeod et al. 2013, PMID 22642570). The child’s own future choice is protected.
Most people at risk choose not to know: in the UK, cumulative uptake among people at 50% risk (1994–2014) was about 17% (Baig et al. 2016, PMID 27165004).
Testing reveals others. A positive result in a grandchild means the parent in between carries the allele too. Testing one identical twin tests both.


Huntington disease is the classic case for the right not to know, and it is the first case in the exercise. Remind students of the genetics: one affected parent, a testcross, one half. With full penetrance for long expanded repeats, a positive result means the person will develop the disease if they live long enough. Predictive testing protocols built for Huntington disease have become the model for other late-onset conditions: counselling before the test, time to reflect, and support afterwards. Point out the two family problems: a 25% at-risk grandchild whose result reveals the status of the 50% at-risk parent, and monozygotic twins, who share the genotype, so one twin’s wish to know collides with the other’s wish not to know. There is no clean solution; the exercise asks students to weigh it.

title: Ethics of genetic knowledge
text:
Prenatal testing and NIPT

Prenatal diagnosis tests fetal cells, obtained by amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling (CVS). Both carry a small risk of miscarriage.
NIPT (non-invasive prenatal testing) analyses cell-free fetal DNA in the mother’s blood. Fetal DNA in maternal plasma was first shown by Lo et al. (1997, Lancet, PMID 9274585). NIPT is a screening test, mainly for trisomies 21, 18 and 13; a positive result is confirmed by a diagnostic test.
In Sweden, all pregnant women must be offered general information about prenatal diagnosis, and the woman decides whether to be tested (Genetic Integrity Act, 2006:351, ch. 4).

Ethical questions: a simple blood test makes testing routine, so is the choice still informed? What does wide screening say to people who live with Down syndrome? Where is the line between serious disease and choosing traits?

The key change NIPT brought is that a screening test with no miscarriage risk can be done from a blood sample early in pregnancy. That is a benefit, but it also lowers the threshold: when something is easy and routine, people may not think of it as a choice. Disability-rights critics argue that routine screening sends a message about the value of people with the conditions screened for. Stress the difference between screening and diagnosis: NIPT gives a risk, not a diagnosis, partly because some of the cell-free DNA comes from the placenta. The Swedish law puts the decision with the woman, after information. Preimplantation genetic testing of IVF embryos is regulated in the same act: only for serious monogenic or chromosomal disease, and not for choosing traits (ch. 4, section 2).

title: Ethics of genetic knowledge
text:
Incidental and secondary findings
Sequence an exome to explain a child’s epilepsy, and you may also find a pathogenic BRCA1 variant in a parent: a high risk of breast and ovarian cancer that nobody was looking for.

Incidental finding: found by chance, unrelated to the question asked.
Secondary finding: deliberately looked for in a short list of actionable genes, where knowing allows prevention. The ACMG publishes such a list (v3.2: Miller et al. 2023, PMID 37347242; updated in v3.3, 2025, PMID 40568962). BRCA1 is on it.
Labs and clinics must decide in advance, with the patient: which findings will be reported, and may the patient opt out?

Principles in tension: beneficence (prevention saves lives; relatives could be tested too) against autonomy and the right not to know.

Whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing look at everything, so they find everything. The American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) keeps a list of genes where a pathogenic variant should be reported even if the test was ordered for something else, because something can be done about it: extra screening, preventive surgery, or drugs. BRCA1 and BRCA2 are standard examples. Guidelines differ between countries on whether to look for such findings at all; the policy choice is: look or not, report or not, and who decides. In the exercise, case 2 asks students to apply this. Note the family dimension again: a BRCA1 result in a mother concerns her sisters and daughters, who each have a half chance of carrying it.

title: Ethics of genetic knowledge
text:
Direct-to-consumer genomics
Companies sell genotyping directly to the public, without a doctor: ancestry, relative matching, traits and some health risks. The customer spits in a tube and gets results online.

Autonomy and access: people can learn about themselves without a gatekeeper.
Without counselling: a health result can frighten or falsely reassure. Genotyping arrays test selected variants, so a “no variant found” for BRCA1 does not mean “no risk”.
Relatives: matching reveals unknown siblings, donor-conceived children, misattributed paternity. Your relatives never agreed to be found.
Data as an asset: the company holds a large genetic database. Its terms of use, a data breach, or a change of owner decide what happens to it.
Raw data mislead: in one clinical lab, 40% of variants from DTC raw data sent for confirmation were false positives (Tandy-Connor et al. 2018, PMID 29565420).

US example, 23andMe: an FDA warning letter stopped its health reports in 2013; the FDA authorised its first health-risk reports in 2017; in 2023 a breach of about 14,000 accounts exposed millions of relative-matching profiles; it filed for bankruptcy in March 2025 and was sold in July 2025.

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) testing removed the doctor and the genetic counsellor from the loop. Benefits: access, curiosity satisfied, and genuinely useful findings for some people. Risks: misinterpretation, false reassurance from limited arrays, and the fact that matching services connect relatives who did not ask to be connected. Stress that a DTC customer’s database entry affects their relatives’ privacy, which leads directly to the next two slides. The 23andMe story shows that a privacy promise is only as durable as the company: when a company is sold or goes bankrupt, the database is an asset. In Sweden, the Genetic Integrity Act bans making a genetic test or genetic information a condition of a contract, and limits insurers’ use of genetic information to narrow cases.

title: Ethics of genetic knowledge
section: Genetic privacy: you cannot anonymise a genome
text:
Genetic privacy: you cannot anonymise a genome

Gymrek et al. (2013, Science, PMID 23329047) recovered surnames from “anonymous” research genomes by reading Y-chromosome STRs and querying public genealogy databases; combined with age and US state, this traced the identities of research participants. They projected that surnames of about 12% of US white males could be recovered this way.

This paper was a turning point in the debate on how genomic data should be shared. The research data had no names, but the Y chromosome carries a surname-like signal: it is passed from father to son, as is the surname in many cultures. That is Y-linked inheritance from the pedigree unit, used as an identifier. Recreational genealogy databases let men upload their Y-STR profiles with their surnames, so matching the anonymous profile gives a likely surname. Add metadata that was published with the research data, such as age and US state, and the candidate list shrinks to one. Two lessons. First, removing names is not anonymisation for genomes. Second, the leak comes through relatives: the people in the genealogy database identified someone else. One response is controlled access: individual-level data are released only to researchers who apply and agree to terms of use.

title: Ethics of genetic knowledge
text:
Genetic genealogy and the police
Investigative genetic genealogy: genotype a crime-scene sample with a SNP array, upload it to a genealogy database, find distant cousins, then build their family trees until one person fits.

Golden State Killer: a suspect in a series of 1970s–80s California murders and rapes was arrested on 24 April 2018 after relatives were found in the free genealogy database GEDmatch (Guerrini et al. 2018, PMID 30278047). He pleaded guilty in 2020 and was sentenced to life without parole. In 2019 GEDmatch made police matching opt-in.
Scale: from 1.28 million consumer genomes, Erlich et al. (2018, PMID 30309907) projected that about 60% of searches for people of European descent would find a third cousin or closer.
Sweden: first used in 2019, on a 16-year-old double murder in Linköping. The Authority for Privacy Protection (IMY) halted further use in 2021; a new law allows the police to use it from 1 July 2025, only for murder and aggravated rape, as a last resort (Ansell & Fagerholm 2025, PMID 40995235).


Explain the genetics: a third cousin shares on average about one 128th of the genome, but in long identical segments that a SNP array can detect. Each cousin match points to a pair of shared great-great-grandparents; genealogists then work down through all their descendants, using public records, until the candidate list is short; a direct DNA test confirms. The ethical issue is consent: the cousins who uploaded their DNA to trace their ancestry did not agree to become police informants, and the suspect never uploaded anything. In favour: serious crimes solved, and innocent suspects cleared. Against: everyone’s privacy depends on what their relatives do; function creep from murder to lesser crimes. Sweden’s approach shows the regulatory answer: a specific law, limited to the most severe crimes. This is case 4 in the exercise.

title: Ethics of genetic knowledge
section: You used these databases all course
text:
You used these databases all course








Database (unit)
What it shares
Who it could identify?




NCBI Gene, Ensembl, OMIM (Part 1)
reference genes and diseases
no one


ClinVar (pedigrees)
variants and their interpretation, without names
rarely, for very rare variants


gnomAD (Part 7)
aggregate allele counts only
very hard


1000 Genomes (Part 4)
individual genotypes, openly
possible: no names or medical data, but open consent to public release


A genealogy site
individual genotypes with names and family trees
you, and your relatives



The same data type, a genotype, can be harmless or identifying depending on how it is shared. Open data speeds up research; controlled access and aggregation protect participants.

Make the link to their own work. Reference genomes and gene records contain nobody’s private data. ClinVar records variants submitted by labs; it contains no names, but a very rare variant together with a rare disease and a hospital could narrow down a family. gnomAD only shows how many people carry each allele, never which people, which is a privacy design choice. The 1000 Genomes Project released full individual genotypes openly, from openly consented samples, without names or medical data. Gymrek’s and Erlich’s studies showed that people in public data sets of this kind can still be identified, through relatives in genealogy databases. Ask the students: which of these would you be happy to have your own genome in? This prepares the discussion of biobank consent at the end.

title: Ethics of genetic knowledge
text:
Germline editing


Somatic editing treats one person. Example: exa-cel, CRISPR-edited blood stem cells for sickle cell disease (Frangoul et al. 2024, PMID 38661449).
Germline editing changes an embryo, so every cell, including the gametes, carries the edit. The change is inherited by Mendel’s rules.


The distinction is the key concept. Somatic editing is ethically like any other new therapy: one consenting patient (or guardian), benefits and risks to that person. Exa-cel edits the patient’s own blood stem cells outside the body to switch fetal haemoglobin back on, a nice link to the sickle cell example in the first unit. Germline editing affects people who cannot consent, the future children and their descendants, and errors cannot be recalled. Mitochondrial replacement, in the right panel, is not gene editing, but it is also a heritable change: a daughter passes on the donor’s mitochondria, by the maternal inheritance we saw in the pedigree unit and will treat in Part 5. In Sweden, experiments and treatments that cause heritable genetic changes in humans are prohibited (Genetic Integrity Act, 2006:351, ch. 2, sections 3–4).

title: Ethics of genetic knowledge
section: He Jiankui and the CRISPR babies
text:
He Jiankui and the CRISPR babies
On 25–26 November 2018, just before an international summit on human genome editing in Hong Kong, He Jiankui announced the birth of twin girls whose embryos he had edited with CRISPR-Cas9 to disrupt CCR5, the co-receptor HIV uses to enter cells (Cyranoski & Ledford 2018, PMID 30482929).

No medical need: the father had HIV, but sperm washing can prevent transmission to the child with no risk.
Not what was intended: neither twin got the natural CCR5-Δ32 deletion; the edits made new mutations, and the children are mosaics (Greely 2019, PMID 31666967).
Consent and oversight: how the parents were informed, and the ethics approval, could not be independently checked; the work was done in secret.
On 30 December 2019 a court in Shenzhen sentenced him to three years in prison and a fine of 3 million yuan for illegal medical practice; it also confirmed a third edited baby (Cyranoski 2020, PMID 31911693).

The response was near-universal condemnation, and calls for a moratorium on heritable editing.

This case is the clearest example of a violation of almost every principle at once. Non-maleficence: unknown risks to healthy children for no medical benefit. Autonomy: questionable consent from the parents, and none from the children or their descendants. Justice and public trust: done in secret, presented to the media before peer review. Point out the genetics: CRISPR makes a double-strand break and the cell repairs it by error-prone end joining, so the alleles created were new small deletions, not the well-studied Δ32 allele, and different cells of an embryo can be repaired differently, which is mosaicism. That is the scientific reason, apart from ethics, why heritable editing is not safe today. Case 5 in the exercise asks students to evaluate a more plausible proposal.

title: Ethics of genetic knowledge
text:
Mitochondrial replacement
Diseases caused by mtDNA mutations pass from mother to all her children (pedigree unit; full story in Part 5, Organelle inheritance). Mitochondrial replacement therapy (MRT) moves the mother’s nucleus into a donor egg with healthy mitochondria.

The child gets nuclear DNA from both parents and mtDNA from the donor: DNA from three people.
The UK allowed it by regulations in force from 29 October 2015, under licence. In 2025 the Newcastle team reported 8 children born after pronuclear transfer, healthy at birth, with mutant mtDNA in blood from undetectable up to 16% (Hyslop et al. 2025, PMID 40673696; McFarland et al. 2025, PMID 40689593).
It is heritable through daughters, and carry-over of some mutant mtDNA means a risk that its level rises again.

Is replacing ~37 genes of mtDNA different from editing a nuclear gene? Should the donor have any status?

MRT is useful for discussion because it is legal and regulated in one country, unlike nuclear germline editing. The genetics: the human mitochondrial genome has 37 genes, all for oxidative phosphorylation and its own translation, so the donor contributes nothing that shapes appearance or personality, which is one argument that it is less problematic. Counter-arguments: it is still a heritable modification; a small amount of the mother’s mitochondria is carried over with the nucleus, and because of the heteroplasmy bottleneck (Part 5) that fraction can rise again in some cells or in the next generation. The donor is anonymous in the UK and has no parental role. A good discussion question: would MRT count as a heritable genetic change under the Swedish Genetic Integrity Act, which bans such changes?

title: Ethics of genetic knowledge
text:
Gene drives

A gene drive cheats Mendel’s law of segregation: a heterozygote passes the drive to nearly all offspring, not half. It could eliminate malaria mosquitoes, or an invasive species.

This links straight back to the Mendel unit: segregation gives each allele a one-half chance of reaching a gamete. A homing gene drive carries the genes for Cas9 and a guide RNA aimed at the same site on the homologous chromosome. In the germline of a heterozygote it cuts the wild-type homolog, and the cell repairs the break using the drive chromosome as a template, so the heterozygote becomes a homozygote and almost every gamete carries the drive. Kyrou and colleagues targeted doublesex in Anopheles gambiae, the main African malaria vector: females homozygous for the disruption are sterile, and caged populations collapsed within 7 to 11 generations. The ethics is different from human germline editing: the benefit could be huge (malaria is a major killer, especially of young children), but a release affects an ecosystem and other countries, and cannot easily be recalled. Who consents for a whole region? That is the justice question.

title: Ethics of genetic knowledge
text:
History: eugenics in Sweden
Eugenics: the idea of “improving” a population by controlling who reproduces. Francis Galton coined the word in 1883. It was mainstream science in many countries in the early 20th century, including Sweden.

The State Institute for Racial Biology (Statens institut för rasbiologi) was set up by a decision of the Riksdag in 1921 and opened in Uppsala in 1922, with Herman Lundborg (director 1921–1935) in charge. It set out to divide the Swedish population into “racial” categories, measuring people and photographing them; Lundborg made repeated trips to Lapland to measure and photograph Sami people.
His successor, Gunnar Dahlberg, questioned the scientific basis of race research, and the institute moved towards medical genetics. In 1958–59 its work was absorbed into Uppsala University’s Department of Medical Genetics.
Its archive, with about 12,000 photographs, is kept by Uppsala University Library.


This is part of Swedish scientific history, and of the history of human genetics itself: the institute is a direct forerunner of a university department of medical genetics. Under Lundborg it used biometric methods to try to give statistical support to the idea that ethnic differences had genetic causes. Make the point that the institute was set up by a broad parliamentary decision, and that the people involved were respected scientists; the lesson is that scientific authority does not protect against serious harm, and that the categories science uses can be shaped by politics. Uppsala University’s own pages give 1958 or 1959 for when the institute’s activities were taken over by the Department of Medical Genetics. Sources: Uppsala University Library’s pages on the archive of the State Institute for Racial Biology, and the university’s news article from December 2021 when the archive was made available.

title: Ethics of genetic knowledge
text:
The Swedish sterilisation laws, 1935–1975

The 1934 act (SFS 1934:171, in force 1 January 1935) allowed sterilisation of people considered mentally ill or “feeble-minded” without their consent if they were judged unable to understand it. The 1941 act (SFS 1941:282) was in principle voluntary, but still allowed sterilisation without consent of people judged legally incapable. The grounds were eugenic, social and medical.
Nearly 63,000 sterilisations were reported in 1935–1975; 93% of those sterilised were women. About 9% were done without consent, and about 24% after a formally voluntary application under coercion-like conditions, e.g. as a condition for leaving an institution or for getting an abortion.
The 1975 act (SFS 1975:580, in force 1976) allows sterilisation only at the person’s own request.
A government inquiry appointed in 1997 (final report SOU 2000:20) investigated, and a 1999 law (SFS 1999:332) gave SEK 175,000 in compensation to people sterilised under compulsion.

The genetics was also wrong: most alleles for recessive conditions are carried by healthy heterozygotes, so sterilising affected people barely changes their frequency (Part 7, Hardy–Weinberg).

Not all of the 63,000 were coerced. The government’s report to the Riksdag (Skr. 2000/01:73, summarising the inquiry) estimates that about half of those sterilised took the initiative themselves, about 9% were sterilised without consent, about 24% under coercion-like conditions and about 10% after persuasion or pressure; the rest could not be classified. Compulsion dominated early on; the 1950s were a turning point towards voluntariness and family-planning motives. The laws were passed with broad political agreement. Sweden was not alone: the first sterilisation law was in the US state of Indiana in 1907, and in the 1930s other Nordic countries and Germany passed laws. The point of the last line is that eugenics failed on its own terms. If a recessive allele has frequency q, affected people have frequency q squared and carriers 2pq; for a rare allele almost all copies are in carriers, who look healthy. Removing affected people from reproduction lowers q only very slowly. Students will be able to compute this after the Hardy-Weinberg unit. The lasting lessons for today: consent cannot be replaced by the state’s idea of the common good, and vulnerable groups need special protection. These lessons are built into the modern ethical review system.

title: Ethics of genetic knowledge
section: Ethical review of research in Sweden
text:
Ethical review of research in Sweden
The Ethical Review Act (Lag (2003:460) om etikprövning av forskning som avser människor, in force 2004). Research must be approved before it starts if it:

processes sensitive personal data (e.g. health or genetic data) or data on criminal offences;
involves a physical intervention, or a method meant to affect a person physically or mentally, or an obvious risk of harm;
uses biological material from a living or dead person that can be traced to them.

Applications go to the Swedish Ethical Review Authority (Etikprövningsmyndigheten, Uppsala, since 1 January 2019). Consent must be voluntary, explicit and specific to the research. Doing such research without approval is a crime.
Internationally: the World Medical Association’s Declaration of Helsinki (1964, last revised October 2024).

Point out what this means for them. Student projects done only within first- or second-cycle education are not “research” under the act, so a bachelor’s project does not need its own application; but a degree project inside a research group often uses data or samples covered by the group’s approval, and they should know where that approval comes from. The criteria are in sections 3 and 4 of the act; the consent rules in sections 16 to 22; breaking the approval requirement can give fines or prison of up to two years (section 38). The authority replaced six regional ethical review boards. The Declaration of Helsinki is the international statement of research ethics for medical research on humans; its core ideas are independent review, informed consent, and that the interests of the individual come before those of science and society. Note that an amendment to the act, decided in 2026, takes effect on 1 July 2027 and changes how some studies are assessed; always check the authority’s website for the current rules.

title: Ethics of genetic knowledge
text:
Biobanks, GDPR and genetic integrity







Law
What it says, in short




Biobanks Act (Biobankslag, 2023:38; replaced 2002:297)
Identifiable human samples may be collected, stored and used, for care or research, with the donor’s informed consent, which can be withdrawn. Includes the PKU biobank of newborn blood spots.


GDPR (EU 2016/679, applies from 25 May 2018)
Genetic data (Art. 4(13)) is a special category of personal data (Art. 9): processing is prohibited unless an exception applies, such as explicit consent or approved research.


Genetic Integrity Act (2006:351)
Nobody may make a genetic test a condition of a contract; insurers may use genetic information only in narrow cases. Heritable genetic changes in humans are banned. Rules for prenatal and preimplantation diagnosis.



Sample re-use is common: newborn blood spots from the Swedish PKU biobank were used to trace PFAS exposure from contaminated drinking water in Ronneby back to 1985 (PMID 40089001).

These three laws are the practical frame for any genetics project in Sweden. The Biobanks Act: a sample taken in health care stays linked to the person; using it for research needs consent and ethical approval. The PKU biobank is special: it stores the newborn screening blood spots of a very large share of the population, so it is a powerful research resource and a sensitive one; the act gives it its own chapter. The Ronneby study is a good example of beneficial re-use: nobody in 1985 could have consented to a PFAS study, so the decision rests on ethical review and the law. GDPR treats genetic data as a special category, alongside health data and ethnic origin. The Genetic Integrity Act protects individuals in contracts: an employer or insurer may not demand a genetic test; the insurance exception only applies to very large policies. Case 6 in the exercise is a biobank re-use request.

title: Ethics of genetic knowledge
text:
Summary

Genetic information is shared, predictive, permanent, identifying and reproductive. That is why it gets special ethical and legal treatment.
Four principles: autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice. Add consent, privacy and the right not to know. Good arguments name the principles in tension and weigh them.
Testing: predictive testing (Huntington disease), prenatal tests and NIPT, incidental findings (BRCA1), and DTC tests each raise different questions.
Privacy: names can be recovered from genomes (Y-STRs, surnames); genealogy databases identify people through their relatives.
Germline: editing an embryo, mitochondrial replacement and gene drives all make heritable changes.
History: Sweden’s racial biology institute and sterilisation laws are why consent and independent ethical review matter.
Sweden today: Ethical Review Act (2003:460), Etikprövningsmyndigheten, Biobanks Act, GDPR, Genetic Integrity Act.


If students remember one structure, it should be: who is affected (including relatives and future generations), which principles conflict, what the genetics really says, and what the law requires. The cases in the exercise are built to make them practise exactly this.

title: Ethics of genetic knowledge
text:
Where this leads

Exercise: six cases for group discussion, a check of when Swedish research needs ethical review, and a PubMed search strategy with MeSH terms to find literature for each case.
Group assignment: a written analysis of one case and an oral presentation (details on Canvas).
Back to the course: Huntington disease (Mendel), Y-linked and mitochondrial inheritance (Pedigree analysis, Organelle inheritance), CRISPR and sequencing (Part 4), allele frequencies and why eugenics failed (Hardy–Weinberg), and every database you used.


The exercise is the main work of the module. Encourage the groups to choose the case for their assignment early, and to use the PubMed strategies to find at least one original paper and one review for it. Remind them that the same case can be argued in different directions; they are assessed on how well they use facts and principles, not on which side they take.

title: Quiz: drift, selection, mutation, migration
text:
Short questions on the forces that change allele frequencies. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Name the four forces that change allele frequencies. Which one has no direction, and which one tends to make populations more similar to each other?






Hint





Compare with the assumptions of Hardy–Weinberg.









Answer





Genetic drift, selection, mutation and migration (gene flow). Drift has no direction: p is as likely to go up as down. Migration makes populations more similar, because alleles move between them. (Non-random mating changes genotype frequencies but not allele frequencies.)




Q2. In the Wright–Fisher model, why does a population of N = 10 drift much faster than one of N = 1000?






Hint





The variance of the change in p per generation is p(1 − p)/(2N).









Answer





Each generation is a random sample of 2N gene copies from the previous one. A small sample deviates more from its source, just as 10 coin tosses deviate more from 50% heads than 1000 tosses. The variance of Δp is pq/(2N): with p = 0.5 the standard deviation is 0.11 for N = 10 and 0.011 for N = 1000.




Q3. A neutral allele has frequency 0.3 in a small isolated population. What is the probability that it is eventually fixed? What is the probability that a single new neutral mutation in a population of N = 50 is eventually fixed?






Hint





Drift has no direction, so the average p over many populations stays at p₀.









Answer





The fixation probability of a neutral allele equals its current frequency: 0.3. A new mutation is one copy among 2N = 100, so it is fixed with probability 1/100, and lost with probability 0.99.




Q4. A breeding herd has 4 bulls and 200 cows. What is its effective population size? Why is it so much smaller than 204?






Hint





Nₑ = 4NmNf/(Nm + Nf).









Answer





Nₑ = 4 × 4 × 200 / 204 = 15.7. Half of every calf’s genes come from one of only 4 bulls, so the paternal half of the gene pool is a very small sample each generation. The herd drifts as fast as an ideal population of about 16 animals.




Q5. Explain how a founder effect can make a rare recessive disease common in one population. Give an example.






Hint





What happens to the frequency of a rare allele when only a few people found a new population?









Answer





A few founders carry a chance sample of the alleles in the source population. If one founder happens to carry a rare disease allele, its frequency among the founders (one copy in, say, 100) can be much higher than in the source (one in 10 000), and it stays high as the population grows. Many other alleles are lost. Most patients then share one founder mutation. Example: the Finnish disease heritage, such as Salla disease (SLC17A5 R39C), which is about 20 times more frequent in Finns than in other Europeans. (Others: Ellis–van Creveld syndrome among the Amish.)




Q6. Fitnesses are wAA = 1, wAa = 1, waa = 0.5, and p = 0.5. What is p after one generation of selection?






Hint





p′ = (p²wAA + pq wAa)/w̄.









Answer





w̄ = 0.25 × 1 + 0.5 × 1 + 0.25 × 0.5 = 0.875. p′ = (0.25 + 0.25)/0.875 = 0.571. Selection against aa raised p from 0.5 to 0.571 in one generation.




Q7. Why does selection against a harmful recessive allele become very slow once the allele is rare?






Hint





Where are most copies of a rare allele?









Answer





When q is small, almost all copies are in heterozygotes (2pq ≫ q²), which have normal fitness. Selection only removes the copies in aa individuals, a tiny fraction. Even if every affected person had no children, q would fall from 0.01 to 0.005 only after about 100 generations.




Q8. A recessive lethal allele arises by mutation at rate μ = 4 × 10−6 per generation. What is its expected equilibrium frequency, and the incidence of the disease? What if the allele were dominant lethal?






Hint





Recessive: q̂ ≈ √(μ/s). Dominant: q̂ ≈ μ/s.









Answer





Recessive: q̂ = √(4 × 10−6) = 0.002; incidence q̂² = 4 × 10−6, equal to μ. Dominant: q̂ = 4 × 10−6, and every case is a new mutation (affected people do not reproduce). The recessive allele is 500 times more frequent because it hides in carriers.




Q9. Why is the HbS allele common in parts of Africa, although HbS/HbS causes sickle-cell disease? What happens to it where malaria disappears?






Hint





Which genotype has the highest fitness where malaria is common?









Answer





Carriers (HbA/HbS) are protected against severe malaria, so where malaria is common they are fitter than both homozygotes: heterozygote advantage. HbS rises when rare (mostly in carriers) and falls when common (many SS), towards a stable equilibrium, about 0.1–0.2 in many malaria regions (0.139 in the 1000 Genomes Yoruba sample). Where malaria disappears, carriers lose their advantage, SS is still selected against, and HbS slowly declines.




Q10. A beneficial mutation gives heterozygotes a 2% advantage (shet = 0.02) in a large population. What is the probability that it is eventually fixed? Why so low?






Hint





Haldane: P(fix) ≈ 2shet.









Answer





About 2 × 0.02 = 0.04, so 96% of such mutations are lost. A new mutation starts as a single copy. In the first few generations, whether its one or two carriers happen to pass it on is mostly chance, and a small advantage hardly changes that. Only once it has reached a few dozen copies does selection reliably take over.




Q11. Island population: p = 0.2. Each generation, 10% of the breeding individuals are migrants from the mainland, where p = 0.6. What is p on the island after one generation? After many?






Hint





p′ = (1 − m)p + m pM.









Answer





p′ = 0.9 × 0.2 + 0.1 × 0.6 = 0.24. The difference from the mainland shrinks by a factor 0.9 per generation (0.4 → 0.36 → …), so after many generations p approaches the mainland value, 0.6, unless drift or selection on the island pulls it away.
