Exercise: drift, selection, mutation, migration
text:
Background
Drift (Wright–Fisher). N diploid individuals, 2N gene copies. Next generation: number of A copies ~ Binomial(2N, p).

P(neutral allele is eventually fixed) = p₀. A new mutation: p₀ = 1/(2N).
Expected heterozygosity: Ht = H₀ (1 − 1/2N)t.
Effective size: Nₑ = 4NmNf/(Nm + Nf); over generations, the harmonic mean Nₑ = t / Σ(1/Ni).

Selection. Fitnesses wAA, wAa, waa (often 1 + s, 1 + hs, 1).
\[
\bar w = p^2 w_{AA} + 2pq\, w_{Aa} + q^2 w_{aa}, \qquad p' = \frac{p^2 w_{AA} + pq\, w_{Aa}}{\bar w}.
\]
Mutation–selection balance (mutation rate μ, selection s against the allele): recessive q̂ ≈ √(μ/s); dominant q̂ ≈ μ/s.
Heterozygote advantage (wAa greater than both homozygotes): \(\hat q = \dfrac{w_{Aa} - w_{AA}}{2w_{Aa} - w_{AA} - w_{aa}}\), where q is the frequency of a.
Migration: p′ = (1 − m)p + m pM; the difference from the source shrinks by (1 − m) per generation.
New beneficial mutation (Haldane): P(fixation) ≈ 2shet, where shet is the advantage of heterozygotes.

title: Exercise: drift, selection, mutation, migration
text:
By hand
B1. (drift in tiny populations) A population of N = 2 individuals (4 gene copies) has p = 0.5. (a) What is the probability that A is lost in the very next generation? That it is fixed? (b) Repeat for N = 10. What does the comparison show?
B2. (fixation) (a) A neutral allele has frequency 0.15 in a population. What is the probability that it is eventually fixed? (b) A new neutral mutation arises in a population of N = 1000. What is the probability that it is eventually fixed, and that it is lost? (c) Which of your answers would change if the allele were in a population of 10 million?
B3. (effective population size) (a) A zoo population has 20 breeding males and 80 breeding females. What is Nₑ? (b) A population has sizes 500, 50, 500 and 500 in four successive generations. What is Nₑ over these generations, and what does the answer say about bottlenecks?
B4. (losing variation) A population of N = 25 starts with heterozygosity H = 0.5 at a neutral locus. What heterozygosity do you expect after 50 generations? After how many generations is half of the heterozygosity lost, roughly? (Hint: (1 − 1/2N)t ≈ e−t/2N.)
B5. (selection, two generations) Fitnesses are wAA = 1, wAa = 0.95, waa = 0.9, and p = 0.4. Compute w̄ and p after one and after two generations of selection. What kind of dominance is this?
B6. (mutation–selection balance) (a) A recessive lethal disease arises by mutation at μ = 10−6 per generation. What allele frequency and incidence would you expect at mutation–selection balance? (b) Cystic fibrosis affects about 1 in 2500 births in north-west Europe, and until recently patients rarely had children (s ≈ 1). What mutation rate would mutation–selection balance require? Is that plausible? Suggest two other explanations for the high frequency.
B7. (heterozygote advantage) In a malaria region, the relative fitnesses for a β-thalassaemia allele t are: TT 0.9, Tt 1, tt 0.1. (a) Which genotype is fittest? What kind of selection is this? (b) Compute the equilibrium frequency of t. (c) What happens to t if malaria is eradicated, so that TT and Tt both have fitness 1?
B8. (migration) A population has p = 0 for an allele. Each generation, 2% of the parents are migrants from a population with p = 0.5. What is p after 1 generation, and after 10 generations?
B9. (a founder disease) A new population is founded by 500 people. Exactly one of them carries a recessive disease allele. (a) What is q among the founders? (b) If the population grows without further change in q, what are the incidence of the disease and the carrier frequency? (c) In one isolated region, drift raises q to 0.02. What are the incidence and the carrier frequency there? Compare with (b).

title: Exercise: drift, selection, mutation, migration
text:
Explore
The demo shows replicate populations evolving by the Wright–Fisher model with selection. Each line is one population: blue lines fixed A (p = 1), red lines lost it (p = 0), grey lines are still segregating. The thick dashed line is what selection alone would do in an infinitely large population. The numbers below are for the default seed; run again gives new random outcomes.



E1. Drift depends on N. Press drift, N = 20. How many of the 20 populations have fixed A, lost A, or are still segregating after 100 generations? Now press drift, N = 500. Same questions. What does the dashed line do in both cases, and why? Compare the mean heterozygosity H in the readout with the drift-theory value H₀(1 − 1/2N)t.
E2. Fixation probability = starting frequency. Set N = 20, s = 0, start p = 0.2, populations = 100 and generations = 500. What fraction of populations fixed A? What does theory predict for a neutral allele? Press run again twice and note the fractions. Then press one new mutation: what is the chance that a single new neutral mutation in a population of N = 20 is eventually fixed?
E3. Selection versus drift. Press selection s = 0.05 (N = 500, start p = 0.1, h = 0.5). Do the lines follow the dashed line? Roughly how many generations does selection need to take A from 0.1 to 0.5? Now change N to 20 (keep everything else). How many of the 20 populations lose the favoured allele? What does this tell you about selection in small populations?
E4. A new beneficial mutation is usually lost. Press new beneficial mutation (N = 500, s = 0.05, h = 0.5, one copy of A, 100 populations, 500 generations). How many populations fixed A? Compare with Haldane’s approximation 2shet, where shet = hs. When are most of the lost mutations lost?
E5. Sickle cell and malaria. Press sickle cell / malaria. Read the fitnesses: which genotype is fittest? Where do the lines settle? Check the equilibrium by hand with the formula in the Background. Why is the HbS allele not lost, even though SS has fitness 0.2? Now set N = 20. What happens, and why?






Solutions: Explore





E1. With N = 20: 9 fixed, 9 lost, 2 segregating after 100 generations. With N = 500: none fixed or lost; all 20 are still segregating and have only spread out a little around 0.5 (mean p 0.536). The dashed line stays flat at 0.5: with s = 0 there is no selection, so an infinite population does not change. All the change is drift, and drift is strong when 2N is small. Heterozygosity: N = 20 gives mean H = 0.024 against the theory value 0.5 × (1 − 1/40)100 = 0.040; N = 500 gives 0.443 against 0.5 × (1 − 1/1000)100 = 0.452. (With only 20 populations the simulated mean is noisy.) The small population has lost almost all its variation in 100 generations; the large one less than 10%.
E2. Default seed: 19 of 100 populations fixed A (0.19); run again gives 0.18 and 0.22. Theory: the fixation probability equals the starting frequency, 0.2. Drift has no direction, so the mean p stays at p₀, and at the end every population is at 0 or 1, so the fraction at 1 must be p₀. A single new mutation starts at p = 1/40 = 0.025, so it is fixed with probability 1/40: in 100 populations expect 2 or 3.
E3. With N = 500 the lines stay close to the dashed line: selection dominates drift (4Ns = 100 ≫ 1). The deterministic curve reaches 0.5 after about 90 generations (0.9 after about 180); at generation 200 the lines average 0.930, against 0.936 for N = ∞. With N = 20, 17 of 20 populations lose the favoured allele and only 3 fix it. In a small population drift can overpower weak selection: an allele that starts rare is often lost by chance before selection can act (4Ns = 4 here).
E4. Default seed: 7 of 100 populations fixed A; run again gives 4 and 4. Haldane: shet = 0.5 × 0.05 = 0.025, so P(fix) ≈ 0.05, about 5 in 100. (A run with 2000 populations gave 0.052.) About 95% of new beneficial mutations are lost, most of them within the first ~10 generations, while there are only one or two copies and chance decides everything. The survivors then rise along an S-shaped curve and fix after roughly 300–360 generations.
E5. wAA (normal) = 1, wAS = 1.16, wSS = 0.20: the heterozygote is fittest. The lines rise from 0.02 and settle around 0.14 (mean 0.142 at generation 300; the dotted line shows p̂ = 0.143). By hand: (1.16 − 1)/(2 × 1.16 − 1 − 0.20) = 0.16/1.12 = 0.143. When HbS is rare it is almost always in fitter heterozygotes, so it increases; when it is common many SS die, so it decreases. The balance keeps the allele. With N = 20 all 20 populations lose HbS: they start with p = 0.02, less than one copy among 40, so drift removes it before selection can protect it. Balancing selection maintains an allele only if the population is large enough for selection to beat drift.

title: Exercise: drift, selection, mutation, migration
text:
Find it
F1. The Finnish disease heritage in PubMed. Search PubMed for "Finnish disease heritage"[title]. Find the three-part review by Norio from 2003. In which journal was it published, and what are the three parts about (read the titles)? Open the abstract of part I. Which historical event in Finland and which feature of the population does it list among the topics? How do they connect to founder effects?
F2. Salla disease in MedGen. Open Salla disease in MedGen (OMIM 604369). What is the mode of inheritance? Which gene is involved, and where is it (read the gene’s location in NCBI Gene)? What does the protein do (read the gene’s full name)?
F3. A Finnish founder allele in gnomAD. The main Finnish Salla allele is SLC17A5 R39C, dbSNP rs80338794. Open it in gnomAD v4. In the Genetic Ancestry Group Frequencies table, compare the allele frequency in European (Finnish) with European (non-Finnish) (use the exome data, which has more people). (a) How many times more frequent is the allele in Finns? (b) Assuming HWE, what is the carrier frequency in Finland (“1 in …”)? (c) Repeat for the CLN1 disease allele PPT1 R122W, rs137852695, in gnomAD. Which drift process explains both?






Solutions: Find it





Checked on 20 November 2026 via PubMed and MedGen (NCBI E-utilities), NCBI Gene and the gnomAD v4 API. gnomAD frequencies may shift slightly between releases; the enrichment in Finns will not.
F1. Norio R. Human Genetics, May 2003, in three parts: “Finnish Disease Heritage I: characteristics, causes, background” (PMID 12627295), “II: population prehistory and genetic roots of Finns” (PMID 12627296) and “III: the individual diseases” (PMID 12627297). The abstract of part I describes the FDH as “a group of rare hereditary diseases that are overrepresented in Finland” and lists among its topics the internal migration of the 1500s and geography and population structure, together with consanguineous marriages, linkage disequilibrium and haplotypes, and the age of the mutations. The connection: when small groups settled new inland regions in the 1500s, each regional population started from few founders, so some rare alleles became common there by founder effects and drift. Patients from one region share the same mutation on the same surrounding haplotype (linkage disequilibrium), inherited from a common ancestor.
F2. MedGen “Salla disease” (C1096903; MIM 604369): autosomal recessive inheritance. Gene SLC17A5, on 6q13 (NCBI Gene ID 26503), “solute carrier family 17 member 5”: according to the RefSeq summary, a membrane transporter that exports free sialic acids from lysosomes. Without it, sialic acid accumulates in lysosomes (a lysosomal storage disease).
F3. Click path: gnomAD → search rs80338794 (or open the link) → variant 6-73644583-G-A → Genetic Ancestry Group Frequencies (exomes). (a) Exomes: Finnish 245/53 410 = 0.0046; non-Finnish European 252/1 111 918 = 0.00023: about 20 times higher in Finns. (Genomes give a similar picture: 0.0044 and 0.0003.) It is absent or nearly absent from the African, East Asian and South Asian groups. (b) 2pq ≈ 2 × 0.0046 = 0.0092, about 1 in 110 Finns carries the allele. (c) PPT1 R122W (1-40091398-T-A), exomes: Finnish 362/53 394 = 0.0068, non-Finnish European 45/1 111 280 = 0.00004: about 170 times higher; carriers ≈ 1 in 74 in Finland. Both are founder effects: a rare allele carried by one of the few founders (or founders of a regional subpopulation) became common by chance as the population grew. (MedGen: CLN1 disease, MIM 256730, autosomal recessive, PPT1 at 1p34.2.)

title: Exercise: drift, selection, mutation, migration
text:
Solutions






Solutions: By hand





B1. (a) The next generation draws 4 copies, each A with probability 0.5. Lost: 0.5⁴ = 1/16 = 0.0625. Fixed: also 1/16. So 1/8 of such populations lose all variation in one generation. (b) With 20 copies: 0.5²⁰ ≈ 10−6 each. Small populations can lose variation in a single generation; larger ones cannot.
B2. (a) 0.15. (b) p₀ = 1/2000, so fixed with probability 0.0005 and lost with probability 0.9995. (c) (a) does not change: the fixation probability of a neutral allele depends only on its current frequency. (b) changes: in 10 million people a new mutation is fixed with probability 1/(2 × 10⁷), and it takes far longer.
B3. (a) Nₑ = 4 × 20 × 80/100 = 64, not 100. (b) Nₑ = 4/(1/500 + 1/50 + 1/500 + 1/500) = 4/0.026 = 154, although the arithmetic mean is 387. The single small generation dominates: a bottleneck has a lasting effect.
B4. H₅₀ = 0.5 × (1 − 1/50)50 = 0.5 × 0.364 = 0.18. Half is lost when e−t/2N = ½, at t = 2N ln 2 ≈ 1.39 × 50 ≈ 35 generations.
B5. Generation 1: w̄ = 0.16 × 1 + 0.48 × 0.95 + 0.36 × 0.9 = 0.940; p′ = (0.16 + 0.24 × 0.95)/0.940 = 0.388/0.940 = 0.413. Generation 2: p² = 0.1704, 2pq = 0.4848, q² = 0.3448; w̄ = 0.941; p″ = (0.1704 + 0.2424 × 0.95)/0.941 = 0.426. The heterozygote’s fitness is exactly halfway between the homozygotes: additive selection (no dominance, h = ½), against a.
B6. (a) q̂ = √(10−6) = 0.001; incidence q̂² = 10−6 (1 in a million). (b) At balance, incidence = q̂² = μ/s, so μ = 1/2500 = 4 × 10−4 per generation. That is far above typical per-gene mutation rates (about 10−6 to 10−5), so mutation–selection balance cannot explain CF’s frequency. Other explanations: a heterozygote advantage in the past (proposed, for example, as resistance to diarrhoeal infections, but not proven), or drift/founder effects in north-west European history. Both are hypotheses.
B7. (a) The heterozygote Tt (fitness 1) is fittest: heterozygote advantage, a kind of balancing selection (thalassaemia carriers are partly protected against malaria). (b) q̂ = (1 − 0.9)/(2 × 1 − 0.9 − 0.1) = 0.1/1.0 = 0.1. (c) With TT = Tt = 1, t is a purely recessive harmful allele; it declines, but slowly, because most copies are in healthy carriers.
B8. After 1 generation: p = 0.98 × 0 + 0.02 × 0.5 = 0.01. After 10: the difference from the source is 0.5 × 0.9810 = 0.409, so p = 0.5 − 0.409 = 0.091.
B9. (a) 1 copy among 1000: q = 0.001. (b) Incidence q² = 10−6 (1 in a million); carriers 2q ≈ 1 in 500. (c) q = 0.02: incidence 4 × 10−4 = 1 in 2500, carriers ≈ 0.039, 1 in 26. A 20-fold rise in q gives a 400-fold rise in incidence: this is how regional founder effects create local “hot spots” of rare recessive disease.

title: Quiz: DNA structure & replication (recap)
text:
Short questions on the evidence for DNA, base pairing, replication and recombination. This is a recap of 5MO103, so focus on the reasoning: what each experiment shows, and what follows from complementarity.

Q1. In Avery, MacLeod and McCarty’s experiment, extract from heat-killed S cells was treated with protease, RNase or DNase before being added to live R cells. Which result showed that the transforming principle is DNA, and why were the other two treatments needed?






Hint





A good experiment rules out the alternatives. What were the alternative candidate molecules?









Answer





Only DNase abolished transformation (no S colonies). The protease and RNase treatments are the controls that rule out the alternatives: destroying protein or RNA left the activity intact, so neither of them can be the transforming principle. Without these controls, one could argue that DNase worked only because of a protein contaminant in the enzyme preparation, or that any harsh treatment kills the activity.




Q2. Hershey and Chase labelled phage with 35S in one experiment and 32P in another. Why these two isotopes? Where did each label end up?






Hint





Which elements are in proteins but not in DNA, and the other way round?









Answer





Protein contains sulphur (in cysteine and methionine) but almost no phosphorus; DNA contains phosphorus (in its backbone) but no sulphur. So 35S labels only the protein coat and 32P labels only the DNA. After infection and blending, the 35S stayed with the empty coats in the fluid, and the 32P went into the bacteria and was passed on to the progeny phage. So DNA carries the information for making new phage.




Q3. A DNA sample is 22 % A. What are the percentages of T, G and C? Would this work for a single-stranded RNA virus?






Hint





Chargaff’s rules: A = T and G = C in double-stranded DNA.









Answer





A = T = 22 %, so A + T = 44 % and G + C = 56 %, giving G = C = 28 %. This only works for double-stranded nucleic acid, where every base has a partner. In a single strand (an RNA virus genome, or one strand of DNA on its own) there is no pairing, and A need not equal U or T.




Q4. Write the reverse complement of 5′-GATTACA-3′. Is 5′-GGATCC-3′ (the BamHI site) its own reverse complement?






Hint





Complement each base (A↔︎T, G↔︎C), then read the result backwards, so that it is again 5′ → 3′.









Answer





Complement: 3′-CTAATGT-5′; reversed: 5′-TGTAATC-3′. For GGATCC: complement CCTAGG, reversed GGATCC. Yes, it is its own reverse complement (a palindrome in the DNA sense), so both strands read the same 5′ → 3′. That is why a restriction enzyme can recognise the site on both strands at once.




Q5. The sickle-cell mutation is written c.20A>T in ClinVar but T>A in dbSNP (rs334, on the chromosome 11 reference). Explain why both are correct.






Hint





Which strand does each description use? On which strand of chromosome 11 is HBB?









Answer





The c. name uses the HBB coding strand, in the direction the gene is read. dbSNP reports alleles on the + strand of the reference chromosome. HBB lies on the − strand of chromosome 11, so its coding strand is the reverse complement of the + strand. The A on the coding strand pairs with a T on the + strand; after the mutation, T on the coding strand pairs with A on the + strand. One base-pair change, A:T → T:A, described from the two strands.




Q6. Meselson and Stahl moved E. coli from 15N to 14N medium. What bands would they have seen after three generations under semiconservative replication? Under conservative replication?






Hint





The two original heavy strands are never broken up or destroyed. How many helices are there after three generations, and how many of them contain an old strand?









Answer





After three generations, one helix has become 23 = 8. Semiconservative: the two old heavy strands sit in two different helices, which are hybrid; the other six are light. So ¼ hybrid, ¾ light. Conservative: the original helix stays intact (heavy), and the other seven are light: ⅛ heavy, ⅞ light, and never a hybrid band.




Q7. An E. coli strain with a mutation in dnaQ (mutD), the proofreading subunit of DNA polymerase III, is called a mutator. What does that mean, and why are mutations in all genes affected?






Hint





What does proofreading do to the error rate of replication?









Answer





Proofreading removes most wrongly inserted bases right after insertion, reducing the error rate by about a hundredfold. Without it, replication errors stay in the DNA, and after the next round of replication they become fixed as mutations. Proofreading works on every stretch of DNA that is replicated, so the mutation rate rises in all genes: the strain is a mutator. (Defects in mismatch repair, the next step, also give mutators, and in humans they cause Lynch syndrome: Mutation unit.)




Q8. Explain in two sentences how a crossover between genes A and B (Part 2) happens at the level of DNA strands. What is a non-crossover, and why was it invisible in mapping crosses?






Hint





Think of the Holliday junctions and the two ways of cutting them.









Answer





In meiosis, a double-strand break in one chromatid is repaired using the homologue as template: a 3′ strand invades the homologue, and the two helices become joined by Holliday junctions. When the junctions are cut one way, the helices swap their flanking regions (crossover: A b, a B). Cut the other way, the flanks stay parental (non-crossover: A B, a b) with only a short heteroduplex patch in between. Mapping crosses score only the flanking markers, so non-crossovers look exactly like no event at all, unless the patch covers a heterozygous site and causes gene conversion.

title: Exercise: DNA structure & replication (recap)
Exercise: DNA structure & replication (recap)
Exercise: DNA structure & replication (recap)
text:
Background
DNA. Two antiparallel strands, each written 5′ → 3′. A pairs with T (2 hydrogen bonds), G with C (3). In double-stranded DNA, A = T and G = C (Chargaff’s rules). The reverse complement of a sequence is its partner strand written 5′ → 3′: complement every base, then reverse the order.
Strands in databases. Genome records (dbSNP, genome browsers) give alleles on the + strand of the reference chromosome. Gene-based names (HGVS c. names, as in ClinVar) use the gene’s own coding strand. For a gene on the − strand, such as HBB, the two are reverse complements.
Replication is semiconservative: each daughter helix has one old and one new strand. Polymerases need a primer and extend only 3′ ends, so one strand is made continuously (leading) and the other in Okazaki fragments (lagging). Proofreading and mismatch repair bring the error rate down to about 1 in 109–1010 bases.
Homologous recombination. A double-strand break → a 3′ end invades the homologue → two Holliday junctions → cut one way (crossover: flanking markers swapped) or the other (non-crossover: flanks parental, short heteroduplex). Mismatch repair of a heteroduplex can cause gene conversion (3 : 1 instead of 2 : 2 in a tetrad).

title: Exercise: DNA structure & replication (recap)
text:
By hand
B1. (the evidence) In Griffith’s experiment, a mouse injected with live R cells plus heat-killed S cells died, and live S cells were recovered from it.

Which two control injections are needed to conclude that the R cells were transformed, and what does each rule out?
Hershey and Chase found 32P, but very little 35S, inside the infected bacteria. Suppose instead that both labels had entered the cells equally. What could you then conclude about the genetic material of the phage?

B2. (Chargaff)

DNA from the bacterium Micrococcus luteus is about 72 % G + C. Give the percentage of each of the four bases.
A DNA sample from a small phage has 25 % A, 33 % T, 24 % G and 18 % C (invented numbers). What is unusual about this DNA?

B3. (reverse complement) The HBB coding sequence, positions c.16–24 (codons 6–8), reads 5′-CCTGAGGAG-3′.

Write the partner strand 5′ → 3′.
In HbS, c.20 is changed from A to T. Write the mutant coding sequence and its reverse complement. Which base changes on the partner strand, and to what?
dbSNP lists rs334 as T>A on the chromosome 11 reference. On which strand of chromosome 11 does HBB lie?

B4. (Meselson–Stahl) Draw the expected bands (heavy, hybrid, light) in a CsCl gradient for each model of replication:

cells grown for many generations in 15N, then for one generation in 14N;
the same cells, then returned to 15N for one more generation.

B5. (polymerase direction) A template strand reads 3′-TACGGATTC-5′.

Write the new strand that a DNA polymerase makes on it, with its 5′ and 3′ ends.
In which direction (left to right, or right to left) does the polymerase move along the template?

B6. (recombination and gene conversion) A yeast diploid is heterozygous at three loci in a row on one chromosome: A — m — B on one homologue and a — m+ — b on the other. (m is a mutation in a gene for an amino acid; m+ is wild type.)

A single crossover between A and B happens in a meiosis. What combinations of the flanking markers do the four spores carry?
Another tetrad gives 3 m+ : 1 m spores, and all spores have the parental flanking combinations A B or a b. Explain this result with the model of recombination from the lecture.

Find it
NCBI Nucleotide stores nucleotide sequences, each with a stable accession and a version (the number after the dot, raised whenever the sequence changes). RefSeq records curated by NCBI start with NM_ (mRNA), NP_ (protein) or NC_ (complete chromosome). A record opens in GenBank format: a header (LOCUS, DEFINITION, ACCESSION, KEYWORDS), a FEATURES table and the sequence at the bottom.

What is on the first line, and what character does it start with?

title: Exercise: DNA structure & replication (recap)
text:
Solutions






Solutions: By hand





B1. a) Heat-killed S alone (the mouse lives): rules out that a few S cells survived the heating. Live R alone (the mouse lives): rules out that R cells turn into S on their own in the mouse. With both controls, the live S cells must have come from R cells changed by something in the dead S cells. Showing that the recovered S cells keep breeding true to S makes it a heritable change. b) Nothing clear. If both protein and DNA entered, either could carry the information for new phage. The experiment works because only one of the two enters.
B2. a) G = C = 72/2 = 36 %; A = T = 28/2 = 14 %. b) A ≠ T and G ≠ C, so the bases are not paired: the phage has single-stranded DNA. (Real examples exist, such as phage ΦX174.)
B3. a) Complement 3′-GGACTCCTC-5′, written 5′ → 3′: 5′-CTCCTCAGG-3′. b) Mutant coding sequence 5′-CCTGTGGAG-3′ (GAG → GTG); its reverse complement 5′-CTCCACAGG-3′. On the partner strand, the T opposite c.20 becomes an A. The base pair A:T became T:A. c) dbSNP gives the + strand of chromosome 11, and shows T>A. That is the partner strand of the HBB coding sequence, so HBB lies on the − strand. (The R exercise checks a–b with code.)
B4. a) Semiconservative: one hybrid band. Conservative: one heavy and one light band, 1 : 1. Dispersive: one hybrid band. b) After one more generation in 15N, each hybrid helix separates into a heavy strand and a light strand, and each gets a new heavy partner. Semiconservative: ½ heavy, ½ hybrid. Conservative: the parental heavy helix stays heavy and makes a new heavy copy; the light helix stays light and makes a new heavy copy: ¾ heavy, ¼ light, no hybrid. Dispersive: one band between hybrid and heavy.
B5. a) New strand 5′-ATGCCTAAG-3′ (complement of each base, antiparallel: its 5′ end lies opposite the template’s 3′ end). b) The polymerase adds to the 3′ end of the new strand, so it moves along the template from the template’s 3′ end to its 5′ end: here left to right.
B6. a) Only two of the four chromatids take part in a crossover. The spores are A B and a b (parental, from the two chromatids that did not cross over) and A b and a B (recombinant). b) Gene conversion in a non-crossover. A strand from one homologue invaded the other at the m gene, making a heteroduplex (one m strand paired with one m+ strand) at that site. The Holliday junctions were cut the non-crossover way, so the flanking markers stayed parental. Mismatch repair then “corrected” the mismatch using the m+ strand as template, turning one m chromatid into m+. The result: 3 m+ : 1 m instead of the Mendelian 2 : 2.









Solutions: Find it





These facts were checked against NCBI E-utilities (record updated 2026-09-06).
F1. Click path: NCBI Nucleotide → search NM_000518 → the record opens in GenBank format. a) DEFINITION: “Homo sapiens hemoglobin subunit beta (HBB), mRNA”. VERSION: NM_000518.5 (if the version is higher when you look, the sequence has been updated since this exercise was written). b) LOCUS: 628 bp, mRNA, linear. c) KEYWORDS: “RefSeq; MANE Select”. MANE Select (Matched Annotation from NCBI and EMBL-EBI) is the one transcript per gene that NCBI and Ensembl agree to use as the default; this record matches Ensembl ENST00000335295.4. d) CDS 51..494, protein_id NP_000509.1. 494 − 51 + 1 = 444 nt = 148 codons, of which the last is the stop codon, so 147 amino acids. (The features also show the three exons: 1..142, 143..365, 366..628.)
F2. a) The header line, starting with >: >NM_000518.5 Homo sapiens hemoglobin subunit beta (HBB), mRNA. The sequence follows on lines of 70 characters. b) Positions 51–53 are ATG, the start codon, as the CDS feature said. The sequence is in DNA letters (T, not U), as in all NCBI nucleotide records.
F3. Genomic context: NC_000011.10 (5225464..5227071, complement). “Complement” means that the gene lies on the − strand, so it is read from right to left on the chromosome’s coordinates. This agrees with B3c: the + strand shows the reverse complement of the HBB coding sequence, which is why dbSNP writes rs334 as T>A.

title: Exercise: DNA structure & replication (recap)
text:
Where this leads
Every mutation in the next unit is a change in this double-stranded text: a wrong base inserted during replication and not repaired, or damage that is copied before it is fixed. In Mutation & complementation you classify such changes by what they do to the protein, and use the complementation test to ask whether two mutations hit the same gene. In Part 4, revcomp() and base pairing come back in primer design and restriction mapping.
Next: Exercise in R: read the HBB FASTA into R, write a revcomp() function, and compute GC content with stringr.

title: Quiz: digital analysis of DNA
text:
Short questions on restriction enzymes, gels, PCR and sequencing. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Write the complementary strand of the BamHI site 5’-GGATCC-3’ and read it 5’→3’. What do you notice, and why does it matter for the enzyme?






Hint





Complement each base (A↔︎T, G↔︎C), then reverse the order to read the other strand 5’→3’.









Answer





The complement is 3’-CCTAGG-5’, which read 5’→3’ is GGATCC: the same as the top strand. The site is a palindrome (it equals its reverse complement). Restriction enzymes like BamHI work as dimers of two identical subunits, each recognising one half-site and cutting one strand, so a symmetric site suits a symmetric enzyme. It also means that the sticky ends left by BamHI (5’-GATC overhangs) can pair with any other BamHI end.




Q2. How often would you expect the site of HindIII (AAGCTT) to occur in random DNA? About how many HindIII sites would you expect in the 3.1 × 109 bp human genome?






Hint





Each of the 6 positions must match by chance, probability ¼ each.









Answer





(¼)6 = 1/4,096, so about once every 4,096 bp. In 3.1 × 109 bp: 3.1 × 109 / 4,096 ≈ 760,000 sites. Real genomes deviate from this estimate because the base composition is not 25% each and because some short sequences are over- or under-represented.




Q3. A circular plasmid has 3 EcoRI sites. A linear DNA molecule also has 3 EcoRI sites. How many fragments does each give?






Hint





Draw both and cut them.









Answer





Circular: 3 fragments (each cut opens the circle; k cuts give k pieces). Linear: 4 fragments (k cuts give k + 1 pieces, because the two ends are already free). In both cases the fragment sizes add up to the total length.




Q4. On a 1% agarose gel, a ladder band of 1,000 bp ran 40 mm and a band of 4,000 bp ran 22 mm. An unknown band ran 31 mm. Estimate its size.






Hint





Distance is roughly linear in log(size). 31 mm is half-way between 22 and 40 mm.









Answer





Half-way in distance means half-way in log size: log10(1,000) = 3.0 and log10(4,000) = 3.6, so the unknown has log10(size) ≈ 3.3, that is about 2,000 bp (the geometric mean of 1,000 and 4,000), not 2,500 bp (the arithmetic mean).




Q5. Why does a 37-bp fragment look much fainter on a gel than a 381-bp fragment, even when both come from the same PCR product and are present in the same number of copies?






Hint





The stain binds along the DNA. What does the amount of stain in a band depend on?









Answer





DNA stains bind along the length of the double helix, so the signal is proportional to the mass of DNA in the band, which is copies × length. The same number of 37-bp molecules carries about 1/10 the mass of 381-bp molecules, so the band is about ten times fainter.




Q6. A PCR starts from 100 copies of a template and runs 25 cycles at 100% efficiency. How many copies are there at the end (if no plateau)? And at 90% efficiency?






Hint





N = N0 (1 + E)n. 210 ≈ 1,000.









Answer





100% efficiency: 100 × 225 = 100 × 3.36 × 107 ≈ 3.4 × 109 copies. 90%: 100 × 1.925 = 100 × 9.3 × 106 ≈ 9.3 × 108 copies, about 3.6 times fewer. A small loss of efficiency per cycle compounds over many cycles.




Q7. In qPCR, sample X crosses the threshold at cycle 22 and sample Y at cycle 25. Assuming 100% efficiency, how much more template did X have?






Hint





Each cycle doubles the product.









Answer





X reached the threshold 3 cycles earlier, so it started with 23 = 8 times more template. (A ten-fold difference would be about 3.3 cycles.)




Q8. A student designs the primer 5’-GCGCGCGCAATATTGCGCGC-3’. Name two problems with it.






Hint





Check the GC content and compare the primer with its own reverse complement.









Answer






The primer is self-complementary: its reverse complement is GCGCGCAATATTGCGCGCGC, almost the same sequence, so it will fold into a hairpin and pair with copies of itself (primer-dimers). (2) Its GC content is 14/20 = 70%, above the 40–60% guideline, with long GC runs at both ends, so it will bind stably to many partly matching sites. A good primer also has to be unique in the genome, which you would check with Primer-BLAST.





Q9. Why must the polymerase used in PCR be heat-stable, and why does a ddNTP stop DNA synthesis in Sanger sequencing?






Hint





Think about the temperature profile of one PCR cycle, and about which chemical group DNA polymerase needs on the growing strand.









Answer





Each PCR cycle heats the reaction to ~95 °C to separate the strands; most enzymes would be destroyed, so you would have to add new enzyme every cycle. Taq polymerase, from the hot-spring bacterium Thermus aquaticus, survives this. DNA polymerase adds each new nucleotide to the 3’-OH of the growing strand. A dideoxynucleotide has no 3’-OH, so once it has been built in, nothing can be added after it: the chain terminates at that base.




Q10. At the sickle-cell site, a Sanger trace from one person shows a single A peak, from another a single T peak, and from a third an A and a T peak of about half height at the same position. What are their genotypes?






Hint





c.20A>T: A is the HbA allele, T is the HbS allele. Both of a person’s alleles are amplified by PCR.









Answer





Single A: HbA/HbA. Single T: HbS/HbS (sickle-cell disease). Double A + T peak: HbA/HbS, a carrier (sickle-cell trait). PCR copies both alleles, so a heterozygote gives a mixed signal at the variant position.




Q11. You sequence a 5 Mb bacterial genome with 2 million reads of 150 bases. What is the average coverage? Will every base be covered?






Hint





Coverage = number of reads × read length / genome length.









Answer





2 × 106 × 150 / 5 × 106 = 60×. On average each base is read 60 times, but reads land at random positions, so coverage varies: some bases have far more reads and some fewer. At 60× it is very unlikely that any base has none, but at low coverage (say 2×) a noticeable fraction of the genome would be missed.

title: Exercise: digital analysis of DNA
Exercise: digital analysis of DNA
Exercise: digital analysis of DNA
text:
Background
Restriction enzymes cut at short, usually palindromic sites: EcoRI G^AATTC, BamHI G^GATCC, HindIII A^AGCTT, PstI CTGCA^G, DdeI C^TNAG (N = any base). In random DNA, a site with n specified bases occurs about once every 4n bp. A linear molecule with k sites gives k + 1 fragments, a circular one gives k. The fragment sizes add up to the total length.
Gels. Fragments run towards the + electrode; distance is roughly linear in log(size). Read unknown sizes from a ladder by interpolating on the log scale. Band brightness is proportional to DNA mass (copies × length).
PCR. Two primers define the product. Each cycle multiplies the product by (1 + E), where E is the efficiency: N = N0(1 + E)n, until a plateau. Ten times more template reaches a threshold log(10)/log(1 + E) cycles earlier: 3.3 cycles at E = 1, 3.6 at E = 0.9. Primer rules: 18–25 nt, 40–60% GC, Tm ≈ 55–65 °C and matched, no 3’ complementarity, unique in the genome. Wallace rule: Tm ≈ 2 °C × (A + T) + 4 °C × (G + C).
Sickle-cell PCR-RFLP. A 500-bp PCR product around HBB exon 1 has DdeI sites at 37, 217 and 418 bp. The HbS change (codon 7 GAG → GTG, c.20A>T) destroys the site at 217:

381, 82, 37



Sequencing. Sanger: dye-labelled ddNTPs stop synthesis; products are sorted by length and the colours read in order; a heterozygote gives a double peak. Next-generation sequencing: coverage = number of reads × read length / genome length.

title: Exercise: digital analysis of DNA
text:
Explore: restriction digest and gel
Do the by-hand part first. Pick a DNA and one or two enzymes; the gel shows the ladder (M), the uncut DNA (U), each single digest and, with two enzymes, the double digest. Fragment sizes come from the real sequences: phage λ (NCBI NC_001416.1), the plasmid pUC19 (NCBI M77789.2) and the 500-bp HBB PCR product (human genome GRCh38). Band brightness is proportional to DNA mass. Leave “show fragment sizes” off until you have made your own estimate.



E1. Start with “HBB PCR, HbA/HbA” (DdeI, 2% gel, 100 bp ladder). Estimate the sizes of the bands from the ladder, then tick “show fragment sizes”. Now click through HbA/HbS and HbS/HbS. Which band tells you that an HbS allele is present, and which bands tell you an HbA allele is present? Compare with your answer to B7.
E2. Choose “phage λ”, the enzyme HindIII only, and the “λ / HindIII” ladder. The ladder is itself a HindIII digest of λ DNA. Which of your HindIII bands does not match a ladder band? Can you explain the difference? (Hint: the λ DNA sold for ladders comes from a mutant strain. Look at what the sizes add up to.)
E3. Choose “pUC19 plasmid”. a) Why do EcoRI alone and HindIII alone each give a single band of 2,686 bp? b) Why does the uncut plasmid run faster than the linear 2,686 bp band? c) What does the double digest EcoRI + HindIII cut out, and why is it hard to see?
E4. Choose “phage λ” with DdeI on a 0.7% gel, then on a 2% gel. Why does the lane look like a smear rather than clear bands? Which gel percentage separates the λ EcoRI fragments best, and which one separates the HBB DdeI fragments best?






Solutions: Explore (gel)





E1. HbA/HbA: 201, 180, 82 and a faint 37 bp band. HbS/HbS: 381, 82, 37. HbA/HbS: all five. The 381 band (uncut at the codon 7 site) shows an HbS allele; the 201 + 180 pair (cut at codon 7) shows an HbA allele. The 82 and 37 bp bands come from the two other DdeI sites, which are the same in both alleles: they act as a built-in check that the enzyme worked. Note that 201 and 180 run close together; on a 1% gel they would be hard to separate.
E2. The λ reference sequence gives seven HindIII fragments: 23,130, 9,416, 6,682, 4,361, 2,322, 2,027 and 564 bp. The ladder has 6,557 and 125 instead of 6,682, and 6,557 + 125 = 6,682. So the ladder DNA has one extra HindIII site. The NCBI record NC_001416.1 notes at position 37,589 a C in wild type and a T in the ind1 mutant, which turns AAGCTC into the HindIII site AAGCTT. Commercial λ DNA comes from a strain carrying ind1, so its HindIII digest has eight fragments. A single point mutation has created a restriction fragment length polymorphism, just like HbS but the other way round (a site gained instead of lost).
E3. a) pUC19 has exactly one site for each of these enzymes, in the multiple cloning site, and a circle cut once becomes one linear molecule of full length. b) The uncut plasmid is supercoiled: twisted into a compact form that moves through the gel faster than the same DNA when linear. So an uncut circle does not tell you its size. c) EcoRI and HindIII are 51 bp apart in the MCS, so the double digest gives 2,635 + 51 bp. The 51-bp fragment has about 2% of the mass of the large one, so its band is very faint, and on a 1% gel it runs near the bottom. In cloning, this small piece is simply replaced by the insert.
E4. DdeI has a 4-base specific site (C, T, A, G with any base in the middle), so it cuts λ 104 times. The 105 fragments, none longer than about 1.8 kb, overlap into a smear. A 0.7% gel spreads the large λ EcoRI fragments (3.5–21 kb) best; a 2% gel spreads the 37–381 bp HBB fragments best. A 2% gel squashes all fragments above about 3 kb together near the well.

title: Exercise: digital analysis of DNA
text:
Explore: PCR cycles
The second demo follows the number of copies of the PCR product, cycle by cycle. Each cycle multiplies the product by 1 + E × (1 − total/K), so growth is exponential at first and stops at a plateau K = 1012 copies. The dashed line is a detection threshold (1010 copies); the readout gives the cycle at which each curve crosses it (the Ct). With “primer-dimer” ticked, the primers occasionally prime on each other and the short dimer product then amplifies too.



E5. On the “realistic (E = 90%)” preset, read the Ct for 1,000 start copies and for 10× less template. What is the difference? Now set the efficiency to 100%: what is the difference now? Compare with log(10)/log(1 + E).
E6. Untick “log y-axis”. Describe the curve. At which cycle could you first see any product on the linear axis? Why do qPCR machines measure the Ct instead of the final amount of product?
E7. Click “10 templates + primer-dimer” and then “no-template control”. At which cycle does the primer-dimer cross the threshold in each case? What does this mean for a diagnostic test that runs 40 cycles, and why does every PCR experiment include a no-template control?
E8. Back on “realistic”, raise the start to 106 copies. What is the Ct now, and what happens in the last 15 cycles? If you ran this reaction on a gel after 35 cycles, could you tell 105 from 106 starting copies?






Solutions: Explore (PCR)





E5. At E = 90%: Ct 25.1 for 1,000 copies and 28.7 for 100 copies, a difference of 3.6 cycles; log(10)/log(1.9) = 3.59. At E = 100%: Ct 23.3 and 26.6, a difference of 3.3 cycles; log(10)/log(2) = 3.32. Lower efficiency means more cycles per ten-fold, and a later Ct for the same template.
E6. On a linear axis the curve sits at zero for about 25 cycles, then rises steeply and bends over into the plateau: an S shape. The product is only visible above roughly 1010–1011 copies, around cycle 25–28 here. The final amount is almost the same for very different starting amounts (all reactions plateau near 1012), whereas the Ct, in the exponential phase, depends directly on the starting amount. That is why quantitative PCR reads the Ct.
E7. With 10 template copies, the target crosses the threshold at cycle 32.3 and the primer-dimer at 39.8. With no template, the primer-dimer crosses at 38.9 (a little earlier, since it does not have to compete with the target). A 40-cycle test with a weak or absent target can therefore show a late signal that is not the target at all. The no-template control (water instead of DNA) shows whether primer-dimers or contaminating DNA give a signal; a signal in it means the run cannot be trusted. In practice, a melting curve or a gel also separates the short dimer from the real product.
E8. 106 copies: Ct 14.4 (105 gives 17.9). From about cycle 20 the curve bends and from about cycle 25 it is flat at the plateau: primers and nucleotides are used up, so the last 15 cycles add almost nothing. After 35 cycles both reactions have reached the plateau, so the bands on a gel would look the same: end-point PCR is not quantitative.
