Where this leads
In Part 7 the same developmental genes come back as cancer genes: SHH, WNT1, CTNNB1, NOTCH1 and TP53 are all in this table. The join-and-fill pattern you used here works whenever “missing” means “zero”, for example when you count mutations per gene and per tumour.

title: Complex traits, heritability & GWAS
text:
About this lecture
Height, blood pressure and the risk of type 2 diabetes do not fall into Mendel’s neat classes. They vary continuously, and depend on many genes and the environment: they are complex (quantitative, polygenic) traits.

The polygenic model: many loci of small effect give a normal distribution.
Heritability: broad (H²) and narrow (h²); twin studies; parent–offspring regression (slope = h²).
What heritability does not mean.
Finding the loci: QTL mapping in crosses, and genome-wide association studies (GWAS): association, linkage disequilibrium, 5 × 10⁻⁸, Manhattan and QQ plots.
Polygenic scores and the missing heritability.

Book: Hartwell, the chapter on complex traits. You need χ² and multiple testing (Part 1, Hardy–Weinberg), LOD scores (Part 2) and lm from your data-analysis course.

This last unit of Part 7 ties together everything in the course. The Mendelian traits of Part 1 are the special case where one locus has a large effect. Most traits of medical and agricultural interest are complex. The statistics students already know, regression with lm, is exactly what Galton invented for this problem. The second half moves from heritability, a property of a population, to finding the actual loci, which is what GWAS do and what the GWAS Catalog records.

title: Complex traits, heritability & GWAS
section: From Mendel’s classes to a continuous trait
text:
From Mendel’s classes to a continuous trait


One locus with additive alleles gives 3 classes; k loci give 2k + 1 classes, and their frequencies follow a binomial, which approaches a normal curve.
Add environmental variation and the steps blur: a smooth bell curve, as for height.
This polygenic model (Fisher, 1918) reconciled Mendel’s discrete inheritance with Galton’s continuous variation.


In the early 1900s there was a real conflict between Mendelians, who studied discrete traits, and biometricians, who studied continuous ones like height. Fisher showed in 1918 that many Mendelian loci, each with a small additive effect, produce continuous normal variation and the correlations between relatives that Galton had measured. The figure assumes each locus has two equally frequent alleles and that each “+” allele adds the same amount. With 20 loci there are already 41 classes; with environmental noise, nobody would see the steps. Nilsson-Ehle’s wheat kernel colour with three loci is the textbook example of the transition. Students simulate this in R.

title: Complex traits, heritability & GWAS
text:
Genes and environment
The phenotype of one person: P = G + E, the sum of a genetic value and an environmental deviation.

Environment here means everything that is not the DNA sequence: nutrition, disease, climate, chance events in development, measurement error.
Height in many countries rose by roughly 10 cm over the 20th century: far too fast for genes, so this is environment (nutrition, health).
Genes and environment can interact: the effect of a genotype may depend on the environment (G × E). Example: PKU is harmful only on a normal diet.

Across a population, we split the variance of P, not one person’s height, into genetic and environmental parts.

The key conceptual move: heritability is about variation among individuals in a population, not about how much of one person’s height comes from genes. That question makes no sense, because genes and environment are both needed for any height at all. The secular increase in height is a good example of why high heritability does not mean a trait cannot change. The PKU example from Part 1 is the classic gene–environment interaction: the genotype causes disease only on a diet with phenylalanine.

title: Complex traits, heritability & GWAS
text:
Heritability: partitioning the variance


VA, additive variance: the part due to the average effects of alleles. This is what makes children resemble their parents.
VD, dominance variance: interactions between the two alleles at a locus, which are not passed on as such (each parent passes one allele).
Narrow-sense heritability h² = VA/VP predicts the response to selection and the parent–offspring resemblance.


Two heritabilities: broad sense, all genetic variance over phenotypic variance; narrow sense, additive variance only. Why does dominance variance not pass to children? A parent passes one allele, not a genotype. If Aa has a special effect because of the combination, the child does not get that combination from one parent. Breeders care about narrow-sense heritability, because the response to selection is R = h² S, the breeder’s equation: if you select parents that are S units above the mean, the offspring will be h² S above the mean. Epistasis, from the extensions-to-Mendel unit, adds a further interaction component, which we ignore here.

title: Complex traits, heritability & GWAS
text:
Twin studies


MZ twins share all their genes; DZ twins half, like ordinary siblings. Both share a family environment.
If MZ twins are more alike than DZ twins, the difference reflects genes: Falconer’s formula h² ≈ 2 [r(MZ) − r(DZ)].
Assumption: MZ and DZ twins have equally similar environments. Twins reared apart and adoption studies test it.


Twins are a natural experiment. The correlation of MZ twins includes all the genetic variance plus the shared environment; DZ twins share half of the additive genetic variance plus the same shared environment. The difference, doubled, estimates the additive part. The numbers in the figure are illustrative; for height in many studies MZ correlations are around 0.9. The equal-environments assumption is the main criticism: MZ twins may be treated more similarly. Twins reared apart, as in the Minnesota study, and adopted children compared with their biological and adoptive parents, are designs that separate genes from family environment. Scandinavian twin registries, including the Swedish Twin Registry, are among the largest sources of such data.

title: Complex traits, heritability & GWAS
text:
Parent–offspring regression


Regress offspring on the midparent (mean of the parents): the slope = h². On one parent, slope = h²/2.
Galton’s 205 families (1886): slope 0.71. Children of tall parents are tall, but less extreme: regression towards the mean, Galton’s original use of the word “regression”.
Shared family environment also makes parents and children alike, so this is an upper estimate of h².


This is lm from the data-analysis course, applied to the problem it was invented for. Why is the slope h squared? The covariance between midparent and offspring is half the additive variance, and the variance of the midparent is half the phenotypic variance, so the ratio is VA over VP. With one parent, the covariance is the same but the variance is the full VP, so the slope halves. The data are Galton’s original family heights, from the HistData R package; students fit this model themselves. Galton multiplied daughters’ heights by 1.08 to put them on the male scale; we follow him. Note that Galton’s slope of 0.71 is probably inflated by shared environment and by assortative mating; modern estimates of the narrow-sense heritability of height in well-nourished populations are around 0.7 to 0.8 from family data.

title: Complex traits, heritability & GWAS
text:
Demo: parent–offspring regression




The demo starts at h squared 0.6 with 200 families: the fitted slope is 0.58 plus or minus 0.10. Drag h squared to 0: the cloud becomes round, the slope near zero. Tick single parent: the slope halves. Then the shared environment preset, h squared 0.3 and c squared 0.3: the slope is about 0.6, so we would wrongly double the heritability. This is the main weakness of family designs.

title: Complex traits, heritability & GWAS
text:
What heritability does not mean

It is not the fraction of one person’s trait caused by genes. It describes variation in a population.
It is specific to a population and environment. If everyone gets the same good food, VE shrinks and h² rises.
High heritability does not mean unchangeable: height is highly heritable and rose ~10 cm in a century; PKU is genetic and treated with diet.
Heritability within groups says nothing about the cause of differences between groups. (Lewontin: seeds from one sack grown in two fields of different soil.)
h² = 0 does not mean genes are unimportant: the number of fingers has heritability near 0, because almost all variation is accidental.


This slide is the ethics content of the unit, and links to the ethics module. Lewontin’s thought experiment: take a sack of genetically varied seeds, plant half in good soil and half in poor soil. Within each field, height differences are mostly genetic: high heritability. Between the fields, the difference is entirely environmental. So a high heritability within human groups gives no support to genetic explanations of differences between groups. The fingers example: humans almost all have five fingers because of genes, but the rare variation is mostly due to accidents, so heritability is low. Heritability measures what causes differences, not what causes the trait.

title: Complex traits, heritability & GWAS
text:
Finding the loci: QTL mapping
A quantitative trait locus (QTL) is a locus that affects a quantitative trait.

In a cross between two inbred lines (for example a tall and a short strain of mice or maize), the F2 or backcross offspring carry different combinations of the parents’ chromosome segments.
Genotype markers along the genome; for each marker, compare the trait between genotype classes (a t-test or regression).
A marker linked to a QTL shows a difference; unlinked markers do not. The evidence is summarised as a LOD score along the chromosome, as in Part 2 (LOD scores).

QTL mapping needs a cross and gives broad regions (tens of cM). In humans we use association in unrelated people instead.

QTL mapping is linkage mapping for quantitative traits. Students know linkage, recombination fractions and LOD scores from Part 2; the only change is that the phenotype is a number, so instead of counting recombinants we compare means. Because an F2 has had only one or two meioses since the parents, linkage blocks are long, so a QTL peak covers a large region. Fine mapping needs many more generations of recombination. Classic successes include fruit size in tomato and domestication genes in maize.

title: Complex traits, heritability & GWAS
text:
Genome-wide association studies (GWAS)
Genotype hundreds of thousands to millions of SNPs in thousands of unrelated people. For each SNP, test whether the trait differs between genotypes:

Quantitative trait: regress the trait on the number of copies of the allele (0, 1, 2), with lm.
Disease: compare allele frequencies in cases and controls (a 2 × 2 χ² test, or logistic regression).

Unrelated people share only tiny stretches of chromosome from common ancestors, so association is local: only SNPs in linkage disequilibrium (LD) with a causal variant show a signal.
Linkage disequilibrium: alleles at nearby SNPs are correlated in the population, because they sit on the same ancestral haplotypes that recombination has not yet broken up.

The contrast with QTL mapping and with family-based LOD scores is the number of meioses: in a population, the haplotypes around a variant have been broken up by recombination over thousands of generations, so only SNPs very close to the causal variant, typically within tens of kilobases, are still correlated with it. That gives much finer resolution, but needs very many markers and very many people. LD is what makes GWAS work with a SNP array: we do not need to genotype the causal variant itself, only a SNP correlated with it.

title: Complex traits, heritability & GWAS
text:
Manhattan and QQ plots


One test per SNP, so about a million tests. At p < 0.05 we would expect ~50 000 false hits. The genome-wide threshold is 5 × 10⁻⁸ ≈ 0.05 / 1 000 000 (a Bonferroni correction for about a million independent tests).
Manhattan plot: −log10 p against position. Causal loci appear as towers: the causal variant and its LD neighbours.
QQ plot: observed against expected −log10 p. Null SNPs follow the line; true signals lift off at the top. If all points lift off, suspect population structure (the Wahlund effect of the Hardy–Weinberg unit) or genotyping errors.


Recall from the Hardy–Weinberg exercise: one of 15 tests was significant at 5 percent, which was just chance. With a million tests, chance alone would give tens of thousands of hits. 5 times 10 to the minus 8 is the conventional threshold; it corresponds to roughly a million independent common variants in the genome of European-ancestry populations. Population structure is a classic trap: if cases come more often from one population than controls, every SNP with an allele frequency difference between the populations looks associated. Modern GWAS correct for this with principal components of the genotypes.

title: Complex traits, heritability & GWAS
text:
Demo: a simulated GWAS




Five causal loci with small effects. At N equals 50 000, two of five pass the genome-wide line with the default seed. Press N equals 5 000: none. N equals 500 000: all five, and no false loci. The expected z of a causal SNP is beta times the square root of 2 f (1 − f) N, so halving the effect requires four times the sample. Then the null preset: the QQ plot follows the diagonal and nothing passes 10 to the minus 5. Point out the towers: many SNPs in LD with each causal one.

title: Complex traits, heritability & GWAS
text:
What GWAS have found

Type 2 diabetes: the strongest association is rs7903146 in an intron of TCF7L2 (10q25). In a 2024 multi-ancestry study of about 2.5 million people (Suzuki et al., Nature), its p-value was about 10⁻¹³¹⁵. Each copy of the risk allele raises the risk only modestly.
The GWAS Catalog lists thousands of T2D associations (KCNQ1, CDKAL1, CDKN2B, FTO, IGF2BP2, …) and tens of thousands for height (GDF5, ZBTB38, LCORL, HMGA2, …).
Most hits are non-coding: they change regulation of nearby genes (Part 6), not protein sequence.
Each variant explains a tiny fraction of the variance: complex traits are truly polygenic.


These are the facts students look up in the exercise via the GWAS Catalog. A p-value of 10 to the minus 1315 is not a measure of a large effect: it reflects an enormous sample. The odds ratio per allele for TCF7L2 is modest, of the order of 1.3 to 1.4 in European-ancestry studies; check the Catalog entry for the exact estimate in a given study. TCF7L2 is a transcription factor in the Wnt pathway; the risk allele is thought to affect insulin secretion. FTO was first found as an obesity locus, and its T2D signal works mostly through body weight. The height loci include genes of the growth plate and skeletal development, which makes biological sense.

title: Complex traits, heritability & GWAS
section: Polygenic scores and the missing heritability
text:
Polygenic scores and the missing heritability
Polygenic score: add up a person’s risk alleles, each weighted by its GWAS effect size: PGS = Σ βi × (number of risk alleles at SNP i).

Useful for groups (risk stratification, research); weak for individuals: most people with a high score do not get the disease.
Scores built in one ancestry group predict worse in others: allele frequencies and LD differ (drift, previous unit).

Missing heritability: twin and family studies give h² ≈ 0.8 for height, but the first GWAS hits together explained only a few percent. Explanations:

many more loci of tiny effect, below the threshold (larger samples keep finding more);
rare variants that arrays do not capture;
family designs overestimating h² (shared environment, as in the demo).


A polygenic score is a weighted sum, exactly the polygenic model of the first slide turned into a prediction. For height, scores now explain a substantial part of the variance in European-ancestry samples, much less in others. This transferability problem is an equity issue: most GWAS participants have been of European ancestry, so the benefits of genetic prediction are unequally distributed. That links to the ethics module. The missing heritability was a major puzzle around 2010; much of it has since been found by bigger GWAS and by methods that estimate heritability from all SNPs together. The gap that remains is partly rare variants and partly overestimation in family studies.

title: Complex traits, heritability & GWAS
text:
Summary

Complex traits: many loci + environment give continuous, normal variation (Fisher’s polygenic model).
VP = VA + VD + VE. Broad H² = VG/VP; narrow h² = VA/VP.
Estimates: twins h² ≈ 2[r(MZ) − r(DZ)]; offspring on midparent slope = h² (Galton: 0.71); on one parent slope = h²/2.
Heritability is about variation in one population and environment; it says nothing about individuals or differences between groups.
QTL mapping uses crosses and linkage (LOD); GWAS use association and LD in unrelated people, with p < 5 × 10⁻⁸.
Hits such as TCF7L2 for T2D have small effects; polygenic scores add them up; part of the heritability is still missing.


The exam-level skills: compute heritability from twin correlations or a regression slope; interpret a Manhattan plot and a QQ plot; explain why the threshold is 5 times 10 to the minus 8; and explain clearly what heritability does not mean.

title: Complex traits, heritability & GWAS
text:
Where this leads

Ethics module: polygenic scores in embryo selection and insurance, direct-to-consumer genomics, and the misuse of heritability.
Back to Part 6: most GWAS hits sit in regulatory DNA; finding the gene they regulate uses the tools of gene regulation.
In the exercise: heritability by hand, the two demos, the GWAS Catalog for type 2 diabetes and height, and in R: Galton’s families with lm, and a Manhattan plot built from scratch with ggplot2.


This is the last unit before the ethics module, and it gives the ethics module much of its material. Encourage students to read one GWAS paper from the Catalog, which supports the literature outcome of the course.

title: Exercise in R: complex traits, heritability & GWAS
Exercise in R: complex traits, heritability & GWAS
Exercise in R: complex traits, heritability & GWAS
text:
Before you start
This page builds on the by-hand part of the Exercise, so do that first. You need the packages dplyr, readr and ggplot2. Download two files and save them in a data/ folder of your R project:

galton_families.csv: Galton’s family heights in inches, one row per adult child (934 children, 205 families). From the R package HistData 1.1.1, data set GaltonFamilies, which transcribes Galton’s own notebook. midparentHeight is (father + 1.08 × mother)/2.
gwas_catalog_t2d.csv: all associations for type 2 diabetes in the GWAS Catalog, downloaded with the REST API v2 on 20 November 2026 and reduced to one row per SNP (the smallest p-value). neg_log10_p is −log10 of the p-value; pos is the GRCh38 position.

title: Exercise in R: complex traits, heritability & GWAS
text:
Tasks
New this time: lm for heritability and a Manhattan plot built step by step. You know lm from your data-analysis course; here the slope has a genetic meaning. A Manhattan plot needs one trick: positions restart at 1 on every chromosome, so we compute a cumulative position by adding the length of all earlier chromosomes.
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)

The polygenic model
R1. For 10 000 people, simulate the number of “+” alleles at 1, 2, 10 and 100 unlinked additive loci, each with allele frequency 0.5. rbinom(n, size = 2, prob = 0.5) gives the number of “+” alleles at one locus; put one locus per column in a matrix and add up each row with rowSums. Plot the distribution for each number of loci. How many classes do you see, and what shape appears?
set.seed(1)
n_people <- 10000
polygenic <- function(n_loci) {
  # each locus: 2 alleles, each + with probability 0.5, so the genotype adds 0, 1 or 2
  g <- matrix(rbinom(n_people * n_loci, size = 2, prob = 0.5), nrow = n_people)
  rowSums(g)                         # number of "+" alleles per person
}
sims <- bind_rows(
  tibble(loci = "1 locus",    value = polygenic(1)),
  tibble(loci = "2 loci",     value = polygenic(2)),
  tibble(loci = "10 loci",    value = polygenic(10)),
  tibble(loci = "100 loci",   value = polygenic(100))
) |> mutate(loci = factor(loci, levels = c("1 locus", "2 loci", "10 loci", "100 loci")))
sims |> group_by(loci) |> summarise(classes = n_distinct(value), mean = mean(value), sd = sd(value))

ggplot(sims, aes(value)) + geom_bar() +
  facet_wrap(~ loci, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = 'number of "+" alleles', y = "people")


Galton’s families
R2. Read data/galton_families.csv. How many families and children are there? Compute the mean and SD of the children’s height for daughters and sons.
galton <- read_csv("data/galton_families.csv")
galton
galton |> summarise(families = n_distinct(family), children = n())
galton |> group_by(gender) |> summarise(n = n(), mean_height = mean(childHeight), sd = sd(childHeight))
R3. Galton multiplied daughters’ heights by 1.08 to put them on the male scale. Do the same in a new column child_adj, and check that the means of sons and daughters now agree. Then fit lm(child_adj ~ midparentHeight). What is the slope, and its 95% confidence interval (confint)? What is your estimate of h²? Plot the data with the regression line and the line of slope 1.
galton <- galton |>
  mutate(child_adj = ifelse(gender == "female", 1.08 * childHeight, childHeight))
galton |> group_by(gender) |> summarise(mean_adj = mean(child_adj))
fit <- lm(child_adj ~ midparentHeight, data = galton)
summary(fit)
coef(fit)
confint(fit)

ggplot(galton, aes(midparentHeight, child_adj)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0.15, alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "midparent height (inches)", y = "child height (inches, daughters x 1.08)",
       title = "Galton's families: offspring on midparent")
(geom_jitter moves each point a little at random, because Galton rounded heights and many points would otherwise lie on top of each other.)
R4. Regress the children on the father alone and on the mother alone. Which slopes do you expect if h² is what you found in R3? Convert the father slope to an estimate of h². Finally, compute the correlation between the heights of fathers and mothers: did tall men marry tall women (assortative mating)?
coef(lm(child_adj ~ father, data = galton))
coef(lm(child_adj ~ mother, data = galton))
2 * coef(lm(child_adj ~ father, data = galton))[2]
cor(galton$father, galton$mother)


A Manhattan plot from the GWAS Catalog
R5. Read data/gwas_catalog_t2d.csv. How many SNPs and studies are in it? Show the eight strongest associations. How many SNPs are genome-wide significant (−log10 p ≥ −log10(5 × 10⁻⁸) = 7.3)?
t2d <- read_csv("data/gwas_catalog_t2d.csv")
nrow(t2d)
n_distinct(t2d$study)
t2d |> arrange(desc(neg_log10_p)) |> select(rsid, chr, pos, neg_log10_p, mapped_gene) |> head(8)
t2d |> filter(neg_log10_p >= -log10(5e-8)) |> nrow()
R6. Build the Manhattan plot in four steps.

For each chromosome, find its length (here: the largest position in the data) and an offset: the summed length of all earlier chromosomes, with cumsum.
left_join the offsets to the SNPs and compute bp_cum = pos + offset.
Find the centre of each chromosome for the axis labels, and the strongest SNP of the six top genes (skip SNPs mapped to several genes) for text labels.
Plot −log10 p against bp_cum, colour alternate chromosomes with chr %% 2, add the 5 × 10⁻⁸ line, and use a log scale on y because the p-values span from 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻¹³¹⁵.

Which chromosomes have most associations?
chrom_len <- t2d |> group_by(chr) |> summarise(len = max(pos)) |>
  mutate(offset = cumsum(as.numeric(len)) - len)
manh <- t2d |>
  left_join(chrom_len, by = "chr") |>
  mutate(bp_cum = pos + offset)
axis_pos <- manh |> group_by(chr) |> summarise(centre = (min(bp_cum) + max(bp_cum)) / 2)
top_genes <- manh |>
  filter(!grepl(";", mapped_gene)) |>
  group_by(mapped_gene) |> slice_max(neg_log10_p, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |> slice_max(neg_log10_p, n = 6)
top_genes |> select(mapped_gene, chr, neg_log10_p)

ggplot(manh, aes(bp_cum, neg_log10_p, colour = factor(chr %% 2))) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(5e-8), colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_text(data = top_genes, aes(label = mapped_gene), colour = "black", size = 3, vjust = -0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("steelblue4", "steelblue2"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = axis_pos$centre, labels = axis_pos$chr) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(5, 10, 30, 100, 300, 1000)) +
  labs(x = "chromosome", y = "-log10(p) (log scale)",
       title = "Type 2 diabetes: associations in the GWAS Catalog") +
  theme_minimal() + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())

t2d |> count(chr) |> arrange(desc(n)) |> head(5)

title: Exercise in R: complex traits, heritability & GWAS
text:
Where this leads
The same code makes a Manhattan plot from the full summary statistics of any GWAS, which many studies publish (the GWAS Catalog links to them). From there, the next steps are fine-mapping, polygenic scores, and the ethics module’s discussion of what such scores should and should not be used for.

title: Chromosome theory & sex linkage
text:
About this lecture
Mendel’s factors were an abstraction: pairs of “somethings” that separate when gametes form. Around 1900–1915 geneticists found out where genes are: on chromosomes. The key evidence came from a gene that follows the X chromosome.

A careful recap of mitosis and meiosis: ploidy, homologues and sister chromatids, and what each division separates.
The chromosome theory of inheritance: chromosomes behave exactly as Mendel’s factors must.
Morgan’s white-eyed fly (1910): the first gene assigned to a specific chromosome, the X.
Bridges’ nondisjunction (1916): rare exceptions that proved the theory.
Sex determination: XY with SRY, XO, ZW and haplodiploidy.
X-linked inheritance worked by hand, and a pointer to dosage compensation.

Book: Hartwell, Genetics: From Genes to Genomes, chromosome theory of inheritance chapter.

This lecture opens Part 2. Part 1 treated genes as abstract factors; today we put them on chromosomes. The next three units use that to map genes along a chromosome: linkage and recombination, three-point crosses, and human linkage with LOD scores. Mitosis and meiosis were covered at school and in cell biology, so the first slides are a recap, but a careful one: students must be fluent with chromosomes versus chromatids, and with n versus 2n, before mapping makes sense. Sex linkage was introduced just enough for pedigrees in Part 1; here it gets its full story.

title: Chromosome theory & sex linkage
text:
Chromosomes: the vocabulary (recap)








Term
Meaning
Example




Homologous chromosomes (homologues)
the two copies of one chromosome in a diploid cell, one from each parent; same genes in the same order, possibly different alleles
your two chromosome 7s, one carrying CFTR from your mother, one from your father


Sister chromatids
the two identical DNA copies of one chromosome after replication, joined at the centromere
a “metaphase chromosome” is two sister chromatids


Haploid (n)
one set of chromosomes
human gametes: n = 23


Diploid (2n)
two sets, one from each parent
human body cells: 2n = 46


Autosomes / sex chromosomes
chromosomes that are the same in both sexes / that differ (X, Y)
humans: 22 autosome pairs + XX or XY


Karyotype
the chromosome set of a species, as seen in the microscope
Drosophila 2n = 8, garden pea 2n = 14



Count chromosomes by centromeres. A replicated chromosome (two chromatids) is still one chromosome.

Go slowly here: most confusion later in Part 2 comes from mixing up homologues and sister chromatids. Homologues are similar but not identical (they can carry different alleles) and come from different parents. Sister chromatids are identical copies made in S phase. The rule “count centromeres” settles every counting question: after S phase a human cell still has 46 chromosomes, but 92 chromatids. Mention the DNA content notation if useful: a G1 diploid cell is 2C, after S it is 4C, a gamete is 1C.

title: Chromosome theory & sex linkage
text:
Mitosis and meiosis


Mitosis: one division; sister chromatids separate. Two diploid daughters, identical to the parent.
Meiosis: one round of DNA replication, two divisions. Meiosis I separates homologues (2n → n). Meiosis II separates sister chromatids, as in mitosis.


Recap from cell biology. Both start with a replicated cell: 2n = 4 here, so 8 chromatids. Mitosis separates sisters, so each daughter gets one copy of every chromosome from both parents, 2n again. Meiosis I is the special division: homologues pair up and then go to opposite poles, so each daughter gets one homologue of each pair, n chromosomes, but each still has two chromatids. Meiosis II is like mitosis in a haploid cell. Point at the gametes: each has one long and one short chromosome, but in different colour combinations. That is independent assortment, and it is built into meiosis I.

Meiosis I is reductional: the chromosome number halves because homologues separate.
Meiosis II is equational: the number stays at n; each chromosome loses its sister.
Mendel’s segregation happens in anaphase I (for a gene with no crossover between it and the centromere; crossovers are the next unit).


Have them fill in this table before showing it. The common mistake is to say a cell after meiosis I is “still diploid because it has 46 chromatids”. Ploidy counts chromosome sets, not DNA molecules. The last bullet is a small honesty note: if a crossover happens between a gene and its centromere, the two alleles are separated only in meiosis II. That matters for tetrad analysis in fungi, which we skip, and it is a hint that crossing over, next unit, complicates the simple picture.

title: Chromosome theory & sex linkage
text:
Meiosis makes variety
Independent orientation at metaphase I. Each homologue pair faces the poles at random, independently of the others. A gamete gets the father’s or the mother’s copy of each chromosome, ½ each:




Drosophila
Pea
Human




n

Combinations in a gamete, 2^n
16

8 388 608


Combinations in a zygote, (2^n)^2
256

≈ 7 × 1013



Crossing over in prophase I mixes the homologues within a chromosome and adds far more variety. It is the subject of the next unit, Linkage & recombination.
Ignoring crossovers, the probability that a human sperm carries the grandfather’s copy of all 23 chromosomes is ½ × ½ × … = (½)23 ≈ 1 in 8.4 million.

This is Mendel’s independent assortment seen from the chromosome side: 2 to the n gamete types is the same count as for n unlinked heterozygous genes in the Mendel unit. With 23 pairs the number of combinations is about 8.4 million per gamete and about 70 trillion per zygote, before crossing over. In the R exercise students simulate this with sample() and ask how much of a gamete comes from each grandparent: on average half, but with a wide spread when whole chromosomes are the unit of inheritance. Crossing over narrows that spread, which they meet in the next unit.

title: Chromosome theory & sex linkage
section: Try it: meiosis step by step
text:
Try it: meiosis step by step




Step through with the Next button. Blue chromosomes came from the father, red from the mother; long and short are two different chromosomes. Stop at metaphase I and press “flip orientation”: the gametes change from blue-long + red-short to blue-long + blue-short. That is the 2^n of the previous slide. Point out stage 2 (S phase): the count of chromosomes stays at 4 while chromatids double; and stage 6 (telophase I): two haploid cells whose chromosomes still have two chromatids. We come back to the two nondisjunction modes at the end of the lecture.

title: Chromosome theory & sex linkage
text:
The chromosome theory of inheritance
Around 1902–1903, Walter Sutton (grasshoppers) and Theodor Boveri (sea urchins) noticed that chromosomes in meiosis behave exactly as Mendel’s factors must:







Mendel’s factors
Chromosomes




come in pairs in the body
come in homologous pairs in diploid cells


the two members segregate into different gametes
homologues go to opposite poles in meiosis I


one of each pair in each gamete
gametes are haploid


different genes assort independently
different pairs orient independently at metaphase I


one set from each parent
one homologue from each parent



Chromosome theory of inheritance: genes are carried on chromosomes, and the behaviour of chromosomes in meiosis is the physical basis of Mendel’s laws.
A parallel is not a proof. The proof needed one gene whose inheritance follows one identifiable chromosome.

The parallel is striking, but it is correlation: two things that both come in pairs and both segregate. Sceptics, including Morgan himself at first, pointed out that there are many more genes than chromosomes, so genes could not each be a chromosome. The resolution, many genes per chromosome, leads straight to linkage in the next unit. What was needed was a chromosome you could recognise in the microscope, and a gene that went with it. The sex chromosomes provided both.

title: Chromosome theory & sex linkage
text:
Sex chromosomes

In many animals the two sexes differ in one chromosome pair. Human and Drosophila females are XX, males XY.
The X and Y are not true homologues: the Y is small and carries few genes. In humans X ≈ 156 Mb and Y ≈ 57 Mb (you look this up in the exercise).
Short pseudoautosomal regions at the tips of X and Y let them pair and segregate in male meiosis.
A male has only one X, so he is hemizygous for X-linked genes: one recessive allele is enough to show.
Every child gets an X from the mother. The father decides the sex: his sperm carry X or Y, ½ each, so sons and daughters are born 1 : 1.









Mother XX

Father XY




eggs: all X

sperm: ½ X, ½ Y


→ daughters XX get one X from each parent

→ sons XY get their X from the mother




The first part is the hemizygosity rule students already used in pedigrees; now we see its chromosomal basis. The X-Y pairing via the pseudoautosomal regions matters for two reasons: it is how the X and Y segregate from each other in meiosis I, and occasional abnormal crossing over there can move SRY onto an X, which explains some XX males (two slides on). The 1 to 1 sex ratio is a Mendelian testcross: XY times XX is like Aa times aa.

title: Chromosome theory & sex linkage
text:
Morgan’s white-eyed fly (1910)

Thomas Hunt Morgan found a white-eyed male in a culture of red-eyed flies. In the F2 only males were white. Explanation: the eye-colour gene w is on the X, and the Y carries no copy.

Walk through panel a. The F1 are all red, so white is recessive. In the F2, red to white is 3470 to 782, roughly 3 to 1 but with too few whites (we come back to that), and all the white flies are males. That is not what an autosomal gene does. With w on the X the Punnett square works: the F1 female is a carrier, X+Xw; the F1 male is X+Y. Half the F2 sons get Xw from the mother and are white; all F2 daughters get X+ from the father and are red. Panel b is the reciprocal cross: a white female times a red male gives red daughters and white sons, the criss-cross pattern. Reciprocal crosses that differ are the hallmark of sex linkage; Mendel’s reciprocal crosses gave the same result because his genes were autosomal. Morgan’s own data and the correct reference: Morgan 1910, Science 32:120-122.

title: Chromosome theory & sex linkage
text:
Do Morgan’s numbers fit 2 : 1 : 1?
The F2, under X-linkage: ½ red ♀ : ¼ red ♂ : ¼ white ♂. Morgan counted 4252 flies:

Expected

p is far below 0.001: the counts do not fit 2 : 1 : 1. But the pattern fits perfectly: no white females, white males only.
The deficit is in the white classes. In Morgan’s backcross (white ♂ × F1 ♀) the four classes should be 1 : 1 : 1 : 1, but he got 129 : 132 red to 88 : 86 white. White-eyed flies survive less well: reduced viability, as for the lethal alleles in Extensions to Mendel.

This is the chi-square test from Part 1 applied to a real historical data set; students repeat it in R. The expected values are 4252 times 1/2, 1/4, 1/4. With df = 2 the 5 percent critical value is 5.99; 129 is enormous. A good scientist does not throw out X-linkage here: the striking qualitative result, no white daughters at all among thousands, is exactly what X-linkage predicts and an autosomal gene cannot produce. The quantitative misfit has a separate cause, and the backcross shows it: both white classes, female and male, are short by about a third. That points to the white allele lowering survival to adulthood, not to a problem with the inheritance model. The lesson: a significant chi-square tells you the model is incomplete, not which part is wrong.

title: Chromosome theory & sex linkage
section: Bridges: exceptions that prove the rule
text:
Bridges: exceptions that prove the rule

Morgan’s student Calvin Bridges crossed white ♀ × red ♂. Rarely (well under 1 % of offspring) he found exceptional flies: white daughters and red sons. His explanation: the two X chromosomes of the mother occasionally fail to separate in meiosis, nondisjunction, giving XX and no-X (O) eggs.

The regular offspring show criss-cross inheritance: red daughters, white sons. The exceptions are the reverse. Bridges reasoned that a white daughter must have got both her X chromosomes from her white-eyed mother, and a Y from the father; a red son must have got his X from the father and no X from the mother. If that is right, the exceptional females must be XXY and the exceptional males XO. In flies the Y does not determine sex, so XXY is female and XO is male, sterile because the Y carries genes needed for sperm. The XXX and YO zygotes mostly die. The table is the Punnett square with the two abnormal egg types added. Try the nondisjunction mode of the demo: the n+1 and n-1 gametes are the XX and O eggs.

title: Chromosome theory & sex linkage
text:
Why nondisjunction was the proof
Bridges made a prediction about chromosomes from genetic data, then checked it in the microscope:

From the eye colours: exceptional white females should be XXY, exceptional red males XO.
Cytology: the exceptional females had two X chromosomes and a Y.
Further prediction: an XXY female has three sex chromosomes to share out, so she often makes XX and Y eggs. Her offspring should include exceptions at a much higher rate than an ordinary XX female’s (secondary nondisjunction). They did.

A gene’s inheritance followed one visible chromosome, even when that chromosome misbehaved. Genes are on chromosomes.
Bridges published this as the first paper of the first issue of the journal Genetics (Bridges 1916, Genetics 1:1–52).

The strength of the argument is that it links two independent kinds of evidence: breeding results and what you see down the microscope. Correlations can be coincidence; a successful prediction of an unusual chromosome set in exactly the unusual flies is not. Secondary nondisjunction: in an XXY female, the two Xs and the Y must segregate somehow, and sometimes both Xs go together, so the XXY female produces exceptional offspring far more often than a normal XX female. Keep this light: the main point is the logic. The reference is real: volume 1, issue 1, pages 1 to 52, with a continuation in issue 2. Nondisjunction in humans, and the trisomies it causes, is in Part 5.

title: Chromosome theory & sex linkage
text:
How is sex determined?

The sex with two different sex chromosomes is heterogametic: it makes two kinds of gamete, and so decides the sex of the offspring. Many reptiles and fish use temperature or other cues instead.

Four chromosomal systems. XY: mammals and Drosophila; the male is heterogametic. XO: grasshoppers and nematodes; the male simply has one fewer chromosome. ZW: birds, butterflies and moths, some reptiles; here the female is heterogametic, so in chickens it is the hen that decides the sex of the chicks. Haplodiploidy: bees, ants and wasps; males come from unfertilised eggs and are haploid, carrying only their mother’s chromosomes, coloured red here. Note that the same chromosome constitution can mean different things: XY in mammals and in flies looks the same but is read differently, which is the next slide.

title: Chromosome theory & sex linkage
section: SRY: the Y makes a male, in mammals
text:
SRY: the Y makes a male, in mammals








Karyotype
Human
Drosophila




XX
female
female


XY
male
male


XXY
male (Klinefelter syndrome)
female (Bridges’ exceptions)


XO
female (Turner syndrome)
male, sterile


Rule
a Y (with SRY) makes a male
the X : autosome ratio decides



Evidence that one Y gene, SRY (sex-determining region Y, on Yp11.2), is the switch:

XX men usually carry SRY, moved onto an X by an abnormal crossover in the father’s meiosis.
Some XY women carry a mutated or deleted SRY.
XX mice given an Sry transgene develop as males (1991).

SRY starts testis development; the testis hormones then make the body male. A mutation in the androgen receptor (AR, on the X) can give an XY person with testes but a female body (exercise, Find it).

The aneuploid karyotypes are the experiment. In humans one Y makes a male however many Xs there are, and no Y means female. In flies the Y is irrelevant for sex; what matters is the number of X chromosomes relative to the autosome sets. SRY was found in 1990 by mapping the smallest piece of Y present in XX males. The three lines of evidence are the classic genetic triad: the gene is present when the trait appears without the rest of the Y, its loss gives the opposite outcome, and adding it alone is enough. SRY encodes a transcription factor; that is development, Part 6. Androgen insensitivity is a nice example that sex development is a pathway: SRY works, testes form, but the body cannot respond to testosterone.

title: Chromosome theory & sex linkage
text:
X-linked inheritance by hand
Write X-linked genotypes with the allele on the X: XAXa, XaY. Then use the three rules:

A son gets his X from his mother, and his Y from his father.
A daughter gets one X from each parent; the father’s X goes to every daughter.
Males are hemizygous: XaY shows the recessive trait.

Example 1 (Drosophila): X+Xw ♀ × XwY ♂.




½ Xw (sperm)
½ Y (sperm)




½ X+
X+Xw red ♀
X+Y red ♂


½ Xw
XwXw white ♀
XwY white ♂



All four classes ¼ each: ½ of the daughters and ½ of the sons are white.
Example 2 (human haemophilia A, X-linked recessive): carrier mother × unaffected father → ½ of sons affected, ½ of daughters carriers, no affected daughters.

The trick for X-linked problems is to solve sons and daughters separately. Sons: it is all about the mother, because the father gives a Y. Daughters: they always get the father’s X, so look at his allele first, then add the mother’s. In example 1, the father is white, so every daughter gets Xw; whether she is white depends on the mother’s X, half and half. The sons get the mother’s X, half and half. This cross is the one Morgan used to show that white-eyed females exist and are viable. Example 2 is the same pattern students used in pedigrees for Duchenne and haemophilia. Note the notation: the allele symbol goes as a superscript on the X; Y carries no allele.

title: Chromosome theory & sex linkage
text:
Dosage compensation: a pointer
Females have two X chromosomes and males one. Why don’t females make twice as much of every X-linked gene product?



Organism
Solution




Mammals
one X in each female cell is inactivated (a Barr body)


Drosophila
males double transcription from their single X


C. elegans
XX hermaphrodites halve expression from each X



In mammals the choice of which X to silence is random in each early embryonic cell, so a heterozygous female is a mosaic. Calico and tortoiseshell cats are the classic example.
More in Part 6 (Eukaryotic gene regulation), with its own demo.

Only a pointer today. The point to make is that sex chromosomes create a dosage problem that the autosomes do not, and that different lineages have solved it in opposite ways. X inactivation also explains why female carriers of X-linked diseases can show mild symptoms: in some tissues, by chance, most cells may have silenced the normal X. The mechanism (the XIST RNA, chromatin modification) belongs to gene regulation in Part 6.

title: Chromosome theory & sex linkage
text:
Try it: nondisjunction




The demo starts at metaphase I in the nondisjunction mode. Step to the gametes: all four are abnormal, two n+1 and two n-1, and the n+1 gametes carry one father’s and one mother’s copy. Then switch to nondisjunction in MII and step again: two gametes are normal, one n+1 with two identical (same colour) copies, one n-1. Link to Bridges: an XX egg is an n+1 gamete for the X; an O egg is n-1. In humans, the same error for chromosome 21 gives Down syndrome; whether it happened in meiosis I or II can be read from DNA markers, because MI errors give two different parental copies. That is Part 5.

text:

homologues: one from each parent; sisters: identical copies after S phase

2^n gamete combinations; 223 ≈ 8.4 million in humans

Sex determination
XY (SRY in mammals; X : A ratio in flies), XO, ZW, haplodiploidy

Dosage compensation
X inactivation in mammals (Part 6)




The two things to take away: the chromosome mechanics of meiosis (which division separates what) and the logic of the proof (a gene that follows a visible chromosome, even in its exceptions). The rest is applying them: X-linked crosses by hand and the sex-determination systems.

title: Chromosome theory & sex linkage
text:
Where this leads

Next: Linkage & recombination. There are many more genes than chromosomes, so genes share chromosomes. Genes on one chromosome do not assort independently, except when crossing over separates them, and how often that happens measures the distance between them.
Three-point crosses and Human linkage & LOD scores turn this into maps.
Part 5: Rearrangements & aneuploidy. Nondisjunction in humans: trisomy 21, XXY and XO, using the same demo.
Part 6: Eukaryotic gene regulation. X inactivation and dosage compensation.


The exercise has by-hand X-linked crosses and nondisjunction problems, the meiosis demo, database tasks (the karyotype in Ensembl, SRY in NCBI Gene, X-linked diseases in MedGen and OMIM) and an R page where students count gamete combinations, simulate how much of a gamete comes from each grandparent, and test Morgan’s counts with chi-square.

text:
Before you start
This page builds on the by-hand part of the Exercise, so do that first. You need the packages dplyr, ggplot2 and readr. Download two data files and save them in a data/ folder of your R project:

morgan1910.csv: Morgan’s counts from Science 32:120–122 (1910), PMID 17759620. Real data.
human_chromosomes.csv: the lengths of the human chromosomes, from the Ensembl REST API (assembly GRCh38.p14, retrieved 2026-11-20). Real data.

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(readr)

title: Exercise in R: chromosome theory & sex linkage
text:
Tasks
There is no new R idiom on this page. You reuse three from Part 1: a small function of your own (Mendel), sample() and replicate() for simulation (Probability & the χ² test), and chisq.test(). The new thing is to apply them to chromosomes instead of single genes.
R1. (\(2^n\)) Make a tibble with the haploid chromosome number n of Drosophila (4), the garden pea (7) and humans (23). Add columns with the number of different combinations of grandparental chromosomes in a gamete, \(2^n\), and in a zygote, \((2^n)^2\). What is the probability that a human gamete carries the grandfather’s copy of all 23 chromosomes, or the grandmother’s copy of all 23?
species <- tibble(
  species = c("Drosophila melanogaster", "garden pea", "human"),
  n       = c(4, 7, 23)
)
species |>
  mutate(gametes = 2^n,
         zygotes = gametes^2)
2^23
1 / 2^22
R2. (one sperm) A man got one copy of each chromosome from his father (the child’s grandfather) and one from his mother (the grandmother). Ignoring crossing over, each of the 23 chromosomes in one of his sperm comes from the grandfather or the grandmother with probability ½, independently. Write a function one_gamete(n_pairs = 23) that returns 23 random draws of "grandfather" or "grandmother". Run it once and compute the fraction of chromosomes from the grandfather.
(The n_pairs = 23 gives the argument a default value, so one_gamete() means one_gamete(23). Default arguments are the new idiom of the next unit; here you just use one.)
one_gamete <- function(n_pairs = 23) {
  sample(c("grandfather", "grandmother"), n_pairs, replace = TRUE)
}
set.seed(1)
g <- one_gamete()
g
table(g)
mean(g == "grandfather")
R3. (10 000 sperm) Use replicate() to compute the fraction from the grandfather in 10 000 simulated sperm. What are the mean and the standard deviation? What fraction of sperm carry between 40 % and 60 % grandfather chromosomes? Did any sperm carry chromosomes from only one grandparent? Plot a histogram.
set.seed(2)
frac_gf <- replicate(10000, mean(one_gamete() == "grandfather"))
summary(frac_gf)
sd(frac_gf)
mean(frac_gf == 0 | frac_gf == 1)
mean(frac_gf >= 0.4 & frac_gf <= 0.6)

ggplot(tibble(frac = frac_gf), aes(x = frac)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1/23, boundary = -0.5/23, fill = "grey70", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "fraction of chromosomes from the grandfather",
       y = "number of gametes",
       title = "10 000 simulated sperm, 23 chromosomes, no crossing over") +
  theme_minimal()
Compare the standard deviation with the binomial formula \(\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\) with p = ½ and n = 23.
R4. (weighted by length) Chromosomes differ in size, so the fraction of DNA from the grandfather is not the same as the fraction of chromosomes. Read human_chromosomes.csv, keep the 22 autosomes, and simulate the fraction of autosomal DNA (in base pairs) from the grandfather in 10 000 sperm. Is the spread larger or smaller than in R3? Why?
chrom <- read_csv("data/human_chromosomes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
autosomes <- chrom |> filter(!chromosome %in% c("X", "Y"))
nrow(autosomes)
autosomes |> summarise(total_Mb = sum(length_bp) / 1e6,
                       longest_Mb = max(length_bp) / 1e6,
                       shortest_Mb = min(length_bp) / 1e6)
L <- autosomes$length_bp
dna_frac <- function() {
  from_gf <- one_gamete(22) == "grandfather"
  sum(L[from_gf]) / sum(L)
}
set.seed(3)
dna_gf <- replicate(10000, dna_frac())
summary(dna_gf)
sd(dna_gf)
R5. (Morgan’s F2) Read morgan1910.csv. Test Morgan’s F2 (F1 × F1) against the X-linked expectation ½ red ♀ : ¼ red ♂ : ¼ white ♂, and check the expected counts. Leave out the row with 0 white females (an X-linked gene predicts none). Then test the males alone against 1 : 1, and compute the fraction of white among the males.
morgan <- read_csv("data/morgan1910.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
f2 <- morgan |> filter(cross == "F1 x F1", n > 0)
f2 |> select(sex, eye, n)
chisq.test(f2$n, p = c(2, 1, 1) / 4)
chisq.test(f2$n, p = c(2, 1, 1) / 4)$expected
males <- f2 |> filter(sex == "male")
chisq.test(males$n, p = c(1, 1) / 2)
f2 |> summarise(white_share_of_males = n[eye == "white"] / sum(n[sex == "male"]))
R6. (Morgan’s backcross) Morgan also crossed his original white male with F1 daughters. Test the four classes against 1 : 1 : 1 : 1. Then add up red and white across the sexes and test 1 : 1. Together with R5, what is the most likely reason that the F2 does not fit 2 : 1 : 1?
bc <- morgan |> filter(cross == "white male x F1 female")
bc |> select(sex, eye, n)
chisq.test(bc$n, p = rep(1, 4) / 4)
bc |> group_by(eye) |> summarise(n = sum(n))
chisq.test(c(red = 129 + 132, white = 88 + 86), p = c(1, 1) / 2)

title: Exercise in R: chromosome theory & sex linkage
text:
Where this leads
In R2–R4 every chromosome was inherited whole, from one grandparent or the other. In Linkage & recombination crossing over breaks that: you write functions that convert between recombination frequency and map distance, with a default argument method = "haldane", and plot them with map_dbl().

title: Cancer genetics
text:
About this lecture
Cancer is a genetic disease of somatic cells: a clone of cells that has collected mutations which let it divide when it should not.

Two kinds of cancer gene: oncogenes (gain of function, dominant at the cell level) and tumour suppressors (loss of function, recessive at the cell level).
Knudson’s two-hit hypothesis, from the ages at which children get retinoblastoma.
Loss of heterozygosity, and why a “recessive” cancer gene is inherited as a dominant predisposition (BRCA1/2).
Mutator phenotypes, clonal evolution, and driver vs passenger mutations.
The Philadelphia chromosome and imatinib: from a chromosome to a drug.

You already know dominance, penetrance and pedigrees from Part 1, mutation types from Part 3, and translocations from Part 5. Book: Hartwell, the chapter on the genetics of cancer.

The one idea to carry through the lecture: everything they have learnt about alleles in families also happens inside one body, among cells. A tumour is a population of cells, and the rules of dominance and recessiveness apply cell by cell. Oncogenes behave like dominant gain-of-function alleles; tumour suppressors like recessive loss-of-function alleles. The twist is that an inherited, cell-level recessive allele appears dominant in a pedigree. Knudson’s argument is the centrepiece, and it is a lovely example of inferring a mechanism from a simple count of ages. The lecture ends with a link to population genetics: a tumour evolves by mutation and selection, which is the topic of the next two units.

title: Cancer genetics
section: Cancer is a genetic disease, but mostly not inherited
text:
Cancer is a genetic disease, but mostly not inherited

A tumour is a clone: all its cells descend from one cell that escaped normal control of division.
The mutations that drive it are mostly somatic: they arise in that cell lineage during life and are not passed to children.
A minority of cancers (roughly 5–10%) arise in people with an inherited predisposing allele. These families give us the cancer genes.
Most cancers are diseases of old age: a cell must collect several mutations, and that takes time.










Germline mutation
Somatic mutation




In which cells
every cell, including gametes
one cell and its descendants


Passed to children
yes
no


Example
inherited RB1 allele
KRAS G12 in a colon polyp




Start by separating two meanings of “genetic”. Cancer is genetic because it is caused by changes in DNA. But almost all of those changes are somatic: they happen in one cell during life, through replication errors and mutagens such as UV light or tobacco smoke. A tumour is the clone of that cell. The germline, inherited, cases are rare but important for two reasons: they are the patients with the highest risk, and their families let geneticists map the genes. The rise of cancer incidence with age is the first hint that several hits are needed, which is exactly the argument Knudson made for retinoblastoma. The 5 to 10 percent is a commonly quoted rough figure; it varies by cancer type.

title: Cancer genetics
text:
Accelerators and brakes


Proto-oncogenes promote division when the cell is told to (growth-factor receptors, RAS, MYC). A gain-of-function mutation makes an oncogene: one mutant allele is enough, so it is dominant at the cell level.
Tumour suppressors stop division or kill damaged cells (RB1, TP53, APC). A cell becomes abnormal only when both copies are lost: recessive at the cell level.


The car analogy is old but works: an oncogene is a stuck accelerator, a tumour suppressor is a broken brake. Connect to Part 1. A gain-of-function allele is dominant because the one overactive copy does its job regardless of the normal copy; this is the same logic as a dominant gain-of-function disease allele. A loss-of-function allele in a tumour suppressor is recessive at the cell level because one working copy still provides the brake; this is the haplosufficiency argument from the extensions-to-Mendel unit. Most cancers need hits in both kinds of gene. Stress “at the cell level”: we will see that at the level of the pedigree, a tumour suppressor allele looks dominant.

title: Cancer genetics
section: How a proto-oncogene becomes an oncogene
text:
How a proto-oncogene becomes an oncogene
Three routes, all gain of function:

Point mutation that locks the protein on. KRAS codon 12 (G12V, G12D): RAS can no longer switch itself off, so it signals all the time.
Amplification: many copies of a normal gene, so too much protein. ERBB2 (HER2) in some breast cancers; MYC in some neuroblastomas (MYCN).
Translocation that puts a gene under a strong promoter, or fuses two genes. BCR–ABL1 in chronic myeloid leukaemia (end of this lecture).

Each needs only one allele, which is why oncogenes are rarely inherited: an always-on allele in every cell is usually lethal to the embryo.

Each route connects to an earlier part. Point mutations are Part 3. Amplification and translocation are the chromosome rearrangements of Part 5. RAS is a small GTPase: it is on when GTP is bound and turns itself off by hydrolysing GTP to GDP; the codon 12 mutations block that hydrolysis, so the switch sticks in the on position. Amplification is visible in tumour karyotypes and in copy-number data. The last point is a nice question for students: why are inherited cancer genes mostly tumour suppressors? Because a germline loss-of-function allele in a tumour suppressor is harmless in most cells as long as the second copy works, while a germline oncogene would be active everywhere from the start. There are exceptions, such as RET in multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2, but they are few.

title: Cancer genetics
section: Retinoblastoma: two forms of one cancer
text:
Retinoblastoma: two forms of one cancer
Retinoblastoma is a tumour of the developing retina, in young children.




Hereditary (about 40%)
Sporadic (about 60%)




Family history
often; autosomal dominant pattern
no


Eyes
usually both (bilateral)
one (unilateral)


Tumours
often several
one


Age at diagnosis
earlier
later



In 1971 Alfred Knudson asked: what single model explains all four rows?

This table is the observation that Knudson started from. The percentages are approximate and vary between sources; the qualitative pattern is what matters. Hereditary cases are bilateral and multifocal and diagnosed early; sporadic cases are unilateral, single, and diagnosed later. Ask the class to propose a model before the next slide. A good prompt: if the hereditary children inherited something, what did they inherit that makes tumours both more numerous and earlier? Retinoblasts divide only during early childhood; once they stop dividing, no new tumours form, which is why retinoblastoma is a disease of young children.

title: Cancer genetics
text:
Knudson’s two-hit hypothesis


A retinal cell becomes a tumour only when both alleles of one gene are lost: two hits. The gene is RB1, on 13q14.
Hereditary: hit 1 is in the germline, so every retinal cell already has it. One more hit in any of millions of cells is likely: many tumours, both eyes, early.
Sporadic: both hits must strike the same cell by chance. That is rare: one tumour, one eye, later.


Walk through the figure row by row. In the hereditary row the fertilised egg already carries one mutant allele, so after many divisions every retinal cell has it. Each of these cells needs only one more event, and there are about a million retinoblasts, so several cells will get their second hit: hence several tumours, often in both eyes, and early. In the sporadic row every cell starts with two good copies. A tumour needs the same cell to be hit twice, which is so unlikely that it typically happens once, in one eye, if at all. Knudson proposed this before the gene was known; RB1 was cloned in the 1980s, and its protein, pRB, turned out to be a brake on the cell cycle at the G1 to S transition.

title: Cancer genetics
section: Knudson’s argument from the ages at diagnosis
text:
Knudson’s argument from the ages at diagnosis


One hit needed: risk by age t ≈ n·u·t, linear in age. Two hits needed: ≈ n·(u·t)², quadratic. On log–log axes the slope counts the hits (a).
Knudson plotted the fraction of cases not yet diagnosed on a log scale (b). Bilateral cases fell on a straight line, as for a single event at a constant rate; unilateral cases did not.


This is the quantitative core. Use the symbols: n cells at risk, u the hit rate per allele per year. If one hit is still needed, the chance that one cell is hit by age t is about u times t, and there are n cells, so about n u t. If two hits are needed, each has probability u t and both must happen in the same cell, so about n times u t squared. A quadratic curve starts flat, which is why sporadic tumours appear later. Panel b is Knudson’s own kind of plot. If tumours start at a constant rate, the fraction still undiagnosed falls by the same factor each year, like radioactive decay, which is a straight line on a log scale. That is what he saw for bilateral cases. The curves here come from the same model as the demo, with exaggerated rates; in reality the rates are far lower and the cells far more numerous.

title: Cancer genetics
text:
Demo: two hits




Default settings: 200 lineages per child, hit rate 0.0015 per allele per year. Point at the table: about 94 percent of carriers get a tumour by age 10, with about 3 tumours each and two thirds bilateral; about 5 percent of non-carriers get one, almost always a single tumour in one eye. Switch to the log–log view and show the slopes 1 and 2. Then press “rarer hits”: the carrier risk halves, the sporadic risk falls about four-fold, because it depends on u squared. Point out that about 6 percent of carriers never get a tumour: incomplete penetrance from pure chance. Finally Knudson’s plot.

title: Cancer genetics
text:
Loss of heterozygosity


In a carrier, the second hit is often not a new point mutation but the loss of the normal allele, together with a stretch of chromosome around it.
Markers near the gene are heterozygous in blood but homozygous in the tumour: loss of heterozygosity (LOH).
A region with frequent LOH in tumours is a hint that it contains a tumour suppressor. RB1 and many other genes were found this way.


Three ways to lose the normal copy: an interstitial deletion, mitotic recombination proximal to the gene so that the distal part becomes homozygous for the mutant chromosome, or loss of the whole normal chromosome followed by duplication of the mutant one. In all three, polymorphic markers near the gene lose one allele in tumour DNA compared with blood DNA. This links to Part 2 and Part 4: markers are the same kind of polymorphism used for linkage mapping, and today SNP arrays and sequencing show LOH genome-wide. Ask: which allele is lost? Always the normal one, from the parent without the mutation, because only cells that lost the normal allele become tumours. That is selection at the cell level.

title: Cancer genetics
section: Recessive in the cell, dominant in the pedigree
text:
Recessive in the cell, dominant in the pedigree
A retinoblastoma family looks autosomal dominant: about ½ of the children of a carrier are affected, in every generation. Yet the allele is recessive in each cell. Both are true:

What is inherited is a predisposition, a first hit in every cell.
The second hit is so likely in a carrier that most carriers are affected. Some carriers get no tumour: incomplete penetrance (recap: Extensions to Mendel), and the pedigree then skips a generation.
Inherited breast and ovarian cancer works the same way: germline BRCA1 (17q21.31) or BRCA2 (13q13.1), with LOH of the normal allele in the tumour. Lifetime risk is high, but not 100%.


This slide resolves the apparent paradox that confuses many students. Dominant and recessive describe phenotypes at a level. At the level of the person, the phenotype is “gets retinoblastoma”, and a heterozygote usually does: dominant, with high but incomplete penetrance. At the level of the cell, the phenotype is “divides uncontrollably”, and a heterozygous cell does not: recessive. Link to the pedigrees unit: incomplete penetrance makes a dominant trait skip a generation, and an unaffected obligate carrier between two affected relatives is the giveaway. BRCA1 and BRCA2 are the commonest example in adults. Their penetrance is high but varies between studies and families; avoid quoting a single number without a source.

title: Cancer genetics
text:
Caretakers and the mutator phenotype
Some tumour suppressors do not control division directly. They repair DNA, so losing them raises the mutation rate of the cell: a mutator phenotype.

Mismatch repair (MLH1, MSH2): replication errors are not fixed. Inherited loss gives Lynch syndrome (colorectal and endometrial cancer); tumours carry thousands of small mutations.
Homologous recombination (BRCA1, BRCA2): double-strand breaks are repaired by error-prone routes, giving rearrangements.
TP53, “guardian of the genome”: senses DNA damage and stops the cell cycle or triggers apoptosis. It is the most frequently mutated gene in human cancer.

A mutator phenotype does not cause cancer itself; it speeds up the collection of the other hits.

Distinguish gatekeepers, which control division directly, such as RB1 and APC, from caretakers, which keep the genome intact, such as the mismatch repair genes and BRCA1 and 2. Losing a caretaker multiplies the hit rate u in Knudson’s model, so every later step happens faster. Link to Part 3: the mutation unit covered mismatch repair and recombination repair; here we see what happens when they fail. TP53 sits in between: it does not repair DNA itself, but it decides whether a damaged cell may go on dividing. Its loss lets cells with damaged genomes survive. In the Find it task students will see in cBioPortal how often TP53 is mutated.

title: Cancer genetics
text:
Clonal evolution: drivers and passengers


Each driver mutation gives its cell a growth advantage, so its descendants take over: selection among cells. The colorectal sequence APC → KRAS → TP53 is the classic example.
Passenger mutations happen by chance in the same cells and are carried along. They have no effect, but they are the majority of mutations in a tumour.
So a tumour evolves: mutation, selection and drift in a population of cells. This is the topic of the next two units.


A fish plot shows the fraction of cells in each clone over time. Every clone starts as one cell with a new driver mutation and expands because it divides faster or dies less. Most new clones without a driver, like the small green one, stay small or vanish. Drivers can be recognised in sequencing data because they recur across many patients and cluster at specific codons, such as KRAS codon 12 or TP53 R175. Passengers are scattered randomly. The order APC, KRAS, TP53 for colorectal cancer comes from Fearon and Vogelstein’s comparison of polyps of increasing size with carcinomas; real tumours vary. Clonal evolution also explains drug resistance: a pre-existing subclone with a resistance mutation is selected by the treatment.

title: Cancer genetics
text:
The Philadelphia chromosome


In chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) a small chromosome 22 was seen in 1960 (Nowell and Hungerford, Philadelphia). It is a reciprocal translocation t(9;22)(q34;q11).
The join fuses BCR (22q11.23) to ABL1 (9q34.12): a BCR–ABL1 tyrosine kinase that is always on.
Imatinib blocks the ATP pocket of the kinase. It turned CML from a fatal disease into a manageable one: the first big success of a drug designed against a cancer’s driver.


This is the first chromosome abnormality tied to a specific cancer, found by looking at karyotypes, which connects to rearrangements in Part 5. The translocation is reciprocal, but the important product is the der(22), the Philadelphia chromosome, carrying the fusion gene under the BCR promoter. ABL1 is a tyrosine kinase that is normally tightly controlled; the BCR part makes it dimerise and stay active. Imatinib, approved around 2001, binds the kinase’s ATP-binding site in its inactive form. Its success depends on CML being driven by one fusion. Resistance arises through point mutations in the kinase domain, which is clonal evolution again, and second-generation drugs target those. The chromosome bands are the cytogenetic locations listed in NCBI Gene.

title: Cancer genetics
text:
Cancer genomes in public databases
Tumours are sequenced by the thousand. You can browse the results without writing code:

cBioPortal (cbioportal.org): mutations, copy number and survival for public studies such as TCGA PanCancer Atlas. A lollipop plot shows where in the protein the mutations fall.
COSMIC Cancer Gene Census (Sanger, free registration) and OncoKB (MSK): which genes are cancer genes, and whether each acts as an oncogene or a tumour suppressor (TSG).
The pattern tells you the role: oncogenes have hotspots (the same codon in many tumours, KRAS G12); tumour suppressors have truncating mutations spread along the gene, plus some hotspots (TP53 R175H).


This is the bioinformatics thread for the unit. In TCGA ovarian serous carcinoma most samples carry a TP53 mutation; in breast cancer about a third do. The lollipop plot is a quick way to classify a gene: a few tall lollipops at the same position mean selection for a specific gain of function; many nonsense and frameshift mutations spread along the gene mean selection for loss of function. TP53 is unusual because its common missense hotspots, such as R175H and R273H, also act dominant-negatively on the remaining normal protein. In the exercise students find the TP53 hotspots in cBioPortal and check the gene’s role in OncoKB.

title: Cancer genetics
text:
Summary

Cancer is a clone of cells with somatic mutations; a minority of patients carry an inherited first hit.
Oncogenes: gain of function, one allele enough (dominant at the cell level). Tumour suppressors: loss of function, both alleles (recessive at the cell level).
Knudson: hereditary retinoblastoma needs one more hit (early, bilateral, multiple, risk ∝ age); sporadic needs two in one cell (late, unilateral, single, risk ∝ age²).
The second hit is often loss of heterozygosity. An inherited cell-recessive allele gives a dominant predisposition with incomplete penetrance (RB1, BRCA1/2).
Mutator phenotypes raise the hit rate; clonal evolution selects drivers; passengers come along.
t(9;22) makes BCR–ABL1; imatinib targets it.


Go back to the four rows of the retinoblastoma table and ask the class to explain each with the two-hit model. Then ask them to place each gene from the lecture in one of two columns, oncogene or tumour suppressor, and to name the type of mutation that activates or inactivates it.

title: Cancer genetics
text:
Where this leads

Next: Hardy–Weinberg and Drift, selection treat allele frequencies in populations of people. A tumour is a population of cells that evolves by the same rules: mutation, selection, drift.
Part 1 links: penetrance and pedigrees explain why cancer predisposition looks dominant.
Ethics: predictive testing for BRCA1/2 and other cancer genes, and what a positive result means for relatives.
In the exercise: two-hit problems by hand, the demo, RB1 in NCBI Gene, TP53 in cBioPortal and OncoKB, and the two-hit model in R.


The bridge to the next units is explicit: mutation creates variation, selection favours some variants, and drift adds chance. These are exactly the forces of population genetics, applied to cells rather than people. Predictive testing comes back in the ethics module: a BRCA1 result in one person is also information about their siblings and children.

title: Exercise in R: cancer genetics
Exercise in R: cancer genetics
Exercise in R: cancer genetics
text:
Before you start
This page builds on the by-hand part of the Exercise, so do that first. You need the packages dplyr, purrr, readr and ggplot2. Download tp53_tcga_mutations.csv and save it in a data/ folder of your R project.
The file lists every TP53 mutation in three TCGA PanCancer Atlas studies on cBioPortal (ov_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018, brca_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018 and coadread_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018), downloaded through the cBioPortal API in November 2026. The column n_sequenced gives the number of samples with mutation data in each study.

title: Exercise in R: cancer genetics
text:
Tasks
No new idiom today: we reuse rbinom from the pedigrees unit and map_dbl from Extensions to Mendel. The trick is that rbinom(n_people, size = n_cells, prob = p) gives, in one call, the number of tumour lineages in each of n_people people, each with n_cells independent cell lineages. Use the same model as the demo: 200 lineages per child and a hit rate u = 0.0015 per allele per year.
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)

The two-hit model
R1. The probability that a given allele in one lineage has been hit by age t is 1 − (1 − u)t: one minus the chance of escaping every year. Write it as a function p_hit(age, u). Compute it for ages 1, 5 and 10. What is the chance that both alleles of one lineage have been hit by age 10?
u <- 0.0015      # hit rate per allele per year
n_cells <- 200   # cell lineages at risk per person
p_hit <- function(age, u) 1 - (1 - u)^age
p_hit(c(1, 5, 10), u)
p_hit(10, u)^2
R2. Simulate 1000 carriers of an inherited first hit (each lineage needs one more hit) and 1000 non-carriers (each lineage needs two), at age 10. What fraction of each group has at least one tumour? How many tumours does an affected person have on average? Tabulate the number of tumours per person. Compare with the demo’s table.
set.seed(1)
n_people <- 1000
carrier  <- rbinom(n_people, size = n_cells, prob = p_hit(10, u))
sporadic <- rbinom(n_people, size = n_cells, prob = p_hit(10, u)^2)
head(carrier, 10)
head(sporadic, 10)
mean(carrier > 0)
mean(sporadic > 0)
mean(carrier[carrier > 0])
mean(sporadic[sporadic > 0])
table(carrier)
table(sporadic)
R3. Write a function frac_affected(age, hits_needed) that simulates 1000 people at a given age and returns the fraction with at least one tumour. Use map_dbl to compute it for ages 1 to 20 in both groups, collect the results in one tibble, and plot the two incidence curves.
frac_affected <- function(age, hits_needed, n_people = 1000) {
  p_cell <- p_hit(age, u)^hits_needed
  tumours <- rbinom(n_people, size = n_cells, prob = p_cell)
  mean(tumours > 0)
}
set.seed(2)
ages <- 1:20
onset <- bind_rows(
  tibble(age = ages, group = "inherited first hit",
         frac = map_dbl(ages, \(a) frac_affected(a, hits_needed = 1))),
  tibble(age = ages, group = "sporadic",
         frac = map_dbl(ages, \(a) frac_affected(a, hits_needed = 2)))
)
onset |> filter(age %in% c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20))

ggplot(onset, aes(age, frac, colour = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point() +
  labs(x = "age (years)", y = "fraction with at least one tumour", colour = NULL,
       title = "Two-hit model: 200 lineages, u = 0.0015 per allele per year")


Counting hits from the shape of the curve
R4. If k hits are needed, the mean number of tumours per person grows as agek. Taking logs, log(tumours) = constant + k · log(age): a straight line whose slope is the number of hits. Simulate the mean number of tumours per person (100 000 people, so that the rare sporadic tumours are counted well) at ages 1, 2, 5, 10 and 20. Fit lm(log10(tumours) ~ log10(age)) to each group and read the slopes. Plot both on log–log axes.
mean_tumours <- function(age, hits_needed, n_people = 1e5) {
  p_cell <- p_hit(age, u)^hits_needed
  mean(rbinom(n_people, size = n_cells, prob = p_cell))
}
set.seed(3)
ages4 <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20)
counts <- bind_rows(
  tibble(age = ages4, group = "inherited first hit",
         tumours = map_dbl(ages4, \(a) mean_tumours(a, hits_needed = 1))),
  tibble(age = ages4, group = "sporadic",
         tumours = map_dbl(ages4, \(a) mean_tumours(a, hits_needed = 2)))
)
counts
coef(lm(log10(tumours) ~ log10(age), data = filter(counts, group == "inherited first hit")))
coef(lm(log10(tumours) ~ log10(age), data = filter(counts, group == "sporadic")))

ggplot(counts, aes(age, tumours, colour = group)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, formula = y ~ x) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "age (years, log scale)", y = "mean tumours per person (log scale)", colour = NULL)
R5. (Knudson’s test) Knudson (1971) did not count tumours. He plotted the log of the fraction of bilateral cases not yet diagnosed against age, and found a straight line, as expected for a single event at a constant rate. For the carriers from R3 (ages 1 to 10), compute still_free = 1 - frac and fit lm(log(still_free) ~ age). Compare the slope with −n·u. Why should they agree?
inherited <- onset |>
  filter(group == "inherited first hit", age <= 10) |>
  mutate(still_free = 1 - frac)
fit_k <- lm(log(still_free) ~ age, data = inherited)
coef(fit_k)
-n_cells * u
R6. (two eyes) Split the 200 lineages into two eyes of 100 and simulate each eye with its own rbinom call at age 10. Among affected carriers, what fraction have tumours in both eyes? How many bilateral cases are there among 1000 non-carriers?
set.seed(4)
left  <- rbinom(n_people, size = n_cells / 2, prob = p_hit(10, u))
right <- rbinom(n_people, size = n_cells / 2, prob = p_hit(10, u))
affected <- (left + right) > 0
mean(affected)
mean(left > 0 & right > 0) / mean(affected)
left_s  <- rbinom(n_people, size = n_cells / 2, prob = p_hit(10, u)^2)
right_s <- rbinom(n_people, size = n_cells / 2, prob = p_hit(10, u)^2)
mean((left_s + right_s) > 0)
sum(left_s > 0 & right_s > 0)


Real tumours: TP53 in cBioPortal
R7. Read data/tp53_tcga_mutations.csv. For each study, compute the fraction of sequenced samples that carry at least one TP53 mutation (use n_distinct on sample_id; one sample can have two mutations). Then count the mutation types and the five most frequent protein changes over all three studies. Make a bar chart of mutation types, coloured by study. Do these numbers match what you found in cBioPortal (F3 in the exercise)? Is the pattern typical of an oncogene or of a tumour suppressor?
tp53 <- read_csv("data/tp53_tcga_mutations.csv")
tp53 |>
  group_by(study) |>
  summarise(n_sequenced = first(n_sequenced),
            n_mutated = n_distinct(sample_id),
            frac_mutated = n_mutated / n_sequenced)
tp53 |> count(mutation_type, sort = TRUE)
tp53 |> count(protein_change, sort = TRUE) |> head(5)

tp53 |>
  count(study, mutation_type) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = reorder(mutation_type, n), fill = study)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "number of mutations", y = NULL, fill = NULL,
       title = "TP53 mutations in three TCGA PanCancer Atlas studies") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.direction = "vertical")

The missense hotspots are the twist: these mutant proteins also block the remaining normal p53, so they are selected more strongly than a simple null allele.
