Where this leads
rbinom with a large size counts rare events in many independent units: cells here, gene copies in the next units. In Drift, selection the same function draws the next generation of a whole population, inside a loop.

title: Bacterial genetics (recap)
text:
About this lecture
Recap of 5MO103 (Microbiology and basic molecular biology). There you met the three ways bacteria exchange DNA. Today we look at them through the lens of genetics: how they were used to map genes on the bacterial chromosome, and which mutations made that possible.

Bacterial mutants: auxotrophs, resistance markers, replica plating; selection vs screening.
Conjugation: F+, Hfr and F′ strains.
Interrupted mating: a map in minutes, and why it is circular.
Minutes vs base pairs: the E. coli map against the genome sequence.
Transduction and cotransduction: fine mapping.
Transformation, and what each method is still used for.

Book: Hartwell, Genetics: From Genes to Genomes, the bacterial genetics chapter.

This is a short recap unit, so keep the pace up. Students have seen conjugation, transformation and transduction as biology in 5MO103: how DNA gets into a bacterial cell. The new angle is genetic: each mechanism is a way to do a “cross” in an organism that has no meiosis, and the genetic map of E. coli was built with exactly these tools in the 1950s and 1960s. The R exercise then checks that classical map against the genome sequence. Name the earlier course explicitly so students know they are expected to remember the basics.

title: Bacterial genetics (recap)
section: Why bacteria are good for genetics
text:
Why bacteria are good for genetics







Property
Why it helps




Haploid: one copy of each gene
every mutation shows its phenotype at once; no dominance to worry about


Fast: a generation in ~20–30 min
many generations overnight


Huge numbers: ~109 cells per ml
events at 1 in 107 can be found, if you can select them


Grow on defined media
phenotypes are read as “grows / does not grow”



Notation. Genes are three lower-case italic letters plus a capital: lacZ, trpA. A phenotype or marker is written with a superscript: lac+ (can use lactose), lac− (cannot), strr (streptomycin resistant), strs (sensitive). A strain that needs a nutrient, such as Trp−, is an auxotroph; the wild type, which grows on minimal medium, is a prototroph.

Haploidy is the key difference from everything in Parts 1 and 2: a recessive mutation is not hidden by a second copy. The numbers are the second key: with a billion cells on a plate, a recombinant that occurs once in ten million cells is still found, but only if the plate kills or starves everyone else. That is why bacterial genetics is the genetics of selection. Spend a moment on notation, because the exercise uses it: lacZ is the gene, lac+ and lac− are phenotypes or alleles, and r and s mean resistant and sensitive.

title: Bacterial genetics (recap)
section: Mutants: selection, screening and replica plating
text:
Mutants: selection, screening and replica plating

Selection: only the wanted cells grow. Minimal medium without threonine selects Thr+ cells; streptomycin selects strr cells.
Screening: everyone grows, but you can see the wanted ones. On X-gal plates, lac+ colonies are blue and lac− colonies white.
Replica plating (Lederbergs, 1952): press a velvet onto a master plate of colonies, then onto several test plates. A colony that grows on complete medium but not on minimal medium is an auxotroph.

Replica plating also showed that resistance mutations (to phage T1, for example) exist before the selection: the same colony positions were resistant on every replica. Selection finds mutants; it does not cause them (Luria and Delbrück had shown the same with the fluctuation test, 1943).

These are the tools that make every mapping experiment possible. A bacterial cross always ends on a selective plate: we kill the donor and select recipients that gained a donor marker. Replica plating lets us then score unselected markers on many colonies at once. The historical point is worth one sentence, because students often hold the Lamarckian intuition that antibiotics “cause” resistance: Luria and Delbrück, and then the Lederbergs, showed that the resistant mutants were already there. This links back to the Mutation unit in Part 3.

title: Bacterial genetics (recap)
section: Three ways DNA moves between bacteria
text:
Three ways DNA moves between bacteria










Transformation
Conjugation
Transduction




DNA travels as
naked DNA from the medium
DNA copied through a mating bridge
DNA packed in a phage head


Needs
a competent recipient
an F+, Hfr or F′ donor, and contact
a phage that sometimes packs host DNA (P1, P22)


How much DNA
small pieces, a few to ~20 kb
up to the whole chromosome (~100 min)
about one phage genome (P1: ~100 kb ≈ 2 min)


Mapping use
cotransformation of close genes
gene order and long distances (minutes)
fine mapping by cotransduction



In all three, a donor fragment only becomes part of the recipient’s chromosome by homologous recombination: an even number of crossovers (in practice two) between the fragment and the chromosome. No recA, no recombinants.

The table is the whole unit in one view. The mapping logic is the same as in eukaryotes: the closer two genes are, the more often they travel together. What differs is the scale each method can measure. Conjugation transfers long stretches over time, so it gives a coarse map in minutes. Transduction moves about one phage head of DNA, so only genes within about two minutes can travel together, which gives fine distances. The last line ties to recombination in Part 2: a linear fragment entering a circular chromosome must be integrated by two crossovers, otherwise the circle is broken. A recA mutant recipient cannot do this, so it gives no recombinants in any of these crosses.

title: Bacterial genetics (recap)
text:
Conjugation: F+, Hfr and F′

The F factor (~100 kb) carries the genes for the mating bridge and an origin of transfer, oriT. One strand is cut at oriT and sent across, 5′ end first, while it is copied.

Three states of the same plasmid. In an F+ cell, F is a free plasmid and only F itself is transferred, efficiently, so the recipient becomes F+. In an Hfr cell (high frequency of recombination), F has integrated into the chromosome by recombination at an insertion sequence. Transfer starts at oriT inside F, so chromosomal genes follow in a fixed order, and the rest of F would come last; because mating pairs usually break long before 100 minutes, the recipient almost never becomes F+ or Hfr. In an F′ cell, F has looped out again and taken a piece of chromosome with it. The recipient gets a second copy of those genes: a partial diploid, or merodiploid. That is the bacterial way to test dominance, and it is how Jacob and Monod did the cis/trans tests on the lac operon (the prokaryotic regulation unit in Part 6).

title: Bacterial genetics (recap)
section: Interrupted mating: a map in minutes
text:
Interrupted mating: a map in minutes




Wollman and Jacob (1950s):

Mix Hfr strs donors with F− strr recipients that carry recessive markers.
At intervals, shake the pairs apart in a blender.
Plate on streptomycin (kills the donors) plus a medium that selects a donor marker.

Each marker first appears at its time of entry. Earlier entry = closer to the origin. Later markers reach a lower plateau, because pairs break apart at random.


This is the classic experiment. The donor is streptomycin sensitive and the recipient resistant, so streptomycin removes the donors from every plate; the str marker must lie far from the origin, so that it is not itself transferred early. Read the plot: no thr+ recombinants before about 8 minutes, then a linear rise. Extrapolating the rise back to zero gives the time of entry. The map is simply the list of entry times. The numbers here are the simulated Hfr from the R exercise. The lower plateaus for later markers are a gradient of transfer: the longer the transfer must last, the more pairs have broken apart before the marker gets through. That gradient alone already gives the order, even without a blender.

title: Bacterial genetics (recap)
text:
Hfr maps are circular

Each Hfr strain has F inserted at its own place and in its own orientation. Every Hfr gives a linear order, but the orders from different Hfrs overlap and only fit together as a circle: the first genetic evidence that the E. coli chromosome is circular.

Hfr A and B are teaching examples; the gene positions are the real ones from the genome sequence, converted to minutes. Ask the students: Hfr A transfers pyr, thr, lac, gal, trp; Hfr B transfers his, trp, gal, lac, thr. Can both be right on a straight chromosome? Only if the line is read in opposite directions. Add a third Hfr that starts in the str region and the orders wrap around: the only consistent arrangement is a circle. This was shown genetically in the late 1950s, years before Cairns saw the circular replicating chromosome by autoradiography (1963). The map unit, the minute, is still used in EcoCyc and in older papers.

The minute map was drawn by convention from thr = 0. Transfer speed is nearly constant along the chromosome, so minutes and base pairs are almost proportional: a straight line. You fit that line in R.

The coordinates are from NCBI Gene for E. coli K-12 MG1655, checked for this unit. The last column is just the position as a fraction of the genome. The historical minute map (from timed transfers) agrees with these values to within about a minute for most genes, which tells us that DNA transfer runs at a roughly constant speed. Compare with the cM-to-bp relation in eukaryotes in Part 2: there, recombination hot and cold spots make the relation uneven; here the “distance” is time, which tracks DNA length much more faithfully. In the R exercise students regress simulated entry times on real Mb positions and get the slope, about 21 minutes per Mb, or 47 kb per minute.

title: Bacterial genetics (recap)
text:
Generalized transduction

Phage P1 (E. coli) or P22 (Salmonella; Zinder and Lederberg, 1952) sometimes packs a piece of host DNA instead of its own genome. Any part of the chromosome can be packed, so any gene can be transduced (generalized transduction). Specialized transduction, by phage λ, moves only the genes next to its insertion site.

The key point is the size limit: a P1 head holds about 100 kilobases, a little over two minutes of the E. coli map. So two genes can only be transduced together, cotransduced, if they lie within about two minutes of each other. Transduction is therefore a short-range ruler, the opposite of interrupted mating. Note the double crossover again: the fragment must recombine into the chromosome on both sides of the marker. Most transducing fragments that enter a cell are never integrated; that is why transduction frequencies are low, around one transductant per 10^5 to 10^6 phage.

title: Bacterial genetics (recap)
text:
Cotransduction: distance from frequency
Select one donor marker, then score a second, unselected one by replica plating. The cotransduction frequency is the fraction of selected transductants that also got the second marker.

Higher frequency = closer. Unlike recombination frequency in Part 2, the scale is reversed.
Order of three genes: in a three-factor cross, the class that needs four crossovers is the rarest. The gene in the middle of that class’s arrangement is the middle gene.


These qualitative rows match the real positions: leuA at 1.8 min, secA (azi) at 2.3 min, thrA at 0 min, lacZ at 7.8 min. The reversed scale confuses students every year: in eukaryotic mapping a high recombination frequency means far apart; here a high cotransduction frequency means close together, because we count how often two markers travel in the same fragment. For order, the reasoning is the same as the three-point cross in Part 2: the rarest class needs the most crossovers. A widely used approximation (Wu, 1966) relates cotransduction frequency C to distance d and fragment length L: C = (1 − d/L)^3. It is in the exercise as an optional extra.

title: Bacterial genetics (recap)
text:
Transformation

Natural competence: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Bacillus subtilis, Haemophilus influenzae take up DNA from the medium. Griffith’s mice (1928) and Avery, MacLeod and McCarty (1944) used it to show that DNA is the genetic material (DNA recap unit).
Artificial: E. coli is made competent with calcium chloride or an electric pulse. This is how plasmids get into cells in every molecular biology lab.
Mapping: genes close enough to be on one piece of DNA are cotransformed; distant genes are transformed together only as often as two independent events (frequency × frequency).

Transformation and transduction are gene transfer, not sex: only a fragment moves, and the recipient stays haploid apart from that fragment.

Transformation was the first of the three to be discovered and it carried the historical weight of proving that genes are DNA, which students met in the DNA recap unit in Part 3. For mapping, it works like transduction with a smaller and more variable fragment size. The test for linkage in transformation is a comparison with the product of the single frequencies: if a+ alone is transformed in 1 in 1000 cells and b+ alone in 1 in 1000, two independent events together happen in about 1 in a million. If a+ b+ double transformants are much more common than that, the genes are on the same fragment.

Which mutation breaks what
The classic markers are real genes. Their old names describe the phenotype; the new names describe the protein.

Loss of function in a biosynthetic enzyme → auxotroph. A change in a drug or phage target → resistance.

This is the genetics lens the recap is meant to add. Most markers fall into two groups. Biosynthetic genes give auxotrophs when broken: the cell needs the end product in the medium. Resistance markers are changes in a target: an altered ribosomal protein that no longer binds streptomycin, or a missing outer membrane receptor that phage T1 uses to attach. Note that str-r is recessive to str-s in a merodiploid, because one sensitive ribosome population is enough to poison translation; that is a nice F′ dominance test. You will look up several of these genes in NCBI Gene in the exercise, with their positions in the genome.

title: Bacterial genetics (recap)
text:
Where this leads

Next: Organelle inheritance. Mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from bacteria (an alphaproteobacterium and a cyanobacterium) and still carry small circular genomes.
Part 6: Prokaryotic regulation (recap). F′ partial diploids were the key tool of Jacob and Monod’s lac operon experiments.
Back to Part 2. Interrupted mating and cotransduction are the bacterial versions of the linkage and three-point cross mapping.
In the exercise: map genes from Hfr and transduction data by hand, find E. coli genes in NCBI Gene, and in R compare entry times with genome positions using left_join and lm.


Point forward. Endosymbiosis is the bridge to the next unit: the mitochondrial genome is a shrunken bacterial chromosome, circular and without introns, and like bacteria it is inherited without meiosis. The lac operon in Part 6 uses the same F′ trick we met today. In the exercise, students first order markers from Hfr data by hand and then check the classical minute map against the real genome in R.

title: Exercise in R: bacterial genetics (recap)
Exercise in R: bacterial genetics (recap)
Exercise in R: bacterial genetics (recap)
text:
Before you start
This page builds on the by-hand part of the Exercise, so do that first. You need the packages readr, dplyr and ggplot2. Download the two data files and save them in a data/ folder of your R project:

hfr_entry.csv: times of entry for ten markers in an interrupted-mating experiment. These are simulated teaching data, not a real experiment: they were computed from the real gene positions for a hypothetical Hfr whose origin of transfer lies near 4 300 000 bp and which transfers towards increasing coordinates, with some random noise added. The comment lines at the top of the file say so.
ecoli_genes.csv: real positions of 18 classic mapping markers in E. coli K-12 MG1655 (chromosome NC_000913.3, 4 641 652 bp), from NCBI Gene, retrieved 2026-11-20. Each classic marker (lac, str, …) is matched with one gene (lacZ, rpsL, …). See data/README.md.

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

title: Exercise in R: bacterial genetics (recap)
text:
Tasks
This unit reuses two things you already know: left_join from Part 4, and lm from 5KE232. One small new piece is the modulo operator %%: a %% b is the remainder after dividing a by b, so (x - origin) %% genome_length is the distance from the origin going round the circle, even when the gene’s coordinate is smaller than the origin’s.
R1. (order and distances) Read hfr_entry.csv. The file starts with comment lines, which comment = "#" skips. Sort the markers by time of entry and add the gap to the previous marker with lag(). What is the gene order? Which two markers are closest?
hfr <- read_csv("data/hfr_entry.csv", comment = "#", show_col_types = FALSE)
hfr_map <- hfr |>
  arrange(time_of_entry_min) |>
  mutate(gap_min = time_of_entry_min - lag(time_of_entry_min))
hfr_map
paste(hfr_map$marker, collapse = " - ")
R2. (join to the genome) Read ecoli_genes.csv and join it to hfr_map by the column marker. Then compute each gene’s distance from the Hfr origin (4 300 000 bp) in Mb, going in the direction of transfer (increasing coordinates) and round the circle. Why does thrA, at 337 bp, come out at 0.342 Mb and not at a negative distance?
genes <- read_csv("data/ecoli_genes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
genome_length <- 4641652
origin <- 4300000

both <- hfr_map |>
  left_join(genes, by = "marker") |>
  mutate(dist_mb = ((start - origin) %% genome_length) / 1e6)
both |> select(marker, gene, time_of_entry_min, start, dist_mb)
R3. (minutes against megabases) Fit a straight line of time of entry on distance with lm. What are the slope (minutes per Mb) and the intercept? Turn the slope into kb per minute. Then plot the points with the fitted line and gene labels.
fit <- lm(time_of_entry_min ~ dist_mb, data = both)
coef(fit)
summary(fit)$r.squared
1000 / coef(fit)[["dist_mb"]]     # kb per minute

# labels alternately right and left of the points, so close neighbours do not overlap
both <- both |> mutate(label_hjust = if_else(row_number() %% 2 == 0, 1.3, -0.3))

ggplot(both, aes(x = dist_mb, y = time_of_entry_min)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, colour = "#2a6f97") +
  geom_text(aes(label = gene, hjust = label_hjust), fontface = "italic", size = 3.5) +
  labs(x = "distance from the Hfr origin (Mb, clockwise)",
       y = "time of entry (min)",
       title = "Interrupted mating (simulated) vs real genome positions") +
  theme_minimal()
R4. (predict) How long would this Hfr need to transfer the whole chromosome (use the slope only)? Use predict() to estimate when his and str would enter. Why is str a good counterselection marker for this Hfr, and why would you rarely see his+ recombinants in practice?
genome_length / 1e6 * coef(fit)[["dist_mb"]]   # minutes for the whole genome (without the lag)
far <- genes |>
  filter(marker %in% c("his", "str")) |>
  mutate(dist_mb = ((start - origin) %% genome_length) / 1e6)
far |>
  mutate(predicted_min = predict(fit, newdata = far)) |>
  select(marker, gene, dist_mb, predicted_min)
R5. (the minute map) Convert every gene in ecoli_genes.csv to map minutes, 100 × start / genome length, and print the table. Where is the origin of our Hfr, in minutes? Check two or three of the values against the classical map positions you know from the lecture (lac ≈ 8, trp ≈ 28, his ≈ 45 min).
genes |>
  mutate(map_min = round(100 * start / genome_length, 1)) |>
  select(marker, gene, start, strand, map_min) |>
  print(n = Inf)
100 * origin / genome_length

title: Exercise: bacterial genetics (recap)
Exercise: bacterial genetics (recap)
Exercise: bacterial genetics (recap)
text:
Background
Notation. lac+ / lac−: can / cannot use lactose. strr / strs: streptomycin resistant / sensitive. Thr− = needs threonine (an auxotroph).
Conjugation. F+ × F− transfers only F. Hfr × F− transfers the chromosome from oriT, in a fixed order and direction; the whole chromosome would take about 100 min, but pairs break apart long before, so the recipient stays F−. F′ × F− transfers F plus a piece of chromosome and makes a partial diploid (merodiploid).
Interrupted mating. Time of entry = distance from the Hfr origin, in minutes. Later markers are recovered less often (the gradient of transfer). Recombinants are selected on plates that kill the donor (counterselection, usually streptomycin) and select a donor marker.
Minutes and base pairs. E. coli K-12 MG1655 has one circular chromosome of 4 641 652 bp (NC_000913.3). 100 min ≈ the whole chromosome, so 1 min ≈ 46 kb, and position in minutes ≈ 100 × bp / 4 641 652.
Transduction. A P1 phage carries about 100 kb (a little over 2 min). Cotransduction frequency = fraction of selected transductants that also got an unselected donor marker. Higher = closer. In a three-factor cross, the rarest class needs four crossovers. An approximation (Wu, 1966) for fragment length L (in min) and distance d: \(C = (1 - d/L)^3\), so \(d = L\,(1 - C^{1/3})\).
Transformation. Two unlinked markers are cotransformed about as often as the product of their single frequencies. Much more often than that means they are on one DNA fragment.

title: Exercise: bacterial genetics (recap)
text:
Find it
NCBI Gene has a record for every gene in the reference strain E. coli K-12 substr. MG1655. Search with the gene symbol and the strain’s taxonomy ID, for example lacZ[gene] AND 511145[taxid]. On the gene page, the Summary box gives the official symbol, the full name (gene description), the locus tag (a “b number”) and Also known as (older names). The section Genomic context gives the position on the chromosome sequence NC_000913.3, as (start..end), with complement if the gene is on the other strand. EcoCyc has the same information with a map view, in minutes and base pairs.
F1. lacZ. What protein does it encode, what is its locus tag, and where is it (start..end, and strand)? Convert the start to minutes. What does complement mean?
F2. thrA. What protein does it encode, where does it start, and on which strand? Why do you think thr sits at 0 min on the classical map?
F3. Search for the old marker name tonA in E. coli K-12. Which gene is it today, what does the protein do, and where is the gene (minutes)? Why does a mutation here make cells resistant to phage T1?
F4. Search for strA in E. coli K-12. Which gene is it today, what does it encode, and where is it in minutes? Use the answer to explain why str is a good counterselection marker for an Hfr whose origin is at 92.6 min transferring clockwise.

title: Exercise: bacterial genetics (recap)
text:
Solutions






Solutions: By hand





B1. (a) Lining up the overlapping orders gives a circle:
thr – leu – lac – gal – trp – his – thy – xyl – ilv – met – pyr – (back to thr).
Hfr 3 ends with pyr then thr, and Hfr 1 starts with thr; no straight line fits all four strains.

Hfr 1: origin 2 min before thr, transfers thr → trp (“clockwise” if thr is at the top). Hfr 2: origin 5 min on the far side of his, transfers his → lac, the opposite direction. Hfr 3: origin 4 min before thy, clockwise thy → thr. Hfr 4: origin 3 min before met, anticlockwise met → thy.
Hfr 1: 30 − 19 = 11 min; Hfr 2: 33 − 22 = 11 min. They agree, as they must if the time of entry measures distance.
From Hfr 1, thr enters at 2, so the origin is at −2 = 98 min, and trp is at 28 min. Hfr 2: his is 22 − 5 = 17 min before trp, so at 28 + 17 = 45 min. Hfr 3: thr is 36 min after thy, so thy is at 100 − 36 = 64 min (Hfr 3 enters thy at 4 and thr at 40). These match the real positions in MG1655: hisG at 45.0 min and thyA at 63.9 min (100 × start / 4 641 652).

B2. (a) Streptomycin kills the strs Hfr donors (counterselection). No threonine and no leucine means only thr+ leu+ cells grow; the F− recipients are thr− leu−, so only recipients that got the donor’s thr+ leu+ by recombination form colonies. (b) If str entered early, many recipients would also receive strs and be killed, and you would lose exactly the recombinants you want. Being far from the origin, str almost never enters. (c) Replica plating: press the master plate onto a velvet and print it onto a plate that selects lac+ (minimal medium with lactose as the only carbon source, plus threonine, leucine and streptomycin), or screen on X-gal. Every colony is scored at once.
B3. Order origin – (thr leu) – lac – gal – trp. The further a marker is from the origin, the longer the transfer must last for it to arrive, and the more mating pairs break apart before that: the gradient of transfer. Even without a blender, the frequencies give the order.
B4. (a) leu–azi: (4 + 92) / 200 = 48%. leu–ton: (4 + 0) / 200 = 2%. (b) azi is much closer to leu. (c) Two orders are possible with azi near leu: leu–azi–ton or azi–leu–ton. The class azis tonr is absent (0). If the order is leu – azi – ton, getting leu+ and ton+ but not azir needs four crossovers (on either side of leu and on either side of azi), so it should be the rarest class, as observed. If the order were azi–leu–ton, every class would need only two crossovers, and azis tonr (a fragment from leu to ton that stops short of azi) should be at least as common as azir tonr (a longer fragment covering all three). It is not: 0 against 4. The order is leu – azi – ton, as in the genome.
B5. azi: \(d = 2(1 - 0.48^{1/3}) = 2(1 - 0.783) = 0.43\) min ≈ 20 kb. ton: \(d = 2(1 - 0.02^{1/3}) = 2(1 - 0.271) = 1.46\) min ≈ 68 kb. Real distances: 108 279 − 81 958 = 26 321 bp (0.57 min) and 167 484 − 81 958 = 85 526 bp (1.84 min). The formula gets the order and the rough size right, but it underestimates; it assumes every fragment is exactly L long and that crossovers happen anywhere with equal probability.
B6. (a) Independent: 2 × 10−3 × 1 × 10−3 = 2 × 10−6. (b) Observed 8 × 10−4 is 400 times more: a and b are linked, carried on the same DNA fragment. (A further test: dilute the DNA. Linked doubles fall in proportion to the singles; independent doubles fall with the square.)
B7. (a) Lac+: one working lacZ makes β-galactosidase. lac+ is dominant, as most loss-of-function mutations are recessive. (b) Streptomycin sensitive: the sensitive ribosomes bind streptomycin, stall on the mRNA and kill the cell even though resistant ribosomes are also present. Here the sensitive allele is dominant, and the resistance allele is recessive.









Solutions: Find it





All coordinates were checked with the NCBI E-utilities (esummary on db = gene, field genomicinfo) on 2026-11-20, for E. coli K-12 substr. MG1655, chromosome NC_000913.3 (4 641 652 bp). Click path: NCBI Gene → search <symbol>[gene] AND 511145[taxid] → the record “symbol … [Escherichia coli str. K-12 substr. MG1655]” → Summary (name, locus tag, Also known as) → Genomic context (position).
F1. lacZ (Gene ID 945006): β-galactosidase, locus tag b0344. Position NC_000913.3 363231..366305, complement. 100 × 363 231 / 4 641 652 = 7.8 min. complement means the gene is read from the other DNA strand (the minus strand), so it is transcribed towards lower coordinates; its start codon is at 366 305.
F2. thrA (Gene ID 945803): fused aspartate kinase / homoserine dehydrogenase 1 (the first enzymes of threonine synthesis), locus tag b0002, at 337..2799 on the plus strand. The thr operon was the first marker on the classical map, so the map was started there (0 min) by convention. The genome sequence’s coordinate 1 was later put just before it, so thr is at 0 min in both systems.
F3. tonA is today fhuA (Gene ID 944856; also known as T1, T5rec, tonA): the ferrichrome outer membrane transporter / phage receptor, at 167484..169727 (plus strand), 3.6 min. The protein sits in the outer membrane, where it takes up iron bound to ferrichrome; phage T1 (and T5) use it as their receptor to attach. Without a working FhuA, T1 cannot attach, so the cell is resistant. The old name tonA means “T one” resistance.
F4. strA is today rpsL (Gene ID 947845; also known as asuB, strA): 30S ribosomal subunit protein S12, at 3474178..3474552, complement, 74.8 min. Streptomycin binds the small ribosomal subunit; changes in S12 stop it binding, giving resistance. For an Hfr with its origin at 92.6 min transferring clockwise, str at 74.8 min is 100 − 92.6 + 74.8 = 82 min from the origin, so it is almost never transferred before the pairs break: a good counterselection marker. That is the simulated Hfr in the R exercise.

title: Exercise: bacterial genetics (recap)
text:
Where this leads
The minute map of E. coli was built from interrupted mating and cotransduction long before DNA could be sequenced. The genome sequence lets us check it: in the R exercise you put entry times next to real gene positions and fit a line. Organelle inheritance comes next: mitochondria and chloroplasts are descendants of bacteria, with small circular genomes of their own. In Part 6, Prokaryotic regulation uses F′ partial diploids for the classic lac operon experiments.
Next: Exercise in R: order markers from interrupted-mating data, join them to real genome positions with left_join, and fit minutes against megabases with lm.

title: Quiz: bacterial genetics (recap)
text:
Short questions on bacterial mutants, conjugation, transduction and transformation as mapping tools. This unit is a recap of 5MO103. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A colony grows on complete medium but not on minimal medium. What kind of mutant is it, and how would you find out which nutrient it needs?






Hint





Minimal medium contains only salts, a carbon source and water. What can a wild-type cell make by itself?









Answer





It is an auxotroph: it has lost the ability to make some compound that the wild type (a prototroph) makes itself, usually because a biosynthetic enzyme gene is broken. Replica-plate the colony onto minimal plates each supplemented with one compound (threonine, leucine, tryptophan, …). The plate on which it grows names the requirement, for example Trp− if it grows only with tryptophan.




Q2. What is the difference between selection and screening? Give one example of each.






Hint





On which kind of plate do the unwanted cells still form colonies?









Answer





In selection only the wanted cells can grow: minimal medium without threonine selects Thr+ cells, streptomycin selects strr cells. In screening all cells grow, but the wanted ones look different: on X-gal, lac+ colonies are blue and lac− white. Selection can find one cell in 108; screening is limited to the colonies you can look at.




Q3. An F+ cell mates with an F− cell, and separately an Hfr cell mates with an F− cell. In which cross does the recipient usually become a donor, and in which does it gain chromosomal genes? Explain.






Hint





Where is F, and which part of F is transferred first?









Answer





In F+ × F−, the free F plasmid (~100 kb) is transferred whole and quickly, so the recipient becomes F+, but it gains no chromosomal genes. In Hfr × F−, F is integrated in the chromosome and transfer starts at oriT in the middle of F, so the chromosome follows in a fixed order. Transferring the whole chromosome takes about 100 min, and mating pairs nearly always break first, so the end of F rarely arrives: the recipient gains donor genes (by recombination) but stays F−.




Q4. In an interrupted-mating experiment, azir enters at 9 min, tonr at 10 min, lac+ at 16 min and gal+ at 25 min. Draw the map. How far apart are lac and gal in minutes, and roughly in kb?






Hint





Order by time. 1 min ≈ 46 kb in E. coli.









Answer





Origin – azi (9) – ton (10) – lac (16) – gal (25). lac to gal is 25 − 16 = 9 min, about 9 × 46 ≈ 410 kb. (The real distance, from the genome sequence, is 788 831 − 363 231 ≈ 426 kb.)




Q5. Why is an E. coli Hfr donor in a mapping experiment usually strs and the recipient strr? Where should the str gene be relative to the Hfr origin?






Hint





After mating, the plate must contain recombinant recipients only.









Answer





Streptomycin in the plates kills the donors, so every colony comes from a recipient. str must lie far from the origin, so that it enters very late (or never). If it entered early, many recipients would receive the donor’s strs allele and die, and markers near str could not be scored. (strs is also dominant over strr, so even a partial diploid with the donor allele would be killed.)




Q6. In P1 transduction, leu+ transductants are selected and scored for an unselected marker. 50% are also azir, 2% are also thr+, and none are lac+. Which marker is closest to leu? What can you say about lac?






Hint





How large a piece of DNA does one P1 phage carry?









Answer





High cotransduction means close: azi is closest to leu, thr is further away. lac is never cotransduced with leu, so it is more than one transducing fragment (P1: ~100 kb, a little over 2 min) away. Cotransduction cannot say how far; for that you use Hfr mapping. (Real positions: leuA 1.8 min, secA (azi) 2.3 min, thrA 0 min, lacZ 7.8 min.) Note that the scale runs the opposite way from recombination frequency in eukaryotic mapping.




Q7. You transform a recA− trp− strain with DNA from a trp+ strain and get no Trp+ transformants, although a recA+ control works. Why?






Hint





How does a linear piece of donor DNA become part of the recipient’s chromosome?









Answer





A linear donor fragment can only be kept if it is integrated by homologous recombination, two crossovers that swap the donor trp+ region into the circular chromosome. RecA is the recombinase that does this. Without it the fragment is degraded and the cell stays trp−. The same holds for Hfr conjugation and transduction (but not for a plasmid that can replicate on its own).




Q8. How did Hfr mapping show that the E. coli chromosome is circular?






Hint





Different Hfr strains have F inserted at different places and in different orientations.









Answer





Each Hfr strain gives a linear order of entry, starting at its own origin and going in its own direction. When the orders from many Hfrs were lined up, they overlapped, and the only arrangement consistent with all of them was a circle: the last genes of one Hfr were the first genes of another. The circular map was later confirmed physically (Cairns, 1963) and by the genome sequence (4 641 652 bp, one circular chromosome).

title: Exercise: cancer genetics
Exercise: cancer genetics
Exercise: cancer genetics
text:
Background
Two kinds of cancer gene.









Oncogene
Tumour suppressor




Normal job
promote division when signalled
stop division, repair DNA, trigger apoptosis


Mutation
gain of function
loss of function


At the cell level
dominant: one allele enough
recessive: both alleles lost


Typical mutations
hotspot missense, amplification, translocation
nonsense, frameshift, deletion, LOH


Examples
KRAS, MYC, ERBB2, BCR–ABL1
RB1, TP53, APC, BRCA1/2



Two-hit model. A cell lineage becomes a tumour when both alleles of a tumour suppressor are lost. With n cells at risk and a probability u that a given allele is hit (per year, or over a period):

Hereditary (one hit inherited): expected tumours ≈ n·u; for small risks, risk ∝ u and ∝ age.
Sporadic (two hits needed in the same cell): expected tumours ≈ n·u²; risk ∝ u² and ∝ age².
The chance that none of n cells is hit, each with a small probability p, is (1 − p)n ≈ e−np. So the chance of at least one tumour is 1 − e−(expected number).

Loss of heterozygosity (LOH). A tumour loses the normal allele of a tumour suppressor, often with the chromosome region around it. Markers that are heterozygous in blood look homozygous in the tumour.
Penetrance (Part 1): the probability that a person with the genotype shows the phenotype.

title: Exercise: cancer genetics
text:
By hand

B7. (Philadelphia chromosome) (a) Explain the notation t(9;22)(q34;q11). (b) The translocation is balanced: no DNA is lost. Why can it still cause leukaemia? (c) Imatinib inhibits the BCR–ABL1 kinase. Why does it harm leukaemia cells much more than normal cells? (d) Some patients relapse after a few years with a point mutation in the ABL1 kinase domain. Explain this in terms of clonal evolution.
B8. (drivers and passengers) 500 tumours of one cancer type are sequenced. Classify each gene as a likely oncogene, a likely tumour suppressor, or probably neither, and explain. (a) Gene P: mutated in 160 tumours; 140 of the mutations are missense at codon 12 or 13. (b) Gene Q: mutated in 110 tumours; the mutations are nonsense and frameshift, spread along the whole gene. (c) Gene R, a very long gene: mutated in 12 tumours, all different missense mutations at random positions.

title: Exercise: cancer genetics
text:
Explore
The demo follows 1000 children who inherited one mutant RB1 allele and 1000 who did not. Each child has n retinal cell lineages, half in each eye, and each RB1 allele in each lineage is knocked out at rate u per year. A lineage becomes a tumour when it has lost both copies. The rates are exaggerated so that sporadic cases show up in only 1000 children; the shapes are what matter.



E1. With the default settings (n = 200, u = 0.0015, T = 10), read the table. What fraction of each group has a tumour by age 10? How many tumours does an affected child have on average, and what fraction of affected children have tumours in both eyes? Relate this to the clinic: which children get bilateral, multiple tumours, and which get a single tumour in one eye?
E2. Compare the median age at the first tumour in the two groups. Then switch to the log–log view. Which curve rises with slope about 1, and which with slope about 2? Explain, from the number of hits each group still needs, why one curve is linear in age at early ages and the other quadratic.
E3. Press rarer hits (u ÷ 2). By what factor does the fraction affected change in each group? Compare the inherited group at age 1 (linear view) and the sporadic group at age 10. Why does halving the mutation rate reduce the sporadic risk so much more?
E4. Return to default and press Knudson’s plot. Which group gives the (nearly) straight line, and why does a straight line on this plot mean “one event at a constant rate”? Then press new sample a few times: which numbers in the table jump around the most, and why?






Solutions: Explore





E1. (Default, seed 1.) Inherited first hit: 94% have a tumour by age 10, with 3.05 tumours per affected child, and 63% of the affected children have tumours in both eyes. Sporadic: 4.9% have a tumour, with 1.02 tumours per affected child, and only 2% are bilateral (1 of 49). (The model’s expected values are 95% and 4.3%.) With one hit already in every cell, the second hit happens in many of the 200 lineages, so tumours are multiple and bilateral. Without it, two hits in the same lineage are rare, so a sporadic case almost always has one tumour in one eye. This is the clinical picture of hereditary and sporadic retinoblastoma. Note also that about 6% of the carriers never get a tumour: incomplete penetrance, from a purely random process.
E2. The median age at the first tumour is 2.2 years for inherited cases and 7.5 years for sporadic cases. On the log–log view the inherited curve rises with slope about 1 and the sporadic curve with slope about 2. An inherited case needs one more hit, so the chance of a tumour by age t is about n u t, proportional to t. A sporadic case needs two independent hits in the same cell, each with probability about u t, so the chance is about n (u t)², proportional to t². On log–log axes the exponent is the slope, so the slope counts the hits.
E3. Inherited: from 94% to 77% at age 10, and at age 1 from 0.265 to 0.131, almost exactly half. Sporadic: from 4.9% to 1.0% at age 10; the expected values fall from 4.3% to 1.1%, a factor of 4. With one hit needed, risk ∝ u, so halving u halves it. With two hits needed, risk ∝ u², so halving u divides it by 4. (Tumours per affected carrier also fall, from 3.05 to 1.87, and bilateral cases from 63% to 33%.)
E4. The inherited group gives the nearly straight line (it bends down only at the very end, because we look only at cases diagnosed by age 10). If tumours start at a constant rate, the fraction still undiagnosed falls by the same factor each year, like radioactive decay: e−rate × t, a straight line on a log scale. The sporadic curve stays high and then falls steeply: almost nothing happens early, because a cell must first collect one hit before the second can do anything. Knudson read this shape from real cases. With new sample, the sporadic numbers vary most (for example seed 2 gives 4.3% affected, 0% bilateral, median age 6.3 years), because they rest on only 40–50 cases, while the inherited numbers rest on more than 900.

title: Exercise: cancer genetics
text:
Solutions






Solutions: By hand





B1. (a) Oncogene, one allele: a hotspot missense that locks KRAS on. (b) Tumour suppressor, both alleles (a homozygous deletion of CDKN2A, which encodes the cell-cycle brake p16). (c) Oncogene, amplification: too much of a normal growth-factor receptor. (d) Tumour suppressor, both alleles: a point mutation (hit 1) plus loss of the other chromosome, LOH (hit 2). (e) Oncogene: a translocation that creates an always-active fusion kinase; one copy is enough.
B2. (a) Expected tumours per eye = n·u = 106 × 2 × 10−6 = 2; in both eyes 4. (b) P(no tumour) = e−4 = 0.018. Penetrance = 1 − 0.018 ≈ 0.98. (c) The eyes are independent. P(tumour in one given eye) = 1 − e−2 = 0.865. Both eyes: 0.865² = 0.75. (d) Expected tumours = 2n × u² = 2 × 106 × (2 × 10−6)² = 2 × 106 × 4 × 10−12 = 8 × 10−6, about 1 in 125 000 children. That is half a million times less than a carrier’s 4 tumours. Sporadic cases are therefore rare, and nearly always single.
B3. Carriers: risk ∝ age, so by age 2 about 4%. Non-carriers: risk ∝ age², so by age 20 about 0.01% × 2² = 0.04%, and by age 5 about 0.01% × (½)² = 0.0025%. (These approximations hold while the risks are small.)
B4. (a) M2, M3 and M4 show LOH; M1 stays heterozygous. (b) The LOH starts between M1 and M2 and runs to the end of the chromosome. Possible mechanisms: mitotic recombination between M1 and M2, which leaves two copies of the region, both from one parent (copy-neutral LOH), or a terminal deletion from between M1 and M2 to the end, which leaves one copy. Loss of the whole chromosome 13 is ruled out, because M1 is still heterozygous. Copy number tells them apart: two copies of the region in the tumour means recombination, one copy means deletion. (c) The tumour kept allele 3 at M2, which came from the father. The tumour keeps the mutant RB1 allele, so the mutant allele came from the father.
B5. (a) P(child carries) × penetrance = ½ × 0.9 = 0.45. (b) Conditional probability, as in the probability unit: P(carrier and unaffected) = ½ × 0.1 = 0.05; P(non-carrier) = ½. So P(carrier | unaffected) = 0.05 / (0.05 + 0.5) = 0.05/0.55 = 0.091. (c) 0.091 × ½ × 0.9 = 0.041, about 1 in 24. A non-penetrant carrier can pass on the allele: the trait then skips a generation.
B6. (a) ½. (b) ½ × 0.60 + ½ × 0.12 = 0.30 + 0.06 = 0.36. (c) If she does not carry her mother’s allele, her risk is that of a non-carrier: 0.12. A negative test for the family’s variant is informative; a negative test in a family with no known variant is much less so.
B7. (a) A reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, with breakpoints in band q34 of chromosome 9 and q11 of chromosome 22. (b) The breakpoints fall inside ABL1 and BCR and join them, creating a new fusion gene. Nothing is lost, but a new protein is made: the BCR–ABL1 kinase that is always active. (A germline carrier of an unrelated balanced translocation is usually healthy because no gene is broken or fused.) (c) Only leukaemia cells contain BCR–ABL1, and they depend on it to keep dividing. Normal cells have normal ABL1, which is regulated and less critical for them. (d) In a large population of leukaemia cells, a few cells may already carry, or later acquire, a mutation that stops imatinib from binding. The drug kills the others, so this resistant subclone is selected and grows: clonal evolution under treatment.
B8. (a) Gene P: likely an oncogene: frequent, and concentrated at codons 12 and 13 (this is the KRAS pattern). Selection favours specific activating changes. (b) Gene Q: likely a tumour suppressor: frequent truncating mutations anywhere in the gene, all of which destroy the protein. (c) Gene R: probably neither: a few scattered, different missense mutations in a long gene are what passengers look like. A long gene collects passengers just by being a big target.

title: Exercise: cancer genetics
text:
Where this leads
The two-hit model is a statement about how fast rare events accumulate in a population of cells. The next two units, Hardy–Weinberg and Drift, selection, take the same forces (mutation, selection and chance) to populations of people. In the ethics module we return to predictive testing for BRCA1/2.
Next: Exercise in R: simulate the two-hit model with rbinom, recover Knudson’s slopes, and summarise real TP53 mutations from cBioPortal.

title: Quiz: cancer genetics
text:
Short questions on oncogenes, tumour suppressors and the two-hit model. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Cancer is called a genetic disease, yet most cancers are not inherited. Explain how both statements can be true.






Hint





In which cells do the mutations that drive a tumour usually arise?









Answer





Cancer is caused by changes in DNA, so it is genetic. But most of those changes are somatic: they arise during life in one cell lineage (through replication errors or mutagens) and are present only in that cell and its descendants, the tumour. They are not in the germline, so they are not passed to children. Only a minority of patients carry an inherited (germline) predisposing allele.




Q2. Why is an activating mutation in a proto-oncogene dominant at the cell level, while an inactivating mutation in a tumour suppressor is recessive at the cell level?






Hint





What does the remaining normal allele do in each case?









Answer





An oncogenic allele is a gain of function: the mutant protein signals all the time, whatever the normal copy does. One allele is enough. A tumour suppressor mutation is a loss of function: the remaining normal allele still makes enough protein to act as a brake (the gene is haplosufficient). Only when both copies are lost does the cell lose control.




Q3. Name three ways in which a proto-oncogene can become an oncogene, with one example each.






Hint





Think of a change in the protein, a change in the amount of protein, and a change in where the gene sits.









Answer






Point mutation that locks the protein in its active state: KRAS codon 12 (G12V, G12D).
Amplification, many copies of the gene: ERBB2 (HER2) in some breast cancers, MYCN in neuroblastoma.
Translocation that creates a fusion gene or puts the gene next to a strong promoter: BCR–ABL1 from t(9;22) in chronic myeloid leukaemia.





Q4. List the four observations that distinguish hereditary from sporadic retinoblastoma, and explain each with Knudson’s two-hit model.






Hint





Family history, number of eyes, number of tumours, age at diagnosis.









Answer





In hereditary retinoblastoma every retinal cell already carries hit 1, so each needs only one more hit.

Family history: hit 1 is in the germline, so it is passed on (½ of the children of a carrier).
Both eyes: with about a million cells at risk, the second hit is likely to happen somewhere in each eye.
Several tumours: several cells get their second hit independently.
Earlier: one event needed, so risk rises linearly with age from the start.

In sporadic cases both hits must hit the same cell. That is rare, so at most one tumour, in one eye, appearing later (risk rises as age²), and with no inherited allele.




Q5. In a simple two-hit model, a carrier’s risk of a tumour by age t is about n u t and a non-carrier’s is about n(u t)². If the mutation rate u were doubled (for example by a mutagen), by what factor would each risk change?






Hint





Replace u by 2u in each formula.









Answer





Carrier: n(2u)t = 2 × n u t, so the risk doubles. Non-carrier: n(2u t)² = 4 × n(u t)², so the risk is four times higher. The more hits a cell needs, the more strongly its risk depends on the mutation rate. (This holds while the risks are small.)




Q6. What is loss of heterozygosity (LOH)? A patient with hereditary retinoblastoma is heterozygous 1/2 for a DNA marker close to RB1 in her blood. Her tumour shows only allele 1. Which parent passed on the mutant RB1 allele, if allele 1 came from her father?






Hint





Which allele must a tumour cell lose: the mutant or the normal one?









Answer





LOH means that a tumour has lost one of the two alleles at a locus where the person is heterozygous, so markers in that region look homozygous (or hemizygous) in tumour DNA. Mechanisms include deletion, mitotic recombination and loss of the whole chromosome.
The tumour must lose the normal RB1 allele and keep the mutant one. It kept allele 1, which came from the father, and lost allele 2, from the mother. So the mutant RB1 was on the father’s chromosome (assuming no recombination between the marker and RB1).




Q7. BRCA1 is a tumour suppressor, recessive at the cell level. Why does inherited breast and ovarian cancer due to BRCA1 show an autosomal dominant pattern in pedigrees? Why do some carriers never get cancer?






Hint





What is inherited: the cancer, or the first hit? Recall penetrance from Part 1.









Answer





A carrier inherits the first hit in every cell. The second hit (often LOH) is very likely to happen in at least one of the many breast or ovarian cells during life, so most carriers get cancer, and each child of a carrier has a ½ chance of inheriting the allele: an autosomal dominant predisposition. The second hit is a random event, so some carriers never get it: incomplete penetrance. In the pedigree the trait may then skip a generation.




Q8. What is a mutator phenotype? Why does losing a mismatch-repair gene such as MLH1 raise the risk of colorectal cancer, even though MLH1 does not control cell division?






Hint





Think of the hit rate u in Knudson’s model.









Answer





A mutator phenotype is a raised mutation rate in a cell, usually because a DNA-repair gene is lost. With MLH1 gone, replication errors are not repaired, so the cell and its descendants collect mutations much faster: the hit rate u rises for every gene. The hits in gatekeepers such as APC, KRAS and TP53 then arrive sooner. Inherited loss of mismatch repair is Lynch syndrome.




Q9. A tumour genome contains 5000 point mutations. Only a handful are drivers. What distinguishes a driver from a passenger, and how can you tell them apart in data from many tumours?






Hint





Does the mutation give the cell an advantage? Would it be seen again in other patients?









Answer





A driver gives its cell a growth or survival advantage and was selected during tumour evolution. A passenger happened by chance in the same lineage and was carried along; it has no effect. Across many tumours, drivers recur: the same gene is hit far more often than expected by chance, often at the same codon (hotspots such as KRAS G12 or TP53 R175H), or with many truncating mutations in a tumour suppressor. Passengers are scattered at random.




Q10. What is the Philadelphia chromosome, and why does the drug imatinib work so well in chronic myeloid leukaemia?






Hint





Which two genes meet at the junction, and what kind of enzyme does the fusion make?









Answer





It is the small derivative chromosome 22, der(22), from the reciprocal translocation t(9;22)(q34;q11). At the junction BCR (22q11) is fused to ABL1 (9q34), making a BCR–ABL1 tyrosine kinase that is always active and drives white blood cells to divide. Imatinib blocks the kinase’s ATP-binding pocket, so it switches off the one driver on which the leukaemia depends. Normal cells, which have no BCR–ABL1, are affected far less.




Q11. Two cancer genes have these mutation patterns in cBioPortal. Gene X: 80% of mutations are at one codon, all missense. Gene Y: mutations spread along the whole gene, many nonsense and frameshift. Which is likely an oncogene and which a tumour suppressor?






Hint





Which kind of mutation turns a protein on, and which destroys it?









Answer





Gene X is likely an oncogene: a gain of function needs a specific change that activates the protein, so selection favours the same few codons (a hotspot). Gene Y is likely a tumour suppressor: any mutation that destroys the protein will do, so truncating mutations (nonsense, frameshift) appear all along the gene. (TP53 has both: truncating mutations and missense hotspots.)

title: Exercise: chromosome theory & sex linkage
text:
By hand
B1. (counting) The domestic cat has 2n = 38. For one cell, give the number of chromosomes and chromatids, and say whether the cell is haploid or diploid:

a skin cell in G1; b) the same cell in G2; c) a primary spermatocyte in metaphase I; d) a cell just after meiosis I; e) a sperm cell.
Ignoring crossing over, how many different combinations of the tomcat’s maternal and paternal chromosomes can his sperm carry?

B2. (which division?) Each description is of one cell from an organism with 2n = 6. Name the division and the stage (mitosis, meiosis I or meiosis II).

Six chromosomes, each with two chromatids, lined up singly on the equator.
Three pairs of homologous chromosomes, paired side by side on the equator.
Three chromosomes, each with two chromatids, lined up on the equator.
Twelve single-chromatid chromosomes moving to the poles, six to each.

B3. (Morgan’s crosses) In Drosophila, white eye (w) is an X-linked recessive allele; red (w+) is wild type.

Give the genotypes and phenotypes of the F1 and F2 (by sex) from red ♀ (X+X+) × white ♂ (XwY).
Do the same for the reciprocal cross, white ♀ × red ♂.
Morgan crossed his original white male with F1 daughters. Predict the offspring. He got 129 red ♀, 132 red ♂, 88 white ♀, 86 white ♂. Does the result show that white-eyed females can exist?

B4. (X-linked plus autosomal) In Drosophila, vestigial wings (vg) is autosomal recessive. A white-eyed, vestigial female (XwXw vg/vg) is crossed to a red-eyed male with normal wings (X+Y vg+/vg+).

Give the F1 phenotypes, by sex.
The F1 are intercrossed. What fraction of F2 females are white-eyed with vestigial wings? What fraction of F2 males? (Use the branch-line method from Mendel: solve each gene separately, then multiply.)

B5. (human X-linked recessive) Red–green colour blindness is X-linked recessive. A colour-blind man and a woman with normal vision whose father was also colour-blind have children.

Give the genotypes of the parents.
What fraction of their sons, and of their daughters, will be colour-blind?
A son with normal vision has children with a woman who is homozygous for normal vision. What is the risk for his children?

B6. (Bridges, and nondisjunction in the father) White ♀ (XwXw) × red ♂ (X+Y).

Give the four zygote types from a meiosis I nondisjunction in the mother (eggs XwXw and O, fertilised by X+ or Y sperm). Which survive, and what are their sex and eye colour in Drosophila?
Now suppose nondisjunction happens in meiosis I of the father instead, giving X+Y and O sperm. Which offspring do you get with normal Xw eggs? Would Bridges have spotted them as exceptions from their eye colour alone?

B7. (sex determination) Predict the sex of each individual and explain briefly.

A human with karyotype 47,XXY. b) A Drosophila with XXY. c) A human 46,XY whose SRY has a loss-of-function mutation. d) A human 46,XX with a piece of Y containing SRY on one X. e) A Drosophila with XO. f) A honeybee that hatched from an unfertilised egg.

B8. (Z-linkage in chickens) In chickens, barred feathers (B) are dominant to non-barred (b), and the gene is on the Z chromosome. A barred hen is crossed to a non-barred rooster.

Write the genotypes of the parents. (Remember which sex is ZW.)
Predict the phenotypes of the chicks by sex. Why is this cross useful to poultry farmers?

B9. (where did the error happen?) A woman with Turner syndrome (45,X) is colour-blind. Her father has normal colour vision; her mother has normal vision but is a carrier. In which parent did the nondisjunction (or loss of a sex chromosome) happen? Explain.

The chromosome number halves in anaphase I, when homologues go to opposite poles. Chromatids per chromosome go from 2 to 1 in anaphase II, when sisters separate. It is the same pattern as for 2n = 46, with 4 and 2 in place of 46 and 23.
E2. The demo starts with the father’s long and the mother’s short chromosome facing the same pole, so the gametes are (blue long, red short) and (red long, blue short), two of each. After flipping: (blue long, blue short) and (red long, red short). That is 4 combinations in total, \(2^2\). With 3 pairs: \(2^3 = 8\); with 23 pairs: \(2^{23} = 8\,388\,608\). Each cell does only one orientation, so one meiosis gives 2 of the combinations; the others come from other meioses.
E3. All four gametes are abnormal: two n + 1 (3 chromosomes, with both a blue and a red long chromosome) and two n − 1 (1 chromosome, no long one). After fertilisation by a normal gamete (n = 2): 3 + 2 = 5 chromosomes (2n + 1, trisomic for the long chromosome) and 1 + 2 = 3 (2n − 1, monosomic). In Bridges’ crosses the n + 1 gametes are the XX eggs (XwXw) and the n − 1 gametes are the O eggs (no X).
E4. Now two gametes are normal (n = 2), one is n + 1 and one is n − 1. In the n + 1 gamete both long chromosomes have the same colour: they are former sister chromatids, copies of one grandparent’s chromosome. After nondisjunction in MI, the two copies have different colours: one from each grandparent. With DNA markers: if the child has inherited two different chromosome 21s from the mother (both of her marker alleles, near the centromere), the error was in meiosis I; if the child has two copies of the same maternal chromosome 21 (one of her alleles, twice), the error was in meiosis II. (Crossing over blurs this away from the centromere, which is why markers near the centromere are used. Part 5 has more.)
E5. The two gametes on the right, with no copy of the chromosome (n − 1 = 0), are the O eggs. The two on the left carry both homologues (XX eggs).

text:
Find it
Ensembl is a genome browser for vertebrates and model organisms. Its karyotype view (Location → Genome) draws all the chromosomes of a species; click a chromosome and choose “Chromosome summary” to see its Length (bps). NCBI Gene has one record per gene; read Location and Exon count in the Summary box. MedGen and OMIM describe diseases; read Mode of inheritance in MedGen, or the Inheritance column of the Phenotype-Gene Relationships table in OMIM (XLR = X-linked recessive).
F1. The human karyotype in Ensembl. Open the human karyotype view. How many chromosomes are drawn, and what are they called? Click chromosome X and then Y, and read the Length (bps) in each chromosome summary. How many times longer is the X than the Y? Which assembly (genome version) does Ensembl show?
F2. The fly karyotype in Ensembl. Open the Drosophila melanogaster karyotype view. Which chromosome names are shown? Drosophila has 2n = 8, that is, four chromosome pairs. Explain how the names fit four chromosomes. Compare the lengths of the X and the Y.
F3. SRY in NCBI Gene. Open SRY in NCBI Gene (or search Gene for “SRY human”). Read Location and Exon count in the Summary box, and the summary paragraph under “Summary”. On which chromosome arm is SRY? What kind of protein does it encode? According to the summary, what happens when SRY is mutated, and when it is moved to an X chromosome?
F4. Two X-linked diseases in MedGen. Open MedGen for haemophilia A (OMIM 306700) and for androgen insensitivity syndrome (OMIM 300068; MedGen calls it “Androgen resistance syndrome”). For each, read the Mode of inheritance and the gene, and find the gene’s band in NCBI Gene (search “F8 human”, “AR human”).

For haemophilia A, who in a family is usually affected, and why?
Read the definition of androgen insensitivity syndrome. What is the karyotype of the affected individuals? They have SRY, and they develop testes. Why is their body not male? What does this tell you about SRY’s role?







Hint





For F4b, AR is the androgen receptor: the protein that lets cells respond to testosterone. SRY decides whether the gonad becomes a testis; it does not act on every cell of the body.

title: Exercise: chromosome theory & sex linkage
text:
Solutions






Solutions: By hand





B1. a) 38 chromosomes, 38 chromatids, diploid. b) 38 chromosomes, 76 chromatids, diploid. c) 38 chromosomes, 76 chromatids (19 bivalents), diploid. d) 19 chromosomes, 38 chromatids, haploid. e) 19 chromosomes, 19 chromatids, haploid. f) \(2^{19} = 524\,288\).
B2. a) Mitosis, metaphase: all 6 chromosomes, replicated, lined up singly. b) Meiosis I, metaphase I: homologues are paired (bivalents). c) Meiosis II, metaphase II: only n = 3 chromosomes, still with two chromatids. d) Mitosis, anaphase: 12 chromatids separating into 6 + 6 means each pole gets a full diploid set. (In anaphase II there would be 3 + 3.)
B3. a) F1: X+Xw red ♀, X+Y red ♂. F2: daughters X+X+ and X+Xw, all red; sons X+Y red and XwY white, ½ each. Overall ½ red ♀ : ¼ red ♂ : ¼ white ♂.

White ♀ XwXw × red ♂ X+Y. F1: daughters X+Xw red, sons XwY white (criss-cross). F2 (X+Xw × XwY): daughters ½ X+Xw red, ½ XwXw white; sons ½ X+Y red, ½ XwY white. All four classes ¼.
XwY × X+Xw: daughters ½ red (X+Xw), ½ white (XwXw); sons ½ red, ½ white. Expected 1 : 1 : 1 : 1. Morgan’s 88 white females prove that white-eyed females are viable, so their absence in the F2 was due to X-linkage, not to white being lethal in females. (Both white classes are below the red ones: white flies survive less well. See the Exercise in R.)

B4. a) F1 females: X+Xw vg+/vg: red, normal wings. F1 males: XwY vg+/vg: white, normal wings (criss-cross for eye colour).

F1 × F1: X+Xw vg+/vg × XwY vg+/vg. Eye colour: daughters ½ white (XwXw); sons ½ white (XwY). Wings: vg+/vg × vg+/vg → ¼ vestigial, in both sexes. White and vestigial: ½ × ¼ = 1/8 of females and 1/8 of males.

B5. a) Man: XcY. Woman: her father gave her Xc, and she has normal vision, so she is XCXc (a carrier). b) Sons get her X: ½ colour-blind. Daughters get Xc from the father and XC or Xc from the mother: ½ colour-blind (XcXc) and ½ carriers. c) A son with normal vision is XCY; his partner is XCXC. No child is colour-blind, and no daughter is a carrier. (A man cannot pass an X-linked allele to his sons.)

These have the same eye colours as the regular offspring (red daughters, white sons), so Bridges could not spot them by phenotype; he would need to look at the chromosomes or notice that the males are sterile. That is why he used a white mother and a red father: only maternal nondisjunction gives eye colours that stand out.

Farmers can therefore sort chicks by sex from their plumage, without examining their genitals (a sex-linked, or autosexing, cross).
B9. She is colour-blind, so her only X must be Xc. Her father is XCY and could only give XC or Y, so her Xc came from her mother. She got no sex chromosome from her father: the error (nondisjunction or loss of the sex chromosome) happened in the father’s meiosis, giving a sperm with no X and no Y.

These facts were checked via the Ensembl REST API (/info/assembly) and NCBI E-utilities (Gene and MedGen) on 2026-11-20.
F1. Ensembl draws 25 chromosomes for human: 1–22, X, Y and the mitochondrial genome MT. Click path: Ensembl → Human → Location: “Genome” (karyotype view) → click X → “Chromosome summary” → Length (bps). On assembly GRCh38 (GRCh38.p14), X is 156,040,895 bp and Y is 57,227,415 bp: the X is about 2.7 times longer. (Much of the Y is repetitive, and it carries far fewer genes than the X.)
F2. The names are 2L, 2R, 3L, 3R, 4, X, Y (plus the mitochondrial genome). 2L and 2R are the left and right arms of chromosome 2, on either side of the centromere, and likewise for chromosome 3. So the four pairs are X (or X/Y), 2, 3 and 4, which fits 2n = 8. Lengths on the current assembly (BDGP6): X ≈ 23.5 Mb, Y ≈ 3.7 Mb. The Y is mostly repetitive heterochromatin that is hard to assemble, so its real size is larger than the assembled sequence; either way it has few genes. Chromosome 4 is tiny (≈ 1.3 Mb).
F3. NCBI Gene ID 6736: Location Yp11.2 (the short arm, “p”, of the Y), Exon count 1 (the summary calls it an “intronless gene”). It encodes a transcription factor of the HMG-box family of DNA-binding proteins, the testis-determining factor (TDF) that starts male sex determination. Mutations give XY females with gonadal dysgenesis (Swyer syndrome); translocation of the SRY region to the X causes XX male syndrome.
