Haemophilia A affects mainly males: they have one X, so one faulty F8 allele leaves them with no working factor VIII. Heterozygous women are usually carriers who pass the allele to half their sons.
The MedGen definition (from GeneReviews) describes undermasculinised or female external genitalia in individuals with a 46,XY karyotype. They have a Y with a working SRY, so their gonads develop as testes, which make testosterone. But without a working androgen receptor their cells cannot respond to it, so the body develops along the female path (complete AIS) or is partly masculinised. SRY is only the switch that makes the gonad a testis; the rest of male development depends on hormones and their receptors, which are encoded by other genes, here one on the X.

title: Exercise: chromosome theory & sex linkage
text:
Where this leads
Genes sit on chromosomes, and there are many more genes than chromosomes. So genes on the same chromosome should travel together. In Linkage & recombination we see that they do, except when crossing over between homologues separates them, and that the frequency of crossing over can be used to map genes. Nondisjunction in humans (trisomy 21, XXY and XO) returns in Part 5, Rearrangements & aneuploidy, with the same meiosis demo, and X inactivation in Part 6.
Next: Exercise in R: count gamete combinations, simulate how much of a gamete comes from each grandparent, and test Morgan’s counts with χ².

title: Quiz: chromosome theory & sex linkage
text:
Short questions on meiosis, the chromosome theory, X-linkage and sex determination. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Write X-linked genotypes with the allele as a superscript on the X: XAXa, XaY.

Q1. A human cell is in G2, after DNA replication. How many chromosomes and how many chromatids does it have? How many does each cell have after meiosis I, and after meiosis II?






Hint





Count chromosomes by centromeres. Replication doubles the chromatids, not the chromosomes.









Answer





G2: 46 chromosomes, 92 chromatids (2n). After meiosis I: 23 chromosomes, 46 chromatids per cell (n; each chromosome still has two sister chromatids). After meiosis II: 23 chromosomes, 23 chromatids per gamete (n).




Q2. What separates in anaphase I, and what separates in anaphase II? Which of the two divisions is like mitosis?






Hint





One division halves the chromosome number; the other does not.









Answer





Anaphase I: the homologous chromosomes separate (one to each pole); sister chromatids stay together. This is the reductional division, 2n → n. Anaphase II: the sister chromatids separate. Meiosis II is like mitosis (sisters separate), except that the cell has only one set of chromosomes.




Q3. A Drosophila female has 2n = 8. Ignoring crossing over, how many genetically different combinations of her own parents’ chromosomes can her eggs carry? What is the probability that an egg carries only chromosomes she inherited from her mother?






Hint





n = 4 pairs, each oriented independently at metaphase I.









Answer





Each of the 4 pairs contributes the maternal or the paternal homologue, independently: 24 = 16 combinations. Only maternal chromosomes: (½)4 = 1/16.




Q4. Sutton and Boveri listed parallels between Mendel’s factors and chromosomes. Why was that not enough to prove that genes are on chromosomes? What kind of evidence was needed?






Hint





A parallel is a correlation. What would link one particular gene to one particular, visible chromosome?









Answer





Parallel behaviour (pairs, segregation, independent assortment) shows that chromosomes could carry genes, but it is a correlation: something else might behave in the same way. The proof needed a specific gene whose inheritance follows a specific, recognisable chromosome, ideally including its unusual behaviour. Morgan’s white gene followed the X; Bridges then showed that rare exceptional flies had exactly the unusual X chromosome sets (XXY, XO) that their eye colours predicted.




Q5. Morgan’s F1 (red X+Xw females × red X+Y males) gave 2459 red females, 1011 red males and 782 white males. Why do these numbers rule out an autosomal gene, even though red : white is roughly 3 : 1?






Hint





For an autosomal gene, is there any reason the white flies should all be male?









Answer





For an autosomal gene, Ww × Ww gives ¼ white offspring in both sexes, so about half of the white flies should be female. Morgan found no white females at all among 4252 flies. That is exactly the X-linked prediction: every F2 daughter gets X+ from her red father, while sons get their only X from the mother (½ X+, ½ Xw).




Q6. A χ² test of Morgan’s F2 against ½ red ♀ : ¼ red ♂ : ¼ white ♂ gives χ² ≈ 129 with 2 df. Does this mean that the white gene is not X-linked? What is a better explanation?






Hint





Which class contributes most to χ²? Is it too big or too small?









Answer





No. The qualitative pattern (no white females) fits X-linkage and nothing else. The misfit comes mainly from the white males, 782 observed vs 1063 expected, and from the red females (more than expected). A simple explanation is that white-eyed flies survive less well (reduced viability). Morgan’s backcross supports this: the white classes were short in both sexes (88 and 86 against 129 and 132 red). A significant χ² says that the model is incomplete, not which part of it is wrong.




Q7. A white-eyed female Drosophila (XwXw) is crossed to a red-eyed male (X+Y). What do you expect among the daughters and among the sons? Bridges found a few white daughters. What chromosome set did they have, and how did they arise?






Hint





Normally, which parent’s X does a daughter get? A white daughter cannot have the father’s X+.









Answer





Expected: all daughters red (X+Xw), all sons white (XwY): criss-cross inheritance. A white daughter must have got both X chromosomes from her mother and none from her father, so she is XwXwY. Her mother’s two X chromosomes failed to separate in meiosis (nondisjunction), giving an XX egg that was fertilised by a Y-bearing sperm. In flies XXY is female, because sex depends on the X : autosome ratio.




Q8. In humans, XXY individuals are male and XO individuals are female. In Drosophila it is the reverse. What does this tell you about how sex is determined in each species?






Hint





What do XY and XXY have in common? What do XX and XXY have in common?









Answer





In humans the Y decides: any karyotype with a Y (and a working SRY) is male, whatever the number of X chromosomes. In flies the number of X chromosomes relative to the autosomes decides: two X (XX, XXY) gives a female, one X (XY, XO) gives a male; the Y is needed only for male fertility.




Q9. In chickens (ZW system), which parent determines the sex of the chicks? In honeybees, how many sets of chromosomes does a drone (male) have, and who are its parents?






Hint





The heterogametic sex makes two kinds of gamete.









Answer





Chickens: females are ZW (heterogametic) and males ZZ, so the hen decides: her eggs carry Z or W, ½ each. Honeybees: a drone develops from an unfertilised egg, so it is haploid (n) and has a mother (the queen) but no father.




Q10. A woman whose father had haemophilia A (X-linked recessive) has children with an unaffected man. What is the probability that (a) a son is affected, (b) a daughter is affected, (c) a daughter is a carrier?






Hint





What did she get from her father? Solve sons and daughters separately.









Answer





Her father gave her his only X, Xh, so she is a carrier, XHXh (an obligate carrier). Her partner is XHY. (a) Sons get her X: P(affected) = ½. (b) Daughters get XH from the father: P(affected) = 0. (c) Daughters get Xh from her with ½: P(carrier) = ½.




Q11. Nondisjunction of chromosome 21 can happen in meiosis I or in meiosis II. How do the resulting n + 1 gametes differ? (Try both modes in the demo.)






Hint





In meiosis I, what fails to separate: homologues or sisters?









Answer





Meiosis I: the two homologues fail to separate, so the n + 1 gamete carries two different copies, one from each of the parent’s own parents; all four gametes are abnormal (two n + 1, two n − 1). Meiosis II: two sister chromatids fail to separate, so the n + 1 gamete carries two identical copies; the other cell divides normally, giving two normal gametes, one n + 1 and one n − 1. (Ignoring crossing over, which makes the distinction partial near the chromosome ends.)

title: Exercise: complex traits, heritability & GWAS
Exercise: complex traits, heritability & GWAS
Exercise: complex traits, heritability & GWAS
text:
Background
Polygenic model. With k additive loci, the number of “+” alleles (0 to 2k) in an F2 from AaBb… × AaBb… follows Binomial(2k, ½).
Variance components. VP = VG + VE, VG = VA + VD (+ epistasis). Broad sense H² = VG/VP; narrow sense h² = VA/VP.
Estimating h².

Twins: h² ≈ 2 [r(MZ) − r(DZ)]; shared environment c² ≈ 2r(DZ) − r(MZ).
Offspring on midparent: slope b = h². Offspring on one parent: b = h²/2.
Prediction: expected child deviation from the mean = h² × midparent deviation.
Breeder’s equation: response R = h² S, where S is how far the selected parents are above the mean.

GWAS. One test per SNP; genome-wide threshold 5 × 10⁻⁸. For a case–control study, compare allele counts in a 2 × 2 table with a χ² test (df = 1); the odds ratio OR = (risk/other allele in cases) / (risk/other allele in controls). The expected test statistic grows with effect size × √N.

title: Exercise: complex traits, heritability & GWAS
text:
By hand
B1. (three loci) Plant height is controlled by three unlinked additive loci A, B, C. Each capital-letter allele adds 5 cm to a base height of 30 cm (aabbcc). Two AaBbCc plants are crossed. (a) How tall are the shortest and the tallest possible offspring? How many height classes are there? (b) What fraction of the offspring are as tall as the tallest class? As the middle class? (c) Sketch the distribution. What would it look like with environmental variation added?
B2. (variance components) For milk yield in a cattle population: VP = 50, VA = 24, VD = 6, and the rest is environmental. Compute VE, H² and h².
B3. (twins) For body mass index in a twin registry, r(MZ) = 0.74 and r(DZ) = 0.40 (round numbers for this exercise). (a) Estimate h² and the shared-environment component c². (b) What fraction of the variance is left for the unique (non-shared) environment? (c) Give one reason why the estimate of h² might be too high.
B4. (parent–offspring regression) In a study of a bird population, the slope of offspring beak depth on one parent’s beak depth is 0.35. (a) Estimate h². (b) A pair of birds has a midparent beak depth 1.0 mm above the population mean. What do you predict for their offspring? (c) Why is the prediction less extreme than the parents?
B5. (breeder’s equation) In the cattle population of B2, a farmer uses only cows and bulls whose own milk yield is on average 8 units above the population mean. What response do you expect in the next generation? What if the farmer selected on a trait with h² = 0.05?
B6. (multiple testing) A GWAS tests 800 000 independent SNPs, none of which has any real effect. (a) How many SNPs do you expect at p < 0.05, p < 10⁻⁵ and p < 5 × 10⁻⁸? (b) What should the QQ plot look like?
B7. (a case–control test) A SNP is genotyped in 1000 cases of type 2 diabetes and 1000 controls (invented counts). Allele counts:




risk allele T
other allele C
total




cases
700
1300
2000


controls
560
1440
2000




Compute the T allele frequency in cases and controls, and the odds ratio.
Compute χ² for the 2 × 2 table (expected counts from the row and column totals; df = 1).
Is the SNP significant at p < 0.05? Is it genome-wide significant (χ² for p = 5 × 10⁻⁸ with df = 1 is about 29.7)?
Roughly how many people would you need to reach genome-wide significance with the same allele frequencies?

B8. (heritability statements) True or false? Explain each in one sentence. (a) If a trait has h² = 0.9, environmental changes cannot change its mean. (b) If h² is high within two populations, the difference between their means must be genetic. (c) A trait that is entirely determined by genes in every person can have a heritability near 0. (d) h² can differ between populations and between generations.

title: Exercise: complex traits, heritability & GWAS
text:
Explore: parent–offspring regression
Each dot is one simulated family: the midparent value against the child’s value, shown in height-like units (170 + 7z cm). The solid line is the fitted regression, the dashed line the slope expected under the model, the dotted line slope 1. The slider c² adds a shared family environment: the child’s environment resembles the parents’.



E1. At the start (h² = 0.6, n = 200), read the fitted slope and its standard error. Is it close to the true h²? Now set n = 20 and then n = 1000. How do the slope and its SE change? Press new sample a few times at n = 20: how much does the estimate jump?
E2. Why is the fitted line flatter than the dotted slope-1 line? A very tall pair of parents has midparent 185 cm: how tall do you predict their child to be, with h² = 0.6? What is this effect called?
E3. Tick single parent (back at n = 200). What happens to the slope? How do you turn it into an estimate of h², and why? Try n = 1000.
E4. Press shared environment (h² = 0.3, c² = 0.3). What slope do you get, and what would you wrongly conclude about h²? Then set h² = 0 and c² = 0.4. What does this tell you about using parent–offspring resemblance as evidence for genes? Which study design could separate the two?






Solutions: Explore (heritability)





All numbers are for the default seed.
E1. At h² = 0.6, n = 200: b = 0.582 ± 0.099 (SE), r = 0.387: close to 0.6, well within one SE. At n = 20: b = 0.466 ± 0.216; at n = 1000: b = 0.613 ± 0.042. The SE shrinks roughly as 1/√n (5 times more families, SE about 2.3 times smaller). With 20 families an estimate can easily be off by 0.2–0.4. Note that r (about 0.4) is not h²: r also depends on how spread out the midparents are.
E2. The child gets only half of each parent’s genes, and the parents’ deviations are partly environmental, which is not inherited. So children of extreme parents are on average less extreme: regression towards the mean (Galton’s “regression towards mediocrity”). Prediction: 170 + 0.6 × (185 − 170) = 179 cm.
E3. The slope halves: b = 0.309 ± 0.074 at n = 200 (expected 0.30), and 0.290 ± 0.031 at n = 1000. A child shares half its genes with one parent, so Cov(parent, offspring) = h²/2 × VP, while the variance of one parent is the full VP. So h² = 2b = 0.62 (n = 200) and 0.58 (n = 1000). With the midparent the covariance is the same but the variance is halved, so the slope is h² directly.
E4. Shared environment, h² = 0.3, c² = 0.3: b = 0.592 ± 0.104 (n = 200), 0.609 ± 0.042 (n = 1000). You would conclude h² ≈ 0.6, double the truth. With h² = 0 and c² = 0.4: b = 0.457 ± 0.112 (n = 200), 0.383 ± 0.045 (n = 1000), clearly above 0 although no gene affects the trait. Families share genes and environments (food, habits, income), and the regression cannot tell them apart. Adoption studies (adopted children against biological and adoptive parents), twin studies (MZ against DZ), and genomic methods in unrelated people can separate them.

title: Exercise: complex traits, heritability & GWAS
text:
Explore: a simulated GWAS
A simulated GWAS of a quantitative trait with 8 400 SNPs on 22 chromosomes. Up to 10 causal loci have small effects (β per allele, in trait SD units; every second locus has β/2), and neighbouring SNPs are in LD with them. Left: the Manhattan plot with the genome-wide (5 × 10⁻⁸, solid) and suggestive (10⁻⁵, dashed) thresholds; triangles mark the true causal loci. Right: the QQ plot.


E5. Press N = 5 000, then N = 50 000, then N = 500 000. How many of the five causal loci pass the genome-wide line each time? Which loci are found first, and why (look at “(β/2)” in the readout)? What does this tell you about why GWAS of height or type 2 diabetes use hundreds of thousands of people?
E6. At N = 500 000, look closely at one peak. Why is it a tower of many SNPs rather than one dot? Is the SNP at the top of the tower necessarily the causal SNP? What does this mean for the step from “GWAS hit” to “causal gene”?
E7. Press null (no causal loci). About how many of the 8 400 SNPs should have p < 0.05, p < 10⁻³ and p < 10⁻⁵ by chance alone? Compare with what you see. How does the QQ plot look? Why does a real GWAS of about a million SNPs use 5 × 10⁻⁸ rather than 0.05?
E8. Back at N = 50 000 (press the preset), raise β to 0.1, then lower it to 0.02. How many loci are found? The test statistic of a causal SNP is about β√(2f(1 − f)N). How much larger must N be to detect an effect half as large?






Solutions: Explore (GWAS)





Default seed. The causal loci are on chromosomes 2 (61 Mb, allele frequency f = 0.42, effect β), 9 (100 Mb, f = 0.33, β), 10 (113 Mb, f = 0.35, β/2), 14 (71 Mb, f = 0.44, β/2) and 17 (45 Mb, f = 0.11, β).
E5. N = 5 000: 0 of 5 found; no SNP even passes 10⁻⁵ (the highest point, −log10 p ≈ 4.7, is a chance null SNP). N = 50 000: 2 of 5 (chr 2 and chr 9), 3 SNPs above 5 × 10⁻⁸ and 10 above 10⁻⁵. N = 500 000: 5 of 5, 56 SNPs above 5 × 10⁻⁸ in exactly five loci, with no false loci. (N = 100 000 finds 3, adding chr 17; N = 200 000 finds 4, adding chr 14.) The loci with the full β and a common allele come first; the β/2 loci and the rare-allele locus (f = 0.11) need larger samples. The expected z for chr 2 is 2.5 at N = 5 000, 7.8 at 50 000 and 24.7 at 500 000, while 5 × 10⁻⁸ needs |z| ≈ 5.45. Real effects on complex traits are small, so only very large samples find most of them.
E6. SNPs near the causal SNP are in linkage disequilibrium with it, so they carry part of its signal: a tower. The top SNP is often but not always the causal one: noise can lift a neighbour above it, and in real data the causal variant may not be genotyped at all. A GWAS hit points to a region, often with several genes; fine-mapping and functional experiments are needed to find the causal variant and gene (TCF7L2 for type 2 diabetes is a well-studied example).
E7. Expected by chance: 8 400 × 0.05 = 420; 8 400 × 10⁻³ = 8.4; 8 400 × 10⁻⁵ = 0.08. Observed (null preset): 415, 9 and 0; none passes 5 × 10⁻⁸, and the highest point is −log10 p = 4.65. The QQ plot follows the diagonal. With about a million tests, p < 0.05 would give ~50 000 false hits; 5 × 10⁻⁸ = 0.05/10⁶ keeps the chance of even one false hit in the whole scan at about 5%.
E8. At N = 50 000: β = 0.1 finds 4 of 5 loci (32 SNPs above 5 × 10⁻⁸); β = 0.05 finds 2; β = 0.02 finds 0. Halving β halves β√N; to keep the same z, √N must double, so N must be 4 times larger.

title: Exercise: complex traits, heritability & GWAS
text:
Find it
The GWAS Catalog (EMBL-EBI and NHGRI) collects the significant associations from published GWAS. Each association links a SNP (with its risk allele) to a trait, with a p-value, an effect size (odds ratio or beta) and the study. Counts change every month as new studies are added, so give rounded answers.
F1. Type 2 diabetes. Open the trait page for type 2 diabetes mellitus. Roughly how many associations and studies are listed (hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands)? In the Associations table, sort by P-value. Which SNP and which mapped gene come first? The same query through the REST API, which returns machine-readable JSON: www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas/rest/api/v2/associations?efo_trait=type 2 diabetes mellitus&sort=p_value&direction=asc&size=5. (Very small p-values are stored as pvalue_mantissa and pvalue_exponent.)
F2. rs7903146. Open the variant page rs7903146. (a) On which chromosome and at which position (GRCh38) is it? In which gene, and is it coding? (b) In the associations for type 2 diabetes, which allele is the risk allele, and roughly what odds ratios are reported? (c) In NCBI Gene, what is the full name and location of TCF7L2? What kind of protein is it? (d) You met this SNP in the Hardy–Weinberg exercise. What was the T allele frequency in the CEU sample?
F3. Height. Open the trait page for body height or use the API: …/associations?efo_trait=body height&sort=p_value&direction=asc&size=20. Roughly how many associations are there, compared with type 2 diabetes? Name three of the mapped genes among the strongest associations. What does the number of associations tell you about the genetic architecture of height?






Solutions: Find it





Checked on 20 November 2026 through the GWAS Catalog REST API v2 and NCBI Gene (E-utilities). The counts will grow; the top hits are stable.
F1. About 9 700 associations for “type 2 diabetes mellitus” (MONDO_0005148), from about 240 GWAS (study accessions) in about 140 publications: thousands. The top association is rs7903146 in TCF7L2, with a p-value of about 3 × 10⁻¹³¹⁵ in Suzuki et al. 2024 (Nature, PMID 38374256, GCST90492734; about 430 000 cases and 2.1 million controls of six ancestry groups). The next distinct loci include KCNQ1, CDKAL1, CDKN2B-AS1, FTO and IGF2BP2.
F2. (a) Chromosome 10, position 112 998 590 (GRCh38), in an intron of TCF7L2: non-coding. (b) The risk allele is T; most studies report odds ratios of about 1.3–1.4 per T allele (some 1.15–1.6). (c) TCF7L2, “transcription factor 7 like 2”, at 10q25.2–q25.3: a transcription factor in the Wnt signalling pathway. (d) CEU: 52 CC, 32 CT, 15 TT, so q(T) = (32 + 30)/198 = 0.31.
F3. About 45 000 associations for body height: several times more than for type 2 diabetes. Among the strongest: ZBTB38 (3q23), LCORL (4p15.31), GDF5 (20q11.22; rs143384), EFEMP1, CABLES1, LIN28B. Height is extremely polygenic: thousands of loci, each with a tiny effect, together explain a large part of its heritability. GDF5 encodes a TGF-β family growth factor that, according to its NCBI Gene summary, regulates the development of cartilage and joints, and whose mutations cause skeletal disorders such as brachydactyly: a biologically plausible height gene.

title: Exercise: complex traits, heritability & GWAS
text:
Solutions






Solutions: By hand





B1. (a) Shortest aabbcc = 30 cm; tallest AABBCC = 30 + 6 × 5 = 60 cm. 0 to 6 capital alleles: 7 classes (30, 35, …, 60 cm). (b) The number of capital alleles is Binomial(6, ½). Tallest: (½)⁶ = 1/64. Middle class (3 capitals, 45 cm): C(6, 3)/64 = 20/64 = 5/16. (c) A symmetric distribution 1 : 6 : 15 : 20 : 15 : 6 : 1. Environmental variation blurs the classes into a bell-shaped curve.
B2. VE = 50 − 24 − 6 = 20. H² = (24 + 6)/50 = 0.60. h² = 24/50 = 0.48.
B3. (a) h² ≈ 2 × (0.74 − 0.40) = 0.68; c² ≈ 2 × 0.40 − 0.74 = 0.06. (b) 1 − 0.68 − 0.06 = 0.26 (equal to 1 − r(MZ)): unique environment and measurement error. (c) MZ twins may share more similar environments than DZ twins (they are treated more alike), so the excess MZ similarity is not all genetic; also non-additive genetic effects inflate r(MZ) relative to r(DZ).
B4. (a) Slope on one parent = h²/2, so h² = 0.70. (b) 0.70 × 1.0 = 0.7 mm above the mean. (c) Only additive genetic effects are transmitted; the parents’ environmental and non-additive deviations are not. Their offspring regress towards the mean.
B5. R = h² S = 0.48 × 8 = 3.8 units per generation. With h² = 0.05: 0.05 × 8 = 0.4 units. Selection works on heritable variation only; for traits with low h² (many fertility traits, for example) progress is slow.
B6. (a) 800 000 × 0.05 = 40 000; 800 000 × 10⁻⁵ = 8; 800 000 × 5 × 10⁻⁸ = 0.04 (most likely none). (b) The points follow the diagonal: observed = expected −log10 p, with some scatter at the top.
B7. (a) Cases: 700/2000 = 0.35; controls: 560/2000 = 0.28. OR = (700/1300)/(560/1440) = 0.538/0.389 = 1.38. (b) Totals: T 1260, C 2740, N 4000. Expected T in cases = 2000 × 1260/4000 = 630, C in cases 1370; the same for controls. Each cell differs from its expectation by 70: χ² = 70²/630 + 70²/1370 + 70²/630 + 70²/1370 = 7.78 + 3.58 + 7.78 + 3.58 = 22.7. (c) Yes at 5% (critical value 3.84; p ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁶). Not genome-wide significant: 22.7 < 29.7. (d) χ² grows in proportion to N for fixed frequencies, so we need 29.7/22.7 ≈ 1.3 times as many: about 2 600 people (1 300 cases, 1 300 controls).
B8. (a) False: heritability describes variation within a given environment; a change of environment can shift the whole distribution (height rose about 10 cm in a century). (b) False: within-group heritability says nothing about between-group differences (Lewontin’s seeds in two fields). (c) True: if everyone has the same genotype for a trait (five fingers), all the remaining variation is environmental and h² ≈ 0. (d) True: h² depends on the genetic and environmental variance in that population at that time.

title: Exercise: complex traits, heritability & GWAS
text:
Where this leads
Complex traits bring together the whole course: Mendelian segregation at many loci, Hardy–Weinberg allele frequencies, linkage and LD, drift between populations, and gene regulation. The ethics module picks up polygenic scores, direct-to-consumer genomics and the misuse of heritability.
Next: Exercise in R: simulate the polygenic model, estimate h² from Galton’s families with lm, and build a Manhattan plot from GWAS Catalog data with ggplot2.

title: Quiz: complex traits, heritability & GWAS
text:
Short questions on quantitative genetics and genome-wide association studies. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. How can many genes with discrete Mendelian alleles produce a trait such as height, which varies continuously?






Hint





Count the number of genotype classes with 1, 2 and 20 additive loci. Then add the environment.









Answer





With k additive loci there are 2k + 1 classes for the number of “+” alleles, and their frequencies follow a binomial distribution that approaches a normal curve as k grows. Environmental variation blurs the remaining steps, so the trait looks continuous and normally distributed. This is Fisher’s polygenic model (1918).




Q2. Define broad-sense (H²) and narrow-sense (h²) heritability. Which one predicts how much offspring resemble their parents, and why?






Hint





What does a parent pass to a child: a genotype, or one allele at each locus?









Answer





H² = VG/VP, all genetic variance; h² = VA/VP, only the additive part. Narrow-sense h² predicts parent–offspring resemblance and the response to selection, because a parent passes one allele per locus, not a genotype. Dominance (and epistatic) effects depend on combinations of alleles that are broken up in every generation.




Q3. For a trait, the correlation between MZ twins is 0.70 and between DZ twins 0.45. Estimate h² with Falconer’s formula. What assumption does the estimate rely on?






Hint





h² ≈ 2 [r(MZ) − r(DZ)].









Answer





h² ≈ 2 × (0.70 − 0.45) = 0.50. It assumes that MZ and DZ twins have equally similar environments (and no dominance or interaction effects). If MZ twins are treated more alike, h² is overestimated.




Q4. A regression of offspring height on midparent height gives a slope of 0.6. What is h²? What slope would you expect if you regressed offspring on the father only?






Hint





Midparent: slope = h². One parent: slope = h²/2.









Answer





h² ≈ 0.6. On one parent the slope would be about 0.3: a child shares half of its genes with each parent, but the variance of one parent’s height is twice that of the midparent.




Q5. Galton found that children of very tall parents were, on average, shorter than their parents. Explain this “regression towards the mean”. Does it mean that the population gets less variable each generation?






Hint





Part of the parents’ extreme height is due to environment and to non-additive effects, which are not passed on.









Answer





Very tall parents are tall partly because of their additive genetic value and partly because of favourable environment and chance. Only the additive part is passed on, so their children are on average closer to the mean: the predicted deviation is h² times the midparent’s deviation. It does not make the population less variable: each generation, new environmental and segregation variation is added, and some children of average parents are very tall. The variance stays the same.




Q6. The heritability of height in a population is 0.8. Which of these statements are true? (a) 80% of each person’s height is caused by genes. (b) 80% of the variation in height in this population is due to genetic differences. (c) Height cannot be changed by environment. (d) A height difference between two populations must be mostly genetic.






Hint





Heritability is a ratio of variances in one population and environment.









Answer





Only (b) is true (for additive variance, with the caveats of the estimate). (a) is meaningless: a person’s height needs both genes and environment. (c) is false: average height rose by about 10 cm in many countries during the 20th century, with better nutrition. (d) is false: heritability within populations says nothing about the cause of differences between them (Lewontin’s seeds in two fields).




Q7. How does QTL mapping in a cross between two inbred lines differ from a GWAS in a human population? Why does a GWAS give much finer resolution?






Hint





How many meioses separate the individuals studied from the shared ancestors in each design?









Answer





QTL mapping uses a controlled cross (F2 or backcross) and linkage: markers co-segregate with the QTL over long chromosome segments, because there have been only one or two meioses since the parental lines. A GWAS uses unrelated people and association through linkage disequilibrium with ancestral haplotypes that have been broken up by thousands of generations of recombination. Only SNPs very close to the causal variant remain correlated with it, so the peaks are narrow.




Q8. Why is the genome-wide significance threshold 5 × 10⁻⁸ and not 0.05?






Hint





How many tests does a GWAS do, and how many would pass p < 0.05 by chance?









Answer





A GWAS tests about a million independent common variants. At p < 0.05, about 50 000 would be “significant” by chance alone. Dividing 0.05 by 10⁶ (a Bonferroni correction) gives 5 × 10⁻⁸, which keeps the chance of even one false positive in the whole scan at about 5%.




Q9. In a Manhattan plot, a significant locus usually appears as a tall “tower” of many SNPs rather than one point. Why? Is the top SNP the causal variant?






Hint





Think about linkage disequilibrium.









Answer





SNPs near the causal variant are in linkage disequilibrium with it: they lie on the same ancestral haplotypes, so they show the association too, more weakly the further away they are. The top SNP is not necessarily causal: it may just be the best-measured proxy, and the causal variant may not be genotyped at all. Fine-mapping and functional experiments are needed.




Q10. In a QQ plot of a GWAS, all p-values, not just the top few, lie above the diagonal. What could be wrong?






Hint





Recall the Wahlund effect from Hardy–Weinberg.









Answer





Population structure: if cases and controls differ in ancestry, every SNP whose allele frequency differs between the ancestry groups looks associated with the disease. Cryptic relatedness and systematic genotyping differences between cases and controls do the same. (A truly polygenic trait in a very large sample also inflates the QQ plot somewhat, but structure must be ruled out.) Modern GWAS correct for ancestry, for example with principal components of the genotypes.




Q11. rs7903146 in TCF7L2 is the strongest known association for type 2 diabetes, with p-values far below 10⁻¹⁰⁰ in the largest studies. Does this mean that the T allele has a large effect on risk?






Hint





What two things determine the size of a test statistic?









Answer





No. A p-value depends on the effect size and the sample size (and the allele frequency). The odds ratio per T allele is modest, about 1.3–1.4 in many studies in the GWAS Catalog; the tiny p-value comes from samples of hundreds of thousands to millions of people. Most carriers of the risk allele never develop type 2 diabetes.

title: Exercise: Development & model organisms
Exercise: Development & model organisms
Exercise: Development & model organisms
text:
Background
Forward vs reverse genetics. Forward genetics goes from phenotype to gene: mutagenise, screen, then map and clone. Reverse genetics goes from gene to phenotype: knock out or knock down a chosen gene (RNAi, CRISPR) and look. Forward screens are unbiased but miss genes that are redundant or have no visible phenotype. Reverse genetics can show “no phenotype” when a paralog covers for the gene.
Balancers. A balancer chromosome carries several inversions, so it cannot give recombinant products with its homologue. It also carries a dominant marker, such as Curly wings, and a recessive lethal. A stock m/Balancer therefore breeds true: both kinds of homozygote die.
Maternal effect. For a maternal-effect gene, the embryo’s phenotype depends on the mother’s genotype, not its own. The mother loads mRNAs such as bicoid into the egg. Screening for maternal-effect mutants needs homozygous mothers, so it takes one generation more than a zygotic screen.
The segmentation hierarchy. Maternal gradients (Bicoid, Nanos) → gap genes (broad domains; a mutant lacks a block of adjacent segments) → pair-rule genes (7 stripes; a mutant lacks every other segment) → segment-polarity genes (14 stripes; part of each segment is replaced by a mirror image of the rest) → Hox genes (give each segment its identity). Each even-skipped stripe has its own enhancer. Stripe 2 forms where the activators Bicoid and Hunchback are high and the repressors Giant and Krüppel are low.
Hox genes. Homeotic mutations turn one body part into another. The order of Hox genes on the chromosome matches the order of the body regions where they act, from anterior to posterior (colinearity). The Drosophila order is lab, pb, Dfd, Scr, Antp, Ubx, abd-A, Abd-B. Mammals have four Hox clusters.
Epistasis in a pathway. For a pathway where gene A inhibits gene B, which promotes an outcome: when single mutants give opposite phenotypes, the double mutant shows the phenotype of the downstream gene. This is the same logic as in Extensions to Mendel.

title: Exercise: Development & model organisms
text:
By hand
B1. (forward or reverse?) Classify each approach as forward or reverse genetics, and name one limitation of each.

Mutagenise zebrafish with ENU and look for embryos with heart defects.
Inject Drosophila embryos with double-stranded RNA against a gene known to be expressed in the wing.
Make a mouse knockout of the mouse ortholog of a human disease gene.
Screen C. elegans for mutants in which cells that should die survive.

B2. (balancers) A recessive embryonic-lethal mutation m on chromosome 2 is kept in the stock m/CyO. CyO is a balancer with the dominant marker Curly (curled wings), and it is itself lethal as a homozygote.

Cross m/CyO × m/CyO. What fraction of the zygotes have each genotype, and which survive?
What do all the surviving adults look like? Why does this stock never need to be checked for loss of m?
Why does it matter that CyO carries inversions?

B3. (planning a screen) You mutagenise males and want recessive mutations on chromosome 2 that affect the embryo’s segment pattern.

Using a balancer, outline the generations from the mutagenised male (P) until you can see homozygous mutant embryos. In which generation do you look, and what fraction of the embryos in a line are homozygous?
Now you want maternal-effect mutations instead. In which generation can you first score the phenotype? Explain why it is one generation later.

B4. (maternal effect: bicoid) bcd is a recessive maternal-effect mutation. Embryos from bcd/bcd mothers lack head and thorax and die.

bcd/+ female × bcd/+ male: what fraction of the embryos are abnormal?
Among the surviving adult daughters from (a), what fraction are bcd/bcd? What happens to their embryos, whatever the father’s genotype?
bcd/bcd female × +/+ male, and +/+ female × bcd/bcd male: predict the embryos of each cross. What does the difference between these reciprocal crosses tell you?

B5. (classifying segmentation mutants) Larval cuticles of three new mutants:

mutant X: denticle belts are missing in every other segment;
mutant Y: thorax and the first abdominal segments are missing, and the rest is normal;
mutant Z: there are 14 segments, but in each one the posterior half is replaced by a mirror image of the anterior half.

Which class is each mutant? Name one known gene of each class.
B6. (a stripe enhancer) The eve stripe 2 enhancer is activated by Bicoid and Hunchback and repressed by Giant (anterior to the stripe) and Krüppel (posterior to it).

In a Krüppel mutant embryo, how would stripe 2 change? (Look only at stripe 2.)
A fly is heterozygous for a small deletion of the stripe 2 enhancer on one copy of eve. Is eve expressed in the stripe 2 region? From which copy? Use the words cis and trans.
A reporter gene with only the stripe 2 enhancer in front of lacZ is put into flies. Where is β-galactosidase made?

B7. (Hox genes)

Antennapedia gain-of-function alleles (legs instead of antennae) are dominant, while loss-of-function alleles of most Hox genes are recessive. Explain the difference.
Using colinearity and the gene order in the Background, which Drosophila Hox gene acts furthest posterior? Which acts furthest anterior?
Mammals have four Hox clusters. Why do single Hox knockouts in mice often give only mild changes in the vertebrae?

B8. (ordering a pathway by epistasis) In C. elegans, 131 cells die by programmed cell death during development.

ced-3 loss of function: no cell deaths.
ced-9 loss of function: many extra cells die, and the embryo dies.
ced-9; ced-3 double mutant: no cell deaths.
ced-4 loss of function: no cell deaths. The ced-9; ced-4 double mutant also has no cell deaths.

Order ced-3, ced-4 and ced-9 in a pathway leading to cell death, using arrows (→, activates) and ⊣ (inhibits).
B9. (PAX6 and dose) Aniridia (no iris) is autosomal dominant and caused by loss of one copy of PAX6 (haploinsufficiency). Homozygous loss of PAX6 gives no eyes and severe brain defects, and is usually lethal.

Two people with aniridia, each PAX6/−, have children. What are the probabilities of a child with normal eyes, with aniridia, and with complete loss of PAX6?
Mouse Small eye (Sey) behaves the same way. How would you expect Sey/+ × Sey/+ litters to look at birth?

B10. (from a mosaic founder to a homozygous mutant) A CRISPR knockout founder (F0) is usually a mosaic: different cells carry different edits, or none. Explain how you get homozygous mutants of one defined allele from such a founder, and in which generation they first appear. What fraction of that generation’s offspring is homozygous?

title: Exercise: Development & model organisms
text:
Find it
F1. (NCBI Gene and Ensembl) Search NCBI Gene for human PAX6. Give the Gene ID and the cytogenetic location. Then search Ensembl for the same gene and give its Ensembl gene ID (it starts with ENSG).
F2. (MGI, mouse) Search MGI for mouse Pax6. Which chromosome is it on? In the gene’s allele list, find the classic spontaneous allele behind the Small eye phenotype and write its allele symbol.
F3. (FlyBase) In FlyBase, look up eyeless (ey), twin of eyeless (toy), Ultrabithorax (Ubx) and labial (lab). For each, give the chromosome or chromosome arm. Give the FlyBase gene ID (FBgn…) of ey and of Ubx.
F4. (the Alliance of Genome Resources) Open the human PAX6 page at the Alliance of Genome Resources and scroll to Orthology.

With the default (stringent) filter, which fly gene is listed as an ortholog? Is ey there?
Relax the filter. Which fly gene appears now, and how many methods support it?
List the zebrafish and worm orthologs and their chromosomes. Use ZFIN and WormBase if the Alliance page does not show the chromosome.
Now open the fly gene lab and list its stringent human orthologs. What do they have in common?







Hint for F4





The orthology table has a stringency setting above it. “Best” or “stringent” keeps only calls supported by several methods and marked as best matches. Ortholog calls are predictions made by algorithms, so different methods and databases can disagree.

title: Exercise: Development & model organisms
text:
Solutions






Solutions: By hand





B1.

Forward. It finds only genes whose loss gives a visible, specific heart phenotype; it misses redundant genes and genes needed earlier for survival.
Reverse (knockdown). The knockdown may be incomplete, and the dsRNA may hit other genes with similar sequence (off-target effects).
Reverse. The mouse ortholog may be redundant with a paralog, so the knockout can show no phenotype; or the knockout can be lethal, which hides later roles. A conditional (Cre/lox) knockout gets round that.
Forward. This is the screen that found the ced genes. It needs a way to see the surviving cells, and it misses genes that are essential for viability.

B2.

¼ m/m (die as embryos), ½ m/CyO, ¼ CyO/CyO (die).
Every surviving adult is m/CyO and has Curly wings. Because both homozygotes die, every survivor must carry m. The stock cannot lose the mutation without anyone selecting for it.
Without the inversions, crossing over between CyO and the m chromosome would make recombinants that separate m from its neighbours, or that move the lethal and the marker apart. The inversions make crossover products unbalanced, so they do not survive, and the chromosome stays intact.

B3.

P: mutagenised male × balancer female. F1: individual males, each carrying one mutagenised chromosome (m*) over a balancer. Cross each F1 male to the balancer stock again, to found a line. F2: collect m*/Balancer brothers and sisters in each line (identified by the marker). F2 × F2 within the line gives F3 embryos, of which ¼ are m*/m*. You score the F3 embryos (dead embryos with an abnormal cuticle).
A maternal-effect phenotype shows only in the embryos of a homozygous mother. So the F3 m*/m* females must survive to adulthood (they look normal), and you score their embryos, the F4. That is one generation later.

B4.

None. All the mothers are bcd/+, so all the eggs get bicoid mRNA. The embryos’ own genotype does not matter.
¼ of all daughters are bcd/bcd. They look normal, because their bcd/+ mother gave them bicoid mRNA. But all of their embryos lack head and thorax, whatever the father is.
bcd/bcd female × +/+ male: all the embryos are abnormal, although they are bcd/+. +/+ female × bcd/bcd male: all normal. Reciprocal crosses differ, and the mother’s genotype decides. That is the signature of a maternal effect. Compare sex linkage (Part 2), organelle inheritance (Part 5) and imprinting (Part 6).

B5. - X: pair-rule (missing every other segment), e.g. even-skipped or fushi tarazu. - Y: gap (a block of adjacent segments missing), e.g. Krüppel. hunchback or knirps would also do. - Z: segment polarity (a mirror-image duplication within each segment), e.g. wingless or hedgehog.
B6.

Krüppel sets the posterior border of stripe 2. Without it, stripe 2 widens posteriorly into the region where Krüppel would normally repress it.
Yes. The enhancer is cis-acting: it controls only the copy of eve on the same chromosome. In the stripe 2 region, the intact copy is expressed, and the copy with the deleted enhancer is not. The transcription factors (Bicoid, Hunchback, Giant, Krüppel) are trans-acting and reach both copies, but only the intact copy has the binding sites.
Only in stripe 2. The enhancer alone is enough to reproduce that one stripe, which is how enhancers are defined experimentally.

B7.

A gain-of-function allele makes a normal Antp protein in the wrong place (the head). One such copy is enough to switch on a leg programme, so it is dominant. A loss-of-function allele leaves one working copy, and for most Hox genes half the dose is enough, so it is recessive.
Abd-B acts furthest posterior; lab furthest anterior.
The four clusters contain paralogs, for example Hoxa1, Hoxb1 and Hoxd1, which partly cover for each other (redundancy). Full transformations need double or triple knockouts of a paralog group.

B8. ced-9 ⊣ ced-4 → ced-3 → cell death. - ced-3 and ced-4 are needed for death, so loss of either means no deaths. ced-9 prevents death, so its loss means extra deaths. - The ced-9; ced-3 and ced-9; ced-4 doubles look like ced-3 and ced-4: no deaths. So ced-3 and ced-4 act downstream of ced-9. - These data alone don’t order ced-4 and ced-3 relative to each other. Biochemistry shows that CED-4 activates the caspase CED-3. Their human counterparts are BCL2 (ced-9), APAF1 (ced-4) and caspases (ced-3).
B9.

PAX6/− × PAX6/−: ¼ +/+ (normal eyes), ½ +/− (aniridia), ¼ −/− (no eyes, usually lethal).
About ¼ wild-type, ½ Sey/+ with small eyes, and ¼ Sey/Sey with no eyes and no nose, which die at birth. Among the survivors you see roughly 1 normal : 2 small-eyed, the same 2 : 1 logic as the yellow-mouse lethal allele in Extensions to Mendel.

B10. Cross the mosaic F0 to wild type. The F1 offspring that inherited an edited chromosome through the F0’s germ line are heterozygous for one defined allele. Sequence the F1 to find carriers of the allele you want, for example a frameshift. Cross two F1 heterozygotes carrying the same allele: in the F2, ¼ are homozygous mutants. This is Mendel’s monohybrid cross again.









Solutions: Find it





F1. NCBI Gene ID 5080, location 11p13. Ensembl gene ID ENSG00000007372. Click path: NCBI Gene → search “PAX6 human” → the top hit is PAX6, Homo sapiens; the location is in the summary box. In Ensembl, search PAX6 → Human gene.
F2. Mouse Pax6 is on chromosome 2. The Small eye allele is Pax6Sey. Click path: MGI → search Pax6 → gene detail page → Mutations, alleles, and phenotypes.
F3. - ey (FBgn0005558) and toy are both on chromosome 4, the small “dot” chromosome. - Ubx (FBgn0003944) and lab are both on 3R, in the Hox complexes (bithorax and Antennapedia complexes).
The location is in the General Information or Genomic Location section of each FlyBase gene report.
F4.

With the stringent filter, the fly ortholog listed is toy (twin of eyeless). ey is not listed.
With a relaxed filter, ey appears, supported by only one method. Ortholog calls are predictions. ey and toy come from a duplication in the insect lineage, and methods disagree on which one to pair with human PAX6. This is the “two paralogs” complication mentioned in the lecture.
Zebrafish: pax6a on chr 25 and pax6b on chr 7, two copies from the teleost genome duplication. Worm: vab-3 on the X chromosome.
lab → HOXA1, HOXB1 and HOXD1. They are all paralog group 1, the most anterior Hox genes, one in each of three of the four mammalian clusters. One fly gene has several human orthologs because the Hox cluster was duplicated in the vertebrate lineage.

title: Exercise: Development & model organisms
text:
Where this leads
The same genes keep coming back. The ced-9 counterpart BCL2 is an oncogene in follicular lymphoma, and Hox and PAX genes are rearranged in some cancers (Cancer genetics). The ortholog tables you just searched are the input for the R page, where you build the whole table across six species.
Next: Exercise in R: join the gene and ortholog tables and draw a presence/absence heat map across model organisms.

title: Quiz: Development & model organisms
text:
Short questions on the genetic analysis of development. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. What is the difference between forward and reverse genetics? Give one strength of each.






Hint





Which do you start from: a phenotype or a gene?









Answer





Forward genetics starts from a phenotype: random mutagenesis, screen, then identify the gene. Strength: unbiased; it finds genes nobody suspected. Reverse genetics starts from a known gene: disrupt it on purpose (RNAi, CRISPR) and look for a phenotype. Strength: targeted; you can test any gene, including ones whose mutants would never be noticed in a screen.




Q2. In the Nüsslein-Volhard–Wieschaus screen, why were the new mutations kept over a balancer chromosome?






Hint





The mutations were recessive lethals. How do you keep a lethal allele in a stock?









Answer





A recessive lethal can only be kept in heterozygotes. A balancer carries inversions that suppress recombination (so the mutation stays on its chromosome together with nearby markers), a dominant visible marker (so you can see who carries it), and its own recessive lethal (so balancer homozygotes die). A m/balancer stock then breeds true: m/m and balancer/balancer die, and only m/balancer adults survive, generation after generation, without selection.




Q3. A female fly is homozygous for a recessive maternal-effect mutation bcd. She looks normal. Her embryos, from a cross with a wild-type male, all lack head and thorax. Explain both observations.






Hint





Where does bicoid mRNA in the egg come from?









Answer





bicoid mRNA is made by the mother and placed at the anterior of the egg. The bcd/bcd female developed from an egg that her bcd/+ mother supplied with normal bicoid mRNA, so she is normal. She herself cannot supply any, so all her embryos lack the anterior gradient, whatever their own genotype (here all bcd/+).




Q4. Put these in the order in which they act: segment-polarity genes, maternal genes, Hox genes, gap genes, pair-rule genes. How many stripes do pair-rule and segment-polarity genes make?






Hint





The pattern gets finer at each step.









Answer





Maternal → gap → pair-rule (7 stripes) → segment polarity (14 stripes) → Hox (identity of each segment). (Hox genes are switched on by the gap and pair-rule genes, so they act in parallel with the later steps.)




Q5. A fly embryo lacks every other segment. Which class of gene is probably mutated? Which class if a block of several neighbouring segments is missing?






Hint





The class names describe the mutant phenotypes.









Answer





Every other segment missing: a pair-rule gene. A block of adjacent segments missing: a gap gene.




Q6. Deleting the even-skipped stripe 2 enhancer removes stripe 2 but leaves the other six stripes. What does this tell you about how eve is regulated? Is the deletion cis- or trans-acting?






Hint





How many enhancers does eve have?









Answer





eve has separate, modular enhancers for different stripes, each reading a different combination of transcription factors (stripe 2: activated by Bicoid and Hunchback, repressed by Giant and Krüppel). The deletion is cis-acting: it affects only the eve copy on the same chromosome.




Q7. Antennapedia gain-of-function alleles are dominant and give legs instead of antennae. Why are they dominant?






Hint





Is the protein abnormal, or is it in the wrong place?









Answer





The mutations (often rearrangements) put the normal Antp coding sequence under a regulatory region active in the head. One such allele is enough to make Antp protein in the antenna disc, where it switches the disc to a leg (thoracic) identity. A gain of expression in a new place is dominant: the normal allele cannot prevent it.




Q8. What is colinearity of Hox genes?






Hint





Compare the order of genes on the chromosome with the order of body regions.









Answer





The order of Hox genes along the chromosome matches the order of the body regions in which they act, from anterior (3′ end of the cluster) to posterior (5′ end). In vertebrates the 3′ genes are also expressed earlier than the 5′ genes (temporal colinearity).




Q9. Humans heterozygous for a PAX6 loss-of-function mutation have aniridia. What does this tell you about the dosage of PAX6? How would you describe the inheritance of aniridia?






Hint





Extensions to Mendel: haplosufficiency vs haploinsufficiency.









Answer





One working copy is not enough: PAX6 is haploinsufficient. Aniridia is therefore inherited as an autosomal dominant trait, although the mutant allele is a simple loss of function.




Q10. In C. elegans, ced-9 loss-of-function mutants lose many cells by extra cell death, but ced-9; ced-3 double mutants have no extra deaths. Which gene acts downstream?






Hint





Epistasis: which single-mutant phenotype does the double mutant show?









Answer





The double mutant looks like ced-3 (no deaths), so ced-3 is epistatic and acts downstream: CED-9 normally inhibits the death programme, and CED-3 (a caspase) carries it out. Without CED-3, losing the inhibitor makes no difference.




Q11. A CRISPR–Cas9 guide is designed against exon 2 of a mouse gene. Why do most edited alleles behave as null alleles, and why must the founder mice be crossed before you study the phenotype?






Hint





What does end joining usually leave behind? And are all cells of the founder edited the same way?









Answer





Cas9 cuts; error-prone end joining usually leaves a small insertion or deletion. Unless it is a multiple of 3 nt, it shifts the reading frame, giving a premature stop codon and no working protein. Founders are usually mosaics (different cells carry different edits, or none), so you cross them to get offspring that carry one defined allele in every cell, then intercross heterozygotes to get homozygotes (¼ of the progeny).

title: Exercise in R: digital analysis of DNA
Exercise in R: digital analysis of DNA
Exercise in R: digital analysis of DNA
text:
Before you start
This page builds on the Exercise, so do the by-hand part (B1–B3) and the gel demo first. You need the packages dplyr, stringr and ggplot2. Download the two FASTA files and save them in a data/ folder of your R project:

lambda.fasta: the genome of phage λ, NCBI NC_001416.1 (48,502 bp; the same file you get in Find it F5).
hbb_pcr.fasta: the 500-bp HBB PCR product from the sickle-cell test (normal allele), taken from the human genome GRCh38 (chr11:5,226,722–5,227,221, minus strand, Ensembl release 116).

See data/README.md for where the files come from.

title: Exercise in R: digital analysis of DNA
text:
Tasks
New idiom: str_locate_all(). str_locate_all(string, pattern) from stringr finds every match of a pattern in a string and returns, for each string, a matrix with one row per match and the columns start and end. The pattern is a regular expression, so "GAATTC" matches itself, "GAATTC|GGATCC" matches either site, and "CT[ACGT]AG" matches CTAAG, CTCAG, CTGAG and CTTAG (the DdeI site, N = any base). In the DNA recap unit you used stringr for single sequences; here we search a whole genome.
A FASTA file is plain text: one header line starting with >, then the sequence split over many lines. There are packages that read FASTA, but it is easy to do by hand, and doing it once shows you what the format is.
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)
R1. (read a FASTA file by hand) Read the λ genome with readLines(), which gives one string per line. Look at the first line, drop it, and glue the rest together with paste(..., collapse = ""). Check the length with nchar() against the NCBI record (Find it F5).
lines <- readLines("data/lambda.fasta")
length(lines)
lines[1]
lambda <- paste(lines[-1], collapse = "")   # lines[-1]: every line except the first
nchar(lambda)
str_sub(lambda, 1, 12)
The first 12 bases are the single-stranded “cos” end of the λ genome. How many sequence lines does the file have, and how many bases per line?
R2. (find the sites) First check with a reverse-complement function (as in the DNA recap unit) that the EcoRI and BamHI sites are palindromes. Then find all EcoRI sites with str_locate_all(). The result is a list with one matrix per input string; we have one string, so take [[1]]. For BamHI, keep only the start column.
revcomp <- function(s) {
  paste(rev(strsplit(chartr("ACGT", "TGCA", s), "")[[1]]), collapse = "")
}
revcomp("GAATTC")
revcomp("GGATCC")

eco <- str_locate_all(lambda, "GAATTC")[[1]]
eco
bam <- str_locate_all(lambda, "GGATCC")[[1]]
bam[, "start"]
How many sites does each enzyme have? Compare with the lecture table and with REBASE (Find it F4).
R3. (from sites to fragments) EcoRI cuts between the G and the first A (G^AATTC). If a site starts at position s, there are s bases to the left of the cut, so the cut position is s + offset − 1 with offset 1. Write a function digest(seq, site, offset = 1) that returns the fragment sizes of a linear molecule, largest first. diff() gives the differences between neighbouring numbers, which are exactly the fragment lengths if you add the two ends (0 and the length) to the cut positions. Use it for EcoRI, BamHI and the double digest, and check that the fragments add up to the genome.
digest <- function(seq, site, offset = 1) {
  starts <- str_locate_all(seq, site)[[1]][, "start"]
  cuts <- starts + offset - 1                  # bases to the left of each cut
  ends <- c(0, sort(cuts), nchar(seq))
  sort(diff(ends), decreasing = TRUE)
}
digest(lambda, "GAATTC")
digest(lambda, "GGATCC")
sum(digest(lambda, "GAATTC"))
both <- digest(lambda, "GAATTC|GGATCC")
both
length(both)
Compare with the restriction-mapping slide in the lecture and with the gel demo.
R4. (the λ/HindIII ladder) The classic λ/HindIII ladder has the bands 23,130, 9,416, 6,557, 4,361, 2,322, 2,027, 564 and 125 bp. Digest the λ sequence with HindIII (A^AGCTT, offset 1) and compare with setdiff(). Which fragment differs, and what does that tell you about the DNA used to make the ladder? (This is question E2 in the exercise.)
hind <- digest(lambda, "AAGCTT")
hind
ladder <- c(23130, 9416, 6557, 4361, 2322, 2027, 564, 125)
setdiff(hind, ladder)
setdiff(ladder, hind)
6557 + 125
R5. (a virtual gel) Put the ladder and the three digests in one table with bind_rows(), one row per band, and plot each band as a short wide tile. On a log y-axis, large fragments end up at the top and small ones at the bottom, just like a real gel. Use factor(..., levels = ...) to keep the lanes in order.
gel <- bind_rows(
  tibble(lane = "λ/HindIII ladder", size = ladder),
  tibble(lane = "EcoRI", size = digest(lambda, "GAATTC")),
  tibble(lane = "BamHI", size = digest(lambda, "GGATCC")),
  tibble(lane = "EcoRI + BamHI", size = both)
) |>
  mutate(lane = factor(lane, levels = c("λ/HindIII ladder", "EcoRI", "BamHI", "EcoRI + BamHI")))
gel |> count(lane)

ggplot(gel, aes(x = lane, y = size)) +
  geom_tile(width = 0.6, height = 0.012, fill = "#ffe3a3") +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(200, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 20000),
                labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "fragment size (bp, log scale)", title = "Virtual gel of phage λ DNA") +
  theme_dark(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#1f262d"),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
(On a log axis, height = 0.012 is measured in log10 units, so every band has the same thickness.) Which bands in the double digest would you expect to merge on a real gel?
R6. (diagnosing sickle cell in R) Read the HBB PCR product the same way. The A of the ATG start codon is at position 201, so codon 7 (GAG) is at positions 219–221 and the HbS change (A → T) is at position 220. Make the HbS version by replacing that base with str_sub() <-, then digest both alleles with DdeI (pattern "CT[ACGT]AG", offset 1).
hl <- readLines("data/hbb_pcr.fasta")
hbbA <- paste(hl[-1], collapse = "")
nchar(hbbA)
str_sub(hbbA, 201, 221)          # codons 1-7
hbbS <- hbbA
str_sub(hbbS, 220, 220) <- "T"
str_sub(hbbS, 201, 221)
dde <- "CT[ACGT]AG"
str_locate_all(hbbA, dde)[[1]][, "start"]
digest(hbbA, dde)
digest(hbbS, dde)
Translate codons 1–7 in your head (or with the codon table from the Mutation unit) for both alleles. Do the fragments agree with the table in the exercise Background?
