[1] 201 180  82  37
[1] 381  82  37
Codons 1–7 read ATG GTG CAT CTG ACT CCT GAG = Met-Val-His-Leu-Thr-Pro-Glu in HbA and …CCT GTG = …Pro-Val in HbS. The DdeI site at 217 (CTGAG) is lost in HbS (CTGTG), so the 180 and 201 bp fragments become one fragment of 381 bp, as in the Background table and the gel demo.

title: Exercise in R: digital analysis of DNA
text:
Where this leads
In Genome annotation you read a much bigger table: every human protein-coding gene from Ensembl BioMart, with read_tsv(), and you count genes per chromosome. The str_locate_all() idea comes back in the ORF finder demo, which searches all six reading frames for start and stop codons.

title: Digital analysis of DNA
text:
About this lecture
So far we have studied genes through phenotypes: round or wrinkled, affected or not. From here on we also read the DNA itself. Four tools make that possible, and together they turn a gene into data you can store, compare and search.

Cut: restriction enzymes recognise short palindromic sites and cut there.
Sort: gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size; a ladder gives the scale.
Copy: cloning in a plasmid vector (briefly), and the polymerase chain reaction (PCR), which copies one stretch of DNA a billion-fold.
Read: Sanger sequencing reads one PCR product; next-generation sequencing reads millions of short pieces at once.

The running example is the sickle-cell allele of HBB from Genetics as information: we will detect it in a family with PCR and a restriction enzyme.
Book: Hartwell, Genetics: From Genes to Genomes, chapter on digital analysis of DNA.

This lecture opens Part 4, the most bioinformatic block of the course, but the questions stay genetic: which allele does this person carry, and how do we know? Remind students of HbS from the first unit: one base change, GAG to GTG in codon 7 (traditionally codon 6). Today we see how a lab detects that one base. The book calls this “digital” because DNA, once read, is a string of four letters that can be copied, compared and searched like any other digital data. The exercise has two demos (a virtual gel and a PCR curve) and the R part finds restriction sites in the genome of phage lambda.

title: Digital analysis of DNA
text:
Cut, sort, copy, read









Tool
What it does
What it gives you
Used for




Restriction enzyme
cuts at a specific 4–8 bp site
fragments of predictable size
mapping, cloning, detecting some mutations


Gel electrophoresis
separates fragments by size
bands; size from a ladder
checking digests and PCR products


Cloning vector
carries a fragment into bacteria, which copy it
many identical copies, kept for later
libraries, protein expression, transgenics


PCR
copies the DNA between two primers
109-fold more of one region
diagnostics, genotyping, sequencing input


Sanger sequencing
reads one PCR product
~800 bases of high-quality sequence
confirming a variant


Next-generation sequencing
reads millions of short fragments
whole genomes, exomes, transcriptomes
finding variants genome-wide



The tools combine: PCR a region, cut it, run it on a gel; or PCR it and sequence it.

This slide is the map of the lecture. Read it as a pipeline: you usually cannot see one gene in three billion base pairs, so you first make many copies of it (PCR or cloning), then you look at it, either by its size on a gel or by reading the bases. Each tool has a characteristic output, and students should be able to say which tool answers which question. For example: “is this person a carrier of HbS?” can be answered by PCR plus DdeI digestion plus a gel, or by PCR plus Sanger sequencing. “Which variants does this person carry in all 20,000 genes?” needs next-generation sequencing.

title: Digital analysis of DNA
text:
Restriction enzymes cut at palindromes


Bacteria make restriction enzymes to cut invading phage DNA; they protect their own DNA by methylating the same sites.
The site is usually a palindrome: the two strands read the same 5’→3’. The enzyme is a dimer and each half cuts one strand.
A staggered cut leaves sticky ends that can pair with any other end cut by the same enzyme.


Restriction enzymes were discovered as the reason some phages grow poorly on certain bacterial strains: the phage DNA is “restricted”, cut up, on entry. The bacterium’s own DNA carries a methyl group at the same sites, added by a matching methyltransferase, so it is not cut. The names come from the organism: EcoRI from Escherichia coli strain RY13, HindIII from Haemophilus influenzae Rd, BamHI from Bacillus amyloliquefaciens. Palindrome here means the sequence equals its own reverse complement, which students can check with the reverse-complement function from the DNA recap unit. Sticky ends are what made recombinant DNA possible in the 1970s: cut a human gene and a plasmid with EcoRI, mix, and the ends pair; DNA ligase seals them.

title: Digital analysis of DNA
section: How often does an enzyme cut?
text:
How often does an enzyme cut?
If the four bases were equally common and random, a given site of n specified bases would occur once every 4n bp.










Enzyme
Site
Expected spacing
Expected in phage λ (48,502 bp)
Actual in λ




EcoRI
GAATTC
46 = 4,096 bp
11.8
5


BamHI
GGATCC
4,096 bp
11.8
5


HindIII
AAGCTT
4,096 bp
11.8
6


DdeI
CTNAG (N = any)
44 = 256 bp
189
104




6-bp cutters (“six-cutters”) give fragments of a few kb; 4-bp cutters give a few hundred bp.
Real DNA is not random, so actual counts differ from the expectation. In the R exercise you count the λ sites yourself.


The 4 to the n rule is a useful first estimate and a nice probability exercise: each position must match, with probability one quarter, independently, so the product rule from Part 1 gives one quarter to the power n. For DdeI, the N matches anything, so only four positions count. The actual numbers for phage lambda come from the reference sequence NC_001416.1 and agree with REBASE’s own counts. Lambda has fewer sites than expected for all four enzymes. One reason is that many phages avoid the sites of their hosts’ restriction enzymes over evolutionary time, since phages with fewer sites survive restriction better. Do not overclaim this for lambda in particular; the general point is that sequence composition matters.

title: Digital analysis of DNA
section: Gel electrophoresis: sorting fragments by size
text:
Gel electrophoresis: sorting fragments by size


DNA has a negative phosphate backbone, so it moves towards the + electrode. The agarose mesh slows long molecules more.
Distance run is roughly linear in log(size) over the gel’s useful range. Use a ladder of known sizes to read off unknown bands.
Higher % agarose resolves short fragments (100–1,000 bp); lower % resolves long ones (1–20 kb).


Every DNA molecule has the same charge per unit length, so charge alone would not separate them; it is the gel matrix that does, by sieving. That is why distance depends on size, and in practice on the log of size. Show how to read the plot: find the unknown band’s distance, go up to the line, read across. Doing it by eye on a log scale is a skill students will need in the lab. Two practical details: the DNA is invisible until stained, and band brightness depends on mass, so a 37 bp fragment carries much less stain than a 400 bp fragment present in the same number of copies. Very large fragments (above about 20 to 30 kb) all run together near the well on a normal gel; separating them needs pulsed-field electrophoresis.

title: Digital analysis of DNA
section: Restriction mapping: where are the sites?
text:
Restriction mapping: where are the sites?
Phage λ DNA (48,502 bp, linear), digested once with each enzyme and once with both:








Digest
Fragments (bp)
Number




EcoRI
21,226 · 7,421 · 5,804 · 5,643 · 4,878 · 3,530
6


BamHI
16,841 · 7,233 · 6,770 · 6,527 · 5,626 · 5,505
6


EcoRI + BamHI
15,721 · 5,505 · 4,669 · 3,775 · 3,758 · 3,530 · 3,240 · 2,752 · 2,564 · 1,868 · 1,120
11




A linear molecule with k sites gives k + 1 fragments; a circular one gives k.
Fragments always sum to the full length: a check on your reading of the gel.
A fragment that survives the double digest unchanged (5,505; 3,530) contains no site for the other enzyme. Fragments that split show where the other sites are.


Restriction mapping is the oldest kind of physical map, and the logic is a puzzle like the three-point cross in Part 2: you have pieces and must find the order. Walk through one example. The BamHI 5,505 fragment survives the double digest, so it has no EcoRI site; it is at an end of the molecule (it is in fact the left end, positions 1 to 5,505). The EcoRI 21,226 fragment, the left end, is cut by BamHI into 5,505 and 15,721. The numbers are computed from the real sequence; students reproduce them in R. Note that 3,775 and 3,758 differ by only 17 bp and would look like one bright band on a gel: a gel cannot resolve everything.

title: Digital analysis of DNA
text:
Cloning vectors (briefly)


A vector is a small DNA molecule that bacteria copy for you. The classic example is the plasmid pUC19 (2,686 bp, circular):







Part
Job




origin of replication
many copies per cell


antibiotic-resistance gene (bla, ampicillin)
only cells with the plasmid survive


multiple cloning site (MCS)
one site each for EcoRI, BamHI, HindIII, PstI, …


lacZα around the MCS
an insert disrupts it: white instead of blue colonies




Cloning in four steps

Cut vector and insert with the same enzyme(s).
Mix; sticky ends pair; ligase seals them.
Transform E. coli; select on ampicillin.
Pick a white colony, grow it, check the insert with a digest and a gel.


Today PCR has replaced cloning for most diagnostic work; cloning is still used to make proteins and transgenic organisms.

Keep this short: the course book covers vectors in more detail, and the lab course does the practical work. The key ideas are the selectable marker and the unique sites. In pUC19, the EcoRI, BamHI, HindIII and PstI sites each occur once, all inside the multiple cloning site, so one cut opens the circle into a single linear 2,686 bp piece; students can check this in the gel demo. Blue-white screening: the lacZ alpha fragment complements a defective lacZ in the host, giving blue colonies on X-gal; an insert in the MCS breaks lacZ alpha and gives white colonies. This links back to the lac operon from 5MO103. Vectors come back in the BLAST task of the exercise: the mystery read hits fly transformation vectors, because they carry the white gene as a marker.

title: Digital analysis of DNA
section: PCR: copying one region a billion times
text:
PCR: copying one region a billion times


Two primers define the product: one on each strand, 3’ ends pointing towards each other.
Each cycle: denature (~95 °C), anneal primers (~55–65 °C), extend with a heat-stable polymerase (72 °C).
Ingredients: template DNA, two primers, dNTPs, Mg2+, buffer, Taq polymerase.


PCR was invented by Kary Mullis in the 1980s. The trick that made it practical was the polymerase from Thermus aquaticus, a bacterium from hot springs, which survives the denaturation step, so you do not have to add new enzyme every cycle. Make sure students see why the product has defined ends: the first cycles make longer strands that start at a primer but run past the other primer site, but from cycle 3 on, strands that start at one primer and end at the other dominate, and after 30 cycles they are essentially all of the product. The product length is therefore set by the primer positions, which is what Primer-BLAST reports in the exercise.

title: Digital analysis of DNA
text:
Exponential amplification, efficiency and plateau








Cycles
Ideal copies from 1 template (2n)
At 90% efficiency (1.9n)




10
1,024
613


20
1.0 × 106
3.8 × 105


30
1.1 × 109
2.3 × 108




Real reactions copy a fraction E of the molecules per cycle: N = N0 (1 + E)n.
The reaction plateaus (~1012 copies in 50 µl) when primers and dNTPs run out.
qPCR measures the cycle where the product crosses a threshold (Ct). 10× more template crosses about log(10)/log(1 + E) ≈ 3.3 cycles earlier (at E = 1).


The point of this table is that exponential growth is extremely sensitive to both the number of cycles and the efficiency: 90 percent instead of 100 percent efficiency gives five times fewer copies after 30 cycles. That is why quantitative PCR does not read the end point, which saturates, but the threshold cycle, which sits in the exponential phase. The rule of 3.3 cycles per ten-fold is worth deriving on the board: 2 to the power x equals 10 gives x equals log 10 over log 2, about 3.32. At 90 percent efficiency it is log 10 over log 1.9, about 3.6, which the demo shows. Sensitivity has a dark side: a single contaminating molecule can be amplified too, so every PCR has a no-template control.

title: Digital analysis of DNA
text:
Designing primers







Rule of thumb
Why




Length 18–25 nt
long enough to be unique in a 3 × 109 bp genome (418 ≈ 7 × 1010)


GC content 40–60%
stable binding without sticking everywhere


Melting temperature (Tm) ~55–65 °C, the two primers within ~2–5 °C
both bind well at the same annealing temperature


A G or C at the 3’ end, but no run of G/C
the polymerase starts from a firmly paired 3’ end


No complementarity between or within primers, especially at 3’ ends
avoids primer-dimers and hairpins


Unique in the genome (check with Primer-BLAST)
one product, not several



Quick estimate (Wallace rule, for short primers): Tm ≈ 2 °C × (A + T) + 4 °C × (G + C).

The 4 to the 18 argument mirrors the restriction-site calculation: a random 18-mer occurs about once per 7 times ten to the ten bases, more than the genome size, so most 18-mers are unique. Real genomes are full of repeats, so uniqueness must be checked, and that is what Primer-BLAST does: it designs primers and searches them against the genome or the RefSeq transcripts. Primer-dimers are the classic failure: two primers with complementary 3’ ends prime on each other and make a short product that competes with the target, especially when the template is scarce. The second demo shows this. The Wallace rule is crude; Primer-BLAST uses a better model and reports slightly different numbers.

title: Digital analysis of DNA
section: Try it: PCR, cycle by cycle
text:
Try it: PCR, cycle by cycle




Interactive demo. It starts on the “realistic” preset: 1,000 starting copies, 90 percent efficiency, 35 cycles, log axis, with a dashed curve for ten times less template. Point out the straight line on the log axis during the exponential phase, the plateau near 10 to the 12, and that the dashed curve is a parallel line shifted 3.6 cycles to the right. Untick “log y-axis”: on a linear axis nothing seems to happen for 20 cycles, then the curve shoots up and flattens. That is the same data. Then click “10 templates + primer-dimer” and “no-template control”: with almost no template, primer-dimers made from the primers alone can reach the detection threshold by cycle 39 or so. That is why late signals in a no-template control mean trouble, and why diagnostic PCR uses a cycle cut-off.

title: Digital analysis of DNA
section: PCR plus a restriction enzyme: genotyping HbS
text:
PCR plus a restriction enzyme: genotyping HbS

The sickle-cell change (codon 7 GAG → GTG, c.20A>T) destroys a DdeI site (CTGAG → CTGTG). Amplify 500 bp around it, cut with DdeI, run a gel: AA = HbA/HbA, AS = carrier, SS = sickle-cell disease.

This is a classic diagnostic method called PCR-RFLP. It ties together everything so far: the mutation from Genetics as information and from the Mutation unit, PCR to get enough DNA from a cheek swab or a blood spot, a restriction enzyme to “read” one base, and a gel to see the result. The primers and fragment sizes are real: the 500 bp product spans exon 1 and intron 1 of HBB on chromosome 11 (GRCh38), and we checked with Primer-BLAST that the primers give a single product in the human genome. The carrier lane shows both alleles: at the DNA level, HbA and HbS are codominant, even though sickle-cell disease is recessive at the level of the phenotype. Before PCR, the same site was detected with the enzyme MstII on Southern blots. In a pedigree, this test turns “probably a carrier, 2/3” into a yes or no.

title: Digital analysis of DNA
text:
Try it: a virtual gel




Interactive demo. It starts on the HBB PCR product from a carrier, cut with DdeI on a 2 percent gel. Ask the room to estimate the sizes from the 100 bp ladder before ticking “show fragment sizes”. Switch between the three genotypes. Then switch to phage lambda with EcoRI and BamHI on a 0.7 percent gel: six, six and eleven bands, and some of the double-digest bands overlap. Then pUC19: each single enzyme gives one band (one site, circular plasmid, so one linear fragment of 2,686 bp), and EcoRI plus HindIII cuts out the 51 bp stretch of the multiple cloning site, which is too faint and too small to see well. Note that the uncut plasmid runs as a supercoiled band, ahead of its true size.

title: Digital analysis of DNA
text:
Sanger sequencing: reading one product


A primer, a polymerase, normal dNTPs and a small amount of four dye-labelled dideoxynucleotides (ddNTPs). A ddNTP lacks the 3’-OH, so the chain stops there.
The result is a set of products ending at every position; capillary electrophoresis sorts them by length, and the dye colour of each gives the base.


Frederick Sanger published the dideoxy method in 1977, and it read the first human genome together with clever automation. The principle uses the replication chemistry from the DNA recap unit: DNA polymerase needs a free 3’ hydroxyl to add the next nucleotide. A dideoxynucleotide has a hydrogen there instead, so once it is built in, synthesis stops. Because the ddNTPs are rare compared with normal dNTPs, termination happens at random, and among millions of molecules every position is represented. Electrophoresis in a thin capillary separates products that differ by one base, which is much finer than an agarose gel.

title: Digital analysis of DNA
text:
Reading a Sanger trace







What you see
What it means




one clean peak per position
a single sequence: homozygous at that site, or a cloned molecule


two overlapping peaks of about half height at one position
a heterozygous SNP (two alleles in the PCR product)


everything doubles after one point
a heterozygous indel: the two alleles are shifted relative to each other


messy start (first ~30 bases) and fading end (after ~800)
normal limits of the method



An HbA/HbS carrier shows an A and a T peak together at c.20 (forward strand).

Reading a trace is a practical skill students may meet in lab courses and in clinical genetics reports. The double peak is the sequencing version of the carrier lane in the PCR-RFLP gel: both alleles are amplified and both are read at once. Make the link to the pedigree unit: a Sanger trace is how a clinical lab confirms that both parents of a child with a recessive disease are carriers. The indel case is worth a sentence: after a heterozygous one-base deletion, every subsequent position has two different bases, so the trace becomes unreadable from that point on, which itself tells you there is an indel.

title: Digital analysis of DNA
text:
Next-generation sequencing: reads and coverage


Fragment the genome, sequence millions of short reads (typically 100–300 bases) in parallel, and map each read to a reference genome.
Coverage = number of reads × read length ÷ genome length. A human genome at 30× needs about 90 Gb of reads.
Coverage varies by chance, so a heterozygous site is called only where enough reads cover it.


The details of the chemistry vary between platforms and change every few years, so we stay at the level of concepts that do not change: reads, mapping and coverage. Short-read platforms such as Illumina dominate; long-read platforms (PacBio, Oxford Nanopore) give reads of tens of kilobases, which help with repeats and assembly in the next unit. The figure is simulated: 40 reads of 50 bases on a 400 base window, mean coverage 5 times. Even so, some bases are not covered at all. This is why 30 times is the usual target for a human genome: at 30 times, very few bases have so few reads that a heterozygous site could be missed. Calling a heterozygote is like the double peak in Sanger, only counted: about half the reads show each allele. The Genomic variation unit uses data from exactly this kind of sequencing.

title: Digital analysis of DNA
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Restriction enzyme
cuts at a palindromic site; sticky or blunt ends; a 6-bp site every ~4,096 bp in random DNA


Fragments
linear: k sites → k + 1 fragments; circular: k; sizes sum to the total


Gel
distance ∝ −log(size); read sizes from a ladder; brightness ∝ mass


Vector
origin + selectable marker + unique cloning sites (pUC19)


PCR
two primers define the product; N = N0(1 + E)n until a plateau; 3.3 cycles per 10×


Primers
18–25 nt, 40–60% GC, matched Tm, no 3’ complementarity, unique (Primer-BLAST)


PCR-RFLP
HbS destroys a DdeI site: 201 + 180 bp (HbA) vs 381 bp (HbS)


Sanger
ddNTPs stop synthesis; sort by length; a heterozygote gives double peaks


NGS
millions of short reads mapped to a reference; coverage = reads × length / genome




This is the revision table. The numbers students should be able to reproduce: 4 to the 6 equals 4,096; k plus 1 fragments for a linear molecule; 2 to the 30 is about a billion; 3.3 cycles per ten-fold; and the coverage formula. The HbS fragment sizes are not to be memorised, but students should be able to predict which bands a carrier shows.

title: Digital analysis of DNA
text:
Where this leads

Exercise: estimate sizes from a gel, design primers, BLAST a mystery read, and look up an enzyme in REBASE.
Exercise in R: read the phage λ genome from a FASTA file, find the EcoRI and BamHI sites with str_locate_all(), and draw your own virtual gel.
Next: Genome annotation. Once a genome is sequenced, where are the genes? ORFs, homology (BLAST), genome browsers.
Genomic variation. Sequencing many people reveals millions of variants, such as the HbS allele, and how their frequencies differ between populations.


Point forward. The BLAST search of the mystery read in the exercise is the first time students use BLAST; the next unit uses it properly, with proteins. The FASTA file in the R exercise is the format every sequence database uses, so reading one by hand is worth doing once.

title: Exercise in R: DNA structure & replication (recap)
Exercise in R: DNA structure & replication (recap)
Exercise in R: DNA structure & replication (recap)
text:
Before you start
This page builds on the by-hand part of the Exercise, especially B3 and F2. You need the packages stringr and tibble (stringr installs stringi, which we also use). Download HBB_NM_000518.5.fasta, the HBB mRNA from F2, and save it in a data/ folder of your R project.

title: Exercise in R: DNA structure & replication (recap)
text:
Tasks
New idiom: DNA as a string. In R a sequence is just a character string, and the stringr functions work on it like on any text. The ones we need:



Function
What it does
Example




str_length(x)
number of characters
str_length("ATG") is 3


str_sub(x, start, end)
the substring from start to end
str_sub("ATGGTG", 4, 6) is "GTG"


str_count(x, pattern)
how many times a pattern occurs; "[GC]" means G or C
str_count("GATC", "[GC]") is 2


str_c(..., collapse = "")
glue strings together




Two more come from base R and stringi: chartr(old, new, x) replaces each character of old by the character at the same place in new (so chartr("ACGT", "TGCA", x) complements every base at once), and stringi::stri_reverse(x) reverses a string.
library(stringr)
library(tibble)
R1. (read the FASTA) A FASTA file is a header line starting with >, followed by the sequence on one or more lines. Read the file with readLines(), drop the header and glue the rest into one string. How long is the mRNA? Check that positions 51–53 hold the start codon (F2b), and find the stop codon at the end of the CDS (51..494).
lines <- readLines("data/HBB_NM_000518.5.fasta")
lines[1]
hbb <- str_c(lines[-1], collapse = "")   # glue the sequence lines into one string
str_length(hbb)
str_sub(hbb, 1, 60)
str_sub(hbb, 51, 53)      # the start codon
str_sub(hbb, 492, 494)    # the stop codon
(Part 4 reads FASTA files with several sequences; one sequence is all we need here.)
R2. (revcomp()) Complement a short sequence with chartr(), and reverse it with stri_reverse(). Then put both steps in a function revcomp(). Test it on your answer to Q4 of the quiz (the EcoRI site GAATTC is its own reverse complement), and check that taking the reverse complement twice gives back the original HBB sequence.
chartr("ACGT", "TGCA", "ATGGTGCAT")        # complement
stringi::stri_reverse("ATGGTGCAT")         # reverse

revcomp <- function(dna) {
  stringi::stri_reverse(chartr("ACGT", "TGCA", dna))
}
revcomp("ATGGTGCAT")
revcomp("GAATTC")                 # the EcoRI site
revcomp(revcomp(hbb)) == hbb
str_sub(revcomp(hbb), 1, 60)
The last line is the start of the HBB − strand written 5′ → 3′, which is what you would see on the + strand of chromosome 11. Can you find the poly(A) signal AATAAA from the end of the mRNA in it? (Hint: what is the reverse complement of AATAAA?)
R3. (gc_content()) Write a function that returns the fraction of G and C in a sequence. Use it on the whole mRNA, on its reverse complement, and on the three regions of the mRNA: 5′ UTR (1–50), coding sequence (51–494) and 3′ UTR (495–628). Then count all four bases on each strand, and on both strands together, to check Chargaff’s rules.
gc_content <- function(dna) {
  str_count(dna, "[GC]") / str_length(dna)
}
gc_content("ATGC")
gc_content(hbb)
gc_content(revcomp(hbb))

regions <- tibble(
  region = c("5' UTR", "coding sequence", "3' UTR"),
  start  = c(1, 51, 495),
  end    = c(50, 494, 628)
)
regions$seq <- str_sub(hbb, regions$start, regions$end)
regions$length <- str_length(regions$seq)
regions$gc <- gc_content(regions$seq)
regions[, c("region", "start", "end", "length", "gc")]

# Chargaff: count A, C, G, T on one strand, on its partner, and on both
str_count(hbb, c("A", "C", "G", "T"))
str_count(revcomp(hbb), c("A", "C", "G", "T"))
both <- str_c(hbb, revcomp(hbb))
str_count(both, c("A", "C", "G", "T"))
str_sub() and gc_content() work on a whole vector at once, so one line handles all three regions.

Why is the GC content of a sequence and of its reverse complement the same?
Does Chargaff’s rule A = T hold for one strand of the mRNA? For both strands together?

R4. (the sickle mutation on both strands) Take positions c.16–24 of the coding sequence (B3). Make the HbS change c.20A>T by assigning to str_sub(), and compare the reverse complements of the normal and mutant sequences with your answer to B3.
cds <- str_sub(hbb, 51, 494)
str_sub(cds, 16, 24)               # codons 6-8 of the coding sequence
hbs <- cds
str_sub(hbs, 20, 20) <- "T"        # c.20A>T
str_sub(hbs, 16, 24)
revcomp(str_sub(cds, 16, 24))
revcomp(str_sub(hbs, 16, 24))
Which base changes in the reverse complement? Relate it to how dbSNP writes rs334.

title: Exercise in R: DNA structure & replication (recap)
text:
Solutions






Solutions: In R





All output below is from Rscript --vanilla run in the unit folder.
R1.
[1] ">NM_000518.5 Homo sapiens hemoglobin subunit beta (HBB), mRNA"
[1] 628
[1] "ACATTTGCTTCTGACACAACTGTGTTCACTAGCAACCTCAAACAGACACCATGGTGCATC"
[1] "ATG"

628 nt, as on the LOCUS line. Positions 51–53 are the start codon ATG, and 492–494 the stop codon TAA.
R2.
[1] "TACCACGTA"
[1] "TACGTGGTA"
[1] "ATGCACCAT"
[1] "GAATTC"
[1] TRUE

Complementing alone gives TACCACGTA, which is the partner strand written 3′ → 5′; reversing alone gives TACGTGGTA, which is not the partner strand at all. Only both steps together give the reverse complement, ATGCACCAT (as in the lecture). GAATTC is its own reverse complement, and two reverse complements give back the original. The reverse complement starts with the reverse complement of the mRNA’s last bases (…TTGCAA at the end of the FASTA becomes TTGCAA…). The poly(A) signal AATAAA near the end of the mRNA appears in it as its own reverse complement, TTTATT, in …TGTTTTTTATTAGG….
R3.

# A tibble: 3 × 5
  region          start   end length    gc

1 5' UTR              1    50     50 0.44

The mRNA is 51.3 % GC; the coding sequence (56.1 %) is richer in GC than the UTRs (44 % and 38.1 %).

Every G on one strand is a C on the other, and every C a G, so G + C is the same on both strands.
On one strand, A (139) ≠ T (167) and G (165) ≠ C (157): Chargaff’s rule does not hold for a single strand. On both strands together, A = T = 306 and C = G = 322: the rule holds for double-stranded DNA, because each A on one strand is a T on the other.

R4.
[1] "CCTGAGGAG"
[1] "CCTGTGGAG"
[1] "CTCCTCAGG"
[1] "CTCCACAGG"
On the coding strand, c.20 changes A → T (GAG → GTG, Glu → Val). In the reverse complement, CTCCTCAGG becomes CTCCACAGG: the T at the matching position becomes A. The reverse complement is the + strand of chromosome 11, so dbSNP writes rs334 as T>A. It is one base-pair change seen from the two strands.

Where this leads

In the next unit, Mutation & complementation, you use str_sub() to cut a coding sequence into codons, translate it with a genetic-code table, and classify point mutations as silent, missense or nonsense.

title: DNA structure & replication (recap)
text:
About this lecture
Recap of 5MO103 (Microbiology and basic molecular biology), seen through the eyes of a geneticist. In Parts 1 and 2 a gene was an abstract “factor” on a chromosome. Now we open it up.

How we know that genes are made of DNA: Griffith, Avery, Hershey and Chase.
The double helix: base pairing, antiparallel strands, and how to read the partner strand (the reverse complement).
Semiconservative replication and the Meselson–Stahl experiment.
The replication fork in brief, and why copying errors matter to a geneticist.
Homologous recombination at the molecular level: the Holliday junction, the molecular basis of crossing over from Part 2.

Book: Hartwell, Genetics: From Genes to Genomes, DNA structure, replication and recombination chapter.

This is a recap unit. Students have met DNA structure and replication in 5MO103, so do not re-teach the enzymology. The aim is to look at the same material with a geneticist’s questions: what properties must the genetic material have, what experiment showed it, what happens when copying goes wrong (mutation, next unit), and how crossing over, which they used as an abstract event in Part 2, happens at the level of DNA strands. Keep it brisk; about 10 content slides.

title: DNA structure & replication (recap)
section: What must the genetic material do?
text:
What must the genetic material do?
From Parts 1 and 2 we already know what genes do. Any candidate molecule has to explain it:







Property seen in genetics
What the molecule must be able to do




Genes are passed on faithfully, generation after generation
be copied accurately before every cell division


Genes come in different alleles
vary: store information in a sequence that can change (mutate)


Genes control phenotypes (round vs wrinkled, HbA vs HbS)
carry information that the cell reads to make RNA and proteins


Homologues exchange parts (crossing over, Part 2)
be cut and rejoined precisely, at matching positions



Until the 1940s most biologists bet on protein: 20 amino acids seemed a richer alphabet than DNA’s 4 bases.

Frame the whole lecture with this table. Each row is answered later: replication (row 1), sequence and mutation (row 2, the next unit), gene expression (row 3, the gene expression recap) and recombination (row 4, the end of today). The protein hypothesis was reasonable: DNA was thought to be a boring repeat of the four bases (the tetranucleotide hypothesis). The next slide is the evidence that changed minds.

title: DNA structure & replication (recap)
text:
Three experiments: genes are DNA


Griffith: a heritable change (R → S) can be caused by something from dead cells: transformation.
Avery, MacLeod & McCarty: only DNase destroys the transforming activity.
Hershey & Chase: phage DNA, not phage protein, enters the bacterium and directs new phage.


Walk through the three panels left to right. Griffith did not identify the molecule; he showed that a heritable trait (the polysaccharide capsule that makes S strains virulent) can be transferred by something in heat-killed cells, and that the change is inherited by the transformed bacteria’s descendants. That last point is what makes it genetics: the R cells did not just pick up capsules, they gained the ability to make them. Avery and colleagues purified the transforming principle and destroyed each kind of molecule in turn with enzymes. Hershey and Chase used the fact that protein contains sulphur but no phosphorus, and DNA contains phosphorus but no sulphur. After infection they sheared the phage coats off the bacteria in a kitchen blender; the 32P went with the cells and was passed on to progeny phage, the 35S stayed in the coats. Transformation comes back in the bacterial genetics recap in Part 5.

title: DNA structure & replication (recap)
text:
The double helix


Watson and Crick (1953), using X-ray data from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins, and Chargaff’s rules (A = T, G = C):

Two strands, each a sugar–phosphate backbone with a base on every sugar.
Bases pair across: A–T (2 hydrogen bonds), G–C (3).
A purine (A, G) always pairs with a pyrimidine (T, C), so the helix has a constant width.
The strands are antiparallel: one runs 5′ → 3′, the partner 3′ → 5′.




“It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material.” (Watson & Crick, 1953)

The key genetic fact is complementarity: one strand determines the other. That gives a copying mechanism (each strand is a template) and a way to repair damage (the undamaged strand holds the information). The 5’ and 3’ ends refer to the carbon atoms of the deoxyribose: the 5’ end has a free phosphate, the 3’ end a free hydroxyl. Polymerases add only to the 3’ end, which is why the replication fork is asymmetric. G-C pairs have three hydrogen bonds and A-T two, so GC-rich DNA melts at a higher temperature; that matters for PCR primers in Part 4. The quotation is the famous understatement at the end of the 1953 paper.

title: DNA structure & replication (recap)
section: Reading DNA: strands and the reverse complement
text:
Reading DNA: strands and the reverse complement
A sequence is always written 5′ → 3′. To write the partner strand, complement every base, then reverse the order:



this strand
5′-ATGGTGCAT-3′ (start of the HBB coding sequence)


complement, as it lies
3′-TACCACGTA-5′


reverse complement
5′-ATGCACCAT-3′



Why a geneticist cares. A genome database stores only the + strand of each chromosome. HBB lies on the − strand of chromosome 11, so the sickle-cell change looks different depending on which strand you read:

on the HBB mRNA and coding sequence: c.20A>T (GAG → GTG, Glu → Val);
on the chromosome’s + strand (dbSNP rs334): T>A at position 5,227,002 (GRCh38).

Same mutation, same base pair, two strands.

This is the most useful practical skill of the lecture, and the R exercise automates it. Every genome browser, VCF file and dbSNP record reports alleles on the forward (+) strand of the reference chromosome, while gene-centred names (HGVS c. names, ClinVar titles) use the gene’s own coding strand. For a gene on the minus strand, the two descriptions are reverse complements of each other. Students will meet this in the Find it tasks of this and the next unit: dbSNP rs334 is listed as T>A on NC_000011.10, while ClinVar calls it c.20A>T. Neither is wrong. A palindromic site such as GAATTC (EcoRI) is its own reverse complement, which is why restriction enzymes can recognise it on both strands at once (Part 4).

title: DNA structure & replication (recap)
section: Three ways to copy a helix
text:
Three ways to copy a helix
Complementary strands suggest three models of replication. Meselson and Stahl (1958) grew E. coli for many generations in heavy nitrogen (15N), moved the cells to light nitrogen (14N), and separated DNA by density in a caesium chloride gradient.









Model
Generation 1
Generation 2




Semiconservative (each helix = one old + one new strand)
all hybrid
½ hybrid, ½ light


Conservative (old helix stays intact)
½ heavy, ½ light
¼ heavy, ¾ light


Dispersive (old and new mixed along each strand)
all hybrid
all one intermediate band




This is one of the most elegant experiments in biology, and it is a genetics-style experiment: three hypotheses, each with a different quantitative prediction, and one decisive observation. Generation 1 rules out conservative replication (no heavy band). Generation 2 rules out dispersive replication (two bands, not one band moving slowly towards light). Only semiconservative fits both. Ask the room what generation 3 would look like: one quarter hybrid, three quarters light. Semiconservative replication is also why a mutation that arises as a mismatch on one strand ends up in only one of the two daughter helices; that comes back in the next unit.

title: DNA structure & replication (recap)
text:
The replication fork, in brief
Polymerases add nucleotides only to a 3′ end, and need a primer. So one strand is made continuously (leading), the other in short Okazaki fragments (lagging).








Job
Bacterial protein
How genetics found or uses it




Start at the origin
DnaA
dnaA temperature-sensitive mutants cannot start new rounds


Unwind the helix
helicase (DnaB)
dnaB ts mutants stop replication at once at high temperature


Lay down RNA primers
primase (DnaG)



Copy DNA, proofread
DNA polymerase III
the ε subunit (dnaQ, mutD) proofreads: its mutants are mutators


Replace primers, join fragments
DNA polymerase I, ligase




Accuracy: about 1 error in 105 bases from base pairing alone, 1 in 107 after proofreading, about 1 in 109–1010 after mismatch repair.

Do not re-teach the fork in detail; students have the full picture from 5MO103. The genetic lens is the right-hand column: many of these genes were found as conditional (temperature-sensitive) lethal mutants. A mutation that stops replication would be lethal, so you can only keep it if it works at the permissive temperature and fails at the restrictive one. The difference between “fast stop” (elongation, dnaB) and “slow stop” (initiation, dnaA: rounds in progress finish) told geneticists what each gene did before anyone purified the proteins. Mutator strains, in which every gene mutates faster, are the bridge to the next unit. The error rates are order-of-magnitude textbook values; the human germline mutation rate, about 1 in 10^8 per base pair per generation, is the end result after many cell divisions.

title: DNA structure & replication (recap)
text:
Homologous recombination: why and where
Homologous recombination uses a matching (homologous) DNA molecule as a template to repair or exchange DNA.

Repair: a double-strand break is mended by copying the sister chromatid. Defects in this pathway (for example in BRCA1 or BRCA2) raise cancer risk.
Meiosis: the cell deliberately breaks DNA (the enzyme Spo11), and repairs the breaks using the homologue. Some repairs become crossovers: the chiasmata you saw in Part 2.

The model, first proposed by Robin Holliday (1964) and later refined to start from a double-strand break:

A double-strand break; the 5′ ends are trimmed back, leaving 3′ single-strand tails.
A 3′ tail invades the homologue, pairs with its complementary strand, and primes new DNA synthesis.
The two duplexes become joined by Holliday junctions: points where strands cross between helices.
Enzymes cut the junctions to separate the helices.


The genetic question that drove this model was: how can two chromosomes exchange parts at exactly matching positions, without losing or gaining a single base? Base pairing is the answer: the invading strand finds its place by pairing with its complement on the homologue. The DSB-repair model is the one in Hartwell; Holliday’s original 1964 model started from single-strand nicks. Spo11 is the meiotic enzyme that makes the breaks, a few hundred per human meiosis, of which only a few dozen become crossovers. BRCA1 and BRCA2 return in the cancer genetics unit.

title: DNA structure & replication (recap)
section: From Holliday junctions to crossing over
text:
From Holliday junctions to crossing over


Cut one way: crossover, A b and a B. The flanking markers are recombinant: this is what you counted as recombination frequency in Part 2.
Cut the other way: non-crossover. The flanks stay parental (A B, a b), but a short stretch of heteroduplex DNA remains.
If a heteroduplex covers a gene where the homologues differ, mismatch repair may “correct” one strand to match the other: gene conversion. In fungal tetrads this shows up as 3 : 1 instead of the Mendelian 2 : 2.


This slide connects to Part 2. A crossover between two genes swaps the flanking markers, which is the event that linkage mapping counts. Non-crossovers leave no trace in flanking markers, so they were invisible in mapping crosses, but they can still change a gene inside the heteroduplex patch. Gene conversion was discovered in fungi, where all four products of a single meiosis can be recovered (tetrad analysis): an Aa diploid should give 2 A : 2 a spores, but occasionally gives 3 : 1. That non-Mendelian ratio is explained by mismatch repair in the heteroduplex. Gene conversion is rare per gene per meiosis and does not disturb Mendel’s ratios in ordinary crosses.

title: DNA structure & replication (recap)
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Genes are DNA
Griffith (transformation), Avery et al. (only DNase stops it), Hershey–Chase (phage DNA enters the cell)


Double helix
two antiparallel strands; A–T, G–C; one strand determines the other


Reverse complement
the partner strand, written 5′ → 3′: complement every base, then reverse


Strands in databases
genome records use the + strand; gene names (c.) use the gene’s own strand. HBB c.20A>T = + strand T>A


Replication
semiconservative (Meselson–Stahl: hybrid, then hybrid + light)


Fork
leading and lagging strands; polymerase proofreads; mismatch repair finishes; error about 10−9–10−10 per base


Recombination
DSB → strand invasion → Holliday junctions → crossover or non-crossover (heteroduplex, gene conversion)




The revision sheet. If they remember three things: complementarity (one strand determines the other, which explains copying, repair and the reverse complement), semiconservative replication, and that crossing over is a DNA repair event that uses the homologue as template.

text:
Where this leads

That function is reused in Part 4 to find restriction sites and design primers.

title: Exercise in R: drift, selection, mutation, migration
Exercise in R: drift, selection, mutation, migration
Exercise in R: drift, selection, mutation, migration
text:
Before you start
This page builds on the by-hand part of the Exercise, so do that first. You need the packages dplyr, tidyr and ggplot2. No data files are needed: everything is simulated.

title: Exercise in R: drift, selection, mutation, migration
text:
Tasks
New idiom today: the for loop. So far each random draw was independent: rbinom(1000, ...) made 1000 families at once. Drift is different: generation t + 1 is drawn from generation t, so we cannot draw all generations at once. A for loop repeats a block of code once for each value of a counter:
for (t in 1:5) {
  print(t^2)      # runs with t = 1, then t = 2, ..., then t = 5
}
The usual pattern is: make an empty vector with numeric(n), set the first element, and fill in element t + 1 from element t inside the loop. As before, set.seed() makes your numbers match the solutions.
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

One population, one loop
R1. Simulate one Wright–Fisher population of N = 50 diploid individuals (100 gene copies), starting at p = 0.5, for 100 generations. Each generation, the number of A copies is rbinom(1, size = 2 * N, prob = p[t]). Print the first 10 values and the last one, and plot p against generation.
set.seed(1)
N <- 50          # diploid individuals, so 2N = 100 gene copies
gens <- 100
p <- numeric(gens + 1)   # an empty vector to fill in
p[1] <- 0.5
for (t in 1:gens) {
  p[t + 1] <- rbinom(1, size = 2 * N, prob = p[t]) / (2 * N)
}
round(p[1:10], 2)
p[gens + 1]

ggplot(tibble(generation = 0:gens, p = p), aes(generation, p)) +
  geom_line() + ylim(0, 1) +
  labs(y = "allele frequency p", title = "One Wright-Fisher population, N = 50")
R2. Turn the loop into a function wright_fisher(N, p0, gens, s = 0, h = 0.5). Before the drift step, apply selection with fitnesses wAA = 1 + s, wAa = 1 + hs, waa = 1, using the recursion from the lecture. Test it: (a) neutral drift with N = 20 for 10 generations; (b) selection with s = 0.05 in a huge population (N = 10⁶), where drift is negligible. Check the first step of (b) by hand.
wright_fisher <- function(N, p0, gens, s = 0, h = 0.5) {
  w_AA <- 1 + s
  w_Aa <- 1 + h * s
  w_aa <- 1
  p <- numeric(gens + 1)
  p[1] <- p0
  for (t in 1:gens) {
    q <- 1 - p[t]
    w_bar <- p[t]^2 * w_AA + 2 * p[t] * q * w_Aa + q^2 * w_aa
    p_sel <- (p[t]^2 * w_AA + p[t] * q * w_Aa) / w_bar      # selection
    p[t + 1] <- rbinom(1, size = 2 * N, prob = p_sel) / (2 * N)   # drift
  }
  p
}
set.seed(2)
round(wright_fisher(N = 20, p0 = 0.5, gens = 10), 3)
round(wright_fisher(N = 1e6, p0 = 0.1, gens = 10, s = 0.05), 3)


Many populations
R3. Use replicate to run 20 populations of N = 20 for 100 generations. Each run returns a vector of 101 values, so replicate gives a matrix with one column per population. Turn it into a tibble with one column per population and reshape it to long format with pivot_longer (from Part 6), so that ggplot can draw one line per population. How many populations are fixed, lost or still segregating at generation 100? Then do the same with N = 500 and plot both side by side with facet_wrap.
set.seed(3)
runs <- replicate(20, wright_fisher(N = 20, p0 = 0.5, gens = 100))
dim(runs)
lines20 <- as_tibble(runs, .name_repair = \(x) paste0("pop", seq_along(x))) |>
  mutate(generation = 0:100) |>
  pivot_longer(-generation, names_to = "population", values_to = "p")
lines20
final <- runs[101, ]
table(fate = ifelse(final == 1, "fixed", ifelse(final == 0, "lost", "segregating")))

set.seed(4)
runs500 <- replicate(20, wright_fisher(N = 500, p0 = 0.5, gens = 100))
range(runs500[101, ])
both <- bind_rows(
  lines20 |> mutate(N = "N = 20"),
  as_tibble(runs500, .name_repair = \(x) paste0("pop", seq_along(x))) |>
    mutate(generation = 0:100) |>
    pivot_longer(-generation, names_to = "population", values_to = "p") |>
    mutate(N = "N = 500")
)
ggplot(both, aes(generation, p, group = population)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.5) + facet_wrap(~ N) +
  labs(y = "allele frequency p", title = "20 replicate populations, p0 = 0.5")
(.name_repair gives the matrix columns the names pop1, pop2, …; \(x) is the short way to write a function, as in Part 1.)


Checking the theory
R4. Run 1000 neutral populations of N = 20, starting at p = 0.2, for 500 generations (long enough for all to fix or lose A), and keep only the final p. What fraction fixed A? Is it close to 0.2? Then start 4000 populations from a single new mutation, p₀ = 1/40. What fraction fixed it?
set.seed(5)
final_p <- replicate(1000, wright_fisher(N = 20, p0 = 0.2, gens = 500)[501])
table(final_p)
mean(final_p == 1)
set.seed(6)
final_new <- replicate(4000, wright_fisher(N = 20, p0 = 1/40, gens = 500)[501])
mean(final_new == 1)
R5. Heterozygosity: run 1000 populations of N = 20 from p = 0.5 for 100 generations. Compute H = 2p(1 − p) for every population and generation (R does this element by element on the whole matrix), average over populations with rowMeans, and compare with H₀(1 − 1/2N)t at generations 0, 10, 25, 50 and 100.
set.seed(9)
runs1000 <- replicate(1000, wright_fisher(N = 20, p0 = 0.5, gens = 100))
H <- 2 * runs1000 * (1 - runs1000)    # heterozygosity of every population, every generation
het <- tibble(generation = 0:100,
              simulated = rowMeans(H),
              theory = 0.5 * (1 - 1 / (2 * 20))^(0:100))
het |> filter(generation %in% c(0, 10, 25, 50, 100))
R6. Selection and drift together. (a) Run 20 populations with s = 0.05, h = 0.5, p₀ = 0.1 for 200 generations, with N = 500 and with N = 20. Compare with the deterministic curve (use N = 10⁹). What fraction of the N = 20 populations lose the favoured allele? (b) Sickle cell: s = −0.8 and h = −0.2 give wSS = 0.2, wAS = 1.16 and wAA = 1 (the focal allele is HbS). Run 20 populations of N = 1000 from p₀ = 0.02 for 300 generations. Compare the mean final frequency with the equilibrium from the lecture.
set.seed(7)
sel500 <- replicate(20, wright_fisher(N = 500, p0 = 0.1, gens = 200, s = 0.05))
sel20  <- replicate(20, wright_fisher(N = 20,  p0 = 0.1, gens = 200, s = 0.05))
det    <- wright_fisher(N = 1e9, p0 = 0.1, gens = 200, s = 0.05)
round(det[c(51, 101, 201)], 3)
round(mean(sel500[201, ]), 3)
range(sel500[201, ])
table(sel20[201, ])

set.seed(8)
sickle <- replicate(20, wright_fisher(N = 1000, p0 = 0.02, gens = 300, s = -0.8, h = -0.2))
round(mean(sickle[301, ]), 3)
w_AA <- 1 - 0.8; w_Aa <- 1 + 0.16; w_aa <- 1
(w_Aa - w_aa) / (2 * w_Aa - w_AA - w_aa)
