title: Exercise in R: drift, selection, mutation, migration
text:
Where this leads
The for loop is the general tool for anything that depends on its own past: population sizes, epidemics, tumour growth. In Complex traits we go back to vectorised R and to lm, to estimate heritability from family data.

title: Drift, selection, mutation, migration
text:
About this lecture
Hardy–Weinberg keeps the allele frequency p constant. Real allele frequencies change. This lecture is about the four forces that change them:

Genetic drift: chance, strongest in small populations. The Wright–Fisher model; fixation and loss; effective population size; founder effects and the Finnish disease heritage.
Selection: genotypes differ in fitness. The Δp recursion; dominance and the speed of selection.
Mutation and mutation–selection balance: why harmful alleles never disappear.
Migration: gene flow makes populations alike.
Heterozygote advantage: sickle-cell haemoglobin and malaria.

This is syllabus outcome 2: how allele frequencies in populations vary with different factors. Book: Hartwell, the population genetics chapter.

Frame the lecture as “what happens when each Hardy–Weinberg assumption fails”. We dealt with non-random mating last time; today the other four. The thread through the course is HBB: the sickle-cell allele was introduced in Part 1 as a missense variant, it was a codominant example in extensions to Mendel, it was missing as homozygotes from 1000 Genomes samples last time, and today we explain why it is common at all. The tumour from the cancer lecture is also a population: drift and selection act on cell clones exactly as they do here.

title: Drift, selection, mutation, migration
text:
Four forces change allele frequencies









Force
What it does to p
Direction
Strongest when




Drift
random change from generation to generation
none (random)
population is small


Selection
genotypes leave different numbers of offspring
towards the fitter allele, or to a balance
fitness differences are large


Mutation
turns one allele into another
towards new alleles
over very long times (rates ~10⁻⁸ per base)


Migration
brings alleles from other populations
towards the source population’s p
many migrants, very different p



Drift and mutation create and remove variation; selection adapts; migration makes populations similar. Real populations feel all four at once.

A summary slide to come back to. Mutation is the ultimate source of all variation but changes allele frequencies very slowly: per-base mutation rates in humans are about 1 in 100 million per generation. Its effect on frequencies matters only in balance with selection. Drift is directionless: it is just as likely to increase as to decrease p. Selection has a direction. Ask students which forces increase differences between populations (drift, divergent selection) and which decrease them (migration).

title: Drift, selection, mutation, migration
text:
Genetic drift: the Wright–Fisher model


A population of N diploid individuals has 2N gene copies. Each copy in the next generation is a random draw from the copies of this generation.
So the number of A copies next generation is Binomial(2N, p): the same rbinom you used for sibships.
p goes up or down by chance: genetic drift. The expected change is zero, but the variance per generation is p(1 − p)/(2N).


The Wright–Fisher model is the simplest model of drift: discrete generations, a constant population size, and random sampling of gene copies. Some copies leave several descendants, some none, purely by chance. In the figure, p goes 0.5, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.4 with only 10 copies. The variance formula shows why small populations drift faster: the standard deviation of the change per generation is the square root of pq over 2N. For 2N equals 10 and p equals 0.5 that is 0.16; for 2N equals 1000 it is 0.016. In the R exercise this model is a for loop of a few lines.

title: Drift, selection, mutation, migration
text:
What drift does


Each population wanders until the allele is fixed (p = 1) or lost (p = 0). Then drift stops: there is no variation left.
The probability that a neutral allele is eventually fixed equals its starting frequency, p₀. A new mutation (p₀ = 1/2N) is almost always lost.
Heterozygosity H = 2pq falls by a factor (1 − 1/2N) per generation on average. Different populations diverge.


Left: with 40 gene copies, after 100 generations most of the 20 populations have fixed or lost A. Right: with 1000 copies, they have barely spread. Fixation probability equals p0 because drift has no direction: the average of p over many populations stays at p0, and at the end every population is at 0 or 1, so the fraction at 1 must be p0. The heterozygosity formula says how fast variation disappears; time to lose half of it is about 1.4 times 2N generations. Note the divergence: populations that start the same end up different by chance alone. This is part of why human populations differ in allele frequencies, as seen in 1000 Genomes.

title: Drift, selection, mutation, migration
text:
Effective population size
Drift depends on the effective population size Nₑ: the size of an ideal Wright–Fisher population that drifts as fast as the real one. Usually Nₑ is much smaller than the census size.

Unequal sex ratio: N_e = \dfrac{4 N_m N_f}{N_m + N_f}. A herd with 10 breeding males and 90 females: Nₑ = 4 × 10 × 90 / 100 = 36, not 100.
Fluctuating size: Nₑ is close to the harmonic mean over generations, so a single small generation dominates. Sizes 1000, 10, 1000: Nₑ = 3/(1/1000 + 1/10 + 1/1000) ≈ 29.
Variance in family size (some parents have many children, most have few) also lowers Nₑ.

Long-term Nₑ of humans is estimated at roughly 10 000, although billions are alive today: past bottlenecks still shape our genomes.

Ne is the number that goes into all the drift formulas. The sex ratio formula follows because half of the genes come from each sex: if only 10 males breed, the paternal half is drawn from a small pool. This matters for conservation genetics and animal breeding, where a few sires father many offspring. The harmonic mean point is the formal version of a bottleneck: one generation at size 10 counts almost as much as a hundred generations at 1000. The human value of around 10 000 is a commonly quoted estimate from genetic diversity; treat it as an order of magnitude.

title: Drift, selection, mutation, migration
text:
Founder effects and bottlenecks


A new population founded by few people carries only a chance sample of the source’s alleles. A rare allele that happens to be among the founders can become common; many others are lost.
A bottleneck (a population crash and recovery) has the same effect.
Recessive diseases due to that allele are then much more common than elsewhere, and are usually due to one shared (“founder”) mutation.


Founder effects are drift compressed into one generation. In the figure, one red copy among 120 in the source becomes one in seven among the founders, and stays at that frequency as the population grows. Classic examples include Ellis–van Creveld syndrome among the Old Order Amish, Tay–Sachs disease among Ashkenazi Jews (where selection may also play a role), and the Finnish disease heritage on the next slide. A founder mutation can be recognised because all patients share the same mutation on the same surrounding haplotype, inherited from the common ancestor.

title: Drift, selection, mutation, migration
text:
The Finnish disease heritage
Finland’s population grew from a small number of settlers, with further bottlenecks as internal regions were settled. Result:

A few dozen rare recessive diseases are much more common in Finland than elsewhere: the Finnish disease heritage (reviewed by Norio, Hum Genet 2003). Most patients are homozygous for one founder mutation.
Example: Salla disease (free sialic acid storage, SLC17A5, 6q13, autosomal recessive). Founder allele R39C (rs80338794): allele frequency about 0.0046 in Finns in gnomAD v4 exomes, 20 times that in other Europeans (0.00023).
Conversely, some diseases common elsewhere in Europe are rare in Finland: CFTR F508del is about 10 times rarer in Finns than in other Europeans (previous lecture).

Same forces, opposite outcomes: drift raises some alleles and removes others.

This is a textbook founder effect in a well-documented population. The exact number of diseases in the heritage depends on the list; Norio’s reviews describe about three dozen. The gnomAD numbers for Salla R39C are from the v4 exome data and were checked through the gnomAD API; students look them up in the exercise. Another striking one is CLN1 disease, infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, due to PPT1 R122W, which is even more enriched. Point out the symmetry with CF: the same random sampling at foundation made some disease alleles common and others rare. Medical genetics in Finland uses this: a few founder mutations explain most cases, so testing is simple.

title: Drift, selection, mutation, migration
text:
Demo: drift and selection




Start with “drift, N = 20”: with the default seed, 9 fixed, 9 lost, 2 still segregating after 100 generations. Then N = 500: all 20 still segregating. Then “selection s = 0.05”: the lines follow the dashed deterministic curve. Change N to 20 with the same s: most populations lose the favoured allele. Then the sickle-cell preset: lines settle near 0.14. Point out the readout comparing heterozygosity with H0 times (1 − 1/2N) to the t.

title: Drift, selection, mutation, migration
section: Selection: fitness and the Δp recursion
text:
Selection: fitness and the Δp recursion
Relative fitness w: the relative number of offspring a genotype leaves. With selection coefficient s and dominance h:



Genotype
AA
Aa
aa




Fitness w
1 + s
1 + hs
1


Frequency before selection
p²
2pq
q²



After selection, the frequency of A among the parents of the next generation is

p' = \frac{p^2 w_{AA} + pq\, w_{Aa}}{\bar w}, \qquad \bar w = p^2 w_{AA} + 2pq\, w_{Aa} + q^2 w_{aa}.

h = 1: A dominant; h = ½: additive; h = 0: A recessive. Apply the recursion generation after generation (a loop) to follow p.

This is the one formula of the lecture. It is a weighted count: each genotype’s contribution of A alleles is multiplied by its fitness, and we divide by the mean fitness so that frequencies add up to one. The 2pq heterozygotes each carry one A, which is why the heterozygote term is pq, not 2pq. Fitness here combines survival and fertility. Example: s equals 0.05 and h equals 0.5 means AA carriers leave 5 percent more offspring than aa, and heterozygotes 2.5 percent more. Small fitness differences, repeated over hundreds of generations, are enough to change p from rare to common.

title: Drift, selection, mutation, migration
section: Dominance and the speed of selection
text:
Dominance and the speed of selection


A favoured dominant allele rises fast at first (selection sees it in heterozygotes) but slows near fixation: the last a alleles hide in heterozygotes.
A favoured recessive allele barely moves while rare: almost all its copies are in heterozygotes, which selection cannot see.
Same reason as last lecture: for a rare allele, almost all copies are in heterozygotes.


These are deterministic curves: no drift. Same s, three dominance values. The additive allele follows a symmetric S curve. The dominant one wins the race at first and then crawls. The recessive one, starting at 1 percent, hardly changes in 800 generations: with q equals 0.01, only 1 in 10 000 people is a homozygote and visible to selection. The flip side: selection against a harmful recessive allele is also very slow once the allele is rare. Even complete removal of affected people reduces q from 0.01 to 0.005 only after about 100 generations, about 2500 years.

title: Drift, selection, mutation, migration
text:
Mutation–selection balance
Selection removes harmful alleles; mutation creates new ones. They balance at an equilibrium frequency, with mutation rate μ per generation:








Harmful allele
Equilibrium frequency
Example: μ = 10⁻⁵, s = 1 (lethal)




recessive (seen only in aa)
\hat q \approx \sqrt{\mu / s}
q̂ ≈ 0.003, incidence q̂² ≈ 10⁻⁵


dominant (seen in Aa)
\hat q \approx \mu / s
q̂ ≈ 10⁻⁵




A recessive lethal allele is ~300 times more frequent than a dominant one with the same mutation rate: it hides in carriers.
For a dominant lethal, every case is a new mutation (recall achondroplasia and new mutations in the pedigrees unit).


The derivation is beyond this course; the intuition is enough. At equilibrium, the number of copies removed by selection each generation equals the number created by mutation. For a recessive allele, selection removes copies only from aa individuals, at a rate s times q squared, so q squared equals mu over s. For a dominant allele, selection acts on heterozygotes, removing about s times q, so q equals mu over s. Note that in both cases the incidence of the disease is about mu, or 2 mu for the dominant: under this simple model, disease incidence tells you the mutation rate. The figure 10 to the minus 5 is a typical order of magnitude for the per-gene rate of new loss-of-function mutations.

title: Drift, selection, mutation, migration
text:
Migration (gene flow)
If a fraction m of each generation are migrants from a population with allele frequency pM:

p' = (1-m)\,p + m\,p_M, \qquad \Delta p = m\,(p_M - p).


The difference from the source shrinks by a factor (1 − m) each generation: after t generations, (1 − m)t. Example: m = 0.05, after 20 generations 0.95²⁰ = 0.36 of the original difference is left.
A little migration is enough to stop populations from drifting apart: roughly one migrant per generation keeps them from fixing different alleles.
Migration also introduces new alleles, and mixes populations: admixed populations (such as ACB, ASW and PUR in 1000 Genomes) carry alleles from several continents.


Migration is the simplest force to model: the new population is a weighted average of the residents and the migrants. The “one migrant per generation” rule is a classical result from Wright’s island model: it holds whatever the population size, because larger populations drift more slowly and need proportionally more migrants. Link to last lecture: the HbS allele appears in 1000 Genomes populations outside Africa only in admixed populations with recent African ancestry, such as ACB in Barbados and ASW in the south-western US. That is migration.

title: Drift, selection, mutation, migration
section: Heterozygote advantage: sickle cell and malaria
text:
Heterozygote advantage: sickle cell and malaria


HbA/HbS carriers are protected against severe falciparum malaria; HbS/HbS have sickle-cell disease. Where malaria is common, the heterozygote is fittest.
Then q rises when rare and falls when common, to a stable equilibrium \hat q = \dfrac{w_{AS} - w_{AA}}{2w_{AS} - w_{AA} - w_{SS}}. With the illustrative fitnesses 1, 1.16, 0.2: q̂ = 0.16/1.12 = 0.14.
1000 Genomes Yoruba (Nigeria): q(HbS) = 0.139 (previous lecture). This is balancing selection.


This brings together the HBB thread of the course. In Part 1 HbS was a single missense change, glutamate to valine at position 6. Here it is a classic case of balancing selection, first proposed by Allison in the 1950s from the overlap of high HbS frequencies with malaria. The fitness values are illustrative, chosen so that the equilibrium matches the observed frequency; they are the same as in the demo preset. The right panel is the change in q per generation: positive below the equilibrium, negative above, so q returns to 0.14 from either side. Where malaria has gone, as among people of African descent in the Americas, the heterozygote advantage disappears and selection slowly lowers HbS. Other examples: thalassaemias and G6PD deficiency, also linked to malaria.

title: Drift, selection, mutation, migration
text:
Drift versus selection
Which wins? Compare selection (s) with drift (1/2Nₑ):

If 4Nₑs ≫ 1, selection dominates: the allele follows the deterministic curve. If 4Nₑs ≲ 1, the allele behaves almost as if neutral.
A new favourable mutation is still usually lost: its fixation probability is only about 2shet (Haldane), where shet is the heterozygote’s advantage. With shet = 0.025: 5%, so 95% of such mutations are lost by chance while still rare.
In small populations, mildly harmful alleles can drift to high frequency, and favourable ones are lost.

So most variation in the genome is shaped by drift, and selection acts strongly only where fitness effects are large.

This connects the two halves of the lecture. The product 4Ns compares the strength of selection with the strength of drift. For human Ne of about 10 000, alleles with s smaller than about 1 in 40 000 behave as neutral: most of the genome. Haldane’s 2s result is surprising for students: even a clearly beneficial mutation is usually lost, because it starts as a single copy and its first few carriers may simply not pass it on. The demo’s “new beneficial mutation” preset shows this: 7 of 100 populations fix the allele with these settings, close to 5 percent. Small populations accumulating harmful alleles is a concern in conservation genetics, and links back to the founder effect.

title: Drift, selection, mutation, migration
text:
Summary

Drift: random sampling of 2N gene copies each generation. Alleles are fixed or lost; P(fixation) = p₀; heterozygosity decays by (1 − 1/2N) per generation. Use Nₑ, which is usually much smaller than the census size.
Founder effects and bottlenecks make some rare alleles common (Finnish disease heritage, Salla disease) and others rare (CF in Finland).
Selection: p′ = (p²wAA + pq wAa)/w̄. Selection on rare recessive alleles is slow.
Mutation–selection balance: q̂ ≈ √(μ/s) recessive, μ/s dominant.
Migration: Δp = m(pM − p); makes populations similar.
Heterozygote advantage keeps HbS at a stable q̂ where malaria is common.


The exam-level skills: apply the selection recursion for one or two generations by hand; compute an equilibrium for heterozygote advantage; compute Ne for a sex ratio; explain founder effects with an example; state the fixation probability of a neutral allele.

title: Drift, selection, mutation, migration
text:
Where this leads

Next: Complex traits: many loci, each with a small effect, plus environment. GWAS find them, and population structure (Wahlund, drift between populations) is a trap.
Cancer genetics again: a tumour is a population of cells. Drivers are selected, passengers drift along, and resistance to a drug evolves by selection.
In the exercise: drift and selection by hand, the demo, the Finnish disease heritage in MedGen and gnomAD, and a Wright–Fisher simulation in R with a for loop.


The R exercise is where students see drift as code: a loop over generations, with rbinom inside. Then replicate runs the whole population many times, which is how population geneticists explore models that are too hard to solve by hand.

title: Exercise: ethics of genetic knowledge
Exercise: ethics of genetic knowledge
Exercise: ethics of genetic knowledge
text:
Background
Four principles (Beauchamp and Childress): autonomy (respect a person’s informed, voluntary choice), beneficence (do good), non-maleficence (do no harm), justice (be fair in who gets benefits and who carries risks). They often conflict; the work is to weigh them.
What genetics adds. Informed consent (voluntary, informed, can be withdrawn; broad consent for future research is debated). Privacy (genetic data are sensitive and identifying, and partly shared with relatives). The right not to know (a person may decline to learn a genetic result).
Kinds of test. Diagnostic (explains a disease), predictive (forecasts disease in a healthy person, e.g. Huntington disease), carrier (Aa × Aa couples), prenatal (NIPT screening; amniocentesis or CVS for diagnosis), and newborn screening (the PKU test). Incidental findings are found by chance; secondary findings are actionable genes looked for on purpose (the ACMG list, which includes BRCA1).
Swedish law in one table.







Law
Key point for these cases




Ethical Review Act (2003:460)
Research on sensitive personal data, physical interventions, or traceable biological material needs approval from Etikprövningsmyndigheten before it starts. Consent: voluntary, explicit, specific.


Biobanks Act (2023:38)
Identifiable samples may be stored and used with the donor’s consent, which can be withdrawn. Includes the PKU biobank.


GDPR (EU 2016/679)
Genetic data are a special category of personal data (Art. 9).


Genetic Integrity Act (2006:351)
No genetic test as a condition of a contract; insurers only in narrow cases. Heritable genetic changes in humans are banned. Rules for prenatal and preimplantation diagnosis.


Police genetic genealogy (from 1 July 2025)
Allowed only for murder and aggravated rape, as a last resort.



How to analyse a case. (1) Get the genetics right. (2) List who is affected. (3) Name the principles and where they conflict. (4) Check what the law says. (5) List the options, not just yes or no. (6) Argue for one, and state the strongest objection to it.

title: Exercise: ethics of genetic knowledge
text:
Cases
Discuss each case in your group. Start with the genetics, then the guiding questions. Each case ends with a collapsed list of points a good answer considers. It is not “the answer”: good answers can reach different conclusions.

C1. Twins and Huntington disease
Karin and Lisa are 28-year-old identical twins. Their father has Huntington disease. Karin wants a predictive test: she is planning a family and wants to know. Lisa does not want to know; she says she would rather live without the answer. Karin has booked an appointment at the clinical genetics clinic.

What is Karin’s risk of carrying the HTT expansion before the test? What does Karin’s result mean for Lisa? Would the answer be different if they were non-identical twins?
Which principles are in conflict? Whose autonomy counts here?
What should the genetic counsellor do: test Karin, refuse, or something in between?
Karin also asks about testing her future embryos (preimplantation testing) without learning her own status. Does that help?







Points a good answer considers: C1






Genetics: father Aa × mother aa, so each child has a ½ prior risk. Identical (monozygotic) twins have the same genotype, so a test of Karin is a test of Lisa. For non-identical twins the results are independent: each has ½, and Karin’s result says nothing certain about Lisa.
Principles: Karin’s autonomy and her reproductive planning (and beneficence towards her) against Lisa’s right not to know and non-maleficence towards her. Both twins have autonomy claims; neither automatically overrides the other.
Options: counselling for both, together or separately; time to reflect; agreeing in advance how the result is kept and shared (Lisa will see whether Karin goes ahead with family plans); Karin waiting; testing with a commitment to confidentiality. Many clinics would not simply refuse Karin, but would put real effort into protecting Lisa.
The embryo question: tests that select embryos without telling the parent their own status exist (exclusion testing, non-disclosing testing). They partly protect the right not to know, but raise their own problems, for example repeated IVF cycles that might be unnecessary. In Sweden, preimplantation diagnosis is allowed for serious monogenic disease (Genetic Integrity Act, ch. 4).
Huntington-specific facts: no cure; international guidelines recommend structured counselling before and after the test, a free choice without coercion, and a minimum age of 18 (MacLeod et al. 2013, PMID 22642570). Most at-risk people choose not to be tested: in the UK, cumulative uptake among people at 50% risk in 1994–2014 was estimated at 17.4% (Baig et al. 2016, PMID 27165004). Twins are a recognised counselling problem: confidentiality of the co-twin’s result and autonomy of participation (Heimler & Zanko 1995, PMID 11660384).






C2. An incidental BRCA1 finding
A two-year-old boy has developmental delay. His parents agree to trio exome sequencing (child, mother, father) to find the cause. The consent form said that “results related to the child’s condition” would be reported; it did not mention other findings. The analysis finds no clear cause for the boy’s condition, but the mother, Sara (35), carries a pathogenic BRCA1 variant. Sara has two sisters.

What does a pathogenic BRCA1 variant mean for Sara? What is the chance that each of her sisters carries it? That her son does?
Should the lab report it to Sara? Who decides, and when should that decision have been made?
If Sara is told, does she have a duty to tell her sisters? Does the clinic?
Is the boy’s BRCA1 status relevant now? Should he be tested as a child?







Points a good answer considers: C2






Genetics: BRCA1 variants are autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance: a high but not certain lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancer. Each sister has a ½ prior risk (one of Sara’s parents is a carrier); her son has a ½ risk too. Carriers can be offered extra screening and risk-reducing surgery: it is actionable.
Principles: beneficence (prevention can save lives; the sisters can benefit too) against Sara’s autonomy and right not to know, since she did not ask for it. The consent form did not cover this: a consent problem made by the lab, not by Sara.
The ACMG approach: report a fixed list of actionable genes (BRCA1 is on it), but discuss this at consent and let patients opt out. The lesson: decide before sequencing, in the consent.
Relatives: in most systems the patient is encouraged to inform relatives, often with a family letter from the clinic; the clinic does not usually contact relatives directly. Weigh confidentiality against harm to relatives.
Testing the child: adult-onset risk with no action in childhood: most guidance is to wait until he can decide himself (protecting his future autonomy and right not to know).






C3. A DTC result in the family chat
Oskar (24) bought a direct-to-consumer genetic test as a birthday present. He downloaded his raw data and ran it through a free online interpretation tool, which said he has a variant giving “increased risk” for a hereditary heart condition. Worried, he posted a screenshot in the family group chat and urged everyone to get tested. His mother is upset; his older brother says he never wanted to know anything about this.

How reliable is a single variant call from a consumer genotyping array and a third-party tool? What should Oskar do before anything else?
Which principles did Oskar’s post affect, and whose?
What responsibility, if any, does the company or the interpretation tool have?
What happens to Oskar’s DNA data now? What could happen if the company is sold?







Points a good answer considers: C3






Reliability: consumer arrays genotype pre-selected SNPs and are not validated for rare variants. In one clinical lab, 40% of variants from DTC raw data sent for confirmation were false positives, and some “increased risk” calls were common benign variants (Tandy-Connor et al. 2018, Genet Med, PMID 29565420). First step: confirm in a clinical lab, with genetic counselling.
Genetics: if real and autosomal dominant, each first-degree relative has a ½ prior risk. That is why the result concerns them, and also why it is theirs to decide whether to learn.
Principles: the brother’s right not to know and the family’s privacy; Oskar’s good intention (beneficence) based on an unconfirmed result (risk of harm: anxiety, unnecessary tests).
Company: terms of use, quality of the information, whether health results are given with any guidance. DTC data are stored by a company: its privacy policy, research use, data breaches and change of ownership all matter. (The US company 23andMe had a data breach in 2023 that exposed millions of relative-matching profiles, filed for bankruptcy in March 2025, and was sold in July 2025.)
Options: delete the post; speak with relatives individually; clinical confirmation and counselling before spreading results.






C4. The police ask for genealogy access
A woman was found murdered in a Swedish town in 2009. The crime-scene DNA matches nobody in the police DNA register. The Swedish Police Authority wants to use forensic investigative genetic genealogy: generate a SNP profile from the crime-scene sample, compare it with a genealogy database, and build family trees from distant relatives. A colleague then suggests also using it for a series of serious burglaries.

How can a search find a suspect who never took a DNA test? Which relatives are most useful, and why do distant cousins work?
Which interests are involved: the victim’s family, the public, database users, their relatives, the suspect?
What does the Swedish law in force since 1 July 2025 allow? Would the burglary series qualify?
Should genealogy database users have to opt in to police matching? Does it matter whether the database is in Sweden or abroad?







Points a good answer considers: C4






Genetics: relatives share long stretches of DNA identical by descent; even third cousins share detectable segments. Each match points to shared ancestors; genealogists work down their family trees to a few candidates, then a direct DNA test confirms. Erlich et al. (2018) projected that about 60% of searches for people of European descent find a third cousin or closer.
Consent: users consented to genealogy, not to being police informants; their relatives consented to nothing. Privacy is a collective issue here.
Benefits: serious crimes solved, innocent suspects cleared, justice for victims’ families.
Law: Sweden first used the method in 2019, on a 16-year-old double murder in Linköping; IMY stopped further use in 2021 for lack of legal support and because of data transfer to a third country; the law in force from 1 July 2025 limits it to murder and aggravated rape, as a last resort (Ansell & Fagerholm 2025, PMID 40995235). So the burglaries would not qualify: an example of “function creep” that the law blocks.
Opt-in respects database users’ autonomy, but not their relatives’. Data transfer outside the EU is a GDPR question.






C5. An embryo editing proposal
Both Maria and Ali have cystic fibrosis, an autosomal recessive disease. They want a biological child without CF. A clinic abroad offers to correct the CFTR variant in their IVF embryos with CRISPR and transfer the edited embryos.

What genotypes can their children have? Why can preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) not help this couple, when it helps most carrier couples?
What are the scientific risks of editing an embryo? Think of how CRISPR repair works, mosaicism and off-target effects.
Who is affected by the decision, and who cannot consent?
Is this case different from He Jiankui’s? Is it different from mitochondrial replacement? Would it be legal in Sweden?
What alternatives does the couple have?







Points a good answer considers: C5






Genetics: aa × aa gives only aa children. PGT selects among embryos, and here there is nothing to select: every embryo is affected. This is one of the few situations where editing would be the only way to a biological child without the disease, which makes it a stronger case than most.
Science: CRISPR cuts, and the cell may repair by error-prone end joining rather than copying a template, so the intended correction is not guaranteed; different cells can end up different (mosaicism); off-target cuts are hard to rule out in a single embryo. In He Jiankui’s twins, neither got the intended 32-bp deletion (CCR5-Δ32); one was heterozygous for a new edit, and they were described as mosaics (Greely 2019, J Law Biosci, PMID 31666967).
Who is affected: the future child and all descendants (the edit is in the germline), who cannot consent; also society, if heritable editing becomes normal.
Comparison: He Jiankui’s edit had no real medical need: the father’s HIV could be kept from the child by sperm washing, with no risk to the embryo (Greely 2019). MRT replaces mitochondria rather than editing a nuclear gene, and is licensed in the UK; both are heritable.
Law: in Sweden, experiments and treatments causing heritable genetic changes in humans are banned (Genetic Integrity Act 2006:351, ch. 2, §§ 3–4). “Going abroad” raises questions of justice and regulation.
Alternatives: donor gametes, adoption, a child with CF (whose treatment has improved greatly), or no children. Weigh the strength of the wish for a genetically related child.






C6. Re-using biobank samples
A research group wants to genotype 20,000 dried blood spots from the PKU biobank (newborn screening samples from the 1990s) to study whether genetic variants are associated with childhood asthma, linking the genotypes to national health registers. The people sampled are now adults. They were never asked about genetic research; their parents agreed to newborn screening.

Why would a researcher want these particular samples? What is their value?
Which Swedish laws apply? Does the project need ethical approval, and why?
Is the original consent valid for this use? What are the options: new consent from 20,000 adults, an opt-out, or approval without individual consent?
The group wants to deposit the genotypes in an international database to share with other researchers. What are the privacy risks, given what you know about re-identification?







Points a good answer considers: C6






Value: a population-wide, unselected collection with samples from birth, which no new study could recreate. Re-use has served public health, for example tracing exposure to PFAS from contaminated drinking water in Ronneby back to 1985 (PMID 40089001).
Law: traceable biological material and genetic (sensitive) data: ethical review is required (Ethical Review Act §§ 3–4). The Biobanks Act has its own chapter on the PKU biobank and requires consent for storage and use. GDPR applies to the genotypes.
Consent: the parents consented to screening, not to genetic research decades later. Contacting 20,000 adults is costly and may itself feel intrusive; an opt-out respects autonomy at lower cost. Swedish patients rarely refuse biobank research (Johnsson et al. 2008, BMJ, PMID 18617496: about 1 in 690 refused), but that does not settle whether consent is needed. The ethical review board weighs the risk to participants against the scientific value.
Sharing: removing names is not anonymisation for genomes (Gymrek 2013; Erlich 2018). Options: controlled access (researchers apply and sign an agreement), sharing only aggregate results, data staying in Sweden.
Trust: a misuse would affect public trust in the PKU biobank itself, which exists to screen newborns for treatable disease.

title: Exercise: ethics of genetic knowledge
text:
Find it

F1. When does research need ethical review?
Go to the Swedish Ethical Review Authority, etikprovningsmyndigheten.se. In the top menu, open How it works → What the Act says (in Swedish: Vad ska etikprövas?). The act itself is on riksdagen.se: Lag (2003:460).

List the four kinds of research that need ethical approval.
What does the page say about work done by students in first- and second-cycle (bachelor’s and master’s) education?
Which of the six cases above describes research that would need approval in Sweden? For each, name the criterion.
Who decides whether an application is needed: the researcher’s institution or the authority?



F2. A worked PubMed search strategy (case C1)

Task. Run "Huntington Disease"[Mesh] AND "Genetic Testing/ethics"[Mesh]. Then add the Review filter. Among the reviews, find a 2007 review by a researcher at Karolinska Institutet with the title starting “To know or not to know”. F3. Secondary findings (case C2)
Search "secondary findings"[ti] AND ACMG[ti], and filter by Article type → Practice Guideline. Open the 2023 policy statement, ACMG SF v3.2, by Miller et al.

Report its journal, year and PMID.
The full text is free in PubMed Central (link on the PubMed page). In Table 1, find BRCA1. Which phenotype and which inheritance does the table give, and since which list version has it been included? How many genes are on the v3.2 list?

title: Exercise: ethics of genetic knowledge
text:
Group assignment brief
The ethics module is examined by a written group analysis of one case and an oral presentation. This section describes the format in general terms; Canvas has the details: group sizes, which cases are available, deadlines, length, and the assessment criteria.

Choose a case: one of C1–C6 above, or a case given on Canvas.
Written analysis (in English): describe the case and the genetics behind it; identify who is affected; analyse it with the four principles and the concepts of consent, privacy and the right not to know; explain what Swedish law and ethical review say; discuss the options and argue for one, including the strongest counter-argument.
Literature: support the analysis with original literature in English, found with a documented PubMed search (show your search string, as in F2). Use at least one original research paper and one review or guideline.
Oral presentation: present the case and your analysis to the class, and lead a short discussion. Be ready to defend your position and to say what would change your mind.

The assessment is about how well you use facts and principles, not which side you take.

title: Exercise: ethics of genetic knowledge
text:
Solutions






Solutions: Find it





F1. Checked on etikprovningsmyndigheten.se and in the act on riksdagen.se.

Research needs approval if it (1) involves a physical intervention on a living or deceased person; (2) uses a method that aims to affect a person physically or mentally, or carries an obvious risk of harm; (3) is done on biological material from a living or deceased person that can be traced to that person; or (4) processes sensitive personal data (GDPR Art. 9, which includes genetic and health data) or data on criminal offences. (Act 2003:460, §§ 3–4.)
Work done only within higher education at first or second cycle (basic or advanced level) is not “research” under the act’s definition (§ 2), so it does not need its own approval. Work by a student inside a research project is covered by that project’s approval.
C6 clearly: traceable biological material (the blood spots) and sensitive personal data (genotypes, health registers). C1, C2, C3 are clinical care or private decisions, not research, so the act does not apply; but a study of, for example, how twins experience predictive testing would need approval (sensitive personal data). C4 is police work under its own law, not research. C5 would be banned in Sweden under the Genetic Integrity Act, whatever the review.
The institution responsible for the research (forskningshuvudmannen) decides whether an application is needed; the authority does not give advance rulings. (An amendment to the act, SFS 2026:1229, in force 1 July 2027, adds a requirement that the institution documents this assessment.)

Click path: etikprovningsmyndigheten.se/en → How it works → What the Act says.
F2. Click path: PubMed → "Huntington Disease"[Mesh] AND "Genetic Testing/ethics"[Mesh] → left menu Article type → Review. The review is:
Robins Wahlin TB. “To know or not to know: a review of behaviour and suicidal ideation in preclinical Huntington’s disease.” Patient Education and Counseling 2007;65(3):279–287. PMID 17000074. The author is at Karolinska Institutet, Stockholm.
From the abstract (Practice implications): “The professionals should not promote nor advocate presymptomatic DNA-testing”, and counsellors have an obligation to provide adequate information. The review stresses professional counselling and attention to suicide risk.
With the synonyms (OR huntington*[tiab], OR "predictive testing"[tiab]) you get more hits: OR widens each concept, and [tiab] also catches papers that are not (yet) indexed with these MeSH terms. (Exact counts change as papers are added, so we do not give them.)
F3. Miller DT et al. “ACMG SF v3.2 list for reporting of secondary findings in clinical exome and genome sequencing: a policy statement of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG).” Genetics in Medicine 2023;25(8):100866. PMID 37347242.

In Table 1, BRCA1 is listed (with BRCA2 and PALB2) under Hereditary breast and/or ovarian cancer, inheritance AD (autosomal dominant), report all pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants. The column “ACMG SF List Version” shows BRCA1 has been on the list since v1.0. The v3.2 table has 81 genes; v3.2 added CALM1, CALM2 and CALM3 (long QT syndrome). You may also spot FBN1 (Marfan syndrome) from the pedigree exercise. Click path: PubMed record → Free PMC article (right side) → Table 1.
No: ACMG SF v3.3 (Lee K et al., Genet Med 2025;27(8):101454, PMID 40568962) replaces it, with 84 genes. Practice guidelines are updated; always check for the newest version.

F4. a) Tillmar A, Fagerholm SA, Staaf J, et al. “Getting the conclusive lead with investigative genetic genealogy – A successful case study of a 16 year old double murder in Sweden.” Forensic Science International: Genetics 2021;53:102525. PMID 33991867.

Ansell R, Fagerholm SA. “Legislation for forensic investigative genetic genealogy in Sweden.” Forensic Sci Int Synergy 2025;11:100637. PMID 40995235. From the abstract: Sweden was in 2019 the first country outside North America to use the method; in 2021 the Swedish Authority for Privacy Protection (IMY) halted further use, because of a lack of legislative support and issues with transferring sensitive personal data to a third country. The new law passed the Riksdag in February 2025 and applies from 1 July 2025, limited to murder and aggravated rape, as a last resort and only when “absolutely necessary”.
The MeSH search finds fewer of them: the newest papers may not yet be indexed with MeSH terms, and [tiab] searches catch them earlier. A good strategy combines both with OR.

F5. a) Gymrek M, McGuire AL, Golan D, Halperin E, Erlich Y. “Identifying personal genomes by surname inference.” Science 2013;339(6117):321–324. PMID 23329047.

Short tandem repeats on the Y chromosome (Y-STRs), profiled from the personal genomes, were queried against recreational genetic genealogy databases, which are free and public. The recovered surname was combined with metadata such as age and US state to triangulate the person’s identity. The authors traced back, with high probability, the identities of multiple participants in public sequencing projects.
Erlich Y, Shor T, Pe’er I, Carmi S. “Identity inference of genomic data using long-range familial searches.” Science 2018;362(6415):690–694. PMID 30309907. Using data from 1.28 million people tested with consumer genomics, they projected that about 60% of searches for individuals of European descent would result in a third-cousin or closer match.

title: Exercise: ethics of genetic knowledge
text:
Where this leads
The cases draw on the whole course: Huntington disease and segregation (Mendel), Y-linked and mitochondrial inheritance (Pedigree analysis, Organelle inheritance), CRISPR and sequencing (Part 4), and allele frequencies (Hardy–Weinberg). The PubMed strategy in F2 is the one to use for the group assignment, and for finding original literature in any later course.

title: Quiz: ethics of genetic knowledge
text:
Short questions on the facts from the lecture, and on applying the four principles. For the “apply” questions there is often more than one defensible answer: the answer below shows the reasoning we look for, not the only conclusion.

Q1. Name the four principles of biomedical ethics, and give each in a few words.






Hint





One is about the person’s own choice, two are about good and harm, one is about fairness.









Answer






Autonomy: respect a person’s own informed, voluntary choices.
Beneficence: act for the person’s good.
Non-maleficence: do no harm (or avoid harm that is not outweighed by benefit).
Justice: distribute benefits, risks and costs fairly.

They come from Beauchamp and Childress, Principles of Biomedical Ethics. In real cases they conflict, and the work is to weigh them.




Q2. Give three reasons why a genetic test result raises ethical questions that a blood glucose value does not.






Hint





Think of relatives, the future, and what a genome can be used for besides medicine.









Answer





Any three of:

It is shared with relatives (½ of alleles with a parent, child or sibling), so it tells something about people who were not asked.
It can predict disease decades ahead, sometimes with no treatment (Huntington disease).
It is permanent and identifying: a genome cannot be changed, and can identify a person even without a name.
It informs reproductive choices about future people (carrier and prenatal tests).
Its meaning changes as variants are reclassified.





Q3. Anna’s mother has Huntington disease. Anna is 30, healthy, and does not want to be tested. Her daughter Elsa, 20, wants to be tested. (a) What is Elsa’s prior risk of carrying the HTT expansion? (b) If Elsa tests positive, what does it reveal about Anna? (c) Which principles are in conflict?






Hint





Huntington disease is autosomal dominant. Elsa can only have inherited the allele through Anna.









Answer






Anna has a ½ chance of carrying the allele, and if she does, Elsa has a ½ chance: ½ × ½ = ¼.
A positive result in Elsa means Anna must carry the allele too: she is the only route from the grandmother. Anna learns her own status against her will.
Elsa’s autonomy (her right to know about her own future) against Anna’s autonomy in the form of the right not to know, and non-maleficence towards Anna. Genetic counselling would try to find a way through, for example by discussing with Elsa how the result will be kept, and whether she can wait or talk with her mother first. There is no rule that one side always wins.





Q4. What is the difference between an incidental finding and a secondary finding? Give a genetic example of each.






Hint





One is found by chance; the other is looked for on purpose, although it is not why the test was ordered.









Answer





An incidental finding is discovered by chance and is unrelated to the question, for example misattributed paternity discovered when a trio (child and both parents) is sequenced to explain a child’s disease.
A secondary finding is deliberately looked for in a list of actionable genes, although the test was ordered for something else. Example: reporting a pathogenic BRCA1 variant found while sequencing an exome to explain epilepsy. The ACMG publishes the list of such genes (ACMG SF v3.2, Miller et al. 2023, PMID 37347242; later updated to v3.3).




Q5. NIPT is described as a screening test, while amniocentesis gives a diagnostic test. What does NIPT analyse, and why does a positive NIPT result need to be confirmed?






Hint





Where does the DNA come from, and is it all from the fetus?









Answer





NIPT analyses cell-free DNA in the pregnant woman’s blood, part of which comes from the fetus (more exactly, mostly from the placenta). It estimates whether, for example, chromosome 21 is over-represented. Because the DNA is a mixture, and the placenta’s DNA does not always match the fetus, the result is a risk, not a diagnosis. A positive result is confirmed by testing fetal cells (amniocentesis or CVS) before any decision is made.
Presence of fetal DNA in maternal plasma was first shown by Lo et al. 1997 (Lancet, PMID 9274585).




Q6. In Gymrek et al. (2013), how were the identities of “anonymous” research participants recovered? Which mode of inheritance from the pedigree unit made it possible?






Hint





Which chromosome travels with the surname in many families?









Answer





The authors read short tandem repeats on the Y chromosome (Y-STRs) from the genomes, and searched public recreational genealogy databases, where men upload their Y-STR profile with their surname. A match gives a likely surname; combined with metadata such as age and US state, this narrowed the search down to one person.
It works because of Y-linked inheritance: the Y passes from father to every son, as the surname does in many families. Gymrek et al., Science 339:321–324, PMID 23329047.




Q7. A man has never taken a DNA test. Police identify him from a crime-scene sample through a genealogy database. How is that possible, and whose consent is missing?






Hint





Think of what you share with a third cousin, and who uploaded their DNA.









Answer





His relatives uploaded their DNA. Distant cousins share long identical stretches of DNA, which a SNP array detects. From the matches, genealogists build family trees down to a few candidates, and a direct DNA test confirms. This is how the Golden State Killer suspect was found in April 2018. Erlich et al. (2018, PMID 30309907) projected that about 60% of searches for people of European descent would give a third-cousin or closer match.
Missing consent: the relatives agreed to use the database for genealogy, not as police informants; the suspect never agreed to anything. In Sweden, a law in force from 1 July 2025 allows the police to use the method only for murder and aggravated rape, as a last resort.




Q8. Why is editing a human embryo ethically different from editing a patient’s blood stem cells, even when the same gene and the same CRISPR method are used?






Hint





Where does the edit end up, and who inherits it?









Answer





Editing an embryo is germline editing: every cell of the person, including the eggs or sperm, carries the edit, so it is inherited by future generations by Mendel’s rules. Those descendants cannot consent, and mistakes (off-target cuts, mosaicism) cannot be withdrawn. Editing a patient’s own blood stem cells is somatic: it affects only that consenting person, like any other therapy (e.g. exa-cel for sickle cell disease). In Sweden, research and treatment that cause heritable genetic changes in humans are prohibited (Genetic Integrity Act 2006:351, ch. 2).




Q9. A gene drive allele is present in a heterozygote. Under Mendel’s law of segregation, what fraction of its gametes should carry the drive? What does a homing gene drive do instead, and why is that ethically different from editing a single organism?






Hint





Recall the cross Aa × aa from the Mendel unit.









Answer





Mendel: ½ of the gametes. A homing drive encodes Cas9 and a guide RNA that cut the wild-type homolog in the germline; repair copies the drive across, so the heterozygote passes it to nearly all gametes. The allele spreads through a population even if it harms its carriers: Kyrou et al. (2018, PMID 30247490) saw a drive in doublesex reach 100% prevalence in caged Anopheles gambiae within 7–11 generations, collapsing the population.
Ethically, a release affects a whole wild species and ecosystem, crosses national borders, and cannot easily be recalled. Who has the right to decide (justice), and how do you weigh huge potential benefits (malaria control) against uncertain harms?




Q10. Under the Swedish Ethical Review Act (2003:460), which of these research projects need ethical approval? (a) A study of anonymous, aggregated allele counts downloaded from gnomAD. (b) Genotyping blood samples from named patients, stored in a hospital biobank. (c) An interview study on how people experience predictive testing for Huntington disease, recording participants’ health information.






Hint





The act is triggered by sensitive personal data, physical interventions or methods affecting people, and biological material that can be traced to a person.









Answer






(a) No: aggregate counts are not personal data, and no person or sample is involved.
(b) Yes: biological material that can be traced to living persons, and genetic data, which is sensitive personal data. The Biobanks Act also applies to the samples.
(c) Yes: it processes sensitive personal data (health). Interviews are not a physical intervention, but the data trigger the act.

Applications go to the Swedish Ethical Review Authority (Etikprövningsmyndigheten). Work done only as part of a first- or second-cycle course is not “research” under the act, but a student working inside a research project is covered by that project’s approval.




Q11. Between 1935 and 1975, nearly 63,000 sterilisations were reported in Sweden under the sterilisation laws. Apart from the violation of consent, why was the eugenic aim of reducing recessive diseases also genetically mistaken?






Hint





For a rare recessive allele, where are most copies of the allele: in affected people (aa) or in carriers (Aa)?









Answer





For a rare recessive allele with frequency q, affected people (aa) make up about q² of the population and carriers (Aa) about 2q. For q = 0.01, that is 1 in 10,000 affected but about 1 in 50 carriers: almost all copies of the allele are in healthy carriers, who were not targeted. Preventing affected people from reproducing therefore reduces q only very slowly. (You can compute this with Hardy–Weinberg in Part 7.)
The sterilisation laws (1934:171 and 1941:282) were replaced in 1975 by a law that allows sterilisation only at a person’s own request. 93% of those sterilised in 1935–1975 were women.

title: Exercise: the eukaryotic chromosome
Exercise: the eukaryotic chromosome
Exercise: the eukaryotic chromosome
text:
Background
Numbers. B-DNA: 0.34 nm per bp. Nucleosome core: 147 bp around a histone octamer (2 × H2A, H2B, H3, H4); about one nucleosome per 200 bp including linker DNA. Haploid human genome (T2T-CHM13): 3.055 × 109 bp.
Chromatin. Euchromatin is open, gene-rich and replicates early. Heterochromatin is compact, gene-poor, replicates late and is built largely on satellite repeats; constitutive heterochromatin is condensed in all cells, facultative heterochromatin (the inactive X) only in some. Position-effect variegation: a gene moved next to heterochromatin is silenced in some cells and not others.
Bands and karyotypes. Band names read chromosome → arm (p short, q long) → region → band → sub-band: 1p36.33. Karyotype: total number, sex chromosomes, abnormality, e.g. 47,XX,+21; 46,XY,del(5)(p15.2); 46,XY,t(9;22)(q34;q11.2). Dark G bands are AT-rich and gene-poor; light bands are GC-rich and gene-rich.
Centromere position. Metacentric (middle), submetacentric (off-centre), acrocentric (near one end; human 13, 14, 15, 21, 22), telocentric (at the end). A chromosome needs exactly one active centromere: an acentric one is lost, a dicentric one breaks at anaphase.
Telomeres. Vertebrate repeat 5’-TTAGGG-3’ on the strand that runs 5’ → 3’ towards the end, which ends in a single-stranded 3’ overhang. End-replication problem: the last lagging-strand primer cannot be replaced by DNA, so ends shorten each division unless telomerase (protein TERT + RNA template TERC) adds repeats. Human TERC template: 3’-CAAUCCCAAUC-5’.
A minimal chromosome (yeast): an origin (ARS), a centromere (CEN) and a telomere (TEL) at each end. A YAC adds a selectable marker on each arm and carries a large insert.

title: Exercise: the eukaryotic chromosome
text:
By hand
B1. (packing) Chromosome 21 is 45 090 682 bp long in T2T-CHM13. (a) How long would it be as stretched-out B-DNA, in mm? (b) About how many nucleosomes does it carry, and how many histone proteins are in their octamers? (c) At metaphase each chromatid of chromosome 21 is about 1.5 µm long. By what factor is the DNA compacted?
B2. (band names and karyotypes) Decode each, in words. (a) the band 22q11.21 (b) 47,XXY (c) 46,XX,del(5)(p15.2) (d) 46,XY,t(9;22)(q34;q11.2) (e) Write the karyotype of a girl with three copies of chromosome 13.
B3. (G-bands) A region of a chromosome is gene-rich and its DNA is GC-rich. Predict (a) whether it lies in a dark or a light G band, (b) whether it replicates early or late in S phase, and (c) whether it is mainly euchromatin or heterochromatin. Which kind of band would you expect to contain the most genes that are expressed in many tissues?
B4. (centromeres) (a) Classify human chromosomes 1, 5 and 21 by centromere position (use the lecture figure). (b) Two acrocentric chromosomes, 14 and 21, break near their centromeres and the two long arms join into one chromosome. How many chromosomes does the person now have, and what genetic material is lost? Why is this person usually healthy? (You will meet this Robertsonian translocation in the next unit.)
B5. (no centromere, two centromeres) A chromosome breaks in two places, and the broken ends of two different chromosomes are joined. Predict what happens at the next mitosis to: (a) a fragment with no centromere; (b) a chromosome with two active centromeres, if the two centromeres of one chromatid are pulled to opposite poles.
B6. (end replication) A human fibroblast line starts with telomeres of 10 kb. Assume each telomere loses 100 bp per cell division, and that a cell stops dividing (senescence) when its shortest telomere reaches 4 kb. (a) How many divisions can the line go through? (b) In reality, telomere lengths differ between chromosome ends. If one end starts at only 7 kb, how many divisions now? What does this tell you about which telomere matters? (c) Why does a circular bacterial chromosome not have this problem?
B7. (telomerase templates) (a) The template region of the telomerase RNA of the ciliate Tetrahymena reads 3’-AACCCCAAC-5’. Which repeat does Tetrahymena telomerase add? Write it 5’ → 3’. (b) Human TERC has the template 3’-CAAUCCCAAUC-5’. The first five bases (3’-CAAUC) pair with the end of the DNA; the other six are copied. Write the six bases added in one round. (c) A cell has a TERC gene with one base changed so that its template reads 3’-CAAUCCCAGUC-5’. What sequence does it add in one round? How could you detect this in the cell’s DNA?
B8. (artificial chromosomes) Predict how each construct behaves in yeast. Each carries the URA3 marker and cells are grown without uracil; a construct that is lost leaves cells that cannot grow. (a) circular plasmid, URA3 only; (b) circular, URA3 + ARS; (c) circular, URA3 + ARS + CEN; (d) linear, URA3 + ARS + CEN, no telomere sequences; (e) linear, URA3 + ARS + CEN + TEL at both ends, 15 kb long; (f) as (e), but carrying 500 kb of human DNA.
B9. (strands) The reference sequence of chromosome 1 begins CACCCTAAACCCTAACCCCTAACCC… and ends …AGGGTTAGGGTTAGGGTT. The reference shows only one strand, read 5’ → 3’ from the p end to the q end. Explain why the two ends show different repeats, even though both are vertebrate telomeres made of TTAGGG. At which end is the 3’ overhang on the strand shown?

title: Exercise: the eukaryotic chromosome
text:
Find it
You will use NCBI Gene, the UCSC Genome Browser and MedGen. In NCBI Gene, the Summary box gives the official full name, the Gene type and the Location (band); the section Genomic context gives the coordinates on the GRCh38 assembly. The UCSC Genome Browser shows a genome as horizontal tracks under a ruler; type a position like chr1:1-200 in the search box and press Go.
F1. TERT. Search NCBI Gene for TERT human and open the Homo sapiens record. (a) What is the official full name, and the gene type? (b) On which chromosome band does it lie? (c) In Genomic context, read its coordinates on chromosome 5 (GRCh38). Roughly how far is TERT from the end of the short arm of chromosome 5? Is it on the plus or the minus strand (“complement”)?
F2. TERC. Now open the human TERC record. What is its full name, gene type and band? Why does it make sense that its gene type differs from TERT’s?
F3. A telomere and a centromere in the T2T genome. Open the UCSC Genome Browser on the T2T-CHM13 v2.0 assembly: genome.ucsc.edu, genome hs1, chr1:1-200. (a) Zoom in until you see bases (or click the ruler’s “Base Position” track). Which 6-bp repeat do you see? (b) Go to chr1:115,000,000-150,000,000 and find the track CenSat Annotation (Centromeric Satellite Annotation; if it is hidden, set it to “pack” under Mapping and Sequencing). Click the large item in the middle labelled hor_… and the large item to its right labelled hsat2_…. Read the start and end of each and compute their sizes in Mb. Which one is the active centromere, and which band are you in for the other one? (Use the ideogram at the top, or click the Cytobands track.) (c) Now open the same region in the older assembly, hg38 chr1:1-20,000, with the Gap track shown. What does the Gap track say about chr1:1-10,000?
F4. A telomere disease. Dyskeratosis congenita is a telomere biology disorder. In MedGen, open Dyskeratosis congenita, X-linked, Dyskeratosis congenita, autosomal dominant 1 and Dyskeratosis congenita, autosomal dominant 2. (OMIM: 305000, 127550, 613989.) (a) Which gene is listed for each? On which chromosome band is each gene (NCBI Gene)? (b) How is each gene connected to telomerase? (c) The same disease is X-linked in one family and autosomal dominant in another. What is this kind of heterogeneity called, and how would the pedigrees differ?

title: Exercise: the eukaryotic chromosome
text:
Solutions






Solutions: By hand





B1. (a) 45 090 682 × 0.34 nm = 1.533 × 107 nm = 15.3 mm, about 1.5 cm. (b) 45 090 682 / 200 ≈ 225 000 nucleosomes, with 8 histones each: about 1.8 million histone proteins (plus about 225 000 H1). (c) 15.3 mm / 1.5 µm = 15 300 µm / 1.5 µm ≈ 10 000-fold.
B2. (a) Chromosome 22, long arm (q), region 1, band 1, sub-band 2, sub-sub-band 1: near the centromere on 22q. (It is the region deleted in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, next unit.) (b) 47 chromosomes, sex chromosomes XXY: a male with Klinefelter syndrome. (c) A female with 46 chromosomes and a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5, from band 5p15.2 to the end (cri-du-chat syndrome). (d) A male with a reciprocal translocation between chromosome 9 (break at 9q34) and chromosome 22 (break at 22q11.2). In leukaemia cells, this rearrangement makes the Philadelphia chromosome. (e) 47,XX,+13 (trisomy 13, Patau syndrome).
B3. (a) A light (G-negative) band; (b) early replicating; (c) euchromatin. Genes expressed in many tissues (“housekeeping” genes) are concentrated in light, GC-rich bands.
B4. (a) 1: metacentric; 5: submetacentric; 21: acrocentric. (b) 45 chromosomes: the two long arms make one chromosome. What is lost are the two tiny short arms, which carry repeats and copies of the ribosomal RNA genes (rDNA). The rDNA is present on all five pairs of acrocentrics, so losing two short arms leaves plenty, and the person is healthy. The problem comes in the next generation: this carrier can make unbalanced gametes (next unit).
B5. (a) An acentric fragment cannot attach to the spindle. It is not pulled to either pole and is usually lost (left in the cytoplasm, often in a micronucleus). The genes on it are lost from one or both daughter cells. (b) A dicentric chromatid pulled towards both poles is stretched into an anaphase bridge and breaks at a random point. Each daughter gets a broken chromosome with a new unprotected end, which can fuse again: a breakage-fusion-bridge cycle, as McClintock saw in maize.
B6. (a) (10 000 − 4 000) / 100 = 60 divisions. (b) (7 000 − 4 000) / 100 = 30 divisions. The shortest telomere decides, not the average: one critically short end is enough to trigger the DNA damage response. (c) A circle has no ends: every Okazaki primer has another DNA fragment upstream whose 3’ end can be extended to fill the gap.
B7. (a) The DNA complement of 3’-AACCCCAAC-5’ is 5’-TTGGGGTTG-3’: Tetrahymena adds TTGGGG repeats. (b) The copied part is 3’-CCAAUC-5’, so it adds 5’-GGTTAG-3’ (which continues the TTAGGG repeat: …TTAG|GGTTAG|GGTTAG…). (c) The copied part becomes 3’-CCAGUC-5’, so it adds 5’-GGTCAG-3’ instead of GGTTAG. Detect it by sequencing the chromosome ends (or by hybridising a probe for the mutant repeat): new mutant repeats would appear at the outermost part of the telomeres, added on top of the old normal repeats.
B8. (a) No colonies (or almost none): the plasmid cannot replicate, so it is diluted out. (b) Replicates, but has no centromere, so it is distributed unevenly and lost from many cells each division. Colonies grow slowly and are unstable. (c) Stable: replicates once per S phase and segregates like a chromosome, about one copy per cell. (d) Unstable: the bare ends are degraded or joined; it does not survive as a linear molecule. (e) A linear minichromosome. It works, but a short one is lost more often than a natural chromosome. (f) A YAC with a large insert behaves much like a natural yeast chromosome: stable. Length itself improves segregation.
B9. The reference shows the top strand, 5’ → 3’ from the p end to the q end. At the q end, this strand runs 5’ → 3’ towards the end, so it is the G-rich strand: TTAGGG. At the p end, the strand that runs 5’ → 3’ towards that end is the bottom strand, which is G-rich (TTAGGG); the top strand there is its reverse complement, CCCTAA. On the strand shown, the 3’ end is at the q end, so that is where its 3’ overhang is (the p end’s overhang is on the bottom strand). Real chromosome ends have overhangs; a reference assembly writes both strands as fully paired.









Solutions: Find it





These facts were checked with the NCBI E-utilities (Gene, MedGen) and the UCSC REST API (hs1, hg38) on 2026-11-20.
F1. NCBI Gene ID 7015. (a) telomerase reverse transcriptase, gene type protein coding. (b) 5p15.33, the outermost band of 5p. (c) Genomic context: NC_000005.10 (1253167..1295068, complement), so TERT lies on the minus strand, about 1.25–1.3 Mb from the end of 5p. Click path: Gene search → “TERT telomerase reverse transcriptase [Homo sapiens (human)]” → Summary (Official full name, Gene type, Location) → Genomic context.
F2. NCBI Gene ID 7012: telomerase RNA component, gene type ncRNA, band 3q26.2. TERC is the RNA template of telomerase. Its gene is transcribed into an RNA that is used as RNA, never translated, so it is a non-coding RNA gene; TERT encodes the protein. The two parts of one enzyme are encoded on different chromosomes (5 and 3).
