title: Exercise: the eukaryotic chromosome
text:
Where this leads
The elements you met here all come back when chromosomes go wrong. In Rearrangements & aneuploidy (next), a crossover inside an inversion makes dicentric and acentric chromosomes, two acrocentrics fuse into a Robertsonian translocation, and the 9;22 translocation makes the Philadelphia chromosome. Bacterial genetics shows a circular chromosome, with no telomeres, and the F plasmid that BACs are built on. Chromatin returns as a regulator of genes in Part 6.
Next: Exercise in R: read the first and last 10 kb of chromosome 1 from the complete T2T genome, count TTAGGG and CCCTAA repeats with str_count, and plot repeat density along the sequence to see where the telomere ends.

title: Quiz: the eukaryotic chromosome
text:
Short questions on chromatin, banding, centromeres, telomeres and artificial chromosomes. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Chromatin is digested briefly with a nuclease that cuts linker DNA, and the DNA is run on a gel. What pattern of fragment sizes do you expect, and what does it tell you?






Hint





Which parts of the DNA are protected by the histone octamer, and how far apart are they?









Answer





A ladder of fragments at about 200, 400, 600 bp and so on: multiples of the nucleosome repeat. The nuclease cuts only in the exposed linker DNA, so each fragment holds a whole number of nucleosomes. With longer digestion, the linker is trimmed away and a resistant 147-bp core fragment remains. This is how the regular spacing of nucleosomes was discovered.




Q2. Why do histones bind DNA so tightly regardless of its sequence?






Hint





Look at their amino acids, and at what every nucleotide has in common.









Answer





Histones are rich in the positively charged amino acids lysine and arginine. DNA has a negatively charged phosphate in every nucleotide, whatever the base. Much of the binding is electrostatic attraction to the backbone, so it does not depend on the sequence. (Some sequences bend more easily and position nucleosomes better, but every sequence can be wrapped.)




Q3. Give three differences between euchromatin and constitutive heterochromatin.






Hint





Think of packing, genes, time of replication and DNA sequence.









Answer





Heterochromatin is compact in interphase (stains darkly), gene-poor and mostly silent, replicates late in S phase, and is built largely on repetitive satellite DNA (around centromeres, for example). It carries H3K9 methylation bound by HP1. Euchromatin is open, gene-rich, mostly active and replicates early. Constitutive heterochromatin is condensed in every cell; facultative heterochromatin, such as the inactive X, only in some.




Q4. A Drosophila inversion moves white+ next to centromeric heterochromatin, and the eyes become red-and-white mottled. No base of white has changed. Explain the mottling, and why the white areas form patches rather than scattered single cells.






Hint





What can heterochromatin do along a chromosome, and what happens to a cell’s state when it divides?









Answer





Heterochromatin can spread along the chromosome into the moved gene and silence it. Whether it spreads is decided, partly at random, in each cell during eye development. Once decided, the state is inherited by the cell’s descendants, so each early choice gives a patch (a clone) of red or white cells. This is position-effect variegation: the phenotype depends on the gene’s position, not its sequence.




Q5. Decode these: (a) the band 7q31.2, (b) the karyotype 47,XX,+18, (c) 45,X.






Hint





Band: chromosome, arm, region, band, sub-band. Karyotype: total number, sex chromosomes, abnormality.









Answer






Chromosome 7, long arm (q), region 3, band 1, sub-band 2. (It is the location of CFTR.)
47 chromosomes, female (XX), with an extra chromosome 18: trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome).
45 chromosomes with a single X and no second sex chromosome: Turner syndrome. Both are in the next unit.





Q6. A yeast centromere is about 125 bp, but a human centromere spans several megabases. What do human centromeres consist of, and why is the DNA sequence alone not enough to make a centromere in humans?






Hint





What histone variant marks active centromeres? Can a centromere move?









Answer





Human centromeres are long arrays of α-satellite, a 171-bp repeat organised in higher-order repeats. The active centromere is defined by chromatin containing the histone H3 variant CENP-A. Evidence that sequence is not enough: neocentromeres can form on DNA with no α-satellite, and in dicentric chromosomes one α-satellite array can be inactive (no CENP-A). CENP-A marks the centromere epigenetically and is copied to the daughter chromosomes.




Q7. Why does replication shorten a linear chromosome, but not a circular bacterial chromosome?






Hint





What does DNA polymerase need in order to fill the gap left when an RNA primer is removed?









Answer





DNA polymerase can only extend a 3’ end. When the RNA primer of an Okazaki fragment is removed, the gap is filled by extending the fragment upstream of it. At the end of a linear molecule, the last primer has no fragment upstream, so its gap cannot be filled and the new strand is shorter: the end-replication problem. A circle has no ends: every primer has another fragment upstream of it.




Q8. The template region of human telomerase RNA reads 3’-CAAUCCCAAUC-5’. Which repeat does it add, and to which strand? What would change if a mutation turned the template into 3’-CAAUCCCGAUC-5’?






Hint





Write the DNA complement of the template, 5’ → 3’.









Answer





The complement of 3’-CAAUCCCAAUC-5’ is 5’-GTTAGGGTTAG-3’, so telomerase adds TTAGGG repeats to the 3’ end of the G-rich strand. The first five template bases (3’-CAAUC) pair with the DNA end (GTTAG); the other six (CCAAUC) are copied into GGTTAG. In the mutant template 3’-CAAUC CCGAUC-5’, the copied part is CCGAUC, so telomerase adds GGCTAG instead of GGTTAG: mutant repeats appear at the chromosome ends. Blackburn’s lab did this experiment in Tetrahymena and found the mutant repeats at the cells’ telomeres, proving that the RNA is the template.




Q9. Most human somatic cells have no telomerase activity. Why is that thought to protect against cancer, and how do cancer cells get around it?






Hint





What happens to a cell line whose telomeres keep shortening?









Answer





Without telomerase, telomeres shorten with each division until they trigger senescence (or cell death) after a limited number of divisions (the Hayflick limit, about 40–60 for cultured fibroblasts). A cell that starts to divide out of control therefore runs out of divisions. About 85–90% of cancers re-activate telomerase, often through mutations in the TERT promoter; most of the rest use ALT, alternative lengthening of telomeres by recombination.




Q10. You want a linear DNA molecule to be inherited stably in yeast. Which three kinds of element must it carry, and what does each do? Why does a YAC also carry two different selectable markers, one on each arm?






Hint





Replication, segregation, ends.









Answer





An origin of replication (ARS) so it is copied in S phase; a centromere (CEN) so that the two copies go to opposite poles at mitosis; and a telomere at each end so the ends are protected and fully replicated. The two markers (for example TRP1 and URA3) let you select for cells that carry both arms, that is, a complete YAC with the insert between them.




Q11. Why was it impossible to sequence human centromeres with short sequencing reads, and what did the T2T Consortium use instead?






Hint





How do you place a 150-base read inside a 4-Mb array of nearly identical 171-bp repeats?









Answer





A short read from inside a satellite array matches many places equally well, so the assembly cannot tell where it belongs or how long the array is. These regions were left as gaps or as computer models in GRCh38. T2T used long reads: accurate PacBio HiFi reads (about 20 kb) and ultra-long Oxford Nanopore reads (over 100 kb) that span the rare differences between repeats. They also used CHM13, a nearly completely homozygous cell line, so there was only one version of each chromosome to assemble.

title: Exercise: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
Exercise: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
Exercise: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
text:
Background
Cis and trans. Promoters and enhancers are DNA sites: mutations in them affect only the allele on the same chromosome (cis). Transcription factors are proteins: mutations in their genes affect every target, on both chromosomes (trans). An enhancer can be far from its gene and is often tissue-specific.
Motifs. A transcription factor binds a short, degenerate motif. In random DNA with equal base frequencies, a position that allows k of the 4 bases matches with probability k/4; multiply over positions. Remember to count both strands.
Chromatin. Acetylation and H3K4me3 go with active chromatin; H3K9me3, H3K27me3 and promoter CpG methylation with silent chromatin. DNMT1 copies methylation after replication, so the state is inherited through mitosis.
Imprinting. Some genes are expressed only from the maternal or only from the paternal allele. The imprint is set in the parent’s germ line and reset every generation. A loss-of-function allele of a maternally expressed gene causes disease only when inherited from the mother; of a paternally expressed gene, only when inherited from the father.
X inactivation. In female mammals, one X per cell is inactivated (Barr body, coated by XIST RNA). The choice is random and made in a pool of N progenitor cells; descendants keep it. Barr bodies = number of X − 1. The fraction of progenitors that chose the maternal X is binomial: P(k of N) = \(\binom{N}{k}(1/2)^N\). Skewed = at least 80 : 20.
Dosage compensation. Mammals inactivate one X in females; Drosophila males double their single X; C. elegans hermaphrodites halve both X.

title: Exercise: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
text:
By hand
B1. (cis or trans?) In mice, two recessive mutations, m1 and m2, each abolish expression of a liver gene G in homozygotes. m1 maps 40 kb upstream of G; m2 maps to another chromosome. The G gene carries a silent SNP, so its two alleles (Ga and Gb) can be measured separately in RNA.

Which mutation is probably in an enhancer and which in a transcription factor?
In a heterozygote m1 Ga / + Gb (m1 on the same chromosome as Ga), which allele(s) of G are expressed? And in m2/+ ; Ga/Gb?
Why can the m2 mutation be recessive even though it is trans-acting?

B2. (motifs by chance) a) How many matches to the SOX2 core motif ACAAT do you expect in a 10 kb stretch of random DNA, counting both strands? b) How many matches to a 12-bp motif with no degenerate positions do you expect in the 3.1 Gb human genome (both strands)? What does that suggest about why many transcription factors bind as pairs or groups?
B3. (reciprocal crosses with an imprinted gene) In mice, Igf2 (a growth factor) is expressed only from the paternal allele. Igf2− is a null allele; Igf2− mice that lack all Igf2 expression are small.

A heterozygous Igf2+/Igf2− male is crossed to a wild-type female. What fraction of the pups is small?
Do the reciprocal cross: heterozygous female × wild-type male.
Why would Mendel’s reciprocal crosses (Part 1) never have shown this?

B4. (imprinting in a pedigree) A disease is caused by loss of function of a gene that is expressed only from the maternal allele. Grandfather I-1 carries the mutation. He has a son (II-1) and a daughter (II-2); both inherited the mutation. Neither is affected.

Why is neither II-1 nor II-2 affected?
What is the risk that a child of II-1 is affected? A child of II-2?
What is the risk that a grandchild of II-1, through one of II-1’s daughters, is affected?

B5. (calico cats) Orange (XO) and black (Xo) are alleles of an X-linked gene in cats.

An orange male is crossed to a black female. Give the coat colours of their sons and daughters.
A calico female (XOXo) is crossed to a black male. Give the expected offspring by sex and colour.
A male calico kitten is born. Suggest a karyotype, and say how many Barr bodies his cells have.

B6. (Barr bodies and XIST) A lab measures XIST RNA and counts Barr bodies in cultured cells from four people. Predict both for: a) 46,XY; b) 46,XX; c) 47,XXY; d) 45,X. Which of them would you mistake for female on XIST alone?
B7. (skewing by chance) Assume X inactivation is decided in N progenitor cells, each choosing at random.

For N = 8, what is the probability that a female is skewed at least 80 : 20 (that is, k ≤ 1 or k ≥ 7 progenitors chose the maternal X)?
For N = 16, what is the probability that k ≤ 3 or k ≥ 13? (The binomial coefficients are 1, 16, 120, 560 for k = 0–3; \(2^{16}\) = 65536.)
Use your answers to explain why identical-twin sisters can differ for an X-linked trait.

B8. (manifesting carrier) A woman’s brother has Duchenne muscular dystrophy (X-linked recessive); she has mildly weak muscles and a raised creatine kinase level. Her mother is a known carrier.

Before any test, what is the chance that she is a carrier?
Given her symptoms, she is very likely a carrier. Explain how a carrier can show symptoms.
What is the chance that a son of hers is affected, if she is a carrier?

B9. (dosage compensation) In C. elegans, a loss-of-function mutation in dpy-27, a subunit of the dosage compensation complex, kills XX animals but not XO animals. In Drosophila, msl mutations kill XY animals but not XX. Explain both, and predict what a mammal with no working XIST gene would look like in each sex.

title: Exercise: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
text:
Explore
Do the by-hand part first. In the demo, N progenitor cells choose the maternal (orange) or paternal (black) X at random and grow into clonal patches. The panel on the right gives the percentage of cells in this female, and a histogram of the fraction over 1000 simulated females with the same N, with the share that are skewed at least 80 : 20. “cell mixing” moves cells around after the patches have grown.



E1. At N = 16, press “new embryo” ten times and note the percentage of maternal-X cells each time. What range do you see? Compare the share of skewed embryos in the histogram with your answer to B7 b).
E2. Set N = 2, 4, 8, 64 and 256 in turn. Write down the percentage of skewed embryos for each. Why does the histogram for N = 2 have only three bars?
E3. In embryo 1 at N = 16, 9 of 16 progenitors (56 %) chose the maternal X, but the tissue is 50 : 50. Why can the share of cells differ from the share of progenitors?
E4. Click “mixed tissue (blood)”. Compare the mosaic and the numbers with the same N and no mixing. Does cell mixing change the chance of skewing? What does it change?
E5. A calico cat has large orange and black patches; the blood of a woman shows no patches at all, even though both are mosaics. Use the demo to explain the difference.






Solutions: Explore





E1. Most embryos fall between about 30 % and 70 % maternal cells; the histogram is centred on 50 % with a spread of about ±12 % (one standard deviation, \(\sqrt{0.25/16}\) = 0.125). The demo gives 2.3 % of 1000 embryos skewed for embryo 1’s seed; the exact binomial answer from B7 b) is 2.1 %. The small difference is sampling noise in the 1000 simulated embryos.
E2. Skewed share for embryo 1 (press “reset” first; the simulated 1000 embryos change a little with each new embryo): N = 2 51.3 %, N = 4 13.2 %, N = 8 6.1 %, N = 64 0 %, N = 256 0 %. The exact binomial values are 50 %, 12.5 %, 7.0 % (B7 a), and essentially 0. With N = 2 there are only three possible outcomes for the progenitors: 0, 1 or 2 maternal (0 %, 50 %, 100 %), with probabilities ¼, ½, ¼. Half of all females are completely skewed.
E3. Each progenitor grows into a patch, but the patches are not equally big: some progenitors leave more descendants than others (here, by random growth). The tissue fraction therefore varies a bit more than the progenitor fraction. In real tissues, differences in proliferation and selection against cells using a harmful X add to this.
E4. The percentages are the same: mixing does not change which X each cell uses, only where the cells are. It changes the pattern, from big coherent patches to salt-and-pepper. So the skewing statistics depend on N (and selection), while patch size depends on how much cells move after the choice.
E5. Skin pigment cells (melanocytes) in a cat descend from a few precursors that migrate and then proliferate in place, so their clones stay together as patches. Blood cells are made in the bone marrow and circulate, so clones are thoroughly mixed: a blood sample is a mixture of both cell types with no visible pattern, but the proportions can still be measured (and can be skewed).

title: Exercise: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
text:
Find it
JASPAR (jaspar.elixir.no) is an open database of transcription-factor binding profiles. Each profile has an ID such as MA0143 plus a version (.1, .2, …). The page shows the sequence logo (big letters = strongly preferred bases), the Class and Family of the factor, the Species and the Data type (how the sites were found).
F1. Open the JASPAR profile for human SOX2, MA0143.5. Read the Class, the Family and the Data type. Read the logo from left to right: which five-letter core do the big letters spell?
F2. Open the profile for mouse Gata1, MA0035.3. What is the class of the factor? Read the core of the logo, then write its reverse complement. Where is “GATA”? Why does JASPAR not have to show the motif on the strand you expect?
F3. Open the GTEx Portal page for XIST. The violin plot shows expression (TPM) across tissues. In which kinds of tissue is XIST highest? If the plot lets you split the samples by sex, do so: what do you see in, for example, skeletal muscle?
F4. Open NCBI Gene for human XIST. In the Summary, read the Gene type and the cytogenetic Location. Does XIST encode a protein? On which strand of the X is it (Genomic context: is the range marked “complement”)?






Hint





For F2, reverse complement means: complement each base (A↔︎T, C↔︎G) and read the result backwards. TTATCT becomes AGATAA.

title: Exercise: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
text:
Solutions






Solutions: By hand





B1. a) m1, close to G, is probably a cis-acting enhancer mutation; m2, unlinked, is probably in a gene for a transcription factor (trans-acting). b) m1 Ga / + Gb: only Gb is expressed in liver; the enhancer next to Ga is broken (cis). m2/+ ; Ga/Gb: both alleles are expressed, each at the level that one working copy of the factor allows. The factor diffuses to both copies. c) A trans-acting mutation is recessive when one working copy of the factor gene makes enough protein to activate G (haplosufficiency, Extensions to Mendel). Trans means “acts on both copies of the target”, not “dominant”.
B2. a) P(ACAAT) = (¼)5 = 1/1024 per position and strand. 10 000 × 2 / 1024 ≈ 20 matches. b) (¼)12 = 1/16 777 216; 3.1 × 109 × 2 / 1.68 × 107 ≈ 370 matches, still many, and real factors tolerate mismatches, so many more. Factors that bind as dimers or with partners (e.g. OCT4–SOX2) effectively read a longer, combined motif, which is far rarer and so more specific.
B3. a) The father passes Igf2− to ½ of the pups, and the paternal allele is the only one expressed: those pups make no IGF2 and are small. ½ small. b) The mother passes Igf2− to ½ of the pups, but the maternal allele is silent anyway; every pup has an active paternal Igf2+. None small. c) Mendel’s seven pea traits were not imprinted: it did not matter which parent gave which allele. Imprinting makes reciprocal crosses differ even for an autosomal gene. (In mice this exact experiment was done in 1991 and was one of the first demonstrations of imprinting.)
B4. a) Both inherited the mutation from their father. The paternal allele of this gene is silent anyway, so their maternal allele is the active one, and it is normal. b) II-1 is a man: his children receive the mutation on their paternal allele, which is silent. Risk 0. II-2 is a woman: she passes the mutation with probability ½, on the maternal (active) allele. Risk ½. c) A daughter of II-1 inherits the mutation with probability ½ (unaffected herself). Her child gets it from her (maternal) with probability ½. Risk = ½ × ½ = ¼.
B5. a) XOY × XoXo: sons get the mother’s X: all black (XoY). Daughters get XO from the father and Xo from the mother: all calico (XOXo). b) XOXo × XoY: sons ½ orange, ½ black; daughters ½ calico (XOXo), ½ black (XoXo). c) XXY (e.g. XOXoY), with one Barr body. (A chimera of two fused embryos is the other explanation.)
B6. a) 46,XY: no XIST, 0 Barr bodies. b) 46,XX: XIST expressed, 1. c) 47,XXY: XIST expressed, 1. d) 45,X: no XIST, 0. The XXY man would be mistaken for female on XIST alone; the 45,X woman would be mistaken for male. A Y-linked gene such as RPS4Y1 resolves both.
B7. a) P(k = 0) + P(k = 1) + P(k = 7) + P(k = 8) = (1 + 8 + 8 + 1)/256 = 18/256 = 0.070, about 7 %. b) 2 × (1 + 16 + 120 + 560)/65536 = 1394/65536 = 0.021, about 2 %. c) X inactivation happens after the twin embryos have split (or in separate cell pools), so each twin’s choice is an independent random draw. With a small N, one twin can be skewed towards the mutant X and the other not, and they can differ in phenotype although their genomes are identical.
B8. a) Her mother is XDXd; she has a ½ chance of being a carrier (XDXd). b) Skewed X inactivation in muscle: if most of her muscle precursor cells chose the X with the normal allele as the inactive one, most fibres lack dystrophin. She is a manifesting carrier. c) ½, as for any carrier mother: each son gets one of her two X chromosomes.
B9. C. elegans hermaphrodites (XX) halve the expression of both X; without dpy-27 both X are fully active, the hermaphrodite gets twice the right dose, and dies. XO males do not use the complex. Drosophila males (XY) double their single X with the MSL complex; without it, the male X is at half dose and males die. Females do not use MSL. A mammal with no working XIST: males (XY) are normal, because they never inactivate an X; females fail to inactivate either X and would have a double dose of X-linked genes. (In mice, embryos that cannot inactivate an X die early.)









Solutions: Find it





F1. SOX2, MA0143.5 (Homo sapiens): Class High-mobility group (HMG) domain factors; Family SOX-related factors; Data type ChIP-seq. The logo spells ACAAT, then a G (consensus ACAATGG). Click path: jaspar.elixir.no → search “SOX2” → MA0143 → latest version → the logo and the metadata table next to it.
F2. Gata1, MA0035.3 (Mus musculus, ChIP-seq): Class Other C4 zinc finger-type factors, Family C4-GATA-related. The core of the logo reads TTATCT (consensus …CTTATCTG…). Its reverse complement is AGATAA, which contains GATA. A binding site is double-stranded, so a motif is equally valid on either strand; JASPAR shows the orientation in which the matrix was built. (The newest version, MA0035.5, from human GATA1, is a shorter core of the same site.)
F3. XIST is highest in female reproductive tissues (ovary, uterus, fallopian tube, cervix, vagina), with median TPM roughly 50–100 in GTEx v10. In most other tissues the pooled median is close to 0, because most GTEx samples come from men, so the median sample is male. Split by sex, XIST in skeletal muscle is clearly expressed in women (median ≈ 18 TPM in GTEx v10) and essentially absent in men (≈ 0.02 TPM). You compute exactly these numbers in the R exercise.
F4. XIST: Gene type ncRNA (it does not encode a protein; the RNA itself is the product), location Xq13.2. In Genomic context the range on NC_000023.11 is marked complement: XIST is on the minus strand. Click path: ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gene/7503 → Summary → Gene type, Location; Genomic context → Location.

title: Exercise: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
text:
Where this leads
XIST is a long non-coding RNA that silences a whole chromosome. In RNA-mediated regulation we meet much smaller RNAs, microRNAs, that turn down individual mRNAs, and learn how they were found by a genetic screen in a worm.
Next: Exercise in R: reshape a GTEx table with pivot_longer(), summarise it with group_by() and summarise(), and see how a pooled median hides the female XIST signal.

title: Quiz: Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics
text:
Short questions on enhancers, transcription factors, chromatin, imprinting and X inactivation. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A point mutation in an enhancer of gene G is heterozygous. Expression of G drops in the liver but not in the kidney. Does the mutation act in cis or in trans? How could you show it with an allele-specific measurement?






Hint





Think of lacOc. Which copy of G does the enhancer control?









Answer





In cis. An enhancer is a DNA site; it controls only the copy of G on the same chromosome. If the two alleles of G differ at a neutral SNP in the transcript, you can measure each allele’s mRNA in liver (allele-specific expression): the allele on the mutant chromosome will be low and the other normal. A trans-acting mutation (in a transcription factor) would lower both alleles equally. Kidney is unaffected because a different enhancer drives G there.




Q2. GATA1 binds the motif (A/T)GATA(A/G). How often would you expect this 6-bp motif by chance on one strand of random DNA with equal base frequencies? What does that tell you about predicting binding sites from sequence alone?






Hint





Two positions allow 2 of 4 bases; four positions allow 1 of 4.









Answer





P(match at one position) = ½ × (¼)4 × ½ = 1/1024, so about once per kb on each strand: millions of matches in a 3-Gb genome. Only a small fraction are bound in any cell. Binding depends on chromatin accessibility, neighbouring factors and spacing, not on the motif alone.




Q3. Why is lactase persistence (an enhancer variant) inherited as a dominant trait?






Hint





How many active LCT alleles does a heterozygote have in adult gut?









Answer





The variant keeps the enhancer active in adults, so the LCT allele on the same chromosome is still expressed after weaning. A heterozygote has one active allele, which makes enough lactase to digest milk. One copy is enough, so the trait is dominant (a gain of expression in cis).




Q4. Which marks go with active chromatin and which with silent chromatin: H3K27me3, histone acetylation, H3K4me3, methylated CpG islands at the promoter, H3K9me3?






Hint





Two of them are “on”, three are “off”.









Answer





Active: histone acetylation and H3K4me3 (at active promoters). Silent: H3K9me3, H3K27me3 and methylated CpG islands.




Q5. Explain how a DNA methylation pattern can be copied when a cell divides.






Hint





CpG reads the same on both strands. What does each daughter double helix look like right after replication?









Answer





CpG is palindromic, so a methylated site has a methyl-C on both strands. After semiconservative replication each daughter helix is hemi-methylated: the old strand is methylated, the new strand not. The maintenance methyltransferase DNMT1 recognises hemi-methylated CpG and methylates the new strand, restoring the full pattern in both daughters.




Q6. A child has a deletion of 15q11–q13 on the maternal chromosome 15. Which syndrome do you expect, and why? What if the same deletion were on the paternal chromosome?






Hint





Which genes in the region are expressed only from the mother’s copy?









Answer





Angelman syndrome. UBE3A is expressed only from the maternal allele in neurons (the paternal copy is silenced). Losing the maternal copy leaves no active UBE3A in the brain. The same deletion on the paternal 15 removes the paternally expressed genes (the SNRPN cluster) and gives Prader–Willi syndrome.




Q7. How many Barr bodies are in the cells of: a 46,XX woman; a 46,XY man; a 47,XXY man; a 45,X woman; a 47,XXX woman?






Hint





All X chromosomes but one are inactivated.









Answer





X − 1 in each case: 46,XX 1; 46,XY 0; 47,XXY 1; 45,X 0; 47,XXX 2.




Q8. Why are calico (orange-and-black) cats almost always female? What karyotype would you predict for a rare male calico?






Hint





Where is the orange gene?









Answer





The orange locus is on the X. An orange-and-black coat needs both alleles, XO and Xo, active in different patches, so the cat needs two X chromosomes and X inactivation. A normal male (XY) has one X and is either orange or black. A male calico is most likely XXY (or a chimera of two embryos).




Q9. A woman is heterozygous for a recessive X-linked mutation that causes haemophilia A in males. She has a clear bleeding tendency. Give two possible explanations.






Hint





Which X is active in the cells that make clotting factor VIII?









Answer





Skewed X inactivation: by chance (few progenitor cells at the time of inactivation) or by selection, most of her factor-VIII-producing cells use the mutant X. She is a manifesting carrier. Other possibilities: she has only one X (45,X, Turner), or she carries a second mutation on her other X. (In a pedigree, this looks like reduced penetrance of an X-linked recessive allele in females.)




Q10. In the demo, why does skewing become less common as the number of progenitor cells N grows?






Hint





Each progenitor is a coin toss. What happens to the proportion of heads as you toss more coins?









Answer





The fraction of progenitors that chose the maternal X is a binomial proportion with standard deviation \(\sqrt{0.25/N}\). With N = 4 it is 0.25, so 80 : 20 or worse is common (12.5 % of females have all four progenitors choosing the same X); with N = 64 it is 0.0625, and 80 : 20 is many standard deviations away. It is the same law of large numbers as Mendel’s large counts in Part 1.




Q11. Mutations in the Drosophila gene msl-2 kill males but not females. Explain.






Hint





How do fruit flies equalise X expression between the sexes?









Answer





Drosophila males double the transcription of their single X using the MSL complex. Without msl-2, the complex does not form, the male X is expressed at half the needed level, and males die. Females (XX) do not use the MSL complex (its assembly is blocked in females), so they are unaffected.

title: Exercise: Gene expression (recap)
Exercise: Gene expression (recap)
Exercise: Gene expression (recap)
text:
Background
Transcription. RNA polymerase II starts at the promoter (TATA box about 25–30 bp upstream). The mRNA has the sequence of the coding strand (U for T) and is complementary to the template strand.
Processing. A 5′ cap is added; the RNA is cut after an AAUAAA signal and given a poly(A) tail; introns are removed by the spliceosome. An intron starts with GU (donor) and ends with AG (acceptor), with a branch-point A upstream of the AG.
Reading frame. Translation starts at AUG and continues in one frame until a stop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA). Skipping an exon whose length is a multiple of 3 keeps the frame; otherwise the frame shifts. A premature stop codon well before the last exon–exon junction triggers nonsense-mediated decay (NMD).
The code is triplet, non-overlapping, degenerate and nearly universal. Frameshift combinations (Crick and Brenner): (+)(−) or (+)(+)(+) close together restore the frame.
Codon numbering. In a coding sequence, codon n covers c.(3n−2) to c.3n.

title: Exercise: Gene expression (recap)
text:
Solutions






Solutions: By hand





B1. a) Reverse complement: 5′-CTCCTCAGGAGTCAGATGCACCAT-3′. b) mRNA 5′-AUGGUGCAUCUGACUCCUGAGGAG-3′: Met Val His Leu Thr Pro Glu Glu. c) The polymerase makes RNA 5′ → 3′, so it moves along the template 3′ → 5′.
B2. a) The intron starts at the first GU after the exon (GUAAGU…) and ends at the AG before GAAUUC: GUAAGUGACUAACUUUUCCUUUCAG, 25 nt. b) Spliced: AUG GCC AAG GAA UUC UGG UAA: Met Ala Lys Glu Phe Trp Stop. c) Unspliced, with the mutation: AUG GCC AAG AUA AGU GAC UAA: Met Ala Lys Ile Ser Asp Stop. The intron is read as if it were coding, and contains a stop codon three codons in: a short, non-functional protein (and in a real cell the mRNA would likely be destroyed by NMD). (The sequence is invented.)
B3. a) 93 = 3 × 31: in frame. 183 = 3 × 61: in frame. 192 = 3 × 64: in frame. 95 = 3 × 31 + 2: frameshift. 87 = 3 × 29: in frame. b) Skipping exon 12 (95 nt) shifts the reading frame after exon 11. The following codons are misread until a premature stop codon appears, and the mRNA is likely destroyed by NMD: a null allele, like G542X, which lies in the same exon.
B4. a) (+)(+): net +2: mutant. b) (−)(−)(−): net −3: wild type (one amino acid fewer). c) (+)(−)(+): net +1: mutant. d) (+)(+)(+)(+): net +4 = one codon plus +1: mutant. e) (+)(+)(−)(−): net 0: wild type. The rule: the frame is restored downstream when the net change is a multiple of 3. Only the short stretch between the first and last change is misread.
B5. a) 42 = 16 doublets are too few for 20 amino acids. Triplets give 43 = 64, enough (with degeneracy and stops). b) With overlapping triplets, each base would belong to three codons, so one change would alter up to three adjacent amino acids. HbS, and other missense alleles, change exactly one amino acid, so codons do not overlap.
B6. a) Reduced: less transcription of a normal gene (β+). b) Abnormal: β-globin with Val instead of Glu (HbS). c) None: no normal splicing (β0). d) Reduced: most mRNA is mis-spliced, but some normal mRNA is made (β+). e) None: premature stop, mRNA destroyed by NMD (β0). f) Reduced: poor 3′-end processing gives less stable mRNA (β+). Only the missense change gives an abnormal protein; the other five are thalassaemias, diseases of quantity.









Solutions: Find it





These facts were checked with the Ensembl REST API (release 116), the UniProt REST API and NCBI E-utilities on 2026-11-20.
F1. a) Chromosome 7, forward (+) strand (band 7q31.2). The location line gives the span of all transcripts together (7:117,287,120–117,715,971 in release 116). b) 45 transcripts in release 116 (other releases may differ). MANE Select: ENST00000003084 (CFTR-201), matching RefSeq NM_000492.4. c) 27 exons, transcript length 6,070 bp, protein 1,480 aa. Click path: gene page → Show transcript table → click ENST00000003084 → transcript summary (or the Exons link in the left menu).
F2. a) 3 isoforms; the canonical isoform 1 is 1,480 aa. b) Isoform 2 lacks residues 404–464 (“Missing” in the Sequence & Isoforms section, or the alternative-sequence feature VSP_022123), and is 1,419 aa long (1480 − 61). (Isoform 3, 604 aa, differs at the end from residue 589.)
F3. a) Codon 404 starts at c.(3 × 404 − 2) = c.1210; codon 464 ends at c.(3 × 464) = c.1392. So c.1210–c.1392, 183 nt. b) c.1210 is the first base of exon 10, and exon 10 is 183 nt long (B3), so it ends at c.1392. Isoform 2 lacks exactly exon 10: an in-frame exon skip. (The R exercise finds the same with the exon table: the Ensembl transcript CFTR-218, 1,419 aa, has every MANE exon except exon 10.)
F4. NM_000492.4(CFTR):c.1585-1G>A, molecular consequence splice acceptor variant, classification pathogenic (review status: practice guideline), condition cystic fibrosis, dbSNP rs76713772. c.1585-1 is the last base of intron 11, the G of the AG right before exon 12 (exon 12 starts at c.1585: 1209 + 183 + 192 = 1584 coding nucleotides in exons 1–11). G542X (c.1624G>T) lies in the same exon. (Its legacy name is 1717-1G>A, from an older numbering of the cDNA.)

text:
Where this leads
This unit closes Part 3. You have seen how a gene is stored (DNA recap), how it changes (Mutation & complementation) and how it is read (this unit). Part 4: Genome analysis turns to the tools: finding genes and open reading frames in raw sequence, sequencing, and browsing variation across whole genomes. The idea of a gene as exons, introns and alternative transcripts is what a genome browser draws for you.

title: Quiz: Gene expression (recap)
text:
Short questions on transcription, splicing, translation and the genetic code, seen through mutations. This is a recap of 5MO103, so focus on what each step means for a mutation’s effect.

Q1. The template strand of a short stretch of DNA reads 3′-TACCACGTA-5′. Write the mRNA, 5′ → 3′. Which strand has the same sequence as the mRNA?






Hint





RNA is made complementary and antiparallel to the template, with U instead of T.









Answer





mRNA 5′-AUGGUGCAU-3′ (Met Val His, the start of β-globin). It has the same sequence as the coding strand 5′-ATGGTGCAT-3′, with U for T. That is why gene sequences and c. numbering use the coding strand.




Q2. A mutation in the TATA box of the HBB promoter causes β+-thalassaemia (reduced, not absent, β-globin). Why “reduced” rather than an abnormal protein?






Hint





Does the mutation change the coding sequence?









Answer





The promoter is not part of the coding sequence, so the protein is normal. The mutation makes the promoter work less well, so less mRNA, and therefore less β-globin, is made. Promoter mutations change the amount of product, not its sequence. (HBB c.-78A>C is such a variant.)




Q3. HBB c.92+1G>A changes the first base of intron 1 from G to A. Why can a single change in an intron be as harmful as a nonsense mutation?






Hint





What are the conserved bases at the start of nearly every intron?









Answer





Introns start with GU (GT in DNA): the 5′ splice site, or donor. c.92+1G>A turns it into AU, so the spliceosome no longer recognises the donor. The intron is kept, an exon is skipped, or a cryptic site is used, and no normal mRNA is made. The allele makes no β-globin: β0-thalassaemia, just like a nonsense allele.




Q4. An internal exon of 183 nt is skipped. Another internal exon of 95 nt is skipped. Which skip keeps the reading frame, and what happens to the protein in each case?






Hint





Divide by 3.









Answer





183 = 3 × 61, so skipping it keeps the frame: the protein lacks 61 amino acids but is otherwise normal (CFTR exon 10, UniProt isoform 2). 95 is not a multiple of 3 (95 = 3 × 31 + 2), so skipping it shifts the frame: the following codons are misread, usually until a premature stop codon. Such an mRNA is often destroyed by nonsense-mediated decay. (CFTR exon 12 is 95 nt long.)




Q5. Ensembl lists 45 transcripts for CFTR, but UniProt lists only 3 protein isoforms. Give two reasons for the difference, and say what the MANE Select transcript is for.






Hint





Look at the biotypes Ensembl gives the transcripts.









Answer





Many Ensembl transcripts do not make a full protein: some are fragments with no defined coding sequence, some keep an intron, and some contain a premature stop and are labelled nonsense_mediated_decay. Others would code for a protein but there is no protein-level evidence for it, and UniProt lists isoforms only with good evidence. MANE Select is one transcript per gene, agreed by NCBI and Ensembl (for CFTR, ENST00000003084 = NM_000492.4), used as the default for describing variants, so that everyone numbers c.1624G>T the same way.




Q6. The nonsense allele CFTR G542X lies in exon 12 of 27. Why does it usually give almost no CFTR protein, rather than a short protein of 541 amino acids?






Hint





Where is the stop codon relative to the last exon–exon junction?









Answer





The premature stop lies far upstream of the last exon–exon junction, so the mRNA is recognised by nonsense-mediated decay and destroyed before much protein can be made. The allele behaves as a null allele. That is also why most nonsense and frameshift alleles are recessive loss-of-function alleles.




Q7. In Crick and Brenner’s experiment, why did a (+) and a (−) mutation restore wild type only if they were close together?






Hint





Which part of the protein is read in the wrong frame?









Answer





Between the (+) and the (−), the codons are read in the wrong frame, giving a stretch of wrong amino acids (and possibly a stop codon). After the (−), the frame is restored. If the two are close, only a few amino acids are wrong, and if that part of the protein is not critical, the protein still works. If they are far apart, the wrong stretch is long, very likely contains a stop codon, and the protein fails.




Q8. Why was the triplet nature of the code a genetic result, while the meaning of UUU was a biochemical one?






Hint





What did each experiment measure?









Answer





Crick and Brenner used only mutants, crosses and phenotypes (phage that grow or not on a host strain) to infer that the code is read in groups of three from a fixed start; they never saw a protein sequence. Nirenberg and Matthaei used cell-free translation: they added synthetic poly-U RNA to a cell extract and measured which amino acid was built into protein (phenylalanine). Genetics gave the rules of the code; biochemistry gave the dictionary.

title: Exercise: genome annotation
Exercise: genome annotation
Exercise: genome annotation
text:
Background
ORFs. An open reading frame runs from ATG to the next in-frame stop codon (TAA, TAG, TGA). DNA has six frames: +1, +2, +3 on the given strand and −1, −2, −3 on the reverse complement. In random DNA, P(stop) = 3/64 per codon, so stops come every ~21 codons, and P(no stop in n codons) = (61/64)n.
Eukaryotic genes have exons and introns. Introns start with GT and end with AG. Annotation combines ORFs and splice signals with RNA-seq, protein homology and conservation, and it is versioned: always note the release (here Ensembl 116, assembly GRCh38).
BLAST finds local alignments: blastn (DNA vs DNA), blastp (protein vs protein), blastx (translated DNA vs protein), tblastn (protein vs translated DNA). Read Per. Ident, Query Cover and the E value (expected chance hits this good; < 10−10 means homology).
Gene families. Gene duplication makes paralogs (related genes in one genome); speciation makes orthologs (the same gene in two species). The human β-globin locus on chromosome 11 (minus strand) holds, from 5’ to 3’, HBE1 (embryo), HBG2 and HBG1 (fetus), the pseudogene HBBP1, and HBD and HBB (adult). The α-like genes (HBZ, HBA2, HBA1) are on chromosome 16.
Human HBB (Ensembl 116, canonical transcript HBB-201): exons of 142, 223 and 263 nt, introns of 130 and 850 nt; the mRNA is 628 nt, of which 444 nt (147 codons + stop) are coding.

title: Exercise: genome annotation
text:
Explore
The demo translates a sequence in all six frames. Grey ticks are stop codons; coloured bars are ORFs (ATG to stop) at least as long as the minimum you set (blue: given strand, red: reverse strand). The green track shows the genes annotated in GenBank. Click an ORF to see its protein.



E1. The demo starts on 3,340 bp of phage λ (NC_001416.1, positions 36,261–39,600) with a 100-aa minimum. How many ORFs are shown, and which annotated genes do they match? Which annotated gene has no ORF at this cut-off? Lower the minimum until it appears: what length is it?
E2. Compare the ORF in frame +3 near position 2,100–2,400 with the annotated cII gene. Which is longer, and why might an ORF finder get the start wrong?
E3. Click “random DNA” (same length, equal base frequencies). At 100 aa, how many ORFs do you find? Press “new random sequence” a few times. What is the longest ORF you see? Compare with your answer to B2.
E4. Click “HBB mRNA”. How many ORFs of at least 100 aa are there, in which frame, and how long? Click it and check that the protein starts MVHLTPEEK. Why does a mature mRNA give a much cleaner picture than the genomic DNA of a human gene would?






Solutions: Explore





E1. Four ORFs: frame −3, 279 aa (rexA); frame −2, 237 aa (cI, the λ repressor); frame +3, 117 aa (over cII); frame +2, 299 aa (O). The annotated cro gene has no ORF at 100 aa: it encodes only 66 aa. It appears when the minimum is 60 aa or lower, together with a few short ORFs that are not annotated genes.
E2. The ORF (117 aa) is longer than the annotated cII (97 aa); they share the same stop codon. The ORF finder starts at the first ATG after the previous stop, but the real start codon is a later ATG, chosen by the ribosome-binding site. Start codons are the least certain part of a predicted gene.
E3. With seed 1 there are no ORFs of 100 aa or more; the longest is 94 aa (at a 50-aa cut-off you see nine). The next nine random sequences (seeds 2–10) give longest ORFs of 86, 202, 144, 70, 117, 72, 84, 87 and 70 aa: usually under 100 aa, but now and then a long one (seed 3 even has a 202-aa ORF). That fits B2: about 0.8% of open stretches reach 100 codons, and this sequence has about 300 stops, so you expect about 2 such stretches, and only some of them contain an early ATG. Random DNA rarely makes long ORFs, but in a whole genome there are enough random stretches that some do.
E4. One ORF of 147 aa in frame +3 (positions 51–494), which is β-globin: MVHLTPEEKSAVTALWGKVNVDE… The other five frames contain only short ORFs. An mRNA has had its introns removed, so the coding sequence is one continuous ORF. In the genomic DNA the same 147 codons are split across three exons by introns of 130 and 850 bp, which contain stop codons, so no single long ORF would show up.

title: Exercise: genome annotation
text:
Find it
F1. (BLASTp: homologs of β-globin) Open protein BLAST (blastp). As query, enter the RefSeq protein accession NP_000509.1 (human β-globin). Set “Database” to UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot (swissprot) and, under “Organism”, type Homo sapiens. Click BLAST. In the Descriptions table, read the Description, Per. Ident and E value of the hits. Which human globins are found, in which order, and which known globin is missing? Then remove the organism limit and run it again: from which kinds of animals are the top hits?
F2. (one gene in a genome browser) Open the Ensembl gene page for HBB. In the Summary, read the Location (chromosome, coordinates, strand) and look at the transcript table: which transcript is marked as MANE Select / Ensembl canonical, how many exons does it have and how long is its protein? Then open the region in the UCSC Genome Browser (chr11:5,220,000–5,275,000, assembly hg38 = GRCh38). Find the five globin genes in the gene track. In the conservation track, where is the signal highest?
F3. (BioMart: export a gene list) Open Ensembl BioMart and build this query:

Database: Ensembl Genes (the release number is shown, e.g. 116). Dataset: Human genes (GRCh38).
Filters (left menu) → Region → Chromosome/scaffold: 21. → Gene → Gene type: protein_coding.
Attributes → Features → keep only Gene name, Chromosome/scaffold name, Gene start (bp), Gene end (bp), Gene type (untick the default Gene stable ID and Transcript stable ID).
Click Results (top left), tick “Unique results only”, choose TSV and Go to download.

How many genes are in the list? Find APP (amyloid precursor protein): what are its start and end? Why do people with Down syndrome (trisomy 21) have an increased risk of early Alzheimer disease? The file used in the Exercise in R was made exactly like this, but for all chromosomes.
F4. (UniProt: what does the protein do?) Open the UniProt entry P68871 (HBB_HUMAN). In Function, read the first sentence. In Interaction → Subunit, read which chains make up adult haemoglobin A. How long is the protein (Sequence section)?






Hint: Ensembl and UCSC





In Ensembl, the Location field reads like “Chromosome 11: 5,225,464-5,229,395 reverse strand”. The transcript table lists each transcript with its number of exons (in “Transcript ID” → click it) and protein length (“Protein” column, in aa); flags such as “MANE Select” and “Ensembl Canonical” are shown in a column on the right. In UCSC, tracks are listed below the image; right-click a track to change how it is displayed. See the UCSC Browser user guide.

text:
Solutions






Solutions: By hand





B1. a)

AGA CAC CAT GGT GCA TCT GAC TCC TGA GGA
R H H G A S D S stop G


+2
GAC ACC ATG GTG CAT CTG ACT CCT GAG
D T M V H L T P E


+3
ACA CCA TGG TGC ATC TGA CTC CTG AGG
T P W C I stop L L R



Frames +1 and +3 have a stop; the β-globin start (MVHLTPE…) is in frame +2 of this snippet. (In the full mRNA, which starts 43 nt earlier, the same codons are in frame +3, as in the demo.)

Reverse complement: 5’-TCCTCAGGAGTCAGATGCACCATGGTGTCT-3’. Frame −1: TCC TCA GGA GTC AGA TGC ACC ATG GTG TCT = S S G V R C T M V S, no stop.
No. A 10-codon stretch without a stop happens by chance with probability (61/64)10 ≈ 0.62, so it means nothing. You would need to see how long the open stretch is in the full sequence, and other evidence: is that strand transcribed (RNA-seq), does the putative protein resemble a known protein (BLAST), is it conserved? Here we know the other strand is the gene.

B2. a) (61/64)50 ≈ 0.091; (61/64)100 ≈ 0.0082; (61/64)300 ≈ 5.5 × 10−7. b) 470,000 × 0.0082 ≈ 3,900 open stretches of at least 100 codons by chance (somewhat fewer contain an ATG near their start). That is nearly as many as the real genes, so a 100-codon cut-off alone would give many false genes. In real bacterial genomes, ORFs on the opposite strand of real genes are a big part of these; gene finders add codon usage, ribosome-binding sites and homology to reject them.
B3. a) 142 + 130 + 223 + 850 + 263 = 1,608 nt; the mRNA is 142 + 223 + 263 = 628 nt, 39% of the primary transcript. b) 628 − 444 = 184 nt of UTR (50 nt 5’ UTR before the ATG and 134 nt 3’ UTR after the stop). c) Exon 1 spans mRNA positions 1–142, so the start codon (51–53) and codon 7 (69–71) are both in exon 1. (That is why the 500-bp PCR product in the last unit, which spans exon 1, detects HbS.) d) GT at the start of the intron is the splice donor signal. Without it, the spliceosome cannot use this site: intron 2 may be retained in the mRNA, or a nearby cryptic GT used instead. Either way the reading frame is disrupted or stop codons are read, and little or no normal β-globin is made: β0-thalassaemia.
B4. a) Ortholog: mouse β-globin (same gene, different species). Paralogs: human δ, ε, γ, α-globin and myoglobin (related by duplication within the human genome). b) The β/δ duplication: δ-globin is the most similar (93%), so the two copies have had the least time to diverge. c) Myoglobin is homologous to β-globin: the shared fold, gene structure and function show a common ancestor. The E value of 113 only says that BLAST could not detect the relationship from sequence alone: after hundreds of millions of years, too few identical residues remain. No significant hit ≠ not homologous. d) α-globin is 141 residues and β-globin 146 (after the start Met): the two differ in length, and the local alignment does not reach the very ends, so 97% of the query is covered.
B5. a) HBB 1,608 nt; HBD 1,646; HBG1 1,589; HBG2 1,594; HBE1 1,601: the genes are all about 1.6 kb (similar 3-exon structure). The 3’ end of HBE1 is its lowest coordinate (5,268,345), because it is on the minus strand; the 5’ end of HBB is its highest (5,227,071). The distance is 5,268,345 − 5,227,071 ≈ 41 kb. b) On the minus strand, 5’→3’ means from high to low coordinates: HBE1 → HBG2 → HBG1 → HBD → HBB. That is the order in which they are expressed: embryonic ε, fetal γ, adult δ and β. c) Coordinates are counted along the plus strand. For a minus-strand cluster, the lowest coordinate is the 3’ end, so HBB is the last gene of the cluster in the direction of transcription.
B6. Chromosome 13: 322 / 114.4 = 2.8 genes/Mb; 18: 267 / 80.4 = 3.3; 21: 221 / 46.7 = 4.7; 19: 1,479 / 58.6 = 25.2. Chromosomes 13, 18 and 21 carry relatively few genes (21 also because it is the smallest), so an extra copy changes the dosage of fewer genes. A trisomy of a gene-rich chromosome such as 19 upsets the balance of so many genes that the embryo does not survive. (The Rearrangements and aneuploidy unit returns to this.)
B7. (1) Both copies keep the old function, giving more product (the two α-globin genes HBA1 and HBA2 make the same protein; the two γ genes almost the same). (2) One copy takes a new function or a new timing (fetal γ-globin binds oxygen more tightly than adult β-globin; embryonic ε). (3) One copy decays into a pseudogene (HBBP1). A fourth possibility is that the copies split the original functions or expression pattern between them.









Solutions: Find it





F1. Click path: BLAST → Protein BLAST → query NP_000509.1 → Database: UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot, Organism: Homo sapiens → BLAST → Descriptions. The top hit is β-globin itself (HBB_HUMAN, 100%), then δ-globin (HBD, ~93%), the embryonic and fetal β-like globins ε (HBE1, ~76%) and γ (HBG2, HBG1, ~73%), then the α-like globins: α (HBA, ~43%), θ (HBQ1, ~39%), ζ (HBZ, ~36%) and μ (HBM, ~35%), and further down the more distant cytoglobin (CYGB, ~29%). Myoglobin (MB) is not among the significant hits. (Identities checked on 2026-11-20 with BLASTp 2.12 against the UniProt sequences; the web order may differ slightly, and the E values depend on the database size.) Without the organism limit, the list fills up with β-globins of other species, mostly mammals (Swiss-Prot has β-globin sequences for many primates, some identical to ours); the mouse ortholog is about 80% identical. Orthologs from other species rank above human paralogs such as α-globin, because they are more similar.
F2. Ensembl Summary: Location Chromosome 11: 5,225,464–5,229,395, reverse strand (release 116). The canonical transcript is HBB-201 (ENST00000335295), marked MANE Select and Ensembl Canonical, with 3 exons and a protein of 147 aa; it matches RefSeq NM_000518.5. (The number of other transcripts changes between releases.) In UCSC at chr11:5,220,000–5,275,000, the gene track shows, from left to right, HBB, HBD, HBBP1, HBG1, HBG2 and HBE1, all with arrows pointing left (minus strand). The Conservation track (in the “Comparative Genomics” group) is highest over the exons of the globin genes and low in most introns and intergenic DNA.
F3. Click path as listed. With Ensembl 116 the list has 221 protein-coding genes on chromosome 21 (later releases may differ by a few). APP is at about 25.88–26.17 Mb (Gene start 25,880,535, end 26,171,128 in release 116). People with Down syndrome have three copies of chromosome 21 and therefore of APP, so they make about 1.5 times as much amyloid precursor protein; its fragment, β-amyloid, forms the plaques of Alzheimer disease. This is a gene dosage effect.
F4. Function: “Involved in oxygen transport from the lung to the various peripheral tissues.” Subunit: haemoglobin A is a heterotetramer of two α chains and two β chains. Length: 147 aa (146 in the mature protein, after the initial Met is removed).

title: Exercise: genome annotation
text:
Where this leads
The annotation you looked at describes one reference genome. In Genomic variation you look at how genomes differ between people and between populations, starting with the variant you have met in every unit of this part, rs334 (HbS) in HBB, and with lactase persistence.
Next: Exercise in R: read the BioMart export of all human protein-coding genes with read_tsv(), count genes per chromosome, join with chromosome lengths and plot gene density.

title: Quiz: genome annotation
text:
Short questions on assembly, gene finding, BLAST, genome browsers and gene families. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Why does a genome assembled from 150-base reads break into many contigs, even at 50× coverage?






Hint





Think of a sequence that occurs at many places in the genome.









Answer





Repeats. A read that lies entirely inside a repeat (a transposable element, a duplicated gene, centromeric satellite DNA) matches every copy equally well, so the assembler cannot tell which copy it came from or which unique sequences flank which copy. More coverage does not help, because every read is still shorter than the repeat. Reads longer than the repeat (long-read sequencing) solve it.




Q2. How many reading frames does a double-stranded DNA sequence have, and why?






Hint





Codons are read in triplets, and either strand can be the template.









Answer





Six: three on each strand. On one strand you can start reading at the 1st, 2nd or 3rd base (the 4th gives the same frame as the 1st), and the complementary strand, read 5’→3’ in the other direction, gives three more.




Q3. In random DNA with equal base frequencies, what is the chance that a given codon is a stop codon? On average, how long is an open stretch between stops?






Hint





How many of the 64 codons are stop codons?









Answer





3 of the 64 codons are stops (TAA, TAG, TGA), so P(stop) = 3/64 ≈ 0.047. The average distance between stops is 64/3 ≈ 21 codons. An ORF of 300 codons is therefore very unlikely by chance: (61/64)300 ≈ 6 × 10−7.




Q4. Why is it much harder to find genes in the human genome by looking for long ORFs than in E. coli?






Hint





Compare the structure of a human gene with a bacterial one.









Answer





Human genes are split into exons separated by introns, so the coding sequence is broken into short pieces (an average exon is about 150 bp), and introns usually contain stop codons in all frames. Human genes are also far apart (about 6 per Mb, against about 1 per kb in bacteria), so most of the DNA is non-coding. Gene finders therefore need other evidence: splice sites (GT…AG), codon bias, RNA-seq and homology to known proteins.




Q5. Name three kinds of evidence that an annotation pipeline uses to decide that a stretch of human DNA is an exon.






Hint





Look at the tracks in the evidence figure in the lecture.









Answer





Any three of: RNA-seq reads mapping to it (it is transcribed), with split reads marking the exon junctions; protein homology (a known protein from another species aligns to it); conservation across species; sequence signals such as an open reading frame, splice sites (GT at the start and AG at the end of the flanking introns), start or stop codons, and typical codon usage.




Q6. A BLASTp search gives two hits: hit A with 35% identity over 140 of 147 query residues, E = 7 × 10−32; hit B with 60% identity over 20 residues, E = 0.9. Which one is more likely to be a real homolog?






Hint





The E value combines how good and how long the alignment is, given the database size.









Answer





Hit A. Its E value says that a hit this good would be expected by chance about 10−31 times, so it is almost certainly homologous, even though only 35% of positions are identical. (Human ζ-globin against β-globin gives numbers like hit A.) Hit B is more identical but over only 20 residues; an E value of 0.9 means you would expect about one such hit by chance in this database. Short, high-identity matches are often chance.




Q7. What is the difference between orthologs and paralogs? Classify: (a) human HBB and mouse Hbb-b1; (b) human HBB and human HBD; (c) human HBA1 and human HBB.






Hint





What event separated the two genes: a speciation or a gene duplication?









Answer





Orthologs are the “same” gene in different species, separated by a speciation event. Paralogs are related genes that arose by gene duplication, usually within one genome. (a) Orthologs. (b) Paralogs, from a recent duplication (93% identical proteins). (c) Paralogs, from an old duplication that separated the α-like and β-like globins (43% identical, now on chromosomes 16 and 11).




Q8. All five β-globin-like genes are on the minus strand of chromosome 11. HBE1 is at about 5.268 Mb and HBB at about 5.225 Mb. Which gene lies further upstream (5’) in the direction of transcription?






Hint





On the minus strand, genes are transcribed from higher to lower coordinates.









Answer





On the minus strand, transcription runs from higher to lower coordinates, so upstream means higher coordinates. HBE1 (5.268 Mb) is upstream of HBB (5.225 Mb). The cluster reads, 5’ to 3’: HBE1 – HBG2 – HBG1 – (HBBP1) – HBD – HBB, the order in which the genes are switched on during development (embryo, fetus, adult).




Q9. A genome browser shows a gene called HBBP1 in the β-globin cluster, with the biotype “pseudogene”. What is a pseudogene, and how does one usually arise?






Hint





Think about what can happen to an extra gene copy after a duplication.









Answer





A pseudogene is a sequence that looks like a gene (similar to a functional gene, sometimes with exons and introns) but cannot make a working product, because of stop codons, frameshifts or missing control regions. It usually arises after a gene duplication: with a second working copy around, mutations that destroy one copy are not removed by selection, and the copy decays. (Processed pseudogenes arise differently: an mRNA is reverse-transcribed and inserted back into the genome without introns.)




Q10. The Ensembl BioMart export in the R exercise has 20,107 protein-coding genes on 3,088 Mb of chromosome sequence. What is the average gene density? Chromosome 19 has 1,479 genes on 58.6 Mb. How many times denser is it than average?






Hint





Genes per Mb = genes / Mb.









Answer





Average: 20,107 / 3,088 ≈ 6.5 genes per Mb. Chromosome 19: 1,479 / 58.6 ≈ 25.2 genes per Mb, about 3.9 times the average. (Chromosome 13, at 2.8 per Mb, is the least dense autosome.)

title: Exercise: genomic variation
Exercise: genomic variation
Exercise: genomic variation
text:
Background
Kinds of variant. SNP (1 bp), indel (insertion or deletion, 1–50 bp; a frameshift in a coding sequence unless its length is a multiple of 3), STR or microsatellite (a 1–6 bp unit repeated a variable number of times; mutation rate 10−3–10−4 per generation), CNV (a segment of kb to Mb present in a variable number of copies).
Names. dbSNP gives each variant position an rs number. HGVS names give the change relative to a reference sequence: g. (genomic), c. (coding, counted from the A of ATG), p. (protein). Genome databases list alleles on the plus strand. The sickle-cell allele is rs334 = NC_000011.10:g.5227002T>A = NM_000518.5:c.20A>T = p.Glu7Val (HBB is on the minus strand). The lactase persistence allele is rs4988235 = NC_000002.12:g.135851076G>A, known in the literature as LCT −13910C>T.
Haplotypes and LD. A haplotype is the set of alleles on one chromosome. Two sites are in linkage disequilibrium (LD) when their alleles are associated in the population: the frequency of a haplotype differs from the product of its allele frequencies. Recombination breaks up LD, so it decays with distance and time.
Databases. dbSNP (variant IDs and names), 1000 Genomes (2,504 people, 26 populations in 5 continental groups: AFR, AMR, EAS, EUR, SAS), gnomAD (about 800,000 people, grouped by genetic ancestry), ClinVar (clinical interpretation).
From allele to genotype frequencies. If genotypes follow Hardy–Weinberg proportions (Part 7), an allele with frequency q gives q2 homozygotes, 2q(1 − q) heterozygotes and 1 − (1 − q)2 people with at least one copy.

title: Exercise: genomic variation
text:
Find it
The four tasks look up the two variants of this unit. gnomAD and Ensembl list alleles on the plus strand.
F1. (gnomAD: lactase persistence) Open the gnomAD page for rs4988235 (2-135851076-G-A) in dataset gnomAD v4. (You can also search for “rs4988235” in the box on the gnomAD front page.) Which group has the highest and which the lowest frequency? Is the allele found only in genomes, or also in exomes, and why?

Then open the HGVS tab and find the name on NM_000518.5. How many different alternative alleles are known at this position?






Hint: gnomAD pages





At the top of a gnomAD variant page are the overall frequency in Exomes and Genomes and the number of homozygotes. Further down, the “Genetic Ancestry Group Frequencies” table has one row per group, with Allele Count, Allele Number (the number of chromosomes typed), Number of Homozygotes and Allele Frequency.
