title: Exercise: genomic variation
text:
Solutions






Solutions: By hand





B1. a) SNP, missense (Glu7Val): HbS, sickle-cell allele. b) Indel (3-bp deletion), in frame: one amino acid lost (Phe508), the protein misfolds: the commonest cystic fibrosis allele. c) SNP, nonsense: GGA → TGA is a stop codon (this is the CFTR allele G542X). d) Indel, frameshift: every codon after it is read in the wrong frame until a stop appears; usually a truncated or absent protein (often via nonsense-mediated decay). e) STR expansion: 45 repeats is in the fully penetrant Huntington disease range (40 or more). f) SNP in a regulatory element: no protein change, but it changes when LCT is expressed (lactase persistence). g) CNV (a deletion), removing one copy of about 3 Mb with dozens of genes: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome; the phenotype comes from reduced gene dosage.
B2. a) G>A on the plus strand is C>T on the minus strand, the genes’ strand. Papers call it LCT −13910C>T, and the persistence allele “−13910T” (it is 13,910 bp upstream of the LCT start). b) ALDH2 is on the plus strand, so G>A applies directly: GAA → AAA, Lys (Glu504Lys; the allele also called ALDH2*2). c) The reference genome was assembled mostly from a few people, largely of European ancestry. In Europeans the derived A allele (Thr111) is almost fixed (frequency about 1.0 in the 1000 Genomes European samples), so the reference carries it. Reference allele ≠ ancestral allele ≠ “normal” allele.
B3. a) SNP1: A = (5 + 1)/10 = 0.6, G = 0.4. SNP2: C = (5 + 0)/10 = 0.5, T = 0.5. b) Expected pAC = 0.6 × 0.5 = 0.3, so 3 of 10; observed 5. c) D = 0.5 − 0.3 = 0.2, not 0: the SNPs are in LD (A tends to go with C, G with T). d) All four G chromosomes carry T, so predict T. Knowing SNP1 tells you SNP2 (for G perfectly, for A mostly), so genotyping SNP1 “tags” SNP2. This is why an array with fewer than a million SNPs captures much of the common variation in a genome.
B4. Persistent = 1 − (1 − q)2. CEU: 1 − 0.262 = 0.93. FIN: 1 − 0.412 = 0.83. TSI: 1 − 0.912 = 0.17. YRI: 0 (from this allele). Among these, YRI (and among the Europeans, Tuscany) would have the most adults who are lactase non-persistent; YRI does not carry other persistence alleles either, as far as is known. (Lactose intolerance also depends on how much milk people drink.)
B5. a) Carriers: 2 × 0.14 × 0.86 ≈ 0.24. Affected newborns: 0.142 ≈ 0.020, about 1 in 50. b) The partner is a carrier with probability 0.24; two carriers have a child with HbS/HbS with probability ¼. Risk = 0.24 × ¼ ≈ 0.06 (6%). c) 201 + 180 + 82 + 37 and no 381 band: the partner is HbA/HbA, so the risk is 0 (apart from a new mutation, which is negligible).
B6. a) Array: ancestry uses common SNPs, and arrays are cheap for very many people. b) Exome or genome sequencing of the child (and ideally both parents, a “trio”): the cause is probably a rare or new (de novo) variant that no array is designed for. c) Array (or a single-SNP assay such as PCR-RFLP or a TaqMan test): one known SNP, many people. d) Neither short-read approach works well; a targeted PCR across the repeat with sizing of the product on a gel or capillary (or long-read sequencing) measures the repeat length.
B7. For a recessive disease, prevalence ≈ q2. With prevalence 1/50,000, the causal allele can have a frequency of at most about √(1/50,000) ≈ 0.0045 (0.45%), and less if several alleles cause the disease. Variant Y at 8% would give 0.082 = 0.0064, about 1 in 156 homozygotes: far more than the disease prevalence, so Y is almost certainly benign. Variant X, absent from gnomAD, is the better candidate (it still needs other evidence, such as its predicted effect and segregation in the family).
B8. Three genotypes matter: HbA/HbA, HbA/HbS and HbS/HbS. Where falciparum malaria is common, HbA/HbA people are more likely to die of severe malaria; HbA/HbS carriers are protected and otherwise healthy, so they have the highest fitness; HbS/HbS people have sickle-cell disease and, without treatment, low fitness. Selection removes HbS alleles through homozygotes but favours them through heterozygotes, so the allele settles at an intermediate frequency: a balanced polymorphism. In Europe and East Asia there has been no such malaria pressure (or the allele never arose there), so HbS is rare or absent. The quantitative version is in the drift and selection unit (Part 7).









Solutions: Find it





F1. Click path: gnomAD → search rs4988235 → dataset gnomAD v4 → Genetic Ancestry Group Frequencies. In gnomAD v4 (checked 2026-11-20, genomes) the A allele has frequency about 0.64 in European (non-Finnish), 0.58 in European (Finnish), 0.12 in African/African American, 0.16 in South Asian, 0.23 in Admixed American and 0.002 in East Asian. Highest: non-Finnish Europeans; lowest: East Asians. The variant is listed only in genomes: it lies in an intron of MCM6, outside the exons that exome sequencing captures. (The 12% in the African/African American group mostly reflects European admixture in African Americans, who make up most of that group.)
F2. For rs334 (11-5227002-T-A), the African/African American frequency is about 0.04–0.06 (0.044 in genomes, 0.057 in exomes in v4), and about 0.0000–0.0002 in European (non-Finnish). It is lower than the Yoruba’s 0.14 because the gnomAD African/African American group is mostly African Americans, whose ancestry is partly European, and whose African ancestors came from many regions; and because selection by malaria has not acted in the Americas. gnomAD lists homozygotes (people with sickle-cell disease) at the top of the page: 9 in genomes and 31 in exomes on 2026-11-20 (the counts change between versions). There are some because gnomAD excludes people with severe paediatric disease but not adults with sickle-cell disease.
F3. Click path: Ensembl → search rs4988235 → Population genetics → 1000 Genomes Project Phase 3. A allele: CEU 0.737, FIN 0.591, TSI 0.089, YRI 0, CHB 0 (only G is listed). Summary: Most severe consequence intron variant (in MCM6); ancestral allele G. So the persistence allele (A, = −13910T) is the derived allele: it arose by mutation from the ancestral non-persistence allele.
F4. dbSNP rs334: Alleles T>A / T>C / T>G (three alternative alleles: A is HbS; C and G are other, rare variants); position chr11:5227002 (GRCh38); Gene : Consequence HBB: missense variant; Clinical Significance includes pathogenic (and others, such as protective and likely benign, because ClinVar holds several submissions for the different alleles and conditions). HGVS: NM_000518.5:c.20A>T (HbS), as well as c.20A>G and c.20A>C.

title: Exercise: genomic variation
text:
Where this leads
In Part 5 the variants get bigger: deletions, inversions, translocations and whole extra chromosomes. In Part 7, the Hardy–Weinberg and drift and selection units turn today’s stories into numbers: how genotype frequencies follow from allele frequencies, and how heterozygote advantage holds HbS at an equilibrium.
Next: Exercise in R: read allele frequencies of five SNPs in the 26 populations of the 1000 Genomes Project, join them with a population table using left_join(), and plot them by population.

title: Quiz: genomic variation
text:
Short questions on kinds of variants, haplotypes and LD, genotyping and population differences. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Name the type of each variant: (a) a C → T change at one position; (b) the loss of three bases CTT in CFTR; (c) 42 instead of 20 copies of CAG in HTT; (d) a 3-Mb segment of chromosome 22 present in one copy instead of two.






Hint





SNP, indel, STR (microsatellite) or CNV?









Answer






SNP (single-nucleotide variant). (b) Indel (a 3-bp deletion; in frame, so one amino acid is lost: F508del). (c) STR / microsatellite repeat expansion (Huntington disease range). (d) CNV, here a deletion (the 22q11.2 deletion, as in DiGeorge syndrome).





Q2. Why do microsatellites (STRs) have many more alleles per locus than SNPs?






Hint





Compare their mutation rates and how they mutate.









Answer





STRs mutate by slippage of the DNA polymerase on the repeat during replication, which adds or removes a repeat unit. Their mutation rate is about 10−3–10−4 per locus per generation, against ~10−8 per base for SNPs. Each mutation can produce a new repeat number, so many alleles accumulate. A SNP site usually has only two alleles, because a second mutation at the same base is very rare.




Q3. dbSNP lists rs334 as T>A on chromosome 11; the clinical literature calls HbS c.20A>T. Are these different variants?






Hint





On which strand of chromosome 11 is HBB?









Answer





No, it is the same change. Genome databases report alleles on the plus strand of the chromosome; HBB is on the minus strand, so the coding-sequence (c.) name uses the complementary base: plus-strand T>A = coding-strand A>T.




Q4. What is a haplotype, and why are SNPs that are close together often in linkage disequilibrium?






Hint





How often does a crossover fall between two sites 1 kb apart, compared with two sites 10 Mb apart?









Answer





A haplotype is the set of alleles along one chromosome. When a new allele arises, it sits on one particular haplotype. Crossovers between sites very close together are rare (1 cM ≈ 1 Mb in humans, so about 10−5 per meiosis for sites 1 kb apart), so even after many generations the new allele is still found with the same neighbouring alleles: they are associated, in LD. For distant sites, crossovers have had time to mix the alleles, and the association disappears.




Q5. A consumer genetic test (SNP array) reports that you are not a carrier of any cystic fibrosis alleles on its panel. Does that mean you cannot be a carrier?






Hint





What can an array detect?









Answer





No. An array tests only the known variants it was designed for, typically the most common ones (such as F508del). Hundreds of other CFTR variants can cause cystic fibrosis, including rare ones found in only a few families. Only sequencing the gene would find those. The result lowers your carrier probability; it does not make it zero.




Q6. In the 1000 Genomes data, the lactase persistence allele (rs4988235 A) has frequency 0.74 in CEU and 0 in YRI. Does that mean that no Africans can digest milk as adults?






Hint





Is this the only allele that gives lactase persistence? Which African populations are in 1000 Genomes?









Answer





No. Several pastoralist populations in East Africa (and the Middle East) have other variants in the same LCT enhancer that also cause lactase persistence: the same trait evolved independently (convergent evolution). The African populations in 1000 Genomes (Yoruba, Esan, Mende, Gambian, Luhya) are mostly not traditional milk-drinking herders. One SNP is not the whole story of a trait.




Q7. Lactase persistence is dominant. In the Finnish sample (FIN) the persistence allele has frequency 0.59. What fraction of Finns would you expect to be lactase persistent, if genotypes follow Hardy–Weinberg proportions?






Hint





Persistent = at least one persistence allele = 1 − P(two non-persistence alleles).









Answer





P(no persistence allele) = (1 − 0.59)2 = 0.412 = 0.168, so P(persistent) = 1 − 0.168 ≈ 0.83. About 17% would be expected to be lactase non-persistent.




Q8. Why is the HbS allele common in parts of Africa, although HbS/HbS causes a severe disease?






Hint





Compare the survival of the three genotypes where malaria is common.









Answer





Heterozygote advantage (balancing selection). Where falciparum malaria is common, HbA/HbS carriers are protected against severe malaria and survive better than HbA/HbA people, while HbS/HbS people have sickle-cell disease. Selection against HbS in homozygotes is balanced by selection for it in heterozygotes, so both alleles stay in the population, at about 10–14% HbS in the West and East African 1000 Genomes samples.




Q9. About what share of human genetic variation lies within populations rather than between them? Why, then, do a few alleles such as rs4988235 differ so strongly between populations?






Hint





Most variants are neutral. What forces can change the frequency of one allele a lot?









Answer





About 85–90% of variation is within populations. Most variants are neutral and their frequencies differ only modestly between populations, through drift and migration. Large differences at single loci, against that background, usually point to natural selection in some populations: positive selection for lactase persistence where milk was drunk, balancing selection for HbS where malaria was common.




Q10. A patient has a severe dominant disease with a prevalence of 1 in 100,000. Sequencing finds a missense variant in a candidate gene. In gnomAD the variant has an allele frequency of 0.5% in the patient’s ancestry group. Is it likely to cause the disease?






Hint





For a dominant disease, how common could a fully penetrant causal allele be at most?









Answer





Very unlikely. If the variant caused a fully penetrant dominant disease, about 2 × 0.005 = 1% of people in that group would be heterozygous and affected, a thousand times more than the prevalence of 1 in 100,000. A variant that common in healthy people is almost certainly benign (or at most has a very low penetrance). This is why population frequency is one of the first filters in clinical variant interpretation.

title: Exercise: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
Exercise: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
Exercise: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
text:
Background
Frequencies. With counts nAA, nAa, naa and N people:
\[
p = \frac{2n_{AA} + n_{Aa}}{2N}, \qquad q = 1 - p.
\]
Hardy–Weinberg proportions (random mating, large population, no selection, mutation or migration): AA = p², Aa = 2pq, aa = q². Reached after one generation of random mating; p stays constant.
χ² test for HWE. Expected counts Np², 2Npq, Nq² from the estimated p. χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E with df = 1 (3 classes − 1 − 1 estimated parameter). Reject HWE at 5% if χ² > 3.84. Expected counts below about 5 make the test unreliable.
Carriers. If a recessive disease has incidence q², carriers = 2pq ≈ 2q when q is small. X-linked: affected males = q, affected females = q², carrier females = 2pq.
Inbreeding. AA = p² + Fpq, Aa = 2pq(1 − F), aa = q² + Fpq. Observed heterozygosity gives F = 1 − Hobs/Hexp. Child of first cousins: F = 1/16.

title: Exercise: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
text:
By hand
B1. (counting) At the bitter-taste receptor SNP rs713598 in TAS2R38, 103 Han Chinese from Beijing (1000 Genomes CHB) have 13 CC, 41 CG and 49 GG. (a) What are the genotype frequencies and the allele frequencies? (b) What counts does HWE predict? (c) Compute χ² and decide whether to reject HWE at the 5% level.
B2. (another test) At the TCF7L2 SNP rs7903146, the 108 Yoruba from Ibadan (YRI) have 60 CC, 44 CT and 4 TT. Test HWE. Which class contributes most to χ², and why should you be careful with it?
B3. (one generation is enough) A new population is founded by 60 AA and 40 aa individuals, and no heterozygotes. (a) What is p? Is the founding population in HWE? (b) What are the genotype frequencies after one generation of random mating? After two?
B4. (dominant phenotype) In a population, 19% of people show a dominant phenotype (A_), and the rest are aa. (a) Assuming HWE, what are q and p? (b) What fraction of the people with the dominant phenotype are heterozygous?
B5. (carriers from incidence) A recessive disease affects 1 in 40 000 newborns. (a) What is the carrier frequency, assuming HWE? Write it as “1 in …”. (b) Two people from this population, with no family history, have a child. What is the risk that the child is affected? Check that your answer matches the incidence. (c) A woman whose brother has the disease (both parents unaffected) has a child with a man from the population. What is the risk for the child? (Recall the pedigrees unit.)
B6. (X-linked) Red–green colour blindness is X-linked recessive. In a population, 8% of men are colour-blind. (a) What is q? (b) What fraction of women are colour-blind, and what fraction are carriers? (c) A colour-blind man has a daughter with a woman of unknown genotype from this population. What is the probability that a son of that daughter is colour-blind?
B7. (inbreeding) In a plant population with p = 0.6, the observed heterozygote frequency is 0.36. (a) What does HWE predict? What is F? (b) What are the three genotype frequencies? (c) For a rare recessive allele with q = 0.002, compare f(aa) in a child of unrelated parents and in a child of first cousins (F = 1/16).
B8. (population structure) Two equally large villages are each in HWE: in village 1, p = 0.8; in village 2, p = 0.2. (a) What is the heterozygote frequency in each village, and in a sample that pools both villages equally? (b) What does HWE predict for the pooled sample? What is the apparent F? (c) After one generation in which everyone mates at random across both villages, what are the genotype frequencies?

The bars compare the observed counts for a sample of N people with the HWE expectation, and the panel shows the χ² test.

title: Exercise: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
text:
Find it
F1. Genotype counts in Ensembl. Open the sickle-cell variant rs334 in Ensembl and go to Population genetics in the left menu. In the 1000 Genomes Project Phase 3 table, find the populations YRI (Yoruba in Ibadan, Nigeria) and GWD (Gambian in Western Division). Read the allele frequencies, and the genotype counts or frequencies (the genotype columns, or click the population). The same data in machine-readable form: rest.ensembl.org/variation/human/rs334?population_genotypes=1. (a) How many people in YRI and in GWD carry each genotype? (The two alleles are T and A on the forward strand; A is HbS.) (b) Test HWE in YRI by hand. Comment on the number of HbS homozygotes. (c) Which populations outside Africa carry the A allele at all?
F2. A common stop codon. Search Ensembl for rs1815739 in ACTN3. What is its most severe consequence, and what does it do to the protein (R577X)? In the Population genetics view, read the genotype counts in GBR (British). Are the counts consistent with HWE? About what fraction of British people are homozygous for the stop allele?
F3. Homozygotes in gnomAD. Open rs334 in gnomAD v4. In the Genetic Ancestry Group Frequencies table, read the row African/African American, genomes: allele count, allele number and number of homozygotes. (a) Compute the allele frequency q and the number of people (allele number / 2). (b) How many homozygotes does HWE predict? Compare with the number observed. Explain the difference.
F4. Carrier frequency of cystic fibrosis. Open CFTR F508del, rs113993960 in gnomAD. Read the allele frequency in the European (non-Finnish) and the European (Finnish) groups (genomes). (a) Estimate the carrier frequency of F508del in each group (≈ 2q), as “1 in …”. (b) The pedigrees unit used a carrier frequency of 1/50 for PKU. How does the CF carrier frequency in non-Finnish Europeans compare? Why is the carrier frequency for all CF alleles higher than for F508del alone?






Solutions: Find it





Checked on 20 November 2026 via the Ensembl REST API (release 116; 1000 Genomes phase 3 is a fixed data set) and the gnomAD v4 API. gnomAD counts may change slightly in later releases; the conclusions will not.
F1. Click path: ensembl.org → search rs334 → variant page → Population genetics → 1000 Genomes Project Phase 3 table. (a) YRI: 78 T|T, 30 A|T, 0 A|A (108 people). GWD: 87 T|T, 26 A|T, 0 A|A (113 people). (b) q(A) = 30/216 = 0.139. Expected: 108 × 0.861² = 80.1 AA, 108 × 2 × 0.861 × 0.139 = 25.8 AS, 108 × 0.139² = 2.1 SS. χ² = 0.05 + 0.67 + 2.08 = 2.8 (p = 0.09): not significant, but the expected SS count is below 5, so the test is weak. The direction is clear: two SS people are expected and none is seen. People with sickle-cell disease are missing from this sample of healthy adults. (c) Outside the African populations (YRI, GWD, ESN, LWK, MSL), HbS heterozygotes appear only in populations with recent African ancestry: ACB (African Caribbean in Barbados, 9), ASW (African ancestry in the southwestern US, 2), PUR (Puerto Rican, 3) and CLM (Colombian, 2). No European, East Asian or South Asian sample in 1000 Genomes carries it. (Some Mediterranean, Middle Eastern and Indian populations not sampled here do carry HbS.)
F2. rs1815739: most severe consequence stop_gained. The T allele changes codon 577 from arginine (CGA) to a stop codon (TGA): R577X, a truncated α-actinin-3 that is not made in fast muscle fibres. GBR: 26 C|C, 45 C|T, 20 T|T (91 people). p = 0.533; expected 25.9, 45.3, 19.8; χ² = 0.004 (p = 0.95): in excellent HWE. About 22% (20/91) of the British sample is homozygous XX and makes no α-actinin-3, without disease. A common homozygous loss-of-function genotype is a good reminder that not all “knockouts” are harmful.
F3. gnomAD v4 genomes, African/African American: allele count 1810, allele number 41 554, homozygotes 9. (a) q = 1810/41 554 = 0.044; people ≈ 41 554/2 = 20 777. (b) HWE predicts 20 777 × 0.044² ≈ 39 homozygotes; gnomAD has 9, about a quarter. gnomAD aggregates studies of adults, and people with severe childhood disease are mostly excluded; sickle-cell disease (SS) also shortens life. Selection and ascertainment remove SS from the sample, so HWE fails for this genotype even though random mating produced it at conception.
F4. gnomAD v4 genomes: non-Finnish European allele frequency 0.0143 (972/67 954); Finnish 0.0015 (16/10 612). (a) Non-Finnish Europeans: 2pq = 0.028, about 1 in 35. Finns: 0.0030, about 1 in 330. (b) F508del alone gives about 1 in 35, already more common than the PKU carriers (1/50). CF is caused by hundreds of different CFTR alleles. A person is a carrier if they carry any of them, so the carrier frequency for CF as a whole is higher (about 1 in 25–30 in many north-west European populations) than for F508del alone. The low value in Finland is a population-history effect; see Drift, selection and the Finnish disease heritage. (gnomAD also lists 1 F508del homozygote among the non-Finnish Europeans, where HWE predicts about 7: people with CF are under-represented in gnomAD, as for sickle-cell disease.)

title: Exercise: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
text:
Solutions






Solutions: By hand





B1. (a) Genotypes: 13/103 = 0.126, 41/103 = 0.398, 49/103 = 0.476. p(C) = (26 + 41)/206 = 0.325, q(G) = 0.675. (b) Expected: 103 × 0.325² = 10.9 CC, 103 × 2 × 0.325 × 0.675 = 45.2 CG, 103 × 0.675² = 46.9 GG. (c) χ² = (13 − 10.9)²/10.9 + (41 − 45.2)²/45.2 + (49 − 46.9)²/46.9 = 0.41 + 0.39 + 0.09 = 0.89. df = 1, critical value 3.84: do not reject HWE (p = 0.35).
B2. p = (120 + 44)/216 = 0.759, q = 0.241. Expected 62.3, 39.5, 6.3. χ² = 0.08 + 0.52 + 0.82 = 1.42 (p = 0.23): consistent with HWE. The largest contribution comes from TT, where the expected count (6.3) is small: a difference of 2 people gives 0.8. With expected counts near or below 5, single individuals move χ² a lot and the χ² distribution fits poorly.
B3. (a) p = 0.6 (all alleles of the 60 AA, out of 200). Not in HWE: HWE predicts 48% heterozygotes and there are none. (b) After one generation of random mating: 0.36 AA, 0.48 Aa, 0.16 aa. After two generations: the same. p stays 0.6, and one generation is enough to reach HWE.
B4. (a) aa = 0.81 = q², so q = 0.9 and p = 0.1. (b) AA = 0.01, Aa = 2 × 0.1 × 0.9 = 0.18. Among the 0.19 with the dominant phenotype, 0.18/0.19 = 0.95 are heterozygous. A rare dominant phenotype is almost always carried by heterozygotes.
B5. (a) q = √(1/40 000) = 1/200 = 0.005. Carriers 2pq = 2 × 0.995 × 0.005 = 0.00995 ≈ 1 in 100. (b) 1/100 × 1/100 × 1/4 = 1/40 000, the incidence, as it should be. (c) She is an unaffected sibling of a patient, so a carrier with probability 2/3. Risk = 2/3 × 1/100 × 1/4 = 1/600.
B6. (a) q = 0.08 (affected males = q). (b) Colour-blind women q² = 0.0064 (0.64%); carriers 2pq = 2 × 0.92 × 0.08 = 0.147 (about 15%). (c) The daughter gets her father’s Xa, so she is at least a carrier. From her mother she gets Xa with probability q = 0.08. Her son gets Xa from her with probability ½ if she is XAXa and 1 if she is XaXa: 0.92 × ½ + 0.08 × 1 = 0.46 + 0.08 = 0.54.
B7. (a) HWE: 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.48. F = 1 − 0.36/0.48 = 0.25. (b) AA = 0.36 + 0.25 × 0.24 = 0.42, Aa = 0.36, aa = 0.16 + 0.06 = 0.22. (Check: 0.42 + 0.36 + 0.22 = 1, and p = 0.42 + 0.18 = 0.6, unchanged.) (c) Unrelated parents: q² = 0.000004 (1 in 250 000). First cousins: 0.000004 + 0.998 × 0.002/16 = 0.000004 + 0.000125 = 0.000129 (about 1 in 7800), about 32 times higher.
B8. (a) Each village: 2 × 0.8 × 0.2 = 0.32. Pooled: also 0.32. (b) Pooled p = 0.5, so HWE predicts 0.50. Apparent F = 1 − 0.32/0.50 = 0.36: a heterozygote deficit from population structure, the Wahlund effect. (c) With random mating across villages, p = 0.5 for everyone: 0.25, 0.50, 0.25. The deficit disappears after one generation.

title: Exercise: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
text:
Where this leads
Today p stood still. In Drift, selection, mutation, migration we let it move: by chance in small populations, and by selection, including the heterozygote advantage that keeps HbS common where malaria is. In Complex traits, HWE is a quality filter for GWAS data.
Next: Exercise in R: write hwe_test(), apply it to 15 real SNP–population pairs with pmap, and draw the de Finetti triangle in ggplot2.

title: Quiz: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
text:
Short questions on allele and genotype frequencies, the Hardy–Weinberg principle and inbreeding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. In a sample of 200 people, 98 are AA, 84 are Aa and 18 are aa. What are the genotype frequencies and the allele frequencies?






Hint





Genotype frequencies count people. Allele frequencies count gene copies: two per person.









Answer





Genotypes: 98/200 = 0.49, 84/200 = 0.42, 18/200 = 0.09. Alleles: p = (2 × 98 + 84)/400 = 280/400 = 0.7; q = 0.3. (Shortcut: p = 0.49 + 0.42/2 = 0.70.) These genotype frequencies are exactly 0.7², 2 × 0.7 × 0.3 and 0.3²: the sample is in HWE.




Q2. A student says: “A is dominant, so over the generations A will spread until everyone has the dominant phenotype.” What is wrong?






Hint





What happens to p after one generation of random mating?









Answer





Dominance decides how a genotype looks, not how often an allele is passed on. Under random mating, p in the next generation is p² + pq = p: unchanged. An allele only spreads if something else acts on it, such as selection or drift. Huntington disease is dominant and rare; blood group O is recessive and common in many populations.




Q3. List the assumptions of the Hardy–Weinberg principle. Which of them, if broken, changes genotype frequencies but not allele frequencies?






Hint





Think about what inbreeding does to heterozygotes and homozygotes.









Answer





Random mating, a very large population (no drift), no selection, no mutation, no migration (and a single population). Non-random mating, such as inbreeding, shifts genotypes from heterozygotes to homozygotes but leaves p unchanged. Pooling different populations (Wahlund effect) does the same. Drift, selection, mutation and migration change p itself.




Q4. Why does the χ² test for HWE have 1 degree of freedom, although there are three genotype classes?






Hint





In Mendel’s crosses, where did the expected ratio come from?









Answer





We lose one degree of freedom because the three counts must add up to N, and another because the expected frequencies use p, which we estimated from the same data. 3 − 1 − 1 = 1. In a Mendelian cross the ratio came from theory, so no parameter was estimated and df = classes − 1. The 5% critical value for df = 1 is 3.84.




Q5. Phenylketonuria (autosomal recessive) affects about 1 in 10 000 newborns. Assuming HWE, what fraction of people are carriers?






Hint





Incidence = q². Then carriers = 2pq.









Answer





q = √(1/10 000) = 0.01, p = 0.99. Carriers 2pq = 2 × 0.99 × 0.01 = 0.0198 ≈ 1/50. This is the carrier frequency used in the pedigrees unit. For a rare allele, carriers ≈ 2q.




Q6. About 1 in 5000 boys is born with haemophilia A (X-linked recessive). Estimate the frequency of affected girls and of carrier women.






Hint





Males have one X. What is the frequency of affected males in terms of q?









Answer





Affected males = q = 1/5000 = 0.0002. Affected females = q² = 4 × 10−8, about 1 in 25 million. Carrier females = 2pq ≈ 2 × 0.0002 = 0.0004, about 1 in 2500. (In reality many cases are new mutations, which this simple calculation ignores.)




Q7. In a de Finetti triangle, a population lies below the HWE parabola. Give two possible explanations. What could put it above the parabola?






Hint





Below means too few heterozygotes.









Answer





Below (heterozygote deficit): inbreeding (F > 0), or population structure: a sample pooled from populations with different allele frequencies (Wahlund effect). Selection against heterozygotes or genotyping errors that miss heterozygotes also do it. Above (excess): heterozygote advantage acting on the sampled individuals, the offspring of a cross between two different populations, or genotyping errors that call too many heterozygotes.




Q8. What does an inbreeding coefficient F = 1/16 mean for a child of first cousins? How does it change the frequency of aa for an allele with q = 0.01?






Hint





f(aa) = q² + Fpq.









Answer





At any locus, the child’s two alleles are copies of the same ancestral allele (identical by descent) with probability 1/16. f(aa) = 0.0001 + 0.99 × 0.01/16 = 0.0001 + 0.00062 = 0.00072, about 7 times higher than under random mating. The rarer the allele, the larger the relative increase.




Q9. In 1000 Genomes, the Yoruba sample has 78 AA, 30 AS and 0 SS people at the sickle-cell SNP. HWE predicts about 2 SS. A much larger sample (gnomAD) shows the same deficit. Why is the sickle-cell locus not in HWE among adults?






Hint





HWE holds at conception. What happens between conception and the time a person is sampled?









Answer





Selection: SS people have sickle-cell disease, which shortens life (especially without treatment), and people with severe disease are rarely included in studies of healthy adults. So SS genotypes are missing from adult samples, although random mating produced them at conception in HWE proportions.




Q10. Two equally large populations are each in HWE, one with p = 0.9 and one with p = 0.1. You sample both and pool the data. What heterozygote frequency do you observe, and what does HWE predict for the pooled p?






Hint





Compute 2pq in each population and average. Then compute the pooled p.









Answer





Each population has 2 × 0.9 × 0.1 = 0.18 heterozygotes, so the pooled sample has 0.18. Pooled p = 0.5, so HWE predicts 0.50. Apparent F = 1 − 0.18/0.50 = 0.64, a large heterozygote deficit without any inbreeding: the Wahlund effect.

title: Exercise in R: genetics as information
text:
Before you start
This page builds on the by-hand part of the Exercise, so do that first. You need the packages tibble, readr, dplyr and ggplot2. Download genomes.csv and save it in a data/ folder of your R project.

title: Exercise in R: genetics as information
text:
Tasks
The data for this part is in data/genomes.csv (download it and put it in a data/ folder next to your script). It lists ten organisms with genome size and protein-coding gene count. Every value comes from the NCBI Datasets reference genome and its current annotation, and the source column gives the assembly accession for each row.
New idiom: log-scale axes and text labels. When values span many orders of magnitude (here 4.6 to 29,118 Mb), a linear axis squashes most points into a corner. scale_x_log10() and scale_y_log10() space the axis by powers of ten instead, so 10, 100 and 1,000 are equally far apart. geom_text(aes(label = ...)) writes a label at each point, so you can see which organism is which without a legend.
R1. Build the table. Create the tibble with tribble() (one row per line, easy to read) and save it with write_csv(). If you downloaded the CSV, you can skip straight to R2, but read the code so you know where each number came from.
library(tibble)
library(readr)

genomes <- tribble(
  ~organism,                  ~common_name,    ~group,      ~genome_mb, ~protein_coding_genes, ~source,
  "Escherichia coli",         "E. coli",       "bacterium",     4.6,    4290, "NCBI Datasets GCF_000005845.2 K-12 MG1655 (RefSeq annotation 2026-09)",
  "Saccharomyces cerevisiae", "baker's yeast", "fungus",       12.1,    6021, "NCBI Datasets GCF_000146045.2 (SGD R64-5-1)",
  "Caenorhabditis elegans",   "nematode worm", "animal",      100.3,   19983, "NCBI Datasets GCF_000002985.6 (WormBase WS298)",
  "Drosophila melanogaster",  "fruit fly",     "animal",      143.7,   13962, "NCBI Datasets GCF_000001215.4 (FlyBase 6.54)",
  "Arabidopsis thaliana",     "thale cress",   "plant",       119.1,   27562, "NCBI Datasets GCF_000001735.4 (TAIR/Araport)",
  "Danio rerio",              "zebrafish",     "animal",     1455.3,   28509, "NCBI Datasets GCF_052040795.2 (RefSeq annotation 2026-08)",
  "Mus musculus",             "house mouse",   "animal",     2728.2,   22198, "NCBI Datasets GCF_000001635.27 (RefSeq annotation 2024-02)",
  "Homo sapiens",             "human",         "animal",     3099.4,   20054, "NCBI Datasets GCF_000001405.40 (RefSeq annotation 2026-11)",
  "Triticum aestivum",        "bread wheat",   "plant",     14566.5,  103793, "NCBI Datasets GCF_018294505.1 (RefSeq annotation 2025-04)",
  "Ambystoma mexicanum",      "axolotl",       "animal",    29117.8,   24121, "NCBI Datasets GCF_040938575.1 (RefSeq annotation 2024-10)"
)
genomes
write_csv(genomes, "data/genomes.csv")
R2. Read it back. Load the file with read_csv(). Which columns did read_csv read as numbers (dbl) and which as text (chr)?
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

genomes <- read_csv("data/genomes.csv")
genomes
R3. Genes per Mb. Add a column genes_per_mb with mutate(), then show it sorted from densest to least dense genome with arrange(desc(...)). Check the E. coli, yeast and human values against your answer to B6 in the exercise.
genomes <- genomes |>
  mutate(genes_per_mb = protein_coding_genes / genome_mb)

genomes |>
  select(common_name, genome_mb, protein_coding_genes, genes_per_mb) |>
  arrange(desc(genes_per_mb))
R4. First, a linear plot. Plot gene count against genome size on ordinary axes. Where do most of the organisms end up?
ggplot(genomes, aes(x = genome_mb, y = protein_coding_genes)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = group), size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = common_name), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.5)
R5. Now on log scales. Add scale_x_log10() and scale_y_log10(). hjust = -0.15 in geom_text() puts each label just to the right of its point; limits makes room on the right for the axolotl’s label, and scales::label_comma() writes 10,000 instead of 1e+04.
ggplot(genomes, aes(x = genome_mb, y = protein_coding_genes)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = group), size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = common_name), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_log10(limits = c(3, 100000), labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "Genome size (Mb, log scale)",
       y = "Protein-coding genes (log scale)",
       colour = NULL)

Which organisms lie far to the right of the others with only an average number of genes?
Which organism has many more genes than the rest, and why (see the Background in the exercise)?
Among the animals only, by what factor does genome size vary, and by what factor does gene number vary? Use filter() and summarise() to find out.

R6. The C-value paradox in words. Using your plot and table, write three or four sentences explaining why genome size and gene number are not proportional. Name at least two kinds of DNA that make large genomes large.

title: Exercise in R: genetics as information
text:
Hints






Hint R5c: filter and summarise





Use filter() to keep group == "animal", then summarise() with max(genome_mb) / min(genome_mb) and max(protein_coding_genes) / min(protein_coding_genes).

Run from the unit folder with Rscript --vanilla. The output below is real output from R 4.6.2.

and write_csv writes data/genomes.csv, identical to the file on this page.
R2. read_csv reports:
Rows: 10 Columns: 6
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (4): organism, common_name, group, source
dbl (2): genome_mb, protein_coding_genes
The two numeric columns are genome_mb and protein_coding_genes; the rest are text. The tibble printed is the same as in R1.
R3.
# A tibble: 10 × 4
   common_name   genome_mb protein_coding_genes genes_per_mb
   <chr>             <dbl>                <dbl>        <dbl>
 1 E. coli             4.6                 4290      933.
 2 baker's yeast      12.1                 6021      498.
 3 thale cress       119.                 27562      231.
 4 nematode worm     100.                 19983      199.
 5 fruit fly         144.                 13962       97.2
 6 zebrafish        1455.                 28509       19.6
 7 house mouse      2728.                 22198        8.14
 8 bread wheat     14566.                103793        7.13
 9 human            3099.                 20054        6.47
10 axolotl         29118.                 24121        0.828
E. coli 933, yeast 498 and human 6.47 genes per Mb agree with B6. Gene density falls by more than a thousandfold from E. coli to the axolotl.
R4. On linear axes, the axolotl and wheat sit far to the right, and the eight other organisms are squashed into the bottom-left corner. You cannot read E. coli and yeast apart, or the worm, fly and cress. This is why we need log axes for data that span orders of magnitude.
R5. The log-log plot:


The axolotl (and to a lesser extent wheat, mouse and human) lies far to the right: its genome is about ten times larger than ours with a similar number of genes.
Bread wheat has about 104,000 protein-coding genes. It is hexaploid: it carries three ancestral genomes (A, B and D), so most genes are present in three copies.


genomes |>
  filter(group == "animal") |>
  summarise(size_range = max(genome_mb) / min(genome_mb),
            gene_range = max(protein_coding_genes) / min(protein_coding_genes))
# A tibble: 1 × 2
  size_range gene_range
       <dbl>      <dbl>
1       290.       2.04
Among the animals, genome size varies about 290-fold (worm 100 Mb to axolotl 29,118 Mb), but gene number only about 2-fold (fly 13,962 to zebrafish 28,509).
R6. Example answer: Genome size varies more than 6,000-fold in this table, but gene number only about 25-fold, and among animals 290-fold against 2-fold. Large genomes are not large because they have more genes, but because they have more non-coding DNA: long introns, large intergenic regions and especially repeated sequences such as transposable elements. Polyploidy (wheat) adds whole extra genomes, and with them extra gene copies. So the amount of DNA (the C-value) says little about the number of genes or the complexity of the organism.

title: Exercise in R: genetics as information
text:
Where this leads
The next unit, Mendel, simulates the cross Aa × Aa in R, and scale_x_log10() comes back there in a plot of how simulated ratios approach the expected ones.

title: Genetics as information
text:
About this lecture
Genetics is the study of biological information: how it is stored in DNA, how it is copied and passed on, and how differences in it become differences between individuals.

A short recap of DNA → RNA → protein → phenotype (from 5MO103).
The words we will use all course: gene, allele, locus, genotype, phenotype, homozygous, heterozygous, wild type, mutant, dominant, recessive.
One gene followed all the way from DNA to disease: HBB and sickle-cell disease.
Genomes differ hugely in size, but many genes are shared. That is why model organisms work.
Four ways to study genetics, which are also a map of this course.

Book: Hartwell, Genetics: From Genes to Genomes, introductory chapter (“Genetics: the study of biological information”).

This is the orientation lecture. Nothing here is hard, but almost every later unit leans on the vocabulary, so the aim is precision rather than depth. Say clearly that the molecular part is a recap from 5MO103 and that we will not re-teach transcription or translation; what is new is the genetic way of looking at it: we care about how differences in DNA become differences in phenotype. The sickle-cell example will come back several times in the course (dominance, pedigrees, population genetics), so it is worth setting it up carefully today.

title: Genetics as information
text:
Genetics is about information
Recap from 5MO103. The information in DNA is copied into RNA and read into protein. Proteins do the work that we see as the phenotype.


DNA is the store: it is replicated and passed to the next generation.
RNA and protein are the readout: they are made fresh in each cell.
The genetic question is about differences: a change in the DNA can change the protein, which can change the phenotype.


Keep this brief: students have seen the central dogma in detail in 5MO103. The new emphasis is the last bullet. A geneticist almost never studies a gene by itself; we study a difference (a variant, a mutation) and ask what difference it makes. That comparative mindset is what unites Mendel’s crosses with modern genome sequencing. Point out that “function” on the last arrow hides a lot of biology (metabolism, development, environment), which is why one gene rarely maps simply to one trait; we simplify today and return to it in Extensions to Mendel and Complex traits.

title: Genetics as information
text:
What is a gene?
A gene is a stretch of DNA that carries the information for one functional product, usually a protein (sometimes only an RNA).

A gene has a position on a chromosome. Human HBB, for example, sits on chromosome 11.
A gene is named with a symbol in italics: HBB (human), Cftr (mouse), w (white, fly).
The protein is written in plain type: the β-globin protein, the CFTR protein.




Level
What it is
HBB example




gene
DNA sequence at one position
HBB on chromosome 11


transcript
RNA copy, spliced
HBB mRNA


protein
the product
β-globin, one chain of haemoglobin




The definition of “gene” has moved over a century, from Mendel’s abstract “factor” to a DNA sequence. For this course, a working definition is enough: a DNA segment whose product does something. Stress the notation convention now, because students will meet it in every database: gene symbols in italics, human symbols in upper case, mouse symbols with only the first letter capital, fly genes named after their mutant phenotype. Proteins are not italic. This is a small thing that marks the difference between sloppy and professional writing.

title: Genetics as information
text:
Genes, alleles and loci


Locus (plural loci): the place on a chromosome where a gene sits.
Allele: one version of a gene. Different alleles differ in DNA sequence.
A diploid organism has two copies of each autosomal locus, one from each parent. So it carries two alleles, which can be the same or different.


The classic confusion is between gene and allele. Use the language: “the gene” is HBB; “the alleles” are the normal version and the sickle version. A population can have many alleles at one locus, but one diploid individual carries at most two. The locus is the address, the gene is what lives at the address, and the alleles are the different versions that can live there. The notation A and a is the Mendelian shorthand; we will use it from the next unit onwards.

title: Genetics as information
text:
Genotype and phenotype

Genotype: the alleles an individual carries at a locus, e.g. AA, Aa or aa.
Phenotype: what we can observe or measure: a colour, a disease, an enzyme activity, a protein band on a gel.
Homozygous: two identical alleles (AA or aa). Heterozygous: two different alleles (Aa).

The phenotype depends on the genotype and on the environment. Sickle-cell symptoms, for example, get worse at low oxygen.
The same genotype can be described at different levels of phenotype: the whole organism, the cell, or the protein. We will see that this matters for the word “dominant”.

Phenotype is a much broader word than students expect. It is not only visible traits; a band on a protein gel or the level of an enzyme is also a phenotype. That breadth is important for the sickle-cell example in a few slides, where the “dominance” relationship changes with the level at which we look. Also introduce the environment early: a genotype gives a range of possible phenotypes, and the environment picks one. Homozygous and heterozygous apply to one locus at a time; an individual can be homozygous at one locus and heterozygous at the next.

title: Genetics as information
text:
Wild type and mutant

Wild type: the allele (or phenotype) that is most common in natural or laboratory populations. Written with a plus: w+ in the fly.
Mutant: an allele that differs from wild type, usually because of a mutation, a heritable change in the DNA.
In the fly, the white gene is named after its mutant phenotype: w flies have white eyes, w+ flies have red eyes.

In humans and other natural populations, many loci have several common alleles, and none is the obvious “wild type”. Then we just name the alleles, for example the ABO blood groups.

Wild type is a model-organism idea. It works well in lab stocks of flies, worms or mice, where one standard allele exists. It works less well in humans, where many alleles at a locus are common and calling one of them “normal” is arbitrary. Keep the word mutant neutral: it simply means changed, not harmful. Many mutations have no visible effect at all. The fly white gene is the textbook example of naming genes after the mutant phenotype, which confuses students at first: the white gene is needed to make red eyes.

title: Genetics as information
section: Dominant and recessive: a first pass
text:
Dominant and recessive: a first pass
In a heterozygote Aa:

if Aa looks like AA, then A is dominant and a is recessive;
the recessive phenotype appears only in aa.

Common misunderstandings.

Dominant does not mean common. Huntington disease alleles are dominant and rare.
Dominant does not mean “better” or “stronger”.
Dominance describes the relationship between two alleles for one phenotype. It is not a property of one allele alone.

This is a simplification: complete dominance. Incomplete dominance and codominance come in the Extensions to Mendel unit.

Students come with secondary-school ideas, and the most persistent one is that dominant alleles spread or are common. Kill that early: frequency in the population is a separate question that belongs to population genetics. Also make the point that dominance is a statement about a pair of alleles and a particular phenotype. The sickle-cell example on the next slides shows that the same pair of alleles can be recessive for one phenotype and codominant for another. Flag the simplification honestly and name where the full story comes.

title: Genetics as information
text:
Worked example: sickle-cell disease (1)
The gene. HBB, “hemoglobin subunit beta”, on human chromosome 11 (band 11p15.4).

HBB encodes β-globin. Two β-globin and two α-globin chains make one haemoglobin molecule, which carries oxygen in red blood cells.
The gene is small: 3 exons, about 1.6 kb of DNA.
The normal allele is called HbA. The sickle allele is HbS.

The difference. HbS has one base change: codon 6 is GAG in HbA and GTG in HbS. The amino acid changes from glutamate (Glu) to valine (Val).
You will look HBB up in NCBI Gene and Ensembl in the exercise.

Sickle-cell disease was the first disease explained at the molecular level (Pauling and colleagues in 1949 showed that the haemoglobin was different; Ingram in the 1950s found the single amino-acid change). It is therefore the cleanest possible example of genotype to phenotype. Numbering: the classic name is Glu6Val, which counts amino acids in the mature chain without the initiator methionine. Databases use the HGVS standard, which counts the methionine, so they write p.Glu7Val and c.20A>T. Mention this now so students are not confused when they meet it in ClinVar. All facts on this slide are on the NCBI Gene and Ensembl pages they will open.

title: Genetics as information
text:
Worked example: sickle-cell disease (2)


Walk through the figure from top left. One base (A to T in the coding strand) changes one codon (GAG to GTG) and one amino acid (Glu to Val). Valine is hydrophobic; on the surface of deoxygenated haemoglobin it creates a sticky patch, so HbS molecules polymerise into long fibres when oxygen is low. The fibres bend the red cell into a sickle shape. Sickled cells are stiff, block small vessels, causing pain and organ damage, and are destroyed early, causing anaemia. At the bottom, the three genotypes: two normal alleles, carrier, and two sickle alleles. The carrier state also gives partial protection against severe malaria, which is why HbS is common in regions where malaria is or was common. We return to that in population genetics.

title: Genetics as information
text:
Worked example: sickle-cell disease (3)
Is HbS dominant or recessive? It depends on the phenotype you look at.










Phenotype level
HbA/HbA
HbA/HbS
HbS/HbS
HbS is…




Disease (anaemia, crises)
no
no (usually)
yes
recessive


Red cells sickle at very low O2
no
some
yes
(partly) dominant


Haemoglobin type on a gel
only HbA
HbA and HbS
only HbS
codominant




At the protein level, each allele makes its own product. The heterozygote has both.
So “recessive” is a statement about one phenotype, not about the allele itself.


This slide is the payoff of the vocabulary. The disease is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait; that is how it appears in pedigrees and in OMIM. But a carrier’s red cells can sickle under extreme low oxygen, and on an electrophoresis gel both haemoglobin types are seen side by side, which is codominance. This is not a contradiction; it shows that dominance is defined relative to a phenotype. Students will meet codominance again in the Extensions to Mendel unit, and the electrophoresis view is the cleanest way to understand it. Use this to reinforce that “recessive” does not mean “does nothing” in the heterozygote.

title: Genetics as information
text:
Genomes differ hugely in size


Genome: all the DNA of an organism (one copy of each chromosome).
Genome size runs from about 5 Mb (E. coli) to over 29,000 Mb (axolotl).
The number of protein-coding genes is far less variable: about 4,000 to 28,000 in this set.


The numbers come from NCBI Datasets, the reference genome for each species and its current annotation. Gene counts are approximate and change a little with each annotation release, so we round in speech. The key observation: genome size spans almost four orders of magnitude; gene number varies about sevenfold. A human has roughly the same number of protein-coding genes as a mouse or a worm. The axolotl, a salamander, has a genome ten times larger than ours with a similar gene number. Students will plot these exact data in R in the exercise.

title: Genetics as information
text:
The C-value paradox
The C-value is the amount of DNA in one haploid genome. The paradox: C-value does not follow organism complexity or gene number.
Why? Most of a large eukaryotic genome does not code for protein:

introns inside genes, and large intergenic regions;
repeated sequences, especially transposable elements, which can make up most of a genome;
polyploidy: bread wheat has three ancestral genomes, which is why it has so many genes.

Bacteria are the exception. Their genes are packed tightly: E. coli has about 900 genes per Mb, humans about 6.

The C in C-value originally meant constant: each species has a characteristic amount of DNA per haploid nucleus. The paradox was that this amount is not related to complexity: some amphibians and plants have far more DNA than mammals. Today we understand it mainly as differences in non-coding DNA, especially transposable elements, and in polyploidy. It is sometimes called the C-value enigma, because once we know about repeats it is not really a paradox any more. The genes-per-Mb comparison is the R task in the exercise, so do not give away too many numbers; the two quoted here are rounded.

title: Genetics as information
text:
Many genes are shared
Genes in different species that descend from one gene in their common ancestor are orthologs. Genes that arose by duplication within a genome are paralogs.

Human CFTR (chromosome 7) and mouse Cftr (chromosome 6) are one-to-one orthologs. Their proteins are about 79% identical (Ensembl).
The zebrafish cftr protein is still about 56% identical to the human one.
HBB is part of a gene family: α-, β-, γ-, δ-globins are paralogs, made by old duplications. Families like this can make one-to-one orthologs hard to define.

Because genes and their functions are conserved, what we learn about a gene in one species often holds in others.

Orthology is the reason comparative genetics works. The identity figures come from the Ensembl Compara orthologue pages (release 116). Mention that the globin family is a nice example of duplication: humans have several β-like globin genes expressed at different developmental stages, and the duplications happened separately in different mammal lineages, so the mouse β-like globins do not pair one-to-one with ours. That is why Ensembl does not list a simple mouse ortholog for HBB, and why the exercise uses CFTR for the mouse ortholog task. Paralogs come back in Genome annotation.

title: Genetics as information
text:
Why model organisms work
A model organism is easy to grow, cross and manipulate, and what we learn in it often applies to other species, because many genes are shared.








Organism
Generation time (roughly)
Good for




Yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae
hours
cell cycle, haploid genetics


Worm, Caenorhabditis elegans
days
development, every cell mapped


Fly, Drosophila melanogaster
about 10 days
classical genetics, development


Thale cress, Arabidopsis thaliana
about 2 months
plant genetics


Zebrafish, Danio rerio
months
vertebrate development, transparent embryos


Mouse, Mus musculus
about 2 months
mammalian genetics, disease models



Each has its own database, joined in the Alliance of Genome Resources.

The trade-off is between ease and similarity to humans. Yeast and worms are fast and cheap but distant; mice are close but slow and expensive. Most human disease genes have counterparts in mouse, many in fly and fewer in yeast. Generation times are rough, under lab conditions, and vary with temperature and strain; do not let students memorise them, only the order. Mention the community databases: SGD, WormBase, FlyBase, TAIR, ZFIN and MGI, now joined in the Alliance of Genome Resources, which the exercise uses for an optional task.

title: Genetics as information
text:
Four ways to study genetics

These four approaches are also the map of this course. Each one asks a different question about the same information.

Use the figure as a map. Transmission genetics is Mendel’s approach: crosses and pedigrees, inferring genes from patterns of inheritance, without seeing any DNA. Molecular genetics looks at the DNA and its products directly. Genomics looks at whole genomes at once. Population genetics asks how allele frequencies change over generations and between populations. The approaches complement each other: sickle-cell disease was first recognised by transmission (a recessive pattern in families), explained molecularly (Glu to Val), and its frequency explained by population genetics (malaria). Point out where each part of the course sits.

title: Genetics as information
text:
Where genetic information lives

Sickle-cell disease: HBB, one base change, Glu→Val, recessive disease, codominant on a gel.

The summary table is the vocabulary sheet for the whole course. Ask students to be able to give the sickle-cell version of each word: gene HBB, locus 11p15.4, alleles HbA and HbS, genotypes HbA/HbA, HbA/HbS, HbS/HbS, phenotype disease or no disease, carrier is heterozygous. If they can do that, they are ready for Mendel.

title: Genetics as information
text:
Where this leads

Mendel: alleles segregate into gametes, and we predict genotype ratios in crosses (Aa × Aa).
Extensions to Mendel: incomplete dominance, codominance and the other complications we postponed today.
Gene expression recap and Genome annotation: transcripts, exons and orthologs in more depth.
Hardy–Weinberg and Drift and selection: why HbS is common where malaria is.


Point forward. The next unit starts with Mendel’s peas, which is transmission genetics with no molecular knowledge at all. Ask students to keep the sickle-cell example in mind: every Mendelian rule we learn can be checked against it.

title: Exercise: linkage & recombination
Exercise: linkage & recombination
Exercise: linkage & recombination
text:
Background
Linkage. Genes close together on one chromosome do not assort independently. In a testcross of a dihybrid, the two parental combinations (the allele combinations the dihybrid received from its parents) are more common than the two recombinant combinations.
Phase. Coupling (cis): A B / a b. Repulsion (trans): A b / a B. The slash separates the two homologues. Phase changes which classes are parental, not the RF.
Recombination frequency. \[\text{RF} = \frac{\text{recombinant offspring}}{\text{all offspring}}, \qquad 0 \le \text{RF} \le 0.5\] RF = 0.5 means unlinked (1 : 1 : 1 : 1 in a testcross).
Crossing over happens between non-sister chromatids after DNA replication, at the four-strand stage of prophase I. One crossover makes 2 of the 4 products recombinant. A chromatid is recombinant for two loci if it has an odd number of crossovers between them.
Map distance. 1 centimorgan (cM) = 1 crossover per 100 chromatids on average. For short intervals, 1 cM ≈ 1% RF. Map distance in morgans = ½ × mean number of chiasmata in the interval. Distances add along the chromosome; RF does not, for long intervals.
Map functions (d in morgans; 1 M = 100 cM):










RF from d
d from RF
Assumes




Haldane
RF = ½(1 − e−2d)
d = −½ ln(1 − 2 RF)
independent crossovers


Kosambi
RF = ½ tanh(2d)
d = ¼ ln[(1 + 2 RF) / (1 − 2 RF)]
interference



χ² test for linkage. Check that each gene segregates 1 : 1. Then test parental vs recombinant against 1 : 1 (H0: unlinked), df = 1, critical value 3.84 at α = 0.05.

title: Exercise: linkage & recombination
text:
By hand
B1. (two-point testcross, maize) In maize, C (coloured kernels) is dominant to c (colourless) and Sh (full kernels) is dominant to sh (shrunken). A plant from the cross C Sh / C Sh × c sh / c sh is testcrossed to c sh / c sh. The kernels on the ears are (invented numbers):



Kernels
Number




coloured, full
2008


colourless, shrunken
1990


coloured, shrunken
72


colourless, full
80




Write the genotype of the heterozygous parent with the slash notation. Is it in coupling or repulsion?
Which classes are parental and which recombinant? Compute the RF.
How far apart are the two genes, in cM?

B2. (repulsion, Drosophila) pr (purple eyes) and vg (vestigial wings) are 11.5 cM apart (RF = 0.115). A purple female (pr vg+ / pr vg+) is crossed to a vestigial male (pr+ vg / pr+ vg). Their F1 daughters are testcrossed to pr vg / pr vg males.

What is the genotype and phase of the F1 daughters?
Predict the four offspring classes and their numbers among 1000 offspring.
Which classes would be parental if the F1 had been made from wild type × purple vestigial instead?

B3. (four-strand stage, chiasmata) In 100 meioses of a plant, a cytologist counts the chiasmata between two loci A and B: 64 meioses have none, 32 have one and 4 have two.

What is the mean number of chiasmata in the interval? What is the map distance?
A meiosis with one chiasma gives what fraction of recombinant products? A meiosis with two chiasmata gives, on average, what fraction? (Assume each chiasma involves two random non-sister chromatids.)
What RF do you expect between A and B? Compare it with the map distance, and explain the difference.

B4. (Sturtevant’s map, real data) Sturtevant (1913) measured these percentages of recombinants between X-linked genes of Drosophila: y–w 1.0%, w–v 29.7%, y–v 32.2%, v–m 3.0%, w–m 33.7%.

Find the gene order and draw a map with y at 0.
Using the neighbouring intervals, where are v and m?
y–v measured directly is 32.2%, but y–w + w–v is 30.7%. Give two reasons why they need not agree.

B5. (saturation) In the same paper, v–r was 26.9%, which puts r at 30.7 + 26.9 = 57.6 on the map. But y–r measured directly was only 37.6%.

Explain why the direct measurement is so much smaller.
Two genes are 90 cM apart. What RF would you roughly expect in a testcross? Could you tell from that testcross alone that they are on the same chromosome?

B6. (map functions) Use a calculator.

Convert RF = 0.10, 0.25 and 0.40 into map distances with Haldane’s function and with Kosambi’s function.
Two genes are 30 cM apart. What RF does each function predict?
Why do the two functions agree for RF = 0.10 but not for RF = 0.40?

B7. (χ² test for linkage) A testcross of A a B b gives 58 A B, 52 a b, 47 A b and 43 a B offspring.

Check that each gene segregates 1 : 1.
Test whether the genes are linked (α = 0.05). Give χ², df and your conclusion.
Suppose the same proportions had been found among 2000 offspring. Repeat the test. What do you learn?

B8. (flies: males and the X)

A male Drosophila of genotype pr vg / pr+ vg+ is testcrossed to pr vg / pr vg females. What offspring do you expect, and why?
For X-linked genes, you do not need a tester: a heterozygous female’s sons show her gametes directly. Explain why.
A female Xy w / X^+ +^ (yellow and white on one X, the wild-type alleles on the other) is crossed to a wild-type male. Among 1000 sons, how many do you expect in each class? (y–w: 1.0 cM, as Sturtevant found.)

title: Exercise: linkage & recombination
text:
Explore
Do the by-hand part first. The demo shows one bivalent at the four-strand stage, with two blue sister chromatids from one parent and two red from the other. Loci A, B, (C, D) are spaced evenly; blue chromatids carry the upper-case alleles. “1 meiosis” places crossovers at random: their number is Poisson, each falls at a random position and joins one random blue and one random red chromatid (no interference). Below, the four products are drawn spliced, and marked P (parental) or R (recombinant) for the two outermost loci. The table counts recombinant products for every pair of loci over all meioses so far and compares the observed RF with Haldane’s prediction and with d/100. The plot shows RF against map distance. Changing the loci or the spacing resets the counts; the random sequence always starts from the same seed.



E1. The demo starts with two loci 10 cM apart. Press “1 meiosis” ten times and note, each time, the number of crossovers and the number of recombinant products. How many of the ten meioses had any crossover between A and B? When there was a crossover, were all four products recombinant?
E2. Now press “+1000”. What RF do you observe for A–B, and how does it compare with d/100 = 0.10 and with Haldane’s 0.091? Look at the readout: how many meioses had two or more crossovers between A and B?
E3. Choose 3 loci and set the spacing to 25 cM. Press “+1000”. Compare the observed RF for A–C with the sum of the RFs for A–B and B–C. Which one adds up: the map distances or the RFs? Why?
E4. Choose 4 loci and spacing 40 cM, so A and D are 120 cM apart, and press “+1000”. What is the RF for A–D? From the readout, what fraction of meioses had at least two crossovers between A and D? Would a testcross tell you that A and D are on the same chromosome?
E5. Press “simulate the curve”. The grey points are 500 meioses at each distance from 5 to 200 cM. Above which distance is the RF always above 0.4? Use Haldane’s formula to find the distance at which RF = 0.45, and check it against the points.






Solutions: Explore





E1. With the default seed, 9 of the 10 meioses have no crossover between A and B (all four products P). The fourth meiosis has two crossovers and gives 2 R + 2 P: a three-strand double crossover. Never are all four products recombinant from one crossover: a crossover involves only two of the four chromatids. (With 10 cM, the expected number of chiasmata per bivalent is 0.2, so about 2 meioses in 10 have one; this run was a little unlucky.)
E2. After “+1000” (on top of your 10 meioses): RF ≈ 0.081 (326/4040), against Haldane 0.091 and d/100 = 0.10. The readout shows about 845 meioses with no crossover, 150 with one, 14 with two and 1 with three or more: double crossovers are rare at 10 cM, so RF ≈ map distance. (The numbers depend slightly on how many single meioses you ran first.)
E3. Observed: A–B 0.194, B–C 0.197, A–C 0.314. The sum of the RFs would be 0.391, much more than 0.314. The map distances add (25 + 25 = 50 cM), but RFs do not: a chromatid with one crossover in A–B and one in B–C is recombinant for both short intervals but parental for A–C. Haldane’s prediction for 50 cM is 0.316, matching the simulation.
E4. A–D: RF ≈ 0.462 (Haldane 0.455). Of 1000 meioses, 281 had two and 406 had three or more crossovers between A and D: 69% had at least two. An RF of 0.46 is hard to distinguish from 0.5 without a very large sample, so a two-point testcross would suggest the genes are unlinked. You would only see that they share a chromosome by mapping the genes in between (B and C, each 40 cM from its neighbours).
E5. From about 80 cM on, the points are at or above 0.4 (0.406 at 80 cM). Haldane: 0.45 = ½(1 − e−2d) → e−2d = 0.1 → d = ½ ln 10 = 1.15 M = 115 cM; the simulated point at 115 cM is 0.451. Beyond that, the points scatter between about 0.44 and 0.50: RF has saturated, and the scatter from 500 meioses is larger than the remaining slope.

title: Exercise: linkage & recombination
text:
Find it
FlyBase is the database for Drosophila genes. Every gene has a gene report page. At the top, the General Information box gives the gene’s symbol and name, and three locations: the Recombination map (the genetic map position, written as chromosome-position in cM, where chromosome 1 is the X), the Cytogenetic map (the band on the giant polytene chromosomes) and the Sequence location (in base pairs). Click “full details” next to the recombination map to jump to the section Genomic Location and Detailed Mapping Data, which lists published estimates of the position.
F1. Open the gene report for white, FBgn0003996 (or type w in the search box on the FlyBase home page and pick the D. melanogaster gene w). Read the Recombination map field. What are the chromosome and the map position? Which chromosome is “1”?
F2. Do the same for yellow (y, FBgn0004034), crossveinless (cv, FBgn0000394), vermilion (v, FBgn0003965) and forked (f, FBgn0262111). Make a table with the five genes in map order, and the distance between neighbours.

What RF would you expect between w and cv in a testcross?
y and f are both on the X. What RF would you expect between them? Use a map function.

F3. On the cv page, click “full details” next to the recombination map. Under Genomic Location and Detailed Mapping Data, find the older recorded positions of cv and the publications they come from. Why does a gene have more than one recombination-map position?
F4. Compare FlyBase with Sturtevant’s 1913 map (y 0.0, w 1.0, v 30.7, m 33.7, r 57.6). Look up miniature (m, FBgn0002577) and rudimentary (r, FBgn0003189) as well. Is the gene order the same? Which interval differs most?

title: Exercise: linkage & recombination
text:
Solutions






Solutions: By hand





B1. a) C Sh / c sh: coupling (the two dominant alleles came in together from one parent). b) Parental: coloured full (C Sh, 2008) and colourless shrunken (c sh, 1990), the two largest classes. Recombinant: coloured shrunken (C sh, 72) and colourless full (c Sh, 80). Total 4150. RF = (72 + 80)/4150 = 152/4150 = 0.037 = 3.7%. c) About 3.7 cM. The interval is short, so RF ≈ map distance.
B2. a) pr vg+ / pr+ vg: repulsion. b) Parental: purple (pr vg+) and vestigial (pr+ vg), each (1 − 0.115)/2 = 0.4425 → 442.5 each, about 443 and 442. Recombinant: wild type (pr+ vg+) and purple vestigial (pr vg), each 0.115/2 = 0.0575 → 57.5 each. c) Wild type and purple vestigial would be parental (coupling), as in the lecture example.
B3. a) Chiasmata: (0 × 64 + 1 × 32 + 2 × 4)/100 = 0.40 per meiosis. Map distance = ½ × 0.40 = 0.20 M = 20 cM. b) One chiasma: ½ of the products recombinant (2 of 4). Two chiasmata: on average also ½ (two-, three- and four-strand doubles give 0, 2, 2 and 4 recombinants out of 4, average 2). c) RF = ½ × (32 + 4)/100 = 0.18: lower than the map distance (0.20), because the 4 meioses with two chiasmata contribute twice to the distance but only once (½) to the recombinants. Double crossovers are partly hidden.
B4. a) y–w is small and w–v is large, and y–v ≈ y–w + w–v, so w is between y and v. v–m is 3.0 and w–m (33.7) ≈ w–v + v–m (32.7), so v is between w and m. Order: y – w – v – m. b) y 0, w 1.0, v 1.0 + 29.7 = 30.7, m 30.7 + 3.0 = 33.7 (Sturtevant’s own map). c) (1) Sampling noise: the RFs come from different crosses with different numbers of flies, each with its own random error. (2) Double crossovers: a long interval measured directly hides some double crossovers, so a direct RF tends to be smaller than the sum of shorter intervals. (Here the direct value is actually larger than the sum, so noise dominates: the 29.7% interval itself already hides some double crossovers.)
B5. a) The y–r interval is long. Many chromatids have two (or another even number of) crossovers between y and r, which restores the parental combination. Those crossovers are invisible with only two markers. RF saturates towards 0.5, so it underestimates the distance. b) Haldane: ½(1 − e−1.8) = ½(1 − 0.165) = 0.42; Kosambi: ½ tanh(1.8) = 0.47. So 42–47%, close to 50%. From a testcross alone you could not distinguish this reliably from unlinked genes; you need genes in between (or a very large sample).
B6. a)








RF
Haldane d = −½ ln(1 − 2 RF)
Kosambi d = ¼ ln[(1 + 2 RF)/(1 − 2 RF)]

−½ ln 0.5 = 34.7 cM
¼ ln(1.5/0.5) = 27.5 cM


0.40
−½ ln 0.2 = 80.5 cM

d = 0.30 M. Haldane: ½(1 − e−0.6) = ½(1 − 0.549) = 0.226. Kosambi: ½ tanh(0.6) = ½ × 0.537 = 0.269.
For small RF, double crossovers are rare whatever the model, so both functions give d ≈ RF. For large RF, the answer depends on how many hidden double crossovers you assume: many (Haldane, no interference) or fewer (Kosambi, interference). The difference grows quickly as RF approaches 0.5.

B7. a) Gene A: A 58 + 47 = 105, a 52 + 43 = 95. χ² = (105 − 100)²/100 + (95 − 100)²/100 = 0.5. Gene B: B 58 + 43 = 101, b 52 + 47 = 99, χ² = 0.02. Both fine (< 3.84). b) Parental (A B + a b) = 110, recombinant (A b + a B) = 90, expected 100 : 100. χ² = (10² + 10²)/100 = 2.0, df = 1, p ≈ 0.16 > 0.05. Not significant: no evidence for linkage (RF estimate 0.45). c) With 2000 offspring: 1100 : 900, expected 1000 : 1000. χ² = (100² + 100²)/1000 = 20, df = 1, p < 0.001: linked, RF ≈ 0.45. Loose linkage is real but needs large samples to detect. The χ² value grows in proportion to the sample size for the same proportions.
B8. a) Only the two parental classes, ½ wild type and ½ purple vestigial, with no recombinants, because Drosophila males have no meiotic crossing over. b) A son gets his X from his mother and his Y from his father. The Y carries no alleles of X-linked genes, so the son’s phenotype for X-linked traits shows exactly which X (and so which gamete) he got from his mother. Males are hemizygous for the X (Chromosome theory & sex linkage). c) Parental: yellow white (Xy w Y) and wild type (X^+ +^ Y), each (1 − 0.01)/2 → 495 each. Recombinant: yellow only (X^y +^ Y) and white only (X^+ w^ Y), each 0.005 → 5 each.

Under Genomic Location and Detailed Mapping Data, cv has several recombination-map positions: 1-13.7 (Buzzati-Traverso, 1947), 1-14.4 (Comeron et al., 2012), and the FlyBase estimate 1-12 (FlyBase, 2016) shown at the top.
