title: Exercise: linkage & recombination
text:
Where this leads
With two markers, double crossovers are invisible; with three, they show up as the rarest class of offspring. In Three-point crosses you use them to order three genes in one experiment and to measure interference, which explains why Kosambi’s map function fits better than Haldane’s. In Human linkage & LOD scores the same RF is estimated from families instead of testcrosses, with the LOD score replacing the χ² test.
Next: Exercise in R: write cM_to_rf() and rf_to_cM() with a default method = "haldane", plot both map functions, and re-analyse Sturtevant’s 1913 data.

title: Quiz: linkage & recombination
text:
Short questions on linkage, recombination frequency and map distance. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. A calculator with ln and exp helps for Q9 and Q10.

Q1. A dihybrid AaBb is testcrossed to aabb. What ratio do you expect if the genes are unlinked? What tells you that they are linked?






Hint





The testcross classes are the gametes of the dihybrid. What does independent assortment say about those gametes?









Answer





Unlinked: four classes in 1 : 1 : 1 : 1, so 50% of the offspring carry new combinations. Linked: two classes (the parental combinations) are clearly more common than the other two (the recombinants), and recombinants are less than 50%. Two large plus two small, with each pair about equal, is the signature of linkage.




Q2. A testcross of Drosophila females heterozygous for b (black body) and vg (vestigial wings) gives: 405 black vestigial, 393 wild type, 92 black, 110 vestigial (invented numbers). Which classes are parental? What is the RF? Was the mother in coupling or repulsion?






Hint





Parental classes are the two largest.









Answer





Parental: black vestigial (b vg) and wild type (b+ vg+), the two largest classes. Recombinant: black (b vg+) and vestigial (b+ vg). RF = (92 + 110) / 1000 = 0.202 = 20.2%. The mother was b+ vg+ / b vg: coupling.




Q3. Same genes, but the F1 mother came from black × vestigial parents (b vg+ / b vg+ × b+ vg / b+ vg). Predict the four classes of her testcross, with approximate fractions.






Hint





RF does not depend on the phase. Only which classes are called parental changes.









Answer





She is b vg+ / b+ vg: repulsion. Parental classes are now black (b vg+) and vestigial (b+ vg), about (1 − 0.2)/2 = 40% each. The recombinants are wild type and black vestigial, about 0.2/2 = 10% each. The same RF, opposite labels.




Q4. One crossover happens between genes A and B in a meiosis. What fraction of the four products of that meiosis is recombinant for A and B? Why?






Hint





How many chromatids does the bivalent have, and how many take part in one crossover?









Answer





Half (2 of 4). Crossing over happens at the four-strand stage, after DNA replication. One crossover involves only two non-sister chromatids; the other two chromatids stay parental. So even if every meiosis had exactly one crossover between A and B, RF would be 50%, not 100%.




Q5. In 30% of meioses there is one chiasma between genes C and D; in the rest there is none. What is the RF, and what is the map distance?






Hint





Use Q4.









Answer





Each meiosis with a chiasma gives ½ recombinant products, so RF = 0.30 × ½ = 0.15. With at most one crossover, RF equals map distance: 15 cM. (Equivalently: map distance in morgans = ½ × mean number of chiasmata = ½ × 0.30 = 0.15 M.)




Q6. RFs among three linked genes: A–B 8%, B–C 5%, A–C 13%. What is the gene order?






Hint





For short distances, map distances add. Which gene’s two distances add up to the third?









Answer





8 + 5 = 13, so B is in the middle: A – B – C, with A–B 8 cM and B–C 5 cM.




Q7. Two genes are on the same chromosome, 80 cM apart. A student predicts 80% recombinants in a testcross. What will she really see, and why?






Hint





A chromatid is recombinant if it has an odd number of crossovers between the two genes.









Answer





Far fewer than 80%, and certainly no more than 50%: Haldane’s map function predicts ½(1 − e−1.6) = 0.40, Kosambi’s ½ tanh(1.6) = 0.46. RF can never exceed 0.5: with many crossovers in the interval, an odd number (recombinant) and an even number (parental) become about equally likely, and double crossovers restore the parental combination. The two genes will look nearly unlinked, although they are on the same chromosome.




Q8. Why does every map distance shorter than about 10 cM almost equal the RF, while long distances do not?






Hint





How likely are two crossovers in a short interval?









Answer





In a short interval, two crossovers on one chromatid are very rare, so nearly every crossover produces a visible recombinant, and RF ≈ expected number of crossovers = map distance. In a long interval, double (and higher even) crossovers are common; they restore the parental combination and are invisible with two markers, so RF is lower than the map distance. That is why maps are built by adding up short intervals.




Q9. Use Haldane’s map function, RF = ½(1 − e−2d) with d in morgans. (a) What RF do you expect for 20 cM? (b) What map distance corresponds to RF = 0.30?






Hint





For (b), use d = −½ ln(1 − 2 RF). Remember to convert morgans to centimorgans.









Answer






d = 0.20 M: RF = ½(1 − e−0.4) = ½(1 − 0.670) = 0.165.
d = −½ ln(1 − 0.6) = −½ ln(0.4) = −½ × (−0.916) = 0.458 M = 45.8 cM. (Kosambi would give ¼ ln(1.6/0.4) = ¼ ln 4 = 0.347 M = 34.7 cM.)





Q10. Kosambi’s map function gives a shorter map distance than Haldane’s for the same RF. Explain why, in terms of interference.






Hint





Which function expects more double crossovers?









Answer





Haldane assumes crossovers are independent, so double crossovers are as common as chance allows, and many crossovers are hidden. To explain a given RF, Haldane must assume a lot of hidden crossovers, hence a long distance. Kosambi allows for interference (one crossover makes another nearby less likely), so fewer doubles are hidden and fewer extra crossovers are needed: the distance is shorter. Interference is measured directly in Three-point crosses.




Q11. A testcross gives 31 parental and 19 recombinant offspring. Test the hypothesis that the genes are unlinked (α = 0.05). Assume each gene alone segregates 1 : 1.






Hint





Under H0 (unlinked), parental : recombinant = 1 : 1. df = 1; the 5% critical value is 3.84.









Answer





Expected 25 : 25. χ² = (31 − 25)²/25 + (19 − 25)²/25 = 1.44 + 1.44 = 2.88, df = 1, below 3.84 (p ≈ 0.09). We cannot reject independent assortment. This does not prove that the genes are unlinked: an RF of 0.38 is quite plausible, and with 50 offspring the test has little power.




Q12. Why do Drosophila geneticists use heterozygous females, not males, in mapping testcrosses?






Hint





What is unusual about meiosis in male flies?









Answer





Drosophila males have no meiotic crossing over. A heterozygous male in coupling gives only the two parental gamete types, so his testcross shows complete linkage (RF = 0) for any two genes on the same chromosome, whatever their distance. Females cross over normally, so their testcross measures RF.

title: Exercise: human linkage & LOD scores
Exercise: human linkage & LOD scores
Exercise: human linkage & LOD scores
text:
Background
Informative meiosis. The parent is heterozygous at the disease locus (Dd) and at the marker (e.g. 1/2), so each child shows which disease allele and which marker allele it received from that parent. The other parent should carry different marker alleles (e.g. 3/3), so the child’s two alleles can be told apart.
Phase. Which marker allele sits on the same homologue as D. Written D 1 / d 2 (coupling of D with 1). It is known if the grandparents show it, and unknown otherwise.
Scoring. With the parent D 1 / d 2: children who got D 1 or d 2 are non-recombinant (NR); D 2 or d 1 are recombinant (R).
Likelihood and LOD. For a phase-known family with n informative meioses and k recombinants, with θ the recombination fraction (the RF of Linkage & recombination):
\[
L(\theta) = \theta^{k}(1-\theta)^{n-k}, \qquad
\text{LOD}(\theta) = \log_{10}\frac{\theta^{k}(1-\theta)^{n-k}}{0.5^{\,n}} = k\log_{10}\theta + (n-k)\log_{10}(1-\theta) + 0.301\,n.
\]
The maximum is at θ̂ = k/n. LOD(0.5) = 0. If k = 0, LOD(0) = 0.301 n; if k ≥ 1, LOD(0) = −∞.
Phase unknown. Average over both phases: L(θ) = ½ θk(1 − θ)n−k + ½ θn−k(1 − θ)k.
Decisions. LOD ≥ 3: linkage (odds 1000 : 1). LOD ≤ −2: linkage at that θ excluded. In between: inconclusive. LODs of independent families add at the same θ; find the maximum of the sum.
Useful logs: log10 0.1 = −1, log10 0.2 = −0.699, log10 0.25 = −0.602, log10 0.3 = −0.523, log10 0.7 = −0.155, log10 0.75 = −0.125, log10 0.8 = −0.097, log10 0.9 = −0.046, log10 2 = 0.301.

text:
Explore
Do the by-hand part first. In the demo, each row is one family, with sliders for the number of informative meioses n and recombinants k; tick “phase ?” for an unknown phase. The plot shows each family’s LOD curve (thin), the total (thick), the thresholds +3 and −2, and the maximum with θ̂. “+ random family” adds a family simulated under true linkage at θ = 0.05.



E1. The demo starts with your family from B1 (n = 8, k = 2). Check your θ̂ and maximum LOD from B2. Then set k = 0: what is the maximum now, and where? Set n = 10 with k = 0: why is this the smallest family that passes 3?
E2. Rebuild the three families of B4 (use “+ add family” and the sliders). Check your answers to B4 a–c. Then remove F1: do F2 and F3 together reach 3?
E3. Tick “phase ?” for the B1 family (n = 8, k = 2) and compare with B6. Then tick it for each family in “five families”. How much does the maximum total LOD fall when every phase is unknown?
E4. Click “unlinked marker”. Where is the maximum, and how large is it? Over which range of θ is linkage excluded? Now add families with k = n/2 until linkage is excluded up to θ = 0.3.
E5. Press “reset”, click “one family (10, 1)”, then press “+ random family” until the total LOD passes 3. How many families and meioses did it take? Is θ̂ close to the true value of 0.05?






Solutions: Explore





E1. n = 8, k = 2: max 0.45 at θ̂ = 0.25, as in B2. With k = 0 the maximum is at θ̂ = 0, LOD = 8 × 0.301 = 2.41. With n = 10, k = 0: 3.01; 9 meioses give 2.71, so 10 is the minimum.
E2. The total peaks at 4.24 at θ̂ = 0.083 (= 2/24). The table gave 4.13 at 0.05 and 4.22 at 0.1, on either side of the true maximum. Without F1, F2 + F3 peak at about 1.7 (at θ ≈ 0.14): not enough.
E3. Phase unknown, n = 8, k = 2: max 0.16 at θ̂ ≈ 0.26, compared with 0.45 for phase known (B6 gives LOD(0.25) = 0.16). In “five families” the total maximum drops from 6.35 (all phase known) to 4.85 (all phase unknown), still at θ̂ ≈ 0.083 and still above 3. Families with k = 0 lose least (6, 0: 1.81 → 1.51), because the other phase would mean that all n children are recombinant, which is very unlikely at small θ. Families with recombinants lose most (7, 1: 0.86 → 0.56).
E4. “unlinked marker” (24 meioses, 11 recombinants): max about 0.04 at θ̂ = 0.458, essentially 0. LOD < −2 for θ < about 0.18, so linkage closer than that is excluded. Adding families with k = n/2 pushes the excluded range further out; reaching 0.3 needs many more meioses (several more families of n = 10, k = 5), because the curve near 0.3 is flat.
E5. With the demo’s fixed seed, the first random family is (9, 1): total max 2.94 at θ̂ ≈ 0.105, just short of 3. The second is (8, 0): total 5.03 at θ̂ ≈ 0.074, so two random families (27 meioses in all, 2 recombinants) were enough. θ̂ = 2/27 = 0.074 is close to the true 0.05, but with so few recombinants it is a rough estimate: one more or one fewer recombinant would move it a lot. (“reset” restarts the random families from the same seed, so everyone gets these numbers.)

Find it
The UCSC Genome Browser shows a region of the human genome with tracks of genes and other features. The top line gives the position (chromosome:start-end) and the genome assembly (use hg38, also called GRCh38). Genes are drawn as boxes (exons) joined by lines (introns), with arrows showing the strand. PubMed searches the biomedical literature (see Probability & the χ² test for the search syntax).
F1. The HTT region. Open the UCSC Genome Browser at HTT, hg38 (or go to the browser, choose human hg38 and type HTT in the search box). Read: a) the position of HTT (chromosome, start, end) and its approximate length in kb; b) which strand it is on (do the arrows point right, +, or left, −?), and how many exons the main transcript has (click the gene, read “Exon count”); c) the chromosome band (the red box on the chromosome ideogram at the top, or the “Chromosome Band” track). How far is HTT from the end of 4p?
F2. Neighbours. Zoom out 3× twice. Name the protein-coding gene immediately to the left of HTT and the one immediately to the right. Linkage in families placed HD within a few cM; roughly how many base pairs is that, and how many genes like these could such a region hold?
F3. The 1983 paper. In PubMed, search Gusella[au] AND Huntington AND 1983[dp]. Find the Nature paper. Report its title, volume, pages and PMID, and summarise the abstract in one sentence. What kind of marker was used (read the title)?
F4. The 1993 paper. Search trinucleotide repeat expanded unstable Huntington's disease chromosomes. Open the 1993 Cell paper. Who are the authors? What did the gene they found (IT15) contain, and in how many HD families was it expanded?
F5. An exclusion. Search DRPLA D4S10. Find the 1990 J Med Genet paper. What LOD score did the authors report, at which θ, and what did they conclude?






Hint





In UCSC, click on the gene in the “GENCODE” or “NCBI RefSeq” track to open its details page. In PubMed, [au] restricts a term to authors and [dp] to the publication date.

These facts were checked against the UCSC Genome Browser API (hg38, NCBI RefSeq Select track and cytoBand track) and PubMed (E-utilities).
F1. a) HTT is at chr4:3,074,681-3,243,957 (hg38, MANE Select transcript NM_001388492.1; the gene record in GENCODE/HGNC starts slightly earlier, at about 3.04 Mb), about 169 kb long. b) + strand (arrows point right); the main transcript has 67 exons. c) Band 4p16.3, which runs from the start of chromosome 4 to 4.5 Mb. HTT starts about 3.1 Mb from the tip of 4p: close to the telomere, in the “distal portion of the short arm” where linkage had placed HD. Click path: UCSC → Genomes → Human hg38 → search HTT → choose the RefSeq/MANE match → click the gene → details page (Position, Strand, Exon count).
F2. To the left: GRK4 (G protein-coupled receptor kinase 4, ends at about 3.04 Mb). To the right: MSANTD1 (starts at about 3.25 Mb). (There is also an antisense RNA gene, HTT-AS, at the start of HTT on the − strand.) A few cM in humans is roughly a few million base pairs (on average about 1 cM per Mb); in the 1 Mb around HTT alone there are more than ten genes, so a linked region can hold dozens of candidate genes.
F3. “A polymorphic DNA marker genetically linked to Huntington’s disease.” Gusella JF, Wexler NS, Conneally PM, et al. Nature 1983 Nov 17–23; 306(5940):234–238. PMID 6316146. Abstract: family studies show that the HD gene is linked to a polymorphic DNA marker that maps to human chromosome 4, a first step towards identifying the defect with recombinant DNA technology. The marker is a polymorphic DNA marker (an RFLP, detected by the probe G8; later named locus D4S10).
F4. “A novel gene containing a trinucleotide repeat that is expanded and unstable on Huntington’s disease chromosomes.” The Huntington’s Disease Collaborative Research Group (a consortium; PubMed lists no individual authors). Cell 1993;72(6):971–983, PMID 8458085. The gene IT15 (now HTT) contains a polymorphic (CAG)n trinucleotide repeat that is longer than normal on HD chromosomes, in all 75 HD families examined. The repeat lies within the coding sequence of a predicted ~348 kDa protein.
F5. Kondo et al. 1990, “Exclusion mapping of the hereditary dentatorubropallidoluysian atrophy gene from the Huntington’s disease locus”, J Med Genet 27(2):105–108, PMID 1969487. Four families; negative LOD scores at all recombination fractions, −2.215 at θ = 0.15. Conclusion: the DRPLA locus is not closely linked to D4S10, so DRPLA is a distinct disease from HD.

Where this leads

title: Quiz: human linkage & LOD scores
text:
Short questions on linkage analysis in human families. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Unless the question says otherwise, assume full penetrance, a phase-known affected parent, and that log10 2 = 0.301.

Q1. Give three reasons why geneticists mapping a human disease gene cannot simply compute RF = recombinants / total and test it with χ², as in Drosophila.






Hint





Think about who chooses the crosses, family size, and what we know about the parent’s chromosomes.









Answer





Any three of these. (1) No designed crosses: we cannot set up a testcross with a double heterozygote of known phase. (2) Families are small, so each gives only a few meioses, too few for χ² (expected counts below 5). (3) The phase of the affected parent is often unknown, so we cannot say which children are recombinant. (4) Not every meiosis is informative: the parent must be heterozygous at the marker. The LOD score solves this by computing a likelihood for each family and adding across families.




Q2. What makes a meiosis informative for linkage between a dominant disease gene and a marker?






Hint





You need to be able to say, for each child, which of the parent’s two homologues it received.









Answer





The parent must be heterozygous at both loci: Dd at the disease locus (an affected parent with a dominant disease) and heterozygous at the marker (e.g. 1/2). Then each child shows which disease allele (affected or not) and which marker allele it received from that parent. If the parent were 1/1 at the marker, every child would get a 1, and we could not tell recombinants from non-recombinants. It also helps if the other parent’s marker alleles differ from the affected parent’s, so that the child’s paternal allele can be read.




Q3. An affected father is D 1 / d 2 (phase known). His wife is unaffected and 3/3 at the marker. Classify each child as recombinant (R) or non-recombinant (NR): (a) affected, 1/3; (b) unaffected, 1/3; (c) affected, 2/3; (d) unaffected, 2/3.






Hint





The 3 always comes from the mother. Which combination of D/d and 1/2 did the child get from the father?









Answer






D with 1: NR. (b) d with 1: R. (c) D with 2: R. (d) d with 2: NR.





Q4. Write the likelihood L(θ) for a phase-known family with 8 informative meioses and 2 recombinants. What is θ̂? What is L(0.5)?






Hint





Each meiosis is R with probability θ and NR with probability 1 − θ, independently.









Answer





L(θ) = θ2 (1 − θ)6. The maximum is at θ̂ = k/n = 2/8 = 0.25. L(0.5) = 0.58 = 1/256 ≈ 0.0039.




Q5. For a phase-known family with no recombinants, LOD(0) = n × 0.301. How many such meioses do you need to reach LOD 3? What happens to LOD(0) if a single recombinant turns up?






Hint





L(0) = 1 if k = 0. If k ≥ 1, what is 0k?









Answer





With k = 0, LOD(0) = log10(1 / 0.5n) = n log10 2 = 0.301 n. For LOD ≥ 3 you need n ≥ 3 / 0.301 = 9.97, so 10 meioses. With one recombinant, L(0) = 0, so LOD(0) = −∞: a single recombinant rules out complete linkage (θ = 0). The maximum then moves to θ̂ = 1/n.




Q6. A family gives LOD(0.1) = 1.2. In words, what does this number mean? Is it evidence of linkage?






Hint





Undo the logarithm.









Answer





101.2 ≈ 16: the family is about 16 times more probable if the disease gene and the marker are linked at θ = 0.1 than if they are unlinked. It points towards linkage, but it is far below the threshold of 3 (odds 1000 : 1). On its own it is inconclusive; add more families.




Q7. Why is the threshold for linkage as high as LOD 3, when odds of 20 : 1 would correspond to the usual 5 % level?






Hint





Before you look at any family, how likely is it that a randomly chosen marker is linked to the disease gene?









Answer





Because linkage is unlikely a priori: only about 1 marker in 50 lies close enough to a given gene to show linkage. Prior odds of about 1 : 49, multiplied by a likelihood ratio of 1000 : 1 (LOD 3), give posterior odds of roughly 20 : 1 in favour of linkage, so about a 5 % chance that the “linkage” is false. A lower threshold would give many false linkages.




Q8. Three families have maximum LODs of 1.4 (at θ = 0.05), 1.1 (at θ = 0.10) and 0.9 (at θ = 0.15). A student adds the maxima, gets 3.4, and declares linkage. What is wrong?






Hint





Which θ does each number belong to?









Answer





LODs add at the same θ. The three maxima are at different θ, so their sum is not a LOD at any single θ. Add the three curves θ by θ, then find the maximum of the sum. That maximum is always ≤ 3.4, and may well be below 3.




Q9. What does a total LOD of −2.5 at θ = 0.10 (and lower at smaller θ) tell you?






Hint





What is the threshold for exclusion?









Answer





Since LOD < −2 for every θ ≤ 0.10, linkage at θ ≤ 0.10 is excluded: the disease gene is not within about 10 cM of this marker. It does not exclude looser linkage (larger θ). A real example: four DRPLA families gave LOD −2.215 at θ = 0.15 with the HD-linked marker D4S10, showing that DRPLA is not caused by the HD gene.




Q10. Why does an unknown phase make a family less informative? Write L(θ) for a phase-unknown family with n = 6 and 1 or 5 recombinants depending on the phase.






Hint





Each phase has prior probability ½.









Answer





L(θ) = ½ θ1 (1 − θ)5 + ½ θ5 (1 − θ)1. We must average over the two possible arrangements, and the wrong one also gets weight. The maximum LOD drops from 0.63 (phase known) to 0.33. Typing the grandparents to determine phase is therefore worth a lot.




Q11. Why did microsatellites replace RFLPs as markers for human linkage mapping?






Hint





How many alleles does each have? What fraction of parents will be heterozygous?









Answer





An RFLP usually has only two alleles (site present or absent), so many parents are homozygous and their meioses are uninformative. A microsatellite (e.g. (CA)n) has many alleles of different lengths, so most people are heterozygous and almost every meiosis is informative. Microsatellites are also typed quickly by PCR instead of Southern blots.




Q12. In 1983 Gusella and colleagues showed that Huntington disease is linked to a DNA marker on chromosome 4. Why did it still take until 1993 to find the gene?






Hint





How precisely can linkage in families locate a gene? How big is 1 cM in base pairs in humans?









Answer





Linkage only gives a region: with the meioses available, a gene is placed within a few cM, which in humans is millions of base pairs holding many genes. In 1989 HD was still placed only “about 4 cM distal to D4S10”, near the tip of 4p (4p16.3). Finding the gene required more markers, a physical map of the region, and searching it for genes. In 1993 the gene (IT15, now HTT) was found to carry an expanded CAG repeat on HD chromosomes in all 75 families examined.

title: Exercise: extensions to Mendel
text:
By hand
B1. (incomplete dominance) In snapdragons, CRCR is red, CRCW pink and CWCW white. Give the phenotype ratios from (a) pink × pink, (b) pink × white, (c) red × white. Which of the three crosses would you use to get the most pink seed?
B2. (ABO) A woman with blood type AB has a child with a man of blood type O. (a) Which blood types are possible for the child, and in what proportions? (b) Could this couple have a child with type O? With type AB?
B3. (allelic series) In rabbits, C (full colour) > cch (chinchilla) > ch (Himalayan) > c (albino). A chinchilla rabbit crossed with a Himalayan rabbit gives 1/2 chinchilla, 1/4 Himalayan and 1/4 albino offspring. What are the genotypes of the two parents?
B4. (lethal allele) Yellow mice (AYa) are crossed with each other, and give litters with on average 8 live pups. (a) What fraction of the zygotes die? (b) Among the live pups, what fraction are yellow? (c) If each litter of yellow × agouti also starts from the same number of zygotes, which cross gives larger litters, and by how much?
B5. (penetrance) Polydactyly in a family is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with 70% penetrance. A man without extra digits has an affected father and an unaffected mother who does not carry the allele. His partner does not carry the allele. (a) What is the probability that the man carries the allele? (Hint: use the fact that he is unaffected.) (b) What is the probability that their first child has extra digits?
B6. (recessive epistasis) In Labradors, B_ gives black and bb brown (chocolate) pigment, but ee dogs are yellow whatever their B genotype. (a) Give the F₂ phenotype ratio from BbEe × BbEe, and explain it with a pathway. (b) A black dog is crossed with a yellow bbee dog. Their pups are 3 black, 2 chocolate and 5 yellow. What is the genotype of the black dog? (c) Can two yellow Labradors have a black pup? Explain.
B7. (complementary genes) Two pure-breeding white-flowered sweet pea lines, W1 and W2, are crossed. All F₁ plants are purple, and the F₂ has 9 purple : 7 white. (a) Give the genotypes of W1, W2 and the F₁. (b) What fraction of the white F₂ plants would breed true if selfed (give only white offspring)? (c) A third white line, W3, crossed with W1 gives only white F₁ plants. What does that tell you about the mutation in W3?
B8. (identify the ratio) Summer squash plants from a dihybrid cross give an F₂ of 205 white, 52 yellow and 15 green fruit. (a) Express the counts in 16ths and suggest a ratio. (b) Test it with χ² by hand. (c) Draw a pathway that explains the ratio, and say which genotypes give green fruit.
B9. (dominant suppression and duplicate genes) (a) White Leghorn chickens (CCII) are crossed with White Wyandottes (ccii). C is needed for coloured feathers, and I suppresses colour. What are the F₁ and F₂ phenotypes? (b) A dihybrid F₂ gives 15 : 1 for triangular : ovoid seed capsules. What ratio would an F₁ test cross give, and why can a test cross not separate 15 : 1 from 13 : 3?

title: Exercise: extensions to Mendel
text:
Explore
The demo shows the 16 squares of AaBb × AaBb coloured by phenotype, next to the pathway that explains the colours. Click a square to see which enzymes that genotype has and how far down the pathway it gets.



E1. In recessive epistasis 9 : 3 : 4, click aaBB, then aabb. Both are yellow. Which enzyme is missing in each, and why does the B genotype not matter? Which class of 16ths has merged with which?
E2. Switch to complementary 9 : 7. Click AAbb and aaBB (the two white parents) and then AaBb (their F₁). Explain why two white parents can give a purple F₁. How many different genotypes are white?
E3. Compare dominant epistasis 12 : 3 : 1 with dominant suppression 13 : 3. In both, A_ switches an inhibitor on. Click aabb in each. Why is aabb a class of its own in one preset and merged with white in the other?
E4. Go through all six presets and, for each one, write down which of the four classes A_B_, A_bb, aaB_, aabb are merged. Check your answers against the table in the Background.
E5. In duplicate genes 15 : 1, how many of the 16 squares have no working enzyme? How many have exactly one kind of working enzyme? Why would a geneticist who knocked out only gene A see no phenotype?






Solutions





E1. aaBB lacks enzyme A, so the yellow precursor is never turned into brown, and enzyme B has nothing to work on. aabb lacks both enzymes. Both stop at yellow. The B genotype only matters if step A happens, so aa hides B/b: aa is epistatic. The 3 aaB_ and the 1 aabb merge into 4.
E2. AAbb has enzyme A but not B; aaBB has B but not A. Both are white. The F₁ AaBb gets a working A from one parent and a working B from the other, so both steps work and it is purple: the two mutations complement each other. White squares: AAbb, Aabb, aaBB, aaBb, aabb, which are 5 genotypes in 7 of the 16 squares.
E3. In dominant epistasis, the inhibitor blocks the first step (white → green). aabb has no inhibitor, so it makes green, but it has no enzyme B to make yellow: it stays green, a class of its own (1/16). In dominant suppression, the pathway has only one step, done by enzyme B. aabb has no inhibitor but also no enzyme B, so it is colourless, like the inhibited plants: 9 + 3 + 1 = 13.
E4. None merged: 9 : 3 : 3 : 1. Recessive epistasis: aaB_ + aabb. Complementary: A_bb + aaB_ + aabb. Dominant epistasis: A_B_ + A_bb. Dominant suppression: A_B_ + A_bb + aabb. Duplicate: A_B_ + A_bb + aaB_.
E5. Only 1 square (aabb) has no working enzyme. Squares with only enzyme A are the 3 A_bb, and squares with only enzyme B are the 3 aaB_: 6 squares have exactly one kind. An aa knockout still has enzyme B (if it is B_), which makes the product on its own. Redundant genes have to be knocked out together before a phenotype appears.

title: Exercise: extensions to Mendel
text:
Find it
F1. The ABO gene. Open NCBI Gene and search for ABO[sym] AND human[orgn]. Open the ABO entry. In the Summary box, read the Location field and the full gene name. On which chromosome is ABO, and in which cytogenetic band? What kind of enzyme does the gene encode, according to its name?
F2. A disease with incomplete penetrance. Open MedGen and search for hereditary breast ovarian cancer syndrome. Open the entry with that name. Read the Mode of inheritance field. Then open the BRCA1 gene in NCBI Gene and read Location. The OMIM entry for the BRCA1-related disease is MIM 604370 (Breast-ovarian cancer, familial, susceptibility to, 1). Does everyone who inherits a pathogenic BRCA1 variant get cancer? What word from the lecture describes this?
F3. Achondroplasia. Open the MedlinePlus Genetics page on achondroplasia and read the Causes and Inheritance sections. Then check the mode of inheritance in MedGen (entry Achondroplasia). OMIM: MIM 100800. (a) What is the mode of inheritance, and which gene is involved? (b) About what fraction of people with achondroplasia have parents of average height? What does that tell you about where their allele came from? (c) What happens to a child who inherits two altered copies? Which idea from the lecture is this? (d) Is the altered protein less active or more active than normal? Which molecular kind of dominance is it?
F4. Where is FGFR3? In NCBI Gene, read the Location of human FGFR3. Is it on the same chromosome as ABO?






Solutions





F1. NCBI Gene → search ABO[sym] AND human[orgn] → ABO (Gene ID 28) → Summary. Location: 9q34.2, so chromosome 9, long arm (q), band 34.2. The full name is “ABO, alpha 1-3-N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase and alpha 1-3-galactosyltransferase”: a glycosyltransferase. The A allele adds N-acetylgalactosamine and the B allele galactose to the H antigen, which is why A and B are codominant.
F2. MedGen → Hereditary breast ovarian cancer syndrome (concept C0677776) → Mode of inheritance: autosomal dominant inheritance. NCBI Gene BRCA1 (Gene ID 672): Location 17q21.31. Not everyone who carries a pathogenic BRCA1 variant develops cancer: they inherit a raised risk, not the disease itself. This is incomplete penetrance. (We do not ask for a penetrance number, because the estimates differ between studies and change over time.)
F3. (a) Autosomal dominant; gene FGFR3 (MedlinePlus Inheritance section; MedGen Achondroplasia, C0001080: “Autosomal dominant inheritance”). (b) About 80% of people with achondroplasia are born to parents of average height. Their FGFR3 allele is a new (de novo) mutation, usually arising in a parent’s germ line. (c) Children with two altered copies have a severe form, with very short bones and a small rib cage; they are usually stillborn or die soon after birth. The allele is dominant for short stature and recessive lethal, like AY in mice. (d) MedlinePlus: the variants “cause the FGFR3 protein to be overly active”. This is a gain-of-function allele.
F4. NCBI Gene → FGFR3 (Gene ID 2261) → Location 4p16.3: chromosome 4, short arm. Not the same chromosome as ABO (9q34.2).

title: Exercise: extensions to Mendel
text:
Solutions






Solutions: By hand





B1. (a) Pink × pink (CRCW × CRCW): 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. (b) Pink × white (CRCW × CWCW): 1 pink : 1 white. (c) Red × white (CRCR × CWCW): all pink. Cross (c) gives the most pink seed (100%), and since pink plants do not breed true you must make this cross every season.
B2. The mother is IAIB and the father ii. (a) The child gets IA or IB from the mother (1/2 each) and i from the father: 1/2 type A (IAi) and 1/2 type B (IBi). (b) Neither O nor AB is possible: every child gets exactly one of IA or IB from the mother, and i from the father.
B3. Albino offspring (cc) mean both parents carry c. A chinchilla parent cchc × a Himalayan parent chc gives 1/4 cchch (chinchilla), 1/4 cchc (chinchilla), 1/4 chc (Himalayan), 1/4 cc (albino) = 1/2 chinchilla : 1/4 Himalayan : 1/4 albino. The parents are cchc and chc.
B4. (a) AYa × AYa gives 1/4 AYAY, which die: 1/4 of the zygotes. (b) The survivors are 2 AYa : 1 aa: 2/3 yellow. (c) Yellow × agouti (AYa × aa) gives 1/2 AYa and 1/2 aa, with no deaths. If 8 live pups are 3/4 of the zygotes, a litter starts from about 8 / (3/4) ≈ 10.7 zygotes, so yellow × agouti litters are about 4/3 times as large (≈ 10.7 pups instead of 8).
B5. (a) Before we know his phenotype, P(carrier) = 1/2 (affected father is heterozygous; mother is +/+). Then use the fact that he is unaffected: P(unaffected and carrier) = 1/2 × 0.3 = 0.15; P(unaffected and not carrier) = 1/2 × 1 = 0.5. P(carrier | unaffected) = 0.15 / (0.15 + 0.5) = 0.15 / 0.65 ≈ 0.23. (b) P(child affected) = P(man carrier) × P(passes it on) × penetrance = 0.23 × 1/2 × 0.7 ≈ 0.081, about 8%.
B6. (a) 9 black (B_E_) : 3 chocolate (bbE_) : 4 yellow (B_ee + bbee). Pathway: E_ is needed to put dark pigment in the hair at all; B_ makes that dark pigment black rather than brown. ee stops the pathway before B matters, so ee is epistatic to B. (b) Chocolate pups (bbE_) mean the black parent carries b; yellow pups (ee) mean it carries e. So the black dog is BbEe, and this is a test cross: expected 1 black : 1 chocolate : 2 yellow, close to 3 : 2 : 5 in a litter of 10. (c) No. Yellow dogs are ee, so all their pups are ee and yellow (whatever their B genotype; their noses may differ).
B7. (a) W1 = AAbb, W2 = aaBB (or the other way round), F₁ = AaBb. (b) White F₂ plants: 1 AAbb, 2 Aabb, 1 aaBB, 2 aaBb, 1 aabb (7/16). Every one of them lacks a working copy of at least one gene for good: A_bb plants are bb, so all their offspring are bb and white; aaB_ plants are aa, so all offspring are white; aabb likewise. So all 7/7 white F₂ plants breed true for white. (c) W3 × W1 gives a white F₁, so W3 does not complement W1: the W3 mutation is in the same gene as W1’s (gene B if W1 is AAbb).
B8. (a) Total = 272. In 16ths: 205/272 × 16 = 12.06, 52/272 × 16 = 3.06, 15/272 × 16 = 0.88. Suggests 12 : 3 : 1 (dominant epistasis). (b) Expected: 272 × 12/16 = 204, 272 × 3/16 = 51, 272 × 1/16 = 17. χ² = (205 − 204)²/204 + (52 − 51)²/51 + (15 − 17)²/17 = 0.0049 + 0.0196 + 0.2353 = 0.26, df = 2. Since 0.26 < 5.99, do not reject; p ≈ 0.88. (For comparison, 9 : 3 : 4 in the same order gives χ² ≈ 46.8, clearly rejected.) (c) White precursor → (step 1) → green → (enzyme from Y) → yellow, and the dominant W allele blocks step 1. W_ is white; wwY_ is yellow; wwyy is green.
B9. (a) F₁ CcIi: white (I suppresses colour). F₂: coloured only if C_ii (3/16); C_I_ (9), ccI_ (3) and ccii (1) are white: 13 white : 3 coloured. (b) F₁ test cross AaBb × aabb gives AaBb, Aabb, aaBb, aabb in 1 : 1 : 1 : 1. Under 15 : 1 only aabb lacks the product: 3 triangular : 1 ovoid. Under 13 : 3 (coloured only aaBb) the test cross is also 3 : 1. Both merge three of the four test-cross classes, so the test cross cannot tell them apart; only the F₂ (15 : 1 vs 13 : 3) can.

title: Exercise: extensions to Mendel
text:
Where this leads
Incomplete penetrance and de novo mutations (as in achondroplasia) come back in Pedigree analysis, where they make human family trees harder to read. The 9 : 7 cross of two white lines is the logic of the complementation test in Mutation. And when a dihybrid F₂ is not 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 because the genes sit close together on a chromosome, that is linkage, which starts Part 2.
Next: Exercise in R: test several candidate ratios on a Labrador F₂ at once with your own χ² functions and map_dbl().

title: Quiz: extensions to Mendel
text:
Short questions on dominance, multiple alleles, lethal alleles, penetrance and epistasis. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. For the two-gene questions, start from the 16 squares of a dihybrid Punnett square: 9 A_B_ : 3 A_bb : 3 aaB_ : 1 aabb.

Q1. Red snapdragons crossed with white snapdragons give an all-pink F₁. What phenotypes, in what ratio, do you expect in the F₂? Why does this show that the parental alleles did not blend?






Hint





With incomplete dominance, each genotype has its own phenotype. What is the genotype ratio of an F₂?









Answer





1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. The F₁ is CRCW, and the F₂ genotypes are 1 CRCR : 2 CRCW : 1 CWCW. With incomplete dominance the phenotype ratio equals the genotype ratio. Red and white come back unchanged in the F₂, so the alleles stayed separate in the pink F₁. Only the phenotype of the heterozygote was intermediate.




Q2. What is the difference between incomplete dominance and codominance? Give one example of each.






Hint





Is the heterozygote an average of the two homozygotes, or does it show both of them?









Answer





In incomplete dominance the heterozygote is intermediate (pink snapdragons, from red × white). In codominance the heterozygote shows both parental phenotypes in full (blood type AB: IAIB red cells carry both A and B antigens). In both cases the F₂ phenotype ratio is 1 : 2 : 1.




Q3. A mother has blood type A and a father has blood type B. Their first child has type O. What are the parents’ genotypes, and what is the probability that their next child has type AB?






Hint





A type O child is ii. Where did each i come from?









Answer





The child is ii, so each parent carries i: the mother is IAi and the father IBi. The next child gets IA from the mother with probability 1/2 and IB from the father with probability 1/2, so P(AB) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. (The four blood types A, B, AB and O are equally likely from this cross.)




Q4. Most loss-of-function alleles are recessive. Explain why, and name two ways in which a mutant allele can still be dominant.






Hint





How much protein does a heterozygote make, and is that usually enough?









Answer





A heterozygote for a null allele still makes about half the normal protein, and for most genes that is enough for a normal phenotype (the gene is haplosufficient). A mutant allele can be dominant through any of:

haploinsufficiency: half the protein is not enough;
dominant negative: the mutant protein spoils the normal protein, for example in a dimer or a collagen triple helix;
gain of function: the mutant protein is over-active or does something new, as with FGFR3 in achondroplasia.





Q5. A protein works as a dimer. A heterozygote makes normal and dominant-negative subunits in equal amounts, and they pair at random. What fraction of the dimers is fully normal? Compare with a heterozygote for a null allele that makes no protein.






Hint





Each subunit in a dimer is normal with probability 1/2. Use the product rule.









Answer





A dimer is fully normal only if both subunits are normal: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. A null heterozygote makes only normal subunits, at half the amount, so it has 1/2 of the normal amount of working dimer. The dominant-negative allele does more damage than losing the gene altogether. (For a tetramer, the fraction would be (1/2)⁴ = 1/16.)




Q6. Yellow mice crossed with yellow mice give 2 yellow : 1 agouti, never 3 : 1. Explain. What would you expect from yellow × agouti?






Hint





Which genotype class of a 1 : 2 : 1 is missing?









Answer





All yellow mice are AYa. Yellow × yellow gives 1 AYAY : 2 AYa : 1 aa, but AYAY embryos die. The survivors are 2 yellow : 1 agouti. AY is dominant for coat colour and recessive for lethality (pleiotropy). Yellow × agouti (AYa × aa) gives 1 yellow : 1 agouti, with no deaths, because no AYAY offspring can form.




Q7. A dominant allele causes a disorder with 80% penetrance. A heterozygous parent and a homozygous normal parent have a child. What is the probability that the child is affected?






Hint





Two things must both happen: the child must inherit the allele, and the allele must show.









Answer





P(inherits the allele) = 1/2. P(affected | has the allele) = 0.8. P(affected) = 1/2 × 0.8 = 0.4. So 40% of children are affected and 10% carry the allele without showing it, which is how a dominant trait can skip a generation.




Q8. What is the difference between dominance and epistasis?






Hint





How many genes are involved in each?









Answer





Dominance is a relation between two alleles of the same gene: which allele’s phenotype shows in the heterozygote. Epistasis is a relation between two different genes: the genotype at one gene hides the effect of the other gene (as ee hides B/b in Labrador coat colour).




Q9. Two pure-breeding white-flowered sweet pea lines are crossed. The F₁ is all purple. The F₁ is selfed and gives 9 purple : 7 white. Explain with a pathway, and give the genotypes of the two white parents.






Hint





Which of the 16 squares are purple? What must the F₁ have that neither parent has?









Answer





Colour needs two steps in a row, enzyme A and then enzyme B (colourless → colourless → purple). Only A_B_ plants (9/16) make pigment. A_bb, aaB_ and aabb are all white (3 + 3 + 1 = 7). The parents were AAbb and aaBB. Each lacks a different enzyme, so the F₁ AaBb has both and is purple: the two white mutations complement each other.




Q10. In summer squash, WwYy × WwYy gives white, yellow and green fruit in 12 : 3 : 1. Which genotypes are green, and which gene is epistatic?






Hint





Which class of 16ths is the “1”?









Answer





Green is the 1/16 class, wwyy. Yellow is wwY_ (3/16). Everything with at least one W is white (W_Y_ + W_yy = 9 + 3 = 12). The dominant W allele is epistatic to Y/y (dominant epistasis). Y only shows its effect in ww plants.




Q11. An F₂ from a dihybrid cross has 151 plants with triangular seed capsules and 9 with ovoid capsules. Which ratio would you test first, and why?






Hint





Convert to 16ths: count ÷ total × 16.









Answer





The total is 160. In 16ths: 151/160 × 16 = 15.1 and 9/160 × 16 = 0.9. So test 15 : 1 (duplicate genes): only aabb lacks the product. Expected counts are 150 and 10, and χ² = 1²/150 + 1²/10 = 0.107, df = 1, p ≈ 0.74, which fits. (This is the shepherd’s purse pattern.)




Q12. A dihybrid F₂ has three phenotype classes in 9 : 3 : 4. A student says: “9 : 7 also fits, with p = 0.6, so both models are fine.” What is wrong with this?






Hint





How do you get 9 : 7 from 9 : 3 : 4?









Answer





9 : 7 is 9 : 3 : 4 with the “3” and the “4” merged. If the finer ratio fits, the coarser one will usually fit too, because merging classes throws information away. But you can see three phenotypes, and 9 : 7 predicts only two. A model has to explain every phenotype class you can tell apart. So 9 : 3 : 4 is the answer, and χ² alone cannot make that choice for you.

title: Exercise: Mendel, segregation & assortment
Exercise: Mendel, segregation & assortment
Exercise: Mendel, segregation & assortment
text:
Background
Notation. Each gene has two alleles; upper case is dominant (R, round), lower case is recessive (r, wrinkled). A diploid genotype has two alleles: RR and rr are homozygous, Rr is heterozygous. R_ means “RR or Rr”, that is, the dominant phenotype. Throughout, we assume complete dominance (the Extensions to Mendel unit relaxes this) and unlinked genes (Linkage, Part 2, relaxes this).
Law of segregation. The two alleles of a gene separate into different gametes, so an Rr plant makes ½ R and ½ r gametes. The reason is meiosis I: the two homologous chromosomes, one carrying R and one carrying r, go to opposite poles.
Law of independent assortment. Alleles of different genes go into gametes independently. An Rr Yy plant makes RY, Ry, rY, ry, ¼ each. The reason: at metaphase I, each homologue pair lines up independently of the others. This holds for genes on different chromosomes.
Key ratios.








Cross
Genotypes
Phenotypes




Aa × Aa
1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa
3 : 1


Aa × aa (testcross)
1 Aa : 1 aa
1 : 1


AaBb × AaBb
9 genotypes, 1 : 2 : 1 : 2 : 4 : 2 : 1 : 2 : 1
9 : 3 : 3 : 1


AaBb × aabb (testcross)
1 : 1 : 1 : 1
1 : 1 : 1 : 1



Product rule. For independent genes, the probability of a combination is the product of the per-gene probabilities: P(aa bb cc) = ¼ · ¼ · ¼ = 1/64. An individual heterozygous for n genes makes \(2^n\) gamete types; a cross between two such individuals gives \(3^n\) genotypes.
Mendel’s numbers. Seed shape F2: 5474 round : 1850 wrinkled. Dihybrid F2 (shape × colour): 315 round yellow : 108 round green : 101 wrinkled yellow : 32 wrinkled green.

title: Exercise: Mendel, segregation & assortment
text:
By hand
B1. (monohybrid, peas) In peas, yellow seeds (Y) are dominant to green (y). Mendel crossed a true-breeding yellow line with a true-breeding green line, then selfed the F1.

Give the genotypes of the P plants, the F1 and the F1 gametes.

Mendel counted 8023 F2 seeds. How many yellow and green seeds do you expect? He observed 6022 yellow and 2001 green.

What offspring do you expect if the male is BB? If he is Bb?
The litter has 4 black and 3 brown pups. What is the male’s genotype?
Another black male sires 6 pups, all black, with brown females. Can you be sure he is BB? What is the probability of this result if he is actually Bb?

What gametes does the F1 make, and in what proportions? Which law are you using?

Give the expected offspring phenotypes and their ratio.

Suppose instead that R and Y were so close together on one chromosome that they never separated. What would the testcross give?

B6. (branch-line) Use the branch-line method for Rr Yy × Rr yy. Give every phenotype class and its probability.
B7. (product rule, three genes) Tall stem (T) is dominant to dwarf (t). Consider Tt Rr Yy × Tt Rr Yy.

How many kinds of gamete does each parent make? How many different genotypes can the offspring have?
What fraction of the offspring is tall, round and green?
What fraction is tt rr yy? What fraction is Tt Rr Yy?
What fraction is dominant for all three traits?

B8. (working backwards) In peas, purple flowers (P) are dominant to white (p), and axial flowers (A) are dominant to terminal (a). Two plants are crossed, giving offspring in the ratio 3 purple axial : 3 purple terminal : 1 white axial : 1 white terminal. What are the parents’ genotypes?
B9. (humans) Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive; Huntington disease is autosomal dominant.

Two unaffected parents have a child with cystic fibrosis. What are the parents’ genotypes? What is the chance that their next child is affected? That their next two children are both unaffected?
An unaffected sister of the affected child wants to know if she is a carrier. What is the probability?
A man with Huntington disease (heterozygous) and an unaffected woman have a child. What is the risk for the child? Which kind of cross is this?

title: Exercise: Mendel, segregation & assortment
text:
Explore
Do the by-hand part first. In the demo you choose 1 or 2 genes and each parent’s genotype. You see each parent’s gametes with their frequencies, the Punnett square (coloured by phenotype, assuming complete dominance), and the genotype and phenotype ratios. Below, the demo simulates N offspring: filled bars are the observed counts, dashed bars the expected ones. “draw again” gives a new random sample (the seed number goes up by one).



E1. The demo starts on the monohybrid F1 × F1 (Aa × Aa). Check the gametes, the Punnett square and both ratios against your answer to B1. Now set N = 16 and press “draw again” a few times, writing down the number of aa offspring each time. How often do you get exactly the expected 4?
E2. Set N = 1000. Compare the proportion of aa offspring with N = 16 and with N = 1000. In which case is the proportion closer to ¼? Which of Mendel’s seven traits would you expect to deviate most from 3 : 1?
E3. Click “dihybrid F1 × F1”. How many distinct gametes does each parent make, how many cells does the square have, and how many genotypes and phenotypes are there? Switch the bars to “genotypes”: which genotype is the most common, and why?
E4. Click “dihybrid testcross”. Why does the Punnett square have only one row? Compare the four phenotype classes with the gametes of the AaBb parent. Then look at N = 100: are the four classes equal?
E5. Before you click, predict the phenotype ratio of AA Bb × aa bb. Then set it up with the genotype buttons and check.






Solutions: Explore





E1. Each parent makes A and a, ½ each; the square has 4 cells: genotypes 1 : 2 : 1 (¼ AA, ½ Aa, ¼ aa) and phenotypes 3 : 1 (¾ A_, ¼ aa), as in B1. With N = 16, seed 1 gives exactly 12 A_ : 4 aa, but the next draws give 15 : 1 (seed 2) and 13 : 3 (seed 3). Hitting the expected count exactly is the exception, not the rule. A 3 : 1 mechanism does not guarantee a 3 : 1 sample.
E2. At N = 1000 (seed 1) there are 757 A_ : 243 aa, so the proportion of aa is 0.243. At N = 16 the proportion jumped between 1/16 = 0.06 and 4/16 = 0.25 in the first three draws. Larger samples come closer to ¼ in proportion, even though the difference in counts (here 7) can be larger than at N = 16. Among Mendel’s traits, pod colour (580 plants: 2.82 : 1) and stem length (1064 plants: 2.84 : 1) have the smallest samples and deviate most; seed shape and seed colour (7324 and 8023 seeds) are closest to 3 : 1.
E3. Each parent makes 4 gametes (AB, Ab, aB, ab, ¼ each), so the square has 4 × 4 = 16 cells. There are 9 genotypes (32), with ratio 1 : 2 : 1 : 2 : 4 : 2 : 1 : 2 : 1, and 4 phenotypes (9 : 3 : 3 : 1). The most common genotype is AaBb (4/16 = ¼): it is heterozygous for both genes, and heterozygous is the most likely outcome for each gene (½ · ½ = ¼).
E4. The aabb parent makes only one kind of gamete (ab), so there is one row. The four cells (AaBb, Aabb, aaBb, aabb) correspond one to one to the four gametes of the AaBb parent (AB, Ab, aB, ab): the testcross reads off the gametes. Expected 1 : 1 : 1 : 1, that is 25 each at N = 100, but seed 1 gives 24 : 18 : 34 : 24. Even at N = 100, a class can be off by 9 by chance.
E5. AA Bb makes AB and Ab gametes (½ each); aa bb makes only ab. Offspring: ½ AaBb (A_B_) and ½ Aabb (A_bb), so the phenotype ratio is 1 : 1, and all offspring show the dominant A phenotype. The square is 2 × 1.

text:
Find it
The Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man database (OMIM) has one entry per human genetic disease, each with a stable six-digit MIM number. At the top of a disease entry, the Phenotype–Gene Relationships table gives the chromosome location, the Inheritance (for example AR = autosomal recessive, AD = autosomal dominant) and the Gene/Locus. OMIM sometimes asks for a login or blocks heavy use; if so, use the NCBI pages linked in each task, which give the same facts.
F1. Open the OMIM entry for cystic fibrosis, MIM 219700. In the Phenotype–Gene Relationships table, read the Inheritance column and the Gene/Locus column. What is the mode of inheritance, and which gene is it? (Alternative: NCBI MedGen, cystic fibrosis, section “Modes of inheritance”.)

F3. Open the NCBI Gene pages for the two genes, CFTR and HTT. In the Summary box at the top, read the Location field. On which chromosomes are the two genes? Would you expect them to assort independently in a family that carries both disease alleles?

A Huntington family with one affected parent is a testcross (Aa × aa: ½ affected). b) For a recessive disease, carriers (Aa) are unaffected, because one working allele is enough. Two carrier parents each pass a with probability ½, so ¼ of their children are aa and affected, although neither parent is. title: Exercise: Mendel, segregation & assortment
text:
Where this leads
Every simulated cross in the demo was a little off from its expected ratio, and so were all of Mendel’s. In Probability & the χ² test we turn “a little off” into a number: the χ² goodness-of-fit test (chisq.test() in R) asks whether a deviation like 5474 : 1850 against 3 : 1 is the size that chance usually produces. Later, Linkage (Part 2) shows what happens when two genes sit close together on one chromosome and independent assortment fails.
Next: Exercise in R: write a function that simulates crosses with sample(), and watch observed ratios approach the expected ones as the number of offspring grows.

title: Quiz: Mendel, segregation & assortment
text:
Short questions on monohybrid and dihybrid crosses and the two laws. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Unless the question says otherwise, assume complete dominance and unlinked genes.

Q1. What is a true-breeding line, and why did Mendel need true-breeding parents?






Hint





What happens when a true-breeding plant is self-fertilised? What genotype must it have?









Answer





A true-breeding line gives only offspring like itself when self-fertilised, generation after generation. That means it is homozygous (RR or rr). Mendel needed this so that he knew exactly what each parent passes on: every gamete of a true-breeding round plant carries R. Without that, the F1 and F2 ratios could not be interpreted.




Q2. Mendel crossed round ♀ × wrinkled ♂ and also wrinkled ♀ × round ♂. What are these called, and what did the identical results tell him?






Hint





Which parent supplies the egg, and which the pollen?









Answer





They are reciprocal crosses. Getting the same F1 (all round) either way showed that the egg and the pollen contribute equally to the trait: it does not matter which sex the allele comes from. (This is not always true: sex-linked and mitochondrial genes, later in the course, give different results in reciprocal crosses.)




Q3. In Mendel’s F2 for seed shape there were 5474 round and 1850 wrinkled seeds. What are the expected numbers under a 3 : 1 ratio? Does the deviation prove that the model is wrong?






Hint





Total = 5474 + 1850. Multiply by ¾ and ¼.









Answer





Total = 7324. Expected: 7324 × ¾ = 5493 round and 7324 × ¼ = 1831 wrinkled. Observed is 19 fewer round and 19 more wrinkled. A small deviation like this is expected from random sampling: each seed is an independent draw, and a sample of draws almost never matches the probabilities exactly. Whether 19 is “too big” needs a test, the χ² goodness-of-fit test, in the next unit.




Q4. An F2 plant from Rr × Rr has round seeds. What is the probability that it is heterozygous?






Hint





You already know it is not rr. Of the ¾ that are round, how much is Rr?









Answer





Among all F2 plants: ¼ RR, ½ Rr, ¼ rr. Given round, only RR and Rr remain, in a ratio of ¼ : ½ = 1 : 2. So P(Rr | round) = ½ ÷ ¾ = ⅔. Mendel confirmed this: when he selfed 565 round F2 plants, 193 bred true and 372 gave both round and wrinkled offspring, close to 1 : 2.




Q5. State the law of segregation and name the event in meiosis that makes it true.






Hint





Where are the two alleles of one gene in a diploid cell?









Answer





The two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation, so each gamete gets one allele, and each allele goes to half of the gametes. The two alleles sit on the two homologous chromosomes, and in anaphase of meiosis I the homologues move to opposite poles. Every gamete therefore gets one homologue, and so one allele, of each pair.




Q6. A purple-flowered pea plant (purple P is dominant over white p) is crossed to a white-flowered plant. The cross gives 12 purple and 0 white offspring. What is the purple plant’s genotype? How sure can you be?






Hint





This is a testcross. If the purple plant were Pp, what is the chance that all 12 offspring are purple?









Answer





This is a testcross. The result fits PP (all offspring Pp, purple). It does not prove it: if the plant were Pp, each offspring would be purple with probability ½, so all 12 purple has probability (½)12 = 1/4096 ≈ 0.00024. That is unlikely, so PP is very probably right. One white offspring would have proved Pp.




Q7. Why is the F2 of a dihybrid cross 9 : 3 : 3 : 1? Answer in one line, using the monohybrid ratio.






Hint





Multiply (¾ + ¼) by (¾ + ¼).









Answer





Each gene on its own gives 3 : 1, and the two genes are independent, so the classes are ¾ · ¾ = 9/16, ¾ · ¼ = 3/16, ¼ · ¾ = 3/16 and ¼ · ¼ = 1/16. In short, 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 = (3 : 1) × (3 : 1). Mendel’s 315 : 108 : 101 : 32 collapses to 423 : 133 for shape and 416 : 140 for colour, both close to 3 : 1.




Q8. An Rr Yy plant makes four kinds of gamete, ¼ each. Explain this with what the chromosomes do in meiosis. When would it not be true?






Hint





Think of two homologue pairs at metaphase I. How many ways can they line up?









Answer





If R/r and Y/y are on different chromosomes, the two homologue pairs line up at metaphase I independently of each other. Half of the meioses put R and Y on the same side (giving RY and ry gametes); the other half put R with y (giving Ry and rY). Overall each of the four types is ¼. This fails when the genes are linked, that is, close together on the same chromosome. Then the parental combinations (RY, ry) are more common than ¼ each. That is the Linkage unit in Part 2.




Q9. In Aa Bb Cc × Aa Bb Cc, what fraction of the offspring is (a) aa bb cc, (b) dominant for all three traits, (c) Aa Bb Cc?






Hint





Answer each gene as its own monohybrid cross, then use the product rule.









Answer






¼ · ¼ · ¼ = 1/64. (b) ¾ · ¾ · ¾ = 27/64. (c) ½ · ½ · ½ = 1/8. A Punnett square would need 8 × 8 = 64 cells; the branch-line method or product rule needs three fractions.





Q10. A plant is heterozygous for 4 unlinked genes (Aa Bb Cc Dd). How many kinds of gamete does it make? If it is selfed, how many different genotypes can the offspring have?






Hint





Per gene: how many alleles can a gamete carry? How many genotypes can an offspring have?









Answer





Gametes: 2 choices per gene, so 24 = 16 kinds. Offspring genotypes: 3 per gene (AA, Aa, aa), so 34 = 81. With complete dominance there are 24 = 16 phenotypes, and the fully recessive class is (¼)4 = 1/256 of the offspring.




Q11. Two parents without cystic fibrosis (an autosomal recessive disease) have a child with cystic fibrosis. What are the parents’ genotypes, and what is the risk for their next child?






Hint





The child must have received a faulty allele from each parent. Which of Mendel’s crosses is this?









Answer





The child is aa, so each parent gave an a. Both parents are unaffected, so both are carriers: Aa × Aa. This is Mendel’s monohybrid F1 × F1 cross, and the risk for each child is ¼. The previous child does not change this: each child comes from a new, independent fertilisation.




Q12. “Dominant alleles are more common in the population than recessive ones.” True or false? Give an example from Mendel’s seven traits or from human disease.






Hint





What does “dominant” describe: a relation between two alleles in one individual, or a frequency in a population?









Answer





False. Dominance describes what the heterozygote looks like; it says nothing about how common an allele is. The Huntington disease allele is dominant but rare, while recessive alleles can be very common (in peas, all plants of a wrinkled line carry only r). Allele frequencies in populations are the topic of the Hardy–Weinberg unit.

text:
Background
Point mutations. A transition replaces a purine by a purine (A↔︎G) or a pyrimidine by a pyrimidine (C↔︎T); a transversion swaps a purine for a pyrimidine. In a coding sequence a substitution can be silent (same amino acid), missense (another amino acid) or nonsense (a stop codon). An insertion or deletion that is not a multiple of 3 is a frameshift.
Numbering. Database (HGVS) names count from the A of the start codon (c.1) and from the start methionine (p.1). So the sickle-cell allele, traditionally Glu6Val, is HBB c.20A>T, p.Glu7Val. Codon n covers c.(3n−2) to c.3n.

Mutagens. EMS: G:C → A:T transitions. Base analogues (5-bromouracil): transitions. Intercalators (proflavin): frameshifts. UV: pyrimidine dimers. X-rays: breaks, deletions.
Fluctuation test. If mutations arise at random during growth, before selection, parallel cultures give very variable counts of mutants (jackpots: variance much larger than the mean). If the selective agent induced them, counts would vary like a Poisson distribution (variance ≈ mean).
Complementation test. Cross two recessive mutants with the same phenotype. F1 wild type (+): they complement, the mutations are in different genes. F1 mutant (−): they fail to complement, same gene. A set of mutations that fail to complement each other is a complementation group = one gene.
Auxotrophs. A mutant blocked at one step of a pathway grows on any compound made after the block.

title: Exercise: Mutation & complementation
text:
Explore
The demo shows a complementation matrix: every pair of recessive mutants has been crossed, and each cell shows whether the offspring is mutant (−, fail to complement) or wild type (+, complement). Click the grey chip to the left of each row to put that mutant in group A, B, C… (click again to change), then press check grouping. Cells that contradict your grouping are outlined. Sort by group reorders rows and columns, and reveal genes shows the true answer. Click a cell to read that cross in words. The mutant sets are invented.



E1. Start with 6 mutants. Group them, check, and then press sort by group. Describe the pattern of − and + in the sorted matrix. Why does each gene become a square block?
E2. Click 8 mutants. How many complementation groups are there, and which mutants are in each? Before you check, use the rule “if x fails with y, and y fails with z, then x fails with z” to predict some cells.
E3. Click 8, harder. One gene is hit by only one mutation. Which mutant is it, and how can you recognise it in the matrix? If you were screening for all the genes of a pathway, what would a group with a single mutant suggest about how complete your screen is?
E4. On any set, put two mutants that fail to complement into different groups on purpose and press check grouping. Read the explanation. Then press new random set a few times and solve each set. How many cells do you actually need to read to solve a set of 8 mutants, if you use the rule from E2?






Solutions: Explore





E1. Groups: A = {1, 4, 6} and B = {2, 3, 5}: two genes. After sorting, all − cells sit in two square blocks along the diagonal, and every cell outside the blocks is +. A block is square because every mutant in a gene fails to complement every other mutant in the same gene (a full set of − among them), and complements every mutant in other genes.
E2. Three groups: {1, 3, 6}, {2, 5, 8} and {4, 7}. Using the rule: 1 × 3 is − and 1 × 6 is −, so 3 × 6 must be − too, and the matrix confirms it. Each new − in a row adds a mutant to an existing group.
E3. Mutant 5 is alone in its gene: its row has − only on the diagonal, and + everywhere else. The four groups are {1, 6}, {2, 4, 7}, {3, 8} and {5}. A group with a single mutant suggests the screen is not saturated: if some genes have been hit only once, there are probably other genes that have not been hit at all. When every gene has been hit several times, new mutants keep falling into known groups, and you can be more confident you have found them all.
E4. The check outlines every cell that disagrees: a − between different groups (they should be in the same gene) or a + within a group (they should be in different genes), and explains the first one. With the transitivity rule you do not need all 28 cells of the half matrix: compare each new mutant with one representative of each group found so far. For 8 mutants in 3 genes that is at most 1 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 18 crosses instead of 28, and often fewer, because you can stop as soon as a mutant fails to complement a representative. (This only works for simple recessive loss-of-function mutations; Q9 of the quiz shows a mutant that breaks the rule.)

The phage selected mutants that were already there.
B5. a) Yes, P is a mutagen: with liver extract it raises revertants of the substitution strain about 16-fold (410 vs 25). P itself is not mutagenic, but liver enzymes convert it into a mutagen (a “promutagen”, like benzo[a]pyrene). b) Q raises revertants only in the frameshift strain, so it causes frameshifts (insertions or deletions of a base), like an intercalating agent (proflavin, acridines). c) Cancer is caused by somatic mutations in genes that control cell division (Part 7). A chemical that mutates bacterial DNA is likely to mutate human DNA as well, so most carcinogens are positive in the Ames test.
B6. a) Recessive: a heterozygote makes about half the enzyme, which is enough to break down phenylalanine; PKU is autosomal recessive. b) Dominant (gain of function): the always-on receptor signals even when a normal receptor is present too. (This is how the achondroplasia allele of FGFR3 works.) c) Dominant (dominant negative): one faulty chain spoils whole triple helices, so most collagen in a heterozygote is defective, not just half.
B7. a) 1 × 4 −, 1 × 7 −, 4 × 7 −: group {1, 4, 7}. 2 × 6 −: group {2, 6}. 3 and 5 complement everyone: {3} and {5}. So four complementation groups: four genes. b) We can only find genes in which our screen produced a mutation. Genes that were not hit, or whose mutations are lethal or give another phenotype, are missed. Two groups have just one mutant, which suggests the screen is far from saturated. c) It fails to complement 2, so it is in group {2, 6} (a new allele of that gene). It should also give − with 6; if it did not, something is wrong with the data or the assumptions.
B8. a) Count how many compounds rescue each mutant: the more compounds, the earlier the block. c is rescued by all four, a by three (E, G, T), d by two (G, T), b only by T. The compound that rescues the earliest-blocked mutant but not the next one comes first: F → E → G → T. b) c: before F (precursor → F). a: F → E (rescued by E, G, T but not F). d: E → G (rescued by G and T). b: G → T (rescued only by T). c) Mutant c is blocked before F, at a step whose product is not among the compounds tested. All four compounds come after its block, so all rescue it.









Solutions: Find it





All facts were checked with the NCBI E-utilities on 2026-11-20. Classifications and review statuses can be updated as evidence accumulates; the consequences and identifiers are stable.
F1. Click path: ClinVar → search HBB[gene] AND c.20A>T (or the direct link) → Variation ID 15333. a) NM_000518.5(HBB):c.20A>T (p.Glu7Val); protein change E7V (Glu7Val), the classic Glu6Val. b) Missense variant. c) Pathogenic; review status criteria provided, multiple submitters, no conflicts. (The conditions list includes “Hb SS disease”, that is, sickle-cell anaemia.) d) rs334; GRCh38 chr11:5,227,002 (band 11p15.4). c.20A>T swaps a purine (A) for a pyrimidine (T): a transversion.
F2. Variation ID 15126: NM_000518.4(HBB):c.19G>A (p.Glu7Lys), missense variant, dbSNP rs33930165. The title uses transcript version .4, because the record was named before NM_000518.5 existed. The two versions differ only outside the coding sequence, so c.19 is the same base in both. G→A is a transition. GRCh38 position 5,227,003: next to HbS (5,227,002), one base further along chromosome 11, which is one base earlier in the HBB coding sequence (c.19 vs c.20), because the gene runs on the − strand. (Classification on 2026-11-20: pathogenic/likely pathogenic.)
F3. Click path: ClinVar → search CFTR[gene] AND G542X → the record titled with (p.Gly542Ter). a) NM_000492.4(CFTR):c.1624G>T (p.Gly542Ter), Variation ID 7115 (VCV000007115). b) Nonsense; condition cystic fibrosis. c) Pathogenic; review status practice guideline (the highest level, four stars). d) rs113993959. Legacy names use one-letter amino acid codes and X for a stop codon: glycine (G) at position 542 becomes a stop (X). Unlike the globins, CFTR legacy numbering already counts the start methionine, so 542 is the same in both names.
F4. dbSNP rs334: alleles T>A / T>C / T>G on NC_000011.10 at position 5,227,002 (GRCh38). a) dbSNP reports alleles on the + strand of chromosome 11. HBB lies on the − strand, so its coding sequence is the reverse complement of the + strand. The A of codon 7 (GAG) pairs with a T on the + strand; the HbS change A>T on the coding strand is T>A on the + strand. b) T>A is HbS (c.20A>T). T>C and T>G on the + strand would be c.20A>G and c.20A>C, other changes at the same base that dbSNP also records (they give Gly or Ala at codon 7).

title: Exercise: Mutation & complementation
text:
Where this leads
Every change in this exercise was described by what it does to a codon. In Gene expression (recap) we follow mutations that act elsewhere: in promoters, splice sites and poly(A) signals, and the frameshift experiments of B2 become Crick and Brenner’s proof that the code is read in triplets. Complementation comes back in the lac operon (Part 6), where it is used with partial diploids, and in cancer genetics (Part 7), where loss of both copies of a tumour suppressor gene is a loss-of-function story.
Next: Exercise in R: load the genetic code as a named vector, translate HBB, and write a function that classifies any point mutation as silent, missense or nonsense.

title: Quiz: Mutation & complementation
text:
Short questions on kinds of mutation, mutagens, the fluctuation test, dominance and the complementation test. Have the genetic code table at hand (Hartwell, or the Exercise in R table).

Q1. Classify each substitution as a transition or a transversion: (a) A→G, (b) C→A, (c) T→C, (d) G→T.






Hint





Purines: A, G. Pyrimidines: C, T. Does the base stay in its class?









Answer






A→G: purine to purine, transition. (b) C→A: pyrimidine to purine, transversion. (c) T→C: pyrimidine to pyrimidine, transition. (d) G→T: purine to pyrimidine, transversion.





Q2. The codon TGG (Trp) mutates at one position. Which single-base changes give a nonsense mutation, and which give a missense mutation?






Hint





The stop codons are TAA, TAG and TGA. Try changing each position of TGG.









Answer





Nonsense: TGG → TAG (2nd position G→A) and TGG → TGA (3rd position G→A). Every other single change is missense, because TGG is the only codon for Trp: for example TGG → TGT (Cys), CGG (Arg), GGG (Gly), TTG (Leu), TCG (Ser), TGC (Cys). No change of TGG is silent.




Q3. Why does a single-base deletion near the start of a coding sequence usually destroy the protein, while a deletion of three bases often does not?






Hint





The ribosome reads in triplets from the start codon, with no punctuation.









Answer





Deleting one base shifts the reading frame: every codon after the deletion is read in a different frame, giving a run of wrong amino acids that usually ends at a premature stop codon. Deleting three bases removes one codon (or changes two codons into one) but keeps the frame, so the rest of the protein is normal. The most common cystic fibrosis allele, F508del, is such an in-frame deletion of three bases; the protein is made but folds badly.




Q4. Luria and Delbrück plated 20 small parallel cultures of E. coli on phage T1. Most plates had 0–2 resistant colonies, but one had 107. Why does this result argue against “the phage induces resistance”?






Hint





If each cell had the same small chance of becoming resistant only on the plate, how much should the counts vary between cultures?









Answer





If phage induced resistance on the plate, every cell in every culture would have the same small chance of becoming resistant, so the counts per culture would follow a Poisson distribution, with variance about equal to the mean: no culture should have 107 when the others have 0–2. A jackpot like 107 is expected if a resistance mutation arose early in the growth of that culture, before it met phage, so that the mutant cell left a large clone. Very skewed counts (variance much larger than the mean) mean that mutations arise at random during growth, and the phage only selects them. (The numbers in this question are invented.)




Q5. In the Ames test, why are the bacteria treated with rat liver extract as well as the chemical? Why does the test count reversions rather than forward mutations?






Hint





What does the liver do to foreign chemicals? On which medium can only revertants grow?









Answer





Many chemicals are not mutagenic themselves, but liver enzymes convert them into mutagens. The extract imitates this metabolism, so the test also catches these chemicals. Reversions of a his− mutation can be selected: on a plate without histidine only revertants form colonies, so one revertant among about 108 cells is easy to see. A forward mutation in a random gene would have no such selection and would be hard to find.




Q6. A mutation in an enzyme gene is recessive. Explain why, in terms of the amount of enzyme. Give one reason a loss-of-function allele can instead be dominant.






Hint





How much enzyme does a heterozygote make, and how much does the cell need?









Answer





A heterozygote makes about half the normal amount of enzyme, and for most enzymes half is enough to keep the pathway going, so the phenotype is wild type: the allele is recessive. A loss-of-function allele is dominant if half the product is not enough (haploinsufficiency), or if the faulty product interferes with the normal one, for example as a defective subunit of a complex (dominant negative).




Q7. Why can only recessive mutations be used in a complementation test?






Hint





What does the F1 look like if one of the two mutations is dominant?









Answer





The test reads the F1 phenotype: wild type means each parent supplied what the other lacked. If one mutation is dominant, the F1 is mutant whatever the other mutation is, because one copy of the dominant allele is enough to give the mutant phenotype. So the F1 is mutant even when the two mutations are in different genes, and the test cannot tell them apart.




Q8. Four recessive mutants with yellow leaves give these F1 (+ = green, − = yellow): 1×2 −, 1×3 +, 1×4 +, 2×3 +, 2×4 +, 3×4 −. How many genes? Which mutants are in each?






Hint





Group together mutants that fail to complement (−).









Answer





1 and 2 fail to complement: one gene. 3 and 4 fail to complement: a second gene. Every cross between the pairs is +. So two complementation groups, {1, 2} and {3, 4}: at least two genes are needed for green leaves.




Q9. In Q8, a fifth mutant fails to complement mutants 1 and 3 (and, as it turns out, 2 and 4). Suggest an explanation.






Hint





A simple point mutation hits one gene. What kind of mutation could knock out two genes at once?









Answer





Mutant 5 cannot be a simple recessive mutation in one gene, because then it would fail to complement only one group. Likely explanations: a deletion that removes both genes (if they lie close together), or a dominant mutation (which gives a mutant F1 with anything). A test cross of mutant 5 with wild type distinguishes these: a dominant mutation gives a mutant F1 even with wild type, a recessive deletion does not. Deletions and other rearrangements are in Part 5.




Q10. Three Neurospora mutants need arginine. Mutant X grows on citrulline or arginine; mutant Y grows only on arginine; mutant Z grows on ornithine, citrulline or arginine. In which order are their blocks in the pathway precursor → ornithine → citrulline → arginine?






Hint





A mutant grows on every compound made after its block.









Answer





Z is blocked earliest (before ornithine), since ornithine rescues it. X is blocked between ornithine and citrulline (citrulline rescues it, ornithine does not). Y is blocked at the last step, citrulline → arginine. The order of blocks is Z, X, Y. Each blocked step is one enzyme and, if the three are in different complementation groups, one gene: Beadle and Tatum’s one gene–one enzyme.

title: Exercise: organelle inheritance
Exercise: organelle inheritance
Exercise: organelle inheritance
text:
Background
Organelle genomes. Human mtDNA is circular, 16 569 bp, with 37 genes: 13 protein-coding, 22 tRNA and 2 rRNA. A cell has hundreds to thousands of copies. Chloroplast genomes of land plants are about 120–160 kb. Most proteins of both organelles are encoded in the nucleus and imported; disease caused by such nuclear genes follows Mendel.
Uniparental inheritance. Organelles pass with the cytoplasm. In humans, mtDNA comes from the mother: every child of a carrier mother inherits the variant, no child of a carrier father does. Reciprocal crosses differ, and the difference depends on the sex of the parent, not of the offspring. Other patterns: most flowering plants maternal, many conifers paternal (cpDNA), Chlamydomonas cpDNA from the mt+ parent and mtDNA from the mt− parent, baker’s yeast biparental.
Heteroplasmy. A cell or person with a mixture of normal and mutant copies is heteroplasmic; the heteroplasmy level \(h\) is the fraction of mutant copies. Homoplasmic: \(h = 0\) or \(h = 1\).
The bottleneck (binomial model). Each oocyte is founded by \(N\) copies drawn at random from the mother’s pool, then amplified. With \(k\) mutant founders:
\[
P(k) = \binom{N}{k} h^k (1-h)^{N-k}, \qquad \text{level} = k/N, \qquad \text{mean} = h, \qquad \text{variance} = \frac{h(1-h)}{N}.
\]
Threshold. Symptoms appear when the level in a tissue exceeds a threshold, often 60–90 %, lowest in tissues with high energy demand (brain, muscle, heart, retina).
