title: Exercise: organelle inheritance
text:
Explore
The demo simulates the bottleneck. A mother has heteroplasmy level h. Each oocyte draws N copies at random from her mtDNA (binomial sampling), which are then amplified, so its level is k/N. The histogram shows the levels of many oocytes. The dashed line is the mother’s level, the red line the disease threshold (move it with the slider, or drag the handle); oocytes at or above the threshold are red. The readout gives the simulated fraction at or above the threshold, the exact binomial probability, and the mean and spread against \(\sqrt{h(1-h)/N}\). “draw again” gives a new random sample (the seed goes up by one); a preset resets the seed to 1.



E1. The demo starts with a mother at 30 %, \(N = 20\), 200 oocytes and a threshold of 60 %. How many oocytes are at or above the threshold? Compare the simulated mean and SD with what you expect from the formulas. Press “draw again” twice: how much do the numbers change?
E2. Click “tight: N = 5”, then “wide: N = 200”. For each, note the fraction at or above 60 %, the SD, and how many oocytes are at 0 %. Why does the histogram for \(N = 5\) have only a few, widely spaced bars?
E3. Click “mother 70 %”. The mother is now above the threshold herself. What fraction of her oocytes are at or above 60 %? Drag the threshold to 80 %: what fraction now? What does this say about the importance of knowing the threshold in genetic counselling?
E4. Set \(N = 1\) (mother 30 %). What do you see? How does the variance compare with \(h(1-h)/N\)? What does a bottleneck of a single copy do to heteroplasmy in one generation?
E5. Click “homoplasmic”. Change \(N\) and the threshold. Does anything change? Which of the two diseases from the lecture, MELAS or LHON, does this preset resemble, and what does the demo not explain about that disease?






Solutions: Explore





E1. On seed 1, 1 of 200 oocytes (0.5 %) is at or above 60 %; the exact binomial probability is also 0.5 %. The mean is 30.0 % (expected \(h\) = 30 %) and the SD is 9.9 percentage points, against \(\sqrt{0.3 \times 0.7 / 20} = 0.102\), that is 10.2 points. Seed 2 gives 2 of 200 (1.0 %), mean 30.7 %, SD 10.6; seed 3 gives 1 of 200, mean 30.0 %, SD 10.1. With 200 oocytes the summary numbers are stable to within about a point; the rare high-level oocytes vary more, because they are so few.

A small bottleneck gives a wide spread: about one oocyte in six is at or above 60 %, and about one in six (0.75 = 0.17) has lost the variant altogether. E3. With the threshold at 60 %, 181 of 200 (90.5 %; exact 88.7 %) are at or above it. With the threshold at 80 %, only 52 of 200 (26 %; exact 23.8 %) are. The same mother, the same eggs, but a very different risk estimate. The threshold depends on the variant and the tissue and is not known precisely, which is one reason why genetic counselling for mtDNA disease relies on observed outcomes in many families rather than on a formula.

Real bottlenecks are larger, but rapid shifts between generations have been observed, first in Holstein cattle.
E5. Nothing changes: all oocytes are at 100 %, whatever \(N\), and all are above any threshold. Sampling from a pool in which every copy is mutant can only give mutant copies. This resembles LHON, where m.11778G>A is usually homoplasmic. The demo would predict that every child is affected, but in real LHON families only about a third to a half of the maternal relatives lose their sight, mostly men. The incomplete penetrance and the male bias come from factors outside the model (nuclear genes, sex, environment).

Find it
The human mitochondrial genome is in NCBI Nucleotide under the RefSeq accession NC_012920.1 (the revised Cambridge Reference Sequence). Variants are named by their position in this sequence with the prefix m., for example m.3243A>G. ClinVar and MedGen work as in the pedigree unit. MITOMAP is a database devoted to human mtDNA variation.
F1. The genome. Open NC_012920.1. Read the title and the length at the top of the GenBank record (first line, LOCUS). Is the molecule linear or circular? Then count the genes: in the Graphics view, or by searching the record (Ctrl+F) for /gene= features, how many protein-coding (CDS), tRNA and rRNA features are there?

Why can one variant be listed with so many different conditions?
F3. LHON. Search ClinVar for m.11778G>A and open NC_012920.1(MT-ND4):m.11778G>A. Report the gene, the protein change, the classification and review status, and the dbSNP ID. Read the expert panel’s comment (in the section with the classification evidence): what does it say about heteroplasmy, penetrance and sex?

Which locus and which diseases are listed? Does the table show the variant as homoplasmic, heteroplasmic, or both? Compare with ClinVar (F2).






Solutions: Find it





The NCBI facts were checked with the NCBI E-utilities (Nucleotide, ClinVar and MedGen) in November 2026. MITOMAP refuses automated access, so its page could not be checked by us; the locus and diseases in F5 agree with the ClinVar record.
F1. Title: Homo sapiens mitochondrion, complete genome; length 16 569 bp; the LOCUS line says circular. The feature table has 13 CDS, 22 tRNA and 2 rRNA features (37 genes; plus one D-loop). Click path: Nucleotide → search NC_012920.1 → GenBank view → LOCUS NC_012920 16569 bp DNA circular; features listed below FEATURES. In RefSeq the genes are named ND1, COX1 and so on; HGNC adds the prefix MT- (MT-ND1), which is what ClinVar shows.
F2. ClinVar Variation ID 9589 (VCV000009589). (a) MT-TL1, the gene for tRNA-Leu (UUR), at positions 3230–3304. A tRNA gene, so the variant impairs translation of all 13 mtDNA-encoded proteins. (b) Pathogenic, reviewed by expert panel, for “Mitochondrial disease”. (c) rs199474657. (d) Submitted conditions include MELAS syndrome, maternally inherited diabetes and deafness (MIDD), MERRF, sensorineural hearing loss, stroke and seizures, among others. One variant gives many conditions because its effect depends on the heteroplasmy level and its distribution among tissues: low levels in some tissues give diabetes and deafness, high levels in brain and muscle give MELAS.
F3. ClinVar Variation ID 9708 (VCV000009708). Gene MT-ND4 (NADH dehydrogenase subunit 4, complex I); protein change p.Arg340His (R340H), a missense change; Pathogenic, reviewed by expert panel; dbSNP rs199476112. The expert panel’s comment says that it is the most common MT-ND4 variant in LHON, that it is seen in both homoplasmic and heteroplasmic states, that it has reduced penetrance (it is even present in the healthy population), and that males are more commonly affected than females. (The OMIM text quoted in the record: 33–60 % of maternal relatives affected, about 80 % of them male.)
F4. MELAS syndrome (MedGen C0162671, OMIM 540000) and Leber optic atrophy (MedGen C0917796, OMIM 535000) both have Mode of inheritance Mitochondrial inheritance, defined as inheritance “observed for traits related to a gene encoded on the mitochondrial genome. Because the mitochondrial genome is essentially always maternally inherited, a mitochondrial condition can only be transmitted by females, although the condition can affect both sexes. The proportion of mutant mitochondria can vary (heteroplasmy).” The genes listed are all mitochondrial genes (prefix MT-): for MELAS for example MT-TL1, MT-ND1, MT-ND5, MT-CO2; for LHON MT-ND1, MT-ND4, MT-ND6 and others. (MedGen also lists “Not genetically inherited” for MELAS, from the Orphanet record, a reminder that some cases arise from new mutations.)
F5. MITOMAP lists position 3243 in the locus MT-TL1 (tRNA Leucine 1, UUR), with MELAS and related conditions such as MIDD. Read the homoplasmy and heteroplasmy columns yourself; m.3243A>G is typically found heteroplasmic, as the lecture says. The locus and disease agree with ClinVar (F2).

This egg happened to get a larger share of mutant copies, 70 %, above the threshold of about 60 %. She herself is just below it. (d) X-linked recessive is ruled out by the 70 % granddaughter: an affected daughter needs an affected father, and her father (who married in) has 0 % and is unaffected. X-linked dominant is ruled out by the 85 % son: an affected son needs an affected mother, and his mother (40 %) is unaffected; the right-hand family rules it out too, since an affected father would have only affected daughters. The pattern that fits is the maternal one: every child of a carrier mother carries the variant, at very different levels, and no child of a carrier father does.

(c) \(N = 4\): \(P(k) = \binom{4}{k}/16\), so levels 0, 25, 50, 75, 100 % with 1/16, 4/16, 6/16, 4/16, 1/16. At or above 60 %: 75 % and 100 %, 5/16 ≈ 0.31. A slightly larger bottleneck gives a slightly larger risk here, because with \(N = 2\) the only level above 60 % is 100 %.
B6. (a) \(h(1-h) = 0.16\). \(N = 4\): \(\sqrt{0.16/4} = 0.20\) (20 points). \(N = 25\): \(\sqrt{0.16/25} = 0.08\) (8 points). \(N = 100\): \(\sqrt{0.0016} = 0.04\) (4 points). (b) \(P(k = 3) = 4 \times 0.2^3 \times 0.8 = 0.0256\); \(P(k = 4) = 0.2^4 = 0.0016\). Sum 0.0272, about 1 in 37. (c) 60 % is 40 points above the mean of 20 %, that is 5 SD for \(N = 25\). Very unlikely: the exact binomial probability is about 1.4 × 10−5. A bottleneck of 25 practically protects a 20 % mother from having a child at 60 %; a bottleneck of 4 does not.
B7. (a) Nuclear, autosomal recessive: two affected children of healthy parents, recurrence within one sibship and nobody else affected. The father’s side is equally involved; with a mtDNA variant you would expect the mother’s relatives to be affected too. (b) mtDNA (maternal): it passes from mother to children of both sexes, with variable severity, but the affected brother’s children are unaffected. Hearing loss with diabetes in a maternal line fits m.3243A>G (MIDD). (c) Not mtDNA: a man cannot pass on mtDNA. It is a nuclear gene, for example autosomal dominant.
B8. (a) The girl’s eggs would have a mean level of 2 % and an SD of \(\sqrt{0.02 \times 0.98 / 20} = 0.031\), about 3 points. 60 % is about 18 SD above the mean: under the binomial model this is essentially impossible: it needs 12 of 20 founders to be mutant, with probability about 4 × 10−16. (b) A rise that the binomial model cannot explain points to selection: the mother’s mtDNA (or the haplotype it is on) may replicate faster than the donor’s in some cells. Random sampling alone does not favour either kind of copy. (c) A boy does not pass on his mtDNA, so any carried-over copies end with him.

text:
Where this leads
The bottleneck is genetic drift inside one woman’s germline: random sampling of a finite number of copies, with variance \(h(1-h)/N\). In Part 7 (Drift and selection) exactly the same model, repeated over generations in a population, drives allele frequencies to 0 or 1. Mitochondrial donation is discussed in the Ethics module.
Next: Exercise in R: simulate the bottleneck with rbinom and replicate, compare bottleneck sizes, compute risk curves with pbinom, and explore the 37 mtDNA genes from the RefSeq record.

title: Quiz: organelle inheritance
text:
Short questions on organelle genomes, maternal inheritance, heteroplasmy, the bottleneck and the threshold effect. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A trait gives different results in reciprocal crosses: mutant ♀ × normal ♂ gives only mutant offspring, but normal ♀ × mutant ♂ gives only normal offspring, of both sexes. Which kind of inheritance does this suggest? Why is it not X-linked?






Hint





For an X-linked recessive trait, what would the sons and daughters of the first cross look like?









Answer





Maternal (organelle) inheritance: the offspring always look like the mother, whatever their sex. For an X-linked trait the result depends on the sex of the offspring: a mutant mother (XaXa) × normal father gives mutant sons but normal (carrier) daughters. Here both sexes follow the mother, so the trait goes with the cytoplasm of the egg.




Q2. Give two reasons why human mtDNA is inherited from the mother.






Hint





Compare the number of mtDNA copies in an egg and a sperm. What happens to the sperm’s mitochondria after fertilisation?









Answer






Numbers: the egg carries a very large number of mtDNA copies (of the order of 100 000), the sperm very few. (2) Elimination: the few sperm mitochondria that enter the egg are tagged and destroyed in the early embryo. So, apart from very rare exceptions (paternal leakage), all of a child’s mtDNA comes from the mother.





Q3. A man has Leber hereditary optic neuropathy caused by m.11778G>A. His wife does not carry the variant. What is the risk that their children carry it? What about the children of his sister, who carries it too?






Hint





Who passes on mtDNA?









Answer





His children: essentially zero. A father does not pass on his mtDNA, whatever the sex of the child. His sister passes it to all her children (m.11778G>A is usually homoplasmic, so at about 100 %). But not all of them will lose their sight: LHON has incomplete penetrance, and her sons are at higher risk than her daughters.




Q4. What is heteroplasmy? Why does it make no sense to describe a person’s mtDNA genotype as AA, Aa or aa?






Hint





How many copies of mtDNA does a cell have?









Answer





Heteroplasmy is a mixture of normal and mutant mtDNA copies in the same cell or person (homoplasmy: all copies the same). A cell has hundreds to thousands of mtDNA copies, not two, so the “genotype” is a proportion, the heteroplasmy level, anywhere from 0 to 100 %. It can also differ between tissues and change over time.




Q5. In Correns’ experiments with Mirabilis jalapa, what seedlings do you expect from (a) a flower on a variegated branch pollinated with pollen from a green branch, and (b) a flower on a green branch pollinated with pollen from a variegated branch?






Hint





Which parent supplies the chloroplasts?









Answer






Green, white and variegated seedlings: the egg cell can contain normal chloroplasts, defective ones, or both. (b) All green: the chloroplasts come from the seed parent, and the pollen contributes none. The pollen source does not matter.





Q6. A woman has 40 % heteroplasmy for a mtDNA variant. Assume a bottleneck of N = 10 copies, sampled at random. What are the mean and the standard deviation of the heteroplasmy level in her eggs?






Hint





Mean = \(h\); variance = \(h(1-h)/N\).









Answer





Mean = 40 %. Variance = 0.4 × 0.6 / 10 = 0.024, so SD = √0.024 = 0.155, about 15.5 percentage points. Many of her eggs will be between about 25 % and 55 %, but values of 0 % or 80 % are not rare. (With N = 10 the possible levels are 0 %, 10 %, …, 100 %.)




Q7. In Q6, how would the standard deviation change if the bottleneck were N = 40 instead of N = 10? What does that mean for the risk of a child above a threshold of 70 %?






Hint





The SD is proportional to \(1/\sqrt{N}\).









Answer





Four times as many copies gives an SD √4 = 2 times smaller: about 7.7 points. The eggs cluster more tightly around 40 %, so far fewer reach 70 %. A narrow bottleneck (small N) is what makes high-level children possible from a low-level mother.




Q8. A woman with 30 % m.3243A>G in her blood has no symptoms, but her son has severe MELAS. Explain how this is possible, using two concepts from the lecture.






Hint





How is his level related to hers? When do symptoms appear?









Answer






The bottleneck: each egg is founded by a small random sample of her mtDNA copies, so her son’s level can be much higher than hers (for example 80 %). (2) The threshold effect: symptoms appear only when the mutant fraction in a tissue exceeds a threshold. She is below it, he is above it. (Her blood level may also underestimate her level in other tissues, as m.3243A>G levels in blood fall with age.)





Q9. A child has a mitochondrial respiratory chain disease. Her parents are both healthy, and her brother is affected too. Later testing shows a variant in POLG, a nuclear gene for the mtDNA polymerase. Which mode of inheritance is most likely, and what is the risk for the next child?






Hint





Where is the gene?









Answer





The gene is in the nucleus, so the disease follows Mendel. Two affected children of unaffected parents suggests autosomal recessive inheritance: both parents are carriers, and the risk for each further child is ¼. “Mitochondrial disease” does not automatically mean maternal inheritance: most mitochondrial proteins are encoded in the nucleus.




Q10. Give three pieces of evidence that mitochondria descend from bacteria. Which group of bacteria?






Hint





Think of the genome, the ribosomes, the membranes and how mitochondria divide.









Answer





Any three of: a small circular genome; bacteria-like ribosomes, sensitive to antibiotics such as chloramphenicol; a double membrane; division by fission (mitochondria are never made from scratch); and, most convincingly, sequence: mitochondrial rRNA and protein genes group with the alphaproteobacteria in phylogenetic trees. (Chloroplasts group with the cyanobacteria.)




Q11. A child is born after mitochondrial donation (pronuclear transfer). How many of her genes come from the donor? If she later has children, whose mtDNA will they inherit? And if a boy is born this way?






Hint





How many genes does mtDNA have? Who passes it on?









Answer





The donor contributes the mtDNA: 37 genes (13 proteins, 22 tRNAs, 2 rRNAs), against about 20 000 protein-coding nuclear genes from the two parents. The girl’s children inherit the donor’s mtDNA (plus any small carried-over fraction of her mother’s), and so will all her descendants through the female line. A boy does not pass on his mtDNA, so the change ends with him. That is why some have suggested transferring only male embryos, and why the method is regulated as a germline change.




Q12. In the green alga Chlamydomonas, a mt+ strain with a streptomycin-resistance mutation in its chloroplast DNA is crossed with a streptomycin-sensitive mt− strain. What do the progeny look like? What about the reciprocal cross (sensitive mt+ × resistant mt−)?






Hint





Which mating type passes on its chloroplast DNA?









Answer





Chloroplast DNA comes from the mt+ parent. So the first cross gives all resistant progeny and the reciprocal cross gives all sensitive progeny. (A nuclear gene would give a 1 : 1 ratio among the haploid progeny in both crosses; so does the mating type itself.)

B9. (X-linked risk) A woman’s brother has Duchenne muscular dystrophy (X-linked recessive). Her parents are unaffected, and we assume it was not a new mutation. (a) What is the probability that she is a carrier? (b) What is the probability that her first son is affected?

title: Exercise: pedigree analysis
text:
Explore
The demo draws a random pedigree under a hidden mode of inheritance. Click a mode to test it. If the mode is consistent, the demo shows one set of genotypes that fits everyone (– means either allele) and draws the obligate carriers half-filled. If it is ruled out, the parents and child that make it impossible are ringed in red. The demo assumes full penetrance and no new mutations; people who married in may be carriers.



E1. Test all four modes on the first pedigree. Which are ruled out? For each, write the trio that breaks it, in the form “II-1 × II-2 → III-3”.
E2. Two modes are consistent. Under each, which people must be carriers? Which of them married into the family? Which mode do you favour, and why? Note the double line: does it change your mind? Then press reveal true mode.
E3. Press new pedigree once. Which mode is ruled out now, and by which trio? Of the three modes left, which is most likely? Look at the children of the affected men I-1 and III-3. Under autosomal dominant inheritance, how likely is that pattern?
E4. Press new pedigree about ten times, and test AR each time. How often is AR ruled out? Using the rule-out table, explain why AR is so hard to rule out.
E5. The demo assumes full penetrance. Sketch a small autosomal dominant family that the demo would wrongly rule out as AD if one person in it were non-penetrant. Which of the demo’s verdicts would change?






Solutions: Explore





E1. The pedigree is seed 2. AD is ruled out by II-1 × II-2 → III-3 (an affected son of two unaffected parents), and again by III-4 × III-5 → IV-4. XD is ruled out by II-1 × II-2 → III-3: an affected son needs XA from his mother, and II-2 is unaffected. The same holds for III-5 → IV-4.
E2. AR and XR are consistent.

Under AR, II-1 and II-2 (the parents of III-3) and III-4 and III-5 (the parents of IV-4) must be carriers. II-1 married into the family, so AR needs a second, unrelated carrier of the same rare allele.
Under XR, I-2, II-2, II-3 and III-5 must be carriers. They are all blood relatives, linked through women, so nobody who married in needs to be a carrier.

XR needs fewer coincidences, so it is favoured. The double line (III-4 and III-5 are first cousins) is a classic hint for AR, and it does explain IV-4 under AR. But it does not explain III-3, whose parents are not related. The true mode is X-linked recessive: affected males related through unaffected women.
E3. (Seed 3.) XR is ruled out by II-1 × II-2 → III-1 (and → III-2): II-2 is an affected woman, so under XR she is XaXa and every son must be affected. AR, AD and XD remain. AR needs two people who married in (II-1 and III-4) to be carriers, so it is unlikely. I-1 has two affected daughters and one unaffected son; III-3 has an affected daughter and an unaffected son. That is exactly the XD pattern. Under AD, each of these five children independently has a ½ chance of matching it: (½)5 = 1/32. XD is the best explanation, and reveal confirms it. One affected son or one unaffected daughter of an affected father would have ruled XD out.
E4. AR is ruled out only rarely. The only trio that excludes it is two affected parents with an unaffected child, because aa × aa can only give aa. Any unaffected person can be a carrier, so an affected child of unaffected parents, or a skipped generation, never contradicts AR. This is why the second step of the strategy (count the carriers a mode needs) matters so much for AR.
E5. For example: I-1 affected, his son II-1 unaffected (but non-penetrant, Aa), and II-1’s daughter III-1 affected, with an unaffected mother II-2. The trio II-1 × II-2 → III-1 is “affected child, both parents unaffected”, so the demo rules out AD, and XD as well, even though the true mode is AD. AR would stay consistent (II-1 and II-2 as carriers). A real geneticist would treat II-1 as an obligate carrier with incomplete penetrance. This is a limit of any rule-out table that assumes full penetrance.

title: Exercise: pedigree analysis
text:
Find it
Each disease has a record in OMIM (Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man), which gives a six-digit MIM number, and in MedGen at NCBI. Orphanet is a European portal for rare diseases with similar information. The gene record is in NCBI Gene. In OMIM, the table Phenotype-Gene Relationships near the top of a disease entry lists the chromosome location, the gene and the inheritance (AD, AR, XLR, XLD). In MedGen, read the section Mode of inheritance. In NCBI Gene, read Location in the Summary box.
F1. Duchenne muscular dystrophy: OMIM 310200, or MedGen “Duchenne muscular dystrophy”. What is the mode of inheritance? Which gene is mutated, and on which chromosome band does it lie (NCBI Gene: search “DMD human”)? Which hallmark from the lecture fits the fact that most patients are boys?
F2. Marfan syndrome: OMIM 154700, or MedGen “Marfan syndrome”. Mode of inheritance, gene and chromosome band? What pedigree pattern would you expect to see?
F3. Phenylketonuria: OMIM 261600, or MedGen “Phenylketonuria”. Mode of inheritance, gene and chromosome band? What does the gene’s protein do (read the gene’s full name)?
F4. X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets: OMIM 307800, or MedGen “Familial X-linked hypophosphatemic vitamin D refractory rickets”. Mode of inheritance, gene and chromosome band? An affected father has two sons and two daughters with an unaffected woman: what do you predict?
F5. ClinVar. ClinVar collects reports on human variants and what they do. Search ClinVar for PAH[gene] R408W, a common PKU variant, and open the record named NM_000277.3(PAH):c.1222C>T (p.Arg408Trp). Click path (MedGen). Open the MedGen link (or search MedGen for the disease name) → the page for the disease → section Mode of inheritance (for example “X-linked recessive inheritance”) → the Genes field names the gene. Click path (NCBI Gene). Search Gene for “DMD human” → “DMD dystrophin [Homo sapiens (human)]” → Summary → Location: Xp21.2-p21.1. In OMIM the same facts are in the Phenotype-Gene Relationships table (Location, Phenotype, Inheritance, Gene/Locus).

F1. X-linked recessive: males are hemizygous, so one Xa is enough. Affected boys are related through carrier mothers, and there is no father-to-son transmission.
F2. Autosomal dominant: affected people in every generation, about ½ of the children of an affected parent affected, both sexes, and male-to-male transmission possible.
F3. Autosomal recessive. PAH encodes phenylalanine hydroxylase, the liver enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine. Without it phenylalanine builds up. (This is why newborns are screened and treated with a low-phenylalanine diet.)
F4. X-linked dominant. An affected father gives his X to both daughters, so both are affected, and his Y to both sons, so neither is.

F5. ClinVar Variation ID 577 (accession VCV000000577). Click path: ClinVar search → PAH[gene] R408W → the record NM_000277.3(PAH):c.1222C>T (p.Arg408Trp).

HGVS name NM_000277.3(PAH):c.1222C>T (p.Arg408Trp). NM_000277.3 is the reference transcript (version 3) of PAH. c.1222C>T means position 1222 of the coding sequence changes from C to T. p.Arg408Trp means amino acid 408 of the protein changes from arginine to tryptophan (R408W in one-letter code).
Germline classification Pathogenic; review status reviewed by expert panel (three stars; the highest level below practice guideline).
Condition phenylketonuria; molecular consequence missense variant.
dbSNP rs5030858. (It is also OMIM allelic variant 612349.0002. On GRCh38 it lies at chr12:102,840,493.)

A ClinVar record joins a variant (its HGVS names on transcript and protein, its genomic location and identifiers) with interpretations submitted by laboratories and expert groups: the classification (pathogenic, likely pathogenic, uncertain significance, likely benign, benign), the condition, and the evidence. The review status tells you how much to trust the classification: a single lab’s submission with no criteria counts for less than agreement among several labs, or an expert-panel review. The number of submissions changes over time; the classification of a well-studied variant such as R408W is stable.

title: Exercise: pedigree analysis
text:
Solutions






Solutions: By hand





B1. Pedigree A.

AR: consistent. II-1 and II-2 are both carriers.
AD: ruled out by II-1 × II-2 → III-1 (and → III-3): affected children of two unaffected parents.
XR: ruled out by II-1 × II-2 → III-1: an affected daughter (XaXa) needs Xa from her father, but II-2 is unaffected.
XD: ruled out by II-1 × II-2 → III-1 (affected daughter of two unaffected parents) and → III-3 (affected son of an unaffected mother).

Only autosomal recessive remains. An affected daughter of unaffected parents is enough on its own.
B2. (a) II-1 and II-2, the parents of the affected children. (b) III-2 is an unaffected child of Aa × Aa: 2/3. (c) II-2 is Aa, so one of his parents is a carrier. If exactly one of I-1 and I-2 is Aa (and the other AA), each of their children is a carrier with probability 1/2. So II-3 is a carrier with probability 1/2.
B3. Pedigree B.

AD: ruled out, for example by I-1 × I-2 → II-3 (affected son of unaffected parents), and again by II-1 × II-2 → III-1 and II-4 × II-5 → III-4.
XD: ruled out by I-1 × I-2 → II-3: an affected son needs an affected mother.
XR: consistent. Carriers needed: I-2, II-2, II-4, all blood relatives; nobody who married in.
AR: consistent. Carriers needed: I-1, I-2, II-2 and II-4, and also II-1 and II-5, who married in. Two unrelated people from outside the family would both have to carry the same rare allele.

XR is most likely: only males are affected, and they are related through unaffected women. Duchenne muscular dystrophy and haemophilia A are inherited like this.
B4. (a) Under XR, II-4 is an obligate carrier (XAXa), and II-5 is XAY. III-5 gets XA from her father and either X from her mother: carrier with probability 1/2. (b) Her son is affected only if she is a carrier and passes Xa: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
B5. Pedigree C.

XR: ruled out by II-1 × II-2 → III-3: II-2 is an affected woman (XaXa), so every son should be affected, but III-3 is not. Also II-5 × II-6 → III-5, and II-1 × II-2 → III-4 (affected daughter, unaffected father).
XD, AD and AR are consistent. Ranking:

XD is most likely. The affected father I-1 has both daughters affected and both sons unaffected, exactly as XD predicts. The affected mothers pass it to about half of their sons and daughters, which also fits.
AD fits, but the pattern among I-1’s children is a coincidence under AD: (½)4 = 1/16.
AR needs I-2 and two people who married in (II-1 and II-6) all to be carriers, which is very unlikely for a rare allele.


To rule out XD, find an affected father with an unaffected daughter or an affected son (whose mother is unaffected).
B6. (a) II-2 is an unaffected child of two obligate carriers: 2/3. (b) 2/3 × 1/50 × 1/4 = 2/600 = 1/300. (c) An affected child proves that both parents are Aa. So the risk for the next child is 1/4. Each child is an independent event, and the earlier child does not change the next one.
B7. Each is an unaffected sibling of a patient, so each is a carrier with probability 2/3: 2/3 × 2/3 × 1/4 = 4/36 = 1/9.
B8. (a) Each child of the carrier grandfather is a carrier with probability 1/2. Each grandchild then gets the allele with probability 1/2. So each cousin is a carrier with probability 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. (b) 1/4 × 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/64 ≈ 0.016. (c) 1/4 × 1/50 × 1/4 = 1/800 ≈ 0.00125. Marrying a cousin raises the risk about 12.5-fold here, because the allele is in the family. In a random family, where nobody is known to be a carrier, the absolute risk is much smaller.
B9. (a) Her brother is XaY and got Xa from their mother, who is therefore an obligate carrier (XAXa). The woman got one of her mother’s two X chromosomes: carrier with probability 1/2. (b) 1/2 (she is a carrier) × 1/2 (she passes Xa to the son) = 1/4.

title: Quiz: pedigree analysis
text:
Short questions on reading pedigrees and on simple risk calculations. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Unless a question says otherwise, assume one gene, full penetrance and no new mutations.

Q1. Why do human geneticists use pedigrees, when geneticists studying peas or flies use controlled crosses?






Hint





Think about who chooses the parents, how many children there are, and how long a generation takes.









Answer





We cannot set up crosses in humans: people choose their own partners, families have only a few children, and a generation takes 25–30 years. So we collect the crosses that have already happened: who is affected and how they are related. With so few children, ratios such as 3:1 are hardly visible within one family. Instead we look for transmissions that are impossible under a mode.




Q2. Two unaffected parents have an affected daughter. Which modes of inheritance does this rule out: AR, AD, XR, XD?






Hint





Take each mode in turn. Under that mode, what genotype must the daughter have, and could two unaffected parents give it to her?









Answer






AD is ruled out: an affected child needs at least one affected parent.
XD is ruled out: the daughter needs an XA from one parent, and both are unaffected.
XR is ruled out: an affected daughter is XaXa, so she got Xa from her father, who would then be affected.
AR remains: both parents are carriers (Aa × Aa).

One trio with an affected daughter of unaffected parents leaves only autosomal recessive.




Q3. An affected man has an affected son. The son’s mother is unaffected. Which mode does this rule out, and why? Does it rule out X-linked recessive?






Hint





Which chromosome does a father give to his son?









Answer





A father gives his son a Y, not his X. So the son cannot have got an X-linked allele from his father.

XD is ruled out: the son needs XA from his mother, and she is unaffected, so she has none.
XR is not strictly ruled out: the son could have got Xa from a carrier mother, who is unaffected. But this needs a carrier to marry into the family, which is unlikely for a rare allele. So male-to-male transmission makes XR very unlikely.

Male-to-male transmission is the classic evidence for autosomal inheritance.




Q4. An affected woman with an X-linked recessive disease has children with an unaffected man. What do you expect among their sons and their daughters?






Hint





Write her genotype with Xa and XA, then make a Punnett square with his XA and Y.









Answer





She is XaXa and he is XAY.

All sons get Xa from her and Y from him: XaY, all affected.
All daughters get Xa from her and XA from him: XAXa, unaffected carriers.

So an affected woman with even one unaffected son rules out XR.




Q5. Look at the autosomal recessive pedigree in the lecture (fig02). Why are III-2 and III-3 called obligate carriers, even though nobody has tested them?











Hint





What genotype must IV-1 have, and where did each of her two alleles come from?









Answer





IV-1 and IV-3 are affected, so they are aa. Each got one a from each parent. Both parents are unaffected, so each must be Aa. The logic of the pedigree forces it: no test is needed. “Obligate” means must be.




Q6. Two unaffected parents have a child with cystic fibrosis (autosomal recessive). What is the probability that their unaffected son is a carrier? Why is it not 1/2?






Hint





Start from Aa × Aa. Which part of the outcomes can you cross out, given that he is unaffected?









Answer





Aa × Aa gives ¼ AA, ½ Aa, ¼ aa. He is unaffected, so he is not aa. Conditional on that:
\[P(Aa \mid \text{unaffected}) = \frac{1/2}{1/4 + 1/2} = \frac{2}{3}.\]
It is not 1/2 because the 1/2 is a share of all children, including the affected ones. Once we know he is unaffected, the aa quarter is gone, and two of the three remaining quarters are Aa.




Q7. The son from Q6 has a child with a woman from a population with a carrier frequency of 1/25. She has no family history. What is the risk that their child has cystic fibrosis?






Hint





Three things must all happen. Multiply their probabilities (product rule).









Answer





\[P = \underbrace{\tfrac23}_{\text{he is }Aa} \times \underbrace{\tfrac1{25}}_{\text{she is }Aa} \times \underbrace{\tfrac14}_{\text{both pass }a} = \frac{2}{300} = \frac{1}{150} \approx 0.0067.\]




Q8. An affected man with an X-linked dominant disease has four children with an unaffected woman. Predict the phenotypes of his sons and daughters. Under autosomal dominant inheritance, what is the probability of exactly the same outcome?






Hint





Under XD, what does a father give to each daughter and to each son? Under AD, each child is an independent coin toss.









Answer





Under XD he gives his XA to every daughter and his Y to every son: all daughters affected, all sons unaffected.
Under AD (Aa × aa) each child is affected with probability ½, independently of sex. The chance that the four children show exactly the XD pattern (every daughter affected, every son unaffected) is (½)4 = 1/16. One such family is suggestive; several such families make XD much more likely than AD.




Q9. Why does consanguinity (for example, a first-cousin marriage) increase the risk of recessive disease, but not of dominant disease?






Hint





For a recessive disease, both parents must carry the same rare allele. How likely is that for unrelated partners, and for cousins?









Answer





Relatives share alleles inherited from common ancestors. If a grandparent carried a rare recessive allele, it can reach both cousins and meet again in their child: the child of first cousins is homozygous by descent at about 1/16 of its genes. For unrelated partners, both carrying the same rare allele is very unlikely. A dominant disease needs only one copy, so it shows in the carrier parent anyway; the parents being related adds no new risk.




Q10. An autosomal dominant disease shows up in generations I and III of a family, but the person in generation II who links them is unaffected. Give two explanations.






Hint





One explanation is about the link between genotype and phenotype; the other is about where the allele came from.









Answer






Incomplete penetrance: the person in generation II carries the dominant allele but does not show the disease. They are an obligate carrier.
New mutation in generation III, so the allele in III was not inherited through generation II. (It is also possible that the disease in generation I has a different cause, or that biological parentage differs from the drawn pedigree.)

These are the cases where the strict rule “every affected person has an affected parent” breaks down.




Q11. A clinic collects families with three children, in which both parents are carriers of a recessive disease. It finds them through an affected child. Is the fraction of affected children among these families 1/4? If not, is it higher or lower, and why?






Hint





Which Aa × Aa families never come to the clinic?









Answer





It is higher, about 0.43 rather than 0.25. Aa × Aa families with three unaffected children (probability (3/4)3 ≈ 0.42) never come to the clinic, so they are missing from the count. Among the families that are seen, the expected number of affected children is
\[\frac{nq}{1 - (1-q)^n} = \frac{3 \times 1/4}{1 - (3/4)^3} \approx 1.30,\]
that is 1.30/3 ≈ 0.43 per child. This is ascertainment bias: how families are found changes the ratio we observe.

title: Exercise: probability & the χ² test
Exercise: probability & the χ² test
Exercise: probability & the χ² test
text:
Background
Probability rules.

Product rule: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B), if A and B are independent.
Sum rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B), if A and B are mutually exclusive.
Conditional probability: P(B | C) = P(B and C) / P(C). In practice, cross out the outcomes that are ruled out, and count among the rest.
Complement: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none).

Binomial. In n independent offspring, each with probability p of a given phenotype,
\[P(k \text{ of } n) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}, \qquad \binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}.\]
\(\binom{n}{k}\) (“n choose k”) is the number of birth orders with exactly k affected children. For example \(\binom{4}{2} = \frac{4 \times 3}{2 \times 1} = 6\).
χ² goodness-of-fit test against a ratio given in advance:

State H0 as a ratio, for example 3:1, and turn it into proportions (¾, ¼).
Expected counts: E = N × proportion, where N is the total observed count. Do not round E.
\(\chi^2 = \sum (O - E)^2 / E\) over all classes.
df = number of classes − 1.
Compare with the critical value, or compute the p-value = P(χ² ≥ observed | H0).
Conclude in words: “reject H0” (p < 0.05) or “fail to reject H0: the data are consistent with …”.

title: Exercise: probability & the χ² test
text:
By hand
B1. (product rule) In Drosophila, the cross AaBbCcDd × AaBbCcDd involves four unlinked genes. What is the probability of an offspring that is (a) aabbccdd; (b) dominant in phenotype for all four traits; (c) heterozygous at all four genes?
B2. (sum rule) From Aa × Aa, what is the probability that a child is homozygous (either AA or aa)? Which rule do you use, and why does it apply?
B3. (conditional probability) Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive. Anna is unaffected, as are both her parents, but her brother has cystic fibrosis. (a) What is the probability that Anna is a carrier? (b) Anna’s partner has been tested and is a carrier. What is the probability that their first child has cystic fibrosis?
B4. (binomial) Two carriers of oculocutaneous albinism (autosomal recessive) plan five children. (a) What is the probability that exactly 2 of the 5 children have albinism? Write out \(\binom{5}{2}\) first. (b) What is the probability that at least one child has albinism?
B5. (binomial, sexes) Assume each child is a girl with probability ½. In a family of 4 children, what is the probability of exactly 3 girls and 1 boy? Is it more or less likely than exactly 2 girls and 2 boys?
B6. (χ², 3:1) Mendel’s F2 for cotyledon colour gave 6022 yellow and 2001 green seeds. Test H0: 3:1. Give E for each class, the χ² value, the df, and your conclusion.
B7. (χ², test cross) A Drosophila test cross vg⁺/vg × vg/vg gives 230 offspring with normal wings and 170 with vestigial wings. Test H0: 1:1. If you reject H0, suggest one biological reason.
B8. (χ², three classes) Flower colour in snapdragons (Antirrhinum majus) shows incomplete dominance. An F2 from red × white gives 52 red, 109 pink and 39 white plants. Test H0: 1:2:1. How many degrees of freedom does the test have?
B9. (which ratio?) An F2 from two white-flowered sweet pea (Lathyrus odoratus) lines gives 382 purple and 269 white plants (illustrative numbers). Test the data against 3:1 and against 9:7. Which hypothesis do you reject, and which is consistent with the data? (The 9:7 ratio comes from two genes that are both needed for colour; see Extensions to Mendel.)

title: Exercise: probability & the χ² test
text:
Explore
Do the χ² problems by hand first. The demo starts with Mendel’s seed-shape data (5474 round : 1850 wrinkled) tested against 3:1. Filled bars are the observed counts, and dashed outlines are the expected counts. Change a count with − and +, or drag the top of a bar. The right panel shows the χ² curve for the current df, with the observed χ² marked and the tail (the p-value) shaded.



E1. Read off χ², df and p for Mendel’s data. Which class contributes more to χ², and why, when both classes deviate from E by the same 19 seeds?
E2. Press N: 100. The counts are set to exactly 75 : 25. Now drag the aa bar upwards (or press +) until p drops below 0.05. How many aa do you need? Then go back to 25 and lower the aa count until p < 0.05. Does the ratio “look” wrong to you at these points?
E3. With 3:1 and N = 100, press simulate under H0 ten times and write down p each time. How many of the ten are below 0.05? How many would you expect in the long run?
E4. Press simulate 1000×. Compare the grey histogram with the curve, and compare “% ≥ observed” with the p-value in the title. Then choose 9:3:3:1 and N: 20 and simulate 1000× again. What warning appears, and why does the histogram no longer follow the curve as well?
E5. Choose 1:1 and N: 20, then make the counts 12 : 8 (60% : 40%). Note p. Now choose N: 1000 and set 600 : 400 (drag the bars). Note p again. What does this tell you about using percentages in a χ² test?






Solutions: Explore





E1. χ² = 0.26, df = 1, p = 0.608, the same as on the lecture slide. The wrinkled class contributes 0.20 and the round class 0.07. The squared deviation is 361 in both, but it is divided by E: 361/1831 is larger than 361/5493. The same absolute deviation weighs more in a class where fewer seeds are expected.
E2. Note that N changes as you change a count, and E follows it. With 75 A_, p first drops below 0.05 at 37 aa (75 : 37, χ² = 3.86, p = 0.0495). Going down, it drops below 0.05 at 14 aa (75 : 14, p = 0.043). So with about 100 seeds, ratios from roughly 2:1 to 5:1 are all consistent with 3:1. Small samples cannot tell close ratios apart.
E3. Your ten values depend on how often you have clicked, but most will be well above 0.05; often none or one of the ten is below. In the long run 5% of honest samples give p < 0.05: that is exactly what the 5% level means. Each of those is a “false rejection” of a true H0.
E4. For 3:1 and N = 100, the histogram follows the df = 1 curve closely, and the fraction of simulations with χ² ≥ the observed one is close to the p-value. This fraction is a p-value estimated by brute force. For 9:3:3:1 with N = 20, the note under the buttons turns red: the aabb class expects only 20/16 = 1.25 (and the 3/16 classes 3.75), which is below 5. The simulated χ² values are then lumpy (only a few distinct values are possible) and do not follow the smooth df = 3 curve well, so the curve’s p-value is unreliable.
E5. 12 : 8 gives χ² = 0.80, p = 0.37 (fail to reject 1:1). 600 : 400 gives χ² = 40, p < 0.0001 (reject). The proportions are identical, but the evidence is not: χ² grows in proportion to N. Percentages throw N away, so χ² must always be computed from counts.

title: Exercise: probability & the χ² test
text:
Find it
Mendel’s numbers fit his ratios remarkably well. In 1936 the statistician R. A. Fisher argued that they fit too well. Fisher’s paper appeared in Annals of Science, which is not indexed in PubMed, but the debate has continued in genetics journals that are. You will find some of these papers.
PubMed search syntax. Type into the search box at https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/:

"Mendel's data": quotes search for the exact phrase, not the separate words.
Mendel AND Fisher: AND requires both words. (OR accepts either; NOT excludes a word.)
Mendel[ti]: the field tag [ti] searches only the title. Without a tag, PubMed searches all fields and maps your words to related terms.

Click a title to open the record. The abstract is under the title. The journal and year are in the line just above the title, and the PMID is listed below the abstract.
F1. Search for "Mendel's data"[ti]. You should get only a couple of hits. Open the one from the Journal of Heredity. Report its title, year, journal and PMID, and summarise its conclusion from the abstract in one or two sentences.
F2. Now search for Mendel's data without quotes and without [ti]. Look at the line “results” near the top of the page. Do you get more or fewer hits than in F1, and why? (Look at “Search details” under “Advanced”, or just compare the titles.)
F3. Search for Mendel[ti] AND Fisher[ti]. Find the paper by E. Novitski in Genetics (2004). Report its title. Then find a hit in the list that has nothing to do with peas, and explain why it matched your search.
F4. Search for "too good to be true" AND Mendel. Find the 2022 paper by G. Radick. Report its title and journal, and, from the abstract, when the “too good to be true” problem became widely discussed.






Solutions: Find it





F1. Click path: PubMed → type "Mendel's data"[ti] → Search. The two hits are Weeden 2016 and Hartl & Fairbanks 2007. The Journal of Heredity paper is:

“Are Mendel’s Data Reliable? The Perspective of a Pea Geneticist.” N. F. Weeden, J Hered 2016;107(7):635–646. PMID 27578843.
Conclusion (abstract): Mendel’s data do show a bias towards the predicted ratios. Real pea crosses do not naturally give ratios closer to expectation than chance (if anything the opposite), and omitting some experiments cannot explain the close fit either. The author could not decide between misclassification of ambiguous phenotypes and deliberate falsification, and suggests that Mendel’s paper is best read as a simplified, persuasive presentation of his model rather than an exact record of his methods.

The other hit is “Mud sticks: on the alleged falsification of Mendel’s data”, Hartl & Fairbanks, Genetics 2007 (PMID 17384156). It has no abstract in PubMed, but the full text is free in PubMed Central (PMC1840063).
F2. Without quotes and without the tag you get more hits. PubMed now searches all fields (title, abstract, keywords, MeSH terms) and maps “Mendel’s” to variants such as “mendel”, “mendels” and “mendelism”. The quotes and [ti] together ask for the exact phrase in the title only, which is much stricter. (The exact numbers grow as new papers appear, so we do not give them.)
F3. Novitski’s paper is “On Fisher’s criticism of Mendel’s results with the garden pea.” Genetics 2004;166(3):1133–1136, PMID 15082533. An off-topic hit is “Bioactivation, toxicokinetics and acute effects of chloroform in Fisher 344 and Osborne Mendel male rats” (J Appl Toxicol 2004, PMID 15211614). Fisher 344 and Osborne-Mendel are names of laboratory rat strains. Field tags match words, not meanings, so always read the titles of your hits. You may also see “Programs for Pedigree Analysis: MENDEL, FISHER, and dGENE” (1988), where MENDEL and FISHER are names of computer programs.
F4. “Mendel the fraud? A social history of truth in genetics.” G. Radick, Studies in History and Philosophy of Science 2022;93:39–46, PMID 35313209. The abstract says the too-good-to-be-true problem was understood almost immediately after the 1900 rediscovery of Mendel’s work, but became widely discussed only from the 1960s, for reasons linked to Cold War geopolitics as much as to concerns about the objectivity of science.

title: Exercise: probability & the χ² test
text:
Solutions






Solutions: By hand





B1. Take one gene at a time and multiply (the genes are unlinked, so independent). (a) P(aa)⁴ = (¼)⁴ = 1/256. (b) P(A_)⁴ = (¾)⁴ = 81/256 ≈ 0.32. (c) P(Aa)⁴ = (½)⁴ = 1/16.
B2. P(AA or aa) = ¼ + ¼ = ½. The sum rule applies because a child cannot be both AA and aa: the events are mutually exclusive.
B3. (a) Both parents must be carriers (Aa × Aa), because they are unaffected and have an affected child. Anna is unaffected, so aa is ruled out, and of the three remaining equally likely cells two are carriers: P = 2/3. (b) The child is affected only if Anna is a carrier and passes on a and her partner passes on a: 2/3 × ½ × ½ = 1/6 ≈ 0.17.
B4. p = ¼ per child. (a) \(\binom{5}{2} = \frac{5 \times 4}{2 \times 1} = 10\). P = 10 × (¼)² × (¾)³ = 10 × 1/16 × 27/64 = 270/1024 ≈ 0.264. (b) 1 − (¾)⁵ = 1 − 243/1024 = 781/1024 ≈ 0.763.
B5. P(3 girls, 1 boy) = \(\binom{4}{3}\) (½)⁴ = 4/16 = ¼. P(2 girls, 2 boys) = \(\binom{4}{2}\) (½)⁴ = 6/16 = ⅜, which is more likely, because there are more birth orders with 2 and 2.
B6. N = 8023. E(yellow) = 8023 × ¾ = 6017.25, E(green) = 8023 × ¼ = 2005.75. Both deviations are ±4.75 (22.5625 when squared). χ² = 22.5625/6017.25 + 22.5625/2005.75 = 0.0037 + 0.0112 = 0.015, df = 1. This is far below 3.84 (p = 0.90). Fail to reject: the data are consistent with 3:1. (A χ² this close to 0 is also part of Fisher’s point: see R6 in the Exercise in R.)
B7. N = 400, E = 200 for each class. χ² = 30²/200 + 30²/200 = 4.5 + 4.5 = 9.0, df = 1. This is above 3.84 and also above 6.63 (p = 0.0027). Reject 1:1. There are too few vestigial flies. A likely reason is that vg/vg flies survive less well (reduced viability) than vg⁺/vg flies, so some died before they were counted.
B8. N = 200, E = 50 : 100 : 50. χ² = (52 − 50)²/50 + (109 − 100)²/100 + (39 − 50)²/50 = 0.08 + 0.81 + 2.42 = 3.31. df = 3 − 1 = 2, critical value 5.99. Fail to reject (p = 0.19): the data are consistent with 1:2:1.
B9. N = 651. Against 3:1: E = 488.25 and 162.75. χ² = 106.25²/488.25 + 106.25²/162.75 = 23.1 + 69.4 = 92.5, df = 1. Reject (p ≈ 10⁻²¹). Against 9:7: E = 651 × 9/16 = 366.19 and 651 × 7/16 = 284.81. χ² = 15.81²/366.19 + 15.81²/284.81 = 0.68 + 0.88 = 1.56, df = 1. Fail to reject (p = 0.21). The data are consistent with 9:7, which fits a model where two genes are both needed for purple colour.

title: Exercise: probability & the χ² test
text:
Where this leads
The χ² test returns in almost every unit of Part 1 and Part 2. In Extensions to Mendel you use it to choose between modified ratios such as 9:7 and 12:3:1, in Linkage a test against 1:1:1:1 is the first sign that two genes are linked, and in Hardy–Weinberg you lose one more degree of freedom because the allele frequency is estimated from the data.
Next: Exercise in R: check your χ² and binomial answers in R, and simulate Mendel’s experiments to see whether his data fit too well.

title: Quiz: probability & the χ² test
text:
Short questions on the probability rules and the χ² goodness-of-fit test. Try each one on paper first, then open the answer. Unless stated otherwise, assume complete dominance and genes on different chromosomes.

Q1. Two parents are both Aa. A couple says: “We already have three unaffected children, so our fourth is bound to be affected.” What is the probability that the fourth child is affected (aa)?






Hint





Does one child’s genotype change the gametes that form the next child?









Answer





¼, exactly as for every other child. Each child comes from an independent egg and sperm, so earlier children have no effect. The 3:1 ratio is a probability for each child, not a quota for a family.




Q2. In AaBbCc × AaBbCc, what is the probability of an offspring with genotype AaBbcc?






Hint





Take one gene at a time. What is P(Aa) from Aa × Aa? Then use the product rule.









Answer





P(Aa) × P(Bb) × P(cc) = ½ × ½ × ¼ = 1/16. The three genes assort independently, so their probabilities multiply.




Q3. In the same cross AaBbCc × AaBbCc, what is the probability that an offspring shows the dominant phenotype for all three traits?






Hint





P(A_) for one gene is the sum of three Punnett cells.









Answer





P(A_) = ¼ + ½ = ¾ by the sum rule (AA or Aa). For all three genes: (¾)³ = 27/64 ≈ 0.42 by the product rule.




Q4. Two carriers of cystic fibrosis (Aa × Aa) have an unaffected daughter. What is the probability that she is a carrier? Why is the answer not ½?






Hint





Which cell of the Punnett square can you rule out, now that you know she is unaffected?









Answer





2/3. Knowing she is unaffected rules out aa. Three equally likely cells are left (AA, Aa, aA), and two of them are carriers. The ½ is the carrier probability before we knew her phenotype. As a formula: P(carrier | unaffected) = (½)/(¾) = 2/3.




Q5. Two Aa parents have 3 children. What is the probability that at least one child is affected?






Hint





What is the opposite of “at least one affected”?









Answer





1 − P(none affected) = 1 − (¾)³ = 1 − 27/64 = 37/64 ≈ 0.58. Adding ¼ + ¼ + ¼ = ¾ is wrong, because “child 1 affected” and “child 2 affected” can both happen, so these events are not mutually exclusive.




Q6. Same parents, 3 children. What is the probability that exactly one is affected?






Hint





How many birth orders have exactly one affected child? What is the probability of each order?









Answer





There are 3 orders (the affected child is first, second or third), so (3 choose 1) = 3. Each order has probability ¼ × ¾ × ¾ = 9/64. Total: 3 × 9/64 = 27/64 ≈ 0.42. In R: dbinom(1, size = 3, prob = 1/4).




Q7. A student tests 9:3:3:1 on four phenotype classes. How many degrees of freedom does the test have, and what is the 5% critical value?






Hint





For a goodness-of-fit test with a ratio given in advance, df = number of classes − 1.









Answer





df = 4 − 1 = 3, and the 5% critical value is 7.81. (For df = 1, 2 and 4 it is 3.84, 5.99 and 9.49.)




Q8. A test cross gives 62 Aa and 38 aa offspring. Test H0: 1:1 by hand. Do you reject H0 at the 5% level?






Hint





E = 50 in each class. Compute (O − E)²/E for each class and add.









Answer





χ² = (62 − 50)²/50 + (38 − 50)²/50 = 144/50 + 144/50 = 5.76, with df = 1. This is larger than 3.84, so p < 0.05 (exactly, p = 0.016) and we reject 1:1. The excess of Aa is larger than chance usually gives. One possible biological reason is that aa individuals survive less well.




Q9. A student reports “70% purple, 30% white” and computes χ² = (70 − 75)²/75 + (30 − 25)²/25 = 1.33 against 3:1. What is wrong with this?






Hint





What does χ² depend on besides the proportions?









Answer





χ² must be computed from counts, not percentages. Using percentages silently sets N = 100. With 1000 plants in the same proportions (700:300), χ² = 13.3, a clear rejection. With 10 plants (7:3), χ² = 0.13. The same proportions are stronger evidence when there is more data.




Q10. A χ² test gives p = 0.40. Which of these statements are correct? (a) The probability that H0 is true is 0.40. (b) If H0 were true, a χ² at least this large would occur in about 40% of experiments. (c) The data prove the hypothesised ratio. (d) We fail to reject H0.






Hint





A p-value is computed assuming H0 is true.









Answer





(b) and (d) are correct. (a) is the most common misreading: a p-value is a probability about the data given H0, not about H0 itself. (c) is wrong: “fail to reject” means the data are consistent with H0, and other ratios may fit as well.




Q11. In a cross with 12 offspring, a student tests 9:3:3:1 and R prints “Chi-squared approximation may be incorrect”. Why?






Hint





Compute the expected count of the rarest class.









Answer





The smallest expected count is 12 × 1/16 = 0.75, and even the 3/16 classes expect only 2.25. The χ² curve is a good approximation only when every expected count is about 5 or more. Collect more offspring, pool classes, or estimate the p-value by simulation (chisq.test(..., simulate.p.value = TRUE)).




Q12. Fisher found that over many of Mendel’s experiments, the total χ² was much smaller than its degrees of freedom. Why is a fit that is too good suspicious?






Hint





If H0 is true, what is the average value of χ²? How often should p be above 0.9?









Answer





If H0 is true and sampling is honest, χ² averages about df, and p-values are spread evenly between 0 and 1: only about 10% of experiments should have p > 0.9. Mendel’s results sit near χ² = 0 again and again, which chance rarely produces. For his seven monohybrid experiments the total is 2.14 on 7 df, and P(χ² ≤ 2.14) ≈ 0.05. This suggests the data were filtered or classified with the expected ratio in mind, though not necessarily deliberately.

title: Exercise: Prokaryotic regulation (recap)
Exercise: Prokaryotic regulation (recap)
Exercise: Prokaryotic regulation (recap)
text:
Background
This is a recap of 5MO103, seen through genetics. The lac operon has a promoter (P), an operator (O) and three genes transcribed as one mRNA: lacZ (β-galactosidase), lacY (permease) and lacA. The repressor gene lacI has its own promoter and is expressed all the time. Repressor binds O and blocks transcription; the inducer (allolactose, or IPTG in the lab) binds the repressor and releases it.
Alleles.








Allele
Defect
Haploid phenotype




lacI−
no working repressor
constitutive


lacIs
repressor cannot bind inducer (super-repressor)
uninducible


lacOc
operator cannot bind repressor
constitutive


lacZ−
no active β-galactosidase
no β-gal; permease normal


lacY−
no active permease
no permease; β-gal normal



Merodiploids carry a second lac region on an F′ plasmid. We write F′ genotype / chromosome genotype; genes not mentioned are wild type.
The logic. Repressor diffuses, so lacI alleles act in trans on both copies: I+ is dominant over I−, and Is is dominant over I+. The operator is a DNA site, so lacO alleles act only in cis on the genes of their own copy. To predict a merodiploid: (1) decide which repressor is in the cell; (2) for each copy, decide whether its operator is free; (3) a copy that is transcribed makes β-gal if it is Z+ and permease if it is Y+.
Simplifications. The inducer reaches the repressor whatever the lacZ/lacY genotypes (as with IPTG). We ignore CAP–cAMP (glucose) and leaky basal expression.

title: Exercise: Prokaryotic regulation (recap)
text:
By hand
B1. (haploids) For each haploid strain, give β-galactosidase and permease as inducible, constitutive or none: a) I+ O+ Z+ Y+; b) I− Z−; c) Is; d) Oc Y−; e) Is Oc.
B2. (merodiploids) Do the same for:

F′ I+ Z− / I− Z+

title: Exercise: Prokaryotic regulation (recap)
text:
Explore
Do the by-hand part first. In the demo, set the chromosome and the F′ genotypes with the buttons (or “no F′” for a haploid), and switch lactose on and off. The demo draws the repressor on each operator, the mRNA, and the proteins made from each copy, then sums up the phenotype for both inducer states and explains it. The presets are classic strains.



E1. Click the presets “I⁻” and then “F′ I⁺ / I⁻”. What changes in the drawing between the two, and why is this called acting in trans?
E2. Click “F′ O⁺ Z⁻ / Oᶜ Z⁺” and then “F′ O⁺ Z⁺ / Oᶜ Z⁻”. Compare the β-galactosidase phenotypes. Which copy makes the active enzyme in each case?
E3. Click “F′ I⁺ / Iˢ” and toggle lactose. Then, keeping the chromosome Is, change the F′ operator to c. Which copy is now transcribed, and why can the super-repressor not stop it?
E4. Set up your answers to B2 c) and d) in the demo and check them.
E5. Click “F′ Z⁺ Y⁻ / Z⁻ Y⁺”. Which copy makes β-gal and which makes permease? Is the strain able to use lactose?






Solutions: Explore





E1. In the I− haploid there is no repressor, so the operator is free and the operon is transcribed with or without lactose: both enzymes constitutive. Adding F′ I+ puts normal repressor into the cell, and it sits on both operators, the F′ one and the chromosomal one, until lactose is added: both enzymes become inducible. The repressor made from one DNA molecule acts on the other, which is what trans means.
E2. F′ O+ Z− / Oc Z+: β-gal constitutive, made from the chromosome, whose Oc operator never binds repressor. F′ O+ Z+ / Oc Z−: β-gal inducible; the chromosome is still transcribed all the time, but its β-gal is inactive (Z⁻), and active β-gal comes only from the F′, which is repressed until lactose is added. In both strains, permease is constitutive (the Oc copy is Y+ and always transcribed).
E3. F′ I+ / Is: the purple super-repressor sits on both operators, with and without lactose: no β-gal and no permease. Inducer binds the normal repressor (drawn with an orange diamond) but not Is. With F′ Oc, the F′ copy is transcribed all the time: both enzymes constitutive. Oc is a change in the DNA that the repressor binds; a repressor of any kind cannot bind it.
E4. c) β-gal inducible (from the chromosome, O+ Z+), permease constitutive (from the F′, Oc Y+). d) β-gal constitutive (from the F′, Oc Z+), permease none (the only Y+ is on the chromosome, whose O+ is blocked by the Is repressor).
E5. β-gal from the F′ (Z+), permease from the chromosome (Y+), both inducible. The cell has both proteins, so it can use lactose: the two mutations complement.

text:
Find it
NCBI Gene has one entry per gene and organism. For E. coli, use the reference strain K-12 MG1655, whose chromosome is the RefSeq sequence NC_000913.3. In a gene page, the Genomic context section gives the location as a range on that sequence; “complement” means that the gene is on the minus strand, read from right to left.
F1. Open NCBI Gene for lacZ in E. coli K-12. In the Summary, read the Gene description. In Genomic context, read the Location. Is lacZ on the plus or the minus strand?
F2. Open NCBI Gene for lacI and read its Location the same way. Using F1 and F2, draw the order of lacI and lacZ along the chromosome and show the direction in which each is transcribed. Is lacI upstream or downstream of lacZ? Does lacI belong to the lac operon mRNA?
F3. On the lacZ and lacI pages, scroll to NCBI Reference Sequences (RefSeq), protein (the NP_ accession). How many amino acids long are β-galactosidase and the repressor? (The protein pages say this as “aa” in the first line.) Alternatively, use EcoCyc, the curated E. coli database, for lacI.






Hint





A gene on the minus strand at complement(a..b) starts at b (its 5′ end) and ends at a. A gene “upstream” of lacZ lies before the lacZ start in the direction of lacZ transcription.

title: Exercise: Prokaryotic regulation (recap)
text:
Solutions






Solutions: By hand





B1. a) wild type: both inducible. b) I− Z−: β-gal none (no working lacZ), permease constitutive. c) Is: both none (uninducible). d) Oc Y−: β-gal constitutive, permease none. e) Is Oc: both constitutive; the super-repressor cannot bind an Oc operator.
B2. a) β-gal inducible: the only Z+ is on the chromosome, and the F′ I+ repressor reaches that operator in trans. Permease inducible. b) both none: Is on the F′ is trans-dominant and blocks the chromosome’s operator. c) β-gal inducible (chromosome O+ Z+), permease constitutive (F′ Oc Y+). d) β-gal constitutive (F′ Oc Z+), permease none (the chromosome’s Y+ is behind an O+ blocked by Is). e) No working repressor at all (both I−). β-gal constitutive (F′ Z+); permease constitutive (both copies Y+ and transcribed).
B3. If c1 is lacI−: the F′ supplies I+ repressor in trans, which controls the chromosome’s O+ Z+ → β-gal inducible (c1 is recessive). If c1 is lacOc: the chromosome’s Z+ sits next to an operator that repressor cannot bind, whatever the F′ provides → β-gal constitutive (c1 is cis-dominant). The F′ must be Z− so that all active β-gal comes from the chromosome; otherwise the F′ copy’s own inducible β-gal would muddy the result.
B4. a) If u1 is Is: the super-repressor blocks the F′ operator too → none (dominant, trans). If u1 is P−: the F′ copy is normal and regulated by the normal repressor → inducible (u1 recessive; it only fails to transcribe its own copy). b) P− is cis-acting: a promoter is a DNA site that only drives the genes next to it.
B5. m1 and m3 fail to complement, so they are in the same gene (lacZ, since both lack β-gal). m2 complements both, so it is in a different gene (lacY). Two genes. Caution: a polar nonsense mutation early in lacZ reduces expression of the downstream lacY from the same mRNA. Such an allele can fail to complement a lacY mutation even though the lacY gene on that copy is intact, which would wrongly suggest that the two are in the same gene.
B6. No. Attenuation reads tryptophan through ribosome stalling at the Trp codons. Without Trp codons in the leader peptide, tryptophan starvation no longer stalls the ribosome there, so the 3:4 terminator forms as usual (the repressor still responds to tryptophan). Instead, alanine starvation would now stall the ribosome in region 1 and allow read-through. (Leader peptides of other amino-acid operons use exactly this trick: the his leader has seven His codons in a row.)









Solutions: Find it





F1. Gene description: beta-galactosidase. Location: NC_000913.3 (363231..366305, complement), on the minus strand. Click path: ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gene/945006 → Summary → Gene description; Genomic context → Location.
F2. lacI: NC_000913.3 (366428..367510, complement), also on the minus strand. Both genes are read from higher to lower coordinates, so the order in the direction of transcription is lacI (366428–367510) → lacZ (363231–366305) → lacY → lacA. lacI lies upstream of lacZ, right next to the operon, but it has its own promoter and its own mRNA; it is not part of the lacZYA transcript. (That the repressor gene sits next to its target is a convenience of evolution, not a requirement: as the merodiploids show, the repressor works in trans from anywhere in the cell.)
F3. β-galactosidase (NP_414878) is 1024 aa; the lac repressor (NP_414879) is 360 aa. Click path: gene page → NCBI Reference Sequences (RefSeq) → mRNA and Protein(s) → the NP_ link → first line of the protein record. (EcoCyc gives the same lengths on its lacI and lacZ pages, IDs EG10525 and EG10527.)

title: Exercise: Prokaryotic regulation (recap)
text:
Where this leads
The same reasoning works in eukaryotes. An enhancer is a cis-acting DNA site, like lacO; a transcription factor is a trans-acting protein, like LacI. In Eukaryotic regulation & epigenetics we add chromatin, DNA methylation and X inactivation, which bacteria do not have.
Next: Exercise in R: write the Jacob–Monod logic as one R function, run it over every possible merodiploid with expand_grid(), and check it against the classic table.

title: Quiz: Prokaryotic regulation (recap)
text:
Short questions on the genetic analysis of the lac operon. As in the lecture, “lactose” means an inducer that reaches the repressor whatever the lacZ and lacY genotypes (in the lab: IPTG), and we ignore CAP and basal expression. Merodiploids are written F′ genotype / chromosome genotype; any gene not mentioned is wild type.

Q1. A haploid E. coli strain makes β-galactosidase and permease with and without lactose. Name two different mutations that could cause this.






Hint





What two things must both work for the repressor to switch the operon off?









Answer





The strain is constitutive. Either the repressor is missing or broken (lacI−), or the operator cannot bind the repressor (lacOc). In a haploid cell the two give the same phenotype; a merodiploid tells them apart.




Q2. What is a merodiploid, and why did Jacob and Monod need one?






Hint





Bacteria are haploid. How do you test whether an allele is dominant in a haploid?









Answer





A merodiploid (partial diploid) is a bacterium that carries a second copy of part of its genome, here on an F′ plasmid carrying the lac region. With two copies in one cell you can test dominance (which allele wins), complementation, and whether a mutation acts in cis or in trans. A haploid cell has only one allele of each gene, so none of these questions can be asked.




Q3. Predict the phenotype of F′ I+ / I− for β-galactosidase. What does that tell you about the lacI gene product?






Hint





Can the repressor made from the F′ reach the operator on the chromosome?









Answer





Inducible. The repressor made from the F′ lacI+ diffuses through the cell and binds both operators, so I+ is dominant over I− and acts in trans. A gene whose effect works in trans makes a diffusible product: the lacI product is a protein (the repressor).




Q4. Predict β-galactosidase in F′ O+ Z− / Oc Z+, and in F′ O+ Z+ / Oc Z−.






Hint





Which copy carries the working lacZ? Is that copy’s operator normal?









Answer






F′ O+ Z− / Oc Z+: constitutive. The working lacZ is next to the broken operator.
F′ O+ Z+ / Oc Z−: inducible. The working lacZ is next to a normal operator; the Oc copy is always on but makes inactive enzyme.

Oc only affects the genes on its own DNA molecule: it acts in cis, so lacO is a DNA site, not a product.




Q5. Why is lacIs dominant over lacI+, while lacI− is recessive?






Hint





In each merodiploid, which kinds of repressor are present, and what does each do?









Answer





In I+/I− the cell still has normal repressor, enough to control both operators: the I− allele just fails to contribute, so it is recessive (a loss of function, as in Extensions to Mendel). In I+/Is the super-repressor cannot bind inducer, so it stays on both operators even when lactose is present. The normal repressor cannot remove it, so the cell is uninducible: Is is dominant (a gain of an abnormal function).




Q6. A strain is F′ Z+ Y− / Z− Y+. Which enzymes does it make, and when? Which test from Part 3 is this?






Hint





Each copy can make one of the two proteins.









Answer





Both β-galactosidase (from the F′) and permease (from the chromosome), inducibly. Z− and Y− complement: they are mutations in different genes. This is the complementation test from the Mutation unit. (A polar nonsense mutation in lacZ could fail to complement lacY−, because it also reduces lacY expression from the same mRNA.)




Q7. Which strain is uninducible even though both of its lacZ genes are wild type: (a) F′ I+ / Is, (b) F′ I+ Oc / Is, (c) F′ I− / I+?






Hint





Look for an Is allele with no Oc to escape it.









Answer





(a). The Is repressor blocks both normal operators. In (b) the F′ copy has Oc, which the super-repressor cannot bind, so that copy is constitutive. (c) is inducible: I+ is dominant over I−.




Q8. In the trp leader, what happens to transcription of trpE–trpA when tryptophan is scarce, and why?






Hint





Where does the ribosome stop on the leader, and which hairpin can then form?









Answer





Transcription continues. With little tryptophan, few charged tRNATrp are available, so the ribosome stalls at the two Trp codons in leader region 1. Region 2 is then free to pair with region 3 (the antiterminator), so the 3:4 terminator hairpin cannot form and RNA polymerase goes on into the structural genes. With plenty of tryptophan the ribosome covers region 2, 3:4 forms, and transcription stops.

title: Exercise: rearrangements & aneuploidy
Exercise: rearrangements & aneuploidy
Exercise: rearrangements & aneuploidy
text:
Background
Kinds of change. Deletion (del), duplication (dup), inversion (inv; paracentric if the centromere is outside the inverted segment, pericentric if inside), translocation (t; reciprocal between two chromosomes, Robertsonian fusion of two acrocentrics: 13, 14, 15, 21, 22). Deletions and duplications are unbalanced; inversions and translocations are balanced but give unbalanced gametes.
Inversion heterozygotes. One crossover inside the loop gives two non-crossover chromatids (balanced) and two crossover chromatids: a dicentric + an acentric (paracentric), or two chromosomes with a duplication + deficiency (pericentric).
Reciprocal translocation carriers. The four chromosomes form a cross at meiosis I; two go to each pole. Alternate (N1 + N2 or T1 + T2): balanced. Adjacent-1 (N1 + T2 or N2 + T1) and adjacent-2 (N1 + T1 or N2 + T2): unbalanced.
Nondisjunction. In MI, both homologues go to one pole: 2 gametes n + 1 (two different homologues) and 2 gametes n − 1. In MII, sister chromatids stay together in one cell: 1 gamete n + 1 (two identical copies), 1 n − 1 and 2 normal. In females only one of the four products becomes the egg.
Polyploidy. A triploid sends 1 or 2 copies of each of its x chromosome types to a gamete, ½ each: P(balanced gamete) = 2 × (½)x.

title: Exercise: rearrangements & aneuploidy
text:
Explore
The demo follows two chromosome pairs through meiosis, the long pair labelled 21 and the short pair labelled 2 (a cell with n = 2), coloured by origin: blue from the father of the person making the gametes, red from the mother. Step through the nine stages with Next ▶. Each gamete is labelled n = 2, n + 1 = 3 or n − 1 = 1. The Mode buttons switch between normal meiosis and nondisjunction of chromosome 21 in meiosis I or II; the pairs buttons show one or two pairs; flip orientation swaps which homologue of the second pair faces which pole.



E1. The demo starts with nondisjunction in meiosis I. Step to Anaphase I and then to Gametes. How many gametes are n + 1 and n − 1? What colours are the two chromosomes 21 in an n + 1 gamete, and what does that mean?
E2. Switch to nondisjunction in MII and step through again. List the four gametes. In the n + 1 gamete, are the two copies alike or different? Compare with your answer to B6.
E3. The person making these gametes is a woman. Her egg with two chromosomes 21 is fertilised by a normal sperm. For MI and for MII nondisjunction, which of the child’s four grandparents contributed the child’s chromosomes 21? Relate your answer to B7.
E4. Watch chromosome 2 in both nondisjunction modes. What happens to it? Press flip orientation and repeat. What does this tell you about whether nondisjunction of chromosome 21 affects other chromosomes?
E5. A trisomic zygote sometimes loses one of its three chromosomes 21 early in development (“trisomy rescue”). If each of the three copies is equally likely to be lost, what is the probability that the rescued embryo has both its chromosomes 21 from the same parent (uniparental disomy)? After MII nondisjunction, what is special about such a pair?






Solutions: Explore





E1. At anaphase I both homologues of 21 go to the left pole. The gametes are two n + 1 = 3 (each with one blue and one red chromosome 21, plus one chromosome 2) and two n − 1 = 1 (no chromosome 21). Blue and red mean that the n + 1 gametes carry the father’s and the mother’s homologue: two different chromosomes 21. All four gametes are abnormal.
E2. Meiosis I is normal. In meiosis II, the sister chromatids in one cell stay together. Gametes: one n + 1 with two copies of the same colour (two identical sister chromatids), one n − 1, and two normal (n). Only half of the products are abnormal, which fits B6: an egg from MII nondisjunction is disomic with probability ¼, compared with ½ for MI.
E3. The child gets one chromosome 21 from the father, plus two from the mother. After MI nondisjunction the mother’s two copies are her father’s and her mother’s homologues, so the child has chromosome 21 from three grandparents (both maternal grandparents and one paternal). After MII nondisjunction the two maternal copies are identical, both from one maternal grandparent (near the centromere; crossing over can mix further out). That is the logic of B7: two different maternal alleles at a centromere marker means MI, two identical ones MII.
E4. Chromosome 2 separates normally in both modes: every gamete has exactly one chromosome 2. Flipping its orientation only changes which parent’s copy goes with which gamete. Nondisjunction of one chromosome does not drag the others along: the gametes are n + 1 or n − 1 for chromosome 21 only. Each chromosome pair segregates independently, as in Mendel’s second law.
E5. Two of the three copies come from the parent with the nondisjunction. The embryo has uniparental disomy if it loses the single copy from the other parent: probability 1/3. (With probability 2/3 it loses one of the two copies from the same parent and ends up normal.) After MII nondisjunction the two remaining copies are identical (isodisomy) near the centromere, so any recessive allele there is now homozygous. Uniparental disomy also matters for imprinted genes; on chromosome 15 it causes Prader–Willi or Angelman syndrome.

(b) Balanced; paracentric inversion (both breakpoints on 3q). (c) Unbalanced; an interstitial deletion within 22q11.21: the 22q11.2 deletion. (d) Balanced; a Robertsonian translocation of 13 and 14, hence 45 chromosomes. (e) Unbalanced; a duplication within 17p12 (the CMT1A duplication).

A mutation lies in the bands that are removed by every deletion that uncovers it, and not removed by any deletion that does not. - m1: in A (1–3) and B (2–5), not C or D → bands 2–3. - m2: in B (2–5) and C (4–7), not A → bands 4–5. - m3: in C (4–7) and D (6–8), not B → bands 6–7. - m4: only D → band 8. - m5: only A → band 1.
