Three kinds survive, so the naive expectation would be 1/3 of births with Down syndrome. The observed risk for a male carrier is only about 1% (about 10–15% for a female carrier). The six gametes are not equally frequent: the unbalanced combinations are rare, and sperm or embryos with them are selected against. This is why genetic counsellors use empirical risks for translocation carriers.

B6. (a) After MI nondisjunction, two of the four products are n + 1 and two n − 1, so the egg has two copies with probability ½, none with ½, one with 0. (b) After MII nondisjunction in the secondary oocyte, the egg has two copies or none, depending on which product becomes the egg. If we treat all four products of the meiosis as equally likely to become the egg, as in the demo: ¼ two copies, ¼ none, ½ one. (c) 0.04 × ½ + 0.01 × ¼ = 0.02 + 0.0025 = 0.0225, about 2.3% of her eggs.
B7. 1: The child has 12 and 15 from the mother (both of her alleles, two different homologues) and 14 from the father: maternal meiosis I. 2: The child has two copies of the mother’s 12 (identical) and 13 from the father: maternal meiosis II. 3: The child has 15 from the mother and both 13 and 14 from the father: paternal meiosis I.
B8. (a) Father MI: sperm XY and O (no sex chromosome). With an X egg: 47,XXY (Klinefelter) and 45,X (Turner). (b) Father MII of the Y-bearing cell: sperm YY and O (plus normal X sperm from the other cell). With an X egg: 47,XYY and 45,X. (c) Mother MI: eggs XX and O. With an X sperm: 47,XXX (triple X) and 45,X; with a Y sperm: 47,XXY and 45,Y. 45,Y cannot survive: genes on the X are essential.
B9. (a) 2 × (½)4 = 2/16 = 1/8. (b) 2 × (½)11 = 2/2048 ≈ 0.001. (c) The tetraploid makes 2x (diploid) gametes, the diploid x (haploid) gametes; the seed is 3x. The triploid plant is nearly sterile, so its fruit has no mature seeds, and it cannot be propagated from its own seed: new triploid seed must be produced from the 4x × 2x cross each year.









Solutions: Find it





These facts were checked with the NCBI E-utilities (ClinVar, MedGen, Gene) on 2026-11-20.
F1. (a) ClinVar variation 57594, GRCh38/hg38 22q11.21(chr22:18339130-21086225)x1. Variant type copy number loss (one copy, a deletion), on GRCh38 at chr22:18,339,130–21,086,225, band 22q11.21. Germline classification Pathogenic (criteria provided, single submitter). Size: 21 086 225 − 18 339 130 + 1 = 2 747 096 bp ≈ 2.7 Mb. Click path: ClinVar → search 57594 or follow the link → the top of the record (Variant type, Variation ID, location) and the Germline classification box. (b) TBX1: chr22:19,756,703–19,783,593 (22q11.21): inside the deletion. BCR: chr22:23,180,509–23,318,037 (22q11.23): outside, about 2 Mb further along 22q. Click path: NCBI Gene → the gene → Genomic context (NC_000022.11). (c) MedGen C0012236 lists the gene TBX1. Major features from the description: congenital heart disease (conotruncal malformations such as tetralogy of Fallot), palatal abnormalities, immune deficiency, characteristic facial features and learning difficulties (also hearing loss, psychiatric illness and autoimmune disorders).
F2. (a) MedGen C0175702: autosomal dominant inheritance; genes ELN, LIMK1, GTF2I, GTF2IRD1 and NCF1. (b) ELN is elastin, at 7q11.23 (NCBI Gene ID 2006). The feature is supravalvar aortic stenosis (a narrowing of the aorta just above the valve), together with peripheral pulmonary stenosis and the connective-tissue problems. With only one copy of ELN, the walls of large arteries have too little elastin: haploinsufficiency. (c) The deletion is heterozygous: one copy of the region is enough to cause the syndrome, so it behaves as a dominant trait. An affected person passes the deleted chromosome to half of their children. Most cases are new deletions (by NAHR between the repeats that flank the region), so most patients have unaffected parents.
F3. (a) BCR: BCR activator of RhoGEF and GTPase, 22q11.23 (Gene ID 613). ABL1: ABL proto-oncogene 1, non-receptor tyrosine kinase, 9q34.12 (Gene ID 25). (b) ABL1 encodes the tyrosine kinase. The fusion gene sits on the der(22), the small Philadelphia chromosome: the start of BCR on chromosome 22 is joined to the part of ABL1 that moved from 9q34. (The reciprocal ABL1::BCR on der(9) is not needed for the leukaemia.) (c) 46,XY,t(9;22)(q34;q11), or with the finer bands from NCBI Gene, 46,XY,t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2). Click path: NCBI Gene → gene → Summary (Official full name, Location).

title: Exercise: rearrangements & aneuploidy
text:
Where this leads
Many of the patterns here come back. The empirical risks for translocation carriers and the maternal-age effect are the kind of numbers used in genetic counselling and prenatal screening, discussed in the Ethics module. Fusion genes return in Cancer genetics (Part 7), and X inactivation, which makes sex-chromosome aneuploidy survivable, in Eukaryotic regulation (Part 6). Next in this part, Bacterial genetics shows a genome that is one circle and is mapped in minutes.
Next: Exercise in R: plot the Danish registry data on fetal aneuploidy against maternal age on a log scale, and simulate the gametes of a translocation carrier and a triploid.

title: Quiz: rearrangements & aneuploidy
text:
Short questions on deletions, duplications, inversions, translocations, aneuploidy and polyploidy. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Which of these rearrangements are balanced, and which are unbalanced: deletion, duplication, paracentric inversion, pericentric inversion, reciprocal translocation, Robertsonian translocation?






Hint





Does the carrier have exactly two copies of every part of the genome (apart from repeats)?









Answer





Unbalanced: deletion (too little) and duplication (too much). Balanced: both kinds of inversion, reciprocal translocations, and Robertsonian translocations (only the repetitive short arms of two acrocentrics are lost, and copies of them remain on the other acrocentrics). Balanced carriers are usually healthy, but they make unbalanced gametes.




Q2. A Drosophila female heterozygous for a deletion is crossed to a male homozygous for a recessive mutation m. Half of the offspring show the mutant phenotype. What does that tell you about m, and what is this phenomenon called?






Hint





Which offspring have only one copy of the region, and which allele is it?









Answer





m lies inside the deleted region. The offspring that got the deletion chromosome from their mother have only the father’s m allele in that region, so the recessive phenotype shows: pseudodominance. Overlapping deletions that do or do not uncover m map it to a small interval: deletion mapping.




Q3. Why do 22q11.2 deletions in unrelated patients usually have almost the same breakpoints?






Hint





What sits at the ends of the deleted segment?









Answer





The segment is flanked by low-copy repeats (segmental duplications). When homologues pair at the wrong copy, crossing over between the mispaired repeats, non-allelic homologous recombination, deletes (or duplicates) exactly the segment between them. The repeats set the breakpoints, so the same deletion arises again and again as a new mutation.




Q4. An individual is heterozygous for a paracentric inversion. One crossover happens inside the inversion loop in a meiosis. What are the four products of that meiosis, and how many of them can give a normal offspring?






Hint





Two chromatids take part in the crossover, two do not.









Answer





The two non-crossover chromatids are one normal and one inverted chromosome, both balanced. The two crossover chromatids become a dicentric chromosome (with two centromeres, torn apart at anaphase I) and an acentric fragment (lost). Only the two non-crossover products give viable, balanced gametes, so at most 2 of 4. That is why recombinants inside the inversion are missing among the offspring.




Q5. How do the crossover products differ if the inversion is pericentric?






Hint





Where is the centromere? Count centromeres in each crossover product.









Answer





Each crossover chromatid has one centromere, so there is no dicentric or acentric. But each has a duplication of one end of the chromosome and a deficiency of the other end. Gametes with them are unbalanced, and often give inviable zygotes. The result is the same: the crossover products are lost.




Q6. A healthy man is a carrier of a balanced reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 4 and 11. Explain why his partner has had several miscarriages, and what kinds of gametes he makes.






Hint





Two of four chromosomes go to each pole. Which combinations are balanced?









Answer





His four chromosomes (normal 4, normal 11, and the two translocated ones) pair as a cross at meiosis I. Alternate segregation gives balanced gametes: either both normal chromosomes, or both translocated ones (a balanced carrier like him). Adjacent-1 and adjacent-2 segregation give gametes with a duplication of one translocated segment and a deficiency of the other. Zygotes from these are unbalanced, and most miscarry; some may be born with malformations.




Q7. A child with Down syndrome has 46 chromosomes. How is that possible, and why does it matter for the parents?






Hint





Can a third copy of 21q sit on another chromosome?









Answer





The child has translocation Down syndrome: two normal chromosomes 21 plus a Robertsonian translocation chromosome that carries a third copy of 21q, fused to another acrocentric (for example rob(14;21)). The total count is 46, but there are three copies of 21q. One parent may be a balanced carrier (45 chromosomes), so the recurrence risk in the family is much higher than for ordinary trisomy 21. Both parents should be offered a karyotype.




Q8. At markers near the centromere of chromosome 21, a child with trisomy 21 has two different alleles from the mother. In which maternal meiotic division did nondisjunction most likely occur? And if the two maternal alleles were identical?






Hint





Which division separates homologues, and which separates sister chromatids?









Answer





Different alleles mean the child got both homologues of the mother: nondisjunction in meiosis I. Identical alleles mean two copies of the same homologue, that is, two sister chromatids: nondisjunction in meiosis II. Markers near the centromere are used because crossing over can make sister chromatids differ further out on the arm.




Q9. The risk of trisomy 21 rises steeply with the mother’s age, but the risk of 45,X (Turner syndrome) does not. Suggest a reason for each.






Hint





How long does an oocyte wait in meiosis I? Which parent’s chromosome is usually missing in 45,X?









Answer





Human oocytes start meiosis I before the mother is born and stay arrested in prophase I until ovulation, up to about 50 years. The cohesin that holds homologues together is not renewed and wears out, so older oocytes are more likely to nondisjoin in meiosis I. Most trisomy 21 is of maternal origin. In 45,X, the missing sex chromosome is usually the paternal one (lost in the father’s meiosis or early after fertilisation), so the mother’s age has little effect.




Q10. Why do individuals with 47,XXY or 47,XXX have far milder phenotypes than individuals with a trisomy of an autosome of similar size?






Hint





What happens to extra X chromosomes in a cell?









Answer





X inactivation: in every cell, all X chromosomes except one are silenced and condensed into Barr bodies, so most extra X genes are not expressed. (A few genes escape inactivation, which explains the remaining symptoms.) The Y carries few genes. Autosomes have no such dosage compensation, so an extra autosome raises the dose of hundreds of genes.




Q11. Bread wheat is hexaploid (2n = 6x = 42, AABBDD) and fully fertile. A triploid banana (2n = 3x = 33) is almost sterile. Explain the difference.






Hint





How many partners does each chromosome have in meiosis?









Answer





Wheat is an allopolyploid: each chromosome pairs only with its exact partner from the same ancestral genome (A with A, B with B, D with D), so meiosis forms 21 bivalents and every gamete gets one complete ABD set. In a triploid, each chromosome has three homologues; each trivalent sends 2 to one pole and 1 to the other at random, so a gamete is balanced only if all 11 chromosome types happen to go the same way: probability 2 × (½)11 ≈ 0.001.

title: Exercise: RNA-mediated regulation
Exercise: RNA-mediated regulation
Exercise: RNA-mediated regulation
text:
Background
Biogenesis. pri-miRNA (RNA pol II) → Drosha → pre-miRNA hairpin → Exportin-5 → Dicer → ~22-nt duplex → guide strand in Argonaute (RISC). siRNAs come from long double-stranded RNA, also through Dicer and Argonaute.
Seed and sites. The seed is nucleotides 2–8 of the mature miRNA, counted from its 5′ end. An mRNA site pairs antiparallel with it, so the site is the reverse complement of the seed, written 5′→3′ in the mRNA. To get it: take nt 2–8, complement each base (A↔︎U, G↔︎C), then read backwards. Site types, from strongest to weakest:



Site
mRNA pairs with
Example for let-7 (seed GAGGUAG)




8mer
nt 2–8, plus an A opposite nt 1
CUACCUCA


7mer-m8
nt 2–8
CUACCUC


7mer-A1
nt 2–7, plus an A opposite nt 1
UACCUCA


6mer
nt 2–7
UACCUC



Chance. In random sequence with equal base frequencies, a given k-nt word occurs about once every 4k nt.
Genetics. A 3′UTR site acts in cis (only on its own mRNA); a miRNA acts in trans. Loss of sites gives a dominant gain of function of the target (lin-14(gf), HMGA2 in tumours). RNAi gives a knockdown (hypomorph), with possible off-target effects through the siRNA’s seed.

title: Exercise: RNA-mediated regulation
text:
By hand
B1. (seeds) The mature miRNAs below are written 5′→3′. For each, write the seed (nt 2–8) and the 7mer-m8 site in the target mRNA (5′→3′).

human miR-21-5p: UAGCUUAUCAGACUGAUGUUGACU
human miR-1-3p: UGGAAUGUAAAGAAGUAUGUAU
C. elegans lin-4: UCCCUGAGACCUCAAGUGUGA

B2. (site types) Here are four 9-nt stretches from 3′UTRs, 5′→3′. Which contain a let-7 site, and of which type? a) GCUACCUCA; b) AUACCUCAG; c) GCUACCUCU; d) AUACCUCGU.
B3. (chance) a) How many 7mer-m8 matches to one given seed do you expect by chance in a 3′UTR of 1200 nt? b) In all human 3′UTRs together (about 30 Mb)? c) What does that mean for predictions based on a single site? Name two features that make a predicted site more believable.
B4. (heterochronic genetics) In C. elegans, lin-4(lf) is retarded (cells repeat L1 fates), lin-14(lf) is precocious (cells skip L1 fates), and lin-14(gf) alleles, which delete part of the 3′UTR, are retarded.

Which of the three classes would you expect to be dominant? Why?
Predict the phenotype of the double mutant lin-4(lf); lin-14(lf). What does it tell you about the pathway?
A lin-14(gf) / lin-14(lf) heterozygote: which allele’s mRNA makes protein in L3? Predict the phenotype.

B5. (HMGA2 in tumours) In some benign tumours a translocation breaks chromosome 12 within HMGA2, after the exons that encode the DNA-binding domains, so the mRNA lacks its normal 3′UTR. The other HMGA2 allele is intact.

Why could this make HMGA2 behave as an oncogene, even if the protein is normal or nearly so?
Is this a dominant or a recessive change? Cis or trans?
Which experiment would show that the loss of let-7 sites is the key change?

B6. (designing an siRNA) You want to knock down a human mRNA that contains the 19-nt stretch 5′-GCAAGCUGACCCUGAAGUU-3′.

Write the 19-nt guide (antisense) strand that pairs with it, 5′→3′.
What is the seed of that guide, and what kind of off-target mRNAs could it hit?
Name two controls that would convince you that a phenotype is due to the intended target.

B7. (RNAi vs mutants) a) Why is an RNAi phenotype genetically like a hypomorphic allele and not a null? b) Give one advantage and one drawback of this for a geneticist. c) Why can you not do a classical complementation test with RNAi knockdowns?
B8. (miRNA mutations) A seed mutation in the human MIR96 gene causes dominant, progressive hearing loss. A deletion of a miRNA gene that has a close paralog with the same seed elsewhere in the genome often has no visible phenotype. Explain both observations.

title: Exercise: RNA-mediated regulation
text:
Find it
miRBase (mirbase.org) is the registry of microRNAs. Each hairpin (precursor) has an accession MI…, each mature miRNA an accession MIMAT…. Names start with a species code (hsa = human, cel = C. elegans), and -5p/-3p says which arm of the hairpin the mature RNA comes from.
TargetScan (targetscan.org) predicts targets by searching 3′UTRs for seed matches. Results are grouped by miRNA family (miRNAs with the same seed).
F1. Open the miRBase page of human hsa-let-7a-5p (MIMAT0000062). Read the Sequence. Then look at Hairpins: how many different hairpin genes produce this same mature miRNA? Open each and read the Genome context: on which chromosomes are they?
F2. Open the worm precursor cel-let-7 (MI0000001) (the very first entry in miRBase) and read the mature sequence (upper case in the hairpin, or follow the link to the mature miRNA). Compare it with the human sequence from F1. What do you conclude?
F3. In TargetScanHuman, choose human and enter the miRNA name let-7a-5p, then submit. In the table of predicted targets, find HMGA2. How many conserved sites does it have in total, and how are they split between 8mer, 7mer-m8 and 7mer-A1? Is LIN28B also on the list?
F4. Still in TargetScan, why is the table titled for a miRNA family (let-7-5p/miR-98-5p) rather than for let-7a alone?






Hint





For F3, the columns of the TargetScan table are grouped: “Conserved sites” has a total column followed by one column per site type (8mer, 7mer-m8, 7mer-A1). Use the browser’s find function (Ctrl/Cmd-F) to jump to HMGA2.

title: Exercise: RNA-mediated regulation
text:
Solutions






Solutions: By hand





B1. a) miR-21-5p: seed (nt 2–8) AGCUUAU; complement UCGAAUA; reversed: site AUAAGCU. b) miR-1-3p: seed GGAAUGU; site ACAUUCC. c) lin-4: seed CCCUGAG; complement GGGACUC; reversed: site CUCAGGG.
B2. The let-7 7mer-m8 site is CUACCUC; the 8mer is CUACCUCA; the 6mer core is UACCUC. a) GCUACCUCA contains CUACCUCA: an 8mer. b) AUACCUCAG: UACCUC followed by A, preceded by A (not C): a 7mer-A1. c) GCUACCUCU: CUACCUC, followed by U: a 7mer-m8. d) AUACCUCGU: UACCUC with neither the C before nor the A after: a 6mer only.
B3. a) 1200/47 = 1200/16 384 ≈ 0.07. b) 3 × 107/16 384 ≈ 1800 sites by chance for every seed. c) A single 7-nt match is weak evidence on its own. More believable: conservation of the site across species (TargetScan’s “conserved sites”), several sites in the same UTR, a stronger site type (8mer), sites away from the very middle of long UTRs, and co-expression of the miRNA and the mRNA in the same cells.
B4. a) lin-14(gf) is dominant: the mutant mRNA escapes lin-4 in cis, whatever the other allele does. lin-4(lf) and lin-14(lf) are recessive losses of function: one working copy of lin-4 makes enough RNA to repress both lin-14 alleles; one working copy of lin-14 is enough in L1. b) Precocious, like lin-14(lf). lin-14 is epistatic, so it acts downstream; lin-4 acts by repressing lin-14. c) In L3, the lin-14(gf) allele’s mRNA, which lacks the sites, still makes protein; the lin-14(lf) allele makes no working protein anyway. LIN-14 stays high: retarded, like lin-14(gf) homozygotes (the gf allele is dominant even over a null).
B5. a) Without its 3′UTR the HMGA2 mRNA has none of its seven let-7 sites, so it escapes repression and the cell makes far more HMGA2, a protein that promotes growth. Over-expression of a normal protein can be oncogenic. b) Dominant (one rearranged allele is enough) and cis (only the rearranged allele’s mRNA escapes; the intact allele is still repressed). Just like lin-14(gf). c) Express HMGA2 with its normal 3′UTR, with the 3′UTR removed, and with the 3′UTR but point mutations in the seed matches only. If the version with mutated sites behaves like the truncated one (more protein, more growth), the sites are what matter. (This is the experiment of Mayr, Hemann and Bartel, 2007.)
B6. a) Guide = reverse complement of the target: target 5′-GCAAGCUGACCCUGAAGUU-3′ → complement CGUUCGACUGGGACUUCAA → reversed: 5′-AACUUCAGGGUCAGCUUGC-3′. b) Seed = nt 2–8 of the guide: ACUUCAG. Any mRNA whose 3′UTR contains its reverse complement, CUGAAGU, could be turned down a little, as by a miRNA: off-target effects. c) Two or more independent siRNAs against different parts of the mRNA should give the same phenotype; a rescue construct with silent changes in the target site should reverse it. Also confirm that the target mRNA or protein went down.
B7. a) RNAi lowers the mRNA but rarely removes it completely, so some protein is left: a partial loss of function. b) Advantage: you can see phenotypes for genes whose null alleles are lethal early, and you can adjust the dose. Drawback: weak knockdown can hide a phenotype, and the degree of knockdown varies between experiments and cells. c) Complementation asks whether two mutations in one organism, on homologous chromosomes, can restore function. An RNAi knockdown is not an allele; it acts on all copies of the mRNA in trans, so there is nothing to put in trans to it.
B8. MIR96 seed mutation: the mutant miRNA loses its normal targets (half dose of the normal miRNA) and gains new targets with the new seed; either effect can give a phenotype in a heterozygote, so it is dominant (compare with dominant gain-of-function alleles in Extensions to Mendel). A deleted miRNA with a paralog of the same seed: the paralog represses the same targets, so the loss is compensated: genetic redundancy, like the duplicate genes that give a 15 : 1 ratio.









Solutions: Find it





F1. Sequence of hsa-let-7a-5p in miRBase 23.1: UGAGGUAGUAGGUUGUAUAGUUU (23 nt; older releases list the 22-nt form without the last U). Three hairpins give the same mature miRNA: hsa-let-7a-1 (chr9), hsa-let-7a-2 (chr11) and hsa-let-7a-3 (chr22). Click path: mirbase.org → search “hsa-let-7a” → mature hsa-let-7a-5p → Sequence; Hairpins → each hairpin page → Genome context.
F2. cel-let-7-5p (MIMAT0000001): UGAGGUAGUAGGUUGUAUAGUU (22 nt). It is identical to the first 22 nt of human let-7a-5p, including the whole seed (GAGGUAG). The sequence has been conserved since the last common ancestor of worms and humans, more than 500 million years ago, which suggests strong selection on it (and on its target sites).
F3. TargetScanHuman 8.0: HMGA2 has 7 conserved sites: 1 8mer, 3 7mer-m8 and 3 7mer-A1. It is among the top predicted targets. LIN28B is also on the list (4 conserved sites). Click path: targetscan.org/vert_80 → Species: Human; “Enter a microRNA name”: let-7a-5p → Submit → table → find HMGA2 → “Conserved sites” columns. In the R exercise you find the same seven sites (plus one 6mer) in the Ensembl HMGA2 3′UTR.
F4. All let-7 family members (let-7a to let-7i, miR-98) share the same seed. Because targeting depends mainly on the seed, they are predicted to hit the same sites, so TargetScan reports them together as one family.

title: Exercise: RNA-mediated regulation
text:
Where this leads
Finding lin-4 and let-7 was forward genetics: from a phenotype to a gene. RNAi made the opposite direction, reverse genetics, routine. Development & model organisms puts both approaches to work on how an embryo is built.
Next: Exercise in R: read a 3′UTR from a FASTA file, extract the let-7 seed, find every site with str_locate_all(), classify them, plot them along the UTR and compare with chance.

title: Quiz: RNA-mediated regulation
text:
Short questions on microRNAs, RNAi and lncRNAs. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. lin-14(gf) alleles in C. elegans are dominant and delete part of the lin-14 3′UTR. Why are they dominant, and why does that point to a cis-acting site?






Hint





Compare with lacOc. What can the normal lin-14 allele do about the mutant one?









Answer





The mutant mRNA lacks the sites through which lin-4 RNA represses it, so it makes LIN-14 protein in later stages whatever the other allele does: one escaped copy is enough to give the phenotype (dominant). Only the allele that carries the deletion escapes: the 3′UTR acts in cis, on its own mRNA, just as lacOc affects only the genes next to it.




Q2. The double mutant lin-4(lf); lin-14(lf) is precocious, like lin-14(lf) alone. What does that tell you about the order of the two genes?






Hint





Epistasis, as in Extensions to Mendel: which phenotype shows in the double mutant?









Answer





lin-14 is epistatic to lin-4: without lin-14, it does not matter whether lin-4 works. So lin-14 acts downstream, and lin-4 acts by turning lin-14 down (a negative regulator).




Q3. What did Fire and Mello find when they injected sense, antisense or double-stranded RNA into worms?






Hint





Which was much more potent, and how many molecules were needed?









Answer





Sense and antisense RNA alone silenced the target weakly; double-stranded RNA silenced it strongly, with only a few molecules per cell, and the effect spread through the body and into the progeny. This is RNA interference: dsRNA is processed into siRNAs that guide cleavage of the matching mRNA.




Q4. Put in order: Dicer, pri-miRNA, RISC/Argonaute, Drosha, pre-miRNA, Exportin-5, miRNA duplex.






Hint





Start in the nucleus with the primary transcript.









Answer





pri-miRNA → Drosha → pre-miRNA → Exportin-5 (to the cytoplasm) → Dicer → miRNA duplex → guide strand loaded into RISC/Argonaute.




Q5. The mature miR-1 is 5′-UGGAAUGUAAAGAAGUAUGUAU-3′. Write its seed (nt 2–8) and the 7-nt mRNA site (7mer-m8) that matches it, 5′→3′.






Hint





Take nucleotides 2–8, complement them, and read backwards.









Answer





Seed (nt 2–8): GGAAUGU. Complement: CCUUACA; reversed, 5′→3′: ACAUUCC. (An 8mer site would be ACAUUCCA.)




Q6. About how often would you expect a given 7-nt site by chance in random sequence? How many would you expect in a 3000-nt 3′UTR?






Hint





47 = 16 384.









Answer





Once every 47 = 16 384 nt, so in 3000 nt about 3000/16 384 ≈ 0.18 sites. The HMGA2 3′UTR (2999 nt) has four 7mer-m8 matches to let-7 (one of them part of an 8mer) and three more 7mer-A1 sites: far more than chance, which suggests selection to keep them.




Q7. Give two differences between an siRNA and a miRNA.






Hint





Where do they come from, and how do they pair with their targets?









Answer





Any two of: siRNAs come from long double-stranded RNA (viral, transposon or experimental); miRNAs from genome-encoded hairpins processed by Drosha. siRNAs pair perfectly with one target and guide its cleavage; miRNAs pair mainly through the seed with many targets and reduce translation and stability. siRNAs mainly defend against viruses and transposons; miRNAs regulate genes in development.




Q8. A seed mutation in MIR96 causes dominant hearing loss. Why can a mutation in a miRNA gene be dominant?






Hint





What does the mutant miRNA still do in the cell, and what has it lost?









Answer





Two effects, both from one allele. The mutant miRNA no longer recognises its normal targets, so they are repressed only by the miRNA from the normal allele, at half dose (haploinsufficiency of the miRNA). And the new seed makes it repress new targets that it should leave alone: a gain of a wrong function. Either can give a phenotype in a heterozygote.




Q9. RNAi against gene X gives a phenotype in a cell-culture screen. Name two checks before you conclude that X is responsible.






Hint





What else can an siRNA turn down?









Answer






Use two or more independent siRNAs with different sequences against X: they should all give the phenotype, while off-target seed effects differ between them. (2) Rescue: express a version of X that the siRNA cannot target (silent changes in the target site); the phenotype should go away. Also check that X mRNA or protein actually went down, and compare with a CRISPR knockout.





Q10. XIST acts in cis. What would you expect if an XIST transgene, switched on, were inserted into an autosome?






Hint





Which chromosome does XIST RNA coat?









Answer





XIST RNA coats the chromosome it is made from. The autosome carrying the active transgene would be coated and (at least partly) silenced, while the X chromosomes would be unaffected. Experiments like this showed that XIST is sufficient to start silencing in cis.

title: Exercise: three-point crosses
Exercise: three-point crosses
Exercise: three-point crosses
text:
Background
The cross. A heterozygote for three linked genes is crossed to a tester that is recessive for all three. Each offspring shows which of the \(2^3 = 8\) allele combinations it got from the heterozygote. The 8 classes come in 4 reciprocal pairs (exact opposites, similar counts). In Drosophila the heterozygote must be a female, since males do not cross over.
The recipe.

Pair up the classes.
Parentals = the largest pair. They give the phase of the heterozygote.
Double crossovers (DCO) = the smallest pair. Compare a DCO class with the parental class it resembles: the one gene that differs is the middle gene. Rewrite all classes in the correct order.

Explore
Do the by-hand part first. The demo shows the 8 classes of a three-point testcross. Each class is drawn as the chromosome it came from: an allele is blue if it sits on the same parental chromosome as the most common class, red if it came from the other one. A colour switch between two loci is a crossover. Pick a gene order: the demo groups the classes into parental, single crossover (SCO, in region I or II) and double crossover (DCO), computes the distances, the expected DCOs, the CoC and the interference, and draws the map. “random” makes a new simulated data set.



E1. The demo starts on the Drosophila data of the lecture, with no order chosen. Which two classes are a single colour? Which classes have a colour switch between every pair of neighbouring loci in the current column order? Now click each of the three orders. For each, write down the “DCO” count and the CoC. Which order is right, and how does the demo tell you?
E2. In the correct order, how many crossovers (×) does the chromosome of each DCO class show? Switch to a wrong order: how many does the same class show now? Explain in one sentence.
E3. Click “maize”. Check your answers to B1 a)–e) against the demo. Why are the parental classes here all-mutant and all-wild-type, while for the flies they were not?
E4. Click “random” several times. For each data set, call the middle gene before you click an order, by finding the rarest pair and comparing it with the most common pair. Note N, the DCO count and the CoC of the correct order. Do you find data sets with a DCO count of 0, 1 or 2? How much would you trust the CoC there?






Solutions: Explore

With the columns in the data order v, cv, ct, the classes + + ct (66) and v cv + (63) switch colour twice: in this column order they would need two crossovers, yet they are not the rarest pair, a first hint that cv is not in the middle. E2. In the correct order, each DCO chromosome shows two crossovers, one on each side of ct. In a wrong order, the same class (v ct + or + + cv) shows only one, because ct now sits at an end and a single colour switch separates it. Which classes need two crossovers depends on the order; the right order is the one where the classes that need two crossovers are the rarest.
E3. The demo agrees with B1: parentals lg gl bm and + + +, DCO + gl + and lg + bm, order lg–gl–bm, distances 22.3 and 20.3 cM, expected DCO 45.3, CoC 0.29, I 0.71. The maize parent was in coupling (lg gl bm / + + +): all mutant alleles came in on one chromosome. The fly female carried v on one X and cv ct on the other (mixed phase), so the parentals were v + + and + cv ct.
E4. Answers depend on the data set. With N = 500 and two short intervals, the expected DCO count is often only 1–3, and you will see data sets with 0, 1 or 2 DCOs. A CoC computed from such small counts is very noisy: one DCO more or less changes it by 30–100%. The gene order can still be found, as long as the DCO pair is clearly smaller than both SCO pairs. When an SCO pair is also small (a very short interval), the order becomes harder to call, which is exactly the problem with mapping close genes.

title: Exercise: three-point crosses
text:
Where this leads
The Drosophila maps of the 1910s–1930s were built from thousands of crosses like these. In humans we cannot set up a testcross, and families are small. Human linkage & LOD scores keeps the idea of counting recombinants, but adds up the evidence from many small families with a likelihood, the LOD score. In Part 5, Rearrangements & aneuploidy, a chromosomal inversion shows up in three-point data as recombination that has mysteriously vanished.
Next: Exercise in R: write one function that analyses a three-point cross for a given gene order, run it over all three orders with map(), and simulate how noisy the coefficient of coincidence is.

title: Quiz: three-point crosses
text:
Short questions on gene order, map distances and interference from three-point testcrosses. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Unless the question says otherwise, the cross is a testcross of a triple heterozygote to a triple recessive tester.

Q1. Why does a three-point testcross give eight phenotype classes? Why do they come in pairs with similar counts?






Hint





How many allele combinations can one gamete carry for three genes? What does one crossover produce?









Answer





Each gamete of the triple heterozygote carries one allele of each of three genes, so there are \(2^3 = 8\) combinations. The tester adds only recessive alleles, so each combination shows up as its own phenotype. A crossover between two chromatids makes two complementary products (for example A b c and a B C), so the classes come in reciprocal pairs that are equally likely and have similar counts.




Q2. In a three-point testcross, which pair of classes is normally the most common, and which the rarest? Why?






Hint





How many crossovers does each kind of class need?









Answer





The parental pair (no crossover in either interval) is the most common. The double crossover pair (one crossover in each interval) is the rarest, because two crossovers in the same short region are much less likely than one. The two single-crossover pairs are in between.




Q3. The parental classes are A b C and a B c, and the double crossover classes are A B C and a b c. Which gene is in the middle?






Hint





Compare A B C with the parental class it shares two alleles with. Which allele has changed?









Answer





A B C differs from the parental A b C only at the B locus, and a b c differs from a B c only at B. A double crossover swaps only the middle gene, so B is in the middle: the order is A–B–C. Note that the heterozygote was in a mixed phase (A b C / a B c), so the DCO classes here are the “all dominant” and “all recessive” ones. Never assume which classes are parental: read them off the counts.




Q4. Why is the double crossover count added to both interval distances?






Hint





How many crossovers does a DCO chromatid carry, and where?









Answer





A DCO chromatid has one crossover in interval I and one in interval II. RF for an interval counts all chromatids with a crossover in that interval, so the DCOs belong in both. Leaving them out underestimates both distances.




Q5. In a cross, genes A and C are 18.9 cM apart in a two-point cross, but 20.0 cM apart when you add the A–B and B–C distances from a three-point cross with 2000 offspring. Explain the difference. How many DCOs were there?






Hint





What does a double crossover between A and C look like if you ignore B?









Answer





A double crossover leaves A and C in their parental combination. A two-point cross counts it as non-recombinant, so it misses two crossovers for each DCO. The difference is 2 × DCO / N: 0.200 − 0.189 = 0.011 = 2 × DCO / 2000, so DCO = 11. Adding up short intervals gives the better estimate of a long distance.




Q6. Genes A–B are 10 cM apart and B–C 20 cM apart. With no interference, what fraction of the testcross offspring are double crossovers? How many in 1000 offspring?






Hint





Use the product rule with the RFs as fractions.









Answer





P(DCO) = 0.10 × 0.20 = 0.02, so 20 of 1000 offspring, 10 in each of the two DCO classes. (Not 10 × 20 = 200: the product rule works on probabilities, not on cM.)




Q7. In the same cross (A–B 10 cM, B–C 20 cM, 1000 offspring), 8 double crossovers are observed. Compute the coefficient of coincidence and the interference. What does the value mean?






Hint





CoC = observed / expected; I = 1 − CoC.









Answer





Expected 20 (Q6). CoC = 8 / 20 = 0.4; I = 1 − 0.4 = 0.6. Only 40% of the double crossovers expected under independence occurred: a crossover in one interval made a crossover in the other less likely. This is positive interference, the usual situation.




Q8. What would I = 1 mean? And I = 0? Can I be negative?






Hint





Translate each value back to the CoC.









Answer





I = 1 (CoC = 0): complete interference, no double crossovers at all; one crossover blocks a second one in the region. I = 0 (CoC = 1): no interference; crossovers in the two intervals are independent and the product rule holds. I < 0 (CoC > 1): negative interference, more doubles than expected. It is rare in ordinary crosses. If you get a CoC far above 1, first check that you have the gene order right.




Q9. A three-point cross with 300 offspring gives zero double crossovers, although 3 were expected. A student concludes “complete interference”. Is that justified?






Hint





If the expected number is 3, how often do you get 0 just by chance? (For rare events, P(0) ≈ e−expected.)









Answer





No. With 3 expected, zero happens by chance with probability about \(e^{-3} \approx 0.05\), one cross in twenty, even with no interference at all. The data agree with complete interference but do not prove it. Estimating interference needs large crosses, because the DCO count is small and noisy.




Q10. Why do Drosophila geneticists put the triple heterozygote in the female in a three-point testcross?






Hint





What is special about meiosis in Drosophila males?









Answer





Drosophila males do not cross over in meiosis. A heterozygous male would give only the two parental classes, and no map distances. Females cross over normally. (For X-linked genes the heterozygote must be female anyway, since males have only one X.)




Q11. You try the wrong gene order on a data set and compute CoC = 4.9. Why does the wrong order give such a large CoC?






Hint





Which pair of classes does the wrong order call “double crossovers”?









Answer





With the wrong gene in the middle, the “double crossover” classes are really a single crossover pair, which is far more common. Its count is then compared with an expected number computed as if it were rare, so observed ≫ expected and CoC ≫ 1. A CoC far above 1 is a warning sign that the order is wrong, which is why the correct order is the one where the DCO pair is the rarest.
